abellaite.occurrence: A post-mining, secondary mineral that forms sparse coatings from supergene enrichment of a “red-bed”, sediment-hosted U-V-Cu deposit.
abellaite.etymology: Honors amateur mineralogist and mineral collector Joan Abella i Creus (b. 1968) from Sabadell, Catalonia, Spain, who collected the first specimens.

abelsonite.occurrence: Of secondary origin on fracture surfaces in oil shale.
abelsonite.etymology: Honors Philip Hauge Abelson (1913– ), American organic geochemist, President of the Carnegie Institution of Washington, D.C., USA, and Editor of Science.

abernathyite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral coating fractures in bleached asphaltic sandstone hosting a Colorado Plateau-type uranium deposit (Fuemrol No. 2 mine, Utah, USA).
abernathyite.etymology: To honor Jess Abernathy, Moab, Utah, USA, mine owner who found the ﬁrst specimens.

abhurite.occurrence: In blisterlike protuberances on the surface of a tin ingot recovered from a ship wrecked possibly 100 years ago (Sharm Abhur cove, Saudi Arabia).
abhurite.etymology: For the Saudi Arabian locality at Sharm Abhur Cove.

abramovite.occurrence: A product of precipitation from fumarolic gases (600° C) in an active stratovolcano.
abramovite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Dmitry Vadimovich Abramov (1963–) of the A.E. Fersman Museum, Russia.

abswurmbachite.occurrence: In very low-grade, high-pressure metamorphic Mn, Al-rich quartzites.
abswurmbachite.etymology: To honor Dr. Irmgard Abs-Wurmbach (1938{ ), German mineralogist.

abuite.occurrence: In hydrothermally altered, felsic pyroclastic rocks, related to a biotite adamellite intrusion.
abuite.etymology: For the type locality, near the town of Abu, Abu County, Yamaguchi Prefecture, Japan.

acanthite.occurrence: A common silver species in moderately low-temperature hydrothermal sulﬁde veins, and in zones of secondary enrichment.
acanthite.etymology: From the Greek for thorn, in allusion to the shape of the crystals.

acetamide.occurrence: In burning waste coal heaps, formed between 50 ◦C and 150 ◦C.
acetamide.etymology: For ACETic acid and AMIDE, for ammonia in its composition.

achalaite.occurrence: In the intermediate zone of a topaz- and columbite-tantalite-bearing granitic pegmatite which is concordant with the schistosity of regional metasedimentary rocks.
achalaite.etymology: For the type locality, the Achala granite batholith, Argentina.

acmonidesite.occurrence: A fumarolic sublimate on pyroclastic breccia.
acmonidesite.etymology: For Acmonides one of Ovidius’ Cyclops, helpers of Hephaistos, the mythological god of fire whose forge was alleged to be located at Vulcano.

actinolite.occurrence: Produced by low-grade regional or contact metamorphism of magnesium carbonate, ma¯c, or ultrama¯c rocks; also in glaucophane-bearing blueschists.
actinolite.etymology: From the Greek for ray, in allusion to the mineral's common radiating ¯brous habit.

acuminite.occurrence: In a small cavity in a specimen from a strontium-rich portion of a cryolite deposit.
acuminite.etymology: From the Latin acuminis, sharp point , for spear head, the characteristic shape of the crystals.

adachiite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal vein that cuts a lateritic metamorphic emery (corundum and hercynite) deposit.
adachiite.etymology: Honors Tomio Adachi (b. 1923), an amateur mineralogist.

adamite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of zinc- and arsenic-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
adamite.etymology: Honoring Gilbert-Joseph Adam (1795–1881), French mineralogist, who supplied the ﬁrst specimens.

adamsite-y.occurrence: A rare late-stage, low-temperature hydrothermal mineral in an alkalic pegmatite dike associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex.
adamsite-y.etymology: To honor Professor Frank Dawson Adams (1859–1942), McGill University, Montreal, Canada, geologist and petrologist, who studied the Monteregian Hills, of which Mont Saint-Hilaire is one.

adanite.occurrence: Secondary in the oxidation zone of a polymetallic (Au-Ag-Cu-Pb) hydrothermal vein deposit (Tintic).
adanite.etymology: Honors American mineral collector and micromounter Charles (Chuck) Adan (b. 1961) of Salt Lake City, Utah. Mr. Adan discovered the studied samples of pararaisaite, northstarite, and adanite.

addibischoffite.occurrence: In the core of a Ca-Al-rich inclusion (CAI) in the Acfer 214 CH3 carbonaceous chondrite meteorite, presumably a refractory phase from the solar nebula.
addibischoffite.etymology: Honors Addi Bischoff (b. 1955), cosmochemist at University of Münster, Germany, for his many contributions to the mineralogy of carbonaceous chondrites, including CAIs in CH chondrites.

adelite.occurrence: A rare mineral in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L˚ angban, Sweden); on willemite-franklinite ore from a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
adelite.etymology: From the Greek for indistinct, as it typically lacks transparency.

admontite.etymology: For Admont, Austria, near the original locality.

adolfpateraite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit.
adolfpateraite.etymology: Honors Adolf Patera (1819-1894), Czech chemist, mineralogist, and metallurgist, who invented the technology for processing uranium ores from Jáchymov for the production of uraniumbased colors.

adranosite.occurrence: A sublimate on pyroclastic breccia around an active volcanic fumarole.
adranosite.etymology: For the ancient god of fire, Adranos.

adranosite-fe.occurrence: A sublimate found on pyroclastic breccia in volcanic fumaroles (Italy); an anthropogenic product of a burning coal dump (Anna mine, near Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany).
adranosite-fe.etymology: As the Fe3+ analog of adranosite – the base name for the ancient god of fire Adranos.

adrianite.occurrence: In altered areas along veins between primary melilite, spinel, and Ti-Al-diopside in a Type B1 FUN (Fractionation and Unidentified Nuclear effects) Ca-Al-rich inclusion (CAI), Egg-3. Adrianite apparently formed by iron-alkali-halogen metasomatic alteration of primary CAI minerals such as melilite, anorthite, perovskite, and Ti-Al-diopside on the CV chondrite parent asteroid.
adrianite.etymology: Honors Adrian J. Brearley (b. 1958), mineralogist and cosmochemist at the University of New Mexico, in recognition of his many contributions to meteorite mineralogy, specifically the alteration mineralogy of chondritic meteorites.

aegirine.occurrence: Common in alkalic igneous rocks, carbonatites, and pegmatites. From regionally metamorphosed schists, gneisses, and iron formations; in blueschist facies rocks, and from sodium metasomatism in granulites. An authigenic mineral in some shales and marls.
aegirine.etymology: From Àgir, the Scandinavian sea-god, as ¯rst described from Norway.

aegirine-augite.occurrence: Common in alkalic igneous rocks, carbonatites, and pegmatites. From regionally metamorphosed schists, gneisses, and iron formations; in blueschist facies rocks, and from sodium metasomatism in granulites. An authigenic mineral in some shales and marls.
aegirine-augite.etymology: From Àgir, the Scandinavian sea-god, as ¯rst described from Norway.

aenigmatite.occurrence: A primary constituent in sodium-rich alkalic volcanics, pegmatites, and other silica-poor igneous rocks.
aenigmatite.etymology: From the Greek for riddle, apparently an allusion to its (formerly) uncertain chemical composition.

aerinite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral of the zeolite facies, formed at relatively low temperature, in fractures cutting mafic igneous rocks (Saint-Pandelon, France).
aerinite.etymology: From the Greek for sky blue for its distinctive color.

aerugite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in hydrothermal Ni–As–U ore deposits.
aerugite.etymology: From the Greek for copper rust , an allusion to its appearance.

aeschynite-ce.occurrence: In nepheline syenites and alkali syenite massifs; in granite pegmatites; in carbonatites in alkalic rocks; a detrital mineral in placers.
aeschynite-ce.etymology: From the Greek for shame, in allusion to the fact that early chemists had diﬃculty with separations of titanium from zirconium in some samples; cerium for the dominant rare-earth element.

aeschynite-nd.occurrence: In veins in slate and metamorphosed dolostone.
aeschynite-nd.etymology: For similarity to aeschynite-(Ce), with neodymium as the dominant rare-earth element.

aeschynite-y.occurrence: In granite and granite pegmatites; in ankerite-dolomitic carbonatites; as a detrital mineral in placers.
aeschynite-y.etymology: For similarity to aeschynite-(Ce), with yttrium as the dominant rare-earth element.

afghanite.occurrence: In thin veinlets cutting lazurite crystals (Sar-e-Sang, Afghanistan); in silici¯ed limestone xenoliths in pumice (Pitigliano quarry, Italy).
afghanite.etymology: For the country of ¯rst occurrence, AFGHANistan.

afmite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by remobilization and crystallization during lowtemperature hydrothermal activity and/or weathering and ground water activity.
afmite.etymology: Honors the Association Française de Microminéralogie (AFM), an amateur association devoted to the collection and study of micro-minerals.

afwillite.occurrence: A product of contact metamorphism of limestones.
afwillite.etymology: Honoring Alpheus Fuller Williams (1874{1953), General Manager, DeBeers Consolidated Mines, Kimberley, South Africa.

agaite.occurrence: A secondary phase formed by partial oxidation of tellurides, chalcopyrite and galena in quartz veins.
agaite.etymology: For the mine from which the first specimens were collected and for A.G. Andrews, from whose initials the name of the mine is derived.

agakhanovite-y.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in granitic pegmatite and crystallized from late-stage hydrothermal solutions enriched in yttrium.
agakhanovite-y.etymology: Honors Atali A. Agakhanov (b. 1971), mineralogist at the A.E. Fersman Mineralogical Museum, Moscow, Russia, who has worked on a wide variety of pegmatite minerals, including minerals of the milarite group.

agardite-ce.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of polymetallic sulfide deposits.
agardite-ce.etymology: By analogy to agardite-(Y), with a suffix for its rare-earth content dominated by Cerium.

agardite-la.occurrence: In small amounts in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal mineralized breccia and polymetallic mineral deposits (Red Cloud mines, New Mexico, USA).
agardite-la.etymology: By analogy to agardite-(Y), with its rare-earth content dominated by lanthanum.

agardite-nd.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of polymetallic sulfide deposits.
agardite-nd.etymology: By analogy to agardite-(Y), with its rare-earth content dominated by neodymium.

agardite-y.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of some copper deposits.
agardite-y.etymology: Honors Jules Agard, geologist, Bureau de Recherches Géologiques et Minières, Orléans, France, and a suffix for dominant yttrium.

agmantinite.occurrence: In the alabandite zone of a polymetallic hydrothermal mineral deposit.
agmantinite.etymology: For its composition, Ag for silver, man for manganese, and tin.

agrellite.occurrence: In pegmatite lenses and pods and in ma¯c gneisses in a regionally metamorphosed agpaitic alkalic rock complex (Villedieu Township, Canada).
agrellite.etymology: To honor Professor Stuart Olof Agrell (1913{1996), eminent petrologist, Cambridge University, Cambridge, England.

agricolaite.occurrence: A secondary weathering mineral in vugs of ankerite gangue in gneiss.
agricolaite.etymology: Honors Georgius Agricola (1494-1555), German scholar and scientist, “Father of Mineralogy”, and author of De re Metallica Libri XII (1556).

agrinierite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a uranium deposit.
agrinierite.etymology: For Henri Agrinier (1928–1971), an engineer in the Mineralogy Laboratory of the French Atomic Energy Commission, Paris, France.

aguilarite.occurrence: An uncommon, relatively low-temperature, mineral in hydrothermal deposits rich in silver and selenium, but manifestly deﬁcient in sulfur.
aguilarite.etymology: After Ponciano Aguilar (1853–1935), Superintendent of the San Carlos mine, Guanajuato, Mexico, where the material was originally found.

aheylite.occurrence: A late stage hydrothermal mineral in a base-metal-tin deposit (Huanuni mine, Bolivia).
aheylite.etymology: To honor Allen V. Heyl (1918– ), economic geologist, U.S. Geological Survey.

ahlfeldite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of nickel-bearing selenides and sulﬁdes.
ahlfeldite.etymology: To honor Friedrich E. Ahlfeld (1892–1982) German–Bolivian mining engineer and mineralogist.

ahrensite.occurrence: From the transformation of fayalite-rich rims of olivine megacrysts or Fe-rich microphenocrysts in contact with shock melt pockets in an olivine-phyric shergottite meteorite [TL].
ahrensite.etymology: Honors California Institute of Technology geophysicist Thomas J. Ahrens (1936-2010) for pioneering and fundamental contributions to high-pressure mineral physics and planetary sciences, many of which involved the interpretation of shock effects in natural rocks and synthetic materials .

aikinite.etymology: For Dr. Arthur Aikin (1773–1854), English chemist and mineralogist, a founder and long-time Secretary of the Geological Society of London, England.

aiolosite.occurrence: On altered pyroclastic breccia in an active medium-temperature intracrater volcanic fumarole.
aiolosite.etymology: From Aiolos (Αίολοσ, Latinized to Aeolus), the god of the winds in Greek mythology. The type locality, the Aeolian Islands (Isole Eolie in Italian) took their name from him.

ajoite.etymology: For the type occurrence at Ajo, Arizona, USA.

akaganeite.occurrence: Apparently formed from pyrrhotite by ferric-sulfate-bearing solutions (Akagan´ e mine, Japan); an important constituent in some soils, and certain geothermal brines and in sea-ﬂoor nodules; also formed as a corrosion product of some meteorites.
akaganeite.etymology: For the Akagan´ e mine, Japan, its original locality.

akaogiite.occurrence: Within multiphase TiO2 clusters enclosed in biotite in heavily shocked garnetcordierite-sillimanite gneiss in the breccia of a meteorite impact crater.
akaogiite.etymology: Honors Masaki Akaogi, Professor at the Department of Chemistry, Gakushuin University, Tokyo, Japan, for his contributions to experimental petrology, calorimetry, and mineralogy, including experimental characterization of high-pressure polymorphs of TiO2 relevant to planetary deep interiors.

akatoreite.occurrence: In a manganiferous metachert and carbonate lens in schists (Akatore Creek, New Zealand); in manganiferous potassium-rich felsic metavolcanics (Norberg, Sweden).
akatoreite.etymology: For the locality near Akatore Creek, New Zealand.

akdalaite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting amesite-ﬂuorite-muscovite rock and ﬂuorite-magnetite-diopsidevesuvianite skarn.
akdalaite.etymology: For the Kazakh name, Akdala, for the vicinity of Kara-Oba, Kazakhstan.

akermanite.occurrence: A product of contact metamorphism of siliceous limestones and dolostones, and in rocks of the sanidinite facies. Also forms from alkalic magmas rich in calcium.
akermanite.etymology: For Anders Richard ºAkerman (1837{1922), Swedish metallurgist.

akhtenskite.occurrence: In mixtures in “psilomelane” with other manganese oxides in an iron oxide deposit, probably bacterially altered from a previous mineral (Akhtensk deposit, Russia); in incrustations of ferromanganese minerals on oceanic basalt on a guyot (Mt. Zarod, Russia).
akhtenskite.etymology: For the Akhtensk deposit, Russia, where it was ﬁrst noted.

akimotoite.occurrence: In shock-metamorphosed melt veins in chondritic L-6 meteorites.
akimotoite.etymology: Honors Syun-iti Akimoto for his contributions to high-pressure research.

aklimaite.occurrence: In a metasomatically altered limestone xenolith in ignimbrite.
aklimaite.etymology: Derived from a Turkish women’s name, Aklima, which means bright by the mind, in allusion to the mineral’s light color and to the challenge of studying complex crystal structures with imperfect material. The name also honors the Turkish population in the Lakargi region.

akopovaite.occurrence: In a zoned spodumene-bearing pegmatite vein associated with quartz-micaceous schists.
akopovaite.etymology: Honors Anna Vartanovna Akopova (b. 1952), a chemistry teacher in the gymnasium #14, Rostov-on-Don, Russia. Her teaching, including experimental work, has prompted many of her students to choose a career in the Natural Sciences, including the first author of the present paper.

akrochordite.occurrence: A rare mineral in hausmannite ore from a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L˚ angban, Sweden); in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Sterling Hill, New Jersey, USA).
akrochordite.etymology: From the Greek for wart, for its typical habit.

aksaite.occurrence: In ﬁne-grained halite in a salt dome.
aksaite.etymology: From the locality, Ak-sa ˘ ı (“White Glen”), Kazakhstan.

aktashite.occurrence: Uncommon, of hydrothermal origin in complex polymetallic As-Hg-bearing deposits.
aktashite.etymology: For its occurrence at the Aktash deposit, Russia.

alabandite.occurrence: May be in large quantities in epithermal polymetallic sulﬁde vein and especially in low-temperature manganese deposits. An uncommon constituent of a number of meteorites.
alabandite.etymology: For the originally reported locality at Alabanda in Turkey.

alacranite.occurrence: In hydrothermal As-S veins (Alacrán mine, Chile); in the condensation zone of a hydrothermal Hg-Sb-As system as cement in a sandy gravel (Uzon caldera, Russia); formed at low temperatures in a polymetallic hydrothermal deposit on a submarine seamount (Conical Seamount, Papua New Guinea); as sublimates on a burning mine dump (Kateřina mine, Czech Republic).
alacranite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Alacrán deposit, Chile.

alamosite.occurrence: As a rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of lead-bearing base metal deposits.
alamosite.etymology: For the Mexican type locality at Alamos.

alarsite.etymology: For ALuminum and ARSenic in the composition.

albertiniite.occurrence: Coating fractures as an intermediate product of oxidation between iron sulfides (pyrite and arsenopyrite) and sulfates.
albertiniite.etymology: Honors Claudio Albertini, an Italian mineral collector and expert on the systematic mineralogy of the Alps and pegmatites.

albite.occurrence: A major constituent of granites and granite pegmatites, alkalic diorites, basalts, and in hydrothermal and alpine veins. A product of potassium metasomatism and in low-temperature and low-pressure metamorphic facies and in some schists. Detrital and authigenic in sedimentary rocks.
albite.etymology: From the Latin, albus, for white, its characteristic color.

albrechtschraufite.occurrence: On a museum specimen of schr¨ ockingerite.
albrechtschraufite.etymology: To honor Professor Albrecht Schrauf (1837–1897), Austrian crystallographer, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria.

alburnite.occurrence: In an epithermal hydrothermal Au-Ag vein.
alburnite.etymology: From the Latin name for the locality that produced the first specimens, known during the Roman period as Alburnus Maior.

alcantarillaite.occurrence: Secondary in the oxidation zone of a wolframite deposit (ferberite, löllingite).
alcantarillaite.etymology: For the locality where the studied material was collected.

alcaparrosaite.occurrence: Formed by the oxidation of pyritic masses under increasingly arid conditions, likely at a relatively early stage.
alcaparrosaite.etymology: For the Alcaparrosa mine, Chile, from where the first specimens were collected.

aldermanite.occurrence: As a secondary mineral in cavities in a brecciated metamorphosed sedimentary phosphate deposit, formed by the alteration of ﬂuellite (Moculta quarry, Australia).
aldermanite.etymology: Honors Arthur Richard Alderman (1901–1980), Professor of Geology and Mineralogy, University of Adelaide, Adelaide, Australia.

aldridgeite.occurrence: Secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of a galena, Cd-bearing sphalerite, and chalcopyrite deposit.
aldridgeite.etymology: Honors Edward William Aldridge, owner of the Duke of Cornwall Hotel, Broken Hill, Australia and collector of the first major Broken Hill mineral specimen collection (1888-1891).

aleksandrovite.occurrence: In a zoned microcline-calcite vein with aegirine-hedenbergite, quartz, and albite in a glacial moraine boulder. The region contains carbonatites and an alkaline massif.
assoc_parsed: zr and hydroxyl analogues of alexandrovite
aleksandrovite.etymology: Honors the Russian geochemist, geologist, and mineralogist Stanislav Mikhailovich Aleksandrov (b. 1932) for his contributions to the geology, geochemistry, and mineralogy of tin.

aleksite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in sulﬁde-quartz veins (Alekseev mine, Russia).

aleutite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
aleutite.etymology: For the Aleut ethnic group, the original inhabitants of the Commander Islands, Aleutsky District, Kamchatka Krai.

alexkhomyakovite.occurrence: In peralkaline pegmatite in an alkaline igneous complex.
alexkhomyakovite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Alexander Petrovich Khomyakov (1933-2012), a specialist in the mineralogy of alkaline rocks, of the Khibiny and Lovozero alkaline complexes, and a senior author for the descriptions of 73 new minerals discovered there.

alexkuznetsovite-ce.occurrence: As part of rich REE mineralization in polymineralic nodules of the Mochalin Log placer deposit, probably formed during fenitization of granitic pegmatites within granite -gneisses in the exocontact zone of an alkaline intrusion.
alexkuznetsovite-ce.etymology: Honors Russian mineral collector Alexey M. Kuznetsov (b. 1962) who provided samples of the studied material. The suffix is the dominant REE. The Ce-analogue of alexkuznetsovite-(La).

alexkuznetsovite-la.occurrence: As part of rich REE mineralization in polymineralic nodules of the Mochalin Log placer deposit, probably formed during fenitization of granitic pegmatites within granite -gneisses in the exocontact zone of an alkaline intrusion.
alexkuznetsovite-la.etymology: Honors Russian mineral collector Alexey M. Kuznetsov (b. 1962) who provided samples of the studied material. The suffix is the dominant REE. The La analogue of alexkuznetsovite-(Ce).

alflarsenite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in a syenitic pegmatite in larvikite.
alflarsenite.etymology: Honors Alf Olav Larsen (b. 1952), Norwegian self-taught mineralogist who has contributed to the description of six new mineral species.

alforsite.occurrence: In lenses and bands of barium silicate metasediments developed under hornblende-pyroxene hornfels facies near the contact with granite or granodiorite.
alforsite.etymology: To honor Dr. John T. Alfors (1930– ), geologist, California Division of Mines, for his work on the type locality.

alfredopetrovite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the weathered portions of a telethermal vein hosted by sandstones and shales.
alfredopetrovite.etymology: Honors Alfredo Petrov (b. 1955), geologist, mineralogist and avid mineral collector for his contributions to the mineralogy and geology of Bolivia and to the mineral collector’s community.

alfredstelznerite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a cavity in fractured mudstone in a playa-hosted borate deposit.
alfredstelznerite.etymology: Honors Dr. Alfred Wilhelm Stelzner (1840–1895), first professor of geology at the University of Córdoba and founder of the Mineralogical Museum.

algodonite.occurrence: Uncommon in hydrothermal deposits, intimately associated with other copper arsenides.

aliettite.occurrence: An alteration product in serpentinized ophiolites and residual in soils derived therefrom; in altered dolostones.
aliettite.etymology: To honor Professor Andrea Alietti (1923{ ), of the University of Modena, Modena, Italy, who ¯rst studied the structure of the mineral.

allabogdanite.occurrence: A primary phase in nickel-rich ataxite meteorites. In surficial terrestrial pyrometamorphic rocks, possibly formed by transformation from barringerite.
allabogdanite.etymology: Honors Alla N. Bogdanova, (b. 1947), Geological Institute, Kola Science Center, Russian Academy of Sciences, Apatity, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

allactite.occurrence: As a rare secondary mineral in veinlets through metamorphosed manganese deposits (Sweden); in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
allactite.etymology: From the Greek, to change, a reference to the strong pleochroism.

allanite-ce.occurrence: An accessory in some granites and granite pegmatites, syenites, more rarely in gabbroic pegmatites. Rarely in schists, gneisses, and some contact metamorphosed limestones; a clastic component of sediments.
allanite-ce.etymology: For Thomas Allan (1777{1833), Scottish mineralogist who discovered the species.

allanite-la.occurrence: In barite veins that cut a dolomitic metamorphosed limestone.
allanite-la.etymology: For the La-dominant analog of allanite-(Ce).

allanite-nd.occurrence: An accessory phase in the blocky zone of a NYF-type granitic pegmatite (Sweden).
allanite-nd.etymology: The suffix identifies the Nd-analog of allanite-(Ce). Honors Thomas Allan (1777-1833), Scottish mineralogist who discovered the species.

allantoin.occurrence: On rock surfaces as the result of evaporation under the conditions prevailing underground (Rowley mine). In a bat-guano deposit related to an active colony of bats (Kahf Kharrat Najem Cave).
allantoin.etymology: Allantoin is the common name for the organic chemical compound C 4H6N4O3 whose equivalence to the natural material is established by Raman spectroscopy, XRD, and structure analysis, despite no quantitative chemical analysis of natural material.

allargentum.etymology: From the Greek for another and the Latin argentum, silver.

alleghanyite.occurrence: Hydrothermally deposited, in lenses in a manganese-bearing vein (Bald Knob, North Carolina, USA); in veins crosscutting franklinite ore near pegmatites in a metamorphosed stratiform Zn{Mn deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
alleghanyite.etymology: For the occurrence in Alleghany Co., North Carolina, USA.

allendeite.occurrence: As grains in an ovoid-shaped, ultra-refractory inclusion in the Allende meteorite , likely a high-temperature condensate early in the formation of the solar system.
allendeite.etymology: For the meteorite that contained the first specimens.

allochalcoselite.occurrence: Formed by sublimation around a degassing volcanic fumarole.
allochalcoselite.etymology: Derived from the Greek for “different” (allos) and “copper” (chalkos) and from “selenium”, to reflect the different valences and crystallographic behavior of copper in this selenite mineral.

alloclasite.occurrence: In calcite or quartz veins of apparently low-temperature, late-stage hydrothermal origin. Also in siliciﬁed, recrystallized metamorphic rock.
alloclasite.etymology: From the Greek for other, and to break, because its cleavage was believed to be diﬀerent from marcasite, which it resembles.

allophane.occurrence: A weathering product of volcanic ash. In hydrothermally altered igneous rocks, from the breakdown of feldspars, and in hydrothermal veins, typically related to copper deposits. In sedimentary rocks, including chalk and coal beds.
allophane.etymology: From the Greek for other and to appear, referring to a change of appearance under the blowpipe.

alloriite.occurrence: Lining the walls of small miarolitic cavities in a sanidine-syenite volcanic bomb.
alloriite.etymology: Honors Roberto Allori (b. 1933), an amateur mineralogist who has studied the Latium region.

alluaivite.occurrence: In ultra-agpaitic pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
alluaivite.etymology: For its occurrence on Mt. Alluaiv, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

alluaudite.occurrence: Very common in granite pegmatites, formed by sodium metasomatism of triphylite - lithiophilite, heterosite-purpurite, or ferrisicklerite; in phosphatic nodules in shales.
alluaudite.etymology: Honors François Alluaud, mining engineer of Limoges, France, who discovered the species.

almandine.occurrence: The most common garnet, typically in mica schists and gneisses, from regionally metamorphosed argillaceous sediments and pelites; also in contact metamorphic hornfels. In granites and eclogites; in sedimentary rocks; as a detrital mineral.
almandine.etymology: For Alabanda in Turkey, a cutting center in antiquity.

almarudite.occurrence: In metasomatized silica-rich xenoliths in leucite tephrite lava.
almarudite.etymology: Honors the authors’ hosting and supporting institution, “Universität Wien”, derived from the university’s proper name “ALma MAter RUDolphina”.

almeidaite.occurrence: In altered dacite 2 meters from a hydrothermal quartz vein.
almeidaite.etymology: Honors Professor Fernando Flávio Marques de Almeida (1916-2013) for his work on the geology of Brazil and South America.

alnaperbøeite-ce.occurrence: A late primary phase in REE-bearing quartz-microcline pegmatite.
alnaperbøeite-ce.etymology: Emphasizes the chemical relationships with perbøeite-(Ce), the dominance of Al in the M3 site and the role of Na to charge balance the dominance of a trivalent cation in the M3 site of the REE-epidote module. The root name alnaperbøeite should apply to any ET polysome composition in which (1) trivalent cations are dominant at the M3 site and aluminum is dominant among them and (2) the charge balance in A sites is dominantly achieved by substitution of Na for REE (rather than A2+ for REE).

alpeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral crystallized from V- and Mn-rich hydrothermal fluids along fractures during tectono-metamorphism.
alpeite.etymology: For the locality, the Monte Alpe mine, that produced the first specimens.

alpersite.occurrence: An efflorescent secondary mineral, likely widespread and unnoticed in mine wastes that contain copper-bearing sulfides, but in which solubilized Fe2+ is not available for melanterite crystallization because of oxidation to Fe3+ in surface waters of near-neutral pH. Natural material collected at relative humidity = 65% and T = 4° C.
alpersite.etymology: Honors Charles N. Alpers, geochemist with the United States Geological Survey, for his contributions to our understanding of the mineralogical controls of mine-water geochemistry.

alsakharovite-zn.occurrence: In cavities in eudialyte-aegirine-feldspar pegmatite in an alkaline massif.
alsakharovite-zn.etymology: Honors Russian geologist Aleksey S. Sakharov (1910-1996) for his study of the Lovozero alkaline massif and a suffix indicates the predominance of Zn in the D structural site.

alstonite.occurrence: Typically in low-temperature hydrothermal Pb–Zn deposits; rare in carbonatites.
alstonite.etymology: For the original locality near Alston, England.

altaite.occurrence: Typically in hydrothermal vein Au–Te-bearing deposits.
altaite.etymology: After the locality in the Altai Mountains, Kazakhstan.

althausite.etymology: To honor Professor Egon Althaus (1933– ), Karlsruhe University, Karlsruhe, Germany.

althupite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the uraniferous zone of an altered granite pegmatite.
althupite.etymology: For the major cations in the composition, ALuminum, THorium, Uranium, Phosphorus.

aluminite.occurrence: Typically in clays or lignites, formed by the reaction of sulfate-bearing solutions from the decomposition of marcasite or pyrite at moderate temperatures with aluminous silicates; as a volcanic sublimate; in sulfur deposits; rarely in caves.

aluminium.occurrence: In a gabbro-dolerite massif (Billeekh intrusion, Russia); in aluminum-rich rocks; in high-temperature hydrothermal Sn–W deposits and their alteration zones; in volcanic ash.
aluminium.etymology: Named aluminum by Humphry Davy, who discovered the element.

alumino-oxy-rossmanite.occurrence: An early magmatic Al-rich oxy-tourmaline indicative of high-temperature in a relatively dry environment, which is poor in Li and F, in pegmatitic in amphibolite and biotite-rich paragneiss.
alumino-oxy-rossmanite.etymology: Prefixes identify dominant composition of the Y and W sites in a tourmaline related to rossmanite which honors George R. Rossman, Professor of Mineralogy, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA.

aluminocerite-ce.occurrence: In secondary and miarolitic cavities in NYF (niobium-yttrium-fluorine) granite pegmatite veins and pods within pink granite.
aluminocerite-ce.etymology: Alumino for a cerite with dominant aluminum in the M site and a suffix for the dominant REE.

aluminocopiapite.occurrence: A secondary mineral typically formed by the oxidation of pyrite in shales and coal; may be a fumarolic reaction product.
aluminocopiapite.etymology: For its content of aluminum and relation to the copiapite group.

aluminocoquimbite.occurrence: A precipitate from volcanic vapors in a fumarole (< 100° C).
aluminocoquimbite.etymology: For its high aluminum content and relation to coquimbite.

aluminomagnesiohulsite.occurrence: In one thin section from a magnesian, spinel-bearing, kotoite-marble skarn.
aluminomagnesiohulsite.etymology: Describes the mineral as the Al- and Mg-dominant analogue of hulsite.

aluminopyracmonite.occurrence: A sublimate from medium-temperature (~250º C) gases emanating from an intracrater volcanic fumarole.
aluminopyracmonite.etymology: For the essential aluminum and chemical analogy with pyracmonite.

aluminosugilite.occurrence: In interstices in manganiferous ophiolitic metacherts.
aluminosugilite.etymology: The prefix identifies the Al-analogue of sugilite, which honors Ken-ichi Sugi (1901-1948) of the Kyushu Imperial University.

aluminum.occurrence: In a gabbro-dolerite massif (Billeekh intrusion, Russia); in aluminum-rich rocks; in high-temperature hydrothermal Sn-W deposits and their alteration zones; in volcanic ash. In a desilicated zoned gem pegmatite vein intruded between a small serpentinized ultrabasic body and biotite gneiss (Bulgaria).
aluminum.etymology: Named aluminum by Humphry Davy, who discovered the element.

alumnoakermanite.occurrence: As phenocrysts in olivine-free melilite-nephelinitic ashes and lapilli-tuffs produced by a carbonatite volcano.
alumnoakermanite.etymology: For its composition and relationship to other members of the melilite group.

alumoedtollite.occurrence: A sublimate on basaltic scoria at an active volcanic fumarole.
alumoedtollite.etymology: Prefix, alumo, identifies the aluminum analogue of edtollite.

alumohydrocalcite.occurrence: Formed at low temperature by the action of carbonated waters on allophane or dickite in dolomites and limestones; chromian varieties are typically formed near altering chromite from serpentinites.
alumohydrocalcite.etymology: From aluminum; water, hydro; and calcium carbonate, calcite, in the composition.

alumoklyuchevskite.etymology: For aluminum in its composition and its relation to klyuchevskite.

alumopharmacosiderite.occurrence: With other oxidized arsenates on a museum specimen.
alumopharmacosiderite.etymology: As the ALUMinum analog of pharmacosiderite.

alumotantite.occurrence: In albitized areas of highly fractionated rare element-enriched granite pegmatites.
alumotantite.etymology: For ALUMinum and TANTalum in the composition.

alumovesuvianite.occurrence: Lining cavities in rodingite (granular diopside) at the contact with host serpentinite. Likely of low-temperature hydrothermal origin (< 350o C).
alumovesuvianite.etymology: As a member of the vesuvianite group with Al3+ as a dominant cation in the Y1 site.

alunite.occurrence: Formed between 15 ◦C and 400 ◦C by the action of sulfate, which may be generated from pyrite or solfataric action, on aluminous rocks, commonly accompanied by kaolinitization and siliciﬁcation.
alunite.etymology: A contraction of the earlier name aluminilite.

alunogen.occurrence: Forms by reaction of sulfates from decomposing sulﬁdes with aluminous minerals in shales and slates; in gossan or altered wall rock of pyritic deposits in arid regions; in coal seams; in relatively low-temperature fumaroles.
alunogen.etymology: From the Latin for alum and the Greek for to make.

alvanite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a vanadiferous clay-anthraxolite horizon.
alvanite.etymology: For ALuminum and V ANadium in the composition.

alwilkinsite-y.occurrence: A secondary phase formed at ambient temperature by evaporative processes at moderately high relative humidity at the surface of a rock with high relative porosity and in an environment that was relatively oxidizing and generally acidic.
alwilkinsite-y.etymology: Honors Alan (Al) J. Wilkins, MD (b. 1955), of Coto de Caza, California, for discovering the mineral.

amakinite.occurrence: Noted in drill core, in thin veins and pockets in kimberlite.
amakinite.etymology: For the Amakin Expedition, which prospected the Sakhan diamond deposits.

amamoorite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed manganese ore deposit.
amamoorite.etymology: For the locality of the first specimens, the Amamoor mine.

amarantite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed especially in arid climates.
amarantite.etymology: From the Greek for amaranth, an imaginary purplish red undying ﬂower, for its color.

amarillite.occurrence: Formed in the oxidation zones of sulﬁde deposits.
amarillite.etymology: For the locality at Tierra Amarilla, Chile.

amblygonite.occurrence: An uncommon accessory mineral in zoned granite pegmatites; in high-temperature tin veins and greisens.
amblygonite.etymology: From the Greek for blunt and angle, for its ∼90 ◦ cleavage angle.

ambrinoite.occurrence: In an evaporite deposit probably formed by highly alkaline, low-temperature hydrothermal fluids.
ambrinoite.etymology: Honors Pierluigi Ambrino (b. 1947), the mineral collector who provided the specimens.

ameghinite.occurrence: Formed in massive borax in a borate-rich playa.
ameghinite.etymology: Honors two brothers, Carlos Ameghino (1865–1936) and Florentino Ameghino (1854–1911), Argentine geologists.

amesite.occurrence: A product of low-grade metamorphism of Al, Mg-rich rocks.
amesite.etymology: Honors James Ames, a mine owner.

amicite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting melilite-nephelinite volcanic rocks and pyroclastics (Hegau, Germany); in natrolite veinlets cutting ijolite-urtite pegmatites and apatite-nepheline rocks (Kola Peninsula, Russia).
amicite.etymology: To honor Giovan Battista Amici (1786{1863), physicist, optician, and inventor of microscope optical elements.

aminoffite.occurrence: In cavities in massive magnetite (Lºangban, Sweden); in °uorite veins at the contact between marbles and \hornblende" granites associated with hastingsite nepheline syenites (Dugdinsk massif, Russia); in °uorite veins in tinguaite and nephelinite dikes (Bayankolsk dike ¯eld, Russia).
aminoffite.etymology: To honor Dr. Gregori Amino® (1883{1947), Swedish mineralogist and expert on Lºangban mineralogy, associated with the Riksmuseum, Stockholm, Sweden.

ammineite.occurrence: Likely the product of the interaction between NH 3 from guano and Cu from chalcopyrite in underlying igneous rocks.
ammineite.etymology: Recognizes the first mineral described with ammine complex in its crystal structure.

ammonioalunite.occurrence: Formed in hot springs under very acid conditions, rich in ammonium and sulfate, poor in potassium, below 100 ◦C.
ammonioalunite.etymology: As the ammonium analog of alunite.

ammoniojarosite.occurrence: Formed in black lignitic shales containing pyrite (Utah, USA).
ammoniojarosite.etymology: As the ammonium analog of jarosite.

ammoniolasalite.occurrence: Product of postmining oxidation of primary montroseite-corvusite assemblages at ambient temperatures. The ammonium derived from organic matter. In a bedded or roll-front U and V deposit in sandstone containing carbonaceous plant material.
ammoniolasalite.etymology: Ammonio for the composition as the NH4-dominant (over Na) analogue of lasalite.

ammonioleucite.occurrence: In veinlets, fractures, and cavities in hydrothermally altered crystalline schist, as powdery pseudomorphous replacements of analcime crystals.
ammonioleucite.etymology: For ammonia in its chemical composition and its relation to leucite.

ammoniomagnesiovoltaite.occurrence: As efflorescences formed by chemical reactions as ground water interacts with organic matter from coal and oxidizing pyrite and marcasite on a burning coal dump.
ammoniomagnesiovoltaite.etymology: As an analog of voltaite with essential ammonium and magnesium in the composition.

ammoniomathesiusite.occurrence: In a U-V roll-front deposit in sandstone; a product of postmining oxidation of a montroseite-corvusite assemblage with pyrite and chalcopyrite. The NH4+ presumably derived from organic matter.
ammoniomathesiusite.etymology: The prefix indicates the ammonium analogue of K-dominant mathesiusite.

ammoniotinsleyite.occurrence: In a guano deposit in a desert.
ammoniotinsleyite.etymology: The prefix identifies the ammonium analogue of tinsleyite.

ammoniovoltaite.occurrence: As efflorescence that covers walls in cracks around gas/steam (∼100°C.) vents in strongly hydrothermally-altered andesite-basalt in a geothermal region characterized by a high ammonium concentration.
ammoniovoltaite.etymology: Emphasizes that this is the ammonium analogue of voltaite.

ammoniozippeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral on the walls of mines in U-V deposits that replaced wood and other organic material in sandstones and conglomerate (roll-front type U-V deposits).
ammoniozippeite.etymology: As the ammonium analogue of zippeite, with (NH4)+ in place of K+.

amstallite.occurrence: In open ¯ssures cutting pegmatitic schlieren, in hydrothermally altered graphite-bearing metamorphic rocks.
amstallite.etymology: For the type locality at Amstall, Austria.

analcime.occurrence: In the groundmass or vesicles of silica-poor intermediate and ma¯c igneous rocks, typically basalts and phonolites, from late-stage hydrothermal solutions, or disseminated due to deuteric alteration. In lake beds, altered from pyroclastics or clays, or as a primary precipitate; authigenic in sandstones and siltstones.
analcime.etymology: From the Greek for weak, alluding to the weak electrostatic charge developed when heated or rubbed.

anandite.occurrence: As monomineralic veinlets and lenses in a banded magnetite deposit capped by banded magnetite-barite rock. The ore zone and associated interbedded calc-schists and gneisses are of metasedimentary origin, of approximately granulite facies grade.
anandite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Ananda Kentush Coomaraswamy (1877{1947), the ¯rst Director of the Mineral Survey of Ceylon (Sri Lanka).

anapaite.occurrence: In oolitic iron ore, and in the stems of fossil trees (Anapa, Russia); in lacustrine sediments.
anapaite.etymology: For its ﬁrst discovery near Anapa, Russia.

anatacamite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a polymetallic sulfide deposit
anatacamite.etymology: For its triclinic symmetry and polymorphism with atacamite.

anatase.occurrence: Usually secondary, derived from other titanium-bearing minerals. In Alpine veins, derived from the enclosing gneisses or schists by hydrothermal solutions. In igneous and metamorphic rocks; in pegmatites; from a carbonatite. A common detrital mineral.
anatase.etymology: From the Greek meaning extension, for the greater length of the usual pyramid compared with other tetragonal minerals.

anatolyite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
anatolyite.etymology: Honors Russian crystallographer, mineralogist, and mathematician Anatoly Kapitonovich Boldyrev (1883-1946) Professor of Crystallography and Mineralogy, Leningrad Mining Institute.

ancylite-ce.occurrence: An uncommon accessory mineral in some nepheline syenites and carbonatites.
ancylite-ce.etymology: From the Greek for curved, in allusion to the characteristically curved crystals.

ancylite-la.occurrence: A rare mineral in nepheline syenites in diﬀerentiated alkalic massifs.
ancylite-la.etymology: For its relation to ancylite-(Ce) and its dominant content of lanthanum.

andalusite.occurrence: A result of contact metamorphism of argillaceous sediments, also in regionally metamorphosed schists. Rare in granites and pegmatites, which however a®ord the largest crystals. Detrital in some sandstones.
andalusite.etymology: For an occurrence in the Andalusia region, Spain. All rights reserved.
