bermanite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Harry Berman (1902–1944), Professor of Mineralogy, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

bernalite.occurrence: On a museum specimen from a metamorphosed Pb-Zn deposit, probably from the surface oxidation zone.
bernalite.etymology: Honors John Desmond Bernal (1901-1971), British crystallographer and historian of science.

bernardite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal deposit with other As–Tl sulﬁde minerals.
bernardite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Jan H. Bernard, mineralogist, Geological Survey of Czechoslovakia, who ﬁrst noted the mineral.

bernarlottiite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in cavities, to 30 cm, in marble related to tectonometamorphism.
bernarlottiite.etymology: Honors Bernardino Lotti (1847-1933) for his significant contributions to the knowledge of the geology of Tuscany and to the development of the Tuscan mining industry.

berndtite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in tin sulﬁde ores (Cerro de Potos ´ ı, Bolivia); a secondary mineral in a tin-bearing pegmatite (Lagares-do-Estanho tin pegmatite); in a high-temperature deposit, hydrothermally altered (Arandis, Namibia).
berndtite.etymology: For Dr. Fritz Berndt, German mineralogist, Corporati´ on Minera de Bolivia, Oruro, Bolivia.

berryite.occurrence: In quartz veins with other sulﬁdes and sulfosalts, and in siderite-rich cryolite (Ivigtut, Greenland).
berryite.etymology: In honor of Professor Leonard Gascoigne Berry (1914–1982), Canadian mineralogist, Queen’s University, Kingston, Ontario, Canada, who obtained the ﬁrst X-ray powder pattern of the mineral.

berthierine.occurrence: Common in unmetamorphosed marine sediments; in lateritic and polar soils.
berthierine.etymology: Honors the French geologist, Pierre Berthier (1782{1861).

berthierite.occurrence: In low-temperature hydrothermal antimony veins, in portions deﬁcient in sulfur.

bertossaite.occurrence: Thought to be formed during a late calcium-rich phase of mineralization in a lithium-bearing granite pegmatite.
bertossaite.etymology: Honoring Antonio Bertossa, Director of the Geological Survey of Rwanda.

bertrandite.occurrence: In ¯ssures in granites and associated pegmatites and in miarolitic cavities in greisens; commonly an alteration product of beryl, more rarely as a primary mineral.

beryl.occurrence: In granites and granite pegmatites, rarely in nepheline syenites. Also in ma¯c metamorphic rocks, low- to high-temperature hydrothermal veins and in vugs in rhyolite.
beryl.etymology: From the Greek beryllos, original signi¯cance unknown.

beryllite.occurrence: In the center of a zoned pegmatite cutting arfvedsonite-bearing nepheline syenite (Lovozero massif, Russia); in analcime-rich veins (Il¶³maussaq intrusion, Greenland).
beryllite.etymology: In allusion to the BERYLLium in its composition.

beryllonite.occurrence: As a rare secondary mineral in granitic and alkalic pegmatites.
beryllonite.etymology: For one of the major constituents in the composition, BERYLLium.

berzelianite.occurrence: With other selenides in hydrothermal veinlets in dolostone (Clausthal, Germany); in iron ores (Lerbach, Germany); with other selenides in calcite veins in serpentine (Skrikerum, Sweden); in a gold-quartz-orthoclase deposit (Redjang-Lebong, Sumatra).
berzelianite.etymology: For J¨ ons Jacob Berzelius (1779–1848), Swedish chemist, who discovered selenium.

berzeliite.etymology: In honor of the noted Swedish chemist and mineralogist, J¨ ons Jacob Berzelius (1779–1848).

beshtauite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of a hydrothermal vein-type uranium deposit in porphyritic granite.
beshtauite.etymology: For the mine that produced the first specimens.

betafergusonite-ce.occurrence: In magnesian skarn around carbonatite-derived dolomitic marble (“Northern China”); in carbonatite (Chernigovsky region, Ukraine).
betafergusonite-ce.etymology: In allusion to its dimorphous relation to fergusonite-(Ce).

betafergusonite-nd.etymology: In allusion to its dimorphous relation to fergusonite-(Nd).

betafergusonite-y.etymology: In allusion to its dimorphous relation to fergusonite-(Y).

betaroselite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in cobalt-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
betaroselite.etymology: As a monoclinic dimorph of roselite.

betekhtinite.occurrence: In veins cutting the black cupriferous shale (Mansfeld, Germany).
betekhtinite.etymology: For Anatolii Georgievich Betekhtin (1897–1962), Russian mineralogist and economic geologist.

betpakdalite-caca.occurrence: Filling cracks in leached pyrite in the oxidized zone of a mineral deposit (Kara-Oba deposit, Kazakhstan); on vein quartz (Krupka, Czech Republic).
betpakdalite-caca.etymology: For the original occurrence in the Bet-Pak-Dal Desert, Kazakhstan. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

betpakdalite-camg.occurrence: In a deep oxidation zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit, formed by alteration of As, Fe and Mo sulfides by solutions rich in Ca and Mg (Tsumeb, Namibia).
betpakdalite-camg.etymology: For the original occurrence in the Bet-Pak-Dal Desert, Kazakhstan. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

betpakdalite-fefe.etymology: For the Bet-Pak-Dal Desert, Kazakhstan. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

betpakdalite-naca.etymology: For the Bet-Pak-Dal Desert, Kazakhstan. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

betpakdalite-nana.occurrence: From the upper oxidation zone of a porphyry copper deposit.
betpakdalite-nana.etymology: For the Bet-Pak-Dal Desert, Kazakhstan. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

bettertonite.occurrence: Extremely rare, in quartz veins in a multi-stage, polymetallic hydrothermal deposit; probably formed from leaching and the replacement of Al to Fe in pharmacosiderite. Dehydrates to penberthycroftite at temperatures likely on oxidizing mine dumps.
bettertonite.etymology: Honors Mr. John Betterton (b. 1959) a museum geologist/mineralogist at Haslemere Educational Museum, Haslemere, Surrey, England, for his extensive contributions to the characterization of minerals from the Penberthy Croft mine for more than 30 years.

beudantite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of polymetallic deposits.
beudantite.etymology: Honors Fran¸ cois Sulpice Beudant (1787–1850), French mineralogist, University of Paris, Paris, France.

beusite.occurrence: A late-stage accessory mineral in complex granite pegmatites. As euhedral inclusions in troilite nodules in an iron meteorite.
beusite.etymology: Honors Dr. Alexey Alexandrovich Beus, Professor of Mineralogy and Geochemistry, Moscow Polytechnical Institute, for his work on minerals of this group.

beusite-ca.occurrence: A common primary phosphate in a beusite-triphylite nodule (6×5×3 cm) in berylcolumbite-phosphate subtype of zoned rare-element pegmatites, in a small dike, which cuts an interlayered sequence of amphibolite and granodiorite. The product of exsolution from a (Li,Ca)- rich graftonite-like parent phase crystallized at high temperature from P-bearing hydrosaline melts related to anatectic melts, generated by partial melting of metasedimentary-metavolcanics rocks.
beusite-ca.etymology: The suffix indicates the Ca-analogue of beusite.

beyerite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in hydrothermal mineral deposits and granite pegmatites, formed by alteration of bismuth-bearing sulﬁdes and sulfosalts.
beyerite.etymology: To honor Adolph Beyer (1743–1805), mining engineer and mineralogist, Schneeberg, Germany, who ﬁrst recognized bismutite.

bezsmertnovite.occurrence: In the cementation zone of a volcanogenic gold telluride deposit, rarely as rims around grains of gold.
bezsmertnovite.etymology: For Dr. Marianna Sergeevna Bezsmertnaya (1914–1991), Institute of Mineralogy and Geochemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, and Dr. Vladimir Vasil’evich Bezsmertnyi (1912– ), All-Union Pedagogy Institute, Moscow, Russia, Soviet geologists and researchers on ore deposits.

biachellaite.occurrence: Found in cavities in volcanic ejecta.
biachellaite.etymology: For the discovery locality, the Biachella Valley.

biagioniite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal gold deposit along a shear zone.
biagioniite.etymology: Honors Cristian Biagioni (b. 1981), Associate Professor of Mineralogy, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Pisa, Italy, co-author of the descriptions of more than 50 new minerals.

bianchiniite.occurrence: Probably related to the circulation of As-rich hydrothermal fluids during the tectonometamorphism of a pyrite ± baryte ± iron-oxide ore deposit in meta-dolostone.
bianchiniite.etymology: Honors mineral collectors Andrea Bianchini (b. 1959) and Mario Bianchini (b. 1962) who provided specimens for studies of the mineralogy of pyrite ± baryte ± iron-oxide ore deposits from the Apuan Alps.

bianchite.occurrence: A post-mine mineral, typically in eﬄorescences on mine walls, an alteration product of oxidizing sulﬁdes.
bianchite.etymology: To honor Angelo Bianchi (1892–1970), Italian mineralogist, University of Padova, Padova, Italy.

bicapite.occurrence: Formed by the oxidation of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a moist environment on sandstone in a Colorado Plateau type, roll-front uranium/vanadium deposit.
bicapite.etymology: In recognition of this being the only known mineral with a structure based on a bicapped Keggin anion.

bicchulite.occurrence: In skarns in limestones, formed through alteration of gehlenite subjected to later retrograde hydration reactions.
bicchulite.etymology: For Bicchu, the town encompassing the Japanese type locality.

bideauxite.occurrence: Rarely enclosing and replacing boleite, with other oxidized Pb and Cl minerals, from an oxidized base-metal mineral deposit (Tiger, Arizona, USA).
bideauxite.etymology: For Richard August Bideaux (1935– ), of Oro Valley, Arizona, USA, American mineralogist and mineral collector.

bieberite.occurrence: An uncommon oxidation product of cobalt-bearing sulﬁde–arsenides.
bieberite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence at Bieber, Germany.

biehlite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral from an oxidized zone in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
biehlite.etymology: To honor Dr. Friedrich Karl Biehl (1887–?), mineralogist, Westfälische-Wilhelms University, Münster, Germany, who authored an early dissertation on Tsumeb minerals.

bigcreekite.occurrence: Filling fractures in gneiss near the margins of a granodiorite pluton.
bigcreekite.etymology: For the locality that provided the first specimens, Big Creek, California, USA.

bijvoetite-y.occurrence: Very rare, in the lower portion of the oxidation zone developed above uraninite-bearing dolomitic rocks.
bijvoetite-y.etymology: Honors Professor Johannes Martin Bijvoet (1892–1980), Dutch crystallographer.

bikitaite.occurrence: As a late-formed mineral in fractures in lithium-rich pegmatites.

bilibinskite.occurrence: In the zone of weathering of tellurium deposits.
bilibinskite.etymology: For Soviet geologist Yuri Aleksandrovich Bilibin (1901–1952), Karpkinskii All-Union Research Institute, St. Petersburg, Russia, specialist in gold deposits.

bilinite.occurrence: An alteration of iron sulﬁde in lignite (Svˇ etec, Czech Republic); a post-mine mineral with other iron sulfates (Nikitov deposits, Ukraine).
bilinite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence near B ´ ılina, Czech Republic.

billietite.occurrence: An uncommon alteration product of uraninite.
billietite.etymology: Honors Valère Louis Billiet (1903-1945), Belgian crystallographer, University of Ghent, Ghent, Belgium.

billingsleyite.occurrence: Believed to have occurred in a body of high-grade hydrothermal silver ore.
billingsleyite.etymology: For Paul Billingsley (1887-1962), mining geologist, who discovered the North Lily mine, and collected the type material.

billwiseite.occurrence: In a complex zoned granitic pegmatite of the LCT (Li–Cs–Ta) type.
billwiseite.etymology: Honors William Stewart Wise (b. 1933), Professor of Geology Emeritus, University of California at Santa Barbara, USA, for his contributions to mineralogy and his inspiration and mentoring of mineralogy students.

bindheimite.occurrence: Common in the oxidized portions of antimony-bearing lead deposits.
bindheimite.etymology: For Johann Jacob Bindheim (1750–1825), German chemist who made the ﬁrst chemical analysis of the mineral.

biotite.occurrence: An important rock-forming mineral under a wide range of conditions. In regionally metamorphosed schists and gneisses, and in contact metamorphosed rocks; in granites to nepheline syenites; less common in extrusive igneous rocks, from rhyolites to basalts. Characteristic of potassic hydrothermal alteration; in detrital sediments.
biotite.etymology: For the French mineralogist and physicist, Jean Baptiste Biot (1774{1862).

biphosphammite.occurrence: An alteration product of phosphammite in guano, due to loss of NH 4 (Gua˜ nape Island, Peru); a byproduct of the reaction between the liquid fraction of bat guano and urea (Murra-el-elevyn Cave, Australia).

biraite-ce.occurrence: In a vein that cuts fenite fragments in a carbonatite.
biraite-ce.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens, the Biraia cabonatite dike and the dominant rare earth element, Cesium.

biraite-la.occurrence: Formed in polymineralic nodules by metasomatism of primary bastnäsite-(La)/-(Ce) of probable alkaline pegmatitic origin.
biraite-la.etymology: Suffix indicates the lanthanum analog of biraite-(Ce).

birchite.occurrence: A late-stage supergene mineral formed in small cavities and thin seams as part of a suite of secondary phosphate minerals under low-temperature condition in an intensely deformed and metamorphosed stratiform base metal deposit of submarine exhalative origin. In a quartz-garnet matrix with abundant disseminated corroded masses of galena, fluorapatite, chalcopyrite and covellite.
birchite.etymology: Honors William D. Birch, Senior Curator of Geosciences, Museum Victoria, Australia, for his contributions to Australian geological sciences, and his service to several professional organizations.

biringuccite.occurrence: As scales on piping in a geothermal ﬁeld.
biringuccite.etymology: To honor Vannoccio Biringuccio (1480–1538/9), alchemist and metallurgist, author of the Pirotechnia.

birnessite.occurrence: A major manganese-bearing mineral of many soils; a common alteration product of manganese-rich mineral deposits; a component of bacterially-precipitated manganese oxides; an important constituent of “desert varnish” and marine manganese nodules.
birnessite.etymology: For the type locality at Birness, Scotland.

bischofite.occurrence: In saline deposits; probably in part secondary, formed from carnallite.
bischofite.etymology: For Karl Gustav Bischof (1792–1870), German geologist and mineral chemist, University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany.

bismoclite.occurrence: In an alluvial specimen, found near bismuth-bearing granite pegmatites (Jackals Water, South Africa); in greisen (Bygoo, Australia).
bismoclite.etymology: In allusion to its composition, a bismuth oxychloride.

bismuth.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with ores of Co, Ni, Ag, and Sn; in pegmatites and topaz-bearing Sn–W quartz veins.
bismuth.etymology: From the German weisse masse, later wismuth, white mass .

bismuthinite.occurrence: Typically in low- to high-temperature hydrothermal vein deposits, in tourmaline-bearing copper deposits in granite, in some gold veins formed at high temperatures, and in recent volcanic exhalation deposits.

bismutite.occurrence: A relatively common alteration product of other bismuth-bearing minerals in hydrothermal mineral deposits and granite pegmatites.
bismutite.etymology: In allusion to bismuth in the composition.

bismutocolumbite.etymology: For BISMuth in its composition and relation to minerals of the columbite–tantalite series.

bismutoferrite.occurrence: Probably of hydrothermal origin, in veins cutting shale (Schneeberg, Germany).
bismutoferrite.etymology: For BISMUTh and iron, (FERRum), in the composition.

bismutohauchecornite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin; as secondary pore-ﬁllings and replacements of sandstone and conglomerate (Zimmer Lake, Canada); in ultramaﬁc rocks (Liu Zhuang, China).

bismutostibiconite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed as an alteration product of bismuthian tetrahedrite-tennantite.
bismutostibiconite.etymology: For a bismuth-containing member of the stibiconite group.

bismutotantalite.occurrence: In granite pegmatite (Uganda and Mozambique); as stream-rounded pebbles (Acari, Brazil).
bismutotantalite.etymology: For BISMuth in its composition, and relation to tantalite.

bitikleite.occurrence: In the cuspidine zone of high-temperature skarns in a carbonate-silicate xenolith at the contact with ignimbrites.
bitikleite.etymology: For Bitikle, an old fortification near where the new mineral was discovered. Formerly bitikleite-(SnAl).

bityite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in lithium-bearing pegmatites.
bityite.etymology: For the locality, Mt. Bity, Madagascar.

bixbyite.occurrence: In lithophysal cavities in rhyolite; in metamorphosed manganese ores.
bixbyite.etymology: For Maynard Bixby, mineral dealer of Salt Lake City, Utah, USA, who provided the ﬁrst specimens.

bixbyite-fe.occurrence: In lithophysal cavities in rhyolite; in metamorphosed manganese ores.
bixbyite-fe.etymology: For Maynard Bixby, mineral dealer of Salt Lake City, Utah, USA, who provided the ﬁrst specimens.

bixbyite-mn.occurrence: In lithophysal cavities in rhyolite; in metamorphosed manganese ores.
bixbyite-mn.etymology: For Maynard Bixby, mineral dealer of Salt Lake City, Utah, USA, who provided the ﬁrst specimens.

bjarebyite.occurrence: A rare late stage reaction product of triphylite and amblygonite in complex granite pegmatites.
bjarebyite.etymology: Honors Alfred Gunnar Bjareby (1899–1967), Swedish-American student of New England pegmatite minerals, Boston, Massachusetts, USA, who collected the ﬁrst specimen.

blatonite.occurrence: In seams of gypsum in the oxidized portions of a roll-front-type uranium deposit in silty conglomerate.
blatonite.etymology: Honors Dr. Norbert Blaton (1945– ), crystallographer and specialist in uranium minerals, Catholic University of Leuven, Leuven, Belgium.

blatterite.etymology: Honoring Fritz Blatter (1943– ), German mineral collector, who provided the original material.

bleasdaleite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from cavities in weathered uraniferous granitic pegmatite containing partly oxidized copper sulfide minerals.
bleasdaleite.etymology: Honors the Reverend John I. Bleasdale (1822-1884) for of his promotion of mineralogy in Victoria.

blixite.occurrence: In hausmannite-rich dolomite and manganophyllite skarn in a metamorphosed Fe-Mn orebody (Långban, Sweden); a reaction product in slag immersed in sea water (Laurium, Greece).
blixite.etymology: For Dr. Ragnar Blix (1898-1985), chemist at the Swedish Museum of Natural History, who performed analyses of many Långban minerals.

blodite.occurrence: In lacustrine salt deposits and salt eﬄorescences; probably a product of metamorphism of marine salt deposits; in nitrate deposits; may be a volcanic sublimate.
blodite.etymology: To honor the German chemist Carl August Bl¨ ode (1773–1820).

blossite.occurrence: A very rare sublimate, probably formed between 100–200 ◦C, from the outer sulfate zone of a fumarole in the crater of a basaltic composite volcano.
blossite.etymology: To honor Dr. F. Donald Bloss (1920– ), American mineralogist, Virginia Polytechnic Institute, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA.

bluebellite.occurrence: A secondary copper mineral formed by decomposition of hessite and chalcopyrite under mildly acidic conditions. Source of iodine not known.
bluebellite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens.

bluelizardite.occurrence: An oxidation product as efflorescence on tunnel walls in sulfide-bearing sandstone in an abandoned underground Colorado Plateau-type uranium mine.
assoc_parsed: a few new unnamed uranyl sulfates of na and mg
bluelizardite.etymology: For the mine that produced the first specimens.

bluestreakite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of roll-front U-V deposit in corvusitemontroseite-bearing sandstone.
bluestreakite.etymology: For the mine that produced the first specimens.

bobcookite.occurrence: As efflorescent crusts, on the surfaces of mine walls, derived from the oxidation of primary minerals (uraninite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, bornite and covellite) in a relatively humid underground environment.
bobcookite.etymology: Honors Robert (Bob) B. Cook (b. 1944), Professor Emeritus, Department of Geology and Geography, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama, USA, recognizing his professional achievements.

bobfergusonite.occurrence: An uncommon primary mineral in the intermediate zone of a granite pegmatite enriched in manganese and fluorine.
bobfergusonite.etymology: To honor Emeritus Professor Robert Bury Ferguson (1920- ), Canadian mineralogist, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada, especially for his contributions to pegmatite mineralogy.

bobierrite.occurrence: Formed from the chemical alteration of guano deposits (Mejillones, Chile; Imperial Canyon lava tubes, Kenya), and an elephant tusk (Edgerton, Minnesota, USA). As a rare alteration product of primary phosphate-bearing minerals (Wodgina, Australia; Bendada pegmatite, Portugal).
bobierrite.etymology: In honor of Pierre Adolphe Bobierre (1823–1881), French agricultural chemist, who ﬁrst described the mineral.

bobjonesite.occurrence: On fractures surfaces in a silicified log with coalified margins within mineralized conglomerate. Oxidation of pyrite and montroseite formed a suite of secondary minerals (Utah). As a sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole (Tolbachik volcano).
bobjonesite.etymology: Honors Robert (Bob) Jones (b. 1926) of Arizona, USA, senior editor of Rocks and Gems for contributions to the mineralogical community through his writing, lecturing, and editing books, magazines and videos on minerals and their occurrence.

bobkingite.occurrence: In a quarry on crusts of malachite and azurite that overlie massive cuprite in oxidized waste material containing native copper hosted by diorite in a laccolith.
bobkingite.etymology: Honors mineralogist Robert King (b. 1923), formerly at the Department of Geology, Leicester University, and a founding member of the Russell Society.

bobmeyerite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a polymetallic sulfide deposit.
bobmeyerite.etymology: Honors Robert (Bob) Owen Meyer (b.1956) of Maple Valley, Washington, USA, who collected the specimens used in this study.

bobshannonite.occurrence: A hydrothermal phase in a pegmatite associated with an intrusive alkaline gabbrosyenite complex.
bobshannonite.etymology: Honors Dr. Robert (Bob) D. Shannon (b. 1935) from Boulder, Colorado, USA, for his contributions to crystal chemistry and mineralogy through his development of accurate and comprehensive ionic radii and his work on dielectric properties.

bobtraillite.occurrence: A late hydrothermal mineral in cavities in igneous breccia and nepheline syenite pegmatite.
bobtraillite.etymology: Honors Dr. Robert (“Bob”) James Traill (b. 1921), mineralogist and former head of the Mineralogy Section at the Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa (1953-1986).

bodieite.occurrence: An oxidation-zone mineral in vugs in polymetallic (Au-Ag-Cu-Pb) vein deposits emplaced in contact-metamorphosed dolomite (Tintic) or a volcanogenic fault-breccia deposit emplaced in granodiorite (Pittsbug-Liberty mine).
bodieite.etymology: For the Bodie Hills volcanic field, in which the Pittsburg-Liberty mine, where some of the first specimens were collected, is located.

bogdanovite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of Au–Te deposits.
bogdanovite.etymology: For Soviet geologist Aleksei Alekseevich Bogdanov (1907–1971), Moscow University, Moscow, Russia.

boggildite.occurrence: A rare mineral within greisen formed at the contact zone of a cryolite ore body.
boggildite.etymology: Honoring the Danish mineralogist Ove Balthasar Bøggild (1872–1956), Professor of Geology, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.

boggsite.occurrence: In vesicles in one of a series of porphyritic basalt °ows intercalated with pyroclastics and minor sediments.
boggsite.etymology: After Robert Maxwell Boggs (1918{ ), of Seattle, Washington, USA, and his son, Dr. Russell Calvin Boggs (1952{ ), of Cheney, Washington, USA, mineral collectors.

bogvadite.etymology: For Richard Bøgvad (1897–1952), formerly Chief Geologist for the company Øresund A/S, which mined the Ivigtut cryolite deposit.

bohdanowiczite.occurrence: In a strongly cracked zone formed in crystalline limestone adjacent to magnetitebearing skarns (Kletno, Poland); in reduction halos in red beds (near Zurich, Switzerland).
bohdanowiczite.etymology: Honors Professor Karol Bohdanowicz (1864-1947), economic geologist of Cracow, Poland.

bohmite.occurrence: Formed from aluminosilicates during tropical weathering, commonly a major constituent of bauxites, laterites, or ﬁreclays; a late product of low-temperature hydrothermal decomposition of corundum, nepheline in nepheline pegmatites, syenites, or ocean-ridge basalts.
bohmite.etymology: For Johannes B¨ ohm (1857–1938), German geologist, who ﬁrst studied the species.

bohseite.occurrence: In strongly fractionated parts of zoned anatectic (NYF-LCT) pegmatite dikes that cut amphibolite.
bohseite.etymology: Honors the Danish geologist Hennning Bohse (b. 1942) who has worked for more than 40 years on the mineralogy and geology of the Ilímaussaq alkaline complex.

bojarite.occurrence: Formed in a guano deposit on chalcopyrite-bearing gabbro in a desert.
bojarite.etymology: Honors Austrian mineralogist Dr Hans-Peter Bojar (b. 1967), Department of Mineralogy, Universalmuseum Joanneum, Graz, Austria, for his contributions to Earth Science including the descriptions of several new mineral species.

bokite.occurrence: In carbonaceous vanadiferous shales (Kurumsak area, Kazakhstan); in rich U–V ore in Triassic stream channels and impregnating sandstone (Monument No. 2 mine, Arizona, USA).
bokite.etymology: For Ivan Ivanovich Bok (1898–1983), Kazakh geologist, Institute of Geosciences, Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan.

boleite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed through reaction of chloride with primary sulﬁdes in the oxidized zone of Pb–Cu deposits; in smelter slag immersed in and leached by sea water.
boleite.etymology: For the occurrence at Boleo, Mexico.

boltwoodite.occurrence: In the outer silicate zone of alteration surrounding hydrated uranyl oxides incrusting primary uraninite; also ¯lling fractures at some distance from primary uraninite. From pegmatite and Colorado-Plateau-type sandstone uranium deposits.
boltwoodite.etymology: For Bertram Borden Boltwood (1870{1927), radiochemist of Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, USA, who devised the U{Pb method of measuring geologic time.

bonaccordite.occurrence: In a small tabular body of nickeliferous serpentinite, probably a contact deposit, along the junction of quartzite and an ultramaﬁc intrusive; it appears to have formed at ∼730 ◦C and < 2 kbar during thermal metamorphism, possibly of a nickel-rich meteorite.
bonaccordite.etymology: For the locality at Bon Accord, South Africa.

bonacinaite.occurrence: In a small void in a metamorphosed manganese deposit.
bonacinaite.etymology: Honors Enrico Bonacina (b. 1928), dean of micromineral photography in Italy.

bonattite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a pyrite deposit (Capo Calamita, Elba, Italy).
bonattite.etymology: To honor Stefano Bonatti (1902–1968), Italian petrologist, University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy.

bonazziite.occurrence: Low-temperature hydrothermal mineral probably formed while the system had direct involvement of magmatic volatiles.
bonazziite.etymology: Honors Paola Bonazzi (b. 1960), Professor in Mineralogy, University of Florence, Italy, in recognition of her seminal contributions to the study of arsenic sulfides and their alteration by light.

bonshtedtite.occurrence: In veinlets associated with alkali-carbonate metasomatism of alkalic massifs.
bonshtedtite.etymology: To honor Elsa Maksimilianovna Bonshtedt-Kupletskaya (1897–1974), Russian specialist in mineralogy of alkalic massifs.

boothite.occurrence: An alteration product of chalcopyrite (Alma mine, California, USA).
boothite.etymology: To honor Professor Edward Booth (1857–1917), American chemist, University of California, Berkeley, California, USA.

boracite.occurrence: An uncommon component of bedded sedimentary salt and potash deposits of marine origin, the boron probably derived from nearby volcanic activity.

boralsilite.occurrence: A high-temperature phase in pegmatites cutting granulite-facies metapelitic rocks.
boralsilite.etymology: From the composition, boron, aluminum, and silicon.

borax.occurrence: In evaporite deposits, salt lakes, playas, commonly well-crystallized; as an eﬄorescence on soils in arid regions.

borcarite.occurrence: In kotoite marbles, near the contact with granodiorite (Snezhnoye deposit, Russia); a rare secondary mineral probably formed by reaction of late hydrothermal ﬂuids with brucite (Fuka, Japan).
borcarite.etymology: For BORate and CARbonate in the composition.

borisenkoite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
borisenkoite.etymology: Honors Russian geochemist, mineralogist, and geologist Leonid Fedorovich Borisenko (1922-2000), a specialist in vanadium deposits and the mineralogy and geochemistry of vanadium. He worked in the Institute of Mineralogy, Geochemistry and Crystal Chemistry of Rare Elements (IMGRE) in Moscow.

borishanskiite.occurrence: In massive and disseminated Cu–Ni sulﬁde ores.
borishanskiite.etymology: To honor Seraﬁma Samoylovna Borishanskaya (1907–1988), Russian mineralogist, Moscow University, Moscow, Russia.

bornemanite.occurrence: In the natrolite zone of alkalic pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
bornemanite.etymology: To honor Irina Dmitrievna Borneman-Starynkevich (1891{1988), Russian mineralogist specializing in Khibiny and Lovozero minerals, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrology, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia.

bornhardtite.etymology: Honors Dr. Wilhelm Bornhardt (1864–1946), German student of ore deposits.

bornite.occurrence: Associated with and disseminated in maﬁc igneous rocks, in contact metamorphic skarn deposits, in pegmatites, in medium- to high-temperature hydrothermal deposits, and in sedimentary cupriferous shales; stable below ∼200 ◦C.
bornite.etymology: Honoring Ignaz Edler von Born (1742–1791), distinguished Austrian mineralogist.

borocookeite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in gem-bearing, zoned, complex, Li-bearing granitic pegmatite.
borocookeite.etymology: The prefix indicates the boron-dominant analogue of cookeite.

borodaevite.etymology: To honor Yuri Sergeevich Borodaev (1923– ), Russian mineralogist, Moscow State University, Moscow, Russia.

boromullite.occurrence: Product of granulite facies metamorphism of boron-rich peletic rocks.
boromullite.etymology: Recognizes boron as an essential constituent and for its relationship to mullite.

boromuscovite.occurrence: A coating on other minerals on the °oor of a pegmatite pocket, hydrothermally deposited after rupture of the pocket.
boromuscovite.etymology: Presumably for the BOROn content and relation to muscovite.

borovskite.occurrence: In massive pentlandite-chalcopyrite-pyrrhotite ores of hydrothermal origin.
borovskite.etymology: To honor Igor Borisovich Borovskii (1909–1985), Russian pioneer in microprobe analysis, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrology, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia.

bortnikovite.occurrence: As rims on isoferroplatinum grains in alluvial placer sediment derived from a concentrically zoned, alkaline ultramafic massif.
bortnikovite.etymology: Honors Professor Nikolai Stefanovich Bortnikov, mineralogist and researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences.

bortolanite.occurrence: Of late magmatic origin, in the matrix of evolved subvolcanic phonolites and nepheline syenite pegmatites.
bortolanite.etymology: For the locality, Bortolan quarry, where the studied material was collected.

boscardinite.occurrence: In a quartz vein cutting dolostone, associated with a barite-pyrite-iron oxide deposit in regionally metamorphosed rocks.
boscardinite.etymology: Honors Matteo Boscardin (b. 1939) for his contribution to the knowledge of the regional mineralogy of Italy.

bosiite.occurrence: In a sulfide- and gold-bearing, sub-volcanic, hydrothermal quartz vein.
bosiite.etymology: Honors Dr. Ferdinando Bosi (b. 1967) , University of Rome La Sapienza, Italy, an expert on the crystallography and mineralogy of the tourmaline-supergroup minerals and the spinels.

bosoite.occurrence: Formed under low-temperature conditions during diagenesis of tuffaceous forearc sandstone and mudstone.
bosoite.etymology: For the Boso Peninsula, east of Tokyo across Tokyo Bay.

bostwickite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit, on surfaces of ore and on secondary carbonate minerals.
bostwickite.etymology: For Richard C. Bostwick, collector of Franklin minerals and expert in mineral °uorescence.

botallackite.occurrence: In copper-bearing deposits, in areas with high chlorine concentrations or weathered while exposed to seawater; a reaction product of slag immersed in seawater; a weathering product of sulﬁdes in subsea black smoker deposits.
botallackite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Botallack mine, Cornwall, England.

botryogen.occurrence: A secondary mineral, which may be in great abundance, altered from pyrite, especially in arid climates.
botryogen.etymology: From the Greek for bunch of grapes and to bear, in allusion to the globular forms exhibited by the original material.

bottinoite.occurrence: Adjacent to and incrusting ullmannite in oxidized hydrothermal base-metal deposits.
bottinoite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Bottino mine, Italy.

botuobinskite.occurrence: As inclusions in pyrope from a kimberlite pipe.
assoc_parsed: distribution from the internatsionalnaya kimberlite pipe

bouazzerite.occurrence: A product of the weathering of a hydrothermal As-Co-Ni-Ag-Au vein.
assoc_parsed: a blue-green copper arsenate related to geminite
bouazzerite.etymology: For the Bou Azzer mine and the similarly named district, Morocco.

boulangerite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins formed at low to medium temperatures.
boulangerite.etymology: Honors Charles Louis Boulanger (1810–1849), French mining engineer, who called attention to the species.

bournonite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins formed at medium temperatures.
bournonite.etymology: In honor of Jacques Louis de Bournon (1751–1825), French crystallographer and mineralogist.

bouskaite.occurrence: Secondary, post-mining mineral from a mine dump formed from weathered primary jordisite and pyrite.
bouskaite.etymology: Honors Czech mineralogist and geochemist Professor Dr. Vladimír Bouška (1933-2000), Charles University, Prague, author of more than 630 papers on mineralogy (ore minerals, metamict minerals, recently formed minerals, organic minerals), gemology, geochemistry (especially of coal), and natural glasses (tektites).

boussingaultite.occurrence: A rare sublimate formed under fumarolic conditions.
boussingaultite.etymology: Honoring Professor Jean-Baptiste Joseph Dieudonn´ e Boussingault (1802–1887), French chemist, Lyon University, Lyon, France.

bowieite.occurrence: In platinum alloy nuggets recovered from dredging operations (Salmon River, Alaska, USA); in platinum-bearing ultramaﬁc rocks intruded into a granite gneiss-“hornblende” gneiss complex (Gaositai, China).
bowieite.etymology: To honor the Scottish scientist, Dr. Stanley Hay Umphray Bowie (1917– ), of the Institute of Geological Sciences, London, England.

bowlesite.occurrence: Probably by low-T exsolution of Pt-Sn phases from high-T sulfides crystallized from a sulfide melt in a layered, mafic-ultramafic intrusion.
bowlesite.etymology: Honors Dr. John Frederick William Bowles (b. 1941), Manchester University, United Kingdom, for contributions to ore mineralogy and mineral deposits in mafic-ultramafic rocks.

boyleite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of sphalerite in a hydrothermal Pb–Zn vein (Kropbach quarry, Germany).
boyleite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Robert William Boyle (1920– ), Canadian geochemist, Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa, Canada.

braccoite.occurrence: In mineralized quartz veins cutting quartzite.
braccoite.etymology: Honors Dr. Roberto Bracco (b. 1959), a systematic mineral collector and author with a special interest in manganese minerals.

bracewellite.occurrence: In ﬁne-grained intergrowth with other chromium oxide-hydroxide minerals.
bracewellite.etymology: For Smith Bracewell, formerly Director, British Guyana Geological Survey, who ﬁrst noted the occurrence.

brackebuschite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal Pb–Zn deposits.
brackebuschite.etymology: Honoring Ludwig Brackebusch (1849–1906), Professor of Mineralogy, University of C´ ordoba, C´ ordoba, Argentina.

bradaczekite.etymology: Honors crystallographer Hans Bradaczek (b. 1940), Free University of Berlin, Germany.

bradleyite.occurrence: A rare mineral in oil shale in the Green River formation.
bradleyite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Wilmot Hyde Bradley (1899-1979), geologist, U.S. Geological Survey, who studied the Green River formation.

braggite.occurrence: In layered maﬁc intrusives, formed at high magmatic temperatures.
braggite.etymology: To honor Sir William Henry Bragg (1862–1942) and Professor William Lawrence Bragg (1890–1971), Cambridge University, Cambridge, England, pioneers in the X-ray investigation of crystals, as this was the ﬁrst new mineral to be discovered by X-ray methods alone.

braithwaiteite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the weathering zone of a hydrothermal enargite deposit.
braithwaiteite.etymology: Honors Richard S.W. Braithwaite (b. 1930), chemist and mineralogist at the University of Manchester, England, for his contributions to the chemistry of secondary Cu-Pb minerals.

braitschite-ce.occurrence: In anhydrite at the contact with sylvite in a thick sequence of marine evaporites, at a depth of about 1 km.
braitschite-ce.etymology: Honors Dr. Otto Braitsch (1921-1966), University of Freiburg, Freiburg, Germany, for his contributions to evaporate mineralogy and geochemistry. A suffix indicates the dominant REE.

brandholzite.occurrence: From oxidized portions of hydrothermal gold-antimony-quartz veins.
brandholzite.etymology: For the occurrence in Germany in the Brandholz-Goldkronach mining district.

brandtite.occurrence: In metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (Harstigen mine and L˚ angban, Sweden); in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Sterling Hill, New Jersey, USA).
brandtite.etymology: To honor George Brandt (1694–1768), Swedish chemist.

brannerite.occurrence: A primary mineral in granite pegmatite and in granitic gneiss; in silicified pebble conglomerates; in hydrothermal quartz and calcite veins; detrital in placers.
brannerite.etymology: To honor Dr. John Casper Branner (1850-1922), American geologist, formerly Professor of Geology and President of Stanford University, Palo Alto, California, USA.

brannockite.occurrence: In the late hydrothermal portions of a Li-Sn-rich pegmatite, in vugs and on °at fracture surfaces.
brannockite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Kent Combs Brannock (1923{1973), Kingsport, Tennessee, USA, chemist and mineral collector.

brassite.occurrence: A rare reaction product of arsenic-rich solutions with Ca–Mg carbonates.
brassite.etymology: Honoring R` ejane Brasse, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound.

brattforsite.occurrence: Probably replaced a Mn-rich precursor mineral in mineralized skarn due to alteration by a late- or post-metamorphic, As and Cl-bearing fluid.
brattforsite.etymology: For the mine that produced the studied material.

braunite.occurrence: Formed by metamorphism of manganese silicates and oxides; also a product of weathering.
braunite.etymology: To honor Kammerrath [Advisor of the Chambers] Braun of Gotha, Germany.

brazilianite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral in phosphate-rich zones of granite pegmatites; also in metamorphosed sedimentary deposits.
brazilianite.etymology: For Brazil, the country in which it was ﬁrst found.

bredigite.occurrence: In contact metamorphosed limestones and dolostones intruded by diabase (Scawt Hill, Ireland) or syenite monzonite (Marble Canyon, Texas, USA).
bredigite.etymology: For Max Albrecht Bredig (1902{ ), physical chemist, who studied the polymorphism of Ca2SiO4:

breithauptite.occurrence: In hydrothermal calcite veins associated with Co–Ni–Ag ores.
breithauptite.etymology: To honor Saxon mineralogist Johann Friedrich August Breithaupt (1791–1873).

brendelite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral found on the dumps of a Bi–Co–Ni–Ag deposit.
brendelite.etymology: In honor of Christian Friedrich Brendel (1776–1861), expert in mining equipment, Neust¨ adtel-Schneeberg, Germany.

brenkite.occurrence: In voids and ﬁssures in a porphryritic selbergite [formerly nosean-phonolite].
brenkite.etymology: For Brenk, near the locality in Germany.

brewsterite.occurrence: Hydrothermally deposited in druses lining cavities in basalts and schists; more rarely in ore deposits.
brewsterite.etymology: Honoring Sir David Brewster (1781{1868), Scottish mineralogist.

brewsterite-ba.occurrence: Hydrothermally deposited in druses lining cavities in basalts and schists; more rarely in ore deposits.
brewsterite-ba.etymology: Honoring Sir David Brewster (1781{1868), Scottish mineralogist.

brewsterite-sr.occurrence: Hydrothermally deposited in druses lining cavities in basalts and schists; more rarely in ore deposits.
brewsterite-sr.etymology: Honoring Sir David Brewster (1781{1868), Scottish mineralogist.

breyite.occurrence: The second most abundant mineral inclusion after ferropericlase in diamonds of superdeep origin; only found in super-deep diamonds. Breyite is presumed to be a strong indicator of lower mantle (>670 km depth) or at least lower transition zone (>520 km depth) origin of both the host diamond and the inclusion suite.
breyite.etymology: Previously known as CaSiO3-walstromite. Honors the German mineralogist, petrologist, and geochemist Gerhard P. Brey (b. 1947), Professor of Mineralogy, Institute of Geosciences, Goethe University Frankfurt, Germany (1994- 2014). Brey was a pioneer in experimental petrology at highpressures and developed a comprehensive set of thermobarometers for lherzolites and related rocks.

brezinaite.occurrence: In the metal matrix and contiguous to silicate inclusions (Tucson iron meteorite).
brezinaite.etymology: In honor of Aristides Brezina (1848–1909), past Director of the Mineralogy-Petrology Section of the Natural History Museum, Vienna, Austria.

brianite.occurrence: A very rare component in phosphate nodules in an iron meteorite.
brianite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Brian Harold Mason (1917– ), U.S. National Museum, Washington, D.C., USA, for his contributions to the study of meteorites.

brianroulstonite.occurrence: Very rare in residues from halite–sylvite evaporites.
brianroulstonite.etymology: Honors Brian V. Roulston (1948– ), geologist and specialist in evaporite deposits.

brianyoungite.occurrence: A rare secondary post-mine mineral in limestone-hosted oxidized Pb–Zn ores (Brownley Hill mine, England).
brianyoungite.etymology: Honors Brian Young (1947– ), ﬁeld geologist and mineralogist of the British Geological Survey, who provided the ﬁrst specimens.

briartite.occurrence: As rare inclusions in other Ge–Ga-bearing sulﬁdes.
briartite.etymology: For Gaston Briart, geologist who studied the Kipushi deposit.

bridgesite-ce.occurrence: Secondary, the product of water percolating through sulfide-bearing orebodies and dripping onto waste limestone in a humid mine environment.
assoc_parsed: undifferentiated iron oxyhydroxides. distribution from the tynebottom mine
bridgesite-ce.etymology: Honors Trevor Bridges (1935-2015), chemist, amateur geologist, mineral collector, mountaineer, munroist, founding member of the Russell Society’s northern branch in 1984, and author of many papers on mineralogy and geochemistry in the British Isles. The suffix identifies the dominant rare earth element.

bridgmanite.occurrence: The dominant mineral of the silicate lower mantle of the Earth. As an impact-induced shock-metamorphic phase enclosed in (Mg,Fe)SiO3 glass in meteorites.
assoc_parsed: clinopyroxene with dominant diopside and jadeite components
bridgmanite.etymology: Honors Percy W. Bridgman (1882-1961), 1946 Nobel laureate in Physics for his contributions to high-pressure mineralogy and research in general. Previously MgSiO3-perovskite.

brindleyite.occurrence: As coatings on limestone and as veinlets cutting kaolinitic clays at the base of a bauxite deposit developed on karst; also a signi¯cant component of weathered ultrama¯c rock (Megara, Greece).
brindleyite.etymology: To honor Dr. George William Brindley (1905{1983), Professor of Mineral Science, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, USA.

britholite-ce.occurrence: In nepheline syenites, pegmatites, and contact deposits related to them.
britholite-ce.etymology: From the Greek for weight, in allusion to its density, and its content of cerium.

britholite-y.etymology: For its chemical relation to britholite-(Ce) and dominant yttrium in its composition.

britvinite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Sergey Nikolaevich Britvin (b. 1965).

brizziite.occurrence: A weathering product of stibnite in an antimony deposit in highly siliciﬁed limestone.
brizziite.etymology: Honors Dr. Giancarlo Brizzi (1936–1992), mineral collector who discovered the ﬁrst specimens.

brochantite.occurrence: Common in the oxidized zone of copper deposits, yet rarely an ore; formed under low acidity, principally in arid regions.
brochantite.etymology: Honors Professor Andr´ e Jean Fran¸ cois Marie Brochant de Villiers (1772–1840), French geologist and mineralogist, School of Mines, Paris, France.

brockite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in granite and granite pegmatites.
brockite.etymology: To honor Maurice R. Brock, U.S. Geological Survey, who supplied the ﬁrst specimen.

brodtkorbite.occurrence: Uncommon in telethermal selenium-rich hydrothermal polymetallic deposits, in calcite veins in amphibolites, formed below 112 °C.
brodtkorbite.etymology: To honor Dr. Milka Kronegold de Brodtkorb (1932– ), Professor at the Universities of Buenos Aires and La Plata, Argentina, for her contributions to mineralogy and economic geology.

bromargyrite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidation zones of silver deposits, notably in arid regions.
bromargyrite.etymology: For BROMine and the Greek for silver, argyros, in its composition.

bromellite.occurrence: In hydrothermal calcite veins and veinlets in hematite skarn and skarnized limestones (L ˚ angban, Sweden); in vugs in natrolite, hydrothermally altered from nepheline, in syenite pegmatite (Langesundsfjord, Norway).
bromellite.etymology: For Magnus von Bromell (1679–1731), Swedish physician and mineralogist.

brontesite.etymology: For Brontes, one of the Cyclopes and a son of Uranus, helpers of the Greek god of fire whose workshops were alleged to be located at Vulcano.

brookite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in alpine veins in gneiss and schist; in contact metamorphic zones and hydrothermal veinlets; a common detrital mineral.
brookite.etymology: For Henry James Brooke (1771–1857), English crystallographer and mineralogist.

browneite.occurrence: In an enstatite-rich achondrite meteorite, postdates the impact melting and subsequent crystallization of an enstatite-rich rock.
browneite.etymology: Honors Patrick R.L. Browne (b. 1941), Professor at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, for his contributions to low-temperature mineralogy and petrology.

brownleeite.occurrence: Within an interplanetary dust particle, (IDP), that likely originated from a comet; likely formed as high-temperature condensates either in the early Solar System or in the outflow of an evolved star or supernova explosion.
assoc_parsed: glass with embedded metal and sulfide grains
brownleeite.etymology: Honors Donald E. Brownlee (b. 1943), an American astronomer and a founder of the field of cosmic dust research who is the principal investigator of the NASA Stardust Mission that collected dust samples from Comet 81P/Wild-2 and returned them to Earth.

brownmillerite.occurrence: In thermally metamorphosed limestone blocks included in volcanic rocks (near Mayen, Germany); in high-temperature, thermally metamorphosed, impure limestones (Hatrurim Formation, Israel).
brownmillerite.etymology: The artiﬁcial compound was named for Dr. Lorrin Thomas Brownmiller (1902– ), Chief Chemist of the Alpha Portland Cement Company, Easton, Pennsylvania, USA, in 1932, the name then transferred to the naturally-occurring mineral.

brucite.occurrence: A common alteration of periclase in marble; a low-temperature hydrothermal vein mineral in metamorphic limestones and chlorite schists; formed during serpentinization of dunites.
brucite.etymology: For Archibald Bruce (1777–1818), physician and early American mineralogist, Professor at the College of Physicians and Surgeons (later Columbia University), New York, New York, USA, who ﬁrst described the species.

bruggenite.occurrence: In veins with nitratine and impregnating the enclosing decomposing rhyolite tuﬀ in a small basin ﬁlled with nitrate caliche.
bruggenite.etymology: To honor Professor Juan Br¨ uggen (1887–1953), University of Chile, who wrote the ﬁrst textbook on the geology of Chile.

brugnatellite.occurrence: A hydrothermal alteration product in serpentinite, lining cracks with other magnesium-rich species.
brugnatellite.etymology: For Luigi Vincenzo Brugnatelli (1859–1928), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy.

brumadoite.occurrence: A late fracture-filling mineral in coarse-grained magnesite.
brumadoite.etymology: For Brumado, Bahia, Brazil, near the first described locality.

brunogeierite.occurrence: In the lower oxidation zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit, at a depth of 930 meters (Tsumeb, Namibia).
brunogeierite.etymology: For Dr. Bruno H. Geier (1902–1987), formerly Chief Mineralogist, Tsumeb Corporation, Tsumeb, Namibia.

brushite.occurrence: One of the most common cave minerals, in guano deposits, and in phosphorites, formed at low pH by reaction of phosphate-rich solutions with calcite and clay.
brushite.etymology: To honor Professor George Jarvis Brush (1831–1912), American mineralogist, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, USA.

bubnovaite.occurrence: As sublimate incrustations and/or products of reaction between rock and volcanic gas on the surface of basalt scoria in an active fumarole.
bubnovaite.etymology: Honors Russian scientist, Professor Rimma Sergeevna Bubnova (b. 1951), Institute of Silicate Chemistry, Russian Academy of Sciences, St-Petersburg State University, Russia, for her contributions to the crystal chemistry of vanadates, silicates, borates, borosilicates and other inorganic oxysalts.

buchwaldite.occurrence: As inclusions in troilite nodules in an iron meteorite.
buchwaldite.etymology: To honor Dr. Vagn Fabius Buchwald (1929– ), Technical University of Denmark, Lyngby, Denmark, for his contributions to the study of iron meteorites.

buckhornite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Buckhorn mine, Colorado, USA.

buddingtonite.occurrence: A low-temperature hydrothermal replacement of plagioclase in andesite altered by ammonia-bearing hot springs (Sulfur Bank mine, California, USA); in metasomatized rhyolitic ash-°ow tu®s (Cedar Mountains, Nevada, USA); in the sedimentary Phosphoria Formation (Idaho, Wyoming, and Montana, USA).
buddingtonite.etymology: To honor Emeritus Professor Arthur Francis Buddington (1890{1980), American geologist, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA.

buergerite.occurrence: Of probable pneumatolytic origin, in cavities in a rhyolite.
buergerite.etymology: To honor Professor Martin Julian Buerger (1903{1986), eminent crystallographer, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

bukovite.occurrence: In selenium-bearing veins of hydrothermal origin.
bukovite.etymology: For its occurrence at Bukov, Czech Republic.

bukovskyite.occurrence: A post-mining surﬁcial weathering product of Fe–As sulﬁdes.
bukovskyite.etymology: To honor Anton´ ın Bukovsk´ y (1865–1950), Professor at the secondary school of Kutn´ a Hora, Czech Republic, who ﬁrst analyzed the mineral.

bulachite.occurrence: Initially found on two museum specimens collected on mine dumps.
bulachite.etymology: For the occurrence at Neubulach, Germany.

bulgakite.occurrence: In fenitized amphibole-quartz-feldspar rock from a complex alkaline massif.
bulgakite.etymology: Honors Lev Vasil’evich Bulgak (b. 1938), Russian mineralogist, gemologist, translator of geological literature, and discoverer of several new minerals who worked from 1975 to 2003 at the A.E. Fersman Mineralogical Museum, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia.

bultfonteinite.occurrence: In a large \horse" of diabase and shale fragments in a kimberlite pipe (Bultfontein mine, Kimberley, South Africa); in a contact zone in thermally metamorphosed limestone (Crestmore, California, USA).
bultfonteinite.etymology: For the Bultfontein mine, Kimberley, South Africa, where it was ¯rst discovered.

bunnoite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting metamorphosed iron- and manganese-rich marine sediments.
bunnoite.etymology: Honors the Japanese mineralogist Michiaki Bunno (b. 1942), retired chief curator for the Geological Museum of the Geological Survey of Japan, for his contributions to the museum and to the discovery of a number of new minerals.

bunsenite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal Ni–U vein (Johanngeorgenstadt, Germany); in a small tabular nickel deposit at the contact between quartzite and serpentinized ultramaﬁcs; it apparently formed at ∼730 ◦C and < 2 kbar during thermal metamorphism, possibly of a nickel-rich meteorite (Bon Accord, South Africa).
bunsenite.etymology: For Professor Robert William Eberhard Bunsen (1811–1899), German chemist of the University of Heidelberg, Heidelberg, Germany, who had observed artiﬁcial NiO.

burangaite.occurrence: In corroded aggregates of other phosphates in a zoned granite pegmatite (Buranga pegmatite, Rwanda).
burangaite.etymology: For the initial occurrence in the Buranga pegmatite, Rwanda.

burbankite.occurrence: Typically an abundant accessory mineral in carbonatites; in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex; may be authigenic.
burbankite.etymology: Honors Wilbur Sweet Burbank (1898–1975), geologist of the U.S. Geological Survey.

burckhardtite.occurrence: In a breccia, loosely cemented by dickite, in very thin disseminations on quartz fragments.
burckhardtite.etymology: To honor Mexican geologist Carlos Burckhardt (1869{1935).

burgessite.occurrence: A secondary mineral along fractures in the weathering zone of a polymetallic sulfarsenate deposit.
burgessite.etymology: For David Burgess (b. 1951), of Newington, Connecticut, USA, who brought the sample to the authors’ attention.

burkeite.occurrence: An uncommon product of evaporation in dry lakes, but typical of eﬄorescences on saline soils.
burkeite.etymology: Honors William Edmund Burke (1880–1966), chemical engineer, who ﬁrst prepared the synthetic compound.

burnsite.occurrence: A very rare fumarolic sublimate, formed at an estimated 450 ◦C–500 ◦C.
burnsite.etymology: Honors Professor Peter Carman Burns (1966– ), Canadian mineralogist and structural crystallographer, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, Indiana, USA, for his contributions to structural mineralogy.

burovaite-ca.occurrence: In cavities in microcline in the hydrothermal zone of aegirine-microcline pegmatite.
burovaite-ca.etymology: honors chemist Tat’yana Alexandrovna Burova (1896-1975) who studied minerals of the Khibiny, Lovozero, and Vishnevye gory plutons, including the labuntsovite group.

burpalite.occurrence: In a fenitized hornfelsic sandstone in the contact zone of an alkalic intrusive.
burpalite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Burpala massif, Russia.

burroite.occurrence: From the oxidation of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a moist environment. The NH4+ presumably from organic matter in this roll-front uranium and vanadium deposit in sandstone.
burroite.etymology: For the type locality, the Burro mine, Colorado, USA.

bursaite.occurrence: In a contact metamorphic scheelite deposit (Uluda˘ g, Turkey); in sulﬁde veinlets around a greisen Sn–W deposit in granite (Shumilovsk deposit, Russia); in a volcanogenic massive sulﬁde deposit (Cofer deposit, Virginia, USA).
bursaite.etymology: For the locality in Bursa Province, Turkey.

burtite.occurrence: From a garnetite in a tin-bearing skarn, formed under conditions of relatively low temperature and low X CO2.
burtite.etymology: For Dr. Donald McLain Burt (1943– ), Professor of Mineralogy, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, USA, authority on mineral equilibria in skarn and greisen deposits, who had predicted the natural occurrence of the compound.

buryatite.occurrence: From drill core containing frolovite veinlets in kurchatovite-sakhaite ore.

buseckite.occurrence: In an enstatite-rich achondrite meteorite, likely derived from the breakdown of high-temperature pyrrhotite to form troilite and buseckite after the solidification of sulfide-rich liquids produced by impact melting of an enstatite-rich rock.
buseckite.etymology: Honors Peter R. Buseck (b. 1935) for his contributions to mineralogy, meteorite research, and transmission electron microscopy.

bussenite.occurrence: In a sodalite-natrolite-calcite veinlet that cuts urtite in an alkaline massif.
bussenite.etymology: Honors Russian petrologist Irina V. Bussen (b. 1915), specialist in the petrology and mineralogy of the Khibiny-Lovozero alkaline complex.

bussyite-ce.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral associated with a nepheline syenite-hosted pegmatite.
bussyite-ce.etymology: Honors Antoine Alexandre Brutus Bussy (1794-1882), co-discoverer of beryllium.

bussyite-y.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal product in alkaline pegmatite.
bussyite-y.etymology: The Y analog of bussyite-(Ce), which honors the French chemist and pharmacist Antoine Alexandre Brutus Bussy (1794-1882) who prepared magnesium and isolated the element beryllium.

bustamite.occurrence: In manganese ores formed by metamorphism of manganese-bearing sediments with attendant metasomatism; typically associated with skarns.
bustamite.etymology: In honor of General Anastasio Bustamente (1780{1853), of Mexico.

butianite.occurrence: Very late-stage, vapor-deposited, alteration product in veins and as mono-mineralic crack-filling material in igneous diopside in the Type B1 Ca-Al-rich inclusion (CAI) ACM-2 from the Allende CV3 carbonaceous chondrite.
butianite.etymology: After the Chinese words “Bu Tian,” meaning patching the sky, in allusion to this secondary mineral filling cracks in a primitive refractory inclusion in the early solar system.

butlerite.occurrence: Rarely formed from the oxidation of pyritic ore; may be formed under fumarolic conditions from mine ﬁres.
butlerite.etymology: Honors Professor Gurdon Montague Butler (1881–1961), American mining geologist, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA.

butschliite.occurrence: Formed in fused wood-ash clinkers in partly burned trees.
butschliite.etymology: To honor Johann Adam Otto B¨ utschli (1848–1920), Professor of Zoology at the University of Heidelberg, Heidelberg, Germany, who studied double salts of potassium and calcium.

buttgenbachite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral found in the oxidized portions of copper deposits; the nitrate may be of biological origin.
buttgenbachite.etymology: Honors Professor Henri Jean Fran¸ cois Buttgenbach (1874–1964), Belgian mineralogist, University of Li` ege, Li` ege, Belgium, who long studied Congo minerals.

byelorussite-ce.occurrence: In a salband of a quartz vein in lower Proterozoic metasomatized granosyenites.
byelorussite-ce.etymology: For the occurrence in Belarus (formerly Byelorussia, USSR), and the cerium content.

bykovaite.occurrence: In the core of a zoned pegmatite in poikilitic nepheline-sodalite syenite of the central part of an alkaline igneous complex.
bykovaite.etymology: Honors analytical chemist Alexandra Vasilyevna Bykova (1917-2001), who first discovered that bornemanite could be transformed to a synthetic form of bykovaite upon treatment with water.

byrudite.occurrence: A primary magmatic phase in emerald-bearing, syenitic pegmatite.
byrudite.etymology: For the locality where the first specimens were collected, Byrud farm, Norway.

bystrite.occurrence: As metasomatic lenses in dolomitic marble.
bystrite.etymology: Presumably for the occurrence in the Malaya Bystraya deposit, Russia .

bystromite.occurrence: In quartz veins in an oxidized antimony deposit.
bystromite.etymology: For Dr. Anders Bystr¨ om (1916–1956), Swedish crystal chemist, who made a structural analysis of the synthetic compound.

bytownite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral typical of ma¯c intrusive igneous rocks, as gabbros and anorthosites; as phenocrysts in basalts; rare in metamorphic rocks.
bytownite.etymology: For the \type" locality, in Ottawa (formerly Bytown), Ontario, Canada.

byzantievite.occurrence: In a glacial moraine boulder of coarse-grained alkaline igneous rock.
byzantievite.etymology: Named for the Byzantine Empire, in allusion to the complexity, effectiveness and beauty this mineral’s atomic structure shares with this empire that existed for nearly 12 centuries.

cabalzarite.occurrence: Formed by hydrothermal remobilization of arsenic during retrograde metamorphism, under lowest to sub-greenschist facies conditions, of syn-sedimentary exhalative Mn deposits embedded in radiolarites.
cabalzarite.etymology: Honors Walter Cabalzar (b. 1919) an amateur Swiss collector, who participated in the description of two new minerals from Falotta (grischunite and geigerite).

cabriite.occurrence: In massive mooihoekite ore, also in galena–chalcopyrite veins.
cabriite.etymology: For Dr. Louis J. Cabri (1934- ), Canadian mineralogist at the Canadian Centre for Mineral and Energy Technology, Ottawa, Canada, describer of a number of platinum group minerals.

cabvinite.occurrence: From low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of Mo-Bi mineralization.
cabvinite.etymology: Honors two Italian mineral collectors, Fernando Caboni (b. 1941) and Antonello Vinci (b. 1944), for their contribution to the knowledge of Su Seinargiu mineralogy. Cabvinite is the acronym based on their surnames, CABoni and VINci.

cacoxenite.occurrence: A common accessory mineral in oxidized magnetite and "limonite" iron ores; in Fe,Mn-bearing novaculites; a rare constituent of iron-rich sediments and soils.
cacoxenite.etymology: From the Greek for a bad guest, for the phosphorus content that degrades the quality of iron made from the host ores.

cadmium.occurrence: In the heavy, non-magnetic fraction of a mechanical concentrate from a gabbro intrusive (Ust’-Khann’ya intrusive, Russia); a product of post-magmatic activity in mineralized aleurolites, sandstones, dolostones, and mudstones (Verkhoyan’ya, Russia).
cadmium.etymology: From the Greek for calamine, as the element occurs in slags resulting from smelting smithsonite (formerly calamine) ore.

cadmoindite.occurrence: As the bottom layer in fumarolic sublimate crusts.
cadmoindite.etymology: As the cadmium analogue of indite.

cadmoselite.occurrence: In sedimentary strata, under reducing secondary conditions of medium to high alkalinity (Ust’Uyuk deposit, Russia).
cadmoselite.etymology: For the presence of cadmium and selenium.

cadwaladerite.occurrence: In a sulfate deposit, embedded in halite.
cadwaladerite.etymology: For Charles Meigs Biddle Cadwalader, formerly President of the Academy of Natural Sciences, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA.

caesiumpharmacosiderite.occurrence: Secondary in the oxidation zone of an ore deposit.
caesiumpharmacosiderite.etymology: Identifies a cesium-dominant member of the pharmacosiderite group.

cafarsite.occurrence: On cleft faces in orthogneiss (Cherbadung, Switzerland).
cafarsite.etymology: For elements in the composition, CAlcium, iron (Ferrum), and ARSenic.

cafetite.occurrence: A late mineral in miarolitic cavities in pegmatites cutting a pyroxenite massif.
cafetite.etymology: For CAlcium, iron (FErrum), and TITanium in the composition.

cahnite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in pegmatites cutting a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA); with zeolites in leucitic lava (Capo di Bove, Italy).
cahnite.etymology: To honor Lazard Cahn (1865–1940), mineral collector and dealer, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA, who ﬁrst noted the species.

cairncrossite.occurrence: Formed by metasomatic alteration of a carbonate-rich manganese deposit.
cairncrossite.etymology: Honors Bruce Cairncross, Professor and Head of the Department of Geology, University of Johannesburg, South Africa for his contributions to the mineralogy of the southern African region, particularly the Kalahari Manganese Field.

calamaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the weathering zone of a pyrite deposit. The result of the oxidation of pyrite under the extremely arid conditions of the Atacama Desert.
calamaite.etymology: For Calama commune and Calama city, the capital of El Loa province, where the first specimens were collected.

calaverite.occurrence: Typically in veins in low-temperature hydrothermal deposits, but also in mediumand high-temperature deposits.
calaverite.etymology: For its occurrence in Calaveras Co., California, USA.

calciborite.occurrence: From drillcore into a contact metasomatized limestone near a quartz diorite intrusion associated with a copper deposit in skarn.
calciborite.etymology: For the essential chemical components, CALCIum and BORon.

calcinaksite.occurrence: The product of contact metamorphism (metasomatism) of a xenolith of a calcic carbonate rock hosted in alkaline basalt.

calcioancylite-ce.occurrence: A rare mineral, found in late-stage miaroles in granite (Baveno, Italy); in Alpine-cleft type ﬁssures (Cornog, Pennsylvania, USA; Polar Ural Mountains, Russia); in alkaline igneous rocks (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada; Il ´ ımaussaq intrusion, Greenland; Kola Peninsula, Russia); and in leucite-bearing lamproite dikes (Baﬃn Island, Canada).
calcioancylite-ce.etymology: For its calcium content and from the Greek for curved in allusion to the typical rounded and distorted crystal habit; and for the dominant rare earth element, cerium.

calcioandyrobertsite.occurrence: On a single specimen from a weathered polymetallic mineral deposit.
calcioandyrobertsite.etymology: The prefix, calcio, designates the calcium analog of andyrobertsite.

calcioaravaipaite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of an epithermal Cu–Pb–Ag deposit.
calcioaravaipaite.etymology: For its CALCIum content and relation to aravaipaite.

calcioburbankite.occurrence: A rare late stage mineral associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire).

calciocatapleiite.occurrence: In cavities between crystals of microcline, in syenite pegmatites of a differentiated alkalic massif.
calciocatapleiite.etymology: For its calcium content and close relation to catapleiite. The change from the original name conforms to International Mineralogical Association guidelines.

calciocopiapite.occurrence: In the oxidized weathering zone of a magnetite–pyrite deposit.
calciocopiapite.etymology: As the calcium member of the copiapite group.

calciodelrioite.occurrence: A secondary mineral as crystalline crusts on fracture surfaces in the oxidized portions of corvusite- and montroseite-impregnated sandstone.
calciodelrioite.etymology: As the calcium (Ca) analog of delrioite.

calcioferrite.occurrence: As nodules in a bed of Tertiary clay (The Battenberg, Germany); in phosphatic clay (Moculta quarry, Australia).
calcioferrite.etymology: For CALCIum and iron, FERRum, in the composition.

calciohilairite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in a peralkalic alaskitic border granite of a batholith (Liberty Bell Mountain, Washington, USA); in miarolitic cavities in a nepheline syenite sill (near Saint-Amable, Canada).
calciohilairite.etymology: For the calcium content and relation to hilairite.

calciojohillerite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
calciojohillerite.etymology: The prefix, calcio, identifies the calcium analogue of johillerite.

calciolangbeinite.occurrence: In sublimate crusts around a volcanic fumarole on an active scoria cone.
assoc_parsed: as- and znbearing orthoclase in solid solution with filatovite
calciolangbeinite.etymology: As the Ca-dominant analog of langbeinite.

calciomurmanite.occurrence: Formed by late-stage, low-temperature hydrothermal alteration (hydration and natural cation exchange) of a high-temperature, anhydrous phosphate-bearing titanosilicate, most likely lomonosovite and/or betalomonosovite, in peralkaline (hyperagpaitic) rocks.
calciomurmanite.etymology: As an analogue of murmanite with essential calcium and sodium.

calciopetersite.occurrence: A secondary mineral derived by weathering chalcopyrite and other copper sulfides.
calciopetersite.etymology: For its composition (Ca > Y) and relationship to petersite-(Y).

calciosamarskite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in RE-rich granite pegmatites, common but not abundant.
calciosamarskite.etymology: Honors Colonel Vasilii Evgrafovich von Samarskii-Bykhovets (1803-1870), Chief of Staff of the Russian Corps of Mining Engineers. The prefix, calcio, indicates Ca is dominant in the A-site.

calciotantite.occurrence: In the albite-spodumene zone of granite pegmatites.
calciotantite.etymology: For CALCIum and TANTalum in the composition.

calciouranoite.occurrence: In stringers in felsite, deep in the oxidation zone of a U–Mo deposit, in water-saturated ore-bearing faults.
calciouranoite.etymology: For CALCIum and URANium in the composition.

calcite.occurrence: A major rock-forming mineral; in limestones, marbles, chalks, a common cement in clastic sedimentary rocks, and as gangue in hydrothermal veins; in alkalic to maﬁc igneous rocks; common as speleothems in caves.
calcite.etymology: From the Latin calx, for burnt lime, an allusion to an important commercial use.

calciumcatapleiite.occurrence: In cavities between crystals of microcline, in syenite pegmatites of a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
calciumcatapleiite.etymology: For its calcium content and close relation to catapleiite.

calcjarlite.formula_html: Na2(Ca,   )14(Mg,   )2Al12F64(OH)4
calcjarlite.occurrence: In a ﬂuorite vein in quartz-mica schists.
calcjarlite.etymology: As a CALCium analog of jarlite.

calclacite.occurrence: Forms on calcareous rock and fossil specimens and pottery sherds thorough the action of acetic acid derived from oak storage cabinets.
calclacite.etymology: From the composition, CALcium, chlorine, CL, and ACetate.

calcurmolite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the lower oxidized zone of Mo–U deposits.
calcurmolite.etymology: For the essential chemical components, CALCium, URanium, and MOLybdenum.

calderite.occurrence: In a manganese deposit (Otjosondu, Namibia); in an iron formation (Wabush district, Canada).
calderite.etymology: For James Calder, an early writer on the geology of India; name ¯rst applied to a rock, later transferred to its predominant mineral.

calderonite.occurrence: In the upper oxidation zone of Pb-Zn hydrothermal deposits.
calderonite.etymology: Honors Professor Salvador Calderón, (1852-1911), for his contributions to the mineralogy of Spain.

caledonite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of Pb–Cu deposits.
caledonite.etymology: From the Latin Caledonia, the Roman name for the Highlands of Scotland, the ﬁrst known locality.

calkinsite-ce.occurrence: A weathering product closely associated with burbankite, in calcite veins cutting shonkinite in a composite stock (Big Sandy Creek, Montana, USA).
calkinsite-ce.etymology: Honors Frank Cathcart Calkins (1878–1974), geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey.

callaghanite.occurrence: Disseminated in the contact zone between diorite and serpentinized dolostone.
callaghanite.etymology: Honors Dr. Eugene Callaghan (1904–1990), Director of the New Mexico Bureau of Mines, Socorro, New Mexico, USA, for his work on magnesite deposits.

calomel.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral formed through the alteration of other mercury minerals.
calomel.etymology: Of uncertain origin; possibly from the Greek for beautiful and honey.

calumetite.occurrence: In cavities and fractures in basalt, formed by the action of chlorine-bearing connate waters on copper, cuprite being regarded as an intermediate product in the alteration (Centennial mine, Michigan, USA).
calumetite.etymology: For the town of Calumet, Michigan, USA, near which it was ﬁrst discovered.

calvertite.occurrence: In a highly oxidized, polymetallic, fractured and brecciated dolomite and sandstone pipe.
calvertite.etymology: Honors Lauriston (Larry) Derwent Calvert (1924–1993) of the National Research Council, Ottawa, Canada for his studies of metallic phases and contributions to the Powder Diffraction File (ICDD).

calzirtite.occurrence: A characteristic accessory mineral in alkalic and ultramaﬁc complexes associated with carbonatites; typically found in residual soils and alluvium.
calzirtite.etymology: For CALcium and ZIRconium in its composition.

camanchacaite.etymology: For the ‘camanchaca’, a dense fog that forms along the northern Chilean coast where the Atacama Desert reaches the Pacific Ocean. The moisture particles of the fog are between 1 and 40 μm in diameter - too small to form raindrops.

camaraite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral in the extensively recrystallized contact zone of a fenitized granite.
camaraite.etymology: Honors Fernando Cámara (b. 1967) of Melilla, Spain, in recognition of his contributions to the mineralogy and crystallography of Ti-silicates, amphiboles, and arrojadite-group and cancrinitegroup minerals.

camaronesite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in boulders from a weathered copper sulfide deposit exposed in an arid region.
camaronesite.etymology: For the valley from which the first samples were collected.

camerolaite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of polymetallic mineral deposits.
camerolaite.etymology: Honors Michel Camerola, mineral collector who collected the ﬁrst specimen.

cameronite.occurrence: One of a number of metallic tellurium-bearing minerals in a hydrothermal deposit.
cameronite.etymology: In honor of Professor Eugene Nathan Cameron (1910– ), University of Wisconsin, who ﬁrst recognized the mineral as a new species.

camgasite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a Co–U-rich zone in a polymetallic mineral deposit.
camgasite.etymology: For Ca, calcium, Mg, magnesium, and As, arsenic, in the composition.

caminite.occurrence: Formed by the reaction of sea water with hydrothermal ﬂuids in a midocean ridge submarine chimney vent. Unstable below 130 ◦ C., below which it hydrates and redissolves in sea water.
caminite.etymology: From the Latin caminus, for chimney, as the mineral occurs in undersea black-smoker chimneys.

campigliaite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a metallic sulﬁde skarn deposit.
campigliaite.etymology: For the locality which provided the ﬁrst specimens, Campiglia Marittima, Italy.

campostriniite.occurrence: A sublimate on pyroclastic breccia at a volcanic fumarole.
campostriniite.etymology: Honors Italo Campostrini (b. 1959), a mineralogist active in the study of volcanic sublimates.

canaphite.occurrence: On a museum micromount specimen presumably from a trap-rock quarry (Haledon, New Jersey, USA); in recent lake-bed sediments (La Cruz Lake, Spain).
canaphite.etymology: For CAlcium, sodium, NAtrium, and PHosphate in the composition.

canasite.occurrence: In pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Russia); in charoitic rocks (Murun massif, Russia).
canasite.etymology: For CAlcium, sodium, NAtrium, and SIlicon in the chemical composition.

canavesite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral on tunnel surfaces in an abandoned mine in weathering ludwigite–magnetite skarn.
canavesite.etymology: For the Canavese district, in which the mine that produced the ﬁrst specimens is located.

cancrinite.occurrence: A primary mineral in some alkalic igneous rocks, including pegmatites in nepheline syenites; also as an alteration product of nepheline.
cancrinite.etymology: For Count Egor Frantsevich Kankrin (Georg Cancrin) (1774{1845), German-Russian Minister of Finance of Russia.

cancrisilite.occurrence: In ultra-agpaitic pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
cancrisilite.etymology: For the relatively high ratio of silicon to aluminum, and its relation to cancrinite.

canfieldite.occurrence: In polymetallic veins, formed very late in the paragenetic sequence.
canfieldite.etymology: Honoring Frederick Alexander Canﬁeld (1849–1926), American mining engineer and mineral collector of Dover, New Jersey, USA.

cannizzarite.occurrence: Associated with deep fumarolic activity (Vulcano, Italy); in sulﬁde veinlets in a greisen Sn–W deposit in granite (Shumilovsk deposit, Russia).
cannizzarite.etymology: Honors Stanislao Cannizzaro (1826–1910), celebrated Italian chemist, University of Rome, Italy.

cannonite.occurrence: An alteration product in Cu-Bi-Au-sulfide deposits.
cannonite.etymology: Honors Benjamin Bartlett Cannon, V (b. 1950), amateur mineralogist of Seattle, Washington, USA, who recognized the first specimens.

canosioite.occurrence: From the dumps of a vein-controlled, polymetallic hydrothermal deposit.
canosioite.etymology: For the small municipality of Canosio, of ∼80 inhabitants, near the Valletta mine.

canutite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from the oxidation of native arsenic and other As-bearing primary phases, followed by later alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions.
canutite.etymology: Honors Claudio Canut de Bon Urrutia (b. 1937), Chilean mining engineer and Senior Professor of Geology and Mineralogy, La Serena University, Coquimbo Region, Chile.

caoxite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting metamorphosed Mn–Ba-rich cherts in an obducted ophiolite.
caoxite.etymology: An acronym with two meanings, for the essential chemical components, CAlcium and OXalate, or the Centennial Anniversary Of X-rays, an essential analytical tool in modern mineralogy.

capgaronnite.occurrence: Probably formed from oxidation of Hg–Ag-rich tennantite exposed to seawater (Cap Garonne mine, France).
capgaronnite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Cap Garonne mine, France.

cappelenite-y.occurrence: In a small vein in nepheline syenite pegmatite.
cappelenite-y.etymology: For D. Cappelen of Holden, Norway, a collector who discovered the mineral, and its yttrium content.
