capranicaite.occurrence: A late-stage metasomatic product inside miarolitic cavities in a block of feldspathoidbearing syenite in an ignimbrite unit ejected from a complex volcano.
assoc_parsed: a member of the sodalite-hauyne series
capranicaite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens.

caracolite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of chlorine-rich lead deposits.
caracolite.etymology: For Caracoles, a town near the Beatriz mine, Chile.

carboborite.etymology: For the essential anionic chemical components, CARBOnate and BORate.

carbobystrite.occurrence: From zoned hyperagpaitic pegmatite in an ijolite-urtite body near its contact with apatite-nepheline rocks and apparently crystallized from residual peralkaline pegmatite-forming melt or solution.
carbobystrite.etymology: For the compositional relationship with bystrite {(Na,K)7Ca[Al6Si6O24](S)1.5·H2O} and the essential role of CO3 in the compound. It is a K-deficient, (CO3), and Na analogue of bystrite.

carbocernaite.occurrence: An uncommon accessory mineral in dolomite–calcite carbonatite associated with an alkaline ultramaﬁc massif (Vuoriyarvi massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia); exsolved from calcite and in a carbonatite dike in fenitized melanephelinite (Sarnu-Dandali complex, India).
carbocernaite.etymology: For the essential chemical components, CARBOnate, CERium, and sodium, NAtrium.

carbokentbrooksite.occurrence: In the quartz core of a zoned pegmatite in the Dara-i-Pioz alkaline massif.
carbokentbrooksite.etymology: For the compositional relationship (carbonate) to kentbrooksite.

carbonatecyanotrichite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of copper-bearing deposits.
carbonatecyanotrichite.etymology: As the carbonate-dominant analog of cyanotrichite.

carbonatefluorapatite.occurrence: Typically of secondary origin. An important constituent of fossil bone, teeth, and marine phosphorite deposits. In carbonatites and nepheline syenite pegmatites. In fractures in phosphate-rich nodules.
carbonatefluorapatite.etymology: For a ﬂuorapatite with essential carbonate.

carbonatehydroxylapatite.occurrence: As cement in phosphatic soils and bioclastic limestones. An accessory mineral in carbonatites and alkaline igneous rocks.

cardite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from a sulfide zone with leached sulfide minerals in a weathered Pb-Zn ore deposit.
cardite.etymology: Honors George William Card (1865-1943), petrologist and mineralogist with the Geological Survey of New South Wales and a Curator of the Mining Museum in Sydney (1893-1927).

carducciite.occurrence: In a barite-pyrite-(Pb-Ag-Zn) vein deposit in a metavolcanic-metasedimentary sequence metamorphosed to greenschist facies.
carducciite.etymology: For the town, Valdicastello Carducci, near the mine that produced the first specimens.

caresite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in an alkaline complex.
caresite.etymology: Honors Stephen (b. 1909) and Janet (b. l921) Cares, amateur mineralogists from Sudbury, Massachusetts, USA, co-finders of the mineral, who have contributed significantly to the mineralogy of Mont Saint-Hilaire. Suffixes 2H and 3T denote the hexagonal and trigonal forms, respectively.

carletonite.occurrence: In cores of thermally metamorphosed wall-rock xenoliths of shale and interbedded limestone, now hornfels and siliceous marble, in nepheline syenite in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex.
carletonite.etymology: For Carleton University, Ottawa, Canada, where it was first studied.

carletonmooreite.occurrence: Localized on plessite fields in aubrite metal nodules in a meteorite, probably formed by low-temperature epitaxial growth by solid-state diffusion from kamacite on tetrataenite.
carletonmooreite.etymology: Honors Carleton B. Moore, chemist and geologist, and founding director of the Center for Meteorite Studies, Arizona State University, USA for contributions to cosmochemistry and meteoritics.

carlfrancisite.occurrence: In metamorphosed lenses associated with Cu-Pb-Ag sulfide ores in feldspathic sandstone that have been reworked by late hydrothermal solutions.
carlfrancisite.etymology: Honors Colonel Eckhard D. Stuart (b. 1939) of Madison, Mississippi, USA., a mineral collector who has provided numerous samples for research, including this new species.

carlfriesite.occurrence: In cavities in an oxidized hydrothermal Au–Te deposit in intensely siliciﬁed brecciated rhyolite vitrophyre.
carlfriesite.etymology: Honors Carl Fries, Jr. (1910–1965), U.S. Geological Survey and the Geological Institute of the National University, Mexico City, Mexico, authority on the geology of large areas of Mexico.

carlgieseckeite-nd.occurrence: In small cavities in veins of saccharoidal albite cross-cutting augite syenite.
carlgieseckeite-nd.etymology: Honors Carl Ludwig Giesecke (1761-1833) for pioneering research in the mineralogy of Greenland; the suffix (-Nd) reflects the dominance of Nd over other REE in the composition.

carlhintzeite.occurrence: Formed by hydrothermal alteration of triphyllite in a pegmatite.
carlhintzeite.etymology: For Dr. Carl Hintze (1851-1916), Professor of Mineralogy, Univerity of Breslau, Breslau, Germany, noted for his compilation of the famous Handbuch der Miiierelogie.

carlinite.occurrence: As small grains in brecciated fragments of carbonaceous limestone, a result of epithermal mineralization.
carlinite.etymology: For the Carlin gold deposit, Nevada, USA, in which it was discovered.

carlosbarbosaite.occurrence: A late-stage cavity filling in albite in a complex pegmatite.
carlosbarbosaite.etymology: Honors Carlos do Prado Barbosa (1917-2003), a chemical engineer, who as a dealer in mineral specimens, promoted the discovery and scientific study of rare mineral species.

carlosruizite.occurrence: A rare constituent of nitrate ores.
carlosruizite.etymology: Honors Carlos Ruiz F. (1916– ), ﬁrst Director of the Chilean Geological Survey.

carlosturanite.occurrence: In a network of veins crosscutting a metamorphic antigorite serpentinite, in an ophiolite.
carlosturanite.etymology: For Professor Carlo Sturani (1938{1976), University of Torino, Torino, Italy.

carlsbergite.occurrence: As minute platelets and grain boundary precipitates in kamacite and troilite, and as similar grains ringing daubreelite in iron meteorites.
carlsbergite.etymology: For the Carlsberg Foundation, Copenhagen, Denmark, which supported recovery and cutting of the Agpalilik meteorite.

carlsonite.occurrence: Formed by a natural fire in oil-bearing shale exposed along a cliff.
carlsonite.etymology: Honors Ernest H. Carlson (1933-2010), Professor of Mineralogy, Kent State University, Ohio, USA and author of Ohio Geological Survey Bulletin 69, Minerals of Ohio (1991).

carmeltazite.occurrence: Interstitial to, or included in, skeletal corundum xenocrysts in mafic to ultramafic pyroclastic ejecta in volcanic rocks and associated alluvial placers. The silicate melts parental to this assemblage had previously been progressively desilicated by the exsolution of immiscible Fe-Tioxide melts and Fe-Ti-Zr-silicide melts (found also as inclusions in carmeltazite), and the crystallization of moissanite and khamrabaevite.
carmeltazite.etymology: For the locality, Mt Carmel, where the first specimens were collected and for the dominant metals in the mineral, titanium, aluminum, and zirconium (“taz”).

carmichaelite.occurrence: Thought to form in saline marine deposits by reaction of pre-existing saline minerals with ﬂuids high in potash.
carmichaelite.etymology: For Rudolph von Carnall (1804–1874), Prussian mining engineer.

carminite.occurrence: An uncommon alteration product of arsenopyrite in some oxidized lead-bearing mineral deposits.

carnallite.occurrence: Thought to form in saline marine deposits by reaction of pre-existing saline minerals with fluids high in potash.
carnallite.etymology: For Rudolph von Carnall (1804-1874), Prussian mining engineer.

carnotite.occurrence: An important ore mineral of uranium, typically in paleochannels in sandstone Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits, found near fossil carbonaceous matter, and in calcretes and near playas; an alteration product of uraninite, montroseite, or davidite.
carnotite.etymology: To honor Marie-Adolphe Carnot (1839–1920), French mining engineer and chemist.

carobbiite.occurrence: In stalactites in cavities in lava.
carobbiite.etymology: For Professor Guido Carobbi (1900–1983), Italian geologist, Institute of Mineralogy and Geochemistry, University of Florence, Florence, Italy, who collected the ﬁrst specimens.

carpathite.occurrence: In cavities at the contact of diorite porphyry with argillites (Olenevo, Ukraine); a low-temperature hydrothermal mineral (California, USA).
carpathite.etymology: From the Russian Karpaty, for the place of discovery in the Transcarpathian district, Ukraine.

carpholite.etymology: From the Greek for straw, in allusion to its color.

carraraite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by late-stage hydrothermal alteration of earlier sulﬁdes and sulfosalts.
carraraite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Carrara district, Italy.

carrboydite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of nickel sulﬁde deposits.
carrboydite.etymology: For the Carr Boyd Rocks mine, Australia, the ﬁrst known locality.

carrollite.etymology: For its occurrence in Carroll Co., Maryland, USA. All rights reserved. caryinite.occurrence: In veinlets in skarn in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody.
caryinite.etymology: From the Greek for nut-brown, for its common color.

caryochroite.occurrence: Product of the supergene alteration of an unidentified Fe2+-rich protophase in cavities in the albite zone of a pegmatite.
caryochroite.etymology: From the Greek for “nut” and “color” in allusion to its hazel-brown color.

caryopilite.occurrence: A product of the metamorphism of manganese-bearing minerals.
caryopilite.etymology: From the Greek for walnut and felt, in allusion to its color and habit.

cascandite.etymology: For CAlcium and SCANDium in the composition.

caseyite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by oxidation in a moist, low-temperature, post-mining environment from montroseite-corvusite and/or asphaltum assemblages on sandstone in a Colorado Plateau type, roll-front uranium/vanadium deposit.
caseyite.etymology: Honors the American geochemist William H. Casey (b. 1955), Distinguished Professor in the Departments of Chemistry and Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, USA, for his contributions in aqueous solution chemistry of natural waters, mineral surface chemistry, and reaction kinetics.

casparite-la.occurrence: In veinlets in a layered manganese ore deposit (Ushkatyn-III deposit) or in alpine fissures in a two-mica gneiss (Wanni glacier).
casparite-la.etymology: A suffix designates the dominant lanthanide element, La, and the base name expresses the analogy to gasparite-(Ce). The new mineral is the arsenate-dominant analogy of monazite-(La).

cassagnaite.occurrence: Filling fractures in braunite and quartz layered mineralization developed under prehnite-pumpellyite facies metamorphism.
cassagnaite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens, the Cassagna mine, Italy.

cassedanneite.occurrence: On museum samples from the oxidized zone of gold-bearing quartz veins (Beresovsk, Russia).
cassedanneite.etymology: To honor Prof. Jacques P. Cassedanne (1923– ), mineralogist, Institute of Geoscience, University of Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

cassidyite.occurrence: An alteration product of a highly weathered iron-nickel meteorite, formed by alteration of schreibersite.
cassidyite.etymology: In honor of Dr. William A. Cassidy, who mapped the Wolf Creek, Australia, crater in 1953.

cassiterite.occurrence: In medium- to high-temperature hydrothermal veins and greisen, in granite, granite pegmatite, rhyolite; rarely in contact metamorphic deposits; in large alluvial placers.

castellaroite.occurrence: A secondary mineral precipitated from oxidizing hydrothermal fluids.
castellaroite.etymology: Honors Fabrizio Castellaro (b. 1970), an Italian mineral collector specializing in the minerals of Liguria, who discovered the first specimens.

caswellsilverite.occurrence: As inclusions in enstatite crystals and in the brecciated matrix of a meteorite (Norton County meteorite); between coarse pyroxene grains in chondrules in a meteorite (Qingzhen meteorite).
caswellsilverite.etymology: To honor Dr. Caswell Silver (1916– ), American geologist associated with the University of New Mexico, Institute of Meteoritics, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA.

catamarcaite.occurrence: In an epithermal bornite-rich ore in a copper, silver, and gold deposit.
catamarcaite.etymology: For the Province of Catamarca, where the new mineral species was found.

catapleiite.occurrence: In syenites and nepheline syenites; in pegmatites, typically the result of metasomatic alteration of eudialyte.
catapleiite.etymology: From the Greek kata, for with, and pleios, for many, because it is always accompanied by other rare minerals.

cattierite.etymology: Honors F´ elicien Cattier (1869–1946), former Chairman of Union Mini´ ere du Haut Katanga, Belgium.

cattiite.occurrence: In a dolomite carbonatite vein that cuts forsterite-magnetite ore in a carbonatite massif.
cattiite.etymology: Honors Michele Catti (b. 1945), Professor of Physical Chemistry, University of Milan Bicocca, Milan, Italy, for his contributions to the crystal chemistry of hydrated oxysalts.

cavansite.occurrence: In a brown tu® partly ¯lling a fault ¯ssure (Lake Owyhee State Park, Oregon, USA); in a vesicular basalt and red tu® breccia, as cavity ¯llings and in calcite veinlets (Chapman quarry, Oregon, USA); in pores of altered basalt breccia and tu®aceous andesite (Poona district, India).
cavansite.etymology: For CAlcium, VANadium, and SIlicon in the composition.

cavoite.occurrence: Developed by tectono-metamorphic re-equilibration under prehnite-pumpellyite facies conditions in manganese deposits (braunite-bearing layers within hematite-rich cherts) near the bottom of chert sequences overlaying ophiolites.
cavoite.etymology: Alludes to the essential chemical elements in the composition, CAlcium, Vanadium, Oxygen.

cayalsite-y.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in cavities in yttrian fluorite in granitic NYF-pegmatite .
cayalsite-y.etymology: From the chemical symbols for the essential elements in the mineral (Ca-Y-Al-Si) and a suffex for the dominant rare-earth element.

caysichite-y.occurrence: In perthite surrounding the quartz core of a granite pegmatite, coating fractures and ¯lling cavities in quartz, perthite, or hellandite; apparently of secondary origin.
caysichite-y.etymology: For the chemical composition: Ca, Y, Si, C, H.

cebaite-ce.occurrence: In carbonatite-derived dolomitic marble (Bayan Obo deposit, China); in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia).
cebaite-ce.etymology: For two of the essential elements, CErium and BArium.

cebollite.occurrence: An alteration product of melilite in a carbonatite (Iron Hill, Colorado, USA); along a diabase-chalk contact (Scawt Hill, Ireland); in zeolitized plagioclase-rich gneiss, amphibolite, and basalt xenoliths (Letseng-La-Terai kimberlite, Lesotho); a late-stage primary igneous mineral (Kimberley, South Africa).
cebollite.etymology: For Cebolla Creek, Colorado, in the drainage of which the mineral was ¯rst collected.

cechite.occurrence: On specimens from old mine dumps from a polymetallic ore deposit.
cechite.etymology: To honor Dr. Frantiˇ sekˇCech (1929–1995), Head of the Department of Mineralogy (1976–1990), Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic.

celadonite.occurrence: Replaces primary ferromagnesian silicate minerals in altered intermediate to ma¯c volcanic rocks, developed under low-grade zeolite facies metamorphism; as amygdule ¯llings in basalts or andesites.
celadonite.etymology: From the French celadon, for sea green, its color.

celestine.occurrence: Of primary sedimentary origin, diagenetic, or typically as ﬁssure and cavity ﬁllings (including caves) precipitated by migrating strontium-bearing ground water or basinal brines in carbonate rocks, concretions and nodules; in hydrothermal veins and maﬁc volcanic rocks.
celestine.etymology: From the Latin for celestial, in allusion to the typical bluish color.

celleriite.occurrence: In granitic LCT-type pegmatite. during the latest stage of evolution of pegmatite cavities after an event of a pocket rupture (Elba); in elbaite-subtype granitic pegmatite (Pikárec).
celleriite.etymology: Honors Luigi G. Celleri (1828-1900), from San Piero in Campo, Italy, for contributions to the discovery of pegmatites during the second half of the 19th Century. He also gathered hundreds of magnificent specimens of tourmaline and associated minerals with scientific and collectible interest.

celsian.occurrence: In amphibolite-grade, regional or contact metamorphic, Mn, Ba-rich rocks, some of which probably were submarine exhalatives.
celsian.etymology: To honor the Swedish astronomer and naturalist, Anders Celsius (1701{1744).

centennialite.occurrence: A secondary low-temperature mineral formed by the reaction of acidic water with other copper mineralization and essentially physically indivisible from other copper-containing secondary minerals.
centennialite.etymology: For the Centennial mine, Calumet, Houghton County, Michigan, USA.

cerchiaraite-al.occurrence: Formed on the margins of quartz-sanbornite veins as a result of fluid interactions.
cerchiaraite-al.etymology: For the analog of cerchiaraite with dominant aluminum in the octahedral structural site.

cerchiaraite-fe.occurrence: Developed in small fractures and veinlets within metacherts of an ophiolitic sequence during prehnite-pumpellyite facies metamorphism.
cerchiaraite-fe.etymology: For the analog of cerchiaraite with dominant iron in the octahedral structural site.

cerchiaraite-mn.occurrence: Developed in small fractures and veinlets within metacherts of an ophiolitic sequence during prehnite-pumpellyite facies metamorphism.
cerchiaraite-mn.etymology: For the analog of cerchiaraite with dominant manganese in the octahedral structural site.

cerianite-ce.occurrence: Sparingly, in partially absorbed inclusions of wall-rock in a dikelike zone of carbonate rock cutting nepheline syenite (Sudbury, Canada); a secondary mineral weathered from phonolites and nepheline syenites (Minas Gerais, Brazil); in pegmatite (Kabuland, Norway).
cerianite-ce.etymology: For CERium in its composition, and by analogy to thorianite and uraninite.

cerite-ce.occurrence: In rare-earth-bearing hydrothermal quartz-barite-carbonatite veins in shonkinite (Mountain Pass, California, USA).
cerite-ce.etymology: A suffix, Ce, and base name for the dominant rare earth element, cerium; the element was discovered in this mineral and named for the planetoid Ceres, also then just discovered.

cernyite.occurrence: A rare constituent of complex zoned pegmatites, as a component of a very minor sulﬁde mineral suite.
cernyite.etymology: To honor Dr. Petr ˇCern´ y (1934– ), Czech-Canadian mineralogist specializing in pegmatites, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada.

cerotungstite-ce.etymology: For CERium and TUNGSten in the composition.

cerromojonite.occurrence: In a vein in a shear zone cutting a series of thinly stratified, pyrite-rich black shales, and reddish-gray, hematite-bearing siltstones.
cerromojonite.etymology: For Cerro Mojon, the highest mountain peak near where the first specimens were collected.

ceruleite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of arsenic-rich polymetallic mineral deposits; a post-mine product.
ceruleite.etymology: From cerulean, for the sky-blue color of the mineral.

cerussite.occurrence: Common in the oxidized zone of lead deposits, where it may constitute an important ore.
cerussite.etymology: From the Latin cerussa, for white lead, synthetic lead carbonate.

cervandonite-ce.etymology: After the locality on the border between Italy and Switzerland where the mineral was discovered, Pizzo Cervandone.

cervantite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed from the oxidation of stibnite.
cervantite.etymology: For the supposed original occurrence at Cervantes, Spain, type material from which is not available.

cervelleite.occurrence: In fracture ﬁllings in highly altered and siliciﬁed rhyolite vitrophyre in a hydrothermal Au–Te deposit.
cervelleite.etymology: To honor Dr. Bernard Cervelle (1940– ), French mineralogist, University of Paris, Paris, France, for his work in ore microscopy.

cesanite.occurrence: As vein and cavity ﬁllings in brecciated rock in an active geothermal ﬁeld.
cesanite.etymology: For the locality near Cesano, Italy.

cesarolite.etymology: To honor Giuseppe Raimondo Pio Ces` aro (1849–1939), Professor of Mineralogy and Crystallography at the University of Li` ege, Li` ege, Belgium.

cesbronite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in an oxidized Cu–Te–Pb sulﬁde deposit (Oriental mine, Mexico).
cesbronite.etymology: Honors Dr. Fabian Cesbron (1938– ), French mineralogist with the Bureau de Recherches G´ eologiques et Mini` eres, Orl´ eans, France.

cesiodymite.occurrence: As sublimates on basaltic scoria near a volcanic fumarole (>350-400 °C.).
cesiodymite.etymology: Cesi for the essential cesium content and the Greek δίδυμοζ, which means “a twin brother” in recognition that the mineral is the Cs-K-ordered analogue of cryptochalcite.

cesiokenopyrochlore.occurrence: From a rare-element granitic pegmatite formed by natural cation exchange with a hydrothermal solution at a late stage of pegmatite evolution.
cesiokenopyrochlore.etymology: The first prefix, cesio, indicates the dominant cation at the Y site, the second prefix, keno, indicates the dominant vacancy in the A site of a member of the pyrochlore subgroup.

cesplumtantite.occurrence: In veinlets in a museum specimen from a granite pegmatite.
cesplumtantite.etymology: For CESium, lead (PLUMbum), and TANTalum in the composition.

cetineite.occurrence: From an antimony deposit in highly siliciﬁed evaporites, on ore which has been roasted, then long weathered.

chabazite-ca.occurrence: In volcanic rocks as basalts, andesite; rarer in limestones and schists; hydrothermally deposited in cavities and joints in ore veins. In tuff in lake deposits, altered from volcanic glass.
chabazite-ca.etymology: From the Greek chabazios, an ancient name of a stone. A suffix indicates the most abundant extra-framework cation. Chabazite is the correct name for a member of the chabazite series that is not specifically identified on compositional grounds.

chabazite-k.occurrence: In volcanic rocks as basalts, andesite; rarer in limestones and schists; hydrothermally deposited in cavities and joints in ore veins. In tuff in lake deposits, altered from volcanic glass.
chabazite-k.etymology: From the Greek chabazios, an ancient name of a stone. A suffix indicates the most abundant extra-framework cation. Chabazite without a suffix is the correct name for a member of the chabazite series that is not specifically identified on compositional grounds.

chabazite-mg.occurrence: In cavities in basalt, formed by hydrothermal alteration of feldspar and volcanic glass in a closed system with Mg-rich solutions.
chabazite-mg.etymology: From the Greek chabazios, an ancient name of a stone. A suffix indicates the most abundant extra-framework cation. Chabazite is the correct name for a member of the chabazite series that is not specifically identified on compositional grounds.

chabazite-na.occurrence: In volcanic rocks as basalts, andesite; rarer in limestones and schists; hydrothermally deposited in cavities and joints in ore veins. In tuff in lake deposits, altered from volcanic glass.
chabazite-na.etymology: From the Greek chabazios, an ancient name of a stone. A suffix indicates the most abundant extra-framework cation. Chabazite without a suffix is the correct name for a member of the chabazite series that is not specifically identified on compositional grounds.

chabazite-sr.occurrence: In a K-feldspar and aegirine pegmatite veinlet in an alkaline massif.
chabazite-sr.etymology: From the Greek chabazios, an ancient name of a stone. A suffix indicates the most abundant extra-framework cation. Chabazite without a suffix is the correct name for a member of the chabazite series that is not specifically identified on compositional grounds.

chabourneite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal deposit in dolomitic limestones with other As–Tl minerals (Jas Roux, France).
chabourneite.etymology: For Chabourn´ eou Glacier, near the Jas Roux deposit, France.

chadwickite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a uranium deposit.
chadwickite.etymology: Honors Sir James Chadwick (1891-1974), English Nobel Laureate in physics for his proof of the existence of neutrons.

chaidamuite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of a Pb–Zn–Fe sulﬁde deposit.
chaidamuite.etymology: For the occurrence near Chaidamu, China.

chalcanthite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of copper sulﬁde deposits, commonly of post-mining formation; rarely as a fumarolic deposit.
chalcanthite.etymology: From an older Latin name, chalcanthum, for ﬂowers of copper.

chalcoalumite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of copper deposits.
chalcoalumite.etymology: For essential chemical components, from the Greek chalkos, for copper and Latin alum, for aluminum sulfate.

chalcocite.occurrence: An uncommon primary hydrothermal mineral but important as a secondary mineral. Found in or below the zone of oxidation in hydrothermal veins and in large low-grade porphyry copper orebodies.
assoc_parsed: many other sulﬁdes and their alteration products
chalcocite.etymology: For its composition, from the Greek for chalkos, copper.

chalcocyanite.etymology: From the Greek for copper and azure-blue, in allusion to the composition and color change caused by hydration.

chalcomenite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in oxidized Cu–Se-bearing deposits.
chalcomenite.etymology: From the Greek for copper and moon.

chalconatronite.occurrence: A component of patina on bronze artifacts, apparently characteristic of arid weathering environments (Egypt); an uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of polymetallic deposits.
chalconatronite.etymology: From the Greek chalcos, for copper, and natron, the modern name for naturally occurring sodium carbonate.

chalcophanite.occurrence: A common component of the weathered zones above zinc- and manganese-bearing base- metal deposits.
chalcophanite.etymology: From the Greek for copper and to appear, for the mineral's change in color on ignition.

chalcophyllite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some arsenic-bearing hydrothermal polymetallic deposits.
chalcophyllite.etymology: From the Greek for copper and a leaf, for its prominent micaceous appearance.

chalcopyrite.occurrence: A primary mineral in hydrothermal veins, stockworks, disseminations, and massive replacements; an exsolution product in maﬁc igneous rocks; of sedimentary origin controlled by redox conditions.
chalcopyrite.etymology: From the Greek for brass and pyrite.

chalcosiderite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized zone of some hydrothermal mineral deposits.
chalcosiderite.etymology: From the Greek for copper and iron, for those elements in the mineral’s composition.

chalcostibite.occurrence: Associated with other sulfosalts and sulﬁdes in hydrothermal veins.
chalcostibite.etymology: From the Greek chalkos, copper and stibium, antimony.

chalcothallite.occurrence: In ussingite veins cutting poikilitic sodalite syenite.

challacolloite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral in an epithermal vein-type silver deposit (Chile). Also as a sublimate near volcanic fumaroles (Italy).
challacolloite.etymology: For the Challacollo mine, where the specimens for description of the species were collected .

chambersite.occurrence: In brine residues from extraction wells in salt domes.
chambersite.etymology: For the location of the ﬁrst known occurrence, Chambers Co., Texas, USA.

chameanite.occurrence: As late-stage deposits in veins cutting granite (Cham´ eane mine, France); in a telethermal selenium-rich hydrothermal polymetallic deposit, in calcite veins in amphibolites (Tuminico, Argentina).
chameanite.etymology: For the occurrence at the Cham´ eane mine, France.

chamosite.occurrence: In sedimentary ironstones; authigenically formed under reducing conditions in the presence of decomposed organic material.
chamosite.etymology: For the locality at Chamoson, Switzerland.

chanabayaite.etymology: For the village of Chanabaya near the locality that produced the first specimens.

changbaiite.occurrence: In kaolinite-ﬁlled veins and cavities in a potassic granite.
changbaiite.etymology: For Changbai Mountain, China, on which the mineral occurs.

changchengite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in chromite bodies in dunites and placers derived therefrom.
changchengite.etymology: From the Chinese word for the Great Wall, situated nearby the occurrence.

changoite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized portion of a Cu–Zn sulﬁde deposit.
changoite.etymology: For the Changos, early inhabitants of Chile.

chantalite.occurrence: In rodingite dikes in an ophiolite.
chantalite.etymology: For Chantal Sarp, wife of the mineral's discoverer.

chaoite.occurrence: In shock-metamorphosed graphite gneisses and meteorites.
chaoite.etymology: For Edward Ching-Te Chao (1919– ), Chinese-American petrologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C, USA.

chapmanite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting gneisses containing varying amounts of graphite (Smilkov, Czech Republic).
chapmanite.etymology: To honor Edward John Chapman (1821{1904), Professor of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada.

charleshatchettite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral, probably developed from a niobium-rich precursor on a fracture surface in fine-grained nepheline syenite.
charleshatchettite.etymology: Honors Charles Hatchett (1765-1847), an English chemist who discovered niobium, a dominant element in charleshatchettite.

charlesite.occurrence: Very rare, coating fractures and vugs in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
charlesite.etymology: Honors Dr. Charles Palache (1869–1954), eminent American crystallographer and mineralogist, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

charmarite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a lead-bearing U–V deposit (Mounana mine, Gabon).

charoite.occurrence: In potassic feldspar metasomatites at the contact of nepheline and aegirine syenites with limestones.
charoite.etymology: For the Chara River, Russia, near which the studied material was discovered.

chatkalite.occurrence: As rounded disseminations in tetrahedrite, from a sulﬁde-bearing quartz vein (Kochbulak deposit, Uzbekistan).
chatkalite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Chatkal-Kuramin Mountains, Russia.

chayesite.occurrence: A late-crystallizing mineral, nonuniformly distributed in the groundmass of lamproites.
chayesite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Felix Chayes (1916{1993) of the Geophysical Laboratory, Carnegie Institute, Washington, D.C., USA.

chegemite.occurrence: A product of sanidinite facies metamorphism of calcareous xenoliths in ignimbrite.
chegemite.etymology: For the Chegem River, in the headwater area of which the new mineral was discovered.

chekhovichite.occurrence: A rare oxidation product of earlier tellurium-bearing minerals.
chekhovichite.etymology: Honors Professor Sergei Konstantinovich Chekhovich (1917–1997), mineralogist and geologist, Polytechnical Institute of Alma-Ata, Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan.

chelkarite.occurrence: Very rare, in the insoluble residue of brines from a salt dome.
chelkarite.etymology: For the locality where the ﬁrst samples were collected, the Chelkar salt dome, Kazakhstan.

chenevixite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some hydrothermal polymetallic mineral deposits.
chenevixite.etymology: To honor Richard Chenevix (1774–1830), Irish chemist, who early analyzed a Cornish Cu–Fe arsenate.

chengdeite.occurrence: In chromite ores in ultramaﬁc rocks and in placer concentrates derived therefrom.
chengdeite.etymology: For Chengde Co., China, in which it was found to occur.

chenmingite.occurrence: Formed by solid-state transformation of precursor chromite, near shock-induced melt pockets, under high pressure and high temperature during the Tissint impact event on Mars.
chenmingite.etymology: Honors Ming Chen, a cosmochemist and mineralogist, Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, for his outstanding contributions to research on high-pressure mineralogy of meteorites, shock metamorphism, and terrestrial impact craters.

cheralite.occurrence: Disseminated in a kaolinized pegmatite dike and surrounding kaolinized granite gneiss; alluvial (Kuttankuli, India); in a carbonatite (Mt. Weld, Western Australia).
cheralite.etymology: For Chera (Kerala), an ancient Dravidian kingdom predating Travancore (now Kerala State), India.

cheremnykhite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in the oxidized zone of a tellurium-bearing gold deposit.
cheremnykhite.etymology: To honor I.M. Cheremnykh (1928– ), geologist, a discoverer of the Kuranakh deposit.

cherepanovite.occurrence: In a placer with other platinum group element minerals derived from an ultramaﬁc massif in an ophiolite belt (Northern Pekul’nei River, Russia).
cherepanovite.etymology: In honor of Vladimir Aleksandrovich Cherepanov (1927–1983), Russian geologist and mineralogist, Karpinskii All-Union Research Institute of Geology, St. Petersburg, Russia.

chernikovite.occurrence: In ﬁssures in quartz syenite and around fossil wood (Karakat deposit, Tajikistan); along fractures in tourmaline-bearing granites and granite pegmatites (Perus district, Brazil).
chernikovite.etymology: To honor Dr. Andrei Andreevich Chernikov (1927– ), Institute of Mineralogy and Geochemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia, who ﬁrst described naturally-occurring material.

chernovite-y.occurrence: In piemontite veinlets in liparite porphyry (Nyarta-Syu-Yu River, Russia); in Alpine-type ﬁssures (Binntal, Switzerland).
chernovite-y.etymology: Honoring Professor Aleksandr Aleksandrovich Chernov (1877–1963), Russian geologist, Institute of Geology, Syktyvar, Russia, explorer of the Polar Urals.

chernykhite.occurrence: In small veinlets cutting carbonate rocks interbedded with vanadium-rich lower Paleozoic shales.
chernykhite.etymology: Honoring Viktor Vasil'evich Chernykh (1889{1941), Professor of Mineralogy, the Mining Institute, St. Petersburg, Russia.

chervetite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a vanadium- and lead-bearing uranium deposit (Mounana mine, Gabon).

chesnokovite.occurrence: A late hydrothermal mineral, intergrown with natrophosphate in a ussingite vein in an alkaline igneous complex.
chesnokovite.etymology: Honors mineralogist Boris Valentinovich Chesnokov (1928–2005) of the Ural Department, Russian Academy of Sciences, Miass.

chessexite.etymology: For Professor Ronald Chessex, petrographer, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.

chesterite.occurrence: In black wallrock between chlorite and actinolite zones of a metamorphosed ultrama¯c body.
chesterite.etymology: For the Chester, Vermont, USA, locality.

chestermanite.occurrence: Rare, in veins and disseminated in a brucite marble lens contained in a multiply metamorphosed roof pendant between two plutons in a granodiorite batholith.
chestermanite.etymology: Honors Charles Wesley Chesterman (1913–1991), geologist and mineralogist, California Division of Mines and Geology, San Francisco, USA, who discovered the ﬁrst specimens.

chevkinite-ce.occurrence: As an accessory mineral in some granites, and in pegmatites associated with alkalic granite and syenites; in air-fall ash deposits.
chevkinite-ce.etymology: In honor of General-Major Konstantin Vladimirovich Tschevkin [Chevkin] (1802{1875), Chief of Sta® of the Russian Mining Engineers Corps.

chiappinoite-y.occurrence: In vugs in a block of peralkaline syenitic volcanic ejectum.
chiappinoite-y.etymology: Honors Luigi Chiappino (b. 1950), a distinguished mineral collector of Milan, Italy, who discovered the first specimen.

chiavennite.occurrence: Coating beryl in late-stage pegmatites (Tanno, Italy); in vugs in syenite pegmatites (Norway).
chiavennite.etymology: For the Italian locality at Tanno, Chiavenna.

chibaite.occurrence: As veins cutting tuffaceous sandstone and mudstone in forearc marine sediments deposited near the plate margin of the Paleo-Izu arc and the triple junction of the Pacific, Philippine Sea, and North America plates.
chibaite.etymology: For the Chiba Prefecture in Japan where the first samples were collected.

childrenite.occurrence: In some complex granite pegmatites, typically a low-temperature hydrothermal alteration product of primary phosphate minerals.
childrenite.etymology: In honor of John George Children (1777–1852), English chemist and mineralogist.

chiluite.occurrence: In quartz veins in a molybdenite deposit.
chiluite.etymology: For the occurrence at Chilu, China.

chinchorroite.etymology: For the Chinchorro culture of the inhabitants of the coastal region of northern Chile and southern Peru from 9000 to 3500 years BP that includes the area around Torrecillas. These people suffered extensively from poisoning due to their consumption of water contaminated with arsenic.

chinleite-y.occurrence: A secondary phase formed at ambient temperature by evaporative processes at moderately high relative humidity at the surface of a rock with high relative porosity and in an environment that was relatively oxidizing and generally acidic.
chinleite-y.etymology: For the Chinle Formation of Upper Triassic age and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element, yttrium.

chiolite.etymology: From the Greek for snow and stone, as compared to cryolite, ice-stone.

chirvinskyite.occurrence: In albitized alkaline pegmatites in a foyaite.
chirvinskyite.etymology: Honors Petr Nikolaevich Chirvinsky (1880-1955), Russian geologist and petrographer, head of the Petrography Department, Perm’ State University (1943-1953), for his contributions to mineralogy and petrology, including studies of the Khibiny alkaline massif.

chistyakovaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the weathered zone of a hydrothermal arsenopyrite and ‘pitchblende’ deposit.
chistyakovaite.etymology: Honors N.I. Chistyakova, a senior assistant at the All-Russia Research Institute of Mineral Resources (VIMS), and the dominant rare earth element, Yittrium.

chistyakovaite-y.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the weathered zone of a hydrothermal arsenopyrite and ‘pitchblende’ deposit.
chistyakovaite-y.etymology: Honors N.I. Chistyakova, a senior assistant at the All-Russia Research Institute of Mineral Resources (VIMS), and the dominant rare earth element, Yittrium.

chiyokoite.occurrence: A low-temperature mineral in hydrothermally altered, boron-bearing, low-Fe, calc-silicate skarn.
chiyokoite.etymology: Honors Professor Chiyoko Henmi (1949-2018), Department of Earth Science, Okayama University, Japan, for his contributions to the mineralogy of skarn minerals from the Fuka mine, including the discovery of several new minerals.

chkalovite.occurrence: In veins in pegmatite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia); in sodalite xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
chkalovite.etymology: For Valerii Pavlovich Chkalov (1904{1938), ¯rst to °y nonstop from Moscow to the USA across the North Pole.

chladniite.occurrence: As a single grain in a phosphate-rich inclusion in an iron meteorite (Carleton meteorite); in phosphate-rich portions of an acapulcoite-lodranite meteorite.
chladniite.etymology: Honors Professor Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni (1756–1827), German physicist, University of Riga, Riga, Latvia, who ﬁrst published the hypothesis that meteorites were of extraterrestrial origin.

chloraluminite.occurrence: As crusts around acidic fumaroles (Vesuvius, Italy).
chloraluminite.etymology: For CHLORine and ALUMINum in its composition.

chlorapatite.occurrence: Relatively much rarer than ﬂuorapatite or hydroxylapatite, formed in F-deﬁcient environments. In calcsilicate marble; an accessory mineral in layered maﬁc intrusions; in veins through diabase; replacing triphylite in granite pegmatite. In meteorites.
chlorapatite.etymology: For dominant chlorine and membership in the apatite group; see ﬂuorapatite.

chlorargyrite.occurrence: May be a rich ore in the oxidized zone above silver deposits; commonly preserved in arid climates.
chlorargyrite.etymology: For CHLORine, and the Greek for silver, argyros, in its composition.

chlorartinite.occurrence: In sublimates around a volcanic ﬁssure.
chlorartinite.etymology: For essential chlorine and chemical relation to artinite.

chlorbartonite.occurrence: In an alkaline hydrothermal vein in feldspathic urtite within apatite-nepheline rock.
chlorbartonite.etymology: A prefix, chlor, indicates the chlorine-dominant analog of bartonite.

chlorellestadite.occurrence: The product of pyrometamorphism and metasomatic alteration under sanidinite facies (larnite sub-facies) of a calcium-silicate xenolith in rhyodacite lava.
chlorellestadite.etymology: Signifies the chlorine-end member of the ellestadite group.

chloritoid.occurrence: In regionally metamorphosed pelitic sediments and schists in the biotite, garnet, and lower grade staurolite zones; in quartz-carbonate veins and other hydrothermal environments.
chloritoid.etymology: For its resemblance to members of the chlorite group.

chlorkyuygenite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in Ca-humite zones of calcareous skarn xenoliths in ignimbrite, crystallized initially as chlormayenite and was altered by volcanic gases containing water vapor.
chlorkyuygenite.etymology: Kyuygenite is for the locality, Kyuygen-Kaya Mountain and the prefix indicates the essential chlorine in the species.

chlormagaluminite.occurrence: In iron-ore skarns in an explosion pipe.
chlormagaluminite.etymology: For its principal components, CHLORine, MAGnesium, and ALUMINum.

chlormanganokalite.etymology: For CHLORine, MANGANese, and potassium (KALium), in its composition.

chlorocalcite.occurrence: As a sublimate in volcanic fumaroles (Vesuvius, Italy).
chlorocalcite.etymology: For CHLORine and CALCium in the composition.

chloromenite.etymology: From the Greek for green, in allusion to its color, and for moon, for its selenium content.

chlorophoenicite.occurrence: Along secondary cracks through franklinite ores in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
chlorophoenicite.etymology: From the Greek for green and purple-red, alluding to the mineral’s colors in natural and artiﬁcial light.

chlorothionite.etymology: From the Greek for chlorine and sulfur in the composition.

chloroxiphite.occurrence: A secondary mineral associated with lead- and copper-bearing pods in Mn–Fe deposits developed along ﬁssures in dolomitic conglomerate and limestone.
chloroxiphite.etymology: From the Greek for green and blade or straight sword, for the typical crystal habit.

choloalite.occurrence: With other tellurites and tellurates in the oxidized portions of base and precious metal deposits.
choloalite.etymology: From the Nahua language choloa, for evasive, the mineral having been undetected for many years.

chondrodite.occurrence: In contact metamorphic zones, in limestones and dolostones, associated with felsic to alkalic plutonic rocks, especially with Fe-B-F metasomatism; in a carbonatite.
chondrodite.etymology: From the Greek meaning grain, alluding to its occurrence in isolated grains.

chongite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from the oxidation of native arsenic and other As -bearing primary phases, followed by later alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions.
chongite.etymology: Honors Dr. Guillermo Chong Díaz (b. 1936), a prominent Chilean geologist and academician.

chopinite.occurrence: In a granulite facies paragneiss (East Antarctica). In a transitional acapulcoite meteorite affected by shock metamorphism.
chopinite.etymology: Honors Christian Chopin (b. 1955) of the Ecole Normale Supérieure, Paris, France, for his contributions to the mineralogy of phosphates.

chovanite.occurrence: In hydrothermal vein and stockwork antimony deposits cutting granites, mica schists or silicified mylonitized granitoids. It formed during the third (quartz-ankerite-sphalerite) of 5 stages of hydrothermal mineralization with a moderately high oxygen activity, replacing earlier sulfosalts.
chovanite.etymology: Honors Professor Martin Chovan (b. 1946), Department of Mineralogy and Petrology, Comenius University, Bratislava, Slovakia, for his extensive studies of antimony mineralization in the Western Carpahian region.

chrisstanleyite.occurrence: In gold-bearing calcite veins in limestone (Hope’s Nose, England); in a carbonate matrix (Tilkerode, Germany); in malachite nodules (Copper Hills prospect, Australia). In a telethermal selenide vein deposit (El Chire prospect, Argentina).
chrisstanleyite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Chris J. Stanley (b. 1954), The Natural History Museum, London, England, for his contributions to ore mineralogy.

christelite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of a Cu–Zn sulﬁde deposit.
christelite.etymology: Honors Christel Gebhard-Giesen (1950– ), German mineral collector.

christite.occurrence: In hydrothermal barite veins and in mineralized carbonaceous silty dolostone (Carlin mine, Nevada, USA); in thallium-rich pods in a stratabound mercury deposit (Lanmuchang deposit, China).
christite.etymology: To honor Dr. Charles Louis Christ (1916–1980), American physical chemist, mineralogist, and crystallographer with the U.S. Geological Survey.

chromatite.occurrence: Formed in an arid climate along fractures in limestones and marls by ascending ground water, the chromium derived from underlying bituminous phosphatic marls.

chrombismite.occurrence: A cumulus mineral in ultramaﬁc portions of layered maﬁc igneous rocks; an accessory mineral in alpine-type peridotites; also detrital. Common in all meteorites, except carbonaceous chondrites, and in lunar mare basalts.

chromceladonite.etymology: The prefix, chrom, indicates the chromium analog of celadonite.

chromdravite.etymology: For CHROMium in the composition and similarity to dravite.

chromferide.occurrence: In quartz veins within brecciated amphibolites and schist.
chromferide.etymology: For the chemical composition, CHROMium and FERrum, iron.

chromio-pargasite.occurrence: Along cracks in podiform chromitite deposits scattered in serpentinized dunite associated with rocks of the eclogite metamorphic facies; probably formed during retrograde metamorphism.
chromio-pargasite.etymology: Originally ehimeite for the type locality; subsequently changed to chromio-pargasite to conform to IMA nomenclature for a chromium-dominant analog of pargasite.

chromite.occurrence: A cumulus mineral in ultramafic portions of layered mafic igneous rocks; an accessory mineral in alpine-type peridotites; also detrital. Common in all meteorites, except carbonaceous chondrites, and in lunar mare basalts.

chromium.occurrence: In heavy sands derived from the contact metamorphic zone between a siliceous marble and ultramaﬁc rock (Sichuan Province, China); in a kimberlite pipe (Liaoning Province, China); in podiform chromitites (Luobusha ophiolite, China); in ultramaﬁc dike rocks (Gavasai ore ﬁeld, Russia); in kimberlite (Sakha, Russia); in serpentinite in dunite–peridotite (Far East, Russia).
chromium.etymology: From the Greek chroma, color, as all chromium compounds are colored.

chromium-dravite.occurrence: In heavy sands derived from the contact metamorphic zone between a siliceous marble and ultramaﬁc rock (Sichuan Province, China); in a kimberlite pipe (Liaoning Province, China); in podiform chromitites (Luobusha ophiolite, China); in ultramaﬁc dike rocks (Gavasai ore ﬁeld, Russia); in kimberlite (Sakha, Russia); in serpentinite in dunite–peridotite (Far East, Russia).
chromium-dravite.etymology: From the Greek chroma, color, as all chromium compounds are colored.

chromo-alumino-povondraite.occurrence: A primary mineral in metaquartzite (granulite facies) in marble.
chromo-alumino-povondraite.etymology: For its relation to povondraite with dominant chromium in the Y site and aluminum in the Z site.

chromschieffelinite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a telluride and galena deposit.
chromschieffelinite.etymology: As the chromate analog of schieffelinite.

chrysoberyl.occurrence: Characteristic of some granite pegmatites associated with high-grade mica schists or reaction zones in ultramaﬁc rocks; also detrital in placers.
chrysoberyl.etymology: From the Greek for golden, in allusion to the mineral’s color, and beryl.

chrysocolla.occurrence: In the oxidized portions of many copper deposits.
chrysocolla.etymology: From the Greek for gold and glue, for a substance used in the soldering of gold, including chrysocolla as well as other blue and green minerals.

chrysothallite.occurrence: Formed by the interactions among high-temperature sublimate minerals, fumarolic gas and atmospheric water vapor at temperatures not higher than 150 °C.
chrysothallite.etymology: For its bright golden-yellow color (from the Greek χρυσόϛ for gold) and the presence of thallium as a species-defining constituent.

chubarovite.occurrence: Formed as sublimates on basaltic scoria around active volcanic fumaroles.
chubarovite.etymology: Honors the Russian mineralogist and physicist Valeriy Mikhailovich Chubarov (b. 1948), a specialist in electron microprobe analysis, Institute of Volcanology and Seismology, Far Eastern Branch, Russian Academy of Sciences, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Russia.

chudobaite.occurrence: In a deep oxidation zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
chudobaite.etymology: To honor Dr. Karl Franz Chudoba (1898–1976), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany.

chukanovite.occurrence: In a terrestrially altered meteorite fragment.
chukanovite.etymology: Honors Nikita V. Chukanov (b. 1953), Russian physicist and mineralogist.

chukhrovite-ca.occurrence: From low-temperature hydrothermal crystallization on the surfaces of fractures crosscutting a vein of marcasite and REE-bearing fluorite.
chukhrovite-ca.etymology: For the Ca-dominant species of the chukhrovite mineral group.

chukhrovite-ce.occurrence: In a hydrothermal barite–ﬂuorite vein deposit (Clara mine, Germany); from the oxidized zone of a banded sellaite–tourmaline–ﬂuorite deposit (Yaroslavsk deposit, Russia).
chukhrovite-ce.etymology: For its relation to chukhrovite-(Y) and content of cerium as the dominant rare-earth element.

chukhrovite-y.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a Mo–W deposit.
chukhrovite-y.etymology: Honors Fedor Vasil’evich Chukhrov (1908–1988), Russian mineralogist, Director, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrology, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia, and yttrium, the dominant rare-earth element.

chukochenite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in mineralized skarn at the exocontact of a granite pluton.
assoc_parsed: zinconigerite-2n1s. distribution from the xianghualing tin-polymetallic   deposit
chukochenite.etymology: Honors Chu Kochen (1890-1974), Chinese scientist and educator, the inaugurator of historical climatology, the leader of the “long march of academics,” the founder of the Department of Geosciences at Zhejiang University, and for major contributions to scien ce and education.

chukotkaite.occurrence: From a subvertical, sulfide-sulfosalt-quartz vein to 20 cm thick cutting argillites.
chukotkaite.etymology: For the region of its type locality, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, Russia.

churchite-y.occurrence: Locally abundant; typically derived from meteoric waters, with yttrium weathered or biochemically leached from trace amounts in surrounding rocks or soil, deposited on colloidal Fe–Mn oxides; less commonly a secondary mineral in hydrothermal mineral deposits.
churchite-y.etymology: To honor Arthur Herbert Church (1834–1915), English chemist, who originally analyzed and described the mineral.

chursinite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a Sb–As–Hg deposit.
chursinite.etymology: In honor of the Russian theater and ﬁlm actress Lyudmila Alekseevna Chursina (1941– ).

chvaleticeite.occurrence: Formed in the oxidation zone of a pyrite–manganese silicate deposit (Chvaletice, Czech Republic).
chvaleticeite.etymology: For the locality where the ﬁrst specimens were collected, Chvaletice, Czech Republic.

chvilevaite.etymology: For Tat’yana Nikiforovna Chvileva (1925– ), economic mineralogist, Institute of Mineralogy and Geochemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia.

cianciulliite.occurrence: A very rare mineral on a museum specimen, typical of material from secondary veins in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
cianciulliite.etymology: In honor of John Cianciulli, of Sussex, New Jersey, USA, for his assistance to mineralogists studying Franklin-Sterling Hill minerals.

cinnabar.occurrence: Formed from low-temperature hydrothermal solutions in veins, and in sedimentary, igneous, and metamorphic host rocks.
cinnabar.etymology: From the Medieval Latin cinnabaris, traceable to the Persian zinjifrah, apparently meaning dragon’s blood, for the red color.

ciprianiite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities and voids in alkali-syenitic pyroclastic ejecta. Formed by latestage post-magmatic hydrothermal fluids enriched in Zr, Ti, REEs, and actinide elements.
ciprianiite.etymology: Honors Curzio Cipriani, Professor of Mineralogy and Head of the Museum of Mineralogy, (later of Natural History), University of Florence, Italy, in recognition of his contribution to mineral systematics.

clairite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by alteration of pyrite to ferric sulfate, and reaction, at pH ∼2, with ammonia produced as the result of decay of organic matter ( Hyrax excreta).
clairite.etymology: Honors Claire Zingg Martini (1936– ), wife of the author of the type description, who assisted her husband in cave exploration and mineral collecting.

claraite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in oxidized Cu–Zn deposits.
claraite.etymology: For the Clara mine, Germany, where the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

claringbullite.occurrence: In oxidized copper ore or slag, produced under chlorine-rich conditions.
claringbullite.etymology: Honors Gordon Frank Claringbull (1911–1990), formerly Keeper of Mineralogy and Director of the British Museum (Natural History), London, England.

clarkeite.occurrence: Replacing uraninite, as a late-stage hydrothermal alteration product.
clarkeite.etymology: Honors Frank Wigglesworth Clarke (1847–1931), prominent American geochemist of the U.S. Geological Survey.

claudetite.occurrence: A secondary oxidation product derived from realgar, arsenopyrite, or other arsenic-bearing minerals. Also produced as a sublimate during mine ﬁres.
claudetite.etymology: Honors Frederick Claudet, the French chemist who ﬁrst described naturally occurring material.

clausthalite.occurrence: Associated in low-sulfur hydrothermal deposits with other selenides, also in mercury deposits. Probably of secondary origin in some deposits.
clausthalite.etymology: For the locality at Clausthal, Germany.

clearcreekite.occurrence: Very rare, probably formed as an alteration product of cinnabar.
clearcreekite.etymology: For the Clear Creek mine, California, USA.

clerite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal gold deposit in limestone.
clerite.etymology: To honor Onisima Yegorovicha Klera (1845–1920), Russian geologist, President of the Ural Society of Natural Sciences Amateurs, Ykaterinberg (Sverdlovsk), Russia.

cleusonite.occurrence: In alpine-type cleft veins in greenschist facies metamorphic rocks.
cleusonite.etymology: For the locality, Cleuson, Switzerland, that provided the specimens for complete description of the species.

cliffordite.occurrence: As rare incrustations along fractures in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal Au–Ag telluride deposits.
cliffordite.etymology: Honors Professor Cliﬀord Frondel (1907–2002), Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA, for his contributions to uranium mineralogy.

clino-ferro-suenite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in metamorphosed iron-poor manganiferous rocks.
clino-ferro-suenite.etymology: The prefix clino indicates a monoclinic structure, the prefix ferro indicates that in the C structural site Fe2+ > Mg,Mn2+. The rootname suenoite indicates an amphibole with composition expressed as A□BMn2+2CMg5TSi8O22W(OH)2.

clino-ferro-suenoite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in metamorphosed iron-poor manganiferous rocks.
clino-ferro-suenoite.etymology: The prefix clino indicates a monoclinic structure, the prefix ferro indicates that in the C structural site Fe2+ > Mg,Mn2+. The rootname suenoite indicates an amphibole with composition expressed as A□BMn2+2CMg5TSi8O22W(OH)2.

clino-oscarkempffite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal Ag-Sn vein deposit.
clino-oscarkempffite.etymology: The prefix clino emphasizes the monoclinic symmetry and the base name the structural and chemical similarity to orthorhombic oscarkempffite.

clino-suenoite.occurrence: In Mn-rich quartzite glacial erratics derived from metamorphosed marine radiolaritic sediments.
clino-suenoite.etymology: The rootname suenoite indicates an amphibole with composition expressed as A□BMn2+2CMg5TSi8O22W(OH)2 and the prefix clino indicates a monoclinic structure.

clinoatacamite.occurrence: An oxidation product of other copper minerals.
clinoatacamite.etymology: As the monoclinic polymorph of atacamite.

clinobarylite.occurrence: In pegmatite veins in an alkaline igneous complex.
clinobarylite.etymology: Reflects the relationship to barylite and non-orthogonal appearance of its crystals which were originally incorrectly determined to be monoclinc.

clinobehoite.occurrence: In hydrothermally altered zones in desilicated pegmatites.
clinobehoite.etymology: For its monoclinic symmetry and relation to behoite.

clinobisvanite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in pegmatites, as an oxidization product of other bismuth minerals.
clinobisvanite.etymology: For the mineral’s monoclinic crystal system, and BISmuth and VANadium in its composition.

clinocervantite.occurrence: In vugs in waste rock from an antimony mine.
clinocervantite.etymology: The prefix, clino, indicates the monoclinic analog of cervantite.

clinochalcomenite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit in brecciated carbonaceous slate (China); in a hydrothermal selenium vein deposit (El Drag´ on mine, Bolivia).
clinochalcomenite.etymology: As the monoclinic dimorph of chalcomenite.

clinochlore.occurrence: A hydrothermal alteration product of amphiboles, pyroxenes, biotite. In chlorite schists, serpentinites, marbles, calc-silicate rocks, amphibolites, less commonly in ultrama¯c rocks. In ore veins; a detrital component of sediments.
clinochlore.etymology: For its inclined optic axes and the Greek chloros, for green, its common color.

clinochrysotile.occurrence: Intermixed with orthochrysotile in veinlets cutting serpentinite.
clinochrysotile.etymology: Chrysotile from the Greek for golden and ¯ber; clino in reference to the mineral's crystallization in inclined axis crystal systems.

clinoclase.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some arsenic-rich hydrothermal base-metal deposits.
clinoclase.etymology: From the Greek for to incline and to break, remarking the oblique basal cleavage.

clinoenstatite.occurrence: As phenocrysts, likely inverted from \protoenstatite," in high-magnesium nonfeldspathic andesites. Exsolved in diopside in ultrama¯c rocks and in enstatite in high-grade metamorphic hornfelses. An essential constituent of chondrite and achondrite meteorites, likely formed by stress.
clinoenstatite.etymology: For its monoclinic crystal system and chemical identity to enstatite.

clinoferrosilite.occurrence: As acicular crystals in lithophysae in obsidian (Lake Naivasha, Kenya).
clinoferrosilite.etymology: For its monoclinic crystal system and chemical identity with ferrosilite.

clinohedrite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
clinohedrite.etymology: From the Greek klino, for incline, and hedra, for face, for the inclined facial character of the crystal morphology.

clinoholmquistite.etymology: In allusion to its similarity to holmquistite and its monoclinic structure.

clinohumite.occurrence: In contact metamorphic zones in dolostones and metasomatized limestones adjacent to felsic plutonic rocks; in serpentine and talc schists; in a carbonatite.
clinohumite.etymology: For its monoclinic crystal system and relation to humite.

clinojimthompsonite.occurrence: In the black wallrock between chlorite and actinolite zones of a metamorphosed ultrama¯c body.
clinojimthompsonite.etymology: For its monoclinic crystallography and relation to jimthompsonite.

clinokurchatovite.occurrence: A replacement of kurchatovite in boron-bearing rocks.
clinokurchatovite.etymology: As the monoclinic dimorph of kurchatovite.

clinometaborite.occurrence: Found as a sublimate in an active fumarole (~250 °C) in a volcanic crater.
clinometaborite.etymology: Named for its monoclinic symmetry and compositional identity with metaborite.

clinomimetite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some base-metal deposits.
clinomimetite.etymology: For its monoclinic structure and relation to mimetite.

clinophosinaite.occurrence: Apparently as an alteration product of eudialyte in alkalic pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
clinophosinaite.etymology: For its monoclinic crystallography and chemical similarity to phosinaite.

clinoptilolite-ca.occurrence: Formed by devitri¯cation of volcanic glass, and in cavities in rhyolites and andesites.
clinoptilolite-ca.etymology: For its inclined optics and relation to ptilolite [mordenite].

clinoptilolite-k.occurrence: Formed by devitri¯cation of volcanic glass, and in cavities in rhyolites and andesites.
clinoptilolite-k.etymology: For its inclined optics and relation to ptilolite [mordenite].

clinoptilolite-na.occurrence: Formed by devitri¯cation of volcanic glass, and in cavities in rhyolites and andesites.
clinoptilolite-na.etymology: For its inclined optics and relation to ptilolite [mordenite].

clinosafflorite.occurrence: In hydrothermal Co–Ni sulﬁde ores, typically silver-bearing.
clinosafflorite.etymology: In reference to the monoclinic symmetry of this saﬄoritelike species.

clinotobermorite.etymology: A prefix, clino, for its monoclinic crystal system and chemical identity to tobermorite.

clinoungemachite.occurrence: Very rarely formed by the oxidation of pyrite in an arid climate, in veins and cavities in other massive iron sulfates.
clinoungemachite.etymology: As the probable monoclinic dimorph of ungemachite.

clinozoisite.occurrence: Typically in low- to medium-grade regionally metamorphosed igneous and sedimentary rocks, as well as in contact metamorphosed calcium-rich sediments; an alteration product of plagioclase feldspars (saussuritization).
clinozoisite.etymology: For its monoclinic crystallography and relation to zoisite.

clintonite.occurrence: In chlorite schists; in metasomatically altered limestones; in siliceous skarns near contact metamorphic zones.
clintonite.etymology: For De Witt Clinton (1769{1828), American statesman.

cloncurryite.occurrence: A product of the weathering in silicified goethite-hematite gossan.
cloncurryite.etymology: For the town of Cloncurry, near where specimens were first collected.

coalingite.occurrence: Developed from iron-rich brucite in the surface weathering zone of a serpentinite (near Coalinga, California, USA); formed (after collection) in thin veinlets in serpentinite from a layered ultramafic complex (Muskox intrusive, Canada).

cobaltarthurite.occurrence: Product of oxidation in a near-surface, sulfide-depleted lens.
cobaltarthurite.etymology: For a member of the arthurite group with essential cobalt in the composition.

cobaltaustinite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a copper deposit, an alteration product of arsenides.
cobaltaustinite.etymology: For its content of cobalt and similarity to austinite.

cobaltite.occurrence: In high-temperature hydrothermal deposits, as disseminations, and as veins in contact metamorphosed rocks.
assoc_parsed: numerous other co–ni sulﬁdes and arsenides
cobaltite.etymology: In allusion to the elemental composition.

cobaltkoritnigite.occurrence: A weathering product of glaucodot (Saxony, Germany); altering from cobaltite (Bauhaus district, Germany).
cobaltkoritnigite.etymology: For its relation to koritnigite and high cobalt content.

cobaltlotharmeyerite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of polymetallic ore deposits.
cobaltlotharmeyerite.etymology: The prefix, cobalt, indicates the cobalt analog of lotharmeyerite.

cobaltomenite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of hydrothermal selenium-sulﬁdebearing vein deposits.
cobaltomenite.etymology: For the content of cobalt and the Greek for moon.

cobaltpentlandite.occurrence: With other sulﬁdes and arsenides in hydrothermal deposits.
cobaltpentlandite.etymology: For the cobalt content and the relation with pentlandite.

cobalttsumcorite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of polymetallic ore deposits.
cobalttsumcorite.etymology: The prefix, cobalt, indicates the cobalt analog of tsumcorite.

cobaltzippeite.occurrence: Rarely as eﬄorescences on the mine walls in oxidized portions of a uraninite deposit containing gersdorﬃte.
cobaltzippeite.etymology: For its dominant content of cobalt and relation to other zippeite group species.

cochromite.occurrence: Replacing chromite in a small tabular nickel deposit at the contact between quartzite and serpentinized ultramaﬁcs; it appears to have formed at ∼730 ◦C and < 2 kbar during thermal metamorphism, possibly of a nickel-rich meteorite (Bon Accord, South Africa); an inclusion in corundum from alkalic basalts (Bo Phloi, Thailand).
cochromite.etymology: For a chromite with essential cobalt, Co.

coconinoite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of vanadium-poor Colorado Plateau-type U- V deposits (Utah and Arizona, USA).
coconinoite.etymology: For Coconino Co., Arizona, USA, from which samples were obtained.

coeruleolactite.occurrence: In brown iron ore (Rindsberg mine, Germany).
coeruleolactite.etymology: From the Greek for blue and milk, for its typical color.

coesite.occurrence: Formed at pressures in excess of 20 kbar, as ¯ne-grained intergrowths with quartz and silica glass in impact metamorphosed rocks and tektites. A primary phase in grospydite (kyanite-garnet-clinopyroxene) xenoliths in kimberlite, and intergrown with quartz as inclusions in garnet and clinopyroxene within eclogites of high-grade metamorphic terranes.
coesite.etymology: For Loring Coes, Jr. (1915{ ), American chemist, who synthesized the material prior to the discovery of a natural occurrence.

coffinite.occurrence: In Colorado Plateau-type black unoxidized U{V deposits, replacing organic material in sandstone; in other sedimentary and hydrothermal vein uranium deposits.
coffinite.etymology: Honoring Reuben Clare Co±n (1886{1972), Tulsa, Oklahoma, USA, pioneer geologist in the study of uranium deposits of the Colorado Plateau.

cohenite.occurrence: In iron meteorites. Also in terrestrial iron, in maﬁc volcanic rocks chemically reduced from assimilation of graphite.
cohenite.etymology: Honors Emil Wilhelm Cohen (1842–1905), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Greifswald, Greifswald, Germany.

coiraite.occurrence: A primary mineral in a telescoped Ag-Sn-Zn polymetallic hydrothermal vein deposit.
coiraite.etymology: Honors Beatriz Lydia Coira (b. 1941), Professor of Petrology, University of Jujuy, Argentina, for her research on volcanism, regional geology, and ore-deposit formation in Argentina.

coldwellite.occurrence: In a heavy-mineral concentrate from a Cu-PGE-Au deposit, disseminated in gabbro.
assoc_parsed: ti- and cr-rich magnetite and ilmenite
coldwellite.etymology: For the locality (Coldwell alkaline complex) that produced the first specimens.

colemanite.occurrence: A common constituent in borate deposits formed in arid alkaline lacustrine environments, deﬁcient in sodium and carbonate, typically under warm conditions.
colemanite.etymology: Honors William Tell Coleman (1824–1893), pioneer developer of the borax industry in California, USA.

colimaite.occurrence: A sublimate found in an active volcanic fumarole.
colimaite.etymology: For the discovery locality, the Colima volcano.

colinowensite.occurrence: In a hydrothermally-altered sedimentary manganese deposit.
assoc_parsed: manganese and iron oxides with a dominance of hausmannite and hematite
colinowensite.etymology: Honors Colin R. Owens (b. 1937), Somerset West, South Africa, who collected the first specimens.

collinsite.occurrence: A secondary weathering product typically incrusting other minerals.
collinsite.etymology: Honoring William Henry Collins (1878–1937), formerly Director of the Geological Survey of Canada.

coloradoite.occurrence: In hydrothermal tellurium-bearing precious metal veins.
coloradoite.etymology: For the Keystone and Mountain Lion mines, Magnolia, Magnolia district, and Smuggler mine, Ballerat district, Boulder Co., type localities in Colorado, USA.

colquiriite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Colquiri deposit, Bolivia.

colusite.occurrence: Widespread in small amounts with other sulﬁdes and sulfosalts, typically in hydrothermal vein and disseminated copper deposits.
colusite.etymology: For the Colusa claim, Butte, Montana, USA, near which it occurs in the Leonard mine.

comancheite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in an oxidized mercury deposit.
comancheite.etymology: For the Comanche Indians, the ﬁrst miners of the mercury deposits in which this mineral occurs.

combeite.occurrence: In nephelinite (Mt. Shaheru, Congo); in nephelinite and ash ejecta (Oldoinyo Lengai volcano, Tanzania).
combeite.etymology: To honor Arthur Delmar Combe, Geological Survey of Uganda.

comblainite.occurrence: An alteration product of nickel and cobalt sulﬁdes in the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit.
comblainite.etymology: For Gordon Comblain (1920– ), Royal Museum of Central Africa, Tervuren, Belgium, who discovered the mineral.

compreignacite.occurrence: As a very rare oxidation product of “pitchblende” in uranium deposits.
compreignacite.etymology: For Compreignac, the village near the Margnac mine, France.

congolite.occurrence: Part of insoluble residue from a drill core into sedimentary evaporites (Brazzaville, Congo); in a marine evaporite deposit (Penobsquis mine, Canada).
congolite.etymology: For Congo, the country in which the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

conichalcite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of copper deposits, typically an alteration product of enargite.
conichalcite.etymology: From the Greek for lime and copper, as both elements are essential to the composition.

connellite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of copper deposits.
connellite.etymology: Honors Arthur Connell (1794–1863), Scottish chemist who ﬁrst examined the mineral.

cookeite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal alteration product of lithium-bearing minerals in pegmatites; a primary hydrothermal vein mineral.
cookeite.etymology: For Josiah B. Cooke, Jr. (1827{1894), American mineralogist and chemist, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

coombsite.occurrence: In a manganese-rich rock in metagraywacke-argillite in the pumpellyite-prehnite facies.
coombsite.etymology: For Professor Douglas Saxon Coombs (1924{ ), mineralogist and petrologist, University of Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand.

cooperite.occurrence: A signiﬁcant platinum ore mineral, found in ultramaﬁcs, gabbros, dunites, chromitites, typically layered; in massive chalcopyrite–pyrrhotite orebodies; in alluvial placers.
assoc_parsed: pt–fe alloys and many other pgm species
cooperite.etymology: Honors Richard A. Cooper (1890–1972), South African metallurgist, Johannesburg, South Africa, who ﬁrst described the mineral.

coparsite.occurrence: As sublimates near a volcanic fumarole vent and included within euchlorine.
coparsite.etymology: Alludes to the copper and arsenic in the essential composition.

copiapite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed typically by the weathering and oxidation of pyrite in a wide range of rock types, preserved in arid climates; rarely associated with fumarolic action.
copiapite.etymology: For the city of Copiap´ o, Chile, near which specimens were ﬁrst collected.

copper.occurrence: Commonly associated with porous zones in maﬁc extrusive rocks, less commonly in sandstones and shales, where the copper was probably of hydrothermal origin, precipitated as the result of oxidizing conditions; in the oxidized zone of large, disseminated copper deposits as a result of secondary processes. A rare mineral in some meteorites.
copper.etymology: From the Latin cuprum, in turn from the Greek kyprios, Cyprus, from which island the metal was early produced.

coquandite.occurrence: Probably produced by action of H 2SO4 on stibnite, in a stibnite vein in siliciﬁed limestone (Pereta mine, Italy).
coquandite.etymology: For Henri-Jean-Baptiste Coquand (1813–1881), Professor of Geology and Mineralogy, University of Marseilles, Marseilles, France, for his early work on the antimony deposits of Tuscany, Italy.

coquimbite.occurrence: Typically a secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of weathering iron sulﬁde deposits in arid regions; rarely associated with fumarolic activity.

coralloite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in strataform manganese deposits.
coralloite.etymology: Honors Giorgio Corallo (b. 1937), a mineral collector, who found several new minerals (cassagnaite, gravegliaite, and reppiaite) in this region and is a “teacher” and “tutor” of several Ligurian mineral collectors.

corderoite.occurrence: In lake-bed sediments and underlying siliciﬁed rhyolite tuﬀs, possibly of low-temperature secondary origin (McDermitt mine, Nevada, USA); in an oxidized hydrothermal deposit (Arzak deposit, Russia).
corderoite.etymology: For its occurrence in the McDermitt (formerly Cordero) mine, USA.

cordierite.occurrence: In thermally metamorphosed argillaceous sediments and high-grade regionally metamorphosed schists, gneisses, and granulites; in ma¯c igneous rocks and granites; detrital.
cordierite.etymology: Honoring Pierre Louis A. Cordier (1777{1861), French mining engineer and geologist, who ¯rst studied the species.

cordylite-ce.occurrence: In carbonatite lenses associated with a fenite dike.
cordylite-ce.etymology: For its structural and chemical identity with cordylite and dominance of La among its rare earth elements.

cordylite-la.occurrence: In carbonatite lenses associated with a fenite dike.
cordylite-la.etymology: For its structural and chemical identity with cordylite and dominance of La among its rare earth elements.

cordylitece.occurrence: Rare in an alkali pegmatite (Narssˆ arssuk, Greenland); a late-stage mineral in miarolitic vugs and fractures (Saint-Amable, Canada); in pegmatite dikes associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
cordylitece.etymology: From the Greek for club, in allusion to its typical clublike crytal habit.

corkite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed at low temperatures or by weathering in oxidized hydrothermal base-metal deposits.
corkite.etymology: For its first-noted occurrence, in Co. Cork, Ireland.

cornetite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some hydrothermal copper deposits.
cornetite.etymology: To honor Jules Cornet (1865–1929), Belgian geologist.

cornubite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in oxidized copper deposits.
cornubite.etymology: From Cornubia, the Latin name for Cornwall, source of the ﬁrst specimens.

cornwallite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in oxidized copper deposits.
cornwallite.etymology: For its occurrence in the County of Cornwall, England.

coronadite.occurrence: A primary mineral in hydrothermal veins or from hot springs; of secondary origin in oxidized zones above manganese-bearing rocks; also in bedded sedimentary deposits.
coronadite.etymology: Honors the ﬁrst Spanish explorer of the American southwest, Francisco Vasquez de Coronado (ca. 1500–1554).

correianevesite.occurrence: In cavities in triphylite in a well-zoned, phosphate-rich granite pegmatite.
correianevesite.etymology: Honors Professor José Marques Correia Neves (1929-2011), Geosciences Institute, Federal University of Minas Gerais, Brazil, for his study of Brazilian pegmatites, especially in the region of Conselheiro Pena and Araçuai, as well as in Alto Ligonha in Mozambique.

corrensite.occurrence: From diverse sedimentary environments, which produced clastic, carbonate, volcanoclastic, or evaporite rocks. Also a hydrothermal alteration product, may be formed under retrograde diagenetic conditions; in soils.
corrensite.etymology: For Professor Carl Wilhelm Correns (1893{1980), Director of the Sedimentary Petrography Institute, GÄ ottingenUniversity, GÄ ottingen, Germany.

corundum.occurrence: Characteristic of Al-rich, Si-poor geological environments; in syenite and monzonite, and some quartz-free pegmatites; primary or a reaction product in eclogitic xenoliths in kimberlites. In regional or contact, high-grade metamorphic aluminous rocks, and some advanced argillic and potassic hydrothermal alteration assemblages; detrital in placers.
corundum.etymology: Probably from the Sanskrit kurivinda, for ruby, through the Tamil kurundam.

corvusite.occurrence: In roll-front uranium deposits in sandstone.
corvusite.etymology: From the Latin word for raven, in allusion to the similarity of the mineral’s color to that of a raven.

cosalite.occurrence: In hydrothermal deposits formed at medium temperatures but also found in contact metasomatic replacements, and epithermal replacements, as well as in pegmatites.
cosalite.etymology: For the locality at Cosal´ a, Mexico.

coskrenite-ce.occurrence: Formed by weathering of pyritiferous phyllite with evaporation of the resulting sulfate-rich solutions in soil, the rare earths probably derived from monazite and xenotime.
coskrenite-ce.etymology: Honors Dr. T. Dennis Coskren (1942– ), geologist and geochemist, Columbia, Maryland, USA, who studied the minerals of Alum Cave Bluﬀ, Tennessee, USA.

cossaite.occurrence: A rare phase formed at approximately 350oC by vapor alteration of volcanic breccia in a strongly acidic, fluorine-rich environment.
cossaite.etymology: Honors Alfonso Cossa (1833–1902), an Italian chemist and mineralogist.

costibite.occurrence: Intimately intergrown with other hydrothermal sulﬁdes (Broken Hill, Australia); in Pb–Zn–Cu–Ag ore deposits remobilized by hydrothermal solutions from later granite emplacement (Bergslagen, Sweden).
costibite.etymology: For CObalt and antimony, STIBium, in its composition.

cotunnite.occurrence: A volcanic sublimate or as an alteration of galena in saline environments. Also as an alteration product on leaden archeological objects or slag immersed in seawater.
