cotunnite.etymology: Honors Domenico Cotugno (Cotunnius) (1736–1822), Italian physician and Professor of Anatomy, University of Naples, Naples, Italy.

coulsonite.occurrence: In veinlets of magnetite, with silicate minerals, cutting metamorphosed andesite (Buena Vista Hills, Nevada, USA); exsolved from magnetite in a mantle xenolith in basalt (Panzhihua, China).
coulsonite.etymology: For Dr. Arthur Lennox Coulson (1898–?), geologist of the Indian Geological Survey.

cousinite.occurrence: As an alteration product of molybdenite-bearing uranium ore.
cousinite.etymology: To honor Jules Cousin (1884–1965), President of the Board of Directors of the Union Mini` ere du Haut-Katanga, Congo.

coutinhoite.occurrence: A secondary hydrothermal mineral in a uraninite-bearing granitic pegmatite.
coutinhoite.etymology: Honors José Moacyr Vianna Coutinho (b. 1924), Professor of Mineralogy and Petrography, Instituto de Geociências, Universidade de São Paulo, Brazil, for significant contributions to Brazilian mineralogy and geology.

covellite.occurrence: Most commonly of secondary origin in the zone of oxidation in sulﬁde copper deposits. Rarely of primary hydrothermal origin. Widespread in most copper deposits; common as an iridescent tarnish on other sulﬁdes.
covellite.etymology: To honor Niccol` o Covelli (1790–1829), discoverer of Vesuvian covellite.

cowlesite.occurrence: In cavities in basalts and scoria, typically the only zeolite within a single vesicle.
cowlesite.etymology: To honor John Cowles (1907{1985), amateur mineralogist of Rainier, Oregon, USA.

coyoteite.occurrence: With rare iron sulﬁdes in small pegmatitic clots thought to have crystallized late in the consolidation of the Coyote Peak intrusive, an alkalic maﬁc diatreme.
coyoteite.etymology: For Coyote Peak, California, a local prominence on which the mineral was found.

crandallite.occurrence: In weathered phosphatic aluminous sedimentary rocks and carbonatites. In phosphate-rich nodules; from complex granite pegmatites; in amphibolite-grade metaquartzites. An authigenic mineral in anoxic marine sediments or in clay-rich sediment beneath a tropical swamp.
crandallite.etymology: Honors Milan L. Crandall, Jr., mining engineer, of Provo, Utah, USA.

cranswickite.occurrence: In veins of up to 3 cm in thickness in a fine-grained metasedimetary rock (illite, quartz, and gypsum).
cranswickite.etymology: Honors Lachlan M.D. Cranswick (1968-2010), an Australian crystallographer who helped to develop and maintain the Collaborative Computational Project No. 14 in Powder and Small Molecule Single Crystal Diffraction (CCP14).

crawfordite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral in ultra-agpaitic pegmatites in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
crawfordite.etymology: To honor Adair Crawford (1748–1795), Scottish physician and Professor of Chemistry, discoverer of strontium salts.

creaseyite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a base-metal deposit, in andesite breccia loosely cemented with iron oxides and wulfenite (Tiger, Arizona, USA).
creaseyite.etymology: To honor Dr. Saville Cyrus Creasey (1917{ ), economic geologist, U.S. Geological Survey, expert on Arizona mineral deposits.

crednerite.occurrence: A low-temperature secondary mineral, perhaps indicating a reducing chemical environment.
crednerite.etymology: Honors Karl F.H. Credner (1809–1876), German mining geologist and mineralogist.

creedite.occurrence: Uncommon in ﬂuorite-rich hydrothermal mineral deposits.
creedite.etymology: For the occurrence near Creede, Colorado, USA.

crerarite.occurrence: In an amphibolite boulder, perhaps glacially transported, containing sulﬁdes.
crerarite.etymology: Honors Professor David Crerar (1945–1994), economic geologist, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA.

crichtonite.etymology: For Sir Alexander A. Crichton (1763–1856), Scottish physician and mineral collector, once physician to the Russian Czar Alexander I.

criddleite.occurrence: A primary hydrothermal mineral in a complex gold deposits.
criddleite.etymology: To honor Dr. Alan John Criddle (1944–2002), English mineralogist of the British Museum (Natural History), London, England.

crimsonite.etymology: Alludes to the mineral’s deep red (crimson) color and the fact that it is the phosphate analogue of carminite, a mineral with a very similar deep red color and whose name is also based upon its color (carmine).

cristobalite.occurrence: In vesicles and lithophysae; a late-crystallizing phase in basaltic to rhyolitic volcanic rocks; from acid-sulfate-type hydrothermal alteration of volcanic rocks; precipitated by hot springs. By contact metamorphism of sandstone; developed during diagenesis, recrystallized from siliceous sedimentary rocks.
cristobalite.etymology: For the ¯rst-noted occurrence at Cerro San Crist¶ obal, Mexico.

crocobelonite.occurrence: In paralavas exposed in a phosphorite quarry (Jordan),

crocoite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of lead deposits associated with chromium-bearing rocks; may be of post-mine formation.
crocoite.etymology: From the Greek for saﬀron, an allusion to the distinctive red-orange color.

cronstedtite.occurrence: A low-temperature hydrothermal product in ore veins.
cronstedtite.etymology: To honor the Swedish mineralogist and chemist, Axel Fredrik Cronstedt (1722{1765).

cronusite.occurrence: In an enstatite achondrite meteorite, formed by terrestrial weathering of caswellsilverite.
cronusite.etymology: For Cronus, a Titan in Greek mythology, son of Uranus and Gaea, in allusion to a mixed meteoritic-terrestrial origin of the mineral.

crookesite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, with other selenides.
crookesite.etymology: In honor of William Crookes (1832–1919), English chemist who discovered thallium.

crowningshieldite.occurrence: Part of a multiphase inclusion in a gem-quality, colorless, type IIa (containing less than ~5 ppm N) diamond from a kimberlite pipe.
crowningshieldite.etymology: Honors G. Robert Crowningshield (1919-2006), who at the Gemological Institute of America (GIA) for more than 50 years, advocated for spectroscopy as a valuable tool in gemology and meticulously recorded the absorption patterns of many gems, ultimately publishing them as a key reference for gem mineral identification.

cryobostryxite.occurrence: Formed as sublimates on basaltic scoria around active volcanic fumaroles and with involvement of meteoric water.
cryobostryxite.etymology: Based on the Greek words, κρύος, for cold or ice, and βόστρυξ, for curl, alludes to the very similar appearance of aggregates of the mineral to ice curls.

cryolite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in some granite pegmatites; in tin-bearing alkalic granites; a vapor-phase mineral along fractures and in the groundmass of some ﬂuorine-rich, topaz-bearing rhyolites; in pods in a carbonatite vein cutting fenitized biotite gneiss. Also as a rare authigenic component of the marlstones and shales of the Green River Formation.
cryolite.etymology: From the Greek for ice and stone, alluding to its appearance.

cryolithionite.etymology: For its similarity to CRYOlite and high LITHIum content.

cryptochalcite.occurrence: As sublimates on basaltic scoria near a volcanic fumarole (>350-400 °C.).
cryptochalcite.etymology: From the Greek κρυπτόζ, which means “concealed”, and χαλκόζ, which means “copper” in allusion to the natural association concealed among other green copper oxysulfate minerals.

cryptohalite.occurrence: A volcanic sublimate, or formed from ﬁres in burning coal seams.
cryptohalite.etymology: From the Greek for concealed and salt, for being admixed with sal ammoniac.

cryptomelane.occurrence: Widespread in oxidized manganese deposits as open-space ﬁllings or replacing primary manganese-bearing minerals; commonly replaced by other secondary manganese minerals.
cryptomelane.etymology: From the Greek for hidden and black, alluding to the mineral’s obscure identity as one of several black mineral species in “psilomelane”, the collective term for hard manganese oxides.

cryptophyllite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral along fractures in a high-potassium peralkaline pegmatite in urtite rocks near the contact with nepheline-apatite rock.
cryptophyllite.etymology: Derived from the Greek words “κρυπτοζ”- concealed (crypto) and “φυλλον” - leaf as an allusion to its occurrence in intimate intergrowths with visually indistinguishable shlykovite and to its layered structure.

cualstibite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from oxidation of a hydrothermal polymetallic barite–ﬂuorite deposit.
cualstibite.etymology: From the chemical symbols of the mineral’s major components, copper (CUprum), ALuminum, and antimony (STIBium).

cuatrocapaite-k.occurrence: A secondary alteration phase formed under hyperarid conditions from the oxidation of native arsenic, and possibly other As-bearing primary phases, coupled with reaction with underground brines rich in mobile cations such as K + , Na+ , NH4+, Ca2+ and Mg2+.
cuatrocapaite-k.etymology: An allusion to the structure, which consists of four (cuatro in Spanish) different types of layers (capa in Spanish): (1) [As2O3], (2) [(NH4),K], (3) [Cl6], and (4) [(Na, Mg,)3(H2O)16]. The suffix indicates the dominant cation in the large-cation layer, (2).

cuatrocapaite-nh4.occurrence: A secondary alteration phase formed under hyperarid conditions from the oxidation of native arsenic, and possibly other As-bearing primary phases, coupled with reaction with underground brines rich in mobile cations such as K + , Na+ , NH4+, Ca2+ and Mg2+.
cuatrocapaite-nh4.etymology: An allusion to the structure, which consists of four (cuatro in Spanish) different types of layers (capa in Spanish): (1) [As2O3]; (2) [(NH4),K]; (3) [Cl6]; and (4) [(Na, Mg,)3(H2O)16]. The suffix indicates the dominant cation in the large-cation layer, (2).

cubanite.occurrence: In hydrothermal deposits formed at relatively high temperature, in pyrrhotite–pentlandite ores in which it commonly occurs as intimate oriented intergrowths with chalcopyrite. Cubanite may exsolve from chalcopyrite below about 200 ◦C–210 ◦C. A rare constituent of some carbonaceous chondrite meteorites.

cuboargyrite.etymology: The prefix, cubo, alludes to a cubic polymorphic relation with miargyrite.

cumengeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed through reaction of chloride ions with primary sulfides in the oxidized zone of some Pb-Cu deposits; in smelter slag immersed in and leached by sea water. Of exhalative origin near a volcanic fumarole.
cumengeite.etymology: For Edouard Cumenge (1828-1902), French mining engineer at Boleo, Mexico, who found the first specimens.

cummingtonite.occurrence: Commonly in medium-grade regionally metamorphosed rocks; characteristic of metamorphosed iron formations; a late-stage mineral in some gabbros and norites; rarely in silicic volcanic rocks.
cummingtonite.etymology: For the occurrence at Cummington, Massachusetts, USA.

cupalite.occurrence: In black slick washed from greenish gray cover weathering from serpentine.

cuprite.occurrence: A common mineral in the oxidized portions of many copper deposits.
cuprite.etymology: From the Latin cuprum, for its copper content.

cuprobismutite.occurrence: Rare, of hydrothermal origin with other sulﬁdes and sulfosalts.
cuprobismutite.etymology: For copper, CUPRum, and BISMUTh in the composition.

cuprocopiapite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral probably formed by reaction between copiapite and copper sulfate-bearing solutions, preserved in arid climates.
cuprocopiapite.etymology: As the cuprian member of the copiapite group.

cuprodongchuanite.etymology: The prefix indicates the Cu-analogue of dongchuanite.

cuproiridsite.etymology: For copper, CUPRum, IRIDium, and Sulfur in the chemical composition.

cuprokalininite.occurrence: As disseminated inclusions in quartz from Cr-V-bearing quartz-diopside granulite facies metamorphic rocks.
assoc_parsed: a mineral of the natalyite-kosmochlor series
cuprokalininite.etymology: For its essential copper content and structural identity with kalininite, ZnCr2S4.

cupromakopavonite.occurrence: By exsolution from an originally homogeneous high-temperature phase in quartz veins in a metamorphosed hydrothermal scheelite deposit.
cupromakopavonite.etymology: Suffix, cupro, indicates dominant copper in a phase related to cupromakovickyite and cupropavonite.

cupromakovickyite.occurrence: As exsolution lamellae or discrete grains associated with sulfosalts in contact metamorphic rocks (skarns) around granite and in scheelite-bearing quartz veins in felsic gneisses and amphibolites.
cupromakovickyite.etymology: For its essential copper content and relationship to makovickyite.

cupromolybdite.occurrence: A fumarolic mineral formed during post-volcanic degassing.
cupromolybdite.etymology: For its chemical composition. The name also reflects the stoichiometric relationship with cuprotungstite, Cu3(OH)2(WO4)2.

cuproneyite.occurrence: In diopside skarn hosting polymetallic mineralization related to contact metamorphism.
cuproneyite.etymology: The prefix, cupro, identifies the copper analogy of neyite.

cupropavonite.occurrence: In zoned mesothermal base- and precious-metal veins.
cupropavonite.etymology: For its copper, cuprum, content, and to stress a similarity with pavonite.

cupropolybasite.occurrence: Supergene, in a hydrothermal epithermal silver-gold deposit.
cupropolybasite.etymology: The prefix, cupro, identifies the Cu-dominant analogue of polybasite.

cuprorhodsite.etymology: For copper, CUPRum, RHODium, and Sulfur in the chemical composition.

cuprorivaite.occurrence: Intimately mixed with quartz (Vesuvius, Italy); in a mudstone xenolith ejected from a scoria cone (Sattelberg volcanic cone, Germany).
cuprorivaite.etymology: For a high copper content and presumed similarity to rivaite.

cuprosklodowskite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by alteration of earlier uranium minerals, both in situ and after transport of solutions.
cuprosklodowskite.etymology: A name supplied by Buttgenbach while introducing Vaes' paper, in the mistaken belief that it was the copper analog of sklodowskite.

cuprospinel.occurrence: In highly oxidized material, once spontaneously ignited, in an ore dump.
cuprospinel.etymology: For the mineral’s copper, CUPRum, content and having the spinel structure.

cuprostibite.occurrence: As ﬁne-grained aggregates in a vein of ussingite cutting sodalite syenite (Il ´ ımaussaq intrusion, Greenland); in sulﬁde veins in metamorphic siliceous dolostone (L ˚ angsj¨ on, Sweden).
cuprostibite.etymology: For copper, CUPRum, and antimony, STIBium, in the composition.

cuprotungstite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral typically replacing scheelite.
cuprotungstite.etymology: For copper, cuprum and tungsten in the composition.

curetonite.occurrence: A rare mineral, in veins cutting a replacement barite deposit.
curetonite.etymology: In honor of Forrest Ellsworth Cureton II (1932– ), mineral dealer and collector, Tucson, Arizona, USA, and Michael Edward Cureton (1960– ), mineral collector, Stockton, California, USA, who ﬁrst found the mineral.

curienite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a Pb-bearing U–V deposit (Mounana mine, Gabon).
curienite.etymology: To honor Professor Hubert Curien (1924– ), French mineralogist and crystallographer, Laboratory of Mineralogy and Crystallography, University of Pierre and Marie Curie (Sorbonne), Paris, France.

curite.occurrence: A secondary mineral commonly formed through alteration of uraninite.
curite.etymology: To honor French physicist Pierre Curie (1856–1906), student of radioactivity.

currierite.occurrence: A secondary alteration phase from the oxidation of native arsenic and other As-bearing primary phases, followed by later alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions.
currierite.etymology: Honors Rock Henry Currier (1940-2015), American mineral dealer, collector, author and lecturer for his unrelenting efforts to benefit the greater mineralogical community.

cuspidine.occurrence: In tu® ejecta (Monte Somma, Italy); in contact metamorphosed limestone (Franklin, New Jersey, USA); in melilite skarn (Dupezeh Mountain, Iraq).
cuspidine.etymology: From the Greek cuspis, for a spear, the characteristic shape of the twinned crystals.

cuyaite.occurrence: Formed by the oxidation of As-bearing primary phases and alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions and perhaps assisted by regional coastal fog.
cuyaite.etymology: For a town near the type locality, Cuya, Arica Province, Chile.

cuzticite.occurrence: Very rare in oxidized ore in a matrix of intensely siliciﬁed and brecciated rhyolite vitrophyre cemented by drusy quartz and carrying pyrite and tellurides.
cuzticite.etymology: From the Nahua language for something yellow, in allusion to the color.

cyanochroite.occurrence: A rare product of fumarolic action (Vesuvius, Italy).
cyanochroite.etymology: From the Greek for blue and color, in reference to its appearance in white light.

cyanophyllite.occurrence: A secondary mineral associated with copper mineralization in a hydrothermal polymetallic barite–ﬂuorite deposit.
cyanophyllite.etymology: From the Greek for blue and a leaf, in allusion to the color and habit.

cyanotrichite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of copper sulﬁde deposits.
cyanotrichite.etymology: From the Greek for blue and hair, in allusion to the typical color and habit.

cylindrite.etymology: In allusion to its typical cylindrical habit.

cymrite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting hydrothermal manganese silicate ore (Benallt mine, Wales); in a copper-bearing deposit in dolostones and siderites (Ruby Creek, Alaska, USA); in jadeite graywacke near the contact of an ultrama¯c rock and the Franciscan Formation (San Benito Co., California, USA); a product of high-pressure metamorphism of manganese-rich rocks (Andros Island, Greece).
cymrite.etymology: From Cymru, the Welsh name for Wales, the locality of discovery.

cyprine.etymology: For a member of the vesuvianite group with predominance of Cu2+ at the Y1A, B sites. The historical name cyprine (derived from Latin cuprum, copper) given by J.J. Berzelius in 1821 for Cu-bearing vesuvianite is transferred to this new mineral.

cyrilovite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in some oxidizing phosphate-bearing granite pegmatites and iron deposits.
cyrilovite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Cyrilov pegmatite, Czech Republic.

czochralskiite.occurrence: A primary phase in graphite-bearing nodules, in an iron meteorite.
czochralskiite.etymology: Honors Jan Czochralski (1885-1953), a Polish chemist, crystallographer and metallurgist, the inventor of the method of production of synthetic silicon crystals known as Czochralski’s method .

dachiardite-ca.occurrence: In the walls of opal-chalcedony veins cutting hydrothermally-altered volcanic rocks.

dachiardite-k.occurrence: In the walls of opal-chalcedony veins cutting hydrothermally-altered volcanic rocks.

dachiardite-na.occurrence: In the walls of opal-chalcedony veins cutting hydrothermally-altered volcanic rocks.

dachiarditeca.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in basalt, quartz veins, and pegmatites; in hydrothermally altered pumiceous tu®aceous sediments.
dachiarditeca.etymology: For Antonio D'Achiardi (1839{1902), Italian mineralogist, whose son described the mineral.

dadsonite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other sulﬁdes and lead sulfosalt minerals.
dadsonite.etymology: To honor the Canadian mineralogist, Alexander Stewart Dadson (1906–1958), active in development of the Yellowknife gold deposits.

dagenaisite.occurrence: A late-stage secondary phase formed by the oxidative alteration of earlier Te- and Znbearing minerals, probably hessite and sphalerite in a polymetallic vein deposit.
dagenaisite.etymology: Honors John Dagenais (b. 1945), of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. Mr. Dagenais has been an active mineral field collector for nearly 50 years. He has collected and provided three new mineral species for scientific research.

daliranite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral formed by reaction with orpiment in a Carlin-type , sediment-hosted disseminated Au-As deposit.
daliranite.etymology: Honors Dr. Farahnaz Daliran (b. 1953), mineralogist and economic geologist at the University of Karlsruhe, Germany, for her research on ore deposits in Iran.

dalnegorskite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in boron-bearing calcareous skarns at the contact of limestone with biotite-hornblende granite.
dalnegorskite.etymology: For the locality where the studied material was collected.

dalnegroite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in dolomitic marble.
dalnegroite.etymology: Honors Alberto Dal Negro (b. 1941), Professor in Mineralogy and Crystallography at the University of Padova, Italy, since 1976.

dalyite.occurrence: A rare accessory in ejected blocks of alkalic granite in trachytic and basaltic tu®s (Ascension Island); in syenite (Serra de Agua de Pau, Azores); in lamproite (Cancarix, Spain).
dalyite.etymology: For Reginald Aldworth Daly (1871{1957), Professor of Geology, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

damaraite.occurrence: From a late-stage vein cutting a banded manganese ore lens in Cu–Pb–Ag ores formed by hydrothermal and metasomatic replacement of dolostones (Kombat mine, Namibia).
damaraite.etymology: For the Damara dolostone sequence, which hosts the Kombat deposit.

damiaoite.occurrence: In a contact metasomatic Co–Cu–Pt-bearing vein in garnet-amphibole pyroxenite in contact with anorthosite and granite.
damiaoite.etymology: For its occurrence near the village of Damiao, China.

danalite.occurrence: In granites, granite pegmatites, zones of contact metamorphism, skarns, and gneisses.
danalite.etymology: To honor James Dwight Dana (1813{1895), American geologist and mineralogist, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, USA.

danbaite.occurrence: In a platinum-bearing Cu–Ni deposit in a highly altered ultramaﬁc intrusion.
danbaite.etymology: For the locality at Danba in China.

danburite.occurrence: In granite and metamorphosed carbonate rocks associated with hydrothermal activity; in evaporites.
danburite.etymology: For the locality at Danbury, Connecticut, USA.

danielsite.occurrence: In a gossan pod in a quartz vein, as a weathering product derived from other sulﬁdes.
assoc_parsed: other secondary lead and copper minerals
danielsite.etymology: For Dr. John L. Daniels (1931– ), Geoscan Pty. Ltd., who collected the material in which the species was found.

dansite.occurrence: A component of marine evaporite deposits.
dansite.etymology: Honors Professor Jean D’Ans (1881–1969), German mineralogist, student of salt deposit chemistry, Technical University, Berlin, Germany.

dansite-fe.occurrence: As encrustations on pyroclastic breccia in volcanic fumaroles; also reported as a secondary mineral (Solvenia).
dansite-fe.etymology: As the iron (Fe)-dominant analog of d’ansite.

dansite-mn.occurrence: As encrustations on pyroclastic breccia in volcanic fumaroles.
dansite-mn.etymology: As the manganese (Mn)-dominant analog of d’ansite.

dantopaite.occurrence: From mineralized (metallic sulfosalts) hydrothermal quartz veins.
dantopaite.etymology: Honors Dr. Dan Topa (b. 1955), ore mineralogist and crystallographer, University of Salzburg, Austria, for his work on sulfosalt crystal chemistry and structures.

daomanite.occurrence: A replacement of bornite in contact metasomatic platinum-bearing Co–Cu sulﬁde mineralization in peridotite-pyroxenite at the contact with anorthosite or granite-gneiss.
daomanite.etymology: From the last syllables of its two Chinese localities, SanDAO and TieMA villages.

daqingshanite-ce.occurrence: In rare-earth-bearing carbonatite-derived biotite dolomite at the footwall of an iron orebody (Bayan Obo deposit, China); in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in altered magnesiocarbonatite (Nkombwa Hill, Zambia).
daqingshanite-ce.etymology: For Mt. Daqingshan, near the Bayan Obo deposit, China.

darapiozite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Dara-i-Pioz massif, Tajikistan.

darapskite.occurrence: Widespread in commercial nitrate deposits, ﬁlling veins and cavities in cemented regolith, in an arid region (Chile); in saline arid soil (Death Valley, California, USA; Antarctica); a component of “ﬂowers” and other cave incrustations, the nitrate probably supplied from urine and guano.
darapskite.etymology: Honors Ludwig Darapsky (1857–1916), German–Chilean chemist and mineralogist, Santiago, Chile.

dargaite.occurrence: Pyrometamorphic by-product of gases, fluids and melts transforming earlier mineral associations (larnite rocks) at ∼900 °C (Israel). In an altered carbonate xenolith from the lava bed of the Shadi-Khokh volcano (Southern Ossetia).
dargaite.etymology: For the canyon (Hahal) Darga, near where studied specimens were collected.

darrellhenryite.occurrence: In the central part of a zoned complex, Li-bearing, petalite-type pegmatite dike.
darrellhenryite.etymology: Honors Darrell J. Henry (b. 1951), Professor of Geology, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, USA, and an expert on the mineralogy, petrology, crystal chemistry, and nomenclature of tourmaline-supergroup minerals.

dashkovaite.occurrence: Rare, in hydrothermal veinlets in serpentine in dolomite marble.
dashkovaite.etymology: To honor Ekaterina Romanova Dashkova (1744–1810), Director of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences and President of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

datolite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in ma¯c igneous rocks; in geodes in tu®s; in skarns in limestones; in serpentinites and \hornblende" schists; from some ore veins.
datolite.etymology: From the Greek to divide, in reference to the granular structure of a massive variety.

daubreeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by alteration of bismuth or bismuthinite, intermixed with “clay” (Tazna, Bolivia).
daubreeite.etymology: For Gabriel Auguste Daubr´ ee (1814–1896), French mineralogist and geologist.

daubreelite.occurrence: In small amounts in many meteorites.
daubreelite.etymology: For Professor Gabriel Auguste Daubr´ ee (1814–1896), of Paris, France, French meteorite researcher.

davanite.occurrence: In contact metamorphic rocks in an alkalic massif (Murun massif, Russia); of magmatic origin, lining vugs in lamproites (Smoky Butte, Montana, USA).
davanite.etymology: For the Davan Stream, in the Murun massif, Russia.

davemaoite.occurrence: As remnant inclusions in a IaAB-type diamond. The first known high-pressure silicate mineral recovered from the lower mantle.
davemaoite.etymology: Honors Dave (Ho-kwang) Mao for his contributions to experimental geophysics and leadership in high-pressure mineral physics that have had a direct impact on understanding deep - Earth chemical and physical processes and Earth’s evolutionary history.

davidbrownite-nh4.struct_group: Not in a structural group, Oxalate
davidbrownite-nh4.occurrence: In a bat-guano-related, post-mining assemblage in a hot and humid area of the mine.
davidbrownite-nh4.etymology: Honors British-Canadian crystallographer Dr. I. David Brown (b. 1932) for developing Bond-Valence Theory, now used extensively by mineralogical crystallographers to both validate structural arrangements and to derive crystal-chemical details (e.g., the presence of hydrogen and its speciation in structures and the arrangements of hydrogen bonds) that are not revealed directly by crystal-structure refinement. The suffix indicates (NH4)+ > K+.

davidite-ce.occurrence: In a pegmatite dike, rich in rare-earth minerals, in granite.
davidite-ce.etymology: For its relation to davidite and dominant cerium content.

davidite-la.occurrence: A primary mineral in high-temperature hydrothermal veins; in norite and anorthosite; in alkalic rocks and also granite pegmatites and carbonatites.
davidite-la.etymology: For Professor Tannatt William Edgeworth David (1858–1934), Australian geologist, University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia. All rights reserved.
