davidlloydite.occurrence: Secondary in the oxidation zone of a Cu-Pb-Zn mineral deposit.
davidlloydite.etymology: Honors David Lloyd (b. 1943), a British mineral collector who was a prime mover in the re-opening of the Tsumeb mine for mineral collecting, and for significant contributions to mineralogy through extensive field collecting at many localities in the British Isles.

davidsmithite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in eclogite, now retrograde-altered to amphibolite facies.
davidsmithite.etymology: Honors the contributions to mineralogy and petrology by David Christopher Smith (b. 1946), Emeritus Professor, Natural History Museum, Paris, France.

davinciite.occurrence: As relict inclusions in rastsvetaevite in a hyperalkaline nepheline-sodalite pegmatite.
davinciite.etymology: Honors Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), Italian scientist, painter, sculptor, and architect.

davisite.occurrence: Likely formed through high-temperature condensation in the solar nebula, followed by melting and crystallization in Ca-,Al-rich refractory inclusions in a meteorite.
davisite.etymology: Honors Andrew M. Davis (b. 1950), Professor of Cosmochemistry at the University of Chicago, USA for his contributions to meteorite research.

davreuxite.occurrence: In quartz veins cutting Mn, Al-rich metapelites, derived from shales subjected to low-grade metamorphism.
davreuxite.etymology: For Charles Joseph Davreux (1800{1863), Belgian pharmacist and natural scientist, Professor of Mineralogy at the University of Liµege, Belgium.

davyne.occurrence: In volcanic ejecta and in leucite-rich lavas.
davyne.etymology: For the great English chemist, Sir Humphrey Davy (1778{1829).

dawsonite.occurrence: Coating vug walls and fractures in hydrothermally altered feldspathic dikes and hornfels associated with nepheline syenite (Mont Saint-Bruno, Canada); authigenic in alkaline shales and coal-bearing rocks (Green River Formation, USA; Sydney Basin, Australia); in saline soils on nepheline syenite tuﬀs (Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania).
dawsonite.etymology: Honors John William Dawson (1820–1899), Canadian geologist and Principal of McGill University, Montreal, Canada.

deanesmithite.occurrence: Very rare in a mercury deposit in silicate–carbonate rock hydrothermally altered from serpentinite.
deanesmithite.etymology: Honors Professor Deane Kingsley Smith, Jr. (1930–2001), Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, USA, for his contributions to structural and experimental mineralogy.

debattistiite.occurrence: A rare hydrothermal mineral in dolomitic marble.
debattistiite.etymology: Honors Luca De Battisti (b.1958), a systematic mineralogist and expert on the minerals of Lengenbach quarry who collected the specimens of debattistiite.

decagonite.occurrence: From impact shock metamorphism in a CV3 carbonaceous chondrite meteorite.
decagonite.etymology: For the 10-fold symmetry of its crystal structure.

decrespignyite-y.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a copper deposit, the source of rare-earths enigmatic, perhaps from surrounding sediments.
decrespignyite-y.etymology: Honors Robert James Champion de Crespigny (1950– ), Chairman of Normandy Mining Limited and Chairman of the South Australian Museum, for his contributions to Australian education.

deerite.occurrence: In meta-ironstones and Cu-Fe sul¯de deposits, in blueschist facies metasediments formed at high pressure and low temperature.
deerite.etymology: To honor Professor William Alexander Deer (1910{ ), mineralogist-petrologist, Cambridge University, Cambridge, England.

defernite.occurrence: In skarn at a granite-limestone contact (GÄuneyce-_Ikizdere, Turkey); throughout a body of unbanded, granular massive hausmannite (Kombat mine, Namibia).
defernite.etymology: For Jacques Deferne, Curator of Mineralogy, Museum of Natural History, Geneva, Switzerland.

delafossite.occurrence: Principally as a secondary mineral near the base of the oxidized zone of copper deposits; less commonly a primary mineral.
delafossite.etymology: For the French mineralogist and crystallographer, Gabriel Delafosse (1796–1878).

delhayelite.occurrence: In a kalsilite-bearing melilite-nepheline lava (Mt. Shaheru, Congo).
delhayelite.etymology: Honoring Fernard Delhaye (1880{1946), Belgian geologist, a pioneer in the geological exploration of the northern Kivu region of Congo (Zaire).

delhuyarite-ce.occurrence: As inclusions in a mass of cerite-(Ce) and percleveite-(Ce) in a metasomatic skarn, REE deposit of the ‘Bastnäs-type’.
delhuyarite-ce.etymology: Honors mineral chemists and metallurgists, Juan José (1754-1796) and Fausto Fermín (1755- 1833) de Elhuyar y de Lubice, French-Basque brothers who first isolated tungsten metal in 1783. The suffix, (Ce), indicates the dominant REE in the essential composition.

deliensite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized portions of a uranium deposit.
deliensite.etymology: Honors Dr. Michel Deliens (1939– ), Belgian mineralogist of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels, Belgium, for his contributions to uranium mineralogy.

delindeite.occurrence: In vugs and miarolitic cavities, as a weathering product of titaniferous nepheline syenite.
delindeite.etymology: In honor of amateur mineralogist Henry deLinde of Mabelvale, Arkansas, USA, owner of the Diamond Jo quarry.

assoc_parsed: tubular inclusions of metallic v and v alloys
dellagiustaite.etymology: Honors Professor Antonio Della Giusta (b. 1941), University of Padova, Italy, an expert on the crystal chemistry and cation order-disorder phenomena in spinel group minerals.

dellaite.occurrence: In late-stage, fracture-controlled replacement veins cutting thermally metamorphosed limestones (Scotland). A late-stage hydration product of pre-existing skarn minerals in a silicadeficient environment (Japan).
dellaite.etymology: To honor Della Martin Roy (b. 1926), Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, USA.

deloneite.occurrence: In the natrolite core of a pegmatite in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
deloneite.etymology: To honor Boris Nikolaevich Delone (1890–1980), crystallographer and mathematician, Mathematics Institute, Moscow, Russia.

deloneite-ce.occurrence: In the natrolite core of a pegmatite in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
deloneite-ce.etymology: To honor Boris Nikolaevich Delone (1890–1980), crystallographer and mathematician, Mathematics Institute, Moscow, Russia.

deloryite.occurrence: Very rare in the oxidized portion of a uranium deposit in sandstone.
deloryite.etymology: Honors Jean Claude Delory (1953– ), French mineral collector and land surveyor, Toulon, France, who collected the ﬁrst specimens.

delrioite.occurrence: An eﬄorescence on sandstone of the Salt Wash member of the Jurassic Morrison Formation associated with a U–V deposit.
delrioite.etymology: For Mexican mineralogist Andr´ es Manuel del Rio (1764–1849), who ﬁrst discovered vanadium in North America.

deltalumite.occurrence: In pores of basaltic rock and scoria altered by volcanic fumarolic gas.
deltalumite.etymology: From the name of the synthetic compound δ-Al2O3 .

delvauxite.etymology: In honor of J.S.P.J. Delvaux de Feuﬀe (1782–1863), Belgian chemist, who ﬁrst analyzed the mineral.

demagistrisite.occurrence: In rhythmically interlayered braunite-bearing metasediments and hematite-rich cherts formed as sedimentary-diagenetic deposits and that were re-equilibrated under prehnite-pumpellyite facies conditions.
demagistrisite.etymology: Honors Leandro de Magistris (1906-1990), a leading Italian mineral collector from the 1940s through the 1980s and an expert on the mineral localities of Liguria .

demartinite.etymology: Honors Francesco Demartin (b. 1953), Professor of General and Inorganic Chemistry, State University of Milan, Italy, for contributions to the chemistry of metallic clusters and to the crystal structures of Alpine rare-earth minerals and uranium minerals.

demesmaekerite.occurrence: Rare in the lower oxidized portions of a selenium-bearing Cu–Co deposit.
demesmaekerite.etymology: Honors Gaston Demesmaeker (1911– ), Belgian mining geologist, Director, Geological Department, Union Mini` ere du Haut Katanga.

demicheleite-br.occurrence: A product of fumarolic alteration of pyroclastic breccia.
demicheleite-br.etymology: Honors Vincenzo de Michele (b. 1936), former curator of the Natural History Museum, Milan, Italy, and suffix for its chemical composition.

demicheleite-cl.occurrence: A product of fumarolic alteration of pyroclastic breccia.
demicheleite-cl.etymology: Honors Vincenzo de Michele (b. 1936), former curator of the Natural History Museum, Milan, Italy, and suffix for its chemical composition.

demicheleite-i.occurrence: A product of fumarolic alteration of pyroclastic breccia.
demicheleite-i.etymology: Honors Vincenzo de Michele (b. 1936), former curator of the Natural History Museum, Milan, Italy, and suffix for its chemical composition.

dendoraite-nh4.struct_group: Not in a structural group, Oxalate

denisovite.occurrence: In nepheline syenite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Russia).
denisovite.etymology: Honors Aleksander Petrovich Denisov (1918{1972), Russian specialist in X-ray investigations of minerals, of the Kola Scienti¯c Center, Ruisia.

denningite.etymology: To honor Reynolds McConnell Denning (1916–1967), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA.

depmeierite.occurrence: In a peralkaline hydrothermal veinlet cross-cutting alternating foyaite, urtite, and lujavrite rocks in an alkaline igneous complex.
depmeierite.etymology: Honors Wulf Helmut Heinz Depmeier (b. 1944), professor of mineralogy and crystallography, Christian Albrecht University, Kiel, Germany.

derbylite.occurrence: In cinnabar-bearing placer gravels (Tripuhy, Brazil); in microcrystalline barite and in cavities within metasomatically mineralized dolostones (Buca della Vena mine, Italy).
derbylite.etymology: For the American geologist Orville Adelbert Derby (1851–1915), at one time Director of the Brazilian Geological Survey.

derriksite.occurrence: Very rare in the oxidized portions of a selenium-bearing Cu–Co deposit.
derriksite.etymology: Honors Jean Marie Fran¸ cois Joseph Derriks (1912–1993), Belgian geologist who studied the Shinkolobwe uranium deposit.

dervillite.etymology: For Dr. Henri Derville, French paleontologist, Strasbourg University, Strasbourg, France, who noted the original specimen.

desautelsite.occurrence: Abundantly, in fractures in serpentinite breccia, with other secondary magnesium minerals, the last mineral to form (California, USA); in ultramaﬁcs in faults in sediments (Shiraki, Japan).
desautelsite.etymology: To honor Paul Ernest Desautels (1920–1991), Curator of Mineralogy, National Museum of Natural History (Smithsonian Institution), Washington, D.C., USA.

descloizite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of vanadium-bearing base metal deposits; rarely an ore of vanadium.
descloizite.etymology: To honor Alfred Lewis Oliver Legrand Des Cloizeaux (1817–1897), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Paris, Paris, France, who ﬁrst described the mineral.

despujolsite.etymology: Honors Pierre Despujols (1888–?), founder of the Moroccan Geologic Survey.

destinezite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in gossans and some coal deposits, formed by sulfate-rich solutions acting on earlier phosphates, may be post-mine; in cave deposits, the phosphate derived from guano; widespread in secondary phosphate assemblages in granite pegmatites. As nodular lumps in hematite-rich epiclastic sediments in small crater lakes on the slopes of El Laco volcano.
destinezite.etymology: Honors M. Destinez. Destinezite is visibly crystalline, triclinic Fe2(PO4)(SO4)(OH)·6H2O. Diadochite is massive to earthy, poorly ordered, X-ray amorphous materials that approximate destinezite in composition.

deveroite-ce.occurrence: Precipitated from meteoric waters enriched with oxalic acid likely derived from incomplete oxidation of decaying plant remains (in this case crusty lichens). Rare earth elements provided by the hosting mineral, cervandonite-(Ce), in NYF-type pegmatite dikes.
deveroite-ce.etymology: For the locality, Devero Natural Park in Devero Valley, that produced the first specimens and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

devilline.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of copper sulﬁde deposits; may be of post-mining origin in dumps and on timbers.
devilline.etymology: Honors Henri Etienne Sainte-Claire Deville (1818–1881), French chemist.

devitoite.occurrence: An alteration product of gillepsite along fractures and parting planes in a sanborni tebearing rock.
devitoite.etymology: Honors Alfred (Fred) Devito (1937–2004) a prominent mineral collector (micromounts) , field collector and contributor to the California mineralogical community.

dewindtite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by alteration of uraninite or earlier-formed secondary uranium minerals.
dewindtite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Jean Dewindt, Belgian geologist.

diaboleite.occurrence: In oxidized manganese ores (Mendip Hills, England); a secondary mineral in deeply oxidized Pb-Cu ores (Tiger, Arizona, USA); in slag exposed to seawater.
diaboleite.etymology: From the Greek for separate from, and the related mineral boleite.

diadochite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in gossans and some coal deposits, formed by sulfate-rich solutions acting on earlier phosphates, may be post-mine; in cave deposits, the phosphate derived from guano; widespread in secondary phosphate assemblages in granite pegmatites.
diadochite.etymology: From the Greek for a successor, as it typically is formed from earlier phosphates. Destinezite is visibly crystalline, triclinic Fe2(PO4)(SO4)(OH)·6H2O. Diadochite is massive to earthy, poorly ordered, X-ray amorphous material that approximated destinezite in composition.

diamond.occurrence: Primarily formed in pipes, less commonly in dikes, of deep-seated, igneous origin, composed of kimberlite or lamproite, and in alluvial deposits formed by their weathering. In carbonaceous achondrite and iron meteorites; may be formed by impact.
diamond.etymology: A corruption of the Greek for invincible.

diaoyudaoite.occurrence: In the heavy-mineral (S.G. > 2.8) fraction of the surface layer of sea-ﬂoor muds at about 1500 m water depth.
diaoyudaoite.etymology: For Diaoyudao Island, near which it occurs.

diaphorite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other sulﬁdes formed at medium temperatures.
diaphorite.etymology: From the Greek for diﬀerence, as being distinct from freieslebenite.

diaspore.occurrence: Typically a ﬁnal product of diagenesis in bauxite deposits formed by the tropical weathering of alumino-silicate rocks; from hydrothermal alteration of aluminous minerals; a hydrothermal mineral in some alkalic pegmatites.
diaspore.etymology: From the Greek for to scatter , in allusion to its decrepitation under the blowpipe.

dickinsonite-kmnna.occurrence: In nodular masses in albitic granite pegmatite.
dickinsonite-kmnna.etymology: Dickinsonite indicates a member of the group with Mn2+ dominant at the M site; two suffixes indicate the dominant cation of the dominant valence state at the A and B sites. Honors the Reverend John William Dickinson (1835-1899), Redding, Connecticut, USA, an early collector of Branchville minerals.

dickite.occurrence: Commonly of hydrothermal origin along veins derived in part from the alteration of aluminosilicate minerals; also as an authigenic sedimentary mineral.
dickite.etymology: For Allan Brugh Dick (1833{1926), Scottish metallurgical chemist, who ¯rst described the species.

dicksonite.occurrence: A high-temperature (>::: 800°C) primary mineral in granite pegmatites.
dicksonite.etymology: In honor of the Reverend John William Dickinson (1835-1899), Redding, Connecticut, USA, an early collector of Branchville minerals.

dickthomssenite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a sandstone U–V deposit.
dickthomssenite.etymology: To honor Richard Wyatt?? Thomssen (1933– ), American economic geologist and collector of microscopic mineral specimens, Dayton, Nevada, USA.

diegogattaite.occurrence: In a hydrothermally altered manganese deposit.
diegogattaite.etymology: Honors Professor Diego Gatta (b. 1974), Department of Earth Sciences, University of Milan, Italy, for his contributions in the areas of crystal structures and crystal chemistry of zeolites and related silicates with cage structures.

dienerite.occurrence: Known only from one loose single crystal.
dienerite.etymology: Honors Professor Karl Diener (1862–1928), Austrian paleontologist, the discoverer.

dietrichite.occurrence: As post-mining eﬄorescences in abandoned mine workings.
dietrichite.etymology: To honor Dr. Gustav Heinrich Dietrich, Pˇ r ´ ıbram, Czech Republic, who analyzed the ﬁrst specimens.

dietzeite.occurrence: In nitrate deposits in an arid region.
dietzeite.etymology: Honors August Dietze (?–1893?), German chemist who ﬁrst described this mineral.

digenite.occurrence: In hydrothermal copper deposits of primary and secondary origin. Formed under a wide range of conditions; reported from maﬁc intrusives, as a volcanic exhalation product, and in pegmatites.
digenite.etymology: From the Greek for two kinds or sexes, in reference to the presumed presence of both cuprous and cupric ions.

dimorphite.occurrence: Deposited at a fumerolic vent at temperatures of about 70 ◦C–80 ◦C (Solfatara, Italy); formed in an ore deposit under secondary conditions (Chile).
dimorphite.etymology: From the Greek for two and form, in reference to the two forms in which the species was thought to occur.

dingdaohengite-ce.occurrence: In magnesian skarn in the excontact of granite within dolomitic marble.
dingdaohengite-ce.etymology: Honors Ding Daoheng (1899-1955), who discovered the world-famous Bayan Obo REE-Nb- Fe ore deposit in 1927 and a suffix indicates that Ce is the dominant rare-earth element.

dinite.occurrence: In bituminous fossil wood in unconsolidated river sediment.
dinite.etymology: Honors Professor Olinto Dini (1802–1866), Italian physicist, University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy, who discovered the ﬁrst specimens.

diopside.occurrence: Typical of metamorphosed siliceous Ca, Mg-rich rocks of the pyroxene-hornfels or epidote-amphibolite facies; common in skarns, Ca, Mg-rich gneisses and schists, and some kimberlites and peridotites. Less common in alkalic olivine basalts and andesites.
diopside.etymology: From the Greek for double and appearance, apparently for two possible orientations of the prism zone.

dioptase.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of some copper deposits.
dioptase.etymology: From the Greek for through and to see, as the cleavage directions may be seen on looking through the crystal.

direnzoite.occurrence: Formed by hydrothermal crystallization in the vugs of a highly porphyritic basalt xenolith.
direnzoite.etymology: Honors Dr. Francesco Di Renzo, (b. 1954), Research Director, Laboratoire de Matériaux Catalytiques et Catalyse en Chimie Organique, Ecole Nationale Supérieure de Chimie de Montpellier (France), for his contributions in the fields of zeolites, mesoporous materials, and catalysis.

dissakisite-ce.occurrence: Formed in marble, under amphibolite-facies metamorphism, at about 600 ±C and 7 kbar (Balchen Mountain, Antarctica).
dissakisite-ce.etymology: From the Greek for twice over, for a magnesium analog of allanite being described twice.

dissakisite-la.occurrence: By hydration and enrichment in LILE and LREE of a garnet-bearing peridotite body, in relation to HP-migmatization of the surrounding gneisses during an orogeny.
dissakisite-la.etymology: The suffix, La, indicates the lanthanum analog of dissakisite-(Ce).

disulfodadsonite.occurrence: In pockets with high sulfur fugacity during hydrothermal alteration of marble.
disulfodadsonite.etymology: For the relationship to dadsonite and the presence of the disulfide ion in the crystal structure.

dittmarite.occurrence: In dryer parts of bat guano in caves.
dittmarite.etymology: Honoring William Dittmar (1833–1892), Professor of Chemistry, University of Glasgow, Glasgow, Scotland.

diversilite-ce.etymology: From the Latin diversus for “heterogeneous” and SILIcate, alluding to the compositional diversity, structural complexity and dominant anionic and rare earth compositions of the mineral.

dixenite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed Fe{Mn orebody in serpentine.
dixenite.etymology: From the Greek di, for two, and xenos, for stranger, in reference to the then unique association of silica and arsenious oxide in the mineral.

djerfisherite.occurrence: In meteorites, in hydrothermal Cu–Ni sulﬁde ores, in skarns, in pegmatites, in kimberlites, and alkalic maﬁcs.
djerfisherite.etymology: To honor Professor Daniel Jerome Fisher (1896–1988), American mineralogist, University of Chicago, Chicago, USA.

djurleite.occurrence: With other secondary copper sulﬁdes in enriched zones.
djurleite.etymology: For Dr. Seved Djurle (1918– ), Swedish chemist, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound later found in nature.

dmisokolovite.occurrence: As sublimate incrustations and/or the product of reaction between rock and volcanic gas on the surface of basalt scoria in an active fumarole.
dmisokolovite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist, volcanologist, and geologist, Dmitry Ivanovich Sokolov (1788-1852), Professor of Mineralogy and Geology at St. Petersburg University, and Academician of the Russian Academy of Sciences. One of the founders of the Russian Mineralogical Society (1817) and first editor of Gornyi Zhurnal (Mining Journal), an early Russian periodical on geology, mineralogy and mining sciences (1825). He also authored mineralogy textbooks.

dmisteinbergite.occurrence: An ultra-refractory mineral in a rounded, coarse-grained, igneous Type B2 Ca- Al-rich inclusion (CAI) in a carbonaceous chondrite meteorite, formed early as a high-temperature condensate in the solar nebula. From burned coal dumps (Russia). By friction-melting along pseudotachylite-bearing faults (Italy).
dmisteinbergite.etymology: Honors Dmitrii Sergeevich Steinberg (b. 1910), noted petrologist, Institute of Geology and Geochemistry, Yekaterinberg, Russia.

dmitryivanovite.occurrence: In a Ca,Al-rich inclusion (CAI) in a CH3 chondrite meteorite.
dmitryivanovite.etymology: Honors Dmitriy A. Ivanov (1962-1986), a geologist, mineralogist, and petrologist who died tragically on a field expedition to study igneous rocks in the Caucasus Mountains.

dobsinaite.occurrence: Secondary in siderite-ankerite hydrothermal carbonate-quartz veins with Ni-Fe-Co-Cu mineralization. By oxidation of primary safflorite and arsenopyrite in a Ca-enriched environment (abundant calcite in the matrix) under relatively dry conditions.
dobsinaite.etymology: For the occurrence near Dobšiná where the studied material was collected.

dokuchaevite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
dokuchaevite.etymology: Honors Russian Professor Vasily V. Dokuchaev (1846-1903), a founder of Soil Science who lectured on mineralogy and crystallography at St. Petersburg State University.

dolerophanite.etymology: From the Greek for fallacious and to appear, in allusion to a physical appearance nonsuggestive of the composition.

dollaseite-ce.occurrence: In tactite replacement deposits developed during metamorphism of dolomitic limestone.
dollaseite-ce.etymology: Honors Professor Wayne A. Dollase, University of California, Los Angeles, California, USA, for his crystal chemical research on minerals of the epidote group, and its cerium content.

dolomite.occurrence: Formed by diagenesis or hydrothermal metasomatism of limestone; a primary phase in hypersaline sedimentary environments; a major component of some contact metamorphic rocks and marbles; a gangue in hydrothermal veins; in carbonatites and ultramaﬁc rocks.
dolomite.etymology: Honors Dieudonne (D´ eodat) Sylvain Guy Tancr` ede de Gratet de Dolomieu (1750–1801), French geologist and naturalist, who contributed to early descriptions of the species in dolostone.

doloresite.occurrence: In relatively unoxidized uranium-vanadium ores; from the cores of black, concretionary masses high in uranium and vanadium, surrounded by tyuyamunite-bearing sandstone (La Sal No. 2 mine, Colorado, USA).
doloresite.etymology: For the Dolores River, southwestern Colorado, USA.

domerockite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a weathered Cu As sulfide deposit.
domerockite.etymology: For the mine that produced the first specimens.

domeykite.etymology: Honors Professor Ignacio Domeyko [born Ignacy Domejko] (1802–1889), Polish–Chilean mineralogist, University of Chile, Santiago, Chile.

domeykite-beta.etymology: Honors Professor Ignacio Domeyko [born Ignacy Domejko] (1802–1889), Polish–Chilean mineralogist, University of Chile, Santiago, Chile.

donbassite.occurrence: In the lode walls and crushed zones in ore veins and as coatings on slickensides of coals. In soils and sediments in very aluminum-rich environments.
donbassite.etymology: For occurrences in the DONets BASin, Ukraine.

donharrisite.occurrence: On an old museum specimen from a polymetallic Hg–Pb-rich dolostone stratabound ore deposit.
donharrisite.etymology: To honor Dr. Donald C. Harris (1936– ), Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa, Canada, for his contributions to ore mineralogy.

donnayite-y.occurrence: In pegmatite dikes, miarolitic cavities, and interstices in nepheline syenite in an alkaline complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
donnayite-y.etymology: Honors Dr. Joseph D´ esir´ e Hubert Donnay (1902–1994), Belgian–American–Canadian crystallographer and his wife Dr. Gabrielle Donnay (1920–1987), American–Canadian mineralogist, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland, USA and McGill University, Montreal, Canada, for their contributions to mineralogy and crystallography.

donowensite.occurrence: A secondary mineral found in brown concretionary masses in potassic fenitized, feldspathoidal syenite.
donowensite.etymology: Honors American geologist and mineralogist Don R. Owens (1937-2015). Owens had a distinguished career in vanadium exploration with Union Carbide, retired in 1983 and became an independent consultant and a faculty member in the Department of Earth Sciences, University of Arkansas, at Little Rock.

donpeacorite.occurrence: In manganese-rich siliceous marbles metamorphosed to the upper amphibolite facies.
donpeacorite.etymology: To honor Dr. Donald R. Peacor (1937{ ), University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA.

donwilhelmsite.occurrence: In shock melt pockets of roughly anorthitic bulk composition in a feldspatic lunar meteorite. Formed from primordial feldspathic lunar crust during impact cratering events. Forms in Earth’s mantle during deep recycling of aluminous crustal materials and is a key host for Al and Ca of subducted sediments in most of the transition zone and uppermost lower mantle (460-700 km).
donwilhelmsite.etymology: Honors Don E. Wilhelms (b. 1930) for his seminal and ground-breaking work on the geological history of the Moon.

dorallcharite.occurrence: In oxidized portions of a Tl-bearing hydrothermal sulﬁde-sulfosalt deposit.
dorallcharite.etymology: From the French dor´ e,golden yellow, and the famous mining locality, Alˇ sar (Allchar), Macedonia.

dorfmanite.occurrence: Noted in drill cores into alkalic pegmatites in diﬀerentiated alkalic massifs, as an alteration product of lomonosovite and nacaphite (Kola Peninsula, Russia); in sodalite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
dorfmanite.etymology: To honor Moisei Davidovich Dorfman (1908– ), Russian mineralogist, A.E. Fersman Mineralogical Museum, Moscow, Russia, investigator of Khibiny minerals.

dorrite.occurrence: A product of oxidizing, high-temperature, low-pressure metamorphism of alkalic rocks, in a pyrometamorphic zone in sediments.
dorrite.etymology: To honor Dr. John A. Dorr, Jr., Professor of Geology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA, in recognition of his regional geologic research in Wyoming.

douglasite.etymology: For the locality, Douglashall, Germany, at which it occurs.

dovyrenite.occurrence: An alteration product of Zr-bearing and zirconium minerals in veins of vesuvianitefoshagite skarn in carbonate xenoliths in a subvolcanic layered gabbro-peridotite massif.
dovyrenite.etymology: After the name of the locality Dovyren Bald Mountain, Russia.

downeyite.occurrence: As a rare sublimation product of gases escaping through vents in actively burning culm banks in anthracite coal deposits; forms at about 200 ◦C near the vents.
downeyite.etymology: For Wayne F. Downey, Jr., of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, USA, who ﬁrst collected the mineral.

doyleite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral lining vugs in veins in nepheline syenite associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in vugs within silicocarbonatite sills intruding limestones (Francon quarry, Canada); in miarolitic cavities in a nepheline syenite sill (near Saint-Amable, Canada).
doyleite.etymology: Honors Canadian physician E.J. Doyle, of Ottawa, Canada, who found the mineral at Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada.

dravertite.etymology: Honors the Russian mineralogist and geologist Petr Lyudovikovich Dravert (1879-1945) for his significant contribution to the mineralogy of Siberia.

dravite.occurrence: Commonly in metamorphosed limestones or ma¯c igneous rocks with metasomatically introduced boron; rarely in pegmatites; as authigenic overgrowths in sedimentary rocks.
dravite.etymology: For the district along the Drava (Drave) River in Austria and Slovenia.

dresserite.occurrence: In vugs in an alkalic sill in limestone.
dresserite.etymology: Honors John Alexander Dresser (1866–1954), Canadian geologist who contributed to knowledge of the Monteregian Hills.

dreyerite.occurrence: In rhyolitic tuﬀs, intercalated with carbonaceous matter and siliciﬁed wood.
dreyerite.etymology: In honor of Gerhard Dreyer, Assistant Professor, Johannes Gutenberg University, Mainz, Germany, who found the mineral.

dritsite.occurrence: A result of diagenesis in the halite-carnallite rock salt deposit.
dritsite.etymology: Honors Russian crystallographer and mineralogist Professor Victor Anatol‘evich Drits (b. 1932), Geological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, for contributions to the studies of the crystal chemistry and systematics of layered minerals, including the hydrotalcite supergroup. Professor Drits is a specialist in the mineralogy of sedimentary rocks and crystal chemistry of compounds with layered structures, especially clay minerals.

droninoite.occurrence: In a fragment of a weathered iron meteorite.
droninoite.etymology: For the village of Dronion, Russia near which the sample was collected.

drugmanite.occurrence: Very rare, formed at low temperatures in vugs in mineralized limestones, an oxidation product of disseminated sulﬁdes.
drugmanite.etymology: To honor Dr. Julien Drugman (1875–1950), Belgian mineralogist.

drysdallite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a uranium deposit in a talc schist.
drysdallite.etymology: To honor Dr. A.R. Drysdall (1933– ), Director, Geological Survey of Zambia.

dualite.occurrence: Formed during the final stages of peralkaline pegmatite formation.
dualite.etymology: From Latin dualis (dual) alluding to the dual taxonomic membership of this mineral, at the same time zirconosilicate and titanosilicate.

dufrenite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed principally in iron ore deposits.
dufrenite.etymology: To honor Professor Ours Pierre Armand Petit-Dufr´ enoy (1792–1857), French mineralogist, National School of Mines, Paris, France.

dufrenoysite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral of medium- to low-temperature hydrothermal origin.
dufrenoysite.etymology: To honor Professor Ours Pierre Armand Petit-Dufr´ enoy (1792–1857), French mineralogist, National School of Mines, Paris, France.

duftite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in the oxidized zone of some hydrothermal base-metal deposits.
duftite.etymology: In honor of G. Duft, General Manager of the mine at Tsumeb, Namibia.

dugganite.occurrence: An alteration product of khinite and parakhinite, formed under acid oxidizing conditions from gold-telluride ores in massive vein quartz (Tombstone, Arizona, USA).
dugganite.etymology: To honor Marjorie Duggan (1927– ), American analytical chemist, who ﬁrst analyzed Te6+ from nature.

dukeite.occurrence: On a museum specimen of pucherite.
dukeite.etymology: For Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA, in whose collection the mineral was found and for the contributions of Duke family to the advancement of scientific knowledge.

dumontite.occurrence: In pockets of torbernite in the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit (Shinkolobwe, Congo).
dumontite.etymology: Honoring Andr´ e Hubert Dumont (1809–1857), Belgian geologist.

dumortierite.occurrence: In aluminum-rich regionally metamorphosed rocks, disseminated and in veinlets cutting schists; also in pegmatitic veins.
dumortierite.etymology: For Eugµene Dumortier (1802{1873?), French paleontologist, of Lyons, France.

dundasite.occurrence: Uncommon in the oxidized zone of lead-bearing deposits.
dundasite.etymology: For the occurrence at Dundas, Tasmania, Australia.

durangite.occurrence: In veins in alkalic rhyolite and tin placers derived therefrom; in pegmatite dikes in granite.
durangite.etymology: For the original occurrence in Durango, Mexico.

duranusite.occurrence: In calcite veinlets in marls and siliceous limestones (Duranus, France).
duranusite.etymology: For the locality at Duranus, France.

dussertite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of some base-metal deposits, typically an alteration product of arsenopyrite.
dussertite.etymology: Honors Desiré Dussert (1872–?), French mining engineer who worked in Algeria.

assoc_parsed: distribution in the moraine of darai-pioz glacier
distribution from the fornovolasco metarhyolite formation

duttonite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by the low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of vanadium-bearing minerals.
duttonite.etymology: Honors Captain Clarence Edward Dutton (1841–1912), American geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, an early worker on the Colorado Plateau.

dwornikite.occurrence: In a vanadium sulﬁde deposit, probably by oxidation of associated bravoite.
dwornikite.etymology: Honors Edward J. Dwornik (1920– ), Lunar geologist and mineralogist, U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C., USA, who studied several vanadium deposits.

dymkovite.occurrence: A secondary mineral found in small cavities and cracks in slightly oxidized uraninite-bearing dolomite veins.
dymkovite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist, Yuriy Maksimovich Dymkov (b. 1926), a specialist in the mineralogy and geology of uranium deposits.

dypingite.occurrence: Coats fractures and exposed surfaces in serpentine; may be of recent formation on dump materials.
dypingite.etymology: For the ﬁrst-noted occurrence at Dypingdal, Norway.

dyrnaesite-la.occurrence: An accessory constituent (late magmatic) of hyperagpaitic arfvedsonite lujavrite in an alkaline igneous complex.
dyrnaesite-la.etymology: For the base camp area, Dyrnæs (animal headland), north of Narsaq, Kujalleq Kommune, South Greenland, with the suffix for the dominant REE.

dyscrasite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other silver minerals as both a primary and secondary mineral.
dyscrasite.etymology: From the Greek for a bad alloy.

dzhalindite.occurrence: Probably of secondary origin from its occurrence along fractures through primary hydrothermal minerals associated with brecciated felsic volcanic rocks (Dzhalinda deposit, Russia); in sulﬁdes hosted in greisenized granite (Mangabeira, Brazil).
dzhalindite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Dzhalinda tin deposit, Russia.

dzharkenite.occurrence: In Se–U ores in quartz-sandstone (Seluchekinskoye deposit, Kazakhstan); in a massive sulﬁde deposit (Zapadno-Ozernoe deposit, Russia).
dzharkenite.etymology: For the Dzharkenskaya depression, within which the Seluchekinskoye deposit occurs.

dzhuluite.occurrence: From fluorine metasomatism of a thermally-altered carbonate-silicate xenolith (20 m long) in ignimbrite, the heat from which created sanidinite facies metamorphism in the xenolith.
dzhuluite.etymology: Originally named bitikleite-(SnFe). Subsequently re-named after Dzhulu Mountain, located near the site from which the first specimens were collected.

eakerite.occurrence: Probably of hydrothermal origin, in a seam in spodumene-bearing pegmatite (Foote mine, North Carolina, USA); as exsolved inclusions in stanniferous andradite (Kitel'skoye deposit, Karelia).
eakerite.etymology: In honor of Jack Eaker, mineral collector of Kings Mountain, North Carolina, USA, who discovered the mineral.

earlandite.occurrence: In unconsolidated ocean ﬂoor sediment at 2580 m depth.

earlshannonite.occurrence: A very late-stage secondary mineral in a lithium-rich granite pegmatite (Foote mine, North Carolina, USA).
earlshannonite.etymology: To honor Earl V. Shannon (1895–1981), American mineralogist and chemist, U.S. National Museum, Washington, D.C., USA.

ecandrewsite.occurrence: In quartz-rich metasediments of the amphibolite-granulite facies (Melbourne Rockwell mine, Australia); in a kyanite-bearing pelitic schist (Death Valley, California, USA).
ecandrewsite.etymology: Honors Ernest Clayton Andrews (1870–1948), New South Wales government geologist, who mapped the Broken Hill region.

ecdemite.occurrence: A rare mineral in metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebodies (Sweden).
ecdemite.etymology: From the Greek for unusual, in allusion to the composition.

eckerite.occurrence: In massive to interstitial sulfosalt accumulations in dolostones metamorphosed to upper greenschist to lower amphibolite facies.
eckerite.etymology: Honors Markus Ecker (b. 1966), an expert on the minerals of Lengenbach quarry.

eckermannite.occurrence: In a jadeitite-amphibole fels rock, likely formed under blueschist facies conditions.
eckermannite.etymology: Honors Professor Claes Walther (Harry) von Eckermann (1886-1969), petrologist, Stockholm, Sweden.

eckhardite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in vugs in quartz formed from the partial oxidation of primary sulfides and tellurides during or following the brecciation of quartz veins.
eckhardite.etymology: Honors Colonel Eckhard D. Stuart (b. 1939) of Madison, Mississippi, USA., a mineral collector who has provided numerous samples for research, including this new species.

eclarite.occurrence: In gold-bearing sulﬁde ores of copper located in quartz veins cutting amphibolite facies metamorphosed maﬁc rocks (B¨ arenbad, Austria).
eclarite.etymology: To honor Professor Eberhard Clar (1904– ), Austrian mineralogist, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria.

edenharterite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal deposit in dolostone.
edenharterite.etymology: Honors Dr. Andreas Edenharter (1933– ), University of G¨ ottingen, G¨ ottingen, Germany, who had previously synthesized the compound.

edenite.occurrence: In intermediate plutonic igneous and medium-grade metamorphic rocks, as amphibolites and marbles.
edenite.etymology: For the locality at Edenville, New York, USA, although it is not certain to occur there.

edgarbaileyite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, probably resulting from reaction between mercury and quartz under unknown conditions.
edgarbaileyite.etymology: For Dr. Edgar Herbert Bailey (1914{1983), distinguished geologist and mercury specialist with the U.S. Geological Survey.

edgarite.occurrence: In a feldspar-rich fenitized xenolith in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
edgarite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Alan D. Edgar (1935–1998), Professor of Petrology, University of Western Ontario, London, Canada, for his work on alkaline rocks.

edgrewite.occurrence: In xenoliths of carbonate-silicate rock altered to sanidinite facies metamorphic rock within ignimbrites.
edgrewite.etymology: Honors Edward S. Grew (b. 1944), professor of mineralogy and petrology at the University of Maine, Orono, Maine, USA.

edingtonite.occurrence: In cavities in ma¯c igneous rocks and nepheline syenites; in carbonatites; in hydrothermal veins.
edingtonite.etymology: For James Edington (1787{1844), mineral collector of Glasgow, Scotland, the discoverer of the mineral.

edoylerite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of cinnabar, in a mercury deposit in silicate–carbonate rock hydrothermally altered from serpentinite.
edoylerite.etymology: To honor Edward H. Oyler (1915– ), American mineral collector specializing in mercury minerals.

edscottite.occurrence: In a Ni-rich ataxite iron meteorite belonging to subgroup sLH of the IAB complex (Low-Au, High-Ni subgroup).
edscottite.etymology: Honors Edward (Ed) R.D. Scott (b. 1947), a pioneering cosmochemist at the University of Hawai‘i at Manoa, for his seminal contributions to research on meteorites.

edtollite.occurrence: A sublimate on basaltic scoria at an active volcanic fumarole.
edtollite.etymology: Honors Russian geologist and Arctic explorer Eduard Vasilievich Toll (1858-1902) for contributions to the geology and geography of Polar Siberia and islands in the Arctic Ocean.

edwardsite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized portion of a Ag-Pb-Zn metal deposit.
edwardsite.etymology: Honors Dr. Austin Burton Edwards (1909–1960), mineralogist and petrologist in the Mineragraphic Section of the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research CSIRO), Melbourne, Australia, for his contributions to the study of Australian ore deposits such as Broken Hill.

efremovite.occurrence: As crusts on burning coal mine dumps, formed by the reaction of combustion gases with carbonate rocks.
efremovite.etymology: Honors Dr. Ivan Antonovich Yefremov (1907–1972), Russian geologist and science ﬁction writer.

eggletonite.occurrence: In miarolitic pockets in nepheline syenite pegmatite.
eggletonite.etymology: To honor Dr. Richard A. Eggleton, Australian National University, Canberra, Australia.

eglestonite.occurrence: An oxidation product of other mercury minerals in mercury deposits.
eglestonite.etymology: Honors Thomas Egleston (1832–1900), Professor of Mineralogy and Metallurgy, Columbia University, New York City, New York, USA.

ehrleite.occurrence: A very rare mineral with other secondary phosphates, in the outer to intermediate zone of a complex granite pegmatite.
ehrleite.etymology: In honor of Howard Ehrle, Miles City, Montana, USA, who discovered the mineral.

eifelite.occurrence: In vesicles in contact metamorphosed basement gneiss xenoliths in leucite tephrite.
eifelite.etymology: For the locality in the Eifel district, Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany.

eirikite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in a dike of nepheline syenite pegmatite.
eirikite.etymology: Honors the Viking Eirik Raude (Eric the Red, born ~950, died ~1003), Norwegian emigrant, the discoverer of Greenland, and father of Leiv (Leif) Eirikson, for whom leifite was named.

eitelite.occurrence: An authigenic mineral in dolomitic shale and bituminous marlstone (Utah, USA); from an alkaline igneous pluton (Khibiny massif, Russia).
eitelite.etymology: Honors Wilhelm Hermann Julius Eitel (1891–1979), Director of the Institute of Silicate Research, University of Toledo, Toledo, Ohio, USA, who synthesized the compound.

ekanite.occurrence: Detrital (Sri Lanka); in a glacial erratic syenitic boulder (Tombstone Mountains, Canada); in volcanic ejecta (Case Collina, Italy).
ekanite.etymology: In honor of the mineral's discoverer, F.L.D. Ekanayake, of Colombo, Sri Lanka.

ekaterinite.occurrence: In calcite and calcite–anhydrite veins associated with a mineralized skarn.
ekaterinite.etymology: Honors Dr. Yekaterina Vladimirovna Rozhkova (1898–1979), Russian mineralogist, Research Institute of Mineral Resources, Moscow, Russia.

ekatite.occurrence: In the oxidized portion of a polymetallic sulfide mineral deposit.
ekatite.etymology: Honors Namibian mining engineer Dieter Ekat (1935-1996).

assoc_parsed: distribution from the “in den dellen”   pumice quarry

ekplexite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in fenites formed by a peralkaline fluid, as a source of Nb, reacting with a large xenolith of alumina-rich metamorphic rocks (metapelites) in agpaitic nepheline syenite.
ekplexite.etymology: After the Greek word έκπληξη meaning “surprise”, for its exotic combination of major chemical constituents.

elasmochloite.occurrence: A sublimate on scoria around an active fumarole.
elasmochloite.etymology: From the Greek words ελασμα, meaning “lamella”, and χλοη, meaning “green shoot” or “green grass”, thus alluding to elasmochloite’s green color and lamellar crystal habit.

elbaite.occurrence: In granites, granite pegmatites, and some metamorphic rocks; in high-temperature hydrothermal veins; detrital in sediments.
elbaite.etymology: From the occurrence on the Island of Elba, Italy.

elbrusite.occurrence: In spurrite zones in skarn developed in xenoliths in ignimbrite.
elbrusite.etymology: For the highest peak in Europe, Mt. Elbrus (5642 m), Northern Caucasus, Russia.

eldfellite.occurrence: As a near surface fumarolic encrustation.
eldfellite.etymology: For the first locality, the Eldfell volcano, Iceland.

eleomelanite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
eleomelanite.etymology: From the Greek eleon for ‘oil’, and melas for ‘black’, for its black color and oleaginous luster on crystal faces that is uncommon for sulfate minerals.

eleonorite.occurrence: A supergene mineral formed by solid-state oxidation of beraunite.
eleonorite.etymology: For the mine that produced the first specimens.

elgoresyite.occurrence: In a shock-induced melt vein in a chondrite meteorite. Suggested to be a potential constituent mineral in rocky planets with relatively high MgO + FeO content.
elgoresyite.etymology: Honors Dr. Ahmed El Goresy for his discoveries of shock-induced high-pressure phases in meteorites at terrestrial impact sites and contributions to our understanding of cosmoc hemical processes in the early parts of our solar system.

eliopoulosite.occurrence: In heavy mineral concentrates from massive podiform chromitite hosted in a strongly altered mantle tectonite in an ophiolite complex.
eliopoulosite.etymology: Honors Dr. Demetrios Eliopoulos (1947-2019), Institute of Geology and Mineral Exploration (IGME) and his widow, Professor Maria Eliopoulos (nee Economou, b. 1947), University of Athens, Greece, for their contributions to the knowledge of ore deposits of Greece and to the mineralogical, petrographic, and geochemical studies of ophiolites, including the Othrys complex .

eliseevite.occurrence: A late-stage, hydrothermal mineral formed by alteration of murmanite, in altered ussingite pegmatites within a layered complex of malignites, foyaites, and foidolites with lenses of poikilitic nepheline syenites in peralkaline veins in a differentiated alkaline massif.
eliseevite.etymology: Honors Nikolai Aleksandrovich Eliseev (1897-1966), Russian geologist and petrologist, Professor at Leningrad State University, for his contributions to the geology and petrology of metamorphic and alkaline complexes.

ellenbergerite.occurrence: As inclusions in pyrope porphyroblasts developed during high-pressure (25{30 kbar), medium-temperature (700 ±C{800 ±C) metamorphism of continental crustal rocks.
ellenbergerite.etymology: Honors Professor Fran» cois Ellenberger, Paris, France, for his geological work in the western Alps.

ellinaite.occurrence: In pyrometamorphic paralava (Israel) and spurite marble (Jordan). In a diamond (Brazil). Forms under highly reduced conditions at high temperatures (>1000 °C).
ellinaite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist and petrologist Ellina Vladimirovna Sokol (b. 1961) from IGM, Novosibirsk, Russia, a specialist in the studies of pyrometamorphic and combustion metamorphic rocks worldwide, including the Hatrurim Formation (Mottled Zone), Israel -Jordan.

ellingsenite.occurrence: A low-temperature mineral in vesicles in hydrothermally altered phonolite.
ellingsenite.etymology: Honors Dr. Hans Vidar Ellingsen (b. 1930), who has been chairman of the Norwegian Amateur Geological Society and who collected the first specimens.

elliottite.occurrence: Secondary in phosphate rock derived from weathered argillaceous rocks by alteration of minyulite in near-neutral solutions.
assoc_parsed: an amorphous calcium-magnesium-aluminum phosphate with the composition reported for “angastonite”
elliottite.etymology: Honors Peter Elliott (b. 1954) for his contributions to the characterization and naming of more than 30 new minerals from Australian localities (half of which he collected personally) and particularly his contributions to the descriptions of new phosphate minerals from South Australia.

ellisite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal gold deposit, in mineralized, argillaceous, carbonaceous dolostone beds.
ellisite.etymology: Honors Dr. Albert J. Ellis (1929– ), New Zealand geochemist, Chemistry Division, Department of Scientiﬁc and Industrial Research, New Zealand.

elpasolite.occurrence: Replacing ﬂuorine-bearing minerals in a quartz-microcline pegmatite (Pikes Peak, Colorado, USA); on vein quartz in a hydrothermal antimony deposit in siliciﬁed limestone (Cetine mine, Italy).
elpasolite.etymology: For El Paso County, Colorado, USA, where the mineral was found.

elpidite.occurrence: In albitized nepheline syenite and associated pegmatites, aegirine-rich granite, and fenites, in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
elpidite.etymology: From the Greek hope, named in anticipation of discovery of other interesting minerals.

eltyubyuite.occurrence: From a thermally-altered carbonate-silicate xenolith (20 m long) in ignimbrite that created sanidinite facies metamorphism (Upper Chegem Caldera).
eltyubyuite.etymology: For the historically famous Balkarian village Eltyubyu, which is located near the site from which the first specimens were collected.

elyite.occurrence: Rare in the oxidized zone of base metal sulﬁdes; may be formed in dumps and common in slags.
elyite.etymology: Honors John H. Ely, nineteenth century frontiersman and promoter of an early mining company in Nevada, USA.

embreyite.occurrence: On museum samples from the oxidized zone of gold-bearing quartz veins (Beresovsk, Russia).
embreyite.etymology: To honor Peter Godwin Embrey (1929– ), English mineralogist, British Museum (Natural History), London, England.

emeleusite.occurrence: A minor constituent of a peralkalic trachyte dike, in °ow-banded aegirine-albite-rich layers.
emeleusite.etymology: To honor Dr. Charles Henry Emeleus, University of Durham, Durham, England.

emilite.occurrence: In quartz veins cutting a metamorphosed scheelite deposit.
assoc_parsed: bismuthinite derivatives in the range krupkaite–hammarite
emilite.etymology: Honors Professor Dr. Emil Makovicky (b. 1940) for his contributions to the crystal chemistry and modular description of diverse sulfosalts families, including those from the Felbertal deposit.

emmerichite.occurrence: A high-temperature pneumatolitic mineral in cavities within alkaline basalt.
emmerichite.etymology: Honors Franz-Josef Emmerich (b. 1940), German amateur mineralogist and collector of minerals from the Eifel region.

emmonsite.occurrence: An alteration product formed from earlier tellurium minerals in the oxide zone of some hydrothermal precious metal deposits.
emmonsite.etymology: To honor Samuel Franklin Emmons (1841–1911), American economic geologist, U.S. Geological Survey.

emplectite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other sulﬁdes and sulfosalts formed at medium temperatures.
emplectite.etymology: From the Greek for interwoven or entwined; in reference to its sometimes intimate association with quartz.

empressite.occurrence: In low-temperature gold-poor hydrothermal vein deposits.
empressite.etymology: For the Empress Josephine mine, Colorado, USA.

enargite.occurrence: In hydrothermal vein deposits formed at medium temperatures. Also as a late-stage mineral in low-temperature deposits.
enargite.etymology: From the Greek for distinct, in allusion to its cleavage.

engelhauptite.occurrence: A late mineral growing in cavities in nepheline basalt.
engelhauptite.etymology: Honors the German amateur mineralogist and mineral collector Bernd Engelhaupt (b. 1946) for his contributions to the mineralogy of the Eifel region.

englishite.occurrence: In variscite nodules (Little Green Monster mine, Utah, USA); in a complex granite pegmatite (Tip Top mine, South Dakota, USA).
englishite.etymology: To honor George Letchworth English (1864–1944), New York City, New York, USA, American mineral dealer and collector.

enneasartorite.etymology: For a member of the sartorite homologous series with a nine-fold superstructure.

enstatite.occurrence: In pyroxenites, peridotites, and dunites; in ultrama¯c inclusions in alkalic olivine basalts and kimberlite; in ma¯c volcanics, rarely in felsic volcanics. Characteristic of charnockites and the granulite metamorphic facies, in regionally metamorphosed rocks and metagabbros. Common in chondrite, achondrite, and stony-iron meteorites.
enstatite.etymology: From the Greek for opponent, in allusion to its refractory nature under the blowpipe.

eosphorite.occurrence: Typically a secondary mineral in some phosphate-bearing granite pegmatites.
eosphorite.etymology: From the Greek for dawn-bearing, in allusion to the pink color.

ephesite.occurrence: In an emery deposit (Gumuch-dagh, Turkey); a minor constituent in manganese oxide ore (Postmasburg district, South Africa).
ephesite.etymology: For Ephesus, Turkey, near where it may occur.

epididymite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in nepheline syenite pegmatites.
epididymite.etymology: The pre¯x epi from the Greek for near, referring to the dimorphous relation with eudidymite.

epidote.occurrence: Characteristic of several facies of regionally metamorphosed rocks and some contaminated felsic igneous rocks; in contact zones between igneous and calcareous sedimentary rocks; from alteration of plagioclase (saussuritization).
epidote.etymology: From the Greek for increase, the base of the prism with one longer side.

epidote-sr.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal vein mineral in a tinzenite deposit in metachert (Nagakawara deposit) and in piemontite breccias (Hohnomori deposit).
epidote-sr.etymology: For its chemical composition as a member of the epidote group.

epifanovite.occurrence: A secondary low-temperature mineral formed by alteration of primary minerals in a quartz-phosphate mass ~5 m in diameter within greisenized cassiterite-bearing granodiorite.
epifanovite.etymology: Honors Porphiriy Prokopievich Epifanov, Russian geologist, the discoverer of the Këster, Ege-Khaya, and others tin deposits between 1936-1938.

epistilbite.occurrence: In cavities in basalts and gneisses.
epistilbite.etymology: From the Greek, epi for near, and the quite similar mineral stilbite.

epistolite.occurrence: A low temperature mineral in alkalic pegmatites, albitites, sodalite xenoliths, and hydrothermal veins.
epistolite.etymology: From the Greek for letter, in allusion to the flat rectangular crystal habit and white color.

epsomite.occurrence: As eﬄorescences on the walls of mines, caves, and outcrops of sulﬁde-bearing magnesian rocks; a product of evaporation at mineral springs and saline lakes; a hydration product of kieserite and langbeinite; rarely a fumarolic sublimate.
epsomite.etymology: For the occurrence at Epsom, England.

erazoite.occurrence: In a high-sulfidation, epithermal vein deposit rich in gold, copper, and arsenic, with a strong influence of meteoric waters and hosted in volcanic rocks.
erazoite.etymology: Honors Gabriel Erazo Fernández (b. 1943) a mining engineer and mineralogist. He was professor of geology, crystallography, and metallurgy at Copiapo University, Chile, and was the first director of the Mineralogical Museum of Copiapo University from its opening in 1966 until 1991.

ercitite.occurrence: In a zoned, rare-element granitic pegmatite, as an overgrowth on collinsite-fairfieldite, whitlockite, and other phosphates on a fracture surface that cuts a lithiophyllite nodule altered by strongly oxidizing, low-temperature, hydrothermal fluids.
ercitite.etymology: Honors mineralogist T. Scott Ercit (b. 1957) of the Canadian Museum of Nature, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada for his contributions to the mineralogy of granitic pegmatites.

erdite.occurrence: Found in abundance, typically associated with other sulﬁdes and ﬁne grained magnetite, in discrete, late segregations within an alkalic maﬁc diatreme (Coyote Peak, California, USA); in pegmatites in nepheline syenite (Lovozero massif, Russia).
erdite.etymology: For Dr. Richard Clarkson Erd (1924– ), American mineralogist with the U.S. Geological Survey, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound.

ericaite.occurrence: An uncommon constituent of marine evaporite deposits.
ericaite.etymology: For the typical purple color, characteristic of the heather genus Erica.

ericlaxmanite.occurrence: As complex incrustations on the surface of basalt scoria or in open pockets. Deposited directly from volcanic gas or as the result of gas-rock interactions at temperatures > 380 °C.
ericlaxmanite.etymology: Honors the Russian mineralogist, geologist, geographer, biologist and chemist Eric Laxman (1737-1796) for his contributions to the study of the natural history of Eastern Siberia.

ericssonite.occurrence: A rare mineral, embedded in a ¯ne-grained manganoan aegirine zone in well-banded tephroite-rhodonite-manganoan aegirine skarn, in a metamorphosed Fe{Mn orebody.
ericssonite.etymology: In honor of John E. Ericsson (1803{1889), Swedish-American inventor and designer of the iron-clad ship \Monitor," who was born at Lºangban, Sweden.

erikapohlite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by weathering tennantite-rich veins in the oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted, hydrothermal polymetallic deposit.
erikapohlite.etymology: Honors Erika Pohl (b. 1919) who donated her mineral collection of more than 40, 000 specimens to the Bergakademie Freiberg, Saxony, Germany, on the condition that it should be accessible to a broad public and scientifically supervised. The collection is on display in the Freudenstein Castle in the center of Freiberg.

erikjonssonite.occurrence: In late-stage, zoned veins crosscutting primary hausmannite ores.
erikjonssonite.etymology: Honors Swedish mineralogist Erik Jonsson (b. 1967), Senior Geologist, Geological Survey of Sweden, Department of Mineral Resources, and Adjunct Professor, Department of Earth Sciences, Uppsala University. Erik Jonsson has done extensive field work in both the Fennoscandian shield and Africa (including the Kombat mine).

eringaite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in metasomatic rodingite-like rocks; it forms regular growth zones and irregular spots in complex garnet crystals.
eringaite.etymology: For the Eringa River, the tributary of the Wiluy River directly across from where the first specimens were collected.

eriochalcite.occurrence: As an encrustation around fumaroles (Vesuvius, Italy); a product of weathering in a copper sulﬁde deposit in an arid climate (Quetena, Chile).
eriochalcite.etymology: From the Greek for wool and copper, for the form of aggregates at Vesuvius, Italy.

erionitek.occurrence: In basalts; in altered rhyolitic tu®s and lake-bed sediments formed by alteration of vitric ash fallen into the lakes.
erionitek.etymology: For the Greek word for wool, recalling its common appearance.

erlianite.occurrence: As coatings along fault surfaces cutting a low-grade metamorphosed volcanic-sedimentary iron formation; presumably formed in a high-pressure, low-temperature environment.
erlianite.etymology: Presumably for the town of Erlian, China.

erlichmanite.occurrence: Typically in PGM placers, likely derived from chromitites associated with ophiolites and other Alaskan-type ultramaﬁc complexes.
assoc_parsed: many other pgm alloys and sulﬁdes
erlichmanite.etymology: For Jozef Erlichman (1935– ), American electron probe analyst, Planetary Branch, NASA-Ames Research Branch, who analyzed a number of new minerals.

ernienickelite.occurrence: In an intensely laterized ultramaﬁc intrusion (Siberia, Western Australia); in the weathering zone of ultramaﬁc rocks (Kamennyy Kobchik deposit, Russia).
ernienickelite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Ernest Henry Nickel (1925– ), Canadian-Australian mineralogist with the C.S.I.R.O., Perth, Australia.

erniggliite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal deposit in dolostone.
erniggliite.etymology: In honor of Professor Emeritus Ernie Niggli (1917- ), mineralogist and petrologist, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland

ernstburkeite.occurrence: As solid inclusions in an ice core (from a depth of 576.5 m), presumably formed by the fixation of CH3SO3H on alkaline particles of marine or continental origin during long-range aerosol transport to the polar region.
ernstburkeite.etymology: Honors Ernst A.J. Burke (b. 1943), Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Netherlands, for his contributions to the mineralogy of opaque minerals and Raman spectrometry of fluid inclusions.

ernstite.occurrence: Formed by oxidation of eosphorite in a granite pegmatite (Farm Davib-East, Namibia).
ernstite.etymology: To honor Dr. Theodor K.H. Ernst (1904–1983), Professor of Mineralogy, Erlangen University, Erlangen, Germany.

ershovite.occurrence: In unweathered ultra-agpaitic pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
ershovite.etymology: For Professor Vadim Victorovich Ershov (1939{1989), of the Moscow Mining Institute, Moscow, Russia.

erssonite.occurrence: In a late-stage, low-temperature assemblage likely formed by hydrothermal alteration in cavities of magnetite-bearing dolomitic rock.
assoc_parsed: members of the magnetite-magnesioferrite solid solution series
erssonite.etymology: Honors chemist and amateur mineralogist, Dr. Anders Ersson (b. 1971), Senior Engineer, Materials Technology section at Scania AB, Södertälje, Sweden, who collected the studied material.

ertixiite.occurrence: As linings of miarolitic cavities in a Ta-Nb-Be-bearing granite pegmatite.
ertixiite.etymology: For the Ertixi River, near the occurrence in China.

erythrite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxide zone of some Co–Ni–As-bearing mineral deposits.
erythrite.etymology: From the Greek for red, for its characteristic deep crimson color.

erythrosiderite.occurrence: As sublimates around fumaroles (Vesuvius, Italy); rimming rinneite in bedded salt deposits (Stassfurt, Germany; Kansk-Taseev depression, Russia).
erythrosiderite.etymology: From the Greek for red and iron, in allusion to its color and composition.

erzwiesite.occurrence: In hydrothermal vein type Ag-Pb-Zn deposits.
erzwiesite.etymology: For the district in Austria where the studied samples were collected.

eskebornite.etymology: For the Eskeborn adit, Tilkerode, Germany, where ﬁrst discovered.

eskimoite.etymology: For the Eskimos, early settlers of Greenland.

eskolaite.occurrence: In chromium-rich tremolite skarns, metaquartzites, and chlorite veins (Outokumpu, Finland); on greywacke pebbles in a glacial boulder clay deposit (Callowhill Upper, Ireland); as pebbles in streams (Merume River, Guyana); a very rare component in chondrite meteorites.
eskolaite.etymology: Honors Professor Pentti Eelis Eskola (1883–1964), of the University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland.

espadaite.etymology: From the Spanish, espada, for ‘sword’, in allusion to the shape of the crystals.

esperanzaite.occurrence: Very rare from a tin-bearing rhyolite.
esperanzaite.etymology: For the La Esperanza mine, Mexico, from which the mineral was collected.

esperite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
esperite.etymology: To honor Professor Esper Signius Larsen, Jr. (1879{1961), American petrologist and mineralogist, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

esquireite.occurrence: Formed by low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of sanbornite, during contact metamorphism of Ba-rich sediments.
esquireite.etymology: Named for the Esquire #1 claim, where the first specimens were collected.

esseneite.occurrence: A high-temperature, low-pressure, oxidized and quenched crystallization product derived from fused sediments contiguous to naturally combusted coal seams.
esseneite.etymology: For Dr. Eric J. Essene, Professor at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA, and discoverer of the ¯rst specimens.

ettringite.occurrence: In metamorphosed limestone near igneous contacts or in xenoliths; as weathering crusts on larnite rocks (Hatrurim Formation, Israel).
ettringite.etymology: For the occurrence near Ettringen, Germany.

eucairite.occurrence: Widely distributed in selenium deposits of hydrothermal origin; locally abundant with other selenides.
eucairite.etymology: From the Greek for opportunity, because it was discovered shortly after discovery of the element selenium.

euchlorine.occurrence: A rare sublimate around volcanic fumaroles.
euchlorine.etymology: From the Greek for pale green, in allusion to the typical color.

euchroite.occurrence: A very rare mineral in the oxidized zone of some copper-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
euchroite.etymology: From the Greek for beautiful color.

euclase.occurrence: The product of decomposition of beryl in pegmatites, and in low-temperature alpine veins.
euclase.etymology: From the Greek for easily and fracture regarding its perfect cleavage.

eucryptite.etymology: From the Greek for well and concealed, in reference to its occurrence as intimate intergrowths with albite.

eudialyte.occurrence: In nepheline syenites, alkalic granites, and associated pegmatites; may be a major constituent, of both magmatic and late-stage pneumatolytic origin.
eudialyte.etymology: From the Greek for easily and dissolved, in allusion to its ready dissolution in acids. All rights reserved.
