eudidymite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in alkalic nepheline syenite pegmatites.
eudidymite.etymology: From the Greek for well and twinned, in allusion to its common occurrence in twins.

eugenite.occurrence: In low-grade copper sulﬁde ore in black shale and carbonate rocks (Lubin mine, Poland); in cuprite (Bisbee, Arizona, USA).
eugenite.etymology: To honor Professor Eugen Friedrich Stumpﬂ (1935– ), Austrian mineralogist, Mining University, Leoben, Austria, for his studies of noble metal compounds.

eugsterite.occurrence: As evaporative crusts in carbonate-poor soil, playa sediment and around an active boron-rich spring.
eugsterite.etymology: Honors Professor Hans Peter Eugster (1927–1985), Swiss–American mineralogist, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland, USA, who studied the mineralogy of saline lakes.

eulytine.etymology: From the Greek for good and dissolved, in reference to its low point of fusion.

eurekadumpite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of quartz-sulfide ores containing tellurides (mostly hessite) in small cavities and in fractures in quartz.
eurekadumpite.etymology: Reflects the fact that the first samples were found on the dumps of the Centennial Eureka mine. The mineral name is also related to the Greek word eureka -“I have found it” – in a dump—an allusion to the important role old mine dumps have played in the discovery of new minerals .

euxenite-y.occurrence: From granite pegmatites; as a component of detrital black sands.
euxenite-y.etymology: From the Greek for hospitable, in allusion to the wide variety of rare elements in its composition.

evansite.occurrence: In a graphite deposit (Gross-Tresny, Czech Republic); in graphitic gneiss (Vatoinandry district, Madagascar); in coal seams (Alabama, USA); a coating in caves, the phosphate derived from guano.
evansite.etymology: In honor of Brooke Evans (1797–1862), English mining geologist, Birmingham, England, who provided the ﬁrst specimens.

evdokimovite.etymology: Honors Mikhail Dmitrievich Evdokimov (1940-2010), Department of Mineralogy, St. Petersburg State University, Russia.

eveite.occurrence: Very rare, in ﬁssures in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L˚ angban, Sweden); in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Sterling Hill, New Jersey, USA).
eveite.etymology: Named for the biblical Eve, in contrast to adamite, with which it is isostructural.

evenkite.occurrence: An accessory mineral associated with coal; in geodes associated with a vein cutting vesicular welded tuff (Evenkia district, Russia).
evenkite.etymology: For the locality in the Evenkia district, Lower Tunguska River, Siberia, Russia.

eveslogite.occurrence: In a veinlet that cuts nepheline syenite in an alkaline massif.
eveslogite.etymology: Alludes to the locality, Mt. Eveslogchorr.

assoc_parsed: second scoria cone of the northern breakthrough of the great tolbachik fissure eruption

ewaldite.occurrence: From drill core into trona beds in dolomitic marlstone (Green River Formation, Wyoming, USA); from carbonatites and hydrothermal veins in alkaline igneous rocks (Kola Peninsula, Russia).
ewaldite.etymology: Honors Professor Paul Peter Ewald (1888–1985), German physicist and crystallographer, founder of Zeits. Krist. and Acta Cryst., Polytechnic Institute of New York, Brooklyn, New York, USA.

ewingite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by postmining oxidation of primary uraninite in a wet environment on a damp wall in an abandoned underground mine.
ewingite.etymology: Honors Rodney C. Ewing (b. 1946) mineralogist and material scientist focused on the properties of nuclear materials at Stanford University, California, USA.

eylettersite.occurrence: An alteration product of thorian crandallite in a phosphate-rich granite pegmatite.
eylettersite.etymology: For the wife of the discoverer, Mme. Van Wambeke.

eyselite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by groundwater in a vug on a single specimen of renierite-germanite-tennantite ore from the oxidation zone above a polymetallic sulfide mineral deposit.
eyselite.etymology: Honors Professor Walter Hans Eysel (1935-1999) Professor of Crystallography at the Ruprecht-Karls-Universität, Heidelberg, Germany, for his studies of germinates and his contributions to the X-ray Powder Diffraction File.

ezcurrite.occurrence: Probably formed from solutions derived from dehydration of borax in a discordant deposit in folded playa siltstones and sandstones.
ezcurrite.etymology: Honors Juan Manuel de Ezcurra (1900–1970), Manager of the Compania Productora de Boratos, S.A., owner of the Tincalayu deposit, Argentina.

eztlite.occurrence: Very rare in oxidized ore in a matrix of intensely siliciﬁed and brecciated rhyolite vitrophyre cemented by drusy quartz and carrying pyrite and tellurides.
eztlite.etymology: From the Nahua language for blood, in allusion to the color.

fabriesite.occurrence: In serpentinized peridotite and related to the hydration of trinepheline during the late stage of metamorphism along veins in a jadeite deposit.
fabriesite.etymology: Honors Jacques Fabriés (1932-2000), professor of Mineralogy, National Natural History Museum, Paris, France, where he served as chair of Mineralogy from 1969 until 1998, and was the Museum director (1990-1994).

faheyite.occurrence: A rare late-stage secondary mineral in a complex granite pegmatite (Sapucaia mine, Brazil).
faheyite.etymology: Honoring Joseph John Fahey (1901–1980), American analytical chemist, U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C., USA.

fahleite.occurrence: On oxidized tennantite–chalcocite ore from a deep oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
fahleite.etymology: In honor of Rolf Fahle (1943– ), Munich, Germany, mineral dealer specializing in Tsumeb minerals, who supplied the specimen from which the species was described.

fairbankite.occurrence: Very rare on the mine dump from a hydrothermal Au-Te-bearing ore deposit.
fairbankite.etymology: Honors Nathaniel Kellogg Fairbank (1829-1903), who organized the company that developed the Grand Central lode, Tombstone, Arizona, USA.

fairchildite.occurrence: Formed from fused wood ash in partially burned trees.
fairchildite.etymology: Honors John Giﬀord Fairchild (1882–1965), analytical chemist, U.S. Geological Survey.

fairfieldite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in granite pegmatites.
assoc_parsed: a host of other fe–mn phosphates
fairfieldite.etymology: For Fairﬁeld Co., Connecticut, USA, within which is Branchville, the original locality.

faizievite.occurrence: In a quartz-pectolite boulder in the moraine of a glacier eroding an alkaline massif.
faizievite.etymology: Honors Faiziev Abdulkhak Radzhabovitch (b 1938), professor and member-correspondent of the Academy of Sciences, Republic of Tajikistan.

falcondoite.occurrence: In garnierite veins which cut an extensive laterite, associated with a serpentinized harzburgite massif (near Bonao, Dominican Republic).
falcondoite.etymology: For the familiar name \Falcondo" of the company operating the mine in the Dominican Republic where the mineral was ¯rst found.

falgarite.occurrence: Fumarolic, formed directly from gas emitted by a natural underground coal fire.
falgarite.etymology: After the Falgar, an ancient Sogdian name for an area around the Zeravshan riverhead.

falottaite.struct_group: Not in a structural group, Oxalate
falottaite.occurrence: Presumably from reaction of humus and oxalic acids (from plants) with manganese minerals in synsedimentary lenses of manganese ore in radiolaritic rocks of an ophiolithic zone.
falottaite.etymology: For its type locality, the Falotta mine, Switzerland.

falsterite.occurrence: Formed as the result of secondary alteration of primary triphylite and associated sphalerite in the core-margin of a well-zoned beryl-phosphate granitic pegmatite.
falsterite.etymology: Honors Alexander U. Falster (b. 1952), a Scientific Research Technologist, Department of Earth and Environmental Science, University of New Orleans, Louisiana, USA, in recognition for his research on pegmatites and pegmatite minerals.

famatinite.occurrence: In copper deposits formed at low to medium temperatures.
famatinite.etymology: For the locality, Sierra de Famatina, Argentina.

fangite.occurrence: In a sediment-hosted disseminated gold deposit, in sulﬁde-rich carbonaceous ore, probably formed by alteration of Tl-As-rich sulfosalts or sulﬁdes.
fangite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Jen-Ho Fang (1929– ), crystal chemist, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA.

farneseite.occurrence: In vugs between interlocking sanidine within a syenitic pyroclastic rock.
farneseite.etymology: For the locality, Farnese, that produced the first specimens.

farringtonite.occurrence: A rare component in pallasite meteorites, rimming and cementing olivine nodules.
farringtonite.etymology: To honor Dr. Oliver Cummings Farrington (1864–1933), Curator of Geology, Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago, Illinois, USA, an authority on meteorites.

fassinaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the weathering zone of a polymetallic hydrothermal deposit.
fassinaite.etymology: Honors Bruno Fassina (b. 1943), an Italian mineral collector who found the first samples at the Trentini mine.

faujasite-ca.occurrence: Rare, in vesicles of basalts, phonolites, and tu®s; formed by palagonization or authigenically.
faujasite-ca.etymology: Honoring Barth¶elemy Faujas de Saint Fond (1741{1819), French mineralogist and vulcanologist.

faujasite-mg.occurrence: Rare, in vesicles of basalts, phonolites, and tu®s; formed by palagonization or authigenically.
faujasite-mg.etymology: Honoring Barth¶elemy Faujas de Saint Fond (1741{1819), French mineralogist and vulcanologist.

faujasite-na.occurrence: Rare, in vesicles of basalts, phonolites, and tu®s; formed by palagonization or authigenically.
faujasite-na.etymology: Honoring Barth¶elemy Faujas de Saint Fond (1741{1819), French mineralogist and vulcanologist.

faustite.occurrence: In argillized shales associated with copper mineralization (Copper King mine, Nevada, USA).
faustite.etymology: To honor Dr. George Tobias Faust (1908–1985), mineralogist and geologist, U.S. Geological Survey.

favreauite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by the oxidation of a selenide-bearing hydrothermal vein hosted by sandstones and shales.
favreauite.etymology: Honors Georges Favreau, amateur mineralogist and professional engineer, President of the Association Française de Microminéralogie (1993-2007) and co-discoverer of this new mineral, for his contributions to mineralogy.

fayalite.occurrence: In ultrama¯c volcanic and plutonic rocks, less commonly in felsic plutonic rocks; rarely in granite pegmatite; in lithophysae in obsidian. In metamorphosed iron-rich sediments and impure carbonate rocks.
fayalite.etymology: After Faial (Fayal) Island in the Azores, thought to occur in a local volcanic rock, but probably obtained from slag carried as ship's ballast.

fedorite.occurrence: In ¯ne veinlets in fenitized sandstone (Turii Peninsula, Russia).
fedorite.etymology: For Evgraf Stepanovich Fedorov (1853{1919), eminent Russian crystallographer, Mining Institute, St. Petersburg, Russia.

fedorovskite.occurrence: In veinlets in a skarn-type boron deposit.
fedorovskite.etymology: Honors Nikolai Mikhailovich Fedorovskii (1886–1956), eminent crystallographer and founder of the Russian Research Institute of Mineral Resources, Moscow, Russia.

fehrite.occurrence: Secondary oxidation product in tetrahedrite veinlets.
fehrite.etymology: Honors Karl Thomas Fehr (1954 -2014), Professor of Mineralogy, Department of Geo- and Environmental Sciences, Ludwig-Maximilians-University, Munich, Germany.

feiite.occurrence: From shock metamorphism in Martian meteorites. At the rim of a transformed ilmenite-ülvospinel grain.

feinglosite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral, in a cavity in chalcocite, from an oxidized zone in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
feinglosite.etymology: To honor Dr. Mark N. Feinglos (1948– ), American medical researcher and mineral collector specializing in Tsumeb minerals, Durham, North Carolina, USA, who ﬁrst noted the mineral.

feitknechtite.occurrence: In a mixture with hausmannite, formed by supergene oxidation of and replacing earlier pyrochroite.
feitknechtite.etymology: To honor Dr. Walter Feitknecht (1899–?), Swiss Professor of Chemistry, University of Berne, Berne, Switzerland, who synthesized the compound.

feklichevite.occurrence: In a pegmatoidal cancrinite syenite vein in a phlogopite mine.
feklichevite.etymology: Honors Vladimir Georgevich Feklichev (1933-1999), mineralogist and crystallographer, author of Diagnostic Constants of Minerals (1992).

felbertalite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal tungsten deposit in amphibolites and felsic gneisses, in discordant quartz veins (Felbertal mine, Austria); in a copper deposit in skarn, developed at the contact between a granodiorite complex with quartz sandstone and slate hornfels (Funiushan deposit, China).
felbertalite.etymology: For the valley of Felbertal, Austria, in which the mineral was found.

felsobanyaite.occurrence: A rare product of oxidation of marcasite ores.
felsobanyaite.etymology: For Baia Sprie, Romania (formerly Fels˝ ob´ anya, Hungary).

fenaksite.occurrence: In pegmatites associated with an ijolite-urtite intrusion in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
fenaksite.etymology: For Fe, Na, K, Si in the composition.

fencooperite.occurrence: In gillespite-rich zones in sanbornite-quartz lenses in low-grade metasedimentary rocks.
fencooperite.etymology: Honors mineral collector Joseph Fenimore (“Fen”) Cooper, Jr. (b. 1937), of Santa Cruz, California, USA, who helped collect the samples in which the new phase was identified.

fengchengite.occurrence: In agpaitic nepheline syenite and pegmatite, crystallized directly from a REE-, U-, Th-, and Zr-rich alkaline magma enriched in volatile components.
fengchengite.etymology: For Fengcheng City, China, near the type locality.

feodosiyite.occurrence: As sublimates on basaltic scoria near a volcanic fumarole vent (~100 °C.).
feodosiyite.etymology: Honors Feodosiy Nikolaevich Chernyshev (1856-1914), Russian geologist, Academician of the Russian Academy of Sciences and Director of Russian Geological Committee (1903-1914).

ferberite.occurrence: In high-temperature hydrothermal veins, greisens, and granitic pegmatites; also residual in alluvial and eluvial deposits.
ferberite.etymology: Honors Moritz Rudolph Ferber (1805–1875), amateur mineralogist, Gera, Germany.

ferchromide.occurrence: In quartz veins within brecciated amphibolites and schist.
ferchromide.etymology: For the chemical composition, FERrum, iron, and CHROMium.

ferdowsiite.occurrence: In barite-quartz lenses in a metamorphosed strataform volcanogenic massive sulfide deposit.
ferdowsiite.etymology: Honors Ferdowsi Tousi (935-1020), the great Persian poet for his endeavors to preserve the national identity, language and heritage of his homeland.

fergusonite-ce.occurrence: In a carbonatite (Novopoltavsk massif, Russia); in magnesium-rich skarn of the outer granite contact zone of a carbonatite-derived dolomitic marble (Bayan Obo, China).
fergusonite-ce.etymology: For its relation to fergusonite-(Y), and its dominant cerium content.

fergusonite-nd.occurrence: In veinlets in a carbonatite-derived dolomitic marble.
fergusonite-nd.etymology: For its relation to fergusonite-(Y), and its dominant neodymium content.

fergusonite-y.occurrence: Typical of rare-earth-bearing granite pegmatites; in placers.
fergusonite-y.etymology: Honors Robert Ferguson (1767–1840), landowner, politician, and mineral collector, of Raith, near Kirkaldy, Scotland, and for its predominant yttrium content.

ferhodsite.occurrence: In mineral separates from dunite (Nizhniy Tagil ultramafic massif) and Au-PGEbearing alluvial placer deposits (Konder and along the River Seyba). In grains of Os-Ir-Ru alloy formed from fractionated Fe-Ni-Cu-melt enriched in the PGE. Likely the product of metasomatic replacement of magmatic minerals during serpentinization of ultramafic rocks.
assoc_parsed: commonly mantled and corroded by chengdeite
ferhodsite.etymology: From the first letters of three of its main chemical elements, Fe (iron), Rhodium, and Sulfur.

fermiite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from post-mining oxidation of primary uraninite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, bornite, and covellite deposited as replacement of wood and other organic material and as disseminations in the enclosing sandstone.
fermiite.etymology: Honors Italian-American theoretical and experimental physicist Enrico Fermi (1901-1954), well known for his work for the Manhattan Project during World War II.

fermorite.occurrence: A rare mineral in veinlets through a manganese deposit.
fermorite.etymology: Honors Dr. Lewis Leigh Fermor (1880–1954), former Director of the Geological Survey of India.

fernandinite.occurrence: In a rich vanadium deposit in ﬁssures that cut red shales and that were probably ﬁlled by a remobilized asphaltite deposit.
fernandinite.etymology: For Eulagio E. Fernandini, formerly an owner of the Minasragra, Peru deposit.

feroxyhyte.occurrence: In sea-ﬂoor Fe–Mn concretions. As cement and coatings on clasts in chemically reduced, poorly drained soils and sediments, formed by the rapid oxidation of ferrous compounds.
feroxyhyte.etymology: For the principal components, iron (FERrum), OXYgen, and HYdroxyl, in its composition.

ferraioloite.occurrence: A secondary phase in sugary pegmatite.
ferraioloite.etymology: Honors James (Jim) Anthony Ferraiolo (1947-2014), author of A Systematic Classification of Nonsilicate Minerals (Bulletin 172 of the American Museum of Natural History, 1982).

ferrarisite.occurrence: A post-mine low-temperature reaction product of carbonate gangue with arsenical solutions derived from arsenic (Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, France).
ferrarisite.etymology: To honor Professor Giovanni Ferraris (1937– ), Institute of Mineralogy, Crystallography and Geochemistry, University of Turin, Turin, Italy, who worked on crystal structures of several arsenate minerals from Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, France.

ferri-fluoro-katophorite.etymology: Signifies an amphibole of the katophorite group with Fe3+ in the C site and fluorine greater than OH and/or Cl in the W site.

ferri-fluoro-leakeite.etymology: Signifies an amphibole of the katophorite group with Fe3+ in the C site and fluorine greater than OH and/or Cl in the W site.

ferri-kaersutite.occurrence: In an ultramafic (spinel-bearing lherzolite) mantle xenolith in alkaline mafic rock.
ferri-kaersutite.etymology: For an amphibole with sodium and calcium dominant in the A and B sites respectively, ferric iron in the C site and O2 - dominant in the W site.

ferri-mottanaite-ce.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in feldspathoid-bearing alkali-syenitic pyroclastic ejecta.
ferri-mottanaite-ce.etymology: Honors Annibale Mottana, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Roma Tre, Italy, for his leadership and support of investigations and cataloguing of the Latium minerals, during which the first sample was found; a suffix indicates the dominant REE, a prefix, ferri, for dominant Fe3+.

ferri-obertiite.occurrence: From vesicles in silicate veins within basaltic scoria.
ferri-obertiite.etymology: For an oxo-amphibole with Fe3+ dominant over Fe2+ in the C site.

ferri-winchite.occurrence: In veins cutting pyroxene fenite in an alkaline igneous complex.
ferri-winchite.etymology: As the Fe3+ analog of winchite.

ferriakasakaite-ce.occurrence: In a manganese deposit in metasedimentary rocks.
ferriakasakaite-ce.etymology: A prefix identifies the dominant cation at the M(1) site (other than Al), and a suffix for the dominant REE at the A(2) site in a member of the group with A(1) = Ca and M(3) = Mn2+ which is “akasakaite” (honoring Masahide Akasaka, professor of mineralogy at the Shimane University)

ferriakasakaite-la.occurrence: In tephroite-calcite veinlets in a stratiform Fe-Mn deposit. In volcanic ejecta (Eifel).
ferriakasakaite-la.etymology: Honors Professor Masahide Akasaka (b. 1950) for his study of minerals occurring in Mn-Fe ore deposits, particularly the natural and synthetic epidote-supergroup minerals. The prefix indicates Fe3+ dominant in the M1 site.The suffix indicates the dominant rare earth element. * continues on next page * Mineralogical Society of America Handbook of Mineralogy Revised 8/9/2016

ferriallanite-ce.occurrence: Of metasomatic origin in alkaline granitic pegmatite.
ferriallanite-ce.etymology: The prefix, ferri, indicates that the mineral is the Fe3+ analog of allanite-(Ce).

ferriallanite-la.occurrence: In a void in a sanidinite xenolith in pumice.
ferriallanite-la.etymology: The suffix identifies the La-analogue of ferriallanite-(Ce). Honors Thomas Allan (1777- 1833), Scottish mineralogist who discovered the species. The prefix, ferri, indicates Fe3+ > Al.

ferriandrosite-la.occurrence: In tephroite-calcite veinlets cutting a stratiform ferromanganese deposit.
ferriandrosite-la.etymology: For a member of the allanite group with dominant Mn2+ in the A1 site and Fe3+ in the M1 site, and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

ferribushmakinite.occurrence: A low-temperature, secondary mineral in the oxidized portion of a quartz vein containing argentiferous galena, sphalerite and pyrite, and cutting phosphatic argillite.
ferribushmakinite.etymology: Signifies the Fe3+ analog of bushmakinite.

ferricerite-la.occurrence: A late-stage, low-temperature secondary phase in a symmetrically zoned, aegirinenatrolite-microcline vein in gneissose foyaite.
ferricerite-la.etymology: The prefix, ferri, indicates dominant Fe3+ in the M site of a member of the cerite group and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element. Formerly cerite-(La).

ferricopiapite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed typically by the weathering and oxidation of iron sulﬁde in a wide range of rock types, preserved in arid climates.
ferricopiapite.etymology: For the ferric iron member of the copiapite group.

ferricoronadite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins that cut metamorphic rocks in an orogenic complex.
ferricoronadite.etymology: For a member of the coronadite group with Fe3+ as the major charge-compensating octahedral cation instead of Mn3+.

ferrierite-k.occurrence: In seams and vesicles in deeply weathered basalts, °ow breccias, and andesites; in tu®aceous sediments.
ferrierite-k.etymology: For Dr. Walter Frederick Ferrier (1865{1950), geologist and mining engineer with the Canadian Geological Survey.

ferrierite-mg.occurrence: In seams and vesicles in deeply weathered basalts, °ow breccias, and andesites; in tu®aceous sediments.
ferrierite-mg.etymology: For Dr. Walter Frederick Ferrier (1865{1950), geologist and mining engineer with the Canadian Geological Survey.

ferrierite-na.occurrence: In seams and vesicles in deeply weathered basalts, °ow breccias, and andesites; in tu®aceous sediments.
ferrierite-na.etymology: For Dr. Walter Frederick Ferrier (1865{1950), geologist and mining engineer with the Canadian Geological Survey.

ferrierite-nh4.occurrence: In seams and vesicles in deeply weathered basalts, °ow breccias, and andesites; in tu®aceous sediments.
ferrierite-nh4.etymology: For Dr. Walter Frederick Ferrier (1865{1950), geologist and mining engineer with the Canadian Geological Survey.

ferrihydrite.occurrence: Widespread in the soluble fraction of soils and weathered rock. In precipitates around cold and hot springs, especially those supporting iron-metabolizing bacteria; in acid mine eﬄuent.
ferrihydrite.etymology: For FERRIc iron in its composition, and a HYDRated mineral.

ferrilotharmeyerite.occurrence: Very rare, on museum specimens from a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
ferrilotharmeyerite.etymology: As the ferric iron analog of lotharmeyerite.

ferrimolybdite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of hydrothermal vein and porphyry-type molybdenum-bearing deposits.
ferrimolybdite.etymology: For the essential chemical components, FERRIc iron and MOLYBDate anionic group.

ferrinatrite.occurrence: An oxidation product of iron sulﬁdes, typically in arid regions; rarely fumarolic.
ferrinatrite.etymology: For the essential chemical components, FERRIc iron and sodium, NATRium.

ferriperbøeite-ce.occurrence: In crystal aggregates, largely replacing cerite-(Ce), in a Fe-Cu-REE skarn deposit.
ferriperbøeite-ce.etymology: By analogy to IMA nomenclature for the epidote supergroup, it recognizes a member of the epidote-törnebohmite polysomatic series and emphasizes the relationship with perbøeite-(Ce).

ferriperbøeite-la.occurrence: Nodules of the deposit have a contact metasomatic origin, probably formed during fenitization of granitic pegmatites in the exocontact of an alkaline intrusion.
ferriperbøeite-la.etymology: The suffix indicates the La-analogue of ferriperbøeite-(Ce).

ferriprehnite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in druses developed in hydrothermally altered dolerite .
ferriprehnite.etymology: The prefix indicates the Fe3+ analogue of prehnite.

ferripyrophyllite.etymology: Presumably for its FERRIc iron content and relation to pyrophyllite.

ferrisanidine.occurrence: A sublimate around an active volcanic fumarole (Russia). In lamproite (USA).
ferrisanidine.etymology: The prefix indicates an analogue of sanidine with essential Fe3+ > Al.

ferrisepiolite.occurrence: In late-stage veinlets cutting copper-sulfide ores hosted in layered hedenbergiteandradite-actinolite-vesuvianite contact metamorphic rocks (skarns).
ferrisepiolite.etymology: As the Fe3+-dominant analog of sepiolite.

ferrisicklerite.occurrence: Formed by late hydrothermal alteration or weathering of triphylite-lithiophilite in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
ferrisicklerite.etymology: For its dominant ferric iron content and relation to sicklerite.

ferristrunzite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in argillaceous and clastic sediments, probably as an oxidation product of strunzite (Blaton, Belgium).
ferristrunzite.etymology: For ferric iron in the composition and its relation to strunzite.

ferrisurite.occurrence: In an oxidized lead deposit in contact metamorphosed impure limestone, as an oxidation product of silicates proximate to galena.
ferrisurite.etymology: For a predominance of Fe3+ over Al and its relation to surite.

ferrisymplesite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a Co–Ni sulﬁde deposit (Hudson Bay mine, Canada); in the oxidized zone of a polymetallic hydrothermal ore deposit (Neubulach, Germany).
ferrisymplesite.etymology: For its ferric iron content and supposed relation to symplesite.

ferrivauxite.occurrence: Formed by oxidation of primary fluorapatite and other phosphates in a hydrothermal tin deposit.
ferrivauxite.etymology: Emphasizes that the mineral is an oxidized equivalent (ferric analog) of vauxite. The latter honors George Vaux Jr (1863-1927), American lawyer and mineral collector.

ferro-ferri-hornblende.etymology: Signifies an amphibole in the compositional range of hornblende with essential Fe2+ > Fe3+ and in the C structural site.

ferro-ferri-nybøite.occurrence: The earliest mineral in an igneous microbreccia in an alkaline syenite-gabbro complex .
ferro-ferri-nybøite.etymology: Signifies an amphibole in the compositional range of nybøite with a dominance of Fe 2+ and Fe3+ substituting for Mg and Al respectively.

ferro-fluoro-edenite.occurrence: In cavities in volcanic ejecta probably crystallized during a late-stage hydrothermal phase.
ferro-fluoro-edenite.etymology: Prefixes indicate the Fe2+ analogue of edenite with fluorine dominant in the W site.

ferro-fluoro-pedrizite.occurrence: In cavities in volcanic ejecta probably crystallized during a late-stage hydrothermal phase.
ferro-fluoro-pedrizite.etymology: Prefixes indicate the Fe2+ analogue of edenite with fluorine dominant in the W site.

ferro-obertiite.occurrence: As metasomatic reaction products in lithic-wacke sandstone fragments in an alkali diatreme.
ferro-obertiite.etymology: To conform to IMA nomenclature for a ferrous (ferro)-dominant analog of oberite.

ferro-papikeite.etymology: The prefix identifies an amphibole of the papikeite group with Fe2+ dominant in the C site. Honors James J. Papike (1937-2020), America crystallographer and geochemist whose work catalyzed renewed interest in amphiboles in the 1960s and 1970s.

ferro-pedrizite.occurrence: In veinlets associated with the metasomatism of spodumene-microcline pegmatite hosted by marble.
ferro-pedrizite.etymology: As the Fe2+-dominant analogue of pedrizite.

ferro-tschermakite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in granitic pegmatite in a batholith. In a variety of metamorphic rocks (amphibolite, metacarbonate, schist, gneiss).
ferro-tschermakite.etymology: For ferrous iron in its composition and relation to tschermakite.

ferroactinolite.occurrence: In iron-rich greenschist and blueschist facies metamorphic rocks; in metamorphosed iron formations; as part of a vein assemblage cutting Ca-Fe-Si tactites.
ferroactinolite.etymology: For ferrous iron in its composition and similarity to actinolite.

ferroalluaudite.occurrence: From zoned granite pegmatites; in phosphatic nodules.
ferroalluaudite.etymology: For its dominant content of ferrous iron and relation to alluaudite.

ferroaxinite.occurrence: In low- to high-grade regionally metamorphosed rocks, in contact metamorphosed rocks, and in pegmatites.
ferroaxinite.etymology: From the Greek for axe, referring to the common crystal shape, and for dominant FERROan iron, in a mineral of the axinite group.

ferrobarroisite.occurrence: A primary mineral in some alkalic granites and syenite ring complexes; from blueschist facies metavolcanic rocks.
ferrobarroisite.etymology: For ferroan iron in its composition and similarity to barroisite.

ferroberaunite.etymology: Prefix indicates the Fe2+-analogue of zincoberaunite.

ferrobobfergusonite.etymology: Prefix, ferro, identifies the iron-dominant analog of bobfergusonite.

ferrobustamite.occurrence: Surrounding chert nodules in a skarn in dolostone (Isle of Skye, Scotland).
ferrobustamite.etymology: For FERROan iron in its composition and its relation to bustamite.

ferrocarpholite.occurrence: In quartz veins in blueschists of low metamorphic grade, formed from felsic tu®s at about 250 ±C and 3 kbar.
ferrocarpholite.etymology: The FERROus iron analogue of carpholite.

ferrochiavennite.occurrence: A late hydrothermal stage mineral in alkaline syenite pegmatite.
ferrochiavennite.etymology: As the iron (ferro) analog of chiavennite.

ferrocolumbite.occurrence: An accessory constituent of granite pegmatites; rarely in carbonatites; a detrital mineral in placer deposits.
ferrocolumbite.etymology: For iron (FERRum), and COLUMBia, for America, source of the ﬁrst specimens. All rights reserved.
