ferroedenite.occurrence: An early or deuteric phase replacing pyroxene in syenitic ring complexes; from medium-grade metamorphic amphibolites and gneisses; from plutonic igneous rocks.
ferroedenite.etymology: For its high ferrous iron content and relation to edenite.

ferroericssonite.occurrence: Along cleavage planes of altered gillespite in quartz-sanbornite veins.
ferroericssonite.etymology: As the Fe2+ analogue of ericssonite.

ferrofettelite.etymology: The prefix indicates the Fe-analogue of fettelite.

ferrogedrite.etymology: For ferrous iron in its composition and similarity to gedrite.

ferroglaucophane.occurrence: In metamorphic rocks of the high-pressure, low-temperature blueschist facies, commonly derived from either siliceous sedimentary, alkalic basaltic, or felsic volcanic predecessors.
ferroglaucophane.etymology: For its high ferrous iron content and similarity to glaucophane.

ferrohexahydrite.occurrence: In oxidized ore-bearing sandstone (Soﬁya mine, Ukraine); a dehydration product of melanterite in drill cores (northeastern Tatarstan, Russia).
ferrohexahydrite.etymology: As a ferrous iron sulfate with six essential water molecules per formula unit.

ferrohornblende.occurrence: From granites, granodiorites, and metabasalts; common in amphibolites and schists. As reaction rims on ferroan hedenbergite.
ferrohornblende.etymology: For its ferrous iron content and from the German for horn and to deceive, in allusion to its similarity to valuable minerals in ores.

ferroindialite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed pelitic xenolith in alkaline basalt.
ferroindialite.etymology: As the iron-dominant (ferro) analog of indialite.

ferrokaersutite.etymology: For its high ferrous iron composition and similarity to kaersutite.

ferrokentbrooksite.occurrence: A late-stage phase in agpaitic pegmatite dikes in nepheline syenite associated with an alkaline intrusive complex.
ferrokentbrooksite.etymology: A prefix, ferro, indicates the Fe2+-dominant analog of kentbrooksite.

ferrokesterite.occurrence: In greisen-bordered sulﬁde veins in granite.
ferrokesterite.etymology: For its content of iron, ferrum, and relation to kesterite.

ferrokinoshitalite.occurrence: In massive Pb-Zn-Cu-Ag sulfide orebodies in banded iron formation that underwent high-grade metamorphism.
ferrokinoshitalite.etymology: Prefix, ferro, indicates the Fe2+-dominant analog of kinoshitalite.

ferromerrillite.occurrence: An accessory phase in the basaltic and olivine-phyric subgroups of shergottite meteorites.

ferronickelplatinum.occurrence: In the heavy fraction of Quaternary alluvial deposits associated with ultramaﬁcs from an ophiolite belt (Northern Pekul’nei River, Russia);
ferronickelplatinum.etymology: For iron, FERRum, NICKEL, and PLATINUM in the composition.

ferronigerite-2n1s.occurrence: In quartz-sillimanite rocks closely associated with tin-bearing granite pegmatites (Egbe district, Nigeria); in riebeckite gneiss (La Guia, Spain).
ferronigerite-2n1s.etymology: For Nigeria, the country where it was ﬁrst found.

ferronigerite-6n6s.occurrence: In quartz-sillimanite rocks closely associated with tin-bearing granite pegmatites (Egbe district, Nigeria); in tin-bearing skarns (Mt. Garnet, Australia).

ferronordite-ce.occurrence: In sodalite syenites and in ussingite veins in an alkaline massif.
ferronordite-ce.etymology: Prefix, ferro, indicates the Fe2+-dominant analog of nordite-Ce.

ferronordite-la.occurrence: In the ussingite core of hyperagpaitic pegmatite.
ferronordite-la.etymology: A member of the nordite group with a prefix, ferro, that indicates dominant Fe2+ in the tetrahedral structural site and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

ferropargasite.occurrence: In an amphibolite facies metamorphosed banded iron formation.
ferropargasite.etymology: For its high ferrous iron content and relation to pargasite.

ferrorhodonite.occurrence: Forms during granulite facies metamorphism of a manganese-rich sedimentary exhalative lead-zinc-silver deposit.
ferrorhodonite.etymology: As an analog of rhodonite with Fe2+ dominant in the M4 site of the structure.

ferrorichterite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in sodium-rich syenites and their volcanic equivalents; replacing ferromagnesian minerals in granite.
ferrorichterite.etymology: For the ferrous iron in its composition and similarity to richterite.

ferrorosemaryite.occurrence: In cassiterite and columbite-tantalite-bearing granitic pegmatite.
ferrorosemaryite.etymology: As the Fe2 + analog of rosemaryite.

ferrosaponite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral associated with pillow basalts.
ferrosaponite.etymology: Prefix, ferro, denotes the Fe2+-dominant analog of saponite.

ferroselite.occurrence: In red-bed deposits of the Colorado Plateau type, peripheral to pyrite and uranium concentrations (Utah, USA); in U–V ores in sandstone, with coaliﬁed wood (Colorado, USA); with other sulﬁdes and selenides cementing sandstones and pelites (Tuva, Russia).
ferroselite.etymology: For iron, FERrum, and SELenium in the composition.

ferrosilite.occurrence: In medium- to high-grade metamorphosed iron formations.
ferrosilite.etymology: For FERROus iron and SILicon in the composition; originally a \normative" mineral in rocks.

ferroskutterudite.occurrence: In hydrothermal dolomite-calcite veins and apophyllite-anhydrite-carbonate veins in a magmatic hydrothermal Co-Ni antimonide-arsenide deposit.
ferroskutterudite.etymology: For the high iron content and relation to skutterudite.

ferrostalderite.occurrence: Formed as massive to interstitial sulfosalt accumulations in dolostone by late stage Tl-As-Cu-Fe-rich hydrothermal fluids during upper greenschist to lower amphibolite metamorphism.
ferrostalderite.etymology: The prefix, ferro, indicates the iron isotype of stalderite.

ferrostrunzite.occurrence: Replacing a belemnite (Mullica Hill, New Jersey, USA); a secondary mineral in weathered phosphatic black shale beds (Bethel Church, Indiana, USA).
ferrostrunzite.etymology: For its dominant content of ferrous iron and relation to strunzite.

ferrotaaffeite-2n2s.occurrence: In the wall zone of a granite pegmatite in “hornblende” gabbro.
ferrotaaffeite-2n2s.etymology: To honor Gunnar Pehrman (1895-?), Emeritus Professor of Mineralogy and Geology, ˚Abo University, Turku, Finland, for his work on the Kemi¨ o pegmatites.

ferrotaaffeite-6n3s.occurrence: In the wall zone of a granite pegmatite in “hornblende” gabbro.
ferrotaaffeite-6n3s.etymology: To honor Gunnar Pehrman (1895-?), Emeritus Professor of Mineralogy and Geology, ˚Abo University, Turku, Finland, for his work on the Kemi¨ o pegmatites.

ferrotapiolite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in zoned granite pegmatites; detrital in placers.
ferrotapiolite.etymology: For its dominant FERROus iron content and for Tapio, ancient Finnish god of the forest, as the mineral was ﬁrst found in Finland.

ferrotitanowodginite.occurrence: In complex rare-element pegmatite in locally tourmalinized quartz-mica schist of medium metamorphic grade.
ferrotitanowodginite.etymology: Prefixes, ferro indicates Fe2+-dominant in the A site and titano indicates Ti-dominant in the B site in a member of the wodginite group.

ferrotochilinite.occurrence: Of low-temperature hydrothermal origin coating cavities in pentlandite-mooihoekitecubanite ore with minor magnetite and chalcopyrite.
ferrotochilinite.etymology: As the structural analogue (based on chemical, X-ray, and IR data similarities) of tochilinite with essential ferrous iron.

ferrotorryweiserite.occurrence: In fluvial placers likely derived from chromitites within ultramafic rocks of a layered complex of dunite-peridotite-gabbro.
assoc_parsed: hosted by grains of os-ir alloy
ferrotorryweiserite.etymology: The prefix indicates the Fe-analogue of torryweiserite.

ferrotschermakite.occurrence: A product of medium- to high-pressure metamorphism of highly aluminous rocks, producing schists, gneisses, or amphibolites; from di®erentiated ma¯c plutonic igneous rocks.
ferrotschermakite.etymology: For ferrous iron in its composition and relation to tschermakite.

ferrotychite.occurrence: A rare constituent of a vein cutting ijolite-urtite in an alkaline igneous complex, from a drill core.
ferrotychite.etymology: For essential FERROus iron and the relation to tychite.

ferrovalleriite.occurrence: Of low-temperature hydrothermal origin coating cavities in pentlandite-mooihoekitecubanite ore with minor magnetite and chalcopyrite.
ferrovalleriite.etymology: As the structural analogue (based on chemical, X-ray, and IR data similarities) of valleriite with essential ferrous iron.

ferrovorontsovite.occurrence: In mineralized limestone breccias (calcite-dolomite, up to 85% of volume) in the ores of the sulfide-carbonate type in a gold deposit of uncertain origin.
ferrovorontsovite.etymology: Honors mining engineer Vladimir Vasilyevich Vorontsov (1842-later than 1908) for whom the city and mine are named where the new mineral was discovered. A prefix, ferro, indicates the iron analog of vorontsovite.

ferrowodginite.occurrence: In museum specimens from a granite pegmatite.
ferrowodginite.etymology: For its content of FERROus iron and its relation to wodginite.

ferrowyllieite.occurrence: A primary phosphate in zoned granite pegmatites.
ferrowyllieite.etymology: As a mineral with dominant ferrous iron, and its relation to wyllieite.

ferruccite.etymology: Honors Professor Ferruccio Zambonini (1880–1932), Italian mineralogist, student of fumarolic minerals.

fersmanite.occurrence: In aegirine-rich nepheline pegmatites in a differentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Russia).
fersmanite.etymology: For Academician Aleksandr Evgen'evich Fersman (1883-1945), eminent Russian mineralogist, geochemist, and gemologist.

fersmite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in nepheline syenites and carbonatites. In miarolitic cavities in an albitized pegmatite dike.
fersmite.etymology: For Academician Aleksandr Evgen’evich Fersman (1883–1945), eminent Russian mineralogist, geochemist, and gemologist.

feruvite.occurrence: By hydrothermal replacement of silicates in a pegmatitic rock.
feruvite.etymology: For iron (FERrum), in the formula and the similarity to uvite.

fervanite.occurrence: As an impregnation in sandstone (Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits).
fervanite.etymology: Named for its content of FERric iron and V ANadium.

fetiasite.occurrence: Deposited from arsenic-bearing solutions in Alpine ﬁssures in gneisses of the upper greenschist to lower amphibolite facies.
fetiasite.etymology: For Fe, Ti, As in its composition.

fettelite.occurrence: A rare mineral in low-temperature hydrothermal, silver-sulfosalt veins.
fettelite.etymology: Honors M. Fettel, a field geologist who first noted the mineral.

fianelite.occurrence: In fractures crosscutting veinlets in metamorphosed Fe–Mn ores.
fianelite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Fianel mine, Switzerland.

fibroferrite.occurrence: An uncommon dehydration product of melanterite in oxidized portions of rocks and sediments containing iron sulﬁde, most stable in arid regions; rarely a volcanic sublimate.
fibroferrite.etymology: For the ﬁbrous habit and essential ferric iron.

fichtelite.occurrence: In fossilized pine wood from a peat bog; in organic-rich modern marine sediment.
fichtelite.etymology: For the original locality in the Fichtelgebirge, Bavaria, Germany.

fiedlerite.occurrence: Produced by reaction of halide-bearing seawater and metal-bearing slag.
fiedlerite.etymology: Honors Karl Gustav Fiedler (1791–1853), Saxon Commissioner of Mines.

fiemmeite.struct_group: Not in a structural group, Oxalate
fiemmeite.occurrence: In coalified wood trunks in continental sandstone which were permeated by mineralizing solutions containing Cu, U, As, Pb and Zn. The mineralization is a “sandstone-uranium type” roll front deposit. Oxalate anions came from diagenesis of plant remains in the sandstone.
fiemmeite.etymology: For the locality near where the first specimens were collected.

filatovite.etymology: Honors Stanislav K. Filatov (b. 1940), Saint Petersburg State University, for his studies of exhalation minerals.

filipstadite.etymology: For the town of Filipstad, Sweden, which is near the L ˚ angban mine.

fillowite.occurrence: A primary accessory mineral in a zoned granite pegmatite (Branchville, Connecticut, USA).
fillowite.etymology: In honor of Abijah N. Fillow (1822–1895), Branchville, Connecticut, USA, who early supplied minerals from his quarry at the locality.

fingerite.occurrence: A rare component of vanadium-bearing sublimates in fumaroles on a basaltic volcanic cone, formed between 100 ◦C and 200 ◦C.
fingerite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Larry W. Finger (1940– ), American mineralogist, Carnegie Institution, Washington, D.C., USA.

finnemanite.occurrence: In crevices in hematite in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L ˚ angban, Sweden).
finnemanite.etymology: For K.J. Finneman, of L ˚ angban, Sweden, who found the ﬁrst specimen.

fischesserite.occurrence: In carbonate veins in epithermal precious metal deposits (Pˇ redboˇ rice, Czech Republic).
fischesserite.etymology: For Raymond Fischesser (1911–1991), French mineralogist and crystallographer, Director of the National School of Mines, Paris, France.

fivegite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal phase in high-potassium peralkaline pegmatite in urtite near the contact with nepheline-apatite rock.
fivegite.etymology: Honors Russian geologist and mining engineer, Mikhail Pavlovich Fiveg (1899-1986), the pioneer prospector of the Khibiny apatite deposits.

fizelyite.etymology: For Sandor Fiz´ ely (1856–1918), Hungarian mining engineer, who discovered the mineral.

flagstaffite.occurrence: Lining cracks in decomposing buried pine logs.
flagstaffite.etymology: For Flagstaﬀ, Arizona, USA, near the type locality.

flamite.occurrence: In Ca- and Al-rich paralava, an ultrahigh-temperature combustion metamorphic rock.
flamite.etymology: Derived from “flame”, in allusion to the origin of the mineral by ultrahigh-temperature metamorphism from the natural combustion of fossil fuel.

fleetite.occurrence: In a fluvial Au-PGE placer deposit. Formed originally by reaction of the associated alloy phases with a fluid phase enriched in Sb, As, and S circulating in a cooling ophiolitic rock.
fleetite.etymology: Honors Dr. Michael Edward Fleet (1938-2017), Professor of mineralogy, Department of Earth Sciences, Western University, London, Ontario, Canada. Dr. Fleet had a wide range of mineralogical interests that included the study of platinum group minerals, thermodynamics, apatite minerals, sulfides, and the structure of silicate melts.

fleischerite.occurrence: Very rare in an oxidized portion of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal germanium-bearing polymetallic ore deposit.
fleischerite.etymology: Honors Dr. Michael Fleischer (1908–1998), mineralogist and geochemist, U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C., USA.

fleisstalite.etymology: For its type locality Kleines Fleisstal.

fletcherite.occurrence: Disseminated in copper sulﬁdes, in copper-rich pods replacing dolostone (Fletcher mine, Missouri, USA); in black slates (Kalgoorlie, Australia).
fletcherite.etymology: For the Fletcher mine in Missouri, USA.

flinkite.occurrence: Very rare, in veinlets in magnetite ore (Harstigen mine, Sweden); in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
flinkite.etymology: To honor Gustav Flink (1849–1931), Swedish mineralogist and collector.

flinteite.occurrence: Formed as sublimates on basaltic scoria around active volcanic fumaroles, probably as the result of a phase transition when cooling after the extraction of crystals of its protophase.
flinteite.etymology: Honors the Russian crystallographer Evgeniy Evgenievich Flint (1887-1975) , Professor of Crystallography, Moscow State University (1925-1930), Professor of Mineralogy and Crystallography, Moscow Geological Prospecting Institute (1930-1962) and Senior Researcher, Institute of Crystallography, USSR Academy of Sciences (1938-1962). He was a specialist in goniometry, X-ray crystallography and compiled a catalogue of pyroelectric and piezoelectric crystals including almost 1000 species.

florencite-ce.occurrence: As a weathering product, typically of apatite, in highly argillized igneous rocks, bauxite, saprolite, carbonatites; authigenic in shales and sandstones; formed by the interaction of guano-reacted waters with gabbroic rock.
florencite-ce.etymology: Honors Dr. William Florence (1864–1942), Brazilian mineralogist who made an early analysis, and for the dominant rare earth element, cerium.

florencite-la.occurrence: A secondary mineral in weathered metamorphosed corrensitic siltstone (Shituru deposit, Congo); an authigenic mineral in sandstone.
florencite-la.etymology: For a ﬂorencite with lanthanum as the dominant rare earth element.

florencite-nd.occurrence: Lining surfaces of fractures in a weathered chert layer in shale.
florencite-nd.etymology: For a ﬂorencite with neodymium as the dominant rare earth element.

florencite-sm.occurrence: In quartz veins cutting quartz meta-conglomerate beds near contacts with Al-enriched metasomatites.
florencite-sm.etymology: As the Sm-dominant example of the florencite structure.

florenskyite.occurrence: In one polished section from a meteorite breccia containing a huge variety of fragments of different chondritic types (e.g. CR, CM, CI, R, EH, and EL classes of carbonaceous, Rumaruti, and enstatite chondrites).
florenskyite.etymology: Honors Cyrill P. Florensky (1915-1982), Russian geochemist, a founder of planetology (Colleagues in the Laboratory of Comparative Planetology, 1985).

florensovite.occurrence: Found in a granulite complex, in Cr- and V-rich metasediments.
florensovite.etymology: To honor Nikolai Aleksandrovich Florensov (1909–1986), Ukrainian geologist, Director of the Institute of the Earth’s Crust, Irkutsk, Russia.

fluckite.occurrence: A post-mine low-temperature reaction product of carbonate gangue with arsenical solutions derived from arsenic (Gabe-Gottes mine, France).
fluckite.etymology: In honor of Pierre Fluck, mineralogist, Louis Pasteur University, Strasbourg, France, who found the ﬁrst specimen.

fluellite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral, formed by weathering of earlier phosphates in some complex granite pegmatites.
fluellite.etymology: From the Latin ﬂuate alumine, for its ﬂuorine and aluminum content, phosphorus having been overlooked in early analyses.

fluoborite.occurrence: A rare hydrothermal mineral in skarns developed in metamorphosed boron-rich magnesian rocks.
fluoborite.etymology: For the essential chemical components, FLUOrine and BORon.

fluocerite-ce.occurrence: In hydrothermal quartz veins in granite.
fluocerite-ce.etymology: As the lanthanum analog of ﬂuocerite-(Ce).

fluocerite-la.occurrence: In hydrothermal quartz veins in granite.
fluocerite-la.etymology: As the lanthanum analog of ﬂuocerite-(Ce).

fluor-dravite.occurrence: Formed near the contact between a granitic pegmatite and country rock.
fluor-dravite.etymology: As a dravite with dominant fluorine in the W site.

fluor-elbaite.occurrence: Formed in or near miarolitic cavities by late-stage hydrothermal solutions in a zoned granitic pegmatite.
fluor-elbaite.etymology: As an elbaite with dominant fluorine in the W site.

fluor-schorl.occurrence: A pneumatolytic phase associated with tin mineralization (Zschorlau) and in hightemperature hydrothermal veins in granitic pegmatites (Grasstein).

fluor-tsilaisite.occurrence: As portion of a color-zoned tourmaline crystal in an aplitic dike of an LCT-type (lithium-, cesium- and tantalum-enriched) pegmatite body.
fluor-tsilaisite.etymology: Represents the fluorine-dominant analog of tsilaisite.

fluorannite.occurrence: A rock-forming species in the upper part of an A-type granite.
fluorannite.etymology: Prefix, fluor, indicates the fluorine analog of annite.

fluorapatite.occurrence: The most common rock-forming phosphate mineral. Accessory in most igneous rocks, important in syenites, alkaline rocks, carbonatites, granite pegmatites. Common in marbles and skarns, Ca-rich regional metamorphic rocks, Alpine-type ﬁssures, and hydrothermal tin veins. An essential component of sedimentary phosphorites, common as a detrital or diagenetic component in oolitic ironstones and phosphatic carbonate rocks and shales. Residual in laterites.
fluorapatite.etymology: For dominant ﬂuorine and membership in the apatite group, the group name from the Greek for to deceive, for the ease with which specimens were confused with other minerals.

fluorapophyllite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in amygdules or druses in basalts; in cavities in granite; in tactite and other metamorphic rocks; a late-stage hydrothermal mineral in some mineral deposits.
fluorapophyllite.etymology: For the preponderance of °uorine in the composition, and apophyllite, from the Greek for away from and leaf, in allusion to its manner of exfoliating on heating.

fluorapophyllite-cs.etymology: Suffix indicates the Cs-analogue of fluorapophyllite-(K).

fluorapophyllite-k.occurrence: A secondary mineral in amygdules or druses in basalts; in cavities in granite; in tactite and other metamorphic rocks; a late-stage hydrothermal mineral in some mineral deposits.
fluorapophyllite-k.etymology: For the preponderance of °uorine in the composition, and apophyllite, from the Greek for away from and leaf, in allusion to its manner of exfoliating on heating.

fluorapophyllite-na.occurrence: A secondary mineral in amygdules or druses in basalts; in cavities in granite; in tactite and other metamorphic rocks; a late-stage hydrothermal mineral in some mineral deposits.
fluorapophyllite-na.etymology: For the preponderance of °uorine in the composition, and apophyllite, from the Greek for away from and leaf, in allusion to its manner of exfoliating on heating.

fluorapophyllite-nh4.occurrence: In cavities of quartz-illite-saponite-tobelite xenoliths embedded in pyroxene andesite. A hydrothermal mineral, formed at a late stage of auto-hydrothermal alteration.
fluorapophyllite-nh4.etymology: The prefix indicates the NH4-dominant analogue of fluorapophyllite-(K), fluorapophyllite-(Na) and fluorapophyllite-(Cs).

fluorarrojadite-bafe.occurrence: A high-temperature (≈ 800 ◦C) primary mineral in granite pegmatites.
fluorarrojadite-bafe.etymology: Arrojadite indicates a member of the group with Fe2+ dominant at the M site; two suffixes indicate the dominant cation of the dominant valence state at the A and B sites. The prefix, fluor, indicates dominant F in the W site. Honors Miguel Arrojado Ribeiro Lisbôa (1872-1932), Brazilian geologist.

fluorarrojadite-bana.occurrence: In hydrothermal quartz veins in highly fractionated, topaz-zinnwaldite S-type leucogranite.
fluorarrojadite-bana.etymology: Indicates a member of the arrojadite group (Fe2+ dominant at the M sites) and suffixes for dominant Ba at the A1 and Na at the B1 sites. The prefix “fluor” indicates dominant F in the W site.

fluorbarytolamprophyllite.occurrence: In agpaitic syenites of an alkaline complex.
fluorbarytolamprophyllite.etymology: Indicates the F-dominant analogue of barytolamprophyllite and Ba-dominant analogue of fluorlamprophyllite.

fluorbritholite-ce.occurrence: In vugs in nepheline syenite, marble xenoliths, sodalite syenite xenoliths, and pegmatite dikes (Mont Saint-Hilaire).
fluorbritholite-ce.etymology: As the fluorine-dominant analogue of britholite-(Ce).

fluorbritholite-y.etymology: As the fluorine-dominant analogue of britholite-(Y).

fluorcalciobritholite.occurrence: In veinlets cross-cutting fenitized gneiss xenoliths in foyaite (Khibiny). In alkaline metasomatite.
fluorcalciobritholite.etymology: The prefix, calcio, indicates an analog of fluorbritholite-(Ce) with calcium dominant over rare earth elements.

fluorcalciomicrolite.occurrence: In heavy mineral concentrates from a rare-element granitic pegmatite exceptionally enriched in lithium and rubidium.
fluorcalciomicrolite.etymology: For a member of the microlite group with dominant fluorine in the Y structural site and calcium in the A structural site.

fluorcalciopyrochlore.etymology: For a member of the pyrochlore group with prefixes to indicate dominant fluorine (fluor) in the Y site and dominant calcium (calcio) in the A site.

fluorcanasite.occurrence: In hyperalkaline pegmatite in an alkaline massif.
fluorcanasite.etymology: The suffix, fluor, identifies the fluorine-dominant analogy of canasite.

fluorcaphite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in a hyperagpaitic pegmatite in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
fluorcaphite.etymology: For FLUORine, CAlcium, and PHosphorus in the composition.

fluorcarletonite.occurrence: In an ultra-agpaitic, potassic alkaline complex.
fluorcarletonite.etymology: The prefix indicates the F-dominant analogue of carletonite.

fluorcarmoite-bana.formula_html: Ba   Na2Na2   CaMg13Al(PO4)11(PO3OH)F2
fluorcarmoite-bana.occurrence: In a river pebble derived from phosphate-bearing quartzites.
fluorcarmoite-bana.etymology: For Monte Carmo di Loano, the highest peak in the area where the mineral was found. A member of the arrojadite group with Mg2+ dominant at the M sites and suffixes for dominant Ba at the A1 and Na at the B1 sites. The prefix “fluor” indicates dominant F in the W site.

fluorchegemite.occurrence: Formed in the edgrewite-bearing zone of endoskarn (sanidinite facies) at the edge of an altered calciferous xenolith within ignimbrite.
fluorchegemite.etymology: Indicates the fluorine-dominant analog of chegemite.

fluorellestadite.occurrence: Formed in burned fragments of petri¯ed wood in coal dumps (Kopeysk, Russia).
fluorellestadite.etymology: For °uorine in the chemical composition and analogy to ellestadite.

fluorite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in granite, granite pegmatites, syenites; around fumaroles; in carbonatites and alkaline intrusives. Economic deposits in low- to high-temperature hydrothermal veins and stratabound deposits; a cement in sandstones.
fluorite.etymology: From the Latin to ﬂow, in allusion to its low melting point.

fluorkyuygenite.occurrence: Major constituent of larnite pyrometamorphic rocks of the Hatrurim Complex (Mottled Zone). Crystallized initially as fluormayenite and was altered by vapor-enriched gases during a combustion event.
fluorkyuygenite.etymology: Kyuygenite is for the locality, Kyuygen-Kaya Mountain and the prefix indicates the essential fluorine in the species.

fluorlamprophyllite.occurrence: Embedded in nepheline syenite in an alkaline massif.

fluorluanshiweiite.occurrence: In a Li-Cs-Ta granitic pegmatite deposit formed in the late stage of the evolution of the pegmatite-forming magmatic liquid.
fluorluanshiweiite.etymology: The prefix indicates the F-dominant at the A site analogue of luanshiweiite. Can be described also as the K-dominant at the I site analogue of voloshinite.

fluormayenite.occurrence: Major constituent of larnite-bearing pyrometamorphic rocks.
fluormayenite.etymology: Indicates the fluorine-dominant analog of mayenite.

fluornatrocoulsellite.occurrence: In replacement lenses formed during greisenization.
fluornatrocoulsellite.etymology: Prefixes indicate the dominant cation in the X site, fluor, and B site, natro, the base name honors Ruth Elise Coulsell (1912-2000), a foundation member and honorary life member of the Mineralogical Society of Victoria.

fluornatromicrolite.etymology: As a member of the microlite group with dominant fluorine (fluor) at an anion site and sodium (natro) in the A structural site.

fluornatropyrochlore.occurrence: An accessory phase in niobium-tantalum-rich alkali syenite.
fluornatropyrochlore.etymology: As a member of the pyrochlore supergroup with dominant fluorine in the Y site and sodium in the A site.

fluoro-cannilloite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-cannilloite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-edenite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-edenite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-leakeite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-leakeite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-nyboite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-nyboite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-pargasite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-pargasite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-pedrizite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-pedrizite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-potassic-pargasite.occurrence: Part of a single crystal attributed to a skarn deposit.
fluoro-potassic-pargasite.etymology: Signifies an amphibole in the compositional range of pargasite with F > OH, Cl and K dominant in the A structural site.

fluoro-richterite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-richterite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-riebeckite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-riebeckite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-taramite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-taramite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoro-tremolite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in skarn (Sparta, New Jersey).
fluoro-tremolite.etymology: The fluorine-analog of tremolite. The prefix fluoro indicates dominant fluorine in the W atomic site and the root name indicates the relation to tremolite.

fluoroaluminoleakeite.etymology: For its composition and relationship to leakeite.

fluorocronite.occurrence: A weathering product of hydrothermal Sn-Ag polymetallic veins.
fluorocronite.etymology: For the composition, fluoro (for fluorine) and cron (the alchemical name for lead).

fluorokinoshitalite.occurrence: In metamorphosed carbonate rocks associated with a large REE-Fe-Nb deposit.
fluorokinoshitalite.etymology: The suffix, fluoro, identifies the essential F in a phase related to kinoshitalite.

fluoroleakite.occurrence: By the reaction of alkaline granite with post-magmatic fluids rich in Li and F.
fluoroleakite.etymology: As the fluorine-dominant analogue of leakeite.

fluoromagnesiohastingsite.occurrence: In small cavities in an altered hematite-rich xenolith in trachyandesite.
fluoromagnesiohastingsite.etymology: Signifies an amphibole in the compositional range of magnesio-hastingsite with F > Cl, OH.

fluoropargasite.etymology: Signifies an amphibole in the compositional range of pargasite with F > OH in the W structural site.

fluoropotassichastingsite.occurrence: A product of potassium-halogen metasomatism of a hastingsite and diopside-bearing rock.
fluoropotassichastingsite.etymology: For its composition and relationship to hastingsite.

fluorosodicferropedrizite.occurrence: At the contact of a lithium pegmatite and formed by reaction of the pegmatitic melt with the country rock.
fluorosodicferropedrizite.etymology: For its composition and relationship to pedrizite.

fluorotetraferriphlogopite.occurrence: In metamorphosed carbonate rocks associated with a large REE-Fe-Nb deposit.
fluorotetraferriphlogopite.etymology: The prefix, fluoro, identifies the F-analog of tetraferriphlogopite.

fluorowardite.occurrence: A secondary phase, in a F-rich secondary phosphate assemblage.
assoc_parsed: turquoise/chalcosiderite. minerals separated by slashes exhibit variations in chemistry between the two species
fluorowardite.etymology: The fluorine analog of wardite; with the prefix “fluoro-” rather than “fluor-” to make pronunciation more straightforward.

fluorphosphohedyphane.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a Pb-Cu-Zn-Ag deposit.
fluorphosphohedyphane.etymology: The prefix, fluor, designates the F-analog of phosphohedyphane.

fluorvesuvianite.occurrence: In coarse grained, chloritized diopside skarn.
fluorvesuvianite.etymology: The prefix fluor indicates the F-dominant analog of vesuvianite.

fluorwavellite.etymology: As the fluorine analog of wavellite and with > ½ F per formula unit.

flurlite.occurrence: A secondary mineral probably formed from the hydrothermal reaction of zinc-bearing fluids with primary Fe-Mn phosphate minerals (triphylite or zwieselite).
flurlite.etymology: Honors Mathias von Flurl (1756-1823), the founder of mineralogical and geological studies in Bavaria and author of the first geological map of Bavaria.

foggite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, probably formed at < 300 ◦C, in complex granite pegmatites.
foggite.etymology: To honor Forrest F. Fogg (1920– ), mineral collector of Penacook, New Hampshire, USA, who provided the ﬁrst material.

fogoite-y.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in a syenite xenolith in trachytic ejecta from a stratavolcano .
fogoite-y.etymology: For the Fogo volcano, São Miguel Island, the Azores, where the first specimens were collected.

assoc_parsed: the original specimens are loose crystals without matrix
foitite.etymology: To honor Franklin F. Foit, Jr. (1942{ ), of Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA, for his work on tourmaline group minerals.

assoc_parsed: a mg-analogue of sonolite or jerrygibbsite
folvikite.etymology: Honors Harald O. Folvik (b. 1941), a Norwegian amateur mineralogist with an interest in Långban-type deposits who initially noticed and collected the specimen used for description.

fontanite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of a uranium deposit.
fontanite.etymology: Honors François Fontan (1942-2007), mineralogist specializing in phosphates, University Paul-Sabatier, Toulouse, France.

fontarnauite.occurrence: An early diagenetic phase in borate-bearing marls and tuffs.
assoc_parsed: kalistronite replacing fontarnauite in pseudomorphs after glauberite
fontarnauite.etymology: Honors Dr. Ramon Fontarnau i Griera, in recognition of his efforts to promote the development of scientific facilities focused on mineral characterization.

foordite.occurrence: A very rare mineral, in an alluvial pebble originating from a highly diﬀerentiated granite pegmatite, formed under reducing conditions deﬁcient in Fe, Mn, Na, Ca, and F (Lutsiro, Rwanda).
foordite.etymology: To honor Dr. Eugene Edward Foord (1946–1998), American mineralogist with the U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado, USA, student of granite pegmatites.

footemineite.occurrence: On thin fractures crossing quartz-microcline-spodumene pegmatite.
footemineite.etymology: For the Foote mine, source of the first samples.

formanite-y.occurrence: In granites and albitized, RE-rich pegmatitic veins; a detrital mineral in placers.
formanite-y.etymology: Honors Francis Gloster Forman (1904-1980), government geologist of Western Australia.

formicaite.occurrence: Rare in hydrothermal veinlets cutting kurchatovite-sakhaite ore (Solongo deposit, Russia); in a veinlet in skarnitized marble (Novofrolovskoye deposit, Russia).
formicaite.etymology: Alludes to the composition, a calcium formate.

fornacite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized zones of some hydrothermal base-metal deposits.
fornacite.etymology: In honor of Lucien Louis Forneau (1867–1930), Colonial Governor of the French Congo.

forsterite.occurrence: In ma¯c and ultrama¯c igneous rocks and thermally metamorphosed impure dolomitic limestones.
forsterite.etymology: After Adolarius Jacob Forster (1739{1806), English mineral collector and dealer.

foshagite.occurrence: In thin veins in thermally altered limestone (Crestmore, California, USA; Kilchoan, Scotland) or melilite skarn (Dupezeh Mountain, Iraq).
foshagite.etymology: For William Frederick Foshag (1894{1956), Curator of the Smithsonian mineral collections, Washington, D.C., USA, who studied Crestmore minerals.

foshallassite.etymology: For its relation to foshagite and \centrallassite" [gyrolite].

fourmarierite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed as an alteration product of uraninite in the oxide zone of uranium deposits; a common component of “gummite” replacing uraninite; may replace fossil wood.
fourmarierite.etymology: Honors Paul Fourmarier (1877–1970), Belgian geologist, Professor of Geology, University of Li` ege, Li` ege, Belgium.

fraipontite.etymology: To honor Julien Jean Joseph Fraipont (1857{1910), and Charles Fraipont, of Liµege, Belgium, both geologists and paleontologists.

francevillite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a Pb-bearing U–V deposit (Mounana mine, Gabon).
francevillite.etymology: For its original occurrence near Franceville, Gabon.

franciscanite.occurrence: As sparse, irregular segregations within a sheared sonolite-bearing assemblage in chert.
franciscanite.etymology: For the Franciscan complex of California, USA, where it was found.

francisite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in an oxidized barite lens in Precambrian sedimentary iron formation.
francisite.etymology: Honors Glyn Francis (1939– ), Quality Control Oﬃcer at the Iron Monarch quarry, Australia, who collected the ﬁrst specimen.

franckeite.occurrence: In hydrothermal Ag-Sn deposits (Bolivia); in a limestone contact metamorphic deposit (Kalkar quarry, California, USA).
franckeite.etymology: Honors the mining engineers Carl and Ernest Francke.

francoanellite.occurrence: An alteration product probably formed by reaction between bat guano and clay minerals (Castellana Cave, Italy); in soils developed on granite debris and bat guano mixtures, by reaction of phosphate-rich sea mist with clay minerals (Farallon Islands, USA).
francoanellite.etymology: Honoring Franco Anelli, formerly Professor of Geography, University of Bari, Bari, Italy, who found the Castellana caves.

francoisite-ce.occurrence: A rare alteration product of uraninite in a sedimentary Cu–Co deposit (Kamoto-East mine, Congo).
francoisite-ce.etymology: To honor Dr. Armand Fran¸ cois (1922– ), former Director of Geology for G´ ecamine (the national mining company), and for its dominant neodymium content.

francoisite-nd.occurrence: A rare alteration product of uraninite in a sedimentary Cu–Co deposit (Kamoto-East mine, Congo).
francoisite-nd.etymology: To honor Dr. Armand Fran¸ cois (1922– ), former Director of Geology for G´ ecamine (the national mining company), and for its dominant neodymium content.

franconite.occurrence: In vugs of a dawsonite-bearing sill in a limestone deposit (Francon quarry, Canada); in cavities in altered pegmatite dikes, hornfels, sodalite syenite, or miarolitic cavities, associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
franconite.etymology: For the Francon quarry, Montreal, Canada, where it was ﬁrst found.

frankdicksonite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, encased in quartz veinlets cutting a gold deposit in siliciﬁed carbonaceous arsenic-rich limestone.
frankdicksonite.etymology: To honor Dr. Frank Wilson Dickson (1922– ), Professor of Geochemistry, Stanford University, Palo Alto, California, USA, for his work on low-temperature ore deposits.

frankhawthorneite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral formed by the oxidization of primary Cu–Te-bearing sulﬁdes.
frankhawthorneite.etymology: Honors Frank Christopher Hawthorne (1946– ), Professor of Crystallography and Mineralogy, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada, who has determined the crystal structures of many copper minerals.

franklinfurnaceite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in vugs in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
franklinfurnaceite.etymology: After Franklin Furnace, the former name for Franklin, New Jersey, USA.

franklinite.occurrence: In beds and veins formed by high-temperature metamorphism of Fe, Zn, Mn-rich marine carbonate sediments. As a minor mineral in some manganese and iron deposits.
franklinite.etymology: Named for Franklin Furnace (now Franklin), New Jersey, USA; and in honor of the American statesman, philosopher, and inventor Benjamin Franklin (1706-1790).

franklinphilite.occurrence: In a veinlet crosscutting a breccia of calcite, aegirine, and serpentine in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
franklinphilite.etymology: From the locality Franklin, New Jersey, USA, and the Greek for friend, for the association of elements characteristic of Franklin.

fransoletite.occurrence: Formed by late-stage hydrothermal alteration of beryl and other phosphates in a zoned granite pegmatite.
fransoletite.etymology: To honor Dr. Andr´ e-Mathieu Fransolet (1947- ), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Li` ege, Li` ege, Belgium, for his work with primary phosphate minerals.

franzinite.occurrence: In ejected metasomatized pumice blocks, thought to be the product of a syntectic process between a trachytic magma and carbonate rocks at the volcanic vent.
franzinite.etymology: For Marco Franzini, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy.

freboldite.etymology: In honor of Professor Georg Frebold (1891–?) of Hannover, Germany.

fredrikssonite.etymology: Honors Dr. Kurt A. Fredriksson (1926– ), Swedish–American geochemist and meteoriticist, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., USA.

freedite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in andradite–magnetite ore from a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody.
freedite.etymology: Honors Dr. Robert L. Freed, American mineralogist, of Trinity University, San Antonio, Texas, USA.

assoc_parsed: a wide variety of sulﬁdes and sulfosalts
freibergite.etymology: For the long-known occurrence of silver-rich tetrahedrite at Freiberg, Germany.

freieslebenite.etymology: Honoring Johann Karl Freiesleben (1774–1846), Mining Commissioner of Saxony, Germany, who ﬁrst described the mineral.

freitalite.occurrence: On mine dumps, formed by pyrolysis of coal during spontaneous combustion in a low oxygen fugacity environment and sublimated from the gas phase.
freitalite.etymology: For Freital, the locality near which the studied material was collected.

fresnoite.occurrence: Disseminated in gneissic metamorphic rocks composed mainly of sanbornite and quartz (Rush Creek, California, USA).
fresnoite.etymology: For the original localities in Fresno Co., California, USA.

freudenbergite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in an apatite-bearing alkali syenite.
freudenbergite.etymology: For Professor Wilhelm Freudenberg (1881–?), who studied Katzenbuckel rocks.

friedelite.etymology: For the noted French chemist and mineralogist, Charles Friedel (1832{1899).

friedrichbeckeite.occurrence: In vesicles in pyrometamorphically metasomatized silicate-rich xenoliths in leucitetephrite volcanic rock.
friedrichbeckeite.etymology: Honors Austrian mineralogist and petrographer Friedrich Johann Karl Becke (1855–1931), best known for developing the Becke-line method for determining indices of refraction.

friedrichite.occurrence: As aggregates of granular crystals, in boulders of vein quartz which occur in the scree of a landslip (Salzburg, Austria); in magnesian and calcic skarn deposits (Apuseni Mountains, Romania).
friedrichite.etymology: To honor Professor Dr.-Ing Otmar Michael Friedrich (1902–1991), Austrian geologist of the Mining University, Leoben, Styria, Austria.

fritzscheite.occurrence: In a hematite deposit (Nove Hamry, Czech Republic).
fritzscheite.etymology: To honor Professor Carl Julius Fritzsche (1808–1871), German chemist.

frohbergite.occurrence: In hydrothermal ore deposits, rimming chalcopyrite grains, and as inclusions in gold, petzite, or chalcopyrite.
frohbergite.etymology: Honors Dr. Max Hans Frohberg (1901–1970), Canadian mining geologist, Toronto, Canada.

frolovite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of hydrothermal boron minerals in skarn deposits.
frolovite.etymology: For the ﬁrst-noted occurrence in the NovoFROLOVskoye deposit, Russia.

frondelite.occurrence: An alteration product of primary phosphates in complex granite pegmatites.
frondelite.etymology: To honor Dr. Cliﬀord Frondel (1907–2002), American mineralogist, Professor of Mineralogy, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

froodite.occurrence: In mill concentrates of As–Pb–Cu-rich ores (Frood mine, Canada); in Pd–Pt-bearing layered or pipelike ultramaﬁc intrusives.
froodite.etymology: For the Frood mine in Canada, from where it was ﬁrst noted.

fuenzalidaite.occurrence: A rare constituent of nitrate ores.
fuenzalidaite.etymology: Honors Humberto Fuenzalida P. (1904–1966), ﬁrst Director of the Chilean School of Geology, University of Chile, Santiago, Chile.

fuettererite.occurrence: A secondary phase formed by partial oxidation of tellurides, chalcopyrite and galena in quartz veins.
fuettererite.etymology: Honors Otto Fuetterer (1880-1970), who is largely responsible for the development of the mining claims on Otto Mountain.

fukalite.occurrence: A retrograde mineral and alteration product in skarns formed from metasomatism of limestone.
fukalite.etymology: For the locality where it was ¯rst discovered, Fuka, Japan.

fukuchilite.occurrence: In an ore body of gypsum–anhydrite, in interstices of small masses consisting of barite, covellite, and pyrite.
fukuchilite.etymology: Honors Nobuyo Fukuchi (1877–1934), Japanese mineralogist and geologist, who studied many Japanese Kuroko-type deposits.

fulbrightite.occurrence: A low-temperature secondary phase on montroseite- and corvusite-bearing sandstone.
fulbrightite.etymology: Honors Jess W. Fulbright, Jr., of Nucla, Colorado (b. 1958), Safety Director for Energy Fuels Inc., a company involved in the acquisition, exploration, development, and mining of uranium properties in the Uravan Mineral Belt of the western USA.

fuloppite.etymology: For Dr. B´ ela F¨ ul¨ opp (1863–1938), mineral collector of Hungary.

furongite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a uranium deposit (Hunan Province, China); in a complex granite pegmatite (Kobokobo pegmatite, Congo).
furongite.etymology: From a poetic name for Hunan Province, China.

furutobeite.occurrence: In veinlets of stromeyerite that cut bornite in the Kuroko zone of a stratabound, Kuroko-type, massive sulﬁde deposit (Furutobe mine, Japan).
furutobeite.etymology: For the type locality at the Furutobe mine, Japan.

gabrielite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in vugs in a hydrothermally-altered dolomitic marble.
gabrielite.etymology: Honors Walter Gabriel (b. 1943) of Basel, Switzerland, a mineral photographer and expert on Lengenbach minerals.

gabrielsonite.etymology: To honor Dr. Olof Erik Gabrielson (1912– ), mineralogist, Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm, Sweden.

gachingite.occurrence: In an epithermal gold deposit of the high-sulfidation (HS) type in volcanic rocks.
gachingite.etymology: For the Gaching ore deposit where the studied material was collected.

gadolinite-ce.occurrence: In syenite pegmatite veins along a contact between basalt and monzonite.
gadolinite-ce.etymology: For its cerium content and relation to gadolinite-(Y).

gadolinite-nd.etymology: Suffix indicates the Nd-dominant member of the gadolinite subgroup.

gadolinite-y.occurrence: In granite and alkalic granite pegmatites.
gadolinite-y.etymology: For the Finnish chemist, Johan Gadolin (1760{1852), who discovered yttrium.

gagarinite-ce.occurrence: In a rare-earth-element enriched, peralkaline granitic complex (Strange Lake).
gagarinite-ce.etymology: Honors the ﬁrst cosmonaut, Yuri Alekseevich Gagarin (1934-1968) and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element, cerium.

gagarinite-y.occurrence: As disseminations, segregations, and in veins and miarolitic cavities within Na-metasomatized alkalic granites and quartz-syenites.
gagarinite-y.etymology: In honor of the ﬁrst cosmonaut, Yuri Alekseevich Gagarin (1934–1968).

gageite.occurrence: A late-stage low- to medium-temperature mineral, implanted on other species in ¯ssures and solution cavities, in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
gageite.etymology: For Robert B. Gage, of Trenton, New Jersey, USA, who analyzed the ¯rst specimens.

gahnite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in granites and granite pegmatites; in medium- to high-grade metamorphic rocks and metamorphosed base-metal sulﬁde deposits; in diasporites, formed by the low-grade metamorphism of bauxites; a detrital mineral in placers.
gahnite.etymology: For the Swedish chemist and mineralogist, Johan Gottlieb Gahn (1745–1818), who discovered the mineral.

gaidonnayite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in nepheline syenite and altered pegmatite dikes in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in augite syenite (Narss^ arssuk,Greenland).
gaidonnayite.etymology: For Professor Gabrielle Donnay (1920{1987), mineralogist of McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada.

gaildunningite.occurrence: In a tectonically emplaced section of oceanic crust, the metamorphism of which released Hg-bearing fluids that migrated along fractures within silicified serpentinite and produced the mercury mineralization.
gaildunningite.etymology: Honors Gail E. Dunning (b. 1937), a prominent field-collector from the New Idria mining district who has discovered many new mercury-bearing minerals.

gainesite.occurrence: A very rare accessory mineral in a granite pegmatite.
gainesite.etymology: To honor Dr. Richard Venable Gaines (1917–1999), American mineralogist, economic geologist, and mineral collector, of Earlysville, Virginia, USA, for his interest in beryllium minerals.

gaitite.occurrence: A very rare mineral from a deep oxidized zone in a dolostone-hosted, hydrothermal , polymetallic ore deposit.
gaitite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Robert Irwin Gait (1938– ), South African-Canadian Curator of Mineralogy, Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto, Canada.

gajardoite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from the oxidation of native arsenic and other As -bearing primary phases, followed by later alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions.
gajardoite.etymology: Honors Dr. Anibal Gajardo Cubillos (b. 1945), a prominent Chilean geologist and academician.

galaxite.occurrence: In carbonate-rich, silica-undersaturated parts of metamorphosed manganese deposits.
galaxite.etymology: For Galax, Virginia, USA, close to Bald Knob, North Carolina, and for the plant, galax, after which the town is named.

galeaclolusite.occurrence: A secondary mineral derived from components from mansfieldite or bariopharmacoalumite.
galeaclolusite.etymology: Honors Valérie Galea-Clolus (b. 1964) for her contributions to Cap Garonne mineralogy.

galeite.etymology: Honors Dr. William Alexander Gale (1898–1985), Director of Research of the American Potash and Chemical Corporation.

galena.occurrence: In many diﬀerent types of environments. In hydrothermal veins, formed under a wide range of temperatures; in contact metamorphic deposits, in pegmatites, rarely; limestones and dolostones are common host rocks.
galena.etymology: A Latin word galena, given to lead ore or the dross from melted lead.

galenobismutite.etymology: In allusion to galena and bismuth in its composition.

galgenbergite-ce.occurrence: In small fissures cutting an albite–chlorite schist.
galgenbergite-ce.etymology: For the locality, the Galgenberg railroad tunnel, that produced the first specimens and suffix for the dominant rare earth element, Cesium.

galileiite.occurrence: Very rare, as inclusions within troilite nodules in type IIIAB iron meteorites.
galileiite.etymology: To honor Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italian astronomer and poet.

galliskiite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral that crystallized from fluorine-rich solutions in intragranitic pegmatite.
galliskiite.etymology: Honors Miguel Ángel Galliski (b. 1948), Argentine mineralogist and pegmatite specialist for his research on the pegmatites of the Pampean Pegmatite Province of northwestern Argentina.

gallite.occurrence: In base-metal vein deposits with relatively high gallium content.

gallobeudantite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in vugs in oxidized ore from a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
gallobeudantite.etymology: For its predominant gallium content as a member of the beudantite group.

galloplumbogummite.occurrence: A secondary mineral derived by alteration of Ge-Ga minerals in the oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted, polymetallic, hydrothermal deposit.
galloplumbogummite.etymology: Reflects dominant essential gallium and the mineral’s structural relation to plumbogummite.

galuskinite.occurrence: A retrograde product of skarn alteration found in sanidinite facies contactmetamorphosed silicate carbonate xenoliths intruded by gabbroid rocks (Birkhin complex ).
galuskinite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogists Irina Olegovna Galuskina (b. 1961) and Evgeny Vadimovich Galuskin (b. 1960), Faculty of Earth Sciences, University of Silesia, Poland.

gamagarite.occurrence: Very rare, in banded manganese ore replacing shale (Gloucester Farm, South Africa); in veinlets cutting manganese ore (Molinello mine, Italy).
gamagarite.etymology: For the original occurrence on Gamagara Ridge, South Africa.

gananite.etymology: Presumably for its occurrence in the Ganan area, China.

ganomalite.occurrence: In skarn assemblages (Jakobsberg, Sweden); in manganese ores in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
ganomalite.etymology: From the Greek for luster, in allusion to its appearance.

ganophyllite.occurrence: In manganese-rich portions of metamorphosed Zn-Mn mineral deposits.
ganophyllite.etymology: From the Greek for luster and leaf, for the high luster on cleavages.

ganterite.occurrence: A rock forming mineral in bands and lenses of white-mica schists and in zoisite– celsian gneiss.
ganterite.etymology: For Gantertal, a valley in the Simplon region that produced the first specimens.

gaotaiite.occurrence: In crushed chromite ores and placer concentrates.
gaotaiite.etymology: For Gaotai village, China, near which the mineral was found.

garavellite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal copper deposit with disseminated chalcopyrite in siderite gangue.
garavellite.etymology: In honor of Professor Carlo L. Garavelli (1929– ), Italian mineralogist, University of Bari, Bari, Italy.

garpenbergite.occurrence: In fractured skarn matrix of granular jacobsite, alleghanyite, kutnohorite and dolomite developed in metamorphosed sedimentary and volcanic rocks.
garpenbergite.etymology: For the place of discovery, Garpenberg. In the Middle Ages, ‘garp’ was the colloquial word in Swedish for a German person. The term here alludes to the Swedish recruitment of German miners to increase know-how in their mining industry.

garrelsite.occurrence: Of authigenic origin, in dolomitic shale in drill core from the Green River Formation (Uintah Co., Utah, USA).
garrelsite.etymology: For Professor Robert Minard Garrels (1916{1988), American geochemist and educator.

garronite.occurrence: As amygdule ¯llings in silica-undersaturated olivine basalt °ows (Co. Antrim, Ireland); in lavas rich in phenocrysts of bytownite and in non-porphyritic olivine basalt °ows (Iceland); in diabase porphyry (Angara River, Russia).
garronite.etymology: For the Garron Plateau area, Co. Antrim, Ireland.

garronite-ca.occurrence: As amygdule ¯llings in silica-undersaturated olivine basalt °ows (Co. Antrim, Ireland); in lavas rich in phenocrysts of bytownite and in non-porphyritic olivine basalt °ows (Iceland); in diabase porphyry (Angara River, Russia).
garronite-ca.etymology: For the Garron Plateau area, Co. Antrim, Ireland.

garronite-na.occurrence: In vugs in a hydrothermally-altered zone of the Poudrette pegmatite and in sodalite-rich segregations in nepheline syenite both part of an alkaline igneous intrusive complex. Association Natrolite, gmelinite, aegirine, gonnardite.
garronite-na.etymology: The suffix indicates the Na analog of garronite.

gartrellite.occurrence: A rare mineral in an oxidized mineralized shear zone cutting graywackes and shales (Anticline prospect, Australia); on ﬁne-grained quartz-spessartine rocks (Broken Hill, Australia).
gartrellite.etymology: Honoring Blair J. Gartrell (1950–1994), Australian mineral collector of Beverley, Australia, who found the mineral.

garutiite.occurrence: Of probable secondary origin, formed at low temperatures during post-magmatic processes, such as serpentinization and/or lateritization. Found in heavy mineral concentrates from podiform chromitite deposits in ophiolitic rocks.
assoc_parsed: zaccariniite and unidentified species including ru- os-ir-fe and pt-ni-fe-ir compounds
garutiite.etymology: Honors Professor Giorgio Garuti (b. 1945), University of Leoben, Austria, for his contributions to the understanding of the mineralogy of platinum-group elements.

garyansellite.occurrence: A rare low-temperature mineral in fractures in a sedimentary iron formation.
garyansellite.etymology: Honors H. Gary Ansell (1943– ), Associate Curator, Canadian National Mineral Collection, Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa, Canada.

gasparite-ce.occurrence: In ﬁssures, replacing synchysite, formed by amphibolite-grade metamorphism of metasedimentary rocks (Pizzo Cervandone, Italy).
gasparite-ce.etymology: To honor Giovanni Gaspari, mineral collector of Crodo, Italy, who ﬁrst found the mineral, and for its dominant cerium content.

gasparite-la.occurrence: In ﬁssures, replacing synchysite, formed by amphibolite-grade metamorphism of metasedimentary rocks (Pizzo Cervandone, Italy).
gasparite-la.etymology: To honor Giovanni Gaspari, mineral collector of Crodo, Italy, who ﬁrst found the mineral, and for its dominant cerium content.

gaspeite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in a Ni-sulfide-bearing vein in metamorphosed siliceous dolostone (Gaspe Peninsula, Canada); possibly from alteration of a nickel-rich meteorite (Bon Accord, South Africa).
gaspeite.etymology: For the original locality on the Gaspe Peninsula, Canada.

gatedalite.occurrence: In hausmannite-bearing skarn associated with a regionally-metamphosed Mn-Fe deposit.
gatedalite.etymology: Honors amateur mineralogist Kjell Gatedal (b. 1947) from Nora, Örebro, Sweden, for his contributions to the mineralogy of Långban-type deposits.

gatehouseite.occurrence: As a secondary mineral in cavities in a sedimentary Fe–Mn deposit, probably formed by reaction of phosphorus-rich ﬂuids with hausmannite at low temperature.
gatehouseite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Bryan Michael Kenneth Cummings Gatehouse (1932– ), crystal chemist, Monash University, Melbourne, Australia.

gatelite-ce.occurrence: In dolomitic portions of a talc deposit.
gatelite-ce.etymology: Honors Pierre Gatel, French mineral collector, founder of the Association Française de Microminéralogie.

gatewayite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by the oxidation of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a moist environment.
gatewayite.etymology: For the Gateway mining district in which the Packrat mine is located. Gateway is also the nearest town to the Packrat mine.

gatumbaite.occurrence: From the phosphate assemblage in a complex granite pegmatite (Buranga pegmatite, Rwanda; H˚ alsj¨ oberg, Sweden.); in andesites altered hydrothermally through hydrogen metasomatism (Mt. Perry, Australia).
gatumbaite.etymology: For its occurrence near Gatumba, Rwanda.

gaudefroyite.occurrence: An uncommon hydrothermal mineral in manganese deposits.
gaudefroyite.etymology: Honors Abb´ e Christophe Gaudefroy (1888–1971), French mineralogist who worked in Morocco.

gauthierite.occurrence: A product of the oxidation-hydration weathering of uraninite and presumably formed by the combination of radiogenic lead and uranium from altered uraninite with potassium leached from gangue minerals.
gauthierite.etymology: Honors Gilbert Joseph Gauthier (1924-2006), a Belgian geologist, mineralogist and connoisseur of Katanga minerals. He found the mineral and provided it for study.

gayite.occurrence: In vugs in hydrothermal apatite-(CaF) in a zoned granitic pegmatite.
gayite.etymology: Honors Hebe Dina Gay (b. 1927), Professor Emeritus of Mineralogy, National University of Córdoba, Argentina, whose accomplishments include a 60-year career in teaching, research, and since 1971, curation of the University’s Alfredo Stelzner Museum of Mineralogy and Geology, one of Argentina’s most important geological museums. Type Material Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, California, USA (59843), and the Alfredo Stelzner Museum of Mineralogy and Geology, National University of Córdoba, Argentina (MS003278).

gaylussite.occurrence: Typically in evaporites or shales from alkali lakes; rarely in veinlets cutting alkalic igneous rocks.
gaylussite.etymology: Honors Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac (1778–1850), noted French chemist and physicist.

gazeevite.occurrence: A high-temperature reaction product in carbonate-silicate xenoliths in rhyodacite (Georgia) or in pyrometamorphic rocks associated with volcanism or natural combustion (Israel).
gazeevite.etymology: Honors Viktor Magalimovich Gazeev (b. 1954), research staff of the Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrography, Mineralogy and Geochemistry of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, and of the Vladikavkaz Scientific Centre of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Vladikavkaz, Republic of North Ossetia-Alania, Russia, for his discovery of unique xenoliths within the Upper Chegem Caldera that lead to the description of over 20 new mineral species.

gearksutite.occurrence: In granite and granite pegmatites; may be formed by low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of aluminous rocks by ﬂuorine-bearing hot springs.
gearksutite.etymology: From the Greek ge for Earth, in allusion to the earthy appearance of the mineral, and arksutite (= chiolite), originally thought to be a mineral that gearksutite closely resembled in composition.

gebhardite.occurrence: On a specimen of highly oxidized ore from the lower oxidation zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
gebhardite.etymology: To honor Dr. Georg Gebhard (1945– ), German chemist, mineral collector, and authority on rare minerals, who supplied the specimen.

gedrite.occurrence: Widespread in medium- to high-grade metamorphic rocks; in metasomatized contact metamorphic rocks.
gedrite.etymology: For the occurrence near Gµedre, France.

geerite.occurrence: Replacing sphalerite along cleavage traces (DeKalb Township, New York, USA); in a serpentine-hosted magnetite–chromite deposit (Eretria, Greece).
geerite.etymology: To honor the collector of the original specimens, Adam Geer (1895–1973), of Utica, New York, USA.

geffroyite.occurrence: As late-stage deposits in veins cutting granite (Cham´ eane mine, France).
geffroyite.etymology: To honor Jacques Geﬀroy (1918–1993), metallurgist for the French Atomic Energy Commission.

gehlenite.occurrence: In contact metamorphosed impure limestones; in calcium-rich ultrama¯c volcanic rocks.
gehlenite.etymology: After the German chemist, Adolf Ferdinand Gehlen (1775{1815). All rights reserved.
