geigerite.occurrence: In cavities in radiolarites, formed by metamorphism of manganese oxide ores.
geigerite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Thomas Geiger (1886–1976), Wiesendangen, Switzerland, who studied Falotta manganese ores.

geikielite.occurrence: Forms during contact metamorphism of impure magnesian limestones. Also in carbonatites, kimberlites, serpentinized ultramaﬁc rocks, and in gem-bearing placer deposits.
geikielite.etymology: In honor of Sir Archibald Geikie (1835–1924), Scottish geologist and Director-General of the Geological Survey of Great Britain.

gelosaite.struct_group: Not in a structural group, Gelosaite
gelosaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in the oxidation zone of bismuth-molybdenum deposits.
gelosaite.etymology: Honors Mario Gelosa (1947-2006) from Porto Torres, Sardinia, who first found the mineral.

geminite.occurrence: From an arsenic-bearing oxidized Pb–Cu deposit (Cap Garonne mine, France); on specimens from mine dumps at a gold-bearing arsenic sulﬁde deposit (Salsigne mine, France).
geminite.etymology: From the Latin gemini, for twins, as the mineral is extensively twinned.

genkinite.occurrence: In ultramaﬁcs or ophiolites mineralized with Pt–Fe–Cu–Ni, and placers derived from them.
genkinite.etymology: For Dr. Alexandr D. Genkin (1919– ), Russian mineralogist specializing in platinum group elements.

genplesite.occurrence: A late-stage, low-temperature hydrothermal mineral in cavities in massive chalcopyrite.
genplesite.etymology: Honors Gennadiy Nikolaevich Plesin (b. 1963), a surveyor at the Oktyabr’sky mine and an amateur mineralogist who collected and provided samples of several new species first described from the Norilsk district.

genthelvite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in granite pegmatites; in alkaline granites and syenites, greisens, and skarns.
genthelvite.etymology: The pre¯x for Frederick August Ludwig Karl Wilhelm Genth (1820{1893), German-American mineralogist, who described a zinc-rich helvite (danalite), later renamed genthelvite.

geocronite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with sulﬁdes and other sulfosalt minerals.
geocronite.etymology: From the Greek for Earth and Saturn, the alchemistic name for lead.

georgbarsanovite.occurrence: A late stage reaction product in nepheline-feldspar pegmatite associated with an alkaline massif.
georgbarsanovite.etymology: Honors prominent Russian mineralogist Georgiy Pavlovich Barsanov (1907-1991).

georgbokiite.etymology: To honor Professor Georgiy Borisovich Bokii (1909–2001), Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Moscow, Russia, for his work in mineralogy and crystal chemistry.

georgechaoite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in analcime-bearing nepheline syenite (Wind Mountain, New Mexico, USA); in a carbonatite, in dolomitic veinlets cutting metasomatically altered pyroxenites, apparently altering from catapleiite (Vuoriyarvi complex, Russia).
georgechaoite.etymology: Honors Professor George Y. Chao, of Carleton University, Toronto, Canada, for his studies of zirconium silicates.

georgeericksenite.occurrence: On a museum specimen from a nitrate deposit.
georgeericksenite.etymology: Honors George E. Ericksen (1920–1996), research geologist, U.S. Geological Survey, Reston, Virginia, USA, who studied Chilean nitrate deposits.

georgeite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in oxidized portions of a Ni–Cu sulﬁde deposit.
georgeite.etymology: Honors George Herbert Payne (1912–1989), Chief of the Mineral Division, Government Chemical Laboratories, Perth, Western Australia.

georgerobinsonite.occurrence: In vugs in silicified rock in a deeply weathered gold-silver-molybdenum-lead-zincvanadium, hydrothermal mineral deposit.
georgerobinsonite.etymology: Honors Dr. George Willard Robinson (b. 1946), mineral curator, researcher, teacher, and field collector.

georgiadesite.occurrence: Formed by the action of seawater on lead-bearing slag (Laurium, Greece).
georgiadesite.etymology: In honor of Mr. Georgiad` es, a Director of the mines at Laurium Greece.

gerasimovskite.occurrence: As a secondary mineral formed by the late-stage hydrothermal alteration of Nb–Ti minerals (possibly epistolite) within ussingite-bearing pegmatites, associated with alkaline intrusions.
gerasimovskite.etymology: Honors Vasily Ivanovich Gerasimovskii (1911–1979), Russian mineralogist and geochemist, discoverer of many new minerals from the Lovozero massif.

gerdtremmelite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral from the deep oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
gerdtremmelite.etymology: To honor Dr. Gerd Tremmel (1940– ), of Overath-Steinbr¨ uck, Germany, who submitted the mineral for identiﬁcation.

gerhardtite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in oxidized portions of copper deposits.
gerhardtite.etymology: Honors Charles Frederic Gerhardt (1816–1856), American chemist who ﬁrst prepared the artiﬁcial compound.

germanite.occurrence: In primary Cu–Pb–Zn ores in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia).
germanite.etymology: For the germanium content of the mineral.

germanocolusite.etymology: For its germanium content and relation to colusite.

gersdorffite.occurrence: In hydrothermal vein deposits formed at medium temperatures.
gersdorffite.etymology: To honor Johann von Gersdorﬀ (1781–1849), owner of the nickel mine at Schladming, Austria.

gersdorffite-p213.occurrence: In hydrothermal vein deposits formed at medium temperatures.
gersdorffite-p213.etymology: To honor Johann von Gersdorﬀ (1781–1849), owner of the nickel mine at Schladming, Austria.

gersdorffite-pa3.occurrence: In hydrothermal vein deposits formed at medium temperatures.
gersdorffite-pa3.etymology: To honor Johann von Gersdorﬀ (1781–1849), owner of the nickel mine at Schladming, Austria.

gersdorffite-pca21.occurrence: In hydrothermal vein deposits formed at medium temperatures.
gersdorffite-pca21.etymology: To honor Johann von Gersdorﬀ (1781–1849), owner of the nickel mine at Schladming, Austria.

gerstleyite.occurrence: A low-temperature mineral found embedded in massive borates and clay.
gerstleyite.etymology: Honors James Mack Gerstley (1907– ), President of the Paciﬁc Coast Borax Company.

gerstmannite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal vein cutting franklinite-willemite ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
gerstmannite.etymology: For Ewald Gerstmann (1918{ ), mineral collector of Franklin, New Jersey, USA.

geschieberite.occurrence: As a weathering product from the post-mining alteration of uraninite and sulfides in a Ag-Bi-Co-Ni-U bearing hydrothermal vein deposit.
geschieberite.etymology: For the Geschieber vein, the locality that produced the first specimens.

getchellite.occurrence: In an epithermal gold deposit formed in a narrow, steeply-dipping fault zone cutting interbedded Paleozoic (?) shales, argillites, and limestones, near a granodiorite intrusive (Getchell mine, Nevada, USA).
getchellite.etymology: For the Getchell mine, Nevada, USA, where it was discovered.

geversite.occurrence: In concentrates of platinum minerals derived from Pt–Fe–Ni–Cu deposits in ultramaﬁc rocks (Driekop mine, South Africa).
geversite.etymology: In honor of Professor Traugott Wilhelm Gevers (1900–1991), University of the Witswatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa, eminent South African geologist.

ghiaraite.occurrence: In volcanic ejecta on the surface of a lava flow.
ghiaraite.etymology: Honors Maria Rosaria Ghiara (b. 1948), Head of Real Museo Mineralogico of Napoli and Centro Musei delle Scienze Naturali e Fisiche dell’Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II for promoting scientific research on the mineralogy of Vesuvius volcano.

giacovazzoite.occurrence: Secondary in a weathered, Tl-rich, pyrite-baryte-magnetite-hematite deposit.
giacovazzoite.etymology: Honors Carmelo Giacovazzo (b. 1940), retired Professor of Mineralogy and Crystallography, University of Bari, Italy, for his contributions to crystallography.

gianellaite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral coating fracture surfaces in oxidized portions of a hydrothermal mercury deposit, the nitrogen likely derived from decaying organic matter (Mariposa mine, Texas, USA); in a mercury deposit in silicate–carbonate rock hydrothermally altered from serpentinite (Clear Creek claim, California, USA).
gianellaite.etymology: Honors Professor Vincent Paul Gianella (1886–1983), Head of the Department of Geology, MacKay School of Mines, University of Nevada, Reno, Nevada, USA.

gibbsite.occurrence: A typical product of weathering of aluminous minerals, common in lateritic soils and bauxite. Also formed in low-temperature hydrothermal and metamorphic environments, replacing aluminous minerals.
gibbsite.etymology: Honors Colonel George Gibbs (1776–1833), a prominent mineral collector of New Haven, Connecticut, USA.

giessenite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, with other sulﬁdes.
giessenite.etymology: For Giessen, a village nearby the Binntal, Switzerland.

giftgrubeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, formed by alteration of arsenical minerals after mining.
assoc_parsed: lollingite. distribution from the st jacques vein
giftgrubeite.etymology: For the mine that yielded the studied material.

gilalite.occurrence: A retrograde metamorphic or mesogene mineral formed at the expense of a prograde calc-silicate and sul¯de assemblage; in tactites, commonly incrusting fractures; also ¯lling cracks or interstices in diopside grains (Christmas, Arizona, USA).
gilalite.etymology: For Gila Co., Arizona, USA, where it was found.

gillardite.occurrence: In silicified ferruginous gossan developed on a komatiite-hosted sulfide deposit.
gillardite.etymology: Honors Professor Robert David Gillard (b. 1936), formerly of the Department of Chemistry, Cardiff University, Wales, UK, for his contributions to inorganic coordination chemistry.

gillespite.occurrence: In a glacial moraine (Dry Delta, Alaska, USA); probably from a contact metamorphic zone (Trumbull Peak, California, USA).
gillespite.etymology: For Frank Gillespie, of Richardson, Alaska, USA, who discovered the ¯rst specimen.

gillulyite.occurrence: In a sediment-hosted disseminated gold deposit, in organic-rich unoxidized carbonates.
gillulyite.etymology: To honor James C. Guilluly (1896–1980), U.S. Geological Survey, who worked in the area of the Mercur deposit.

gilmarite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral associated with other copper arsenates and copper arsenides in the oxidized zone.
gilmarite.etymology: To honor Gilbert Mari (1944– ), mineralogist, University of Nice-Sophia Antipolis, Nice, France, who collected the samples in which the mineral was found.

giniite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a complex granite pegmatite.
giniite.etymology: To honor Adelheid (Gini) Keller (1940– ), wife of Paul Keller.

ginorite.occurrence: As eﬄorescences on weathered basalt associated with colemanite-bearing limestone (Death Valley, California, USA); in veins in sandstone (Sasso Pisano, Italy).
ginorite.etymology: Honors Prince Piero Ginori Conti (1865–1939), Florence, Italy, for his contributions to the Tuscan borax industry.

giorgiosite.occurrence: A rare incrustation on recent lava (Th ´ ıra Island, Greece); a weathering product in fractures in sideritic iron formation (Big Fish River-Rapid Creek area, Canada).
giorgiosite.etymology: For Giorgios, a cone formed during the volcanic eruption of 1866 on Th ´ ıra Island.

giraudite.occurrence: A rare late-stage mineral with other selenides and sulﬁdes in uranium deposits.
giraudite.etymology: To honor Roger Giraud (1936– ), French electron microprobe analyst, B.R.G.M.–C.N.R.S., Orl´ eans, France.

giraudite-zn.occurrence: A rare late-stage mineral with other selenides and sulﬁdes in uranium deposits.
giraudite-zn.etymology: To honor Roger Giraud (1936– ), French electron microprobe analyst, B.R.G.M.–C.N.R.S., Orl´ eans, France.

girdite.occurrence: Very rare, coating fractures in oxidized tellurite and tellurate ores.
girdite.etymology: Honors Richard Gird (1836–1910), mining engineer and assayer, a discoverer of the Tombstone district, Arizona, USA.

girvasite.occurrence: A low-temperature hydrothermal mineral ﬁlling solution cavities in dolomite carbonatite in a diﬀerentiated alkaline massif.
girvasite.etymology: For Lake Girvas, northwest of the Kovdor massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

gismondine.occurrence: In cavities in nepheline and olivine basalt and leucite tephrite.
gismondine.etymology: For Professor Carlo Giuseppe Gismondi (1762{1824), Italian mineralogist, Rome, Italy, who ¯rst examined the mineral.

gismondine-ca.occurrence: In cavities in nepheline and olivine basalt and leucite tephrite.
gismondine-ca.etymology: For Professor Carlo Giuseppe Gismondi (1762{1824), Italian mineralogist, Rome, Italy, who ¯rst examined the mineral.

gittinsite.occurrence: In eudialyte-rich pegmatitic lenses in a regionally metamorphosed agpaitic syenite complex (Kipawa River, Canada); an alteration product of eudialyte in syenite, quartz syenite, and alkalic granite (Pajarito Mountain, New Mexico, USA).
gittinsite.etymology: For Professor John Gittins, Canadian petrologist, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada.

giuseppettite.occurrence: As veinlets in a block of sanidinite volcanic ejecta.
giuseppettite.etymology: Honors Giuseppe Giuseppetti, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy.

gjerdingenite-ca.occurrence: As alteration of vuonnemite formed in hydrothermal assemblages of peralkaline pegmatites related to agpaitic feldspathoidal syenites.
gjerdingenite-ca.etymology: Signifies the structural analog of gjerdingenite-Mn with dominant Ca in the D structural site.

gjerdingenite-fe.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in a sodic granite.
gjerdingenite-fe.etymology: For Lake Gjerdingen nearby the first discovered occurrence and with the suffix -Fe to indicate the dominant cation in the D site.

gjerdingenite-mn.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities, with little or no late-stage hydrothermal alteration, in a sodic alkaline granite.
gjerdingenite-mn.etymology: Root name is derived from the nearby Lake Gjerdingen. The suffix -Mn indicates the dominant cation in the D site of the structure.

gjerdingenite-na.occurrence: As alteration of vuonnemite formed in hydrothermal assemblages of peralkaline pegmatites related to agpaitic feldspathoidal syenites.
gjerdingenite-na.etymology: Signifies the structural analog of gjerdingenite-Fe with dominant Na in the D structural site.

gladite.etymology: For the original locality, Gladhammar, Sweden.

gladiusite.occurrence: A rare (only a few hundred mg are known to exist) low-temperature hydrothermal mineral in vugs in veins of dolomitic carbonatite.
gladiusite.etymology: Alludes to the crystal morphology, which resembles a double-edged sword (gladius in Latin).

gladkovskyite.occurrence: In limestone breccias cemented by realgar, orpiment, baryte, pyrite, clinochlore, fluorapatite, quartz, and talc.
gladkovskyite.etymology: Honors Russian geologist Boris Aleksandrovich Gladkovsky (1937-1990), who discovered the Vorontsovskoe gold deposit.

glagolevite.occurrence: In lenses within altered melilitic rocks in a phlogopite deposit in an alkaline massif.

glauberite.occurrence: A common constituent of continental and marine evaporite deposits; as sublimates around fumaroles; in mineral-ﬁlled cavities in basaltic lava; in nitrate deposits in arid climates.
glauberite.etymology: In allusion to Glauber’s Salt (Na 2SO4), the synthetic equivalent of the dominant chemical component, named for Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1668), German alchemist.

glaucocerinite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral on museum specimens from a Cu–Zn sulﬁde deposit.
glaucocerinite.etymology: From the Greek for bluish green and waxlike.

glaucochroite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA); in skarn at the contact between diabase and marble (Anakit Creek, Russia); in calc-silicate rocks with manganese ores (Kuruman, South Africa).
glaucochroite.etymology: From the Greek for blue green and color, in allusion to its color.

glaucodot.occurrence: In deep-seated deposits of high-temperature hydrothermal origin.
glaucodot.etymology: From the Greek for blue, in reference to its use in the dark blue glass called smalt.

glauconite.occurrence: Altered from detrital biotite or other parent materials, by marine diagenesis in shallow water under reducing conditions; especially in loosely consolidated sandstone (greensand), and impure limestone and siltstone.
glauconite.etymology: From the Greek glaucos, for bluish green.

glaucophane.occurrence: Characteristic of the blueschist facies, in former subduction zones in mountain belts; in the greenschist facies and in eclogites that have undergone retrograde metamorphism.
glaucophane.etymology: From the Greek for bluish green and to appear.

glaukosphaerite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposits.
glaukosphaerite.etymology: From the Greek for bluish green and spherical, the typical color and habit.

glikinite.occurrence: A sublimate around an active volcanic fumarole.
glikinite.etymology: Honors Russian Professor Arkady Glikin (1943-2012), Department of Crystallography, St. Petersburg State University, for his work on crystal growth and mineral forming processes.

glucine.occurrence: As segregations in mica-fluorite greisen in illite rocks (Boevskoye deposit, Russia).
glucine.etymology: From the Latin glucinium, beryllium, for its content of that element.

glushinskite.occurrence: As veinlets in brown coal seams impregnated with natural acetic acid (Chai-Tumus deposit, Russia); formed by reaction between Mg-rich minerals and oxalic acid secreted by incrusting lichen, Lecanora atra (Mill of Johnston, Scotland); in desert plants (Lake Huleh basin, Israel).
glushinskite.etymology: To honor Petr Ivanovich Glushinskii (1908– ), coal geologist, Institute of Arctic and Antarctic Geology, St. Petersburg, Russia.

assoc_parsed: southern part of the hatrurim complex

gmelinite-ca.occurrence: Formed from calcium-rich fluids, in basalts and related igneous rocks, also pegmatites.
gmelinite-ca.etymology: For Christian Gottlob Gmelin (1792-1860), mineralogist and chemist of Tübingen, Germany. The suffix indicates the dominance of Ca as the extra-framework cation.

gmelinite-k.occurrence: As drusy aggregates in cavities within brecciated pegmatite.
gmelinite-k.etymology: For Christian Gottlob Gmelin (1792-1860), mineralogist and chemist of Tübingen, Germany. The suffix indicates the predominance of K as the extra-framework cation.

gmelinite-na.occurrence: Formed from sodium-rich fluids, in basalts and related igneous rocks, also pegmatites.
gmelinite-na.etymology: For Christian Gottlob Gmelin (1792-1860), mineralogist and chemist of Tübingen, Germany. The suffix indicates the dominance of Na as the extra-framework cation.

gobbinsite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in amygdules in basalts (Co. Antrim, Ireland); in cavities in sodalite syenite in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
gobbinsite.etymology: For the type locality at The Gobbins, Ireland.

gobelinite.occurrence: From the weathering of cobaltite-gersdorffite and nearby tennantite under acidic conditions.
gobelinite.etymology: Alludes to the Old French word gobelin, equivalent to the German word kobold, from which the designation of the element cobalt was derived.

godlevskite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins, or in peridotite with other nickel sulﬁdes.
godlevskite.etymology: In honor of Mikhail Nikolaevich Godlevskii (1902–1984), Russian economic geologist, Central Institute of Geological Exploration for Base and Precious Metals, Moscow, Russia.

godovikovite.occurrence: As reaction crusts around outlets releasing sulfuric acid from burning coal heaps.
assoc_parsed: unspeciﬁed anhydrous calcium and magnesium sulfates
godovikovite.etymology: Honors Aleksandr Aleksandrovich Godovikov (1927–1995), Russian mineralogist and Director of the Fersman Mineralogical Museum, Moscow, Russia.

goedkenite.occurrence: A rare late-stage secondary hydrothermal mineral in a complex granite pegmatite.
goedkenite.etymology: To honor Dr. Virgil Linus Goedken (1940–1992), Department of Chemistry, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA.

goethite.occurrence: A common weathering product derived from numerous iron-bearing minerals in oxygenated environments; an important component of ore in weathered iron deposits. Also a primary precipitate in hydrothermal, marine, and bog environments upon oxidation of reduced iron-bearing waters.
goethite.etymology: Honors the German poet, dramatist, and philosopher, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832).

gold.occurrence: Widespread in very small quantities in rocks of many kinds throughout the world, and in sea water. In veins of epithermal origin, typically in quartz with pyrite and other sulﬁdes, and with tellurides; in pegmatites; in contact metamorphic deposits. Common in placers.
gold.etymology: An Old English word for the metal; perhaps related to the Sanskrit jval; chemical symbol from the Latin aurum, shining dawn .

goldfieldite.occurrence: In epithermal gold-bearing veins; less commonly in porphyry copper and volcanogenic massive sulﬁde deposits.
goldfieldite.etymology: After the type locality, Goldﬁeld, Nevada, USA.

goldichite.occurrence: Cementing fragments in slope debris from an oxidizing pyritiferous Colorado Plateau-type uranium deposit (Dexter No. 7 mine, Utah, USA); coating mine walls in an argillized sulfur deposit formed by underground fumarole activity (Santa B´ arbara mine, Argentina).
goldichite.etymology: Honors Dr. Samuel Stephen Goldich (1909–2000), American mineralogist, petrologist, and analytical isotope chemist, Professor of Geology, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA, who analyzed the mineral.

goldmanite.occurrence: In a small metamorphosed U{V deposit in sandstone, embedded in vanadium-rich clays and calcite (Sandy mine, New Mexico, USA); in calcareous metapelites and tungsten-bearing skarns (Coat-an-Noz, France); detrital.
goldmanite.etymology: For Dr. Marcus Isaac Goldman (1881{1965), American sedimentary petrologist, U.S. Geological Survey.

goldquarryite.occurrence: A supergene product on and between brecciated and hydrothermally rounded jasperoid fragments lightly cemented by late-stage silicification in a Carlin-type gold deposit.
goldquarryite.etymology: For the quarry where the first specimens were collected.

goldschmidtite.occurrence: An inclusion in a websteritic diamond (whose surface had green and brown radiation damage) from a kimberlite pipe.
goldschmidtite.etymology: Honors geochemist Victor Moritz Goldschmidt (1888-1947), for his wide-reaching contributions in geology, chemistry, mineralogy, crystallography, and petrology. He is widely recognized as the “founder of modern geochemistry”, formalized perovskite crystal chemistry and identified KNbO3 as a perovskite-structured compound.

golyshevite.etymology: Honors сгуstallographer Vladimir Mikhailovich Golyshev (1943-2000), Mordvinian State University, Saransk, Russia.

gonnardite.occurrence: In cavities in basalt, leucite tephrite, and altered skarn.
gonnardite.etymology: For Ferdinand Gonnard, French mineralogist, Lyons, France, who ¯rst noted the mineral.

gonyerite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veinlets cutting skarn (Lºangban, Sweden).
gonyerite.etymology: In honor of Forest A. Gonyer, analytical chemist in the Department of Mineralogy and Petrography, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

goosecreekite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in vugs and fractures in a Triassic diabase (Goose Creek quarry, Virginia, USA); in cavities in basalt (Nasik, India).
goosecreekite.etymology: For the initially described occurrence in the Goose Creek quarry, Virginia, USA.

gorceixite.occurrence: Probably always a secondary mineral; in novaculites and other sedimentary rocks; in carbonatites; from hydrothermal argillic alteration zones; in topaz greisen; in the fine-grained fraction of soils; commonly as favas in diamantiferous river sands.
gorceixite.etymology: To honor Henrique Gorceix (1842-1919), French mining geologist and mineralogist, Director, School of Mines, Ouro Preto, Brazil.

gordaite.occurrence: In the oxidized portions of a Cu-Zn sulfide deposit (San Francisco mine, Chile); on weathered mine dumps (Helbra, Germany); on the outside oxidized portions of a sea floor chimney formed by the mixing of hydrothermal fluids with sea water (Juan de Fuca Ridge).
gordaite.etymology: For the Sierra Gorda, Chile, from which the mineral was first fully characterized.

gordonite.occurrence: Rare in variscite-rich phosphate nodules in limestones ([Little Green Monster mine, near] Fairﬁeld, Utah, USA); a late-stage hydrothermal mineral in a complex granite pegmatite (Tip Top mine, South Dakota, USA).
gordonite.etymology: To honor Samuel George Gordon (1897–1953), American mineralogist, Academy of Natural Sciences, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA.

gorgeyite.occurrence: Typically an uncommon secondary mineral in evaporite deposits; in hydrothermal veins.
gorgeyite.etymology: Honors Rolf von G¨ orgey (1886–1915), mineralogist specializing in Austrian salt deposits.

gormanite.occurrence: As low-temperature fracture ﬁllings in phosphate-ironstones (Yukon Territory, Canada); in fractures in tonalite (Bisbee, Arizona, USA).
gormanite.etymology: Honoring Donald Herbert Gorman (1922– ), Professor of Mineralogy, Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada.

gortdrumite.occurrence: Admixed with other sulﬁde minerals in a vein cutting dolomitized limestone; mineral associations suggest formation at less than 200 ◦C.
gortdrumite.etymology: For the type locality, the Gortdrum deposit, Ireland.

goryainovite.occurrence: In diopside-amphibole skarn in metamorphosed greenstone, metavolcanic and metasedimentary rocks.
goryainovite.etymology: Honors Pavel Mikhailovich Goryainov (b. 1937) of the Geological Institute of the Kola Centre of the Russian Academy of Sciences for his contribution to the knowledge of the geology and petrology of banded iron formation of the Fennoscandian Shield.

goslarite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in oxidized portions of zinc sulfide deposits, particularly as coatings on walls of mine passages.
goslarite.etymology: For the locality at Goslar, Germany.

gottlobite.etymology: For the occurrence in Germany at Gottlob hill.

gotzenite.occurrence: In a nephelinite from the wall of the crater of an extinct volcano (Mt. Shaheru, Congo); in hornfels and marble xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
gotzenite.etymology: For Count Gustav Adolph von GÄ otzen(1886{?), noted German traveller who climbed Mt. Shaheru, Congo (Zaire), in 1894.

goudeyite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in a hydrothermal Cu–Sn orebody in rhyolite porphyries and breccias (Majuba Hill, Nevada, USA).
goudeyite.etymology: To honor Hatﬁeld Goudey (1906–1985), American economic geologist, mineral collector and dealer in microscopic specimens, San Mateo, California, USA, who contributed to knowledge of the type locality.

gowerite.occurrence: A rare weathering product of colemanite and priceite.
gowerite.etymology: To honor Harrison Preston Gower (1890–1967), Mining Manager, U.S. Borax and Chemical Company, for his assistance to scientiﬁc studies of Death Valley borate deposits.

goyazite.occurrence: In granite pegmatites; from hydrothermal argillic alteration zones; in kaolinitic claystones derived from air-fall volcanic tuﬀs; in carbonatites; detrital.

graemite.occurrence: A rare dehydration product of teineite, as pseudomorphs and incrustations.
graemite.etymology: Honors Richard Graeme (1941– ), American mining engineer and mineral collector, Phelps Dodge Corporation, USA, who found the ﬁrst specimen.

graeserite.etymology: Honors Professor Stefan Graeser (b. 1935) of the Mineralogical-Petrographic Institute, University of Basel, Switzerland for his research on oxides and sulfosalts of arsenic in the Binntal region.

graftonite.occurrence: A primary mineral or exsolution product in complex granite pegmatites.
graftonite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence near Grafton, New Hampshire, USA.

graftonite-ca.occurrence: A common primary phosphate in beryl-columbite-phosphate subtype of zoned rareelement pegmatites related to anatectic melts, generated by partial melting of metasedimentarymetavolcanics rocks during amphibolite-facies metamorphism and migmatization.
assoc_parsed: triphylite oxidized topotactically to ferrisicklerite and heterosite
graftonite-ca.etymology: The suffix indicates the M1Ca-analogue of graftonite, M(1)FeM(2),M(3)Fe2(PO4)2.

graftonite-mn.occurrence: A common primary phosphate in beryl-columbite-phosphate subtype of zoned rareelement pegmatites related to anatectic melts, generated by partial melting of metasedimentarymetavolcanics rocks during amphibolite-facies metamorphism and migmatization.
assoc_parsed: triphylite oxidized topotactically to ferrisicklerite and heterosite
graftonite-mn.etymology: The suffix indicates the M1Mn-analogue of graftonite, M(1)FeM(2),M(3)Fe2(PO4)2.

gramaccioliite-y.occurrence: In hydrothermal quartz veins cutting biotite gneiss (Italy); in metamorphosed bodies of brecciated bauxite and marble (Greece).
assoc_parsed: a mineral of the synchysite series
gramaccioliite-y.etymology: Honors Professor Carlo Maria Gramaccioli (b. 1935), University of Milan, Italy and a suffix to designate the dominant rare earth element, Yttrium.

grammatikopoulosite.occurrence: In a heavy mineral concentrate separated from podiform chromitite hosted in strongly serpentinized dunite from a mantle tectonite composed of harzburgite and minor intercalations of plagioclase-bearing lherzolite.
grammatikopoulosite.etymology: Honors Tassos Grammatikopoulos (b. 1966), geoscientist at the SGS Canada Inc., for his contributions to the economic mineralogy and mineral deposits of Greece.

grandaite.occurrence: From a small Fe-Mn-As deposit in metamorphosed quartzites (high-P, low-T blueschist facies).
grandaite.etymology: For the informal appellation of the Province where the Valletta mine is located - called ‘‘la Granda’’ (the Big One) for its considerable areal extent, one of the biggest in Italy.

grandidierite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in aluminous boron-rich rocks, thermally and high-grade regionally metamorphosed under low pressure; in pegmatites, aplites, gneisses; in xenoliths.
grandidierite.etymology: For Alfred Grandidier (1836{1912), French naturalist and explorer, an authority on Madagascar.

grandreefite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in isolated vugs in the oxidized portions of a breccia-hosted hydrothermal Cu–Pb–Ag deposit.
grandreefite.etymology: For the Grand Reef mine, Arizona, USA.

grandviewite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by the oxidation of Cu-bearing sulfides.
grandviewite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens.

grantsite.occurrence: In partially oxidized portions of sandstone seams and coalified wood in vanadiferous uranium deposits of the Colorado Plateau type.
grantsite.etymology: For the town of Grants, New Mexico, USA, near which it was first discovered.

graphite.occurrence: Formed by metamorphism of sedimentary carbonaceous material, by the reduction of carbon compounds; a primary constituent in igneous rocks.
assoc_parsed: a wide variety of minerals stable in the metamorphic conditions under which graphite forms. in meteorites
graphite.etymology: From the Greek to write, in allusion to its use as a crayon.

gratonite.occurrence: In vugs in hydrothermal copper ores.
gratonite.etymology: In honor of Louis Caryl Graton (1880–1970), Professor of Mining Geology, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

grattarolaite.occurrence: Very rare, in microcrystalline nodules in lignite beds which appear to have burned naturally.
grattarolaite.etymology: Honoring Giuseppe Grattarola (1844–1907), Professor of Mineralogy, Florence University, Florence, Italy.

graulichite-ce.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by weathering of arsenopyrite-bearing metaquartzite.
graulichite-ce.etymology: Honors mining engineer Jean-Marie Graulich (1920-2001), honorary Director of the Geological survey of Belgium, particularly for his contribution to the geology of the Stavelot Massif.

graulichite-la.occurrence: In a secondary oxidation assemblage in a sulfide deposit.
graulichite-la.etymology: The suffix indicates the La analogue of graulichite-(Ce).

gravegliaite.occurrence: Very rare, along fractures in metamorphosed manganiferous layers in radiolarian cherts in an ophiolite sequence.
gravegliaite.etymology: For Val Graveglia, Italy, within which the Gambatesa mine is located.

grayite.occurrence: In a lithium-bearing pegmatite (Mtoko district, Zimbabwe); in an oxidized granitic vein in Precambrian rocks (Gunnison, Colorado, USA); in fracture ﬁllings and disseminated through limestone (Fremont Co., Wyoming, USA).
grayite.etymology: In honor of Anton Gray, mining engineer, advisor to the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority.

grechishchevite.etymology: To honor Oleg Konstantinovich Grechishchev (1936– ), Institute of Geology, Novosibirsk, Russia, a student of the Tuva mercury deposits.

greenalite.occurrence: A primary phase in some banded iron formations.
greenalite.etymology: In allusion to its green color.

greenlizardite.occurrence: A secondary mineral on the walls of mines in U-V deposits that replaced wood and other organic material in sandstones and conglomerate (roll-front type U-V deposits).
greenlizardite.etymology: For the Green Lizard mine, the locality that provided the first specimens.

greenockite.occurrence: As earthy coatings, especially on sphalerite, in which it also occurs as a substituent; also rarely as crystals in cavities in maﬁc igneous rocks; in high-temerature hydrothermal vein deposits.
greenockite.etymology: In honor of Charles Murray Cathcart (1783–1859), Lord Greenock.

greenwoodite.occurrence: Part of the prograde assemblage in a green schist facies metamorphosed Mississippi-Valley type base-metal deposit.
greenwoodite.etymology: Honors Professor Hugh J. Greenwood (b. 1931), former head of the Geological Sciences Department, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, for his contributions to petrology.

gregoryite.occurrence: As phenocrysts in lengaite carbonatite lava.
gregoryite.etymology: Honors Professor John Walter Gregory (1864–1932), University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia and University of Glasgow, Glasgow, Scotland, who completed early scientiﬁc studies of the volcanism and structure of the East African Rift system.

greifensteinite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in Li-rich granite pegmatite.
greifensteinite.etymology: For the locality in Germany that provided the first specimens.

greigite.occurrence: Formed in lacustrine beds consisting of interbedded calcareous clays, silts, and ﬁne- to medium-grained arkosic sands; in varvelike laminae of grayish black sulﬁde-bearing clays and ﬁne silts; possibly as the result of seasonal variation in the composition and physical condition of lake waters; also in hydrothermal vein deposits; formed in magnetotactic bacteria, and by sulfate-reducing bacteria.
greigite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Joseph Wilson Greig (1895–1977), mineralogist and physical chemist, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA.

grenmarite.occurrence: An early crystallization product, embedded in microcline and fine-grained albite i n an alkaline nepheline syenite pegmatite dike cutting larvikite.
grenmarite.etymology: For Grenmar, the Norse name of the Langesundsfjord.

grguricite.occurrence: A low-temperature secondary phase in a limestone-hosted, stratiform, Pb-Ba (galenabaryte) deposit.
grguricite.etymology: Honors Australian geologist Ben Grguric (b. 1971), who reported the potentially equivalent ‘Ca-petterdite analogue’ from Happy Jack mine in 2006 and has published on secondary minerals and Australian topographic mineralogy.

griceite.occurrence: In sodalite inclusions in hornfels associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex.
griceite.etymology: Honors Dr. Joel Denison Grice (1946– ), Curator of Minerals at the Canadian Museum of Nature [National Museum of Natural Sciences], Ottawa, Canada.

grigorievite.occurrence: A sublimate on basaltic scoria deposited from fumarolic gas.
grigorievite.etymology: Honors Professor Dmitry Pavlovich Grigoriev (1909-2003), Saint Petersburg Mining Institute, Russia, for his contributions to the mineralogical sciences.

grimaldiite.occurrence: In ﬁne-grained intergrowth with other chromium oxide-hydroxide minerals in alluvial gravels (Merume River, Guyana); in cracks and crevices in penroseite from a hydrothermal mineral deposit (Hiaco, Bolivia).
grimaldiite.etymology: For Dr. Frank Saverio Grimaldi (1915– ), formerly Chief Chemist, U.S. Geological Survey.

grimselite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in veins in mineralized granodiorite.
grimselite.etymology: For the Grimsel region of Switzerland, which produced the first specimens.

griphite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in complex granite pegmatites.
griphite.etymology: From the Greek for enigma, as the chemical composition was originally puzzling.

grischunite.occurrence: An alteration product of sarkinite in a manganese deposit.
grischunite.etymology: From the former Romansch name Grischun for Graub¨ unden Canton.

groatite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral, most likely derived from the dissolution of lithiophosphate and lithiophilite, in a spodumene-rich portion of a zoned petalite-subgroup pegmatite.
groatite.etymology: Honors Lee A. Groat (b. 1959), professor of Mineralogy at the University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, for his extensive contributions to pegmatite mineralogy.

found in the baunt evenk district

grootfonteinite.occurrence: A product of the regional metamorphism of a Pb-Mn-(As-Ba)-rich, chemically heterogeneous, volcanic-hydrothermal assemblage.
grootfonteinite.etymology: For the Grootfontein district, in which the mine that provided the first specimens is located.

grossite.occurrence: In argillaceous limestones metamorphosed at high temperature and low pressure (Hatrurim Formation, Israel); in Ca–Al-rich inclusions thought formed by condensation from a hot gas or molten droplets (meteorites).
grossite.etymology: Honors Dr. Shulamit Gross (1923– ), Geological Survey of Israel, Jerusalem, Israel, who noted the species in the Hatrurim Formation, Israel.

grossmanite.occurrence: Likely formed through high-temperature condensation in the solar nebula, followed by melting and crystallization in Ca-,Al-rich refractory inclusions in a meteorite.
grossmanite.etymology: Honors Lawrence Grossman (b. 1946), Professor of Cosmochemistry, University of Chicago, USA, for his fundamental contributions to meteorite research.

grossular.occurrence: In contact and regionally metamorphosed calcareous rocks, or rocks which have undergone calcium metasomatism; in some schists and serpentinites.
grossular.etymology: From Ribes Grossularium or gooseberry; the botanical name, in reference to a typical greenish color.

groutite.occurrence: A secondary mineral lining vugs in weathered banded iron formations (Minnesota, USA); manganiferous talc schists (Talcville, New York, USA); a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA); and a variety of hydrothermal orebodies (Arizona, USA).
groutite.etymology: Honors Professor Frank Fitch Grout (1880–1958), petrologist, of the University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA.

grumiplucite.occurrence: Very rare, in quartz-carbonate veins in mercury deposist, probably formed during retrograde metamorphism.
grumiplucite.etymology: For the GRUppo MIneralogico e Paleontological LUcchese, a group of amateur mineralogists who provided the specimens for study.

grundmannite.occurrence: A primary mineral, deposited from oxidizing low-temperature hydrothermal fluids at the waning stage of selenide formation in a telethermal vein.
grundmannite.etymology: Honors Günter Grundmann (b. 1947), for his pioneering work on the El Dragón mine.

grunerite.occurrence: Common in medium- to high-grade metamorphosed iron formations. A product of contact metamorphism, and in some blueschist facies metaquartzites.
grunerite.etymology: To honor the French chemist, Louis Emmanuel Gruner (1809{1883), who provided the ¯rst analysis. All rights reserved.
