gruzdevite.occurrence: In veinlets of probable low-temperature hydrothermal origin (Chauvai deposit, Kyrgyzstan).
gruzdevite.etymology: To honor the Russian mineralogist, Vyacheslav Sergeevich Gruzdev (1938–1977), Institute of Mineralogy and Geochemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia.

guanacoite.occurrence: A secondary phase in a high sulfidation-type, Au-rich epithermal deposit hosted by felsic rocks (El Guanaco mine), weathered in an arid and Mg-rich environment.
guanacoite.etymology: For the occurrence at El Guanaco mine, Chile.

guanajuatite.occurrence: In hydrothermal deposits of low to medium temperatures.
guanajuatite.etymology: For the locality in Guanajuato, Mexico.

guanine.occurrence: An uncommon component of phosphatic crusts associated with guano from seabirds or bats.
guanine.etymology: From the Peruvian guanu, for dung, in allusion to its mode of formation in nature.

guarinoite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of a polymetallic sulﬁde deposit.
guarinoite.etymology: Honors Andr´ e Guarino (1945– ), mineral collector and medical technologist, Toulon, France, who ﬁrst collected the mineral.

gudmundite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral formed in sulﬁde deposits.
gudmundite.etymology: For the occurrence at Gudmundstorp, Sweden.

guerinite.occurrence: A recent weathering product in oxidizing arsenic-rich mineral deposits.
guerinite.etymology: Honors Henri Gu´ erin (1906– ), who synthesized the compound.

guettardite.occurrence: Of low-temperature hydrothermal origin, in marbles (Madoc, Canada; Seravezza, Italy).
guettardite.etymology: Honors Jean Etienne Guettard (1715–1786), French mineralogist and geologist.

gugiaite.occurrence: In cavities in skarns and melanite adjacent to an alkalic syenite.
gugiaite.etymology: For the locality near Gugia, China.

guidottiite.occurrence: In a pocket in a hydrothermally altered, bedded manganese deposit.
guidottiite.etymology: Honors Charles V. Guidotti (1935-2005), University of Maine, USA., for his many contributions to phyllosilicate mineralogy.

guildite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed in mine workings by burning pyritic ores.
guildite.etymology: Honors Professor Frank Nelson Guild (1870–1939), American mineralogist and economic geologist, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA.

guilleminite.occurrence: In the oxidized portions of a Cu–Co sulﬁde deposit (Musonoi mine, Congo).
guilleminite.etymology: Honors Dr. Claude Guillemin (1923–1994), eminent French mineralogist, Bureau de Recherches G´ eologiques et Mini` eres, Paris, France.

gungerite.occurrence: By late stage, low temperature, hydrothermal processes in limestone breccias composed of calcite and dolomite cemented by orpiment, pyrite, realgar, stibnite, baryte, quartz.
assoc_parsed: minerals of the chabourneite-dalnegroite and vorontsoviteferrovorontsovite series
gungerite.etymology: Honors Yuri Vladimirovich Gunger (b. 1961), a mining engineer, surveyor, historian, and authority on the Northern Urals.

gunningite.occurrence: Of rare occurrence in dry areas of the oxidized portions of sphalerite-bearing deposits; occurs also as a post-mining eﬄorescence on museum specimens.
gunningite.etymology: Honors Dr. Henry Cecil Gunning (1901–1991), Geological Survey of Canada and Professor of Geology, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada.

gunterite.occurrence: In efflorescencent crusts on mine walls and in fractures in sandstone, formed by the oxidation of montroseite–corvusite assemblages.
gunterite.etymology: Honors Professor Mickey Eugene Gunter (b. 1953), University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA, for his studies in optical mineralogy and the mineralogy of asbestos minerals.

gupeiite.occurrence: Innermost in spheres, surrounded by nickel-iron minerals and their oxidation products, apparently of extraterrestrial origin, found in placers.
gupeiite.etymology: For an eastern passageway, Gupeikou, of the Great Wall of China.

gurimite.occurrence: A common accessory mineral in thin veins of paralava cutting gehlenite-flamite hornfels and formed at >1100° C from the relatively fast crystallization of residual melt.
gurimite.etymology: After the geographical region of Gurim, Israel, its type locality.

gustavite.occurrence: A rare mineral of hydrothermal origin; also in pegmatites.
gustavite.etymology: To honor Gustav Adolf Hageman (1842–1916), chemical engineer for the Cryolite Firm, Ivigtut, Greenland.

guyanaite.occurrence: In ﬁne-grained intergrowth with other chromium oxide-hydroxide minerals (Merume River, Guyana); in chromium-rich tremolite skarns, metaquartzites, and chlorite veins (Outokumpu, Finland).

gwihabaite.occurrence: As crusts and eﬄorescences formed by bacterial action on bat guano in caves.
gwihabaite.etymology: For Gcwihaba Cave where the ﬁrst specimens were collected, although the mineral name is spelled without the “c” (which stands for the “!” or “click” sound spoken by the San people who named the cave).

gypsum.occurrence: A common constituent of sedimentary rocks, particularly marine salt deposits, and soils formed directly by evaporation or later by hydration of anhydrite. Formed by the reaction between sulfuric acid and carbonate rock in oxidizing sulﬁde deposits, and by the action of sulfurous volcanic gases on surrounding Ca-bearing rock. As eﬄorescences in mines and speleothems in caves.
gypsum.etymology: From the Greek for calcined gypsum used as plaster.

gyrolite.occurrence: As replacements of wall rocks and in vugs, amygdules, and veinlets in basalts; in hydrothermally altered rhyolites and sediments; in some ore deposits.
gyrolite.etymology: From the Greek for round, in reference to its common habit.

gysinite-la.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of rare-earth-bearing lead deposits, the rare-earths perhaps supplied from altered uraninite.
gysinite-la.etymology: Honors Marcel Gysin (1891–1974), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.

gysinite-nd.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of rare-earth-bearing lead deposits, the rare-earths perhaps supplied from altered uraninite.
gysinite-nd.etymology: Honors Marcel Gysin (1891–1974), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.

haapalaite.occurrence: As thin scales in the Kokka serpentine and in carbonate; rarely in chrysotile.
haapalaite.etymology: In honor of Paavo Haapala (1906– ), Chief Geologist of the Outokumpu Company, Finland.

hafnon.occurrence: In tantalum-bearing granite pegmatites (Zamb¶ezia district, Mozambique); in a weathered pegmatite (Mt. Holland, Western Australia).

hagendorfite.occurrence: In complex granite pegmatites; in phosphatic nodules in shale.
hagendorfite.etymology: For Hagendorf, Germany, the locality which yielded the ﬁrst specimens.

haggertyite.occurrence: As isolated crystals or in small groups within the reaction rims around serpentinized mafic xenoliths in olivine lamproite (Arkansas); in the groundmass of diamondiferous olivine lamproite pipes (Australia).
haggertyite.etymology: Honors Stephen E. Haggerty (b. 1938), Department of Geology, University of Massachusetts, USA, for his contributions to the understanding of the mineralogy and crystal chemistry of titanate minerals from the Earth’s mantle.

haggite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of Colorado Plateau-type U-V deposits.
haggite.etymology: Honors Gunnar Hagg (1903- ),chemist and crystallographer, of the University of Uppsala, Uppsala, Sweden.

hagstromite.occurrence: A secondary, oxidation zone mineral likely formed by oxidation of earlier tellurides, chalcopyrite, and galena.
hagstromite.etymology: Honors John P. Hagstrom (b. 1953) of Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, a mineral collector who in recent years focused on deposits in the Goodsprings district, Nevada, and the Blue Bell mine and Otto Mountain near Baker, California. He has provided many of his collected specimens for scientific study, especially those from Otto Mountain, including for this work.

haidingerite.occurrence: Formed by dehydration of pharmacolite (Getchell mine, Nevada, USA).
haidingerite.etymology: Honors Wilhelm Karl von Haidinger (1795–1871), Austrian mineralogist.

haigerachite.occurrence: A secondary phosphate formed on a mine dump.
haigerachite.etymology: For the village and valley near the mine.

haineaultite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in altered marble zenoliths and breccia in a complex peralkaline intrusion (nepheline and sodalite syenties).
haineaultite.etymology: Honors Gilles Haineault (b. 1946) of St-Mathieu de Beloeil, Quebec, a collector and dealer of minerals from Mont Saint-Hilaire.

hainite.occurrence: In cavities and embedded in the groundmass of a phonolite.
hainite.etymology: For the locality, formerly named Hoher Hain, in the Czech Republic.

hainite-y.occurrence: In cavities and embedded in the groundmass of a phonolite.
hainite-y.etymology: For the locality, formerly named Hoher Hain, in the Czech Republic.

haitaite-la.etymology: For the town where the studied material was collected and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

haiweeite.occurrence: On fracture surfaces in granite and in voids in neighboring loosely consolidated lake bed sediments (Coso Mountains, California, USA); along fractures in tourmaline-bearing granite and granite pegmatite (Brazil).
haiweeite.etymology: For the Haiwee Reservoir, Coso Mountains, California, USA, above which the mineral was first found to occur.

hakite.etymology: In honor of Jaroslav Hak (1931– ), Czech mineralogist, Institute of Ore Research, Kutn´ a Hora, Czech Republic.

hakite-hg.etymology: In honor of Jaroslav Hak (1931– ), Czech mineralogist, Institute of Ore Research, Kutn´ a Hora, Czech Republic.

halamishite.occurrence: In a phosphide assemblage related to the Fe-Ni-P system in a pyrometamorphic rock (Hatrurim Formation).
halamishite.etymology: For the locality, the Halamish Wadi, Israel, were the mineral was found.

halite.occurrence: Typically in sedimentary rocks of evaporite association, may form immense beds; also as volcanic sublimates, eﬄorescences, cave deposits. Crystals are common in multiphase ﬂuid inclusions; may be included in other minerals as a product of intermediate-grade metamorphism.

hallimondite.occurrence: A secondary mineral found on a museum specimen from an oxidizing As-Pb-bearing deposit, formed by alteration of galena.
hallimondite.etymology: Honors Dr. Arthur Francis Hallimond (1890-1968), British mineralogist, London, England, for his work with secondary uranium minerals.

halloysite.occurrence: A product of hydrothermal alteration or surface weathering of aluminosilicate minerals, as feldspars. Formed by dehydration of endellite above 110 ±C.
halloysite.etymology: To honor Baron Omalius d'Halloy (1707{1789), who ¯rst observed the mineral.

halloysite-10a.occurrence: A product of hydrothermal alteration or surface weathering of aluminosilicate minerals, as feldspars. Formed by dehydration of endellite above 110 ±C.
halloysite-10a.etymology: To honor Baron Omalius d'Halloy (1707{1789), who ¯rst observed the mineral.

halloysite-7a.occurrence: A product of hydrothermal alteration or surface weathering of aluminosilicate minerals, as feldspars. Formed by dehydration of endellite above 110 ±C.
halloysite-7a.etymology: To honor Baron Omalius d'Halloy (1707{1789), who ¯rst observed the mineral.

halotrichite.occurrence: As eﬄorescences in weathering sulﬁde deposits and oxidizing pyritic coals, with persistent accumulations in arid climates; as a precipitate around volcanic fumaroles and hot springs.
halotrichite.etymology: From the Latin, halotrichum, derived from the Old German, Haarsalz, for hair salts ,i n allusion to its common hairlike habit.

halurgite.occurrence: Of rare occurrence in interstices and vugs in a rock salt diapir.
halurgite.etymology: Honors the Institute of Halurgy, St. Petersburg, Russia, for its studies of saline deposits.

hambergite.occurrence: An uncommon accessory mineral in granite pegmatites.
hambergite.etymology: Honors Professor Axel Hamberg (1863–1933), Swedish mineralogist and geographer.

hammarite.etymology: For the locality at Gladhammar, Sweden.

assoc_parsed: distribution from the schone aussicht mine

hanawaltite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of cinnabar, in a mercury deposit in silicate-carbonate rock hydrothermally altered from serpentinite.
hanawaltite.etymology: To honor Dr. Joseph Donald Hanawalt (1903–1987), American metallurgist, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA, for his early work in X-ray powder diﬀraction.

hancockite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA); in a metamorphosed manganese-iron orebody in skarns enclosed in dolomitic marble (Jakobsberg, Sweden).
hancockite.etymology: For Elwood P. Hancock (1836{1916), of Burlington, New Jersey, USA, collector of minerals from Franklin.

hanjiangite.occurrence: Disseminated in lenticular bodies and veins associated with strataform hydrothermal barium deposits.
hanjiangite.etymology: After the Hanjiang River, that flows through the Shiti ore district and is the largest branch of the Yangtze River, China.

hanksite.etymology: Honors Henry Garber Hanks (1826–1907), for his service as ﬁrst State Mineralogist of California, USA.

hannayite.occurrence: As rare druses on guano-derived phosphate mineral crusts in caves.
hannayite.etymology: Honors James Ballantine Hannay (1855–1931), Scottish chemist, University of Manchester, Manchester, England.

hannebachite.occurrence: Lining cavities in blocks of melilite-nepheline-leucitite at the base of a volcano.
hannebachite.etymology: For the locality, Hannebacher Ley volcano, Germany, from which the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

hansblockite.occurrence: In a vein cutting interbedded pyritiferous black shales and hematite-bearing siltstones.
hansblockite.etymology: Honors Hans Block (1881-1953), for his contributions to fostering Bolivian mining.

hansesmarkite.occurrence: On fracture surfaces in a hydrothermally altered syenite pegmatite dike.
hansesmarkite.etymology: Honors Hans Morten Thrane Esmark (1801-1882), a Norwegian priest from the town of Brevik, an enthusiastic mineral collector in the pegmatites of the Larvik Plutonic Complex who discovered several new mineral species including aegirine, leucophanite, and thorite.

hapkeite.occurrence: In a highland regolith breccia clast in the lunar meteorite Dhofar 280, formed by impact-induced, vapor-phase deposition under extreme reducing conditions in lunar soil.
hapkeite.etymology: Honors Bruce Hapke (emeritus, University of Pittsburgh), who first predicted the presence of vapor-deposited elemental Fe as coatings on lunar soil grains.

haradaite.occurrence: In coarse-grained rhodonite ore (Noda-Tamagawa mine, Japan); as veinlets cutting rhodonite-goldmanite ore (Yamato mine, Japan).
haradaite.etymology: For Zyunpei Harada (1898{1992), Emeritus Professor, Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan.

hardystonite.occurrence: In granular ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
hardystonite.etymology: For Hardyston Township in which Franklin is situated.

harkerite.occurrence: In skarns in dolomitic limestones at the contact with granite (Camas Malag, Scotland); in volcanic ejecta (Alban Hills, Italy).
harkerite.etymology: For Alfred Harker (1859{1939), British petrologist, Cambridge University, Cambridge, England.

harmotome.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, in cavities in basalts, phonolites, trachytes; in gneisses, and in some ore veins.
harmotome.etymology: From the Greek harmos, for a joint, and tome, for a cutting, as the twinned crystals may be divided.

harmunite.occurrence: In pyrometamorphic larnite pebbles of a pseudo-conglomerate, the cement of which consists of intensely altered larnite-bearing rocks, likely formed in the presence of sulfate melt .
harmunite.etymology: For Mt. Harmun, from where the first specimens were collected.

harrisonite.occurrence: A minor but wide-spread constituent in a layered iron silicate-quartz-apatite body in gneisses, probably a shaly and phosphatic iron formation metamorphosed to the granulite facies.
harrisonite.etymology: To honor Dr. James Merritt Harrison (1915{1990), former Director of the Canadian Geological Survey.

harstigite.occurrence: A rare mineral found in open ¯ssures in a metamorphosed manganese deposit.
harstigite.etymology: For the Harstigen mine, Sweden, where it was found.

hartite.occurrence: Rare, in lignite seams and fractures in fossil coaliﬁed and siliciﬁed tree trunks. Typically obtained by leaching lignite with organic solvents and reprecipitation.
hartite.etymology: For its discovery locality, Oberhart, Austria.

hashemite.occurrence: Disseminated in veinlets cutting phosphate carbonate rock, the stratigraphic correlative of the Mottled Zone of the Hatrurim Formation, Israel.
hashemite.etymology: Honors the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, within which the species occurs.

hastingsite.occurrence: In nepheline syenite and granite; in schists, gneisses, tactites, and amphibolites.
hastingsite.etymology: For a locality in Hastings Co., Ontario, Canada.

hatchite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, in crystalline dolostone.
hatchite.etymology: To honor Dr. Frederick Henry Hatch (1864–1932), American geologist and mining engineer.

hatertite.occurrence: A sublimate at a volcanic fumarole.
hatertite.etymology: Honors Professor Frédéric Hatert (b. 1973), University of Liège, Belgium, for his contributions to the mineralogy and crystal chemistry of alluaudite-group minerals.

hatrurite.occurrence: In a high-temperature contact metamorphic assemblage in a larnitebrownmillerite-mayenite rock, probably derived from ¯ne-grained sediments.
hatrurite.etymology: For the Hatrurim Formation in Israel.

hauchecornite.etymology: Honors William Hauchecorn (1828–1900), Director of the Geological Survey and the Mining Academy, Berlin, Germany.

hauckite.occurrence: Very rare, found in several diﬀerent parageneses in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
hauckite.etymology: To honor Richard Philip Hauck (1935– ), mineral collector of Bloomﬁeld, New Jersey, USA, for his contributions to preserving scientiﬁcally signiﬁcant specimens from Franklin and Sterling Hill, New Jersey, USA.

hauerite.occurrence: A low-temperature mineral commonly associated with solfataric waters, in clay deposits rich in sulfur, and from decomposed extrusive rocks.
hauerite.etymology: In honor of Joseph Ritter von Hauer (1778–1863), and his son Franz Ritter von Hauer (1822–1899), Austrian geologists.

hausmannite.occurrence: A primary mineral in hydrothermal veins. Also produced by metamorphism of manganiferous rocks.
hausmannite.etymology: Honors Johan Friedrich Ludwig Hausmann (1782–1859), Professor of Mineralogy, University of G¨ ottingen, G¨ ottingen, Germany.

hauyne.occurrence: In phonolites and related leucite- or nepheline-rich igneous rocks; less commonly in nepheline-free extrusives.
hauyne.etymology: To honor Abb¶e Ren¶e Just HaÄuy (1743{1822), French crystallographer and mineralogist.

hawleyite.occurrence: As coatings on ﬁne-grained sphalerite and siderite in vugs; probably of secondary origin, deposited from meteoric waters in vugs and along late fractures.
hawleyite.etymology: To honor Professor James Edwin Hawley (1897–1965), Canadian mineralogist, Queen’s University, Kingston, Ontario, Canada.

hawthorneite.occurrence: Formed during upper-mantle (75–100 km, 900–1100 ◦C, 20–30 kbar) metasomatism of chromian spinel in peridotite xenoliths in a kimberlite pipe.
hawthorneite.etymology: For John Barry Hawthorne (1934– ), formerly Chief Geologist (Diamonds), DeBeers Consolidated Mines, South Africa, in honor of his contributions to studies of the upper mantle.

haxonite.occurrence: In iron meteorites and carbonaceous chondrites.
haxonite.etymology: Honors H.J. Axon, metallurgist at the University of Manchester, Manchester, England.

haycockite.occurrence: In a hortonolite dunite (replacement) pegmatite in the Bushveld complex (Mooihoek mine, South Africa).
haycockite.etymology: To honor Maurice Hall Haycock (1900–?), former Head, Mineralogy Section, Mineral Sciences Division, Department of Energy, Mines, and Resources, Mines Branch, Ottawa, Canada.

haydeeite.etymology: For the Haydee mine, where the first specimens were collected.

haynesite.occurrence: Rare in an oxidized uranium deposit in mudstones and sandstones.
haynesite.etymology: Honors Patrick Eugene Haynes (1953- ), American geologist, mineral collector and dealer, who found the ﬁrst specimens.

hazenite.occurrence: In and/or on completely dried-out or decomposed cyanobacteria on porous calcium carbonate (mainly calcite and aragonite) substrates or tufa in a hypersaline alkaline lake in a hydrologically closed basin.
hazenite.etymology: Honors Robert Miller Hazen, staff scientist at the Geophysical Laboratory, Carnegie Institution of Washington, D.C, USA, for his contributions to Earth sciences in general, and mineralogy in particular, in both research and education, as well as for his contributions to understanding interactions between minerals and organic molecules.

heamanite-ce.occurrence: As inclusions in a diamond, likely derived from the upper mantle.
heamanite-ce.etymology: Honors Larry Heaman (b. 1955), Distinguished University Professor, University of Alberta, Canada, for contributions to radiometric dating applied to diamond-bearing kimberlites, mantlederived eclogites, and lamprophyre dikes. The suffix indicates the dominant rare earth element.

heazlewoodite.occurrence: In serpentinized dunites and lherzolites, and in ophiolites, probably of hydrothermal origin; in layered maﬁc intrusives nd chromitites, where it may be a low-temperature secondary mineral; in mantle xenoliths.
heazlewoodite.etymology: For the locality near Heazlewood, Tasmania, Australia.

hechtsbergite.etymology: For the Hechtsberg quarry, Germany, source of the ﬁrst specimens.

hectorfloresite.occurrence: In dessication cavities in a nitrate deposit; may be more widespread than this single locality indicates.
hectorfloresite.etymology: Honors Professor Hector Flores W. (1906–1984), Chilean economic geologist and teacher, University of Chile, Santiago, Chile.

hectorite.occurrence: In a bentonite deposit, altered from clinoptilolite derived from volcanic tu® and ash with a high glass content, related to hot spring activity (Hector, California, USA).
hectorite.etymology: For the locality at Hector, California, USA.

hedenbergite.occurrence: A common constituent of metamorphosed iron formations or other ferruginous siliceous sediments; common in Fe-Mn skarns. In alkalic granites, syenites, and in xenoliths in kimberlite.
hedenbergite.etymology: To honor the Swedish chemist, M.A. Ludwig Hedenberg, who ¯rst described the species.

hedleyite.occurrence: Typically a late-stage hydrothermal mineral in quartz veins and massive sulﬁdes associated with skarns and breccias; less commonly in pegmatites.
hedleyite.etymology: For the locality being near Hedley, Canada.

hedyphane.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in metamorphosed manganese deposits (Sweden); in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
hedyphane.etymology: From the Greek for beautifully bright, in allusion to the typical luster of specimens.

heftetjernite.occurrence: In vugs in albite in a mixed LCT-NYF type cleavelandite-amazonite pegmatite.
assoc_parsed: dark grayish brown mineral of the pyrochlore-microlite group
heftetjernite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens, Heftetjern pegmatite, Norway.

heideite.etymology: Honors Professor Fritz Heide (1891–1973), meteoriticist of Jena, Germany.

heidornite.occurrence: Very rare, in a cavity in a marine evaporite deposit.
heidornite.etymology: Honors Dr. F. Heidorn, Bentheim, Germany, for his scientiﬁc study of the Zechstein deposits.

heinrichite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in oxidized uranium deposits.
heinrichite.etymology: Honors Professor Eberhardt William Heinrich (1918-1991), mineralogist, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA.

heisenbergite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by weathering.

hejtmanite.occurrence: In arfvedsonite veins in pegmatite cutting alkalic granite and syenite (Mbolwe Hill, Zambia).
hejtmanite.etymology: To honor Dr. Bohuslav Hejtman, Emeritus Professor of Petrology, Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic.

heklaite.occurrence: A sublimate precipitated around fumaroles emitting F-rich volcanic gases.
heklaite.etymology: For the Hekla volcano, Iceland, where the first specimens were collected.

heliophyllite.occurrence: From metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebodies (Sweden); in the oxidation zone above a Pb–Zn deposit (Xitieshan mine, China); in metallic slag exposed to seawater (Laurium, Greece).
heliophyllite.etymology: From the Greek for sun and leaf, in allusion to its color and habit.

hellandite-ce.occurrence: Inside miarolitic cavities in alkali-syenite volcanic ejecta in an ignimbrite.
hellandite-ce.etymology: For geologist Amund Theodor Helland (1846-1918), of Oslo, Norway. The suffix indicates the dominant REE at the Y site.

hellandite-y.occurrence: In granite pegmatite (Norway; Wakefield Lake, Canada).
hellandite-y.etymology: For geologist Amund Theodor Helland (1846-1918), of Oslo, Norway. The suffix indicates the dominant REE at the Y site.

hellyerite.occurrence: Very rare, as coatings on shear surfaces in serpentinite.
hellyerite.etymology: Honors Henry Hellyer (1791–1832), ﬁrst Surveyor-General of the Van Diemen’s Land Company and explorer of northwestern Tasmania.

helmutwinklerite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in corroded tennantite ore from a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
helmutwinklerite.etymology: Honors Professor Helmut G.F. Winkler (1915–1980), University of G¨ ottingen, G¨ ottingen, Germany, for his contributions to petrology, mineralogy, and crystallography.

helvine.occurrence: May be locally abundant in granites, granite pegmatites, gneisses, and contact zones and skarns.
helvine.etymology: From the Greek for sun, in allusion to its yellow color.

hematite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in felsic igneous rocks, a late-stage sublimate in volcanic rocks, and in high-temperature hydrothermal veins. A product of contact metamorphism and in metamorphosed banded iron formations. A common cement in sedimentary rocks and a major constituent in oolitic iron formations. Abundant on weathered iron-bearing minerals.
hematite.etymology: From the Greek for blood, in allusion to its color.

hematolite.occurrence: In ﬁssures in metamorphosed limestone in metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebodies.
hematolite.etymology: From the Greek for blood, in allusion to the color.

hematophanite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed banded Fe–Mn ore deposit in dolostone (Jakobsberg, Sweden).
hematophanite.etymology: From the Greek for blood and visible, presumably for the blood-red color exhibited in transmitted light.

hemihedrite.occurrence: Formed through oxidation of galena, sphalerite, and pyrite, in the oxide zone of hydrothermal lead-bearing veins.
hemihedrite.etymology: In allusion to its distinctive hemihedral morphology.

hemimorphite.occurrence: A secondary mineral typically found in the oxidized zone of zinc-bearing mineral deposits.
hemimorphite.etymology: In allusion to the mineral's hemimorphic morphology.

hemleyite.occurrence: In an unmelted portion of the heavily shocked (<20 GPa; <2000 °C) L6 Suizhou chondrite meteorite. Perhaps relevant to the mineralogy of Earth’s deep interior, it could have a role at the bottom of the Earth’s mantle transition zone and within the uppermost lower mantle.
assoc_parsed: fe-bearing pyroxene with a composition nearly identical to hemleyite
hemleyite.etymology: Honors Russell J. Hemley (b. 1954), former Director of the Geophysical Laboratory, Carnegie Institution, Washington D.C., USA., for his research exploring the behavior of materials under extreme conditions of pressure and temperature.

hemloite.etymology: For the Hemlo deposit, Ontario, Canada, where it occurs.

hemusite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, early formed in the mineral association (Chelopech, Bulgaria); in a polymetallic deposit in carboniferous porphyritic andesites (Kochbulak deposit, Uzbekistan).
hemusite.etymology: After an ancient name for the Balkan Mountains, on the southern slope of which the Chelopech deposit occurs; probably of Thracian origin.

hendekasartorite.etymology: For a member of the sartorite homologous series with an eleven-fold superstructure.

hendersonite.occurrence: In thin seams and veinlets through sandstone at the interface between partially oxidized and unoxidized ore in Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits.
hendersonite.etymology: Honors Dr. Edward Porter Henderson (1898–1992), formerly Curator of Meteorites at the Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., USA, who contributed to the knowledge of the mineralogy of U–V deposits.

hendricksite.occurrence: Restricted to irregular lens- or sheetlike skarn bodies in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
hendricksite.etymology: For Dr. Sterling B. Hendricks (1902{ ), American crystallographer and chemist, a student of micas.

heneuite.occurrence: In a serpentine–magnesite deposit developed in a regional metamorphic terrain.
heneuite.etymology: Honors Professor Henrich Neumann (1914–1983), Mineralogical-Geological Museum, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway.

henmilite.occurrence: Very rare, in cavities in borate veins in contact-metasomatized limestone.
henmilite.etymology: Honors Professor Kitinosuke Henmi (1919–1997), and his daughter Dr. Chiyoko Henmi (1949– ), Department of Earth Science, Okayama University, Okayama, Japan, in recognition of their mineralogical work on the skarn deposit at Fuka, Japan.

hennomartinite.occurrence: From a hand specimen, in veinlets of s¶erandite-pectolite cutting sugilite, probably of hydrothermal origin in a bedded manganese deposit.
hennomartinite.etymology: For Henno Martin, German geologist, who has worked on the Precambrian geology of the general area where the mineral occurs.

henritermierite.occurrence: As small grains ¯lling interstices between crystals of other minerals in a manganese ore deposit (Tachgagalt mine, Morocco).
henritermierite.etymology: For Henri F.E. Termier (1897{ ), Professor of Geology at the Sorbonne, Paris, France.

henryite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, with other Cu–Ag tellurides.
henryite.etymology: In honor of Professor Norman Fordyce McKerron Henry (1909–1983), mineralogist and ore microscopist, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, England.

henrymeyerite.occurrence: In late-stage veins associated with metasomatized phoscorite-carbonatite rocks of an alkaline ultramafic complex (Kovodor, Russia); in carbonate-metasomatized lherzolitic and harzburgitic mantle xenoliths (Prince Charles Mountains, Antarctica).
henrymeyerite.etymology: Honors Professor Henry O.A. Meyer (1937–1995) for his contributions to the petrology and mineralogy of mantle-derived xenoliths and kimberlitic rocks.

hentschelite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in some oxidized copper deposits.
hentschelite.etymology: Honors Dr. Gerhard Hentschel (1930– ), Geological Survey of Hesse, Wiesbaden, Germany.

hephaistosite.occurrence: On fragments of altered pyroclastic breccia in a high temperature (400° C) fumarole , most likely formed as a sublimate.
hephaistosite.etymology: For Hephaistos, the Greek god of fire, whose workshops were believed to be located at Vulcano.

heptasartorite.etymology: For a member of the sartorite homologous series with a seven-fold superstructure.

herbertsmithite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of polymetallic mineral deposits.
herbertsmithite.etymology: Honors G.F. Herbert Smith (1872-1953), British Museum (Natural History), who discovered paratacamite.

hercynite.occurrence: In high-grade metamorphosed ferruginous argillaceous sediments and in some mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks. Also in placers.
hercynite.etymology: From the Latin, Silva Hercynia, for the Bohemian Forest, Czech Republic, where the mineral was first found.

herderite.occurrence: Probably from a complex granite pegmatite.
herderite.etymology: To honor Siegmund August Wolfgang von Herder (1776–1838), mining oﬃcial, Freiberg, Saxony, Germany.

hereroite.occurrence: Most likely a late-stage, low-temperature hydrothermal (epigenetic) reworking of primary Pb-Cu-Zn-Ag sulfides. Known from a single specimen purchased commercially.
hereroite.etymology: For the Herero people, one of the indigenous tribes in the region near the Kombat mine.

hermannjahnite.occurrence: As sublimates around a volcanic fumarole.
hermannjahnite.etymology: Honors Hermann Arthur Jahn, co-author of the Jahn-Teller effect, so pronounced in the structure of hermannjahnite.

hermannroseite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in an oxidize, polymetallic sulfide deposit.
hermannroseite.etymology: Honors Professor Hermann Rose (1883-1976), honorary member of the German Mineralogical Society since 1973 and head of the Mineralogical Institute, University of Hamburg , Germany (1922-1954).

herzenbergite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, later than the deposition of cassiterite.
herzenbergite.etymology: To honor Robert Herzenberg (1885–1956), Latvian–German chemist of Oruro, Bolivia.

hessite.occurrence: In hydrothermal medium- and low-temperature veins; also in small quantities in some massive pyrite deposits.
hessite.etymology: To honor Germain Henri Hess (1802–1850), Swiss-Russian physician and chemist, of St. Petersburg, Russia.

hetaerolite.occurrence: A secondary mineral associated with other manganese minerals, primarily in hydrothermal ore deposits.
hetaerolite.etymology: From the Greek for companion, for its occasional association with chalcophanite.

heterogenite.occurrence: A weathering product of smaltite (Schneeberg, Germany); an alteration product of linnaeite, constituting an important ore of cobalt (Shaba Province, Congo); widespread in residual soils above ultramaﬁc rocks (New Caledonia).
heterogenite.etymology: From the Greek for of another kind, as diﬀering in composition from similar minerals.

heteromorphite.etymology: From the Greek for diﬀerent and form, in allusion to the diﬀerence between this mineral and a proposed dimorphous species.

heterosite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of complex granite pegmatites, replacing primary phosphate minerals, principally triphylite.
heterosite.etymology: From the Greek for another, probably because it was the second manganese-bearing species described from the type locality.

heulandite.occurrence: In cavities in basalts; in highly weathered andesites and diabases; as a devitri¯cation product of volcanic glasses and tu®s.
heulandite.etymology: For the English mineral collector and dealer John Henry Heuland (1778{1856).

heulandite-ba.occurrence: A late stage mineral in hydrothermal quartz-calcite veins.
heulandite-ba.etymology: For its chemical composition and relationship to other heulandite minerals.

heulandite-ca.occurrence: In cavities in basalts; in highly weathered andesites and diabases; as a devitri¯cation product of volcanic glasses and tu®s.
heulandite-ca.etymology: For the English mineral collector and dealer John Henry Heuland (1778{1856).

heulandite-k.occurrence: In cavities in basalts; in highly weathered andesites and diabases; as a devitri¯cation product of volcanic glasses and tu®s.
heulandite-k.etymology: For the English mineral collector and dealer John Henry Heuland (1778{1856).

heulandite-na.occurrence: In cavities in basalts; in highly weathered andesites and diabases; as a devitri¯cation product of volcanic glasses and tu®s.
heulandite-na.etymology: For the English mineral collector and dealer John Henry Heuland (1778{1856).

heulandite-sr.occurrence: In cavities in basalts; in highly weathered andesites and diabases; as a devitri¯cation product of volcanic glasses and tu®s.
heulandite-sr.etymology: For the English mineral collector and dealer John Henry Heuland (1778{1856).

hewettite.occurrence: As an alteration product of patronite (Minasragra, Peru); an alteration product of less-oxidized vanadium minerals in Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits.
hewettite.etymology: For Donnel Foster Hewett (1881–1971), geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, who described the mineralogy of Minasragra, Peru.

hexacelsian.occurrence: A common accessory mineral in thin veins of paralava cutting gehlenite-flamite hornfels and formed at > 1100° C from the relatively fast crystallization of residual melt.
hexacelsian.etymology: Historical name of the synthetic phase with structure and composition analogous to the mineral described in this paper and named after Anders Celsius (1701-1744), Swedish astronomer, physicist, and naturalist.

hexahydrite.occurrence: By dehydration of epsomite; as eﬄorescences on magnesian rock exposures and in mine workings; as speleothems in caves; may be widespread as an evaporative precipitate in saline lakes and soils; rarely a fumarolic precipitate.
hexahydrite.etymology: With the Greek preﬁx, hexa, in recognition of a magnesium sulfate hydrate with six essential water molecules.

hexahydroborite.occurrence: A rare component of boron-enriched skarn deposits in metasomatized limestones.
hexahydroborite.etymology: For the composition, originally thought to contain six waters of hydration (later found by crystal-structure analysis to be incorrect).

hexamolybdenum.occurrence: As grains in an ovoid-shaped, ultra-refractory inclusion in the Allende meteorite , likely a high-temperature condensate early in the formation of the solar system.
hexamolybdenum.etymology: Alludes to the symmetry (primitive hexagonal) and composition (molybdenum-rich).

hexatestibiopanickelite.occurrence: In ore concentrates from Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposits.
hexatestibiopanickelite.etymology: Presumably named for the crystal system and composition.

heyerdahlite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in nepheline-syenite pegmatite hosted by foyaite.
heyerdahlite.etymology: Honors the Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl (1914-2002), who was born and raised in the city of Larvik, which is within the Larvik Plutonic complex - where the first specimens were collected.

heyite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in the oxidized portions of a polymetallic sulﬁde deposit (Betty Jo claim, Nevada, USA); along a fault through a stockwork disseminated gold deposit (Gold Quarry mine, Nevada, USA).
heyite.etymology: Honors Dr. Max Hutchinson Hey (1904–1984), eminent British mineralogist and chemist, British Museum (Natural History), London, England.

heyrovskyite.etymology: In honor of Jaroslav Heyrovsk´ y (1890–1967), Czech Nobel Laureate in chemistry.

hezuolinite.occurrence: In a series of alkaline volcanic and intrusive igneous rocks, associated with aegirine nepheline syenite.
hezuolinite.etymology: Honors He Zuolin (1900-1967), for his contributions to optical mineralogy and rare-earths mineralogy in China. Hezuolinite corresponds to the previously discredited “saimaite”.

hibbingite.occurrence: In serpentinized troctolite and peridotite (Hibbing, Minnesota, USA); in fractures in chlorine-rich portions of a Cu-Ni orebody (Strathcona mine, Canada); in terrestrially weathered iron meteorites.
hibbingite.etymology: For Hibbing, Minnesota, USA, from near where the mineral was first characterized.

hibonite.occurrence: In metamorphosed limestone, pyroxenite, gneiss, and granulite of the amphibolite to granulite facies; also alluvial. A common accessory in Ca–Al-rich inclusions in some carbonaceous chondrites.
hibonite.etymology: For Paul Hibon, who discovered the mineral.

hibschite.occurrence: In a calcareous marl (Mari¶ ansk¶ aHora, Czech Republic); in zeolite-calcite rocks and low-grade metamorphosed marls (Hatrurim Formation, Israel).
hibschite.etymology: After Professor Josef Emanuel Hibsch (1852{1940), German Agricultural Academy, Tetschen, Czech Republic.

hidalgoite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral of the oxide zone of polymetallic sulﬁde deposits.
hidalgoite.etymology: For Hidalgo, the state in Mexico that produced the ﬁrst specimens.

hielscherite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in alkaline basalt or also in xenoliths in volcanic glass.
hielscherite.etymology: Honors German mineral collector Klaus Hielscher (b. 1957) from Steinbach, Hessen, a specialist in the mineralogy of the Zeilberg basalt quarry in Franconia, Bavaria, Germany.

hieratite.occurrence: As a deposit around volcanic fumaroles.
hieratite.etymology: From the Greek Hiera, an ancient name for Vulcano.

hilairite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities and altered pegmatite dikes in nepheline syenite in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
hilairite.etymology: For the locality at Mont Saint-Hilaire, Quebec, Canada.

hilarionite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a sulfide-rich (pyrite, sphalerite, chalcopyrite, galena) orebody.
hilarionite.etymology: For the mine that produced the first specimens.

hilgardite.etymology: Honors Eugene Woldemar Hilgard (1833–1916), German–American geologist, one of the ﬁrst to study the Louisiana salt diapir deposits.

hillebrandite.occurrence: In limestone a®ected by high-grade contact metamorphism.
hillebrandite.etymology: For William Francis Hillebrand (1853{1925), American geochemist and analytical chemist.

hillesheimite.formula_html: (K,Ca,Ba,   )2(Mg,Fe,Ca,   )2[(Si,Al)13O23(OH)6](OH)·8H2O
hillesheimite.occurrence: Encrusts the walls of miarolitic cavities in alkali basalt.
hillesheimite.etymology: For the town of Hillesheim, near where the studied samples were collected.

hillite.occurrence: In a gossan developed on argillaceous siltstone.
hillite.etymology: Honors Dr. Roderick Hill (b. 1949) Chief of the Mineral Research Division, CSIRO at Melbourne, Australia, who described the mineral in 1973 as a potentially new species.

hingganite-ce.etymology: For the predominance of cerium and relation to hingganite-(Y).

hingganite-nd.occurrence: In weathered alluvium from gneissic alkaline A-type granite.
hingganite-nd.etymology: The suffix indicates an analogue of hingganite-(Y), hingganite-(Yb), and hingganite-(Ce), but with Nd dominant among the rare earth elements.

hingganite-y.occurrence: In a RE, Be-bearing granophyre (Greater Khingan Range, China); in “amazonite"-rich pegmatite in a differentiated alkalic massif (Kola Peninsula, Russia).
hingganite-y.etymology: Presumably for the occurrence in the Greater Khingan (Hinggan) Range, China, and predominance of yttrium.

hingganite-yb.occurrence: Formed by very late-stage replacement reactions in \amazonite"-rich pegmatites.
hingganite-yb.etymology: For the predominance of ytterbium and its relation to hingganite-(Y).

hinsdalite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of polymetallic sulfide deposits.
hinsdalite.etymology: For Hinsdale County, Colorado, USA, source of the first specimens.

hiortdahlite.occurrence: A rare mineral in alkalic rocks, their pegmatites, and metamorphosed equivalents; in miarolitic cavities in sanidinites.
hiortdahlite.etymology: After Professor Thorstein Hallager Hiortdahl (1839{1925), mineralogist of Kristiania (now Oslo), Norway.

hiroseite.occurrence: In a quenched shock-melted portion of the heavily shocked (<20 GPa; <2000 °C) L6 Suizhou chondrite meteorite, by the transformation of chemically zoned olivine. Perhaps relevant to the mineralogy of Earth’s deep interior, it could have a role at the bottom of the Earth’s mantle transition zone and within the uppermost lower mantle.
hiroseite.etymology: Honors Kei Hirose (b. 1968) for his fundamental contributions to the discovery of the postperovskite phase and to the mineralogy of mantle perovskite in general.

hisingerite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, formed from the weathering, or late-stage deuteric or hydrothermal alteration, of iron-bearing silicates or sul¯des; by late-stage hydrothermal activity during sul¯de ore deposition.
hisingerite.etymology: For the Swedish chemist and mineralogist, Vilhelm Hisinger (1766{1852).

hitachiite.occurrence: From a volcanogenic massive sulfide deposit (Cu-Zn with small amounts of Pb). The sulfide deposit was metamorphosed to lower epidote-amphibole facies.
hitachiite.etymology: For the mine where the studied samples were collected.

hizenite-y.occurrence: As a druse in alkali olivine basalt.
hizenite-y.etymology: For “Hizen”, the historic name (between the 7 th and 16th centuries) for the locality that produced the first specimens and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

hocartite.occurrence: Of relatively high-temperature origin, typically in hydrothrmal tin-bearing deposits.
hocartite.etymology: Honors Raymond Hocart (1896–1983), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Paris, Paris, France.

hochelagaite.occurrence: In vugs of a dawsonite-bearing sill in a limestone deposit (Francon quarry, Canada); in cavities in altered pegmatite dikes, hornfels, sodalite syenite, or miarolitic cavities, associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in miarolitic cavities in a syenite sill (near Saint-Amable, Canada).
hochelagaite.etymology: For Hochelaga, an early name for Montreal, Canada and its surrounds, within which the mineral occurs.

hodgkinsonite.occurrence: As seams in massive willemite-franklinite granular ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
hodgkinsonite.etymology: For H.H. Hodgkinson, Assistant Underground Superintendent of the Franklin mine, who discovered the mineral.

hodrushite.occurrence: In a polymetallic ore deposit of subvolcanic type, in a quartz vein system developed in propylitized pyroxenite andesite (Bansk´ a Hodruˇ sa, Slovakia).
hodrushite.etymology: For the mining community of Bansk´ a Hodruˇ sa, Slovakia.

hoelite.occurrence: Very rare, in crusts around the surface vents of a burning coal deposit.
hoelite.etymology: Honors Adolf Hoel (1879-1964), leader of the discovery expedition to Spitsbergen during which the mineral was found.

hoganite.occurrence: Formed in ferruginous gossan by reaction of oxidized zone metallic minerals with decaying vegetable matter provided by leaf litter and possibly mine timbers.
hoganite.etymology: To honor Graham P. Hogan (1957– ), Broken Hill, Australia, miner and collector of Broken Hill minerals, who found the ﬁrst specimens.

hogarthite.occurrence: In metasomatically altered marble xenoliths in a breccia zone associated with an alkaline intrusive complex.
hogarthite.etymology: Honors Donald D. Hogarth (b. 1929), Professor Emeritus, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Ottawa, in recognition of his contributions to the mineralogy and geology of the Grenville Province in Quebec and Ontario, and to the nomenclature of the pyrochlore group.

hogtuvaite.occurrence: As a late-stage metamorphic mineral in peraluminous granitic gneisses and ma¯c pegmatites associated with a beryllium deposit (near Mo i Rana, Norway).
assoc_parsed: many minor beryllium and sul¯de minerals
hogtuvaite.etymology: For H¿gtuva Mountain, near the type locality in Norway.

hohmannite.occurrence: An uncommon low-temperature precipitate in oxidized iron sulﬁde deposits.
hohmannite.etymology: Honors Thomas Hohmann (1843–1897), mining engineer of Valparaiso, Chile who discovered the ﬁrst specimens.

holdawayite.occurrence: Locally abundant as a rare vein mineral in low-grade metamorphosed Mn-rich sedimentary rocks intercalated with sedimentary iron deposits.
holdawayite.etymology: Honors Dr. Michael Jon Holdaway (1936– ), Professor of Petrology, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, Texas, USA.

holdenite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in veinlets, on slip surfaces, and as interstitial ¯llings within a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
holdenite.etymology: For the mining engineer Albert Fairchild Holden (1866{1913), of Salt Lake City, Utah, USA, in whose collection the mineral was ¯rst noticed.

holfertite.etymology: Honors John W. Holfert (b. 1949) for his contributions to understanding the mineral occurrences in the Thomas Range, Utah, USA.

hollandite.occurrence: A primary mineral in contact metamorphic manganese ores, and a secondary weathering product of earlier manganese-bearing minerals.
hollandite.etymology: For Dr. Thomas Henry Holland (1868-1947), Director of the Indian Geological Survey.

hollingworthite.occurrence: In platinum deposits in dunite pipes, layered ultramaﬁc intrusives, and chromatites; in Cu–Ni sulﬁde ores.
hollingworthite.etymology: To honor Professor Sidney Ewart Hollingworth (1899–1966), eminent British geologist, University College, London, England.

hollisterite.occurrence: In metal assemblages in a carbonaceous chondrite meteorite.
hollisterite.etymology: Honors Lincoln S. Hollister, Emeritus Professor, Department of Geosciences, Princeton University, USA, for his extraordinary contributions to Earth science in general.

holmquistite.occurrence: As metasomatic replacements near the outer margins of lithium-rich pegmatites.
holmquistite.etymology: To honor the Swedish petrologist, Per Johan Holmquist (1866{1946), of Stockholm.

holtedahlite.occurrence: In a serpentine–magnesite deposit (Tingelstadtjern quarry, Norway); a common accessory mineral, of likely pneumatolytic origin, in an igneous magnetite–apatite deposit (Gole Gohar, Iran).
holtedahlite.etymology: Honors Olaf Holtedahl (1885–1975), Professor of Geology, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway.

holtite.occurrence: As coatings on stibiotantalite and replacing tantalite in a pegmatite (Greenbushes, Western Australia); in pegmatites cutting amphibolites (Voron'i massif, Russia); in alluvial gravels derived from pegmatite.
holtite.etymology: Honors Harold Edward Holt (1908-1967), Prime Minister of Australia (1966-1967).

holtstamite.occurrence: In a manganese-rich calc-silicate contact metamorphic rock.
holtstamite.etymology: Honors Dr. Dan Holtstam (b. 1963) for his contributions to Swedish mineralogy and specifically Mn deposits of the Långban type.

homilite.etymology: From the Greek for to occur together, in allusion to its association with meliphanite and \erdmannite" (allanite).

honeaite.occurrence: In microvugs and microfractures roughly following the metamorphic banding, mainly within areas of epidote and prehnite alteration (greenschist facies) of quartz amphibolite.
honeaite.etymology: Honors Professor Russell M. Honea (1929-2002), University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, USA.

honessite.occurrence: A rare oxidation product of nickel sulﬁde minerals.
honessite.etymology: Honors Professor Arthur Pharoah Honess (1887–1942), American mineralogist, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA.

hongshiite.occurrence: In an actinolized diopside-type of platinum deposit (China); in high-grade hematitic veins in itabirite, typically rimmed by platinum from which copper has been leached (Brazil); in Alpine-type ultramaﬁc intrusives and related placers.
hongshiite.etymology: For its occurrence near Hongshi village, China.

honzaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by weathering of nickelskutterudite and tennantite, under strongly acidic conditions, in a Ag+As+Co+Ni+Bi and U vein-type hydrothermal mineral deposit.
honzaite.etymology: Honors Czech mineralogist and collector of minerals from the Jáchymov ore district, Jan “Honza” Hloušek (1950-2014).

hopeite.occurrence: A rare, late-stage mineral in some hydrothermal zinc deposits and complex granite pegmatites; incrusting bone breccia in a limestone cave.
hopeite.etymology: Honors Thomas Charles Hope (1766–1844), Professor of Chemistry, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, Scotland.

hornesite.occurrence: In limestone blocks, thermally metamorphosed, in a volcanic tuﬀ (Fiano, Italy).
hornesite.etymology: Honors Moritz H¨ ornes (1815–1868), Curator of the Imperial Cabinet, Vienna, Austria.

horomanite.occurrence: Filling space between silicate minerals in lherzolites of a peridotite massif.
horomanite.etymology: For the ultramafic massif (Horoman) from which the first specimens were collected.

horvathite-y.occurrence: A very rare, late-forming mineral in an altered pegmatite dike in nepheline syenite, part of an alkalic igneous complex.
horvathite-y.etymology: Honors Elsa Horv´ ath (1947– ) and L´ aszl´ o Horv´ ath (1937– ), husband and wife collectors of Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada minerals.

hotsonite.occurrence: A weathering product derived from natroalunite and zaherite in an arid climate (Koenabib, South Africa).
hotsonite.etymology: For Hotson 42, the farm in South Africa on which the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

housleyite.occurrence: A secondary phase on fracture surfaces and in small vugs in quartz veins. Formed from the partial oxidation of primary sulfides (e.g., galena) and tellurides (e.g., hessite) during or following brecciation of the quartz veins.
housleyite.etymology: Honors Robert M. Housley (b. 1934), Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA.

howardevansite.occurrence: Forms by sublimation around fumaroles on an andesitic volcano.
howardevansite.etymology: Honors Dr. Howard Tasker Evans, Jr. (1919–2000), American mineralogist and crystallographer, U.S. Geological Survey, Reston, Virginia, USA.

howieite.occurrence: An essential mineral in some of the metamorphosed shales, siliceous ironstones, and impure limestones of the Franciscan Formation (Laytonville district, California, USA).
howieite.etymology: For Professor Robert Andrew Howie (1923{ ), British mineralogist and petrologist, London University, London, England.

howlite.etymology: For Henry How (1828{1879), Canadian chemist, geologist, and mineralogist, University of King's College, Windsor, Nova Scotia, Canada, who ¯rst described the species.

hsianghualite.occurrence: In phlogopite veins in a °uorine-rich metamorphosed Devonian limestone intruded by a beryllium-bearing granite.
hsianghualite.etymology: For the place of discovery; the word means fragrant °ower in Chinese.

huanghoite-ce.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in hydrothermal veins associated with rare-earth-bearing carbonatite deposits in alkaline igneous complexes.
huanghoite-ce.etymology: For the Huang Ho (Yellow River), China, 150 km south of the Bayan Obo deposit, China, where the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

huangite.occurrence: A product of acid sulfate hydrothermal alteration of rhyolite tuﬀs and andesites.
huangite.etymology: Honors Yunhui Huang (1926– ), Chinese mineralogist, Institute of Mineral Deposit Geology and Mineral Resources, Beijing, China, in part for her contributions to the study of contact-metamorphic beryllium deposits.

huanzalaite.occurrence: As inclusions in scheelite in the Mg-metasomatized contact skarns of an intrusive granodiorite and quartz porphyry.
huanzalaite.etymology: For the first described locality, the Huanzala mine, Peru.

hubeite.etymology: For the province in China where the first specimens were collected.

hubnerite.occurrence: Typical of high-temperature hydrothermal vein deposits and pneumatolytically altered granites yielding greisen; in granite pegmatites; also in alluvial and eluvial deposits.
hubnerite.etymology: Honors Adolph H¨ ubner, metallurgist of Freiberg, Germany.

huemulite.occurrence: Formed after opening Cu–U deposits in sandstones and conglomerates; the vanadium may be derived from associated asphalt.
huemulite.etymology: For the Huemul mine, Argentina, where it occurs.

huenite.occurrence: An oxidation product of primary sulfides formed by late-stage hydrothermal fluids as open-space fillings in pipes of tourmalinized quartz porphyry, collapse-breccia.
huenite.etymology: Honors Edgar Huen (b. 1947), an Italian senior mineral collector, and expert in Alpine fissure minerals and worldwide systematic mineralogy.

hugelite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in cavities in hornstone breccia.
hugelite.etymology: To honor Baron Friedrich von H¨ ugel (1852–1925), Austrian-British theologian.

hughesite.occurrence: As efflorescent crusts on the sandstone walls of mine workings and in rock fractures, through the oxidation of primary vanadium oxides (corvusite and montroseite) that react with acidic, oxidizing groundwater in roll-front type U deposits, usually in organic-carbon-rich zones.
hughesite.etymology: Honors John Michael Hughes (b. 1952), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Vermont, USA, for his long and outstanding career in mineralogy, including his extensive work on the pascoite family of minerals and vanadium bronzes.

huizingite-al.occurrence: Formed by a natural fire in oil-bearing shale exposed along a cliff.
huizingite-al.etymology: Honors Terry E. Huizing (born 1938) and Marie E. Huizing (born 1939) of Cincinnati, Ohio , USA, recipients of numerous awards for their diverse service to the international amateur and professional mineralogical communities. The ‘-(Al)’ suffix indicates that this mineral is the Al-dominant member of a series with a not-yet-described Fe-dominant counterpart, for which the name huizingite-(Fe) is proposed.

hulsite.occurrence: Very rare, in a contact-metamorphosed limestone, close by an intrusive granite.
hulsite.etymology: Honors Alfred Hulse Brooks (1871–1924), geologist in charge of the Division of Alaskan Mineral Resources, U.S. Geological Survey.

humberstonite.occurrence: Formed by repeated natural leaching of nitrate ore with reprecipitation in irregular pods above the local regolith.
humberstonite.etymology: Honors James Thomas Humberstone (1850–1939), industrial chemist whose contributions permit economical extraction of nitrate from the Chilean deposits.

humboldtine.occurrence: Typically coating fractures in brown coal deposits; very rarely in granite pegmatites and hydrothermal mineral deposits.
humboldtine.etymology: Honors Friedrich Heinrich Alexander von Humboldt (1769–1859), German naturalist and explorer.

humite.occurrence: Typically in contact metamorphic zones in limestones and dolostones associated with felsic, or more rarely, alkalic plutonic rocks, especially where metasomatism has introduced Fe, B, and F.
humite.etymology: After Sir Abraham Hume (1749{1838), English connoisseur and collector of works of art, gems, and minerals. All rights reserved.
