kapellasite.occurrence: From weathering copper and zinc minerals in the presence of chloride ions.
kapellasite.etymology: Honors Christo Kapellas (1938-2004), collector and mineral dealer from Kamariza, Lavrion, Greece.

kapitsaite-y.occurrence: In a boulder of peralkaline pegmatite in the moraine of a glacier.
kapitsaite-y.etymology: Honors Russian P’yotr Leonidovich Kapitsa (1894-1984), well-known solid-state physicist.

kapundaite.occurrence: In a phosphorite deposit that has undergone metamorphism, followed by weathering and secondary enrichment.
kapundaite.etymology: For the town nearest to the quarry, Kapunda, which is in turn derived from the Australian Aboriginal word “cappie oonda,” which was applied to a spring near the present town site.

kapustinite.occurrence: In hyperagpaitic pegmatite in an alkaline massif.
kapustinite.etymology: Honors mineralogist Yu. L. Kapustin (1933–2002), who extensively studied alkaline massifs.

karasugite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in ﬁssures in the oxidation zone of veins of iron ores in tectonic breccias.
karasugite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Karasug deposit, Russia.

karchevskyite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral, finely intergrown with quintinite-3T, in cavities in dolomite in a carbonatite complex.
karchevskyite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Pavel Karchevsky (1976–2002) for significant contributions to the study of carbonatites.

karelianite.occurrence: In sulﬁde-rich portions of glacial boulders derived from high-grade metamorphic rocks, as schists and quartzites (Outokumpu mine, Finland); in primary unoxidized U–V ores (Mounana mine, Gabon); in vanadiferous anthraxolite bitumen (Guangxi, China).
karelianite.etymology: For the Karelian schist belt, the region of Finland where the mineral occurs.

karenwebberite.occurrence: As late-magmatic exsolution lamellae hosted by graftonite in plagioclase within the central portion of a granitic pegmatite dike.
karenwebberite.etymology: Honors Karen Louise Webber, Assistant Professor Research, in the Mineralogy, Petrology and Pegmatology Research Group, Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of New Orleans, Louisiana, USA, for her contributions to the scientific understanding of the cooling and crystallization dynamics of granitic pegmatites.

karibibite.etymology: For the Karibib pegmatite district, Namibia, where the species occurs.

karlite.occurrence: Probably formed by Alpine metamorphism, in a calcsilicate–carbonate lens in amphibolites (Schlegeistal, Austria).
karlite.etymology: To honor Dr. Franz Karl (1918–1972), Professor of Mineralogy and Petrography, Christian Albrechts University, Kiel, Germany, for his studies of the geology of the eastern Alps.

karnasurtitece.occurrence: In the intermediate replacement zone, composed largely of microcline, of a zoned pegmatite stock in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Mt. Karnasurt, Russia).
karnasurtitece.etymology: For the locality, Mt. Karnasurt, Kola Peninsula, Russia, and its high cerium content.

karpatite.occurrence: In cavities at the contact of diorite porphyry with argillites (Olenevo, Ukraine); a low-temperature hydrothermal mineral (California, USA).
karpatite.etymology: From the Russian Karpaty, for the place of discovery in the Transcarpathian district, Ukraine.

karpenkoite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed during the post-mining oxidation of corvusite and montroseite in a moist environment at ambient temperatures.
karpenkoite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Vladimir Yu. Karpenko (b. 1965), an expert on the mineralogy of vanadium.

karpinskite.etymology: For Alexander Petrovich Karpinsky (1847{1936), Russian geologist and President of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia.

karpovite.occurrence: A sublimate on rock around a volcanic fumarole.
karpovite.etymology: Honors Professor Gennadiy Alexandrovich Karpov (b. 1938), volcanologist at the Institute of Volcanology, Russian Academy of Sciences, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskiy, Russia.

kasatkinite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in cavities in rhodingite.
assoc_parsed: minerals of the tobermorite and hydrotalcite families
kasatkinite.etymology: Honors Russian amateur mineralogist and mineral collector Anatoly V. Kasatkin (b. 1970).

kashinite.occurrence: In placer deposits derived from ultramaﬁc rocks.
kashinite.etymology: To honor Stepan Aleksandrovich Kashin (1900–1981), Central Institute of Geological Exploration for Base and Precious Metals, Moscow, Russia, a Russian investigator of ore deposits in the Ural Mountains.

kaskasite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in fenites formed by the influence of a peralkaline fluid acting as a source of Nb on a large xenolith of alumina-rich metamorphic rocks (metapelites) located inside a huge intrusion of agpaitic nepheline syenite.
kaskasite.etymology: For Mount Kaskasnyunchorr, the locality that produced the first specimens, whose name is based on the word for “juniper” - kaskas - in the Saami language of the Kola aboriginal people.

kasolite.etymology: For the occurrence at Shinkolobwe, near Kasolo Hill, Congo (Zaire).

kassite.occurrence: Lining miarolitic cavities in alkalic pegmatites (Afrikanda massif, Russia); in nepheline syenite (Diamond Jo quarry, Arkansas, USA).
kassite.etymology: Honors Academician Nikolai Grigor’evich Kassin (1885–1949), the geologist who discovered the Afrikanda massif, Russia.

kastningite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in a zoned granite pegmatite.

katerinopoulosite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in the oxidation zone of a sphalerite-rich deposit situated in the contact zone between calcite marble and mica schist.
katerinopoulosite.etymology: Honors Greek geologist and mineralogist Athanassios Katerinopoulos (b. 1950), director of the Museum of Mineralogy and Petrology and of the Laboratory of Museum Studies, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, for significant contributions to the geology and mineralogy of the Lavrion mining district. He is a co-author of several new mineral discoveries from the district.

katiarsite.occurrence: Formed in sublimates encrusting basaltic scoria around a volcanic fumarole.
katiarsite.etymology: For the mineral’s chemical composition, ka lium titanyl arsenate.

katoite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral in cavities in a phonolitic lava °ow that erupted through an argillaceous marl.
katoite.etymology: In honor of Akira Kato, mineralogist of the National Science Museum, Tokyo, Japan.

katophorite.occurrence: In alkalic volcanic and plutonic igneous rocks; in blueschist facies jadeitites.
katophorite.etymology: From the Greek for a carrying down, in allusion to its volcanic origin.

katoptrite.etymology: From the Greek for mirror, for the perfectly re°ecting cleavage surfaces.

kawazulite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, in a quartz veins (Kawazu and Suttsu mines, Japan); in a breccia pipe cutting dacitic ignimbrites (Mazenod Lake, Canada).

kayrobertsonite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in pegmatite as part of a complex suite of Al-rich secondary phosphates.
kayrobertsonite.etymology: Honors German-American mineral collector Gabriella Kay Robertson (b. 1920) of Los Angeles, California, USA. Since the mid-1950s, Kay has been an ardent and sophisticated mineral collector, specializing in German minerals, and a valued resource for professional mineralogists.

kazakhstanite.occurrence: In thin veins or cementing breccia in the weathering zone of vanadiferous black shales (Kara-Tau Mountains, Kazakhstan); in a hydrothermal gold deposit (Gold Quarry mine, Nevada, USA).

kazakovite.occurrence: In sodalite-rich syenites in an alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
kazakovite.etymology: For Mariya E¯movna Kazakova (1913{1982), Institute of Mineralogy and Geochemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia, analytical chemist who provided the mineral's analysis.

kazanskyite.occurrence: In the natrolite zone of a hydrothermally-altered, pegmatite vein cutting nepheline syenite near the contact with ijolite-urtites.
kazanskyite.etymology: Honors Vadim Ivanovich Kazansky (b.1926), a Russian ore geologist and expert in Precambrian metallogeny of the Kola region.

keckite.occurrence: A weathering product of phosphate minerals in a complex granite pegmatite.
keckite.etymology: Honors Erich Keck, Etzenricht, Germany, collector of Hagendorf minerals.

kegelite.occurrence: In a deep oxidation zone in a polymetallic mineral deposit.
kegelite.etymology: For Friedrich Wilhelm Kegel (?{1948), Director of mining operations (1922{1938) at Tsumeb, Namibia.

kegginite.occurrence: A secondary mineral found on asphaltum in a montroseite- and corvusite-bearing sandstone in a roll-front type uranium deposit.
kegginite.etymology: Recognizes the presence of the e-isomer of the Keggin anion in the mineral and also honors J.F. Keggin who first experimentally determined the structure of α-Keggin anions in 1934.

keilite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in enstatite chondrite and achondrite meteorites.
keilite.etymology: Honors Dr. Klaus Keil (b. 1934), Hawaii Institute of Geophysics and Planetology, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, Hawaii, USA, for his research on chondritic meteorites.

keithconnite.occurrence: Rare with other platinum-group minerals in layered ultrabasic complexes and their placers.
keithconnite.etymology: Honors H. Keith Conn (1923– ), the geologist largely responsible for the discovery of Pt–Pd mineralization of parts of the Stillwater complex, Montana.

keiviite-y.occurrence: In ¯ssures in quartz and °uorite in \amazonite" pegmatites.
keiviite-y.etymology: For the relation to keiviite-(Yb) and the yttrium content.

keiviite-yb.occurrence: In microcline-bearing pegmatites; two generations of the mineral are present.
keiviite-yb.etymology: For Keivy on the Kola Peninsula, Russia, and ytterbium in its composition.

keldyshite.occurrence: A primary mineral in foyaites composed of partly albitized microcline, nepheline, sodalite, aegirine, and alkali amphibole, in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
keldyshite.etymology: For Russian mathematician Mstislav Vsevolodovich Keldysh (1911{1978), President of the Academy of Sciences, Russia.

kellyite.occurrence: In banded Ca-Mn carbonate-rich rocks (Bald Knob mine, North Carolina, USA); in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
kellyite.etymology: To honor Professor William Crowe Kelly (1929{ ), geologist, of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA.

kelyanite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a stibnite-cinnabar ore deposit.
kelyanite.etymology: For the Kelyana mine, Russia, where it was first found.

kemmlitzite.occurrence: In a kaolinized quartz porphyry, in a heavy-fraction separate of undetermined origin as to primary or secondary formation.
kemmlitzite.etymology: For the locality of the ﬁrst specimens, Kemmlitz, Germany.

kempite.occurrence: In an erratic boulder with other manganese-bearing species.
kempite.etymology: Honors economic geologist James Furman Kemp (1859–1926), Professor of Geology, Columbia University, New York City, New York, USA.

kenhsuite.occurrence: Along fractures in hydrothermally altered, rhyolitic, tuffaceous lacustrine rocks in a caldera complex.
kenhsuite.etymology: Honors Dr. Kenneth Jinghwa Hsu (b. 1929), Professor Emeritus, Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (E.T.H.), Zurich, Switzerland, for his numerous contributions to the earth sciences.

kenoplumbomicrolite.formula_html: (Pb,   )2Ta2O6[   ,(OH),O]

kentbrooksite.occurrence: In alkaline pegmatitic bodies cutting pulaskite.
kentbrooksite.etymology: Honors geologist C. Kent Brooks for significant contributions to the understanding of the Kangerdlugssuaq area as a rifted continental margin.

kentrolite.occurrence: In a cavity in calcite in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA); in veinlets cutting franklinite ore in bedded manganese deposits (Ushkatyn deposits, Kazakhstan).
kentrolite.etymology: From the Greek for spike or thorn, for its prismatic habit.

kenyaite.occurrence: As concretions, with chert cores, embedded in magadiite; perhaps as a reaction product between the two (Lake Magadi, Kenya); in altered volcanic rocks (Trinity Co., California, USA).

keplerite.occurrence: In some pallasite and angrite meteorites. In brecciated, altered pyroxene paralava (fused sediments) by pyrometamorphism (Israel). An indicator of high-temperature environments characterized by extreme depletion of sodium.
keplerite.etymology: Honors Johannes Kepler (1571-1630), a prominent German naturalist, for his contributions to astronomy and crystallography.

kerimasite.occurrence: A magmatic phase in calcite carbonatite associated with a nephelinitic volcano (Kerimasi) and surrounding pyroclastic rocks (carbonatite agglomerates and tuffs).
kerimasite.etymology: For the Kerimasi volcano in Tanzania.

kermesite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, as an alteration of stibnite, in antimony deposits.
kermesite.etymology: From kermes (after Persian qurmizq, crimson) for red amorphous antimony trisulfide.

kernite.occurrence: An important ore mineral of borax in sedimentary borate deposits, deposited under warm conditions or formed by metamorphism.
kernite.etymology: For Kern Co., California, USA, in which Boron is located.

kernowite.occurrence: Secondary in cavities in quartz-gossan, rich in undifferentiated micro-crystalline gray sulfides. Perhaps related closely to the formation of arsenic-rich gels/mineraloids.
assoc_parsed: poorly crystalline arsenic phases including pharmacosiderite and olivenitegroup minerals
kernowite.etymology: After the world for Cornwall in the Cornish language (Kernow). The Fe3+-analogue of liroconite.

kesebolite-ce.occurrence: In Mn deposits in fine-grained, brecciated, andradite skarn.
kesebolite-ce.etymology: For the discovery locality, the Kesebol mine. The suffix indicates the dominant rare earth element.

kesterite.occurrence: In quartz-sulﬁde hydrothermal veinlets in tin deposits.
kesterite.etymology: For the locality in Russia at the Kester deposit.

kettnerite.occurrence: In a quartz vein cutting pegmatitic potassian feldspar (Krupka, Czech Republic).
kettnerite.etymology: Honoring Radim Kettner (1891–1968), Professor of Geology, Charles University, Czech Republic.

keyite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
keyite.etymology: Honors Charles Locke Key (1935– ), Windhoek, Namibia, American mineral dealer who furnished the ﬁrst specimen.

keystoneite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed in the oxidized zone of a complex polymetallic hydrothermal mineral deposit.
keystoneite.etymology: For its occurrence at the Keystone mine, Colorado, USA.

khademite.occurrence: Rarely formed in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal base-metal deposits.
khademite.etymology: To honor Nasrollah Khadem (1910– ), Director of the Geological Survey of Iran.

khaidarkanite.occurrence: Secondary in highly oxidized, copper-bearing, fluorite-rich veinstone that locally evolved small quantities of hydrofluoric acid (HF) during weathering (Great Sled Dale).
khaidarkanite.etymology: For the locality from which the first samples were collected.

khamrabaevite.occurrence: In amygdaloidal basaltic porphyries (Chatkal Range, Russia); in spheroidal groups in granodiorites that have undergone silica metasomatism (Chinorsaisk massif, Tadzhikistan).
khamrabaevite.etymology: Honors Ibragim Khamrabaevich Khamrabaeva (1920- ), Director, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Tashkent, Uzbekistan.

khanneshite.occurrence: Disseminated in hydrothermally-altered ﬁne-grained carbonatite (Khanneshin complex, Afghanistan); in a drillcore in a carbonatite veinlet from a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia).
khanneshite.etymology: For the Khanneshin complex, Afghanistan, its ﬁrst-noted occurrence.

kharaelakhite.etymology: For the Kharaelakh Plateau, Noril’sk region, Russia.

khatyrkite.occurrence: In black slick washed from greenish gray cover weathering from serpentine.
khatyrkite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Khatyrka ultramaﬁc zone, Russia.

khesinite.occurrence: Formed from melt and as reaction rims in thin veins of paralava within fine-grained gehlenite rocks (pyrometamorphic hornfels).
khesinite.etymology: Honors Azerbaijanian and Israeli geophysicist Boris Emmanuilovich Khesin (1932 -2010), after 1991, at the Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva, Israel.

khibinskite.occurrence: In aegirine-rich metasomatic rocks in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
khibinskite.etymology: For the locality in the Khibiny massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

khinite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral formed under acid oxidizing conditions from goldtelluride ores in massive vein quartz.
khinite.etymology: Honors BaSaw Khin (b. 1931), Burmese-American mineralogist, Phelps Dodge Corporation.

khmaralite.occurrence: In a pegmatite metamorphosed at granulite-facies likely from pre-existing pegmatitic Be phases such as beryllian cordierite.
khmaralite.etymology: For the locality, from which the first samples were collected, named for Ivan Fedorovich Khmara (1936-1956), a tractor driver on the Soviet Antarctic Expedition who perished in Antarctica.

khomyakovite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in nepheline syenite in an alkaline intrusive complex.
khomyakovite.etymology: Honors Dr. Alexander Petrovich Khomyakov (b. 1933), of the Institute of Mineralogy, Geochemistry and Crystal Chemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia, for his contributions to the mineralogy and geochemistry of alkaline rocks, in particular those of agpaitic character.

khrenovite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.

khurayyimite.occurrence: In cavities and veins in altered spurrite marbles of pyrometamorphic origin.
assoc_parsed: minerals of the tobermorite group and ettringite -thaumasite series. distribution from near khurayyim mount
khurayyimite.etymology: For Khurayyim Mount (Jabal al Khurayyim), Um Al-Rasas Sub-district, central Jordan.

khvorovite.occurrence: In the moraine of the Darai-Pioz glacier which erodes a multiphase, boron-enriched, alkaline intrusive complex.
khvorovite.etymology: Honors Pavel Vitalyevich Khvorov (b. 1965), a Russian mineralogist for his contributions to the mineralogy of the Darai-Pioz massif.

kiddcreekite.etymology: For the Kidd Creek mine, Canada.

kidwellite.occurrence: As a late-stage replacement of earlier phosphate minerals.
kidwellite.etymology: Honors Albert Laws Kidwell (1919-2008), Houston, Texas, USA, for his study of Arkansas phosphate deposits.

kieftite.occurrence: In a polymetallic sulﬁde skarn deposit.
kieftite.etymology: Honors Dr. Cornelis Kieft (1924– ), for his contributions to ore mineralogy.

kieserite.occurrence: Typically in marine salt deposits; rarely as a volcanic sublimate or eﬄorescence.
kieserite.etymology: Honoring Dietrich Georg Kieser (1779–1862), President, Jena Academy, Jena, Germany.

kihlmanite-ce.occurrence: In a symmetrically-zoned pegmatite vein of arfvedsonite-aegirine-microcline in fenitized metavolcanic rock. Probably the product of low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of rinkite and loparite-(Ce).
kihlmanite-ce.etymology: Honors Alfred Oswald Kihlman (Kairamo) (1858-1938), a Finnish geographer and botanist, for whom Mt Kihlman and the mineral are named.

kilchoanite.occurrence: In limestones thermally metamorphosed by invasion of gabbro; thought to have formed during retrograde metamorphism following decarbonation of limestone and thus under low pressure of CO2 (Kilchoan, Scotland; Carlingford, Ireland).
kilchoanite.etymology: For Kilchoan, Scotland, where it was ¯rst found.

killalaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in cavities and veins in hydrothermally altered and thermally metamorphosed limestones.
killalaite.etymology: For the locality at Killala Bay, Ireland.

kimrobinsonite.occurrence: The weathering product of an undetermined Ta–Sb pegmatite mineral.
kimrobinsonite.etymology: Honors Kim Robinson (1951– ), Australian geologist of Perth, Australia, who discovered the specimen in which the mineral occurs.

kimuraitey.occurrence: In ﬁssures in an alkali olivine basalt.
kimuraitey.etymology: To honor Professor Kenjiro Kimura (1896–?), Tokyo University, Tokyo, Japan, for his contributions to the mineralogy of rare-earth minerals.

kimzeyite.occurrence: In a carbonatite associated with ijolite (Magnet Cove, Arkansas, USA); in a shoshonitic basaltic lava (Stromboli, Italy).
kimzeyite.etymology: For Joe Kimzey, the mineral's discoverer, and the Kimzey family, of Magnet Cove, Arkansas, USA.

kingite.occurrence: Of secondary origin, precipitated in fractured rock by meteoric water.
kingite.etymology: Honors Mr. D. King (1926–1990), geologist, Department of Mines, Adelaide, South Australia, who collected the ﬁrst specimens.

kingsgateite.occurrence: Part of a suite of secondary bismuth, molybdate, tungstate, phosphate, and arsenate minerals from the weathering of native bismuth-bismuthinite-molybdenite-bearing quartz pipes contained in coarse, hornblende-biotite granite.
assoc_parsed: muscovite. distribution from the old 25 pipe
kingsgateite.etymology: For the locality where the studied material was collected.

kingsmountite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed from alteration of primary phosphates by descending oxidizing ground water in complex granite pegmatites.
kingsmountite.etymology: For the town, KINGS MOUNTain, North Carolina, USA, near which the mineral was ﬁrst collected.

kingstonite.occurrence: In placers derived from platinum-bearing dunite and pyroxenite, as inclusions in a Pt-Fe alloy.
kingstonite.etymology: Honors Dr. Gordon Andrew Kingston (b. 1939), senior lecturer, Department of Geology, University of Wales, College of Cardiff, Wales, U.K., for his contributions to PGE mineralogy.

kinichilite.occurrence: A very rare mineral in low-temperature hydrothermal Au–Ag–Te quartz veins.
kinichilite.etymology: Honors Dr. Kin-ichi Sakurai (1912– ), prominent collector and amateur mineralogist, for his descriptions of tellurium minerals from the Kawazu mine, Japan.

kinoite.occurrence: In vugs and veinlets in skarn (Santa Rita Mountains, Arizona, USA); in amygdules in basaltic lava °ows (Calumet, Michigan, USA).
kinoite.etymology: For Fr. Eusebio Francisco Kino (1645{1711), Jesuit pioneer of the Sonora-Arizona- California frontier.

kinoshitalite.occurrence: In hausmannite-tephroite ore (Noda-Tamagawa mine, Japan); in manganese-rich rocks invaded by silicic pegmatite and carbonate veins (Netra, India).
kinoshitalite.etymology: For Dr. Kameki Kinoshita (1896{1974), investigator of ore deposits in Japan.

kintoreite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a Pb–Zn deposit.
kintoreite.etymology: For the site from which the best specimens were ﬁrst collected, the Kintore open cut, Broken Hill, Australia.

kipushite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a Cu–Zn deposit (Kipushi, Congo).
kipushite.etymology: For Kipushi, Congo, where the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

kircherite.occurrence: A late-stage metasomatic phase within miarolitic cavities in volcanic ejecta.
kircherite.etymology: Honors Athanasius Kircher (1602-1680), a German Jesuit scholar who published ~ 40 works, some of which dealt with magnetism, geology, mineralogy, and volcanology. Kircher founded the museum of the Collegium Romanum in 1651, hereafter named the Museum Kircherianum.

kirchhoffite.occurrence: In a massif composed of a variety of granitic, alkaline granitic and syenitic pegmatites, various hydrothermal rocks (albitites, fenites) and carbonatites.
kirchhoffite.etymology: Honors Professor Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (1824-1887), the German physicist at the universities of Breslau and Berlin, one of the founders of spectral analysis and co-discoverer (with Robert Bunsen) of cesium and rubidium.

kirkiite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal Pb-Zn deposit (Kirki, Greece); in a volcanic fumarole, formed at about 470 °C (Vulcano, Italy).

kirschsteinite.occurrence: In melilite-nephelinite lava (Mt. Shaheru, Congo); in calcareous skarn (Tazheran massif, Russia).
kirschsteinite.etymology: For Dr. Egon Kirschstein, German geologist, a pioneer in the geological exploration of Kivu Province, Congo (Zaire).

kishonite.occurrence: In xenoliths in pyroclastic ejecta from basaltic volcanoes. This ultra-reduced mineral assemblage may reflect the interaction of deep-seated basaltic magmas with mantle derived CH4 + H2 at high fluid/melt ratios.
kishonite.etymology: For the Kishon river, which drains Mt. Carmel and enters the sea near Haifa where the placer gemstone deposits with the studied xenoliths were collected.

kitagohaite.occurrence: In heavy mineral concentrates from river sediment perhaps derived from hydrothermal quartz vein deposits of unknown type.
kitagohaite.etymology: For the Kitagoha river, Democratic Republic of the Congo. The river’s name probably comes from ‘kitahuha’, which in the local Bantu language means ‘the river that does not make noise’.

kitkaite.occurrence: In narrow carbonate-bearing ﬁssure veinlets in albite.
kitkaite.etymology: For the Kitka River, Finland, in the valley of which the mineral was found.

kittatinnyite.occurrence: A secondary mineral coating fractures in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
kittatinnyite.etymology: Derived from kittatinny, which in the language of the Algonquin Indians meant endless hills, in allusion to the topography of the Franklin area.

kladnoite.occurrence: Formed as a result of ﬁres in coal heaps.
kladnoite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Kladno district, Czech Republic.

klajite.occurrence: Formed by the weathering induced decomposition of enargite in material from the ore dumps of an epithermal high-sulphidation Cu-Au-As mineral deposit.
klajite.etymology: Honors Sándor Klaj (b. 1948), the Hungarian mineral collector who provided the first specimens.

klaprothite.occurrence: As efflorescent crusts on mine walls, formed by hydration-oxidation weathering of primary uranium minerals (mainly uraninite) by acidic solutions from the decomposition of sulfides.
klaprothite.etymology: Honors German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth (1743-1817), the discoverer of uranium (1789), zirconium (1789) and cerium (1803).

klebelsbergite.occurrence: An alteration product of stibnite in antimony deposits.
klebelsbergite.etymology: Honoring Kun´ o Klebelsberg (1875–1932), Hungarian Minister of Education.

kleberite.occurrence: In the heavy mineral fractions of marine sand deposits.
kleberite.etymology: Honors Will Kleber (1906-1970), a former director of the Institute of Mineralogy and the Museum of Mineralogy, Humboldt University, Berlin, Germany.

kleemanite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the weathering zone of manganiferous iron ore.
kleemanite.etymology: Honors Dr. Alfred William Kleeman (1913–1982), mineralogist, University of Adelaide, Adelaide, Australia.

kleinite.etymology: To honor Carl Klein (1842–1907), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Berlin, Berlin, Germany.

klockmannite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, in deposits rich in copper and tellurium.
klockmannite.etymology: For Professor Friedrich Ferdinand Hermann Klockmann (1858–1937), German mineralogist, Technical High School, Aachen, Germany.

klyuchevskite.etymology: For the locality, as one of the Klyuchevskaya group of volcanoes.

knasibfite.occurrence: On altered pyroclastic breccia in an active low-temperature volcanic fumarole.
knasibfite.etymology: An acronym based on the chemical symbols for its essential components.

knorringite.occurrence: A rare component of ultrama¯c kimberlite nodules (Kao kimberlite pipe, Lesotho).
knorringite.etymology: To honor Dr. Oleg von Knorring (1915{1994), Department of Earth Sciences, Leeds University, Leeds, England.

koashvite.occurrence: As veinlets replacing lomonosovite in an ultra-agpaitic pegmatite in an alkalic massif.
koashvite.etymology: For the locality, Mt. Koashva, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

kobeite-y.occurrence: In granite pegmatites (Japan); in a stream cobble of graphic granite (Paringa River, New Zealand).
kobeite-y.etymology: For Kobe-Mura [presently Oyama-cho], Japan, from where it was ﬁrst noted.

kobellite.etymology: In honor of Wolfgang Franz von Kobell (1803–1882), German mineralogist.

kobokoboite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by weathering of the upper branch of a zoned albiteberyl-microcline pegmatite of the LCT family, rare-element class, Li subclass, beryl type, beryl– columbite/beryl–phosphate subtype.
kobokoboite.etymology: For the pegmatite body (Kobokobo) from which the first specimens were collected.

kobyashevite.occurrence: As a secondary mineral in pyrite-chalcopyrite veins cutting fenites in an alkaline igneous complex.
kobyashevite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Yuriy Stepanovich Kobyashev (1935-2009), a specialist on the mineralogy of the Urals.

kochite.occurrence: An accessory phase in nephline syenite in an alkaline complex.
kochite.etymology: Honors Danish geologist Lauge Koch (1892-1964), who mapped Werner Bjerge.

kochkarite.occurrence: In the heavy mineral fraction of concentrates (Krokhalin deposit, Russia).
kochkarite.etymology: For the locality near the Kolyma River, Russia.

koechlinite.occurrence: As a rare alteration product in the oxidation zone of Bi–Mo deposits.
koechlinite.etymology: Honors Rudolf Ignatz Koechlin (1862–1939), Austrian mineralogist and Curator of the Vienna Natural History Museum, Vienna, Austria.

koenenite.etymology: Honors Adolph von Koenen (1837–1915), German geologist of G¨ ottingen, Germany, who discovered the ﬁrst specimens.

kogarkoite.occurrence: A sublimate from steam around a hot spring (Hortense Hot Spring, Colorado, USA); in nepheline syenite pegmatite veins in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif (Mt. Alluaiv, Kola Peninsula, Russia); in sodalite–syenite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro–syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
kogarkoite.etymology: Honoring Liya Nikolaevna Kogarko (1936– ), Russian geochemist and petrologist, investigator of alkaline rocks.

kojonenite.occurrence: In a sulfide-rich intercumulus segregation in a Pt-bearing zone in a layered mafic igneous intrusion.
assoc_parsed: intergrown with moncheite and palarstanide as inclusions in chalcopyrite
kojonenite.etymology: Honors Kari K. Kojonen (b. 1949), senior research scientist, Bedrock Geology and Resources Group, Geological Survey of Finland, for contributions to the mineralogy of the platinum group minerals and to ore mineralogy in general. Kojonen also served as Vice-Chair of the Commission on Ore Mineralogy of the International Mineralogical Association.

kokchetavite.occurrence: As inclusions in clinopyroxene and garnet within ultrahigh-grade granitic and biotite gneiss (estimated 900-1000 oC and 5.8-6.5 GPa).
kokchetavite.etymology: For the locality of the first specimens, the Kokchetav Massif.

kokinosite.occurrence: In a moist part of the oxidation zone of a corvusite-montroseite-bearing sandstone.
kokinosite.etymology: Honors Michael (Mike) Kokinos (b. 1927) of Shingle Springs, California, USA., member of the Micromounters’ Hall of Fame, and for his role as a mentor in the collecting community.

koksharovite.occurrence: A sublimate from fumarolic gas deposited on andesitic scoria.
koksharovite.etymology: Honors Professor Nikolay Ivanovich Koksharov (1818-1892), Academician of the Russian Academy of Sciences and former Director of the Russian Mineralogical Society, for his contributions to the mineralogical sciences.

koktaite.occurrence: On waste piles of a lignite mine.
koktaite.etymology: To honor Jaroslav Kokta (1904–1970), Czech chemist who analyzed the synthetic compound.

kolarite.occurrence: Of primary origin, in a hydrothermal gold-quartz vein containing sulﬁdes and selenides.
kolarite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Kolar deposit, India.

kolbeckite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in some hydrothermal metallic veins and phosphate deposits.
kolbeckite.etymology: To honor Dr. Friedrich Ludwig Wilhelm Kolbeck (1860–1943), German mineralogist, Mining Academy, Freiberg, Germany.

kolfanite.occurrence: An alteration product of holtite in a hydrothermally altered granite pegmatite.
kolfanite.etymology: An abbreviation for the Russian KOL’skii Filial Akademii Nauk SSSR [Kola Branch of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR].

kolicite.occurrence: Incrusting willemite-franklinite ore from metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebodies.
kolicite.etymology: For John Kolic, of Rockaway, New Jersey, USA, who ¯rst discovered the mineral.

kolitschite.occurrence: From supergene alteration of primary Pb-Zn ore.
kolitschite.etymology: Honors Dr. Uwe Kolitsch (b. 1966), Curator of Mineralogy, Natural History Museum, Vienna, Austria, for his contributions to mineralogy - in particular the characterization of new minerals, in crystallography, and work on alunite-group minerals.

kolovratite.occurrence: In quartz schists and carbonaceous slates.
kolovratite.etymology: In honor of Lev Stanislovich Kolovrat-Chervinskii (1884–1921), Russian physicist and radiologist, Mineralogical Laboratory, Russian Academy of Science, St. Petersburg, Russia, who studied the Tyuya-Muyun uranium deposit, Kyrgyzstan.

kolskyite.occurrence: Formed in a pegmatite as a result of hydrothermal activity.
kolskyite.etymology: For the Kola Peninsula (Kolsky Poluostrov in Russian).

kolwezite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of some Cu–Co hydrothermal ore deposits.
kolwezite.etymology: For its occurrence at Kolwezi, Congo.

kolymite.occurrence: Found in the heavy mineral fraction of concentrates (Magadan region, USSR).
kolymite.etymology: For the locality near the Kolyma River, USSR.

komarovite.occurrence: With late albite and redeposited fine-grained natrolite in alkalic rocks in a differentiated alkalic massif.
komarovite.etymology: Honors the Russian cosmonaut, Vladimir Mikhailovich Komarov (1927-1967).

kombatite.occurrence: A rare component of layered manganese ores.
kombatite.etymology: For the Kombat mine, Namibia, in which it occurs.

komkovite.occurrence: Apparently altering from catapleiite, in dolomitic veinlets cutting metasomatically altered pyroxenites, in a carbonatite.
komkovite.etymology: To honor Russian mineralogist and crystallographer Aleksandr Ivanovich Komkov (1926{1987), Karpinskii All-Union Research Institute of Geology, St. Petersburg, Russia.

konderite.occurrence: As inclusions in a Pt–Fe alloy from an alkalic ultramaﬁc massif.
konderite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Konder massif, Russia.

koninckite.occurrence: Presumably as a secondary mineral in phosphatic sedimentary rocks (Richelle, Belgium); in a hydrothermally altered andesite enriched in Fe, SO 4, and PO4 (Suwa mine, Japan).
koninckite.etymology: Honors Laurent Guillaume de Koninck (1809–1887), Belgian geologist, University of Li` ege, Li` ege, Belgium.

kononovite.occurrence: Encrusting basaltic scoria around an active fumarole, probably by reaction of volcanic gas with minerals in the scoria.
kononovite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Oleg V. Kononov (born 1932), Moscow State University , Russia.

konyaite.occurrence: Widespread in salt eﬄorescences on saline soils, formed between 30 ◦C and 50 ◦C by evaporation of ground and surface waters.
konyaite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Great Konya Basin, Turkey.

koritnigite.occurrence: A secondary mineral of the lower oxidation zone in a dolostone-hosted polymetallic hydrothermal ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia).
koritnigite.etymology: Honors Professor Sigmund Koritnig (1912–1984), petrologist, University of G¨ ottingen, G¨ ottingen, Germany.

kornelite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral formed by oxidation of pyrite.
kornelite.etymology: To honor Kornel Hlavacsek (1835–1914), Hungarian mining engineer at the pyrite mines, Bansk´ aˇStavnica, Slovakia.

kornerupine.occurrence: In boron-rich volcanic and sedimentary rocks subjected to amphibolite to granulite facies metamorphism; in metamorphosed anorthosite complexes.
kornerupine.etymology: For the Danish geologist, Andreas Nikolaus Kornerup (1857-1883).

kornite.occurrence: From a hand specimen, in veinlets of s¶erandite-pectolite cutting sugilite, probably of hydrothermal origin in a bedded manganese deposit.
kornite.etymology: For Hermann Korn (?{1946), German geologist, professionally associated with Henno Martin, for whom an associated mineral is named.

assoc_parsed: belovite- . at mt. kasnasurt: in nests of a cryptocrystalline na-fe hydrosilicate
korobitsynite.etymology: For amateur mineralogist Mikhail Fyodorovich Korobitsyn (1928-1996), for significant contributions to the mineralogy of the Lovozero massif.

korshunovskite.occurrence: From a drill core taken at 770 m in an iron ore deposit, in low-temperature hydrothermal veinlets in dolomitic marble.
korshunovskite.etymology: For the Korshunov deposit, Russia, where it was first discovered.

koryakite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
koryakite.etymology: For the Koryak, the original inhabitants living on the Kamchatka peninsula.

korzhinskite.etymology: Honoring Dmitrii Sergeevich Korzhinskii (1899–1985), Russian petrologist, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrology, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia.

kosmochlor.occurrence: A major constituent of some jadeitites; an accessory constituent of some iron meteorites.
kosmochlor.etymology: From the German kosmisch, for cosmic, in allusion to its meteoritic occurrence, and the Greek chlor, for green.

kosnarite.occurrence: A very rare mineral, formed by late hydrothermal alteration, probably of beryl and zircon, in complex granite pegmatites.
kosnarite.etymology: For Richard A. Kosnar (1946– ), American mineral dealer of Black Hawk, Colorado, USA, long interested in pegmatite minerals.

kostovite.occurrence: From gold- and tellurium-bearing replacement copper deposits (Chelopech, Bulgaria; Campbell mine, Arizona, USA).
kostovite.etymology: To honor Professor Ivan Kostov (1913– ), Bulgarian mineralogist, University of Sophia, Bulgaria.

kostylevite.occurrence: In alkalic pegmatite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
kostylevite.etymology: For Ekaterina Evtikhievna Kostyleva-Labuntsova (1894{1974), Russian mineralogist, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrology, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia.

kotoite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral typically formed in the contact zone of magnesium-rich skarn borate deposits.
kotoite.etymology: To honor Professor Bundjiro Koto (1856–1935), Japanese geologist and petrographer, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan, who studied the ore deposits of Hol Kol, North Korea.

kottenheimite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in alkali basalt.
kottenheimite.etymology: For the town near the locality that produced the first specimens.

kottigite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of some zinc deposits.
kottigite.etymology: To honor Otto K¨ ottig (1824–1892), chemist, of Schneeberg, Germany, who published the ﬁrst description of the mineral.

kotulskite.occurrence: A minor accessory mineral, of primary or secondary hydrothermal origin, in many Pt–Pd-bearing Cu–Ni deposits in ultramaﬁc rocks.
kotulskite.etymology: To honor Vladimir Klement’evich Kotul’skii (1879–1949), Russian economic geologist and authority on Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposits, of the Mining Institute, St. Petersburg, Russia.

koutekite.etymology: For Jaromir Koutek (1902–1983), Professor of Economic Geology, Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic.

kovdorskite.occurrence: A very rare mineral in an explosive breccia pipe cutting an iron ore deposit in a carbonatized ultramaﬁc-alkalic intrusive.
kovdorskite.etymology: For the Kovdor massif, Russia, in which it was ﬁrst found to occur.

kozoite-la.occurrence: In cavities in an alkali olivine basalt lava flow.
kozoite-la.etymology: A suffix indicates the La-dominant analogue of kozoite-(Nd), which honors Professor Kozo Nagashima (1925-1985).

kozoite-nd.occurrence: By post-magmatic hydrothermal activity in cavities and fissures in alkali olivine basalt.
kozoite-nd.etymology: Honors Kozo Nagashima (1925-1985), a Japanese chemist, for his contributions to the mineralogy, chemistry, and crystallography of rare earth minerals.

kozulite.occurrence: In metamorphosed manganese-rich sediments along the contact of a granodiorite intrusion (Tanohata mine, Japan).
kozulite.etymology: To honor Shukusuke K^ ozu (1880{1955), Professor at Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan.

kozyrevskite.occurrence: As complex incrustations on the surface of basalt scoria or in open pockets. Deposited directly from volcanic gas or as the result of gas-rock interactions at temperatures > 380 °C.
kozyrevskite.etymology: Honors the Russian geographer and traveler, Cossack officer Ivan Petrovich Kozyrevskiy (1680-17 34), one of the first explorers of Kamchatka and the Kuril Islands who made the first map of the East Coast of the Kamchatka Peninsula in 1726.

kraisslite.occurrence: In the zincite zone, as ¯lms and lenses in fractures, probably of secondary origin, in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
kraisslite.etymology: For Frederick Kraissl, Jr. (1899{1986) and Alice L. Kraissl (1905{1986), of Hackensack, New Jersey, USA, American amateur mineralogists who specialized in Franklin and Sterling Hill minerals.

krasheninnikovite.occurrence: A sublimate around an active volcanic fumarole.
krasheninnikovite.etymology: Honors the Russian geographer, ethnographer, and naturalist Stephan Petrovich Krasheninnikov (1711-1755), one of the first scientists who researched and published on Kamchatka.

krasnoshteinite.occurrence: Formed by diagenetic or post-diagenetic processes in halite-carnallite evaporitic rock.
krasnoshteinite.etymology: Honors Russian mining engineer and scientist Arkadiy Evgenievich Krasnoshtein (1937- 2009) specialist in the mining of potassium salts for his contributions to the exploitation of underground mines at the Verkhnekamskoe deposit.

krasnovite.occurrence: A very rare mineral from an iron ore deposit in a carbonatized ultramaﬁc-alkalic intrusive.
krasnovite.etymology: Honoring Natal’ya Ivanovna Krasnova (1941– ), mineralogist and specialist on the Kovdor massif, St. Petersburg University, St. Petersburg, Russia, in whose collection the ﬁrst specimen was found.

kratochvilite.occurrence: Formed as a result of burning pyritic shale (Kladno, Czech Republic).
kratochvilite.etymology: To honor Professor Josef Kratochv ´ ıl (1878–1958), Czech petrographer, Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic.

krausite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in sulfate-bearing cherts (Borate, California, USA); formed on a dump by post-mine oxidation of pyrite (Velarde˜ na mine, Mexico).
krausite.etymology: To honor Dr. Edward Henry Kraus (1875–1973), American mineralogist, Professor of Mineralogy and Crystallography, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA.

krauskopfite.occurrence: In veins cutting sanbornite-quartz-bearing gneissic metamorphic rocks.
krauskopfite.etymology: For Konrad Bates Krauskopf (1910{ ), Professor of Geochemistry, Stanford University, Palo Alto, California, USA.

krautite.etymology: Honors Dr. Fran¸ cois Kraut, mineralogist, Natural History Museum, Paris, France.

kravtsovite.occurrence: In vein-disseminated hydrothermal mineralization in skarn rocks beneath a basaltic sill.
kravtsovite.etymology: Honors Viktor Fomich Kravtsov (1932-2014), one of the discoverers of the Talnakh and Oktyabrsk deposits in the Noril’sk district of Russia.

assoc_parsed: distribution from the moraine of the darai-pioz glacier

kremersite.etymology: Honors the German chemist, Peter Kremers (1827–?), who analyzed the mineral.

krennerite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other tellurides.
krennerite.etymology: For J´ ozsef A. Krenner (1839–1920), Hungarian mineralogist who ﬁrst noted the species.

krettnichite.occurrence: As a primary accessory ore mineral and as free crystals in vugs within a nonmetamorphosed, hydrothermal manganite-quartz vein.
krettnichite.etymology: For the locality that provided the first specimens, Krettnich, Germany.

kribergite.etymology: A contraction of the type locality, the KRlstineBERG mine, Sweden.

krieselite.occurrence: From vugs in tennantite-chalcocite-galena-germanite ore in a complex polymetallic hydrothermal sulfide deposit.
krieselite.etymology: Honors Friedrich Wilhelm Kriesel who was the chief chemist at the Tsumeb mine laboratory around 1920.

krinovite.occurrence: Disseminated within graphite nodules in some octahedrite iron meteorites.
krinovite.etymology: For Evgeny Leonidovich Krinov, noted Russian investigator of meteorites.

krivovichevite.occurrence: A low-temperature hydrothermal alteration product of galena and natrolite by oxidizing solutions in a zoned pegmatite vein within lujavrite. Possibly a metastable ephemeral phase that forms in the early stages of oxidation of galena prior to a transformation to stable plumbojarosite–hinsdalite-like phases.
krivovichevite.etymology: Honors Sergey Vladimirovich Krivovichev (b. 1972), Professor of mineralogy and crystallography, St. Petersburg State University, Russia, for his contributions to the mineralogy of alkaline massifs and the structural mineralogy of sulfate and lead minerals.

krohnkite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral formed in the oxidized zone of copper deposits, typically in very arid climates.
krohnkite.etymology: Honoring B. Kr¨ ohnke, who provided the ﬁrst analysis of the mineral.

krotite.occurrence: Likely formed by condensation or crystallization from a melt in the solar nebula, now a Ca-Al-rich refractory inclusion in a carbonaceous chondrite meteorite. One of the earliest minerals formed in the solar system.
krotite.etymology: Honors Alexander N. Krot (b. 1959), a cosmochemist, University of Hawaii, USA, for his contributions to the understanding of early Solar System processes.

kroupaite.occurrence: Of supergene origin by oxidation-hydration alteration of uraninite.
kroupaite.etymology: Honors mining engineer Gustav Kroupa (1857-1935), who as head of the mining district, approved shipment of 10 tons of leachate from processing pitchblende ore to Marie Curie Sklodowska and Pierre Curie in 1898. They isolated three grams of the new substance radium chloride from this material and subsequently the new element radium.

kruijenite.occurrence: In fragments of altered calcic xenolith from tephra, the product of pyrometamorphic and hydrothermal alteration by magmatic volatiles.
kruijenite.etymology: Honors Dutch collector of Eifel minerals Fred Kruijen (b. 1956), an author of numerous articles in popular scientific periodicals and an outstanding photographer of Eifel micro-minerals.

krupickaite.occurrence: As secondary crusts on cemented fragments with strongly altered relics of primary minerals.
krupickaite.etymology: Honors Professor Jiří “George” Krupička (1913-2014), a polymath, linguist, geologist, and astronomer.

krupkaite.etymology: For the locality in the Czech Republic at Krupka.

krutaite.etymology: For Dr. Tom´ aˇ s Kruˇta (1906– ), Director of the Mineralogy Laboratory, Moravian Museum, Brno, Czech Republic.

krutovite.occurrence: In Co–Ni–As sulﬁde veins of hydrothermal origin.
krutovite.etymology: For Georgi Alekseevich Krutov (1902–1989), Professor of Mineralogy, Moscow State University, Moscow, Russia.

kryachkoite.occurrence: In metal assemblages in a carbonaceous chondrite meteorite.
kryachkoite.etymology: Honors Valery Kryachko who found the first samples of the Khatyrka meteorite in the Koryak Mountains in 1979 and later played a leading role in the expedition to recover more fragments in 2011.

kryzhanovskite.occurrence: A rare low-temperature oxidation product of phosphate minerals in complex granite pegmatites and iron formations.
kryzhanovskite.etymology: Honors Vladimir Il’ich Kryzhanovskii (1881–1947), Russian mineralogist, Curator of the A.E. Fersman Mineralogical Museum, Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia.

ktenasite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral formed by oxidation of chalcopyrite and sphalerite in Cu–Zn hydrothermal mineral deposits and in mine dumps.
ktenasite.etymology: Honoring Professor Konstantin Anton Ktenas (1884–1935), Greek mineralogist.

kuannersuite-ce.occurrence: In albite-lined cavities in veins that cut augite syenite in an alkaline igneous complex .
kuannersuite-ce.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens, the Kuannersuit Plateau, and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element, Cesium.

kudriavite.occurrence: As high-temperature (~ 400 °C) fumarole encrustations on the inner wall of an active andesitic stratovolcanic crater.
kudriavite.etymology: For the volcano from which the first specimens were collected.

kudryavtsevaite.occurrence: In a serpentinized xenolith in kimberlite.
kudryavtsevaite.etymology: Honors Galina Kudryavtseva (1947-2006), founder of the Diamond Mineralogy Laboratory, Lomonosov State University, Moscow, Russia.

kufahrite.occurrence: In heavy mineral concentrate from a fluvial placer derived from a Ural-Alaskan-type ultramafic complex.
kufahrite.etymology: Honors geologist Fahrid Shakirovitch Kutyev (1943-1993), Institute of Volcanology of USSR Academy of Sciences, who played a key role in the discovery of the Koryak -Kamchatka platinum belt, including the Ledyanoy placer platinum deposit.

kukharenkoite-ce.occurrence: In syenitic alkalic massifs and carbonatites.
kukharenkoite-ce.etymology: To honor Professor Aleksandr Aleksandrovich Kukharenko (1914–1993), Russian mineralogist, St. Petersburg University, St. Petersburg, Russia, for his extensive work on the carbonatites of the Kola Peninsula, Russia.

kukharenkoite-la.occurrence: A late hydrothermal mineral in cavities in pegmatite veins cutting an alkaline igneous complex.
kukharenkoite-la.etymology: As the Lanthanum-dominant analog of kukharenkoite-(Ce).

kukisvumite.occurrence: In pegmatite veins cutting ijolite-urtite rocks in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
kukisvumite.etymology: For Mt. Kukisvumchorr, Kola Peninsula, Russia, on which it occurs.

kuksite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in the oxidized zone of a tellurium-bearing gold deposit.
kuksite.etymology: To honor A.I. Kuks (1906– ), a discoverer of the Kuranakh deposit.

kulanite.occurrence: A weathering product in fractures in sideritic iron formation (Cross-cut Creek, Canada); as disseminations and veinlets in granite pegmatite (Xiyuantou, China).
kulanite.etymology: Honors Mr. Alan Kulan, Ross River, Yukon Territory, Canada, a co-discoverer of the Rapid Creek phosphate occurrences.

kuliginite.occurrence: In cavities or veins in weakly serpentinized volcaniclastic and coherent kimberlites of the Udachnaya East kimberlite pipe, Yakutia, Russia.
kuliginite.etymology: Honors Sergey Semenovich Kuligin (1961-2014), Russian geologist, Sobolev Institute of Geology and Mineralogy, Novosibirsk, Russia, who studied Yakutian kimberlites, xenoliths, and alluvial diamond deposits and co-discovered the Nicka diamondiferous placer along the Tyung River, Russia.

kuliokite-y.occurrence: As inclusions in °uorite or on ¯ssures in microcline pegmatites.
kuliokite-y.etymology: For the Kuliok River, Kola Peninsula, Russia, and yttrium in its composition.

kulkeite.occurrence: In dolostone, metamorphosed below 400 ±C, with evaporites.
kulkeite.etymology: For Dr. Holger Kulke, geologist of Essen, Germany, who provided the original specimen.

kullerudite.occurrence: In calcite veins in sills of albite diabase in schist, associated with low-grade uranium mineralization, almost exclusively as an alteration product of wilkmanite.
kullerudite.etymology: In honor of Gunnar Kullerud (1921–1989), Norwegian-American mineralogist, Geophysical Laboratory, Washington, D.C., USA.

kumdykolite.occurrence: As inclusions in omphacite in eclogite (Kazakhstan). Presumed to form under high temperatures with rapid cooling and in the absence of water. As inclusions in garnet in a diamondbearing, felsic garnet-kyanite-feldspar-quartz granulite (Bohemian massif). Also known from an enstatite chondrite meteorite in the core of a concentrically zoned, metal-sulfide nodule.
kumdykolite.etymology: For Kumdy Kol, the source of the first specimens.

kummerite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in pegmatite formed by the reaction of laueite with Al-bearing hydrothermal fluids.
kummerite.etymology: Honors Rudolf Kummer (1924-1982), mining director of the Cornelia mine at Hagendorf Süd from 1964-1982 for his appreciation of and familiarity with the mineral occurrences at the mine and support for researchers and collectors who studied and collected samples from the mine.

kumtyubeite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in contact-metasomatic, spurrite-rondorfite-ellestadite skarn in carbonate-xenoliths in ignimbrites.
kumtyubeite.etymology: Derives from Kum-Tyube, the name of a mountain plateau near where the mineral was found.

kunatite.occurrence: Secondary along fractures and in vugs deposited from circulating groundwaters charged with P, U and Cu that were derived from oxidation of primary fluorapatite in granite.
kunatite.etymology: From the Australian aboriginal words kunat kunat, meaning 'cotton weed’, a species that grows in the region around Lake Boga where studied samples were collected.

kupletskite.occurrence: In the natrolite-rich central part and in the wall rocks of nepheline syenite pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
kupletskite.etymology: For Boris Mikhailovich Kupletskii (1894{1965), Russian geologist, Institute of Geosciences, Moscow, and El'za Maximilianovna Bohnshtedt-Kupletskaya (1898{1974), Russian mineralogist, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrology, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia. kupletskite-cs.occurrence: At the border of aegirine-microcline-quartz pegmatites, and in polylithionite-quartz replacement complexes in pegmatites.
kupletskite-cs.etymology: For the cesium in the composition and similarity to kupletskite.

kuramite.occurrence: In gold–sulﬁde–quartz veins, as inclusions in goldﬁeldite (Kochbulak deposit, Uzbekistan).
kuramite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Kuramin Mountains, Uzbekistan.

kuranakhite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a gold quartz deposit (Kuranakh deposit, Russia; Jialu deposit, China).
kuranakhite.etymology: For the Kuranakh deposit, Russia, where it was ﬁrst found to occur.

kuratite.occurrence: In multiple-phase pockets, located mainly at olivine-augite triple junctions in an angrite meteorite, probably crystallized from an interstitial melt. Terrestrial occurrences include as a component in tephrite glass, basalt and phonolite.
kuratite.etymology: Honors Professor Gero Kurat (1938-2009), former Head of the Mineralogical-Petrographical Department and Curator of the Meteorite Collection, Natural History Museum,Vienna, Austria.

kurchatovite.occurrence: In an iron-bearing skarn (Solongo deposit, Russia).
kurchatovite.etymology: To honor Igor Vasil’evich Kurchatov (1903–1960), Russian physicist, Institute of Nuclear Energy, Moscow, Russia.

kurgantaite.occurrence: In marine evaporite salt deposits and salt domes.
kurgantaite.etymology: For the region, Kargan-tau, Kazakhstan, that produced the first specimens.

kurilite.occurrence: In hydrothermal Au-Ag quartz veins cutting calcalkaline volcanic rocks.
kurilite.etymology: For the islands (Kuril arc) on which the first specimens were collected.

kurnakovite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral, typically in lake-bed borate deposits.
kurnakovite.etymology: To honor Professor Nikolai Semenovich Kurnakov (1860-1941), Russian mineralogist and chemist, Institute of General and Inorganic Chemistry, Moscow, Russia.

kurumsakite.occurrence: In bituminous schists in the walls of cavities and open ¯ssures.
kurumsakite.etymology: For the locality at Kurumsak, Kazakhstan.

kusachiite.occurrence: On calcite crystals in a calcite vein between gehlenite-spurrite skarn and limestone; thought to be of low-temperature hydrothermal origin.
kusachiite.etymology: To honor Dr. Isao Kusachi (1942– ), Professor of Mineralogy, Okayama University, Okayama, Japan, for his work on skarn minerals of the Fuka area.

kushiroite.occurrence: In a refractory inclusion in a CH group carbonaceous chondrite meteorite, perhaps formed by metastable crystallization from refractory melts in the solar nebula.
kushiroite.etymology: Honors Ikuo Kushiro, Professor Emeritus, University of Tokyo, Japan, for his seminal contributions to experimental petrology and mineralogy, including characterization of CaTs-bearing systems, planetary science, and meteoritics.

kutinaite.occurrence: In carbonate-rich hydrothermal veins ( ˇCern´ y D ˚ ul mine, Czech Republic).
kutinaite.etymology: For Dr. Jan Kutina (1924– ), Lecturer at the Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic.

kutnohorite.occurrence: Typically in deposits associated with manganiferous sediments.
kutnohorite.etymology: For its ﬁrst described occurrence at Kutn´ a Hora, Czech Republic [the original label translated as kutnohorite].

kuzelite.occurrence: A rare mineral in carbonaceous xenoliths in basalt, formed above 100 ◦Cb y decomposition of ettringite.
kuzelite.etymology: Honoring Professor Hans J¨ urgen Kuzel (1932–1997), German mineralogist, Mineralogical Institute, Erlangen, Germany, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound.

kuzmenkoite-mn.occurrence: A late hydrothermal phase in minute cavities in albitized murmanite-bearing lujavrites.
kuzmenkoite-mn.etymology: For Russian geochemist and mineralogist M.V. Kuzmenko (1918-1995), the suffix, Mn, for the dominant cation in the D site.

kuzmenkoite-zn.occurrence: A late hydrothermal phase in minute cavities in albitized murmanite-bearing lujavrites.
kuzmenkoite-zn.etymology: For Russian geochemist and mineralogist M.V. Kuzmenko (1918-1995), the suffix, Mn, for the dominant cation in the D site.

kuzminite.occurrence: In vugs in mercury sulﬁdes, in calcite veins in a mercury ore deposit (Kadyrel deposit, Russia).
kuzminite.etymology: Honors Aleksei Mikhailovich Kuzmin (1891–1980), Russian mineralogist of the Tomsk Polytechnic Institute, Tomsk, Russia.

kuznetsovite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of hydrothermal mercury deposits.
kuznetsovite.etymology: Honors Academician Valerii Alekseevich Kuznetsov (1906–1985), Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Novosibirsk, Russia, student of mercury deposits.

kvanefjeldite.occurrence: As patches, streaks, and veinlets cutting arfvedsonite-bearing nepheline syenite; probably of late-stage hydrothermal origin.
kvanefjeldite.etymology: For the type locality, which is Danish for the mountain where the angelica grows.

kyanite.occurrence: In gneisses, schists, included pegmatites, and quartz veins, from moderately high-pressure regional metamorphism of principally pelitic rocks; detrital in sedimentary rocks.
kyanite.etymology: From the Greek for blue, in allusion to its common dark blue color.

kyanoxalite.occurrence: A rock-forming mineral in hydrothermally altered peralkaline rocks and pegmatites of an alkaline massif.
kyanoxalite.etymology: For its color, kyanos (Greek for blue), and presence of species-defining oxalate anion.

kyawthuite.occurrence: Only known from alluvium, the presence of Bi, Sb and small amounts of Ta, as well as trace amounts of Ti, Nb, W and U, suggest an origin in a pegmatite.
kyawthuite.etymology: Honors Dr. Kyaw Thu (b. 1973), a Burmese mineralogist-petrologist-gemologist on the staff of the Geology Department of Yangon University from 1998 to 2005, and has been the owner/operator of the Macle Gem Trade Laboratory since 2003. Dr. Thu found the specimen.

kyzylkumite.etymology: For the Kyzylkum Desert, Uzbekistan, where it was ﬁrst found.

assoc_parsed: intermediate members of the jacobsite-magnetite series
laachite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens.

labradorite.occurrence: In ma¯c igneous rocks and anorthosites. Rarer in metamorphic rocks, as amphibolites. As detrital grains in sedimentary rocks.
labradorite.etymology: For the type locality on Pauls Island, o® the coast of Labrador, Canada.

labuntsovite-fe.occurrence: In K-feldspar-natrolite-calcite veinlets in hydrothermally altered urtite.
labuntsovite-fe.etymology: Suffix, Fe, refers to the iron-dominance in the D site of a member of the labuntsovite subgroup.

labuntsovite-mg.occurrence: In cavities within dolomitic carbonatite in an alkaline massif.
labuntsovite-mg.etymology: Suffix, Mg, refers to the magnesium-dominance in the D site of a member of the labuntsovite subgroup.

labyrinthite.occurrence: A late-stage pegmatitic mineral in an alkaline igneous complex.
labyrinthite.etymology: Alludes to its very complex (labyrinthine) crystal structure.

lacroixite.occurrence: In druses in granite (Greifensteine, Germany); an alteration product rimming natromontebrasite in a complex granite pegmatite (Rusororo, Rwanda).
lacroixite.etymology: Honors Fran¸ cois Antoine Alfred Lacroix (1863–1948), French mineralogist, Natural History Museum, Paris, France.

laffittite.occurrence: With other arsenic sulﬁdes, in hydrothermal deposits.
laffittite.etymology: For Pierre Laﬃtte (1925– ), Director, National School of Mines, Paris, France.

laflammeite.occurrence: In a platinum-group-element deposit in a layered ultramafic intrusive complex, formed under relatively high-Pb, low-S conditions.
laflammeite.etymology: Honors Joseph Hector Gilles Laflamme (1947– ), Canada Centre for Mineral and Energy Technology (CANMET), Ottawa, Canada, for his work on platinum-group minerals.

laforetite.occurrence: In a dump sample from a vein-type hydrothermal ore deposit (Montgros mine, France); in a vein-type hydrothermal ore deposit (Toyoha mine, Japan).
laforetite.etymology: In honor of Claude P. Laforˆ et (1936– ), French metallographer, Bureau de Recherches G´ eologiques et Mini` eres, Orl´ eans, France, who ﬁrst observed the species.

lafossaite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens – La Fossa Crater, Italy.

lahnsteinite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal polymetallic sulfide deposit.
lahnsteinite.etymology: For the city nearby the locality from which the first specimens were collected .

laihunite.occurrence: In a Precambrian metamorphic iron deposit, probably derived by oxidation of fayalite (Little Lai-He Village, China).
laihunite.etymology: For the occurrence at Little Lai-He Village, China.

laitakarite.occurrence: In veinlets in quartz-anthophyllite-cordierite-biotite rocks (Orij¨ arvi mine, Finland).
laitakarite.etymology: For Professor Aarne Laitakari (1890–1975), Director, Geological Survey of Finland, who collected the original material.

lakargiite.occurrence: In high-temperature skarns formed in sanidinite-facies conditions of contact metamorphism in carbonate-silicate rocks occurring as xenoliths in ignimbrites.

lakebogaite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities and on joint surfaces in a weathered uranium and fluorapatitebearing pegmatitic granite.
lakebogaite.etymology: For the nearest township, Lake Boga, whose name was derived from the Bogan tribe of Australian aboriginal people, who were the original inhabitants of the region.

lalondeite.etymology: Honors Professor Andre E. Lalonde, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Ottawa, Canada, for work on mica minerals and alkaline intrusions.

lammerite.occurrence: On an old mineral specimen (Laurani, Bolivia); in an oxidized zone in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia); in volcanic sublimates (Tolbachik ﬁssure volcano, Russia).
lammerite.etymology: Honors Franz Lammer, mineral collector of Leoben, Austria, who provided the ﬁrst specimen.

lammerite-beta.occurrence: On an old mineral specimen (Laurani, Bolivia); in an oxidized zone in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia); in volcanic sublimates (Tolbachik ﬁssure volcano, Russia).
lammerite-beta.etymology: Honors Franz Lammer, mineral collector of Leoben, Austria, who provided the ﬁrst specimen.

lamprophyllite.occurrence: In all rock types and most pegmatites of a differentiated alkalic massif; both polytypes coexist in ussingite-microcline-sodalite veins at Mt. Alluaiv (Lovozero massif, Russia).
lamprophyllite.etymology: From the Greek for shining and leaf, for its lustrous cleavage.

lanarkite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of lead sulﬁde deposits.
lanarkite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Susanna mine, Lanarkshire, Scotland.

landauite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in albite veins cutting syenite pegmatite associated with an alkalic pluton.
landauite.etymology: Honors Lev Davidovich Landau (1908–1968), noted Russian physicist.

landesite.occurrence: Replacing reddingite in a complex granite pegmatite (Berry quarry, Maine, USA).
landesite.etymology: Honors Dr. Kenneth Knight Landes (1899–1984), Professor of Geology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA, for his study of Maine pegmatites.

langbanite.occurrence: In crystalline limestones and manganese-rich skarns in metamorphosed manganese deposits.
langbanite.etymology: For the place of its original discovery, Lºangban, Sweden.

langbeinite.occurrence: A principal ore of potash, mined from marine salt deposits.
langbeinite.etymology: To honor A. Langbein, of Leopoldshall [Stassfurt], Germany.

langhofite.occurrence: In a vug in hematite-pyroxene skarn in a metamorphosed, carbonate-hosted, syngenetic Långban-type, Fe-Mn-(Ba-As-Pb-Sb-W-Be-B) deposit.
langhofite.etymology: Honors curator H. Jörgen S. Langhof (b. 1965), Swedish Museum of Natural History, who collected the discovery sample.

langisite.occurrence: In pockets of ore minerals, mineralized fault gouge, and breccia cemented with calcite and quartz.
langisite.etymology: For the Langis mine in Canada, where it was discovered.

langite.occurrence: An uncommon but widespread secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of copper sulﬁde deposits; may be of post-mine formation.
langite.etymology: Honoring Victor von Lang (1838–1921), physicist and crystallographer, Professor of Physics, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria.

lanmuchangite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a Tl–Hg deposit.
lanmuchangite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Lanmuchang deposit, China.

lannonite.occurrence: A rare post-mine mineral deposited from solutions derived from an oxidizing breccia zone.
lannonite.etymology: Honoring Dan Lannon, who early staked claims in the Wilcox district, New Mexico, USA.

lansfordite.occurrence: Stalactites pendant from the shale roof of an anthracite coal mine (Nesquehoning, Pennsylvania, USA); in a hydromagnesite deposit (Atlin, Canada); a weathering product of an ultramaﬁc body (Sør-Trøndelag, Norway).
lansfordite.etymology: For its occurrence near Lansford, Pennsylvania, USA.

lanthanite-ce.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral typically formed by alteration or weathering from earlier rare-earth-element-bearing minerals.
lanthanite-ce.etymology: For its relation to lanthanite-(La), and preponderance of cerium over other rare-earth elements.

lanthanite-la.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral typically formed by alteration or weathering from earlier rare-earth-element-bearing minerals.
lanthanite-la.etymology: For dominant lanthanum in its composition.

lanthanite-nd.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral typically formed by alteration or weathering from earlier rare-earth-element-bearing minerals.
lanthanite-nd.etymology: For lanthanum in its composition, and preponderance of neodymium over other rare-earth elements.

lapeyreite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in geodes of cuprite in a weathering zone.
lapeyreite.etymology: Honors Laurent Lapeyre (b. 1973), the mineral collector who found the mineral.

laphamite.occurrence: As a secondary incrustation, probably by sublimation, on clinker adjacent to a surface vent on a burning pile of waste material from an anthracite coal mine.
laphamite.etymology: To honor Dr. Davis M. Lapham (1931–1974), former Chief Mineralogist of the Pennsylvania Geological Survey.

lapieite.occurrence: In a highly altered and mineralized glacial erratic (Lapie River, Canada).

laplandite-ce.occurrence: In the natrolite zone of a pegmatite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
laplandite-ce.etymology: For Lappland (Lapland), the region in which the Kola Peninsula lies.

laptevite-ce.occurrence: A mineral of hydrothermal origin, discovered in a glacial moraine boulder of calcitebafertisite-aegirine-microcline rock.
laptevite-ce.etymology: Honors Tatyana Mikhailovna Lapteva (1928-2011), a Russian geologist and petrologist who worked on the geology of Central Asia.

larderellite.etymology: Honoring Francesco de Larderel (1848–1925), principal operator of the Tuscan borax works.

larisaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in an oxidized ‘roll-front’ U deposit in sandstone.
larisaite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Larisa Nikolaevna Belova (1923-1998) for her studies of U minerals.

larnite.occurrence: In contact metamorphic terranes involving sedimentary carbonate rocks.
larnite.etymology: For Larne, Ireland, in the vicinity of which the mineral was initially observed.

larosite.occurrence: In the central portion of a layered hydrothermal vein.
larosite.etymology: To honor Frederick Alfred LaRose, Canadian blacksmith, one of the discoverers of silver ore at Cobalt.

larsenite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in veins cutting and replacing coarse, massive willemite-franklinite ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
larsenite.etymology: For Esper Signius Larsen, Jr. (1879{1961), American petr ologist, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

lasalite.occurrence: As efflorescences in oxidized portions of paleochannel uranium vanadium deposits of the Colorado Plateau type.
lasalite.etymology: For the mining district that provided the first specimens.

lasnierite.occurrence: As inclusions in a 1.97 carat, faceted, oval piece of lazulite-bearing blue quartzite.
lasnierite.etymology: Honors Emeritus Professor Bernard Lasnier (b. 1938), who taught geology, mineralogy, and gemology at the University of Nante, France, and studied lazulite-bearing quartzite from Intremo.

lazarenkoite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a metallic ore deposit.
lazarenkoite.etymology: Honors Academician Evgenii Konstantinovich Lazarenko (1912–1979), mineralogist, Lvov University, Lvov, Ukraine.

lazaridisite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from the weathering of primary hawleyite and greenockite.
lazaridisite.etymology: Honors Stathis Lazaridis (1953-2010), a mineral collector from Lavrion, who contributed significantly to the current understanding of the paragenetic sequences within the Lavrion deposits .

lazulite.occurrence: Disseminated in metamorphic quartzites, schists and quartz veins; in the border zones of complex granite pegmatites; in alluvium and colluvium.
lazulite.etymology: From the German lazurstein, for blue stone.

lazurite.occurrence: A contact metamorphic mineral in limestones.
lazurite.etymology: For its color resemblance to azurite, named from the Persian lazhward, for blue.

lead.occurrence: A rare mineral of hydrothermal origin, and found in placers; possibly also formed by authigenic processes and known to replace tree roots.
lead.etymology: An Old English word for the metal; the chemical symbol from the Latin plumbum.

leadamalgam.occurrence: In heavy concentrates of crushed ores from a platinum-bearing Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposit.
leadamalgam.etymology: For the composition, by analogy to mercury–silver amalgam.

leadhillite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of lead deposits.
leadhillite.etymology: For its initially-noted occurrence at Leadhills, Scotland.

leakeite.occurrence: In a metasediment rich in manganese minerals, crosscut by epigenetic veins.
leakeite.etymology: To honor Bernard E. Leake, Professor of Geology, Glasgow University, Glasgow, Scotland, for his work on amphiboles.

lecontite.occurrence: An early product of the breakdown of bat guano.
lecontite.etymology: Honoring John Lawrence LeConte (1825–1883), American entomologist, University of California, Berkeley, California, USA, who discovered the mineral.

lecoqite-y.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral associated with a hyperagpaitic pegmatite.
lecoqite-y.etymology: Honors the French chemist P.É. Lecoq de Boisbaudran (1838–1912) and for the dominant rare earth element in its composition.

leesite.occurrence: Collected in an abandoned mine tunnel in a roll-front uranium deposit.
leesite.etymology: Honors American mineral dealer and collector Bryan K. Lees (b. 1957), recipient of the Friends of Mineralogy Author of the Year Award (1998), Carnegie Mineralogical Award (1998), the Colorado School of Mines Medal (2003), and the American Mineral Heritage Award (2014).

legrandite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of Zn–As-bearing deposits; rare in granite pegmatite.
legrandite.etymology: Honors a Mr. Legrand, Belgian mine manager, who collected the ﬁrst specimen.

leguernite.occurrence: A sublimate on volcanic rock from the walls of a high-temperature fumarole.
leguernite.etymology: Honors François Le Guern (1942-2011), better known as “Fanfan,” a volcanologist and expert on volcanic gases and sublimates.

lehmannite.occurrence: A sublimate around an active volcanic fumarole.
lehmannite.etymology: Honors Johann Gottlob Lehmann (1719-1767) Academician of the Royal Prussian Academy of Sciences (1754) and the Imperial Russian Academy of Sciences (1761); author of the first mineral description of a new species discovered in Russia - crocoite.

lehnerite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a complex granite pegmatite.
lehnerite.etymology: Honors Ferdinand Lehner (1868–1943), Pleystein, Germany, an early collector of Hagendorf minerals.

leifite.occurrence: In pegmatite (Narss^ arssuk, Greenland); in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia); associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
leifite.etymology: For Leif Ericson, Norse adventurer and discoverer of Greenland in 982.

leightonite.occurrence: Of localized occurrence in the oxidized zone of a copper deposit, probably formed under conditions of low acidity (Chuquicamata, Chile).
leightonite.etymology: Honors Tom´ as Leighton Donoso (1896–1967), Chilean mining engineer and Professor of Mineralogy, University of Santiago, Santiago, Chile.

leisingite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in dump material from the oxidized zone of a tellurium-bearing Cu–Au–Ag deposit.
leisingite.etymology: Honoring Joseph F. Leising (1949– ), Reno, Nevada, USA, geologist and mineral collector, who helped collect the material.

leiteite.occurrence: With other zinc- and arsenic-bearing minerals, apparently formed at low temperatures in an oxidized zone in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
leiteite.etymology: For Luis Antonio Bravo Teixeira-Leite (1942–1999), Portuguese-South African amateur mineralogist of Pretoria, South Africa, who noted the ﬁrst specimen.

lemanskiite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, as nodules or veinlets in gold-bearing quartz veins of a hydrothermal deposit.
assoc_parsed: a mineral of the crandallite group
talc. lavendulan transforms easily to lemanskiite
lemanskiite.etymology: Honors Chester S. Lemanski, Jr. (b. 1947), New Jersey, USA, a mineral collector who first recognized this new mineral.

lemmleinite-ba.occurrence: In alkaline pegmatites in an alkaline massif.
lemmleinite-ba.etymology: Suffix, Ba, refers to the barium-dominance in the D site of a member of the lemmleinite subgroup.

lemmleinite-k.occurrence: In ultra-agpaitic pegmatites in apatite-nepheline in an alkaline massif.
lemmleinite-k.etymology: Honors Georgy Glebovich Lemmlein (1901-1962), Russian mineralogist and crystallographer, the suffix, K, indicates the dominant cation in B site.

lemoynite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral, in pegmatite in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mpnt Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in miarolytic cavities in a nepheline syenite sill (near Saint-Amable, Canada).
lemoynite.etymology: For Charles Lemoyne (1625{1685), Lord of Longuevil, and his four sons, well-known personalities in French-Canadian history.

lenaite.occurrence: In goethite pseudomorphs after magnesian siderite, in quartz-siderite veins (Russia); in an epithermal gold-silver telluride vein deposit (Gies deposit, Montana).
lenaite.etymology: For its occurrence near the Lena River, Russia.

lengenbachite.etymology: For the locality at the Lengenbach quarry, Switzerland.

leningradite.occurrence: In volcanic fumaroles, deposited at about 140◦ C.
leningradite.etymology: For the city of Leningrad (once and again St. Petersburg), in the Universities of which this and related minerals have been studied.

lennilenapeite.occurrence: Apparently as both a primary and a late-stage low-temperature hydrothermal mineral in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
lennilenapeite.etymology: For the Lenni Lenape Indians (original people in the Algonquin Indian language) who inhabited the Franklin area.

lenoblite.occurrence: In a zone of reduction below the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit (Mounana mine, Gabon).
lenoblite.etymology: For Andr´ e Lenoble (?–1968), formerly Head of the Laboratory of Mineralogy and Chief of Exploration, French Atomic Energy Commission.

leogangite.occurrence: A secondary mineral coating limonitic dolostone breccia and filling voids in the oxidized zone of a pyrite, galena, tennantite deposit.
leogangite.etymology: For the city (Leogang) in Austria near the first found specimens.

leonardsenite.occurrence: A sublimated encrustations from fluorine-rich fumarolic gas.
leonardsenite.etymology: Honors Erik Leonardsen (b. 1934), the former leader of the X-ray Diffraction Laboratory of the Geological Institute, University of Copenhagen, Denmark, for his work on the characterization of the fumarolic minerals from Icelandic volcanoes by X-ray diffraction.

leonite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral of metamorphic origin in marine salt deposits; may occur in volcanic fumaroles.
leonite.etymology: To honor Leo Strippelmann, Director of the salt works at Westeregeln, Germany.

lepageite.occurrence: A primary accessory mineral in a lens of granitic LCT (Li-Cs-Ta) pegmatite formed during injection of an evolved LCT-type melt related to anatectic processes within a metasedimentary-metavolcanic complex into serpentinite.
lepageite.etymology: Honors Yvon Le Page (b. 1943) a crystallographer who developed the program MISSYM that has played a major role in the solution of complex mineral structures (including lepageite), solved the structures of many minerals, and was involved in the description of several new minerals.

lepersonnite-gd.occurrence: In the lower portion of the oxidation zone developed above uraninite-bearing dolomitic rocks.
lepersonnite-gd.etymology: For Jacques Lepersonne, honorary Head of the Department of Geology and Mineralogy, Royal Museum of Central Africa, Tervuren, Belgium, and for its gadolinium content.

lepersonnite-nd.etymology: The suffix indicates the Nd-analogue of lepersonnite-(Gd).

lepidocrocite.occurrence: A weathering or oxidation product of other iron-bearing minerals, in soils and mineral deposits; a precipitate from ground water. In marine manganese nodules.
