lepidocrocite.etymology: From the Greek for scale and thread, for the occasionally feathery or scaly habit.

lepidolite.occurrence: In granite pegmatites, derived by metasomatic replacement of muscovite or biotite; in some high-temperature quartz veins, greisens, and granites.
lepidolite.etymology: From the Greek lepidos for scale, in allusion to its micaceous structure.

lepkhenelmite-zn.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in a complex granitic (eudialite, agerine, feldspar) pegmatite.
lepkhenelmite-zn.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens and the dominant element in the D structural site, Zn.

lermontovite.occurrence: In uranium-bearing veins in a granite porphyry stock.
lermontovite.etymology: Honors Mikhail Yur’evich Lermontov (1814–1841), Russian poet.

letovicite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral, formed from burning coal (Czech Republic); deposited from hot springs (The Geysers, California, USA).
letovicite.etymology: For Letovice, Czech Republic, the locality ﬁrst noted for the mineral.

leucite.occurrence: With potassium- rich ma¯c and ultrama¯c lavas and hypabyssal rocks, and may almost entirely compose them.
leucite.etymology: From the Greek leucos for white, in allusion to its color.

leucophanite.occurrence: In pegmatites in augite syenite (Langesundsfjord, Norway); in albitization zones in pegmatites at the contact of alkalic massifs intruding Proterozoic carb onaceous quartz-sericite schists (Baikal massif, Russia).
leucophanite.etymology: From the Greek for white and to appear, its common color.

leucophoenicite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal or contact zone mineral in veins and skarns in a metamorphosed stratiform Zn-Mn orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
leucophoenicite.etymology: From the Greek for pale and purplish red in reference to its conspicuous color.

leucophosphite.occurrence: Formed by reaction between bat or bird guano and earlier iron-bearing minerals; by hydrothermal alteration of iron-rich phosphates in complex granite pegmatites; crosscutting ﬂuorapatite nodules in black shale; replacing fossil wood; in phosphate rock deposits.
leucophosphite.etymology: From the Greek for white and the phosphate in its composition.

leucosphenite.occurrence: In pegmatite in syenite (Greenland, Russia, Canada); in aegirine-feldspar veins (Inagli massif, Russia); an authigenic mineral in shales (Utah and Wyoming, USA).
leucosphenite.etymology: From the Greek for white and wedge, its color and crystal habit.

leucostaurite.occurrence: A secondary mineral by the interaction of evaporitic brines within the oxidation zone of a base-metal deposit.
leucostaurite.etymology: From the Greek “leukos” (white) and “stauros” (cross) in allusion to the white or transparent, colorless cruciform twinned crystals.

levantite.etymology: For the Levant region, a geographical term referring to an area in the eastern Mediterranean that includes parts of Israel, Jordan, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Cyprus , and Turkey.

leverettite.occurrence: As a secondary mineral in a weathered vein of copper and arsenic minerals.
leverettite.etymology: Honors Peter Leverett (b. 1944), professor of Chemistry, University of Western Sydney, Australia, in recognition of his contributions to research and teaching in chemistry and chemical geology.

levinsonite-y.occurrence: Formed by evaporative precipitation during weathering of pyritiferous phyllite, the rare earths probably derived from monazite and xenotime.
levinsonite-y.etymology: To honor Dr. Alfred Abraham Levinson (1927– ), mineralogist, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada, who originated the nomenclature system in use for rare-earth-bearing minerals.

levyneca.occurrence: Typically as a crystalline lining in cavities in basalts.
levyneca.etymology: After Armand L¶evy (1794{1841), French mineralogist and crystallographer.

leydetite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit.
leydetite.etymology: Honors Jean-Claude Leydet (b.1961), an amateur mineralogist and mineral collector from Brest, France, who discovered the new mineral.

liandratite.occurrence: In a zoned pegmatite in amphibolite-grade gneiss, as an oxidized crust over petscheckite.
liandratite.etymology: Honors Professor George Liandrat, of Samo¨ ens, France, who prospected in Madagascar.

liberite.occurrence: In veins cutting a lepidolite-°uorite-magnetite \ribbon rock" in tactite.
liberite.etymology: Presumably for LIthium and BERyllium in the composition.

libethenite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of copper deposits.
libethenite.etymology: For the locality from which it was ﬁrst described, L’ubietov´ a, Slovakia (formerly Libethen, Hungary).

liddicoatite.occurrence: Detrital in soil, an apparent product of the local pegmatites.
liddicoatite.etymology: For Richard Thomas Liddicoat, Jr. (1918{ ), American gemologist.

liebauite.occurrence: In cavities in argillaceous sedimentary xe noliths subjected to very high-grade thermal metamorphism.
liebauite.etymology: For Dr. Friedrich Liebau, Kiel, Germany, prominent worker on silicate minerals.

liebenbergite.occurrence: In a small tabular nickel deposit at the contact between quartzite and serpentinized ultrama¯cs; it appears to have formed at »730 ±C and < 2 kbar during thermal metamorphism, possibly of a nickel-rich meteorite.
liebenbergite.etymology: For W.R. Liebenberg, Deputy Director-General of the National Institute for Metallurgy of South Africa.

liebermannite.occurrence: Shock-generated, high-pressure mineral formed via solid-state transformation of primary igneous K-feldspar in a Martian-enriched basaltic shergottite meteorite.
liebermannite.etymology: Honors Robert C. Liebermann, a high-pressure mineral physicist at Stony Brook University, New York, USA.

liebigite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral typically formed as an alteration product of uraninite in alkaline carbonate solutions.
liebigite.etymology: To honor Professor Justus von Liebig (1803–1873), German chemist, University of Munich, Munich, Germany.

liguowuite.occurrence: Rare in heavy mineral concentrates from hydrothermally (high temperature) altered biotite-quartz monzonite.
liguowuite.etymology: Honors Li Guowu (b. 1964) for his contributions to mineralogical research in this region, including the descriptions of tewite and wumuite.

likasite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of copper deposits.
likasite.etymology: For the locality where it was ﬁrst found, Likasi, Congo.

lileyite.occurrence: Occurs in miarolitic cavities in an alkaline basalt.
lileyite.etymology: For the old name of the first known locality, Liley, Germany.

lillianite.occurrence: In hydrothermal deposits of probable high-temperature origin.
assoc_parsed: at a number of early reported occurrences the “lillianite” was shown to be mixtures
lillianite.etymology: For the Lillian mine, Leadville, Colorado, USA, the discredited type locality.

lime.occurrence: In thermally metamorphosed calcareous ejecta (Vesuvius, Italy); in burning coal measures (Kopeysk, Russia); an accessory phase by oxidative sintering in medium-temperature, combustion metamorphic spurrite-fluorellestadite-fluorapatite marbles (Jordan).

limousinite.occurrence: In vugs in altered primary nodular Li-Fe-Mn phosphates (triplite, alluaudite, and heterosite) in beryl-bearing granitic pegmatite.
limousinite.etymology: For the French historical region Limousin from which studied material was collected. The name Limousin is derived from Lemovices, a native first millenary BC Gaulish tribe .

linarite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of Pb–Cu deposits.
linarite.etymology: For its occurrence at Linares, Spain.

lindackerite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of some arsenic-rich copper deposits.
lindackerite.etymology: To honor Joseph Lindacker, Austrian pharmacist-chemist, who made the first analyses.

lindbergite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in granite pegmatites.
lindbergite.etymology: Honors Marie Louise Lindberg (-Smith) (b. 1918), from the US Geological Survey, who described several new minerals from the nearby Sapucaia quarry (frondelite, faheyite, moraesite, barbosalite, and tavorite).

lindgrenite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of molybdenum-bearing copper deposits.
lindgrenite.etymology: Honors Professor Waldemar Lindgren (1860–1939), Swedish–American economic geologist, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

lindqvistite.occurrence: In a regionally metamorphosed lead-bearing Fe–Mn skarn deposit.
lindqvistite.etymology: For Dr. Bengt Lindqvist (1927– ), formerly Senior Curator of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm, Sweden.

lindsleyite.occurrence: A mantle-derived phase in veinlets in metasomatized kimberlite (South Africa).
lindsleyite.etymology: For Professor Donald Hale Lindsley (1934– ), State University of New York, Stony Brook, New York, USA, for his work in high-pressure petrology.

lindstromite.etymology: Honors Gustav Lindstr¨ om (1838–1916), Swedish mineral chemist of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm, Sweden.

lingbaoite.occurrence: Within pyrite as composite inclusions (<50 μm) probably formed through the cooling of polymetallic melt droplets within the hydrothermal gold-bearing quartz-vein system.
lingbaoite.etymology: After Lingbao city, central China, ~30 km northeast of the mine where the new mineral was discovered.

linnaeite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other cobalt and nickel sulﬁdes.
linnaeite.etymology: In honor of Carl von Linn´ e [Carolus Linnaeus] (1707–1778), Swedish taxonomist.

lintisite.occurrence: Coating and replacing lorenzenite in ultra-agpaitic syenite pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia); in sodalite xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
lintisite.etymology: For LIthium, sodium (Natrium), TItanium, and SIlicon in the composition.

linzhiite.occurrence: In the heavy mineral fraction of a podiform chromitite deposit in the peridotite of an ophiolitic harzburgite. Likely the product of a strongly reducing environment and possibly are xenocrysts derived from a mantle source.
linzhiite.etymology: For Linzhi Prefecture, near the locality that produced the first samples.

liottite.occurrence: In cavities in ejecta blocks of metasomatized carbonate rocks in a pumice deposit.
liottite.etymology: For mineral collector Luciano Liotti, who donated the specimen in which this mineral was ¯rst found.

lipuite.occurrence: In high-grade Wessels-type Mn ore, mainly hausmannite, bixbyite, braunite-II, and manganite, formed by structurally controlled hydrothermal enrichment of low-grade strataform beds.
lipuite.etymology: Honors Chinese geochemist and petrologist, Professor Pu Li (1911-1968), Beijing Institute of Geology and later at the Guiyang Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Professor Li was the founder and pioneer of isotope geochemistry in China and made significant contributions to the development of Chinese geology and petrology.

liraite.occurrence: In the intermediate zone of a muscovite-rare element-class pegmatite. Formed by reaction of phosphate minerals with Na-bearing hydrothermal fluids.
liraite.etymology: Honors Argentinian mineralogist Dr. Raúl Lira (b. 1956), for his contributions to the knowledge of mineralogy and petrology in Argentina.

liroconite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some copper deposits.
liroconite.etymology: From the Greek for pale and powder, for its pale blue to green streak.

lisetite.occurrence: Formed by retrograde metamorphism of a Na, Al-rich and K, Mg-poor eclogite pod in the highest pressure part of the greenschist, amphibolite, or granulite facies.
lisetite.etymology: For the Liset eclogite pod, Norway.

lishizhenite.occurrence: In cavities and veinlets in anhydrite in the oxidation zone of a Pb–Zn deposit.
lishizhenite.etymology: To honor Li Shizhen (1518–1593), famous Chinese pharmacologist.

lisiguangite.occurrence: Of contact metamorphic origin, along veins in an exoskarn associated with mafic igneous rocks (garnet pyroxenite).
assoc_parsed: from a heavy mineral concentrate with chalcopyrite
lisiguangite.etymology: Honors Chinese geologist, Li Siguang (J.S. Lee) (1889–1971), Minister of Geology of China (1952–1971), Vice President of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Chairman of the China National Association of the Sciences.

lisitsynite.occurrence: In the central zone of a hyperagpaitic pegmatite.
lisitsynite.etymology: Honors Russian specialist in boron deposits, Apollon E. Lisitsyn (1928-1999).

liskeardite.occurrence: An oxidation product of arsenic-bearing sulﬁdes.
liskeardite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence, near Liskeard, England.

litharge.occurrence: As an alteration product of other lead-bearing minerals.
litharge.etymology: From the Greek word given by Dioscorides to the lead oxide obtained in parting lead from silver by ﬁre metallurgy; a name long applied to the synthetic product.

lithidionite.occurrence: In lapilli strongly modi¯ed by fumerolic action subsequent to the 1873 eruption of Vesuvius.
lithidionite.etymology: From the Greek for pebble, [Greek diminutive of lithos, for stone; lithidion in English, litidion in Italian] presumably for the size and shape of the lapilli on which the mineral occurs.

lithiomarsturite.occurrence: In small vugs within a complex Li-Sn-rich pegmatite.
lithiomarsturite.etymology: As the lithium analogue of marsturite.

lithiophilite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in some complex granite pegmatites; usually primary but rarely secondary.
lithiophilite.etymology: For its lithium content and the Greek for friend.

lithiophorite.occurrence: A relatively common constituent of “wad” in the oxidized zones of hydrothermal ore deposits and sedimentary manganese deposits; in banded iron formations; from lithium-rich granite pegmatites; in some lateritic soils and bauxites.
lithiophorite.etymology: For its content of LITHIum and the Greek for to bear.

lithiophosphate.occurrence: Formed by hydrothermal replacement of montebrasite in the core of a granite pegmatite in amphibolite (Mt. Okhmyl’k, Russia); in a lithium-rich granite pegmatite (Foote mine, North Carolina, USA).
lithiophosphate.etymology: For its content of lithium and phosphate.

lithiotantite.occurrence: In microcline-albite zones of granite pegmatites.
lithiotantite.etymology: For LITHIum and TANTalum in its composition.

lithiowodginite.occurrence: In the albite zone of granite pegmatites.
lithiowodginite.etymology: For the dominant LITHium content and relation to wodginite.

lithosite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from the weathering of ultraperalkalic pegmatite veins cutting nepheline syenites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
lithosite.etymology: From the Greek lithos, for stone, as the mineral is composed of the most abundant chemical elements of the crust of the earth.

litochlebite.occurrence: A primary phase in hydrothermal veins in a uranium deposit.
litochlebite.etymology: Honors the Czech mineralogist Dr. Jiří Litochleb (b. 1948), currently head of the Department of Mineralogy and Petrology and director of the Natural History Museum, National Museum, Praha, Czech Republic.

litvinskite.occurrence: In a hyperagpaitic pegmatite in an alkaline massif.
litvinskite.etymology: Honors crystallographer Galina P. Litvinskaya (1920-1994), Moscow State University, Russia.

liudongshengite.occurrence: In a highly oxidized quartz-sulfide vein in a Pb-Zn mine.
liudongshengite.etymology: Honors Chinese geologist and archaeologist Professor Liu Dongsheng (1917-2008), a Research Fellow at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology and then at the Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

liuite.occurrence: At the rim of a transformed ilmenite-ülvospinel grain in a shock-melt pocket in a Martian meteorite.

liveingite.etymology: In honor of George D. Liveing (1827–1924), Professor of Chemistry, Cambridge University, Cambridge, England.

liversidgeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in highly weathered portions of a metamorphosed Pb-Zn-Ag sulfide deposit.
liversidgeite.etymology: Honors Archibald Liversidge (1846-1927), Professor of Geology and Mineralogy, and later Professor of Mineralogy and Chemistry at the University of Sydney for his contributions to the mineralogy of New South Wales, in particular that of the Broken Hill deposit, and his contributions to education in mineralogy and chemistry.

livingstonite.etymology: Honors David Livingstone (1813–1873), Scottish explorer and missionary in Africa.

lizardite.occurrence: Typically a product of retrograde metamorphism, replacing olivine, orthopyroxene, or other minerals in ultrama¯c igneous rocks.
lizardite.etymology: For the type locality, the Lizard complex, Cornwall, England.

lobanovite.occurrence: In pegmatitic cavities in a differentiated alkaline igneous massif.
lobanovite.etymology: Honors Dr. Konstantin V. Lobanov, a Russian ore geologist who has worked in the Kola Peninsula for more than 40 years. Previously known under the names monoclinic astrophyllite, magnesium astrophyllite, magnesiumastrophyllite and magnesioastrophyllite.

lokkaite-y.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by alteration of primary rare-earth minerals.
lokkaite-y.etymology: To honor Professor Lauri Lokka (1885–1966), Finnish mineralogist and Chief Chemist, Geological Survey of Finland, Helsinki, Finland.

lollingite.occurrence: In mesothermal deposits associated with other sulﬁdes and with calcite gangue; also in pegmatites.
lollingite.etymology: For the Austrian locality at L¨ olling.

lomonosovite.occurrence: In nepheline syenites and pegmatites cutting them (Lovozero massif, Russia); in lavas and gabbros near contacts with nepheline syenite (Il¶³maussaq intrusion, Greenland).
lomonosovite.etymology: For Mikhail Vasil'evich Lomonosov (1711{1765), Russian mineralogist and naturalist.

londonite.occurrence: An uncommon component of granite pegmatites, in the central zones and in miarolitic cavities.
londonite.etymology: To honor Dr. David London (1953– ), Professor of Geology and Geophysics, University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma, USA, for his contributions to the understanding of granite pegmatites.

lonecreekite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral probably formed by alteration of pyrite and reaction, at pH < 1, with ammonia fumes produced as the result of decay of organic matter ( Hyrax excreta).
lonecreekite.etymology: For Lone Creek Fall Cave, South Africa, its original occurrence.

lonsdaleite.occurrence: Discovered in the residue (ca. 200 mg) from the dissolution of 5 kg of Ca˜ non Diablo meteorite. The mineral may be formed by impact shock, or be a product of direct crystallization in the parent body.
lonsdaleite.etymology: To honor Professor Kathleen (Yardley) Lonsdale (1903–1971), distinguished British crystallographer, University of London, London, England.

loparite-ce.occurrence: A primary phase in diﬀerentiated nepheline syenite massifs and alkalic pegmatites; replacing perovskite in carbonatites.
loparite-ce.etymology: From the Russian name for the Lapps, Lopar, inhabitants of the Kola Peninsula, Russia, ﬁrst noted place of occurrence of the mineral, and for its cerium content.

lopezite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in vugs in massive nitrate rock.
lopezite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Emiliano L` opez Saa (1871–1959), Iquique, Chile, Chilean mining engineer and mineral collector long associated with the Chilean nitrate industry.

lorandite.occurrence: Although rare, the most widespread thallium mineral; of hydrothermal origin, typically formed at relatively low temperatures.
lorandite.etymology: For E¨ otv¨ os Lorand (1848–1919), physicist of Budapest, Hungary.

loranskite-y.etymology: For Apollonie Mikhailovich Loranski (1847–?), Inspector of the Mining Institute, St. Petersburg, Russia.

lorenzenite.occurrence: In nepheline syenites and their associated pegmatites.
lorenzenite.etymology: After Johannes Theodor Lorenzen (1855{1884), Danish mineralogist interested in Greenland minerals.

loseyite.occurrence: A very rare mineral occurring in veinlets in massive ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
loseyite.etymology: To honor Samuel R. Losey (1830–1904), mineral collector of Franklin, New Jersey, USA.

lotharmeyerite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of an arsenic-rich polymetallic base-metal deposit.
lotharmeyerite.etymology: Honors Julius Lothar Meyer (1830-1895), German chemist and physician, Karlsruhe Polytechnic Institute and University of Tübingen, Germany, for his contributions to chemistry.

loudounite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in the alteration of diabase.
loudounite.etymology: For the occurrence in Loudoun Co., Virginia, USA.

loughlinite.occurrence: As replacements in dolomitic medium- to low-grade oil shale of the Green River Formation (Sweetwater Co., Wyoming, USA).
loughlinite.etymology: For Dr. Gerald Francis Loughlin (1880{1946), Chief Geologist, U.S. Geological Survey.

lourenswalsite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed during weathering, in vugs and miarolitic cavities in a titaniferous nepheline syenite.
lourenswalsite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Lourens Wals, mineral collector of Turnhout, Belgium.

lovdarite.occurrence: A late hydrothermal mineral in alkalic pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
lovdarite.etymology: From the Russian phrase dar Lovozera, for a gift of Lovozero.

loveringite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral from residual intercumulus magma in the pyroxene, olivine-chromite, or plagioclase-rich layers of maﬁc intrusions.
loveringite.etymology: Honors Professor John Francis Lovering (1930– ), Australian geochemist, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia, for his work on ﬁssion-track methods in geochemistry.

lovozerite.occurrence: In nepheline syenites and associated pegmatites.
lovozerite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Lovozero massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

loweite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in marine salt deposits; in eﬄorescences and crusts in saline playa deposits; a volcanic sublimation product.
loweite.etymology: To honor Alexander L¨ owe (1808–1895), Austrian chemist, Chief Assayer at the Mint, Vienna, Austria.

luanheite.occurrence: In a placer containing gold and other elements.
luanheite.etymology: For the Luan [Luan He in Mandarin Chinese] River, China, in which it is found.

luanshiweiite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting and the outer zone of a granitic pegmatite dike .
assoc_parsed: na- and ca-poor but li- and oh- or f-rich tourmaline
luanshiweiite.etymology: Honors Chinese pegmatitic petrologist Professor Luanshiwei (1928-2012).

luberoite.occurrence: In concentrates from placers derived from granodioritic source rocks.
luberoite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Lubero district, Congo.

luborzakite.occurrence: In a gold deposit in metasomatites (skarns, argillisites and jasperoids) that replace volcanogenic-sedimentary rocks and limestones. Brecciated metasomatites host Mn-Tl-Hg-As-Sb mineralization.
luborzakite.etymology: Honors Czech crystallographer Professor Lubor Žák (1925-2008), Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic, an expert on the mineralogy and structures of Bi -sulfosalts and on the geology and mineralogy of manganese deposits in the former Czechoslovakia.

lucabindiite.occurrence: As encrustations on pyroclastic breccia around an active volcanic fumarole.
lucabindiite.etymology: Honors Luca Bindi (b. 1971), Professor of Mineralogy and former Head of the Division of Mineralogy, Natural History Museum, University of Florence, Italy, for contributions to the study of the structural complexity in minerals (i.e., incommensurate structures, superstructures, twinned structures) and integrating together mineralogy and the most advanced fields of crystallography.

lucasite-ce.occurrence: In heavy-media concentrates from non-sandy tuﬀ in an olivine lamproite diatreme.
lucasite-ce.etymology: For Hans Lucas, Australian geologist, CRA Exploration Pty. Ltd., who noted the mineral in concentrates.

lucchesiite.occurrence: As graphic intergrowths, in the central parts of a contaminated anatectic pegmatite dike (Czech Republic). In gem-bearing alluvial gravels (“illam”) (Sri Lanka).
lucchesiite.etymology: Honors Sergio Lucchesi (1958-2010), professor of mineralogy, Sapienza University, Rome, Italy, for his contributions to the study of tourmaline and spinel crystal chemistry.

luddenite.occurrence: In thoroughly oxidized Pb{Cu sul¯de ores.
luddenite.etymology: For Raymond W. Ludden, Chief Geologist for Western Exploration, Phelps Dodge Corporation.

ludjibaite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized zone of some copper deposits.
ludjibaite.etymology: For its occurrence at Ludjiba, Congo.

ludlamite.occurrence: In complex granite pegmatites, a common hydrothermal alteration product of earlier phosphates, formed under reducing conditions.
ludlamite.etymology: To honor Henry Ludlam (1824–1880), English mineral collector, London, England.

ludlockite.occurrence: In sulﬁde ore from a complex polymetallic hydrothermal ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia).
ludlockite.etymology: For Fredrick LUDlow Smith III, (1939– ) and Charles LOCKe Key (1935– ), American mineral dealers then resident in New Jersey, USA, who supplied the ﬁrst specimens for study.

ludwigite.occurrence: Typically formed in magnesian iron skarn and contact metamorphic deposits.
ludwigite.etymology: Honoring Ernst Ludwig (1842–1915), Austrian Professor of Chemistry, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria, who analyzed the original material.

lueshite.occurrence: Incrusting a vermiculitelike mica, at the contact of cancrinite syenite with carbonatite (Lueshe, Congo); in sodalite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); a common accessory mineral formed during fenetization of pyroxenite and gabbro (Gem Park, Colorado, USA); in veins cutting nepheline syenites (Il ´ ımaussaq intrusion, Greenland).
lueshite.etymology: For the occurrence at Lueshe, Congo.

luetheite.occurrence: A rare mineral ﬁlling cavities in intensely altered volcanic rock (Patagonia district, Arizona, USA); in the oxidized zone of a copper deposit (Majuba Hill, Nevada, USA).
luetheite.etymology: Honors Ronald D. Luethe (1944– ), geologist for Phelps Dodge Corporation, Douglas, Arizona, USA, who found the ﬁrst material.

lukechangite-ce.occurrence: A very rare mineral found in a pegmatite dike associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex.
lukechangite-ce.etymology: To honor Professor Luke L.Y. Chang (1934– ), University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland, USA, for his studies of carbonate minerals.

lukkulaisvaaraite.occurrence: In veins, veinlets and pods in sulfide-bearing, pegmatoid pyroxenites in a layered gabbronorite intrusion, formed under post-magmatic conditions.
lukkulaisvaaraite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens, the Lukkulaisvaara intrusion.

lukrahnite.occurrence: Secondary in the oxidation zone of polymetallic sulfarsenide deposits.
lukrahnite.etymology: Honors geologist Ludger Krahn (b. 1957), who provided the initial specimen for study.

lulzacite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veinlets associated with metamorphism at the contact between quartzite and ironstone.
lulzacite.etymology: Honors geologist Y. Lulzac (b. 1934), who discovered the mineral.

lumsdenite.occurrence: Post-mining, secondary on asphaltum associated with montroseite- and corvusitebearing sandstone. Deposited where U6+- and V4+/V5+-bearing solutions encountered local, strongly reducing conditions caused by the presence of organic matter.
lumsdenite.etymology: For the location of the Packrat mine at the head of Lumsden Canyon.

luneburgite.etymology: For its first-noted occurrence at Liineburg, Germany.

lunijianlaite.occurrence: Within corundum, in a hydrothermal pyrophyllite deposit in rhyolite.
lunijianlaite.etymology: From the Chinese luni, for the chlorite group, representing cookeite; jian, a connective; and lain for pyrophyllite.

lunokite.occurrence: In fractures and on crusts of mitridatite in granite pegmatites.
lunokite.etymology: For the Lun’ok River, nearby Mt. Vasin-Myl’k, Russia.

luobusaite.occurrence: In the heavy mineral fraction of a podiform chromitite deposit in the peridotite of an ophiolite.
luobusaite.etymology: For the “Luobusa” mine, the site from which the first specimens were collected .

luogufengite.occurrence: An oxidation product of Fe-bearing basaltic glass in vesicles in basaltic scoria.
assoc_parsed: hydronium jarosite. distribution from the menan volcanic complex
luogufengite.etymology: Honors Chinese Professor Luo Gufeng (b. 1933), who has passionately taught crystallography and mineralogy at Nanjing University of China for more than 50 years.

lusernaite-y.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in fractures in regionally metamorphosed gneiss.
lusernaite-y.etymology: Named for the Luserna valley in which the first specimens were collected and a suffix of the chemical symbol of the dominant rare earth element.

lussierite.occurrence: Post-mining, secondary, as efflorescent crusts on the surfaces of mine walls from the oxidation of primary uranium ores in a humid underground environment.
lussierite.etymology: Honors Canadian mineralogist Aaron J. Lussier (b. 1980), Research Scientist, Canadian Museum of Nature, whose articles advanced our understanding of actinide mineralogy and crystal chemistry, and who is senior author of a comprehensive review of uranyl compounds ’ structures.

luxembourgite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins of finely crystallized dolomite and siderite cutting red schists.
luxembourgite.etymology: For the city of Luxembourg, close to where the studied material was collected.

luzonite.occurrence: In hydrothermal Cu–As–Sb-rich vein and disseminated deposits, formed at low to medium temperatures.
luzonite.etymology: For Luzon Island in the Philippines.

lyonsite.occurrence: In summit crater fumaroles, as a sublimate formed at ≤800 ◦C.
lyonsite.etymology: To honor Dr. John Bartholomew Lyons (1916– ), Professor of Mineralogy, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, USA.

macaulayite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in deeply weathered granite.
macaulayite.etymology: For the Macaulay Institute for Soil Research, Aberdeen, Scotland.

macdonaldite.occurrence: As veinlets, fracture coatings, and disseminated in a sanbornite-quartz-bearing metamorphic rock.
macdonaldite.etymology: For Gordon Andrew MacDonald (1911{1978), American vulcanologist, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, Hawaii, USA.

macedonite.occurrence: As a rare accessory mineral in microcline-quartz syenite pegmatite veins cutting pyroxene amphibole schist (Crni Kamen, Macedonia); as inclusions in hematite and magnetoplumbite in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L ˚ angban, Sweden).
macedonite.etymology: For Macedonia, where the mineral was discovered.

macfallite.occurrence: In abundance, replacing calcite in ¯ssures and in lenses in basalt (Manganese Lake, Michigan, USA); replacing braunite under low-temperature metamorphic cond itions (Faggiona, Italy).
macfallite.etymology: For Russell P. MacFall, American amateur mineralogist.

machatschkiite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in crusts on granite.
machatschkiite.etymology: Honors Felix Karl Ludwig Machatschki (1895–1970), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria.

machiite.occurrence: An ultra-refractory phase in matrix of a carbonaceous chondrite meteorite, likely formed in the solar nebula, either by gas-solid condensation or by crystallization from a Ca-Al-rich melt with solar-like oxygen isotopic composition, under high-temperature (~1400-1500 °C) and lowpressure (~10-4-10-5 bar) conditions in the CAI-forming region near the protosun.
machiite.etymology: Honors Chi Ma (b. 1968), mineralogist at California Institute of Technology, USA, for his contributions to meteorite mineralogy and discovery of 45 new minerals, including 14 refractory phases formed in the solar nebula and 11 high-pressure minerals from shock metamorphism of meteorite parent bodies.

mackayite.occurrence: Of rare occurrence in the oxidized zone of Au–Te deposits, an alteration product of tellurium.
mackayite.etymology: For John William Mackay (1831–1902), Irish–American Comstock Lode mining magnate, in honor of his endowment of the School of Mines, University of Nevada, Reno, Nevada, USA.

mackinawite.occurrence: Formed by hydrothermal activity in mineral deposits, during serpentinization of peridotites, and in the reducing environment of river bottom muds; may be produced by magnetotactic and sulfate-reducing bacteria. Rarely in iron and carbonaceous chondrite meteorites.
mackinawite.etymology: For the Mackinaw mine in Washington, USA.

macphersonite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the zone of oxidation of lead deposits.
macphersonite.etymology: To honor Dr. Harry Gordon Macpherson (1925– ), Keeper of Minerals, Royal Scottish Museum, Edinburgh, Scotland.

macquartite.occurrence: On museum specimens from an oxidized Pb-Zn-Cu orebody.
macquartite.etymology: For the French chemist Louis Charles Henri Macquart (1745{1808), who brought to France the Russian crocoite specimens in which chromium was discovered.

madocite.occurrence: In the marbles of the Precambrian Grenville Limestone, at the margin of an intrusive (Madoc, Canada); in a hydrothermal deposit in dolomitic limestones with other As–Tl minerals (Jas Roux, France).
madocite.etymology: For the locality at Madoc, Canada.

magadiite.occurrence: In silts of upper Pleistocene to recent age, precipitated by evaporation of saline brines (Lake Magadi); in veins cutting playa sediments and in muds associated with alkali salts and brines (Alkali Lake Playa, Oregon); in altered volcanic rocks (Trinity Co., California); in marble xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in miarolitic cavities in a nepheline syenite sill (near Saint-Amable, Canada).
magadiite.etymology: For the Kenyan locality, Lake Magadi.

magbasite.occurrence: In thin veins cutting ferrodolomite- and siderite-carbonatites (Canada).
magbasite.etymology: For MAGnesium and BArium in its chemical composition.

maghagendorfite.occurrence: In a complex zoned granite pegmatite.
maghagendorfite.etymology: As the magnesium analog of hagendorﬁte.

maghemite.occurrence: Formed by weathering or low-temperature oxidation of spinels containing ferrous iron, commonly magnetite or titanian magnetite. A widespread yellow pigment in continental sediments, rocks, and soils.
maghemite.etymology: From MAGnetite and HEMatite, in allusion to the mineral’s magnetism and composition.

maghrebite.occurrence: From weathering Co-arsenides in a hydrothermal Co-Ni-As-(Cu-U-Mo) vein in an arid environment.
maghrebite.etymology: The word maghreb, derived from the Arabic al-maghrib, meaning ‘‘region where the sun sets’’, originally signified the region between the high ranges of the Atlas Mountains and the Mediterranean Sea. Now it refers collectively to Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and Mauritania.

magnanelliite.occurrence: Secondary in an oxidized baryte-pyrite-magnetite-hematite deposit in K-bearing rocks.
magnanelliite.etymology: Honors Stefano Magnanelli (b. 1959), chemist and mineral collector, for contributions to the mineralogy of the hydrothermal veins of the Apuan Alps.

magnesio-ferri-fluoro-hornblende.occurrence: In vugs in a welded tuff.
magnesio-ferri-fluoro-hornblende.etymology: For a calcium amphibole with dominant magnesium and ferric iron in the C site and fluorine dominant in the W site.

magnesio-foitite.occurrence: From an alteration zone in a silicified porphyry developed in completely altered andesitic to dacitic volcanic rocks (Japan); in unconformity-type uranium deposits (Canada).
magnesio-foitite.etymology: The prefix, magnesio, indicates the magnesium analogue of foitite.

magnesio-hornblende.etymology: Indicates a calcium amphibole with composition between 0.5 and 1.5 apfu C(Al+Fe3++2Ti) and between 0 and 0.5 apfu (Na+K+2Ca).

magnesio-lucchesiite.occurrence: Within a lamprophyre dike that crosscuts tourmaline-rich metapelites within the exocontact of a batholith (Canada); in hydrothermal veins embedded in meta-serpentinites within the contact aureole of a monzogranite intrusion (Italy).
magnesio-lucchesiite.etymology: Prefix, magnesio, indicates the dominance of Mg over Fe at the Y site in an analog of lucchesiite.

magnesioarfvedsonite.occurrence: As exsolution lamellae in cummingtonite from metamorphosed iron formation; in felsic pegmatites; from sodium metasomatism (fenitization) around some carbonatites; as authigenic or diagenetic overgrowths on detrital igneous \hornblende."
magnesioarfvedsonite.etymology: For its high magnesium content and similarity to arfvedsonite.

magnesioaubertite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by the reaction of volcanic gases and aluminum-bearing rocks.
magnesioaubertite.etymology: For its content of magnesium greater than copper, and relation to aubertite.

magnesioaxinite.occurrence: [Typically a mineral formed during contact metamorphism and boron metasomatism.]
magnesioaxinite.etymology: For dominant magnesium in the composition, and its membership in the axinite group.

magnesiobermanite.occurrence: In zoned granitic pegmatite. Formed from secondary phosphate minerals, that had been formed by metasomatic alteration of magmatic fluorapatite, by hydrothermal alteration and weathering in an oxidizing, low-temperature, and low-pH environment.
magnesiobermanite.etymology: The prefix identifies the Mg-analogue of bermanite.

magnesiocanutite.occurrence: From the oxidation of native arsenic and other As-bearing primary phases, followed by later alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions .
magnesiocanutite.etymology: As the Mg analogue of canutite with Mg rather than Mn dominant in the M2 site.

magnesiocarpholite.occurrence: In veins and in schist, quartzite, and metabauxite formed during high-pressure, low-temperature metamorphism (Vanoise, France).
magnesiocarpholite.etymology: As the magnesium analog of carpholite.

magnesiochloritoid.occurrence: In metapelites and related rocks within high-grade blueschist rocks; stable under metamorphic conditions of near 500 ±C and 18 kbar.
magnesiochloritoid.etymology: For magnesium in its composition and its relation to chloritoid.

magnesiochromite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in ultramaﬁc rocks, as dunites, serpentinites, kimberlites, lamproites, and komatiites. More rarely as xenocrysts in lamprophyres and mid-ocean basalts. May be detrital.

magnesiocopiapite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral, typically formed by oxidation of pyrite.
magnesiocopiapite.etymology: For its magnesium content and relation to copiapite.

magnesiocoulsonite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in Cr–V-bearing metamorphic rocks.
magnesiocoulsonite.etymology: For its dominant MAGNESIum content and relation to coulsonite.

magnesiocummingtonite.occurrence: In metamorphosed ultrama¯c rocks of the amphibolite facies; as exsolution lamellae in magnesio-arfvedsonite.
magnesiocummingtonite.etymology: For magnesium in its composition and similarity to cummingtonite.

magnesioferrite.occurrence: Most commonly of fumarolic origin; also in high-grade (sanidinite facies) combustion-metamorphosed marls and burning coal heaps; in metamorphosed dolostones. An accessory mineral in some kimberlites, carbonatites, and alkali gabbros. As skeletal inclusions in glassy spherules in sediments attributed to bolide impact debris.
magnesioferrite.etymology: From the composition, with dominant MAGNESium and FERRic iron.

magnesiofluckite.etymology: The prefix indicates the magneium analogue of fluckite.

magnesiohastingsite.occurrence: In alkalic basalts; in andesites, latites, tephrites, and their tu®s; in carbonatites.
magnesiohastingsite.etymology: For magnesium in its composition and relation to hastingsite.

magnesiohatertite.occurrence: A sublimate around an active volcanic fumarole.

magnesiohogbomite-2n2s.occurrence: A primary mineral, or replacing spinel or magnetite, in skarns, gabbros, gneisses, “emery” or other rocks formed during medium- to high-grade metamorphism; rarely detrital.
magnesiohogbomite-2n2s.etymology: For Professor Arvid Gustaf H¨ ogbom (1857–1940), of the University of Uppsala, Uppsala, Sweden.

magnesiohogbomite-2n3s.occurrence: A primary mineral, or replacing spinel or magnetite, in skarns, gabbros, gneisses, “emery” or other rocks formed during medium- to high-grade metamorphism; rarely detrital.
magnesiohogbomite-2n3s.etymology: For Professor Arvid Gustaf H¨ ogbom (1857–1940), of the University of Uppsala, Uppsala, Sweden.

magnesiohogbomite-2n4s.occurrence: A primary mineral, or replacing spinel or magnetite, in skarns, gabbros, gneisses, “emery” or other rocks formed during medium- to high-grade metamorphism; rarely detrital.
magnesiohogbomite-2n4s.etymology: For Professor Arvid Gustaf H¨ ogbom (1857–1940), of the University of Uppsala, Uppsala, Sweden.

magnesiohogbomite-6n 12s.etymology: Identifies a mineral with Ti dominant in the N module (rootname högbomite), Mg dominant in the S module (prefix magnesio-), and 6 and 12 as the total number of N and S modules, respectively (hyphenated suffix 6N12S).

magnesiohogbomite-6n12s.occurrence: A primary mineral, or replacing spinel or magnetite, in skarns, gabbros, gneisses, “emery” or other rocks formed during medium- to high-grade metamorphism; rarely detrital.
magnesiohogbomite-6n12s.etymology: For Professor Arvid Gustaf H¨ ogbom (1857–1940), of the University of Uppsala, Uppsala, Sweden.

magnesiohogbomite-6n6s.occurrence: A primary mineral, or replacing spinel or magnetite, in skarns, gabbros, gneisses, “emery” or other rocks formed during medium- to high-grade metamorphism; rarely detrital.
magnesiohogbomite-6n6s.etymology: For Professor Arvid Gustaf H¨ ogbom (1857–1940), of the University of Uppsala, Uppsala, Sweden.

magnesiohornblende.occurrence: Common in amphibolites, schists, and pegmatitic alkalic gabbro. Also from welded tu®s, granodiorites, granites, and tonalites.
magnesiohornblende.etymology: For its high magnesium content and from the German for horn and to deceive, in allusion to its similarity to valuable minerals in ores.

magnesiohulsite.occurrence: In a magnesium skarn borate deposit at the contact between granite and calcite–dolomite rocks.
magnesiohulsite.etymology: As the magnesium analog of hulsite.

magnesiokatophorite.occurrence: In alkalic igneous rocks, including plutonic ring complexes and dikes, and carbonatites.
magnesiokatophorite.etymology: For magnesium in its composition and its relation to katophorite.

magnesiokoritnigite.occurrence: As a secondary mineral derived from the oxidation of native arsenic and other As-bearing primary phases, followed by later alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions.

magnesioleydetite.occurrence: A secondary phase on asphaltum found in efflorescent crusts on the surfaces of mine walls.

magnesioneptunite.occurrence: In volcanic ejecta of hornfelsed fine-grained sandstone as reaction zones between a skarn carbonate xenolith and host ignimbrite by alteration of ilmenite.
magnesioneptunite.etymology: As the magnesium analog of neptunite.

magnesionigerite-2n1s.occurrence: An accessory mineral in high-temperature tungsten ore.
magnesionigerite-2n1s.etymology: To honor Peng Zhizhong, Chinese mineralogist, Wuhan Geological College, Beijing, China, who determined the crystal structure.

magnesionigerite-6n6s.occurrence: An accessory mineral in high-temperature tungsten ore.
magnesionigerite-6n6s.etymology: To honor Peng Zhizhong, Chinese mineralogist, Wuhan Geological College, Beijing, China, who determined the crystal structure.

magnesiopascoite.occurrence: Product of groundwater leaching and oxidation of vanadium oxides in a post-mining environment.
magnesiopascoite.etymology: As the magnesium analog of pascolite.

magnesioriebeckite.occurrence: In granulites, ironstones, ferruginous metacherts, greenschist facies schists, and carbonatites.
magnesioriebeckite.etymology: For its high magnesium content and similarity to riebeckite.

magnesiorowlandite-y.occurrence: In a block of granitic pegmatite collected from a talus slope.
magnesiorowlandite-y.etymology: As the magnesium analog of rowlandite-(Y).

magnesiosadanagaite.occurrence: In a granitic contact aureole composed of dolomitic marble (Japan).
magnesiosadanagaite.etymology: Signifies an amphibole in the compositional range of sadanagaite with Mg dominant in the C structural site.

magnesiostaurolite.occurrence: From an ultra-high-pressure, coesite-bearing metamorphic terrane.
magnesiostaurolite.etymology: The prefix, magnesio, indicates the magnesium analog of staurolite.

magnesiotaaffeite-2n2s.occurrence: In a nodule, perhaps formerly a corundum crystal, in high-grade metapyroxenite, associated with metaperidotites and granulites (Musgrave Ranges, Australia); in pegmatite cutting granulite (Enderby Land, Antarctica).
magnesiotaaffeite-2n2s.etymology: For the Musgrave Ranges, South Australia, from where it was ﬁrst recognized.

magnesiotaaffeite-6n3s.occurrence: In a nodule, perhaps formerly a corundum crystal, in high-grade metapyroxenite, associated with metaperidotites and granulites (Musgrave Ranges, Australia); in pegmatite cutting granulite (Enderby Land, Antarctica).
magnesiotaaffeite-6n3s.etymology: For the Musgrave Ranges, South Australia, from where it was ﬁrst recognized.

magnesiotaramite.occurrence: An unusual product of the retrograde metamorphism of eclogitic rocks.
magnesiotaramite.etymology: For magnesium in its composition and similarity to taramite.

magnesiovesuvianite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in cavities in a garnet-bearing rodingite.
magnesiovesuvianite.etymology: The prefix indicates a member of the vesuvianite group with Mg2+ dominant in the Y1 site.

magnesiovoltaite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal, polymetallic, sulfide vein deposit hosted by volcanic rocks in an arid region.
magnesiovoltaite.etymology: As an analog of voltaite and zincovoltaite with Mg dominant at the M1 structural position.

magnesite.occurrence: A primary mineral in igneous or sedimentary rocks; formed by metamorphism or alteration of serpentine and peridotite; uncommon in marine evaporites and hydrothermal veins; rare in carbonatites.

magnesiumchlorophoenicite.occurrence: A very rare mineral, in open veinlets cutting a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
magnesiumchlorophoenicite.etymology: For its magnesium content and similarity to chlorophoenicite.

magnesiumzippeite.occurrence: A rare post-mine mineral on the walls of mine tunnels.
magnesiumzippeite.etymology: For its content of magnesium and relation to zippeite.

magnetite.occurrence: A common accessory mineral in igneous and metamorphic rocks, in which magmatic segregation or contact metamorphism may produce economic deposits. Extensive deposits in sedimentary banded iron formations; a biogenic product; important detrital deposits.
magnetite.etymology: An ancient term, possibly an allusion to the locality, Magnesia, Greece.

magnetoplumbite.occurrence: In skarns associated with metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebodies (Sweden).
magnetoplumbite.etymology: For being a MAGNETic oxide of iron, manganese, and lead, plumbum.

magnocolumbite.occurrence: In a pegmatite in partially assimilated dolomitic marbles (Kukhi-Lal deposit, Tajikistan).
magnocolumbite.etymology: For dominant MAGNesium in the composition, and its relation to ferrocolumbite.

magnolite.occurrence: A late alteration product of coloradoite, formed at low temperature and oxygen fugacity, in the oxidized zone of complex polymetallic hydrothermal mineral deposits.
magnolite.etymology: For the Magnolia district, Colorado, USA, in which the species was ﬁrst noted.

magnussonite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L ˚ angban, Sweden); very rare in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Sterling Hill, New Jersey, USA).
magnussonite.etymology: For Nils Harald Magnusson (1890–1976), formerly Director, Geological Survey of Sweden, for his contributions to knowledge of the L ˚ angban mine.

mahlmoodite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in vugs in alkaline igneous rock (Wilson Springs mine, Arkansas, USA); in a mineralized ﬁssure vein (Kerriack Cove, Cornwall, England).
mahlmoodite.etymology: Honors Bertha K. Mahlmood, Analytical Assistant, U.S. Geological Survey.

mahnertite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of an arsenic-rich copper deposit (Cap Garonne mine, France).
mahnertite.etymology: To honor Dr. Volker Mahnert (b. 1943), Director, Natural History Museum, Geneva, Switzerland.

maikainite.occurrence: In a gold-bearing, base-metal, massive-sulfide deposit (Maikain); in a germaniumbearing, base-metal, massive-sulfide deposit (Tsumeb).
maikainite.etymology: For the locality, the Maikain deposit, that produced the first specimens studied.

majakite.occurrence: As intergrowths with other platinum-group minerals in chalcopyrite and talnakhite ores (Majak mine, Russia); in sulﬁde mineralization in a strongly metamorphosed layered intrusive (Konttij¨ arvi intrusion, Finland).

majindeite.etymology: Honors mineralogist Ma Jinde (1939-1991), University of Geosciences, Wuhan, China.

majorite.occurrence: Formed from low-calcium, high-aluminum pyroxene, olivine, and shock-induced glass, by high-pressure impact metamorphism in bolides.
majorite.etymology: For Alan Major, who assisted A.E. Ringwood in the high-pressure synthesis of garnet from pyroxene.

majzlanite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
majzlanite.etymology: Honors Professor Dr. Juraj Majzlan (b. 1973), Institute of Geosciences, Friedrich-Schiller- University, Jena, Germany. Among his achievements and contributions to mineralogy and crystallography, in general, are those to the mineralogy of sulfates.

makatite.occurrence: In cores from drill holes in a lacustrine evaporite series (Lake Magadi, Kenya); leached from natrosilite in an alkalic pegmatite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
makatite.etymology: From the Masai word emakut, meaning soda, in allusion to the high sodium content of the mineral.

makinenite.occurrence: In sills of albite diabase in schist, associated with low-grade uranium mineralization (Kuusamo, Finland).
makinenite.etymology: Honors Eero M¨ akinen (1886–1953), Finnish geologist, and former President of the Outokumpu Company.

makovickyite.occurrence: Among other bismuth-bearing sulfosalts in a dolomite skarn (B˘ ai¸ ta, Romania); in a hydrothermal tungsten deposit in amphibolites and felsic gneisses, in discordant quartz veins (Felbertal mine, Austria).
makovickyite.etymology: To honor Professor Emil Makovicky (1941– ), Slovak–Danish mineralogist, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.

malachite.occurrence: A common secondary mineral formed in the oxidation zone of copper deposits; locally may be an ore of copper.
malachite.etymology: From the Greek for mallow, in allusion to its green color.

malanite.occurrence: In peridotite-type platinum ores with Cu–Ni sulﬁdes (Malan Valley, China).
malanite.etymology: Apparently for the Malan Valley, China.

malayaite.occurrence: In tin-rich contact metamorphic skarn deposits, probably a hydrothermal alteration product of cassiterite or other tin-bearing minerals.
malayaite.etymology: For the localities in Malaya, Malaysia.

maldonite.occurrence: Formed below 373 ◦C, under hydrothermal conditions in gold-quartz veins and stockworks, and calc-silicate skarns.
maldonite.etymology: For the locality at Maldon, Australia.

maleevite.occurrence: In a slightly rounded block of pegmatite in syenite within a boulder in the moraine of the Dara-i-Pioz glacier, Alai mountain range, Tien Shan, northern Tajikistan. The Dara-i-Pioz massif at the head of the glacier contains B-rich alkaline rocks and pegmatites.
maleevite.etymology: Honors Bulgarian mineralogist Mikhael Naidenovich Maleev (b. 1940).

maletoyvayamite.occurrence: In heavy-mineral concentrate from a hydrothermal, high-sulfidation epithermal deposit.
maletoyvayamite.etymology: For the type locality, the Maletoyvayam deposit in the Kamchatka peninsula, Russia.

malinkoite.occurrence: In a cavity in the ussingite-rich core of a hyperagpaitic pegmatite.
malinkoite.etymology: Honors Russian specialist in boron minerals, Svetlana V. Malinko (b. 1927).

malladrite.etymology: Honors Professor Alessandro Malladra (1868–1945), Italian vulcanologist, Director, Vesuvius Observatory, Italy.

mallardite.occurrence: A rare mineral formed by oxidation of Fe–Mn sulﬁdes and carbonates under conditions of saturated relative humidity; typically post-mine, when it may be seasonal.
mallardite.etymology: To honor Fran¸ cois Ernest Mallard (1833–1894), French crystallographer, National School of Mines, Paris, France.

mallestigite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal polymetallic base-metal deposit containing galena and tetrahedrite (Austria); in weathered metallic slag (Hartz Mountains, Germany).
mallestigite.etymology: For the town near the dumps from where the mineral was first noted.

malyshevite.occurrence: In the contact aureole of an impact melt sheet (Sudbury); in a U-V-precious metals deposit in albite-mica-carbonate metasomites (Srednyaya Padma).
malyshevite.etymology: Honors Ilya Ilyich Malyshev (1904-1973), discoverer of the Samotkansky titanium ore deposit in the Urals, and his son, Professor V.I. Malyshev (1927-2002).

mambertiite.etymology: Honors Italian mineral collector Marzio Mamberti (b. 1959) for his contributions to Sardinian mineralogical science.

mammothite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal polymetallic base-metal deposit (Tiger, Arizona, USA); in metallic slag, formed by reaction with ocean water (Laurium, Greece).
mammothite.etymology: For the Mammoth vein at Tiger, Arizona, from where the mineral was first noted, and the town of Mammoth, Arizona, USA, named for the mine.

manaevite-ce.occurrence: In skarn-like metasomite in a phlogopite deposit in an alkaline-ultramafic massif.
manaevite-ce.etymology: Honors Nikolay Mikhailovich Manaev (1936-2012), former Chief Geologist, Kovdorslyuda Mining and Dressing Company, for his contribution to the geology, mineralogy, and exploitation of the Kovdor phlogopite deposit, Kola Peninsula, Russia. A suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

manaksite.occurrence: In ultra-agpaitic pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
manaksite.etymology: For MAnganese; sodium, NAtrium; potassium, Kalium; and SIlicon in its composition.

manandonite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities developed in corroded di®erentia ted quartz-microclinetourmaline-bearing pegmatites.
manandonite.etymology: For the Manandona River, nearby the type locality in Madagascar.

manasseite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in ultramaﬁc rocks.
manasseite.etymology: Honors Ernesto Manasse (1875–1922), Italian chemist and mineralogist, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Florence, Florence, Italy, for work on pyroaurite-related minerals.

mandarinoite.occurrence: Probably formed by the simultaneous oxidation of penroseite and pyrite in a selenium-rich ore deposit (Pacajake mine, Bolivia).
mandarinoite.etymology: To honor Dr. Joseph Anthony Mandarino (1929– ), American–Canadian mineralogist, Emeritus Curator of Mineralogy, Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto, Canada.

maneckiite.occurrence: In the outer zone of phosphate nodules. A product of Na- and Ca-metasomatism in a weakly fractionated anatectic lithium-cesium-tantalum pegmatite induced by a hydrothermal fluid in the presence of Al3+ from a neighboring aluminosilicate melt.
maneckiite.etymology: Honors Andrzej Manecki (b. 1933), eminent Polish mineralogist and emeritus Professor, Department of Mineralogy, Petrography, and Geochemistry, Faculty of Geology, Geophysics and Environmental Protection, AGH University of Science and Technology , Cracow, Poland.

manganarsite.occurrence: Coating armangite, and ﬁlling fractures, in a museum specimen from a metamorphosed Fe–Mn deposit.
manganarsite.etymology: For MANGANese and ARSenic in the composition.

manganaxinite.occurrence: Typically a mineral formed by contact metamorphism and boron metasomatism; from a pegmatite vein cutting metamorphosed iron formation at a contact with gabbro (Minnesota, USA).
manganaxinite.etymology: For dominant manganese in a mineral of the axinite group, named from the Greek for axe after their sharp crystal forms.

manganbabingtonite.occurrence: In thin stringers in amphibolized garnet-pyroxene-magnetite skarn associated with an iron deposit (Rudnyi Kaskad deposit, Russia); replacing hedenbergite-johannsenite skarn (Iron Cap mine, Arizona, USA).
manganbabingtonite.etymology: For the manganese content and relation to babingtonite.

manganbelyankinite.etymology: For its MANGANese content, and relation to belyankinite.

manganberzeliite.occurrence: In metamorphosed manganiferous skarns (Sweden); in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
manganberzeliite.etymology: For the manganese dominant analogue of berzeliite.

manganesehornesite.occurrence: In ﬁssure veins in skarn in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L˚ angban, Sweden).
manganesehornesite.etymology: For the dominant manganese content and its relation to h¨ ornesite.

manganeseshadlunite.occurrence: In Cu–Ni sulﬁde ores (Noril’sk region, Russia).
manganeseshadlunite.etymology: For its manganese content and relation to shadlunite.

manganflurlite.occurrence: A late-stage, relatively low-temperature, secondary hydrothermal mineral in a zoned granitic pegmatite.
manganflurlite.etymology: The prefix, mangan, indicates the Mn-analog of flurlite.

mangangordonite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
mangangordonite.etymology: As the manganese analog of gordonite.

manganhumite.occurrence: A late-stage skarn mineral formed in recrystallized limestone banded between layers of manganese ore minerals (Brattfors mine, Sweden); in a manganese deposit metamorphosed to the amphibolite facies (Bald Knob, North Carolina, USA).
manganhumite.etymology: For manganese in the composition and relation to humite.

mangani-dellaventuraite.occurrence: In a regionally metamorphosed, submarine, volcanogenic Fe-Mn oxide deposit in silicate-impregnated, calcitic carbonate rock.
mangani-dellaventuraite.etymology: Prefix identifies a pargasite analog with Mn3+ dominant among the trivalent C cations.

mangani-obertiite.occurrence: In a regionally metamorphosed, submarine, volcanogenic Fe-Mn oxide deposit in silicate-impregnated, calcitic carbonate rock.
mangani-obertiite.etymology: Prefix identifies a pargasite analog with Mn3+ dominant among the trivalent C cations.

mangani-pargasite.occurrence: In a regionally metamorphosed, submarine, volcanogenic Fe-Mn oxide deposit in silicate-impregnated, calcitic carbonate rock.
mangani-pargasite.etymology: Prefix identifies a pargasite analog with Mn3+ dominant among the trivalent C cations.

manganiakasakaite-la.occurrence: In a manganese deposit in metasedimentary rocks.
manganiakasakaite-la.etymology: A prefix identifies the dominant cation at the M(1) site (other than Al), and a suffix for the dominant REE at the A(2) site in a member of the group with A(1) = Ca and M(3) = Mn2+ which is “akasakaite” (honoring Masahide Akasaka, professor of mineralogy at the Shimane University)

manganiandrosite-ce.occurrence: In metamorphosed (eclogite facies) lenses near Mn deposits associated with ophiolite.
manganiandrosite-ce.etymology: The Ce analogue of manganiandrosite-(La). An epidote-group mineral in which Mn2+ is dominant in A1, REE are dominant in A2, Mn3+ in M1, Al in M2, and in which Mn2+ is the dominant charge-compensating (i.e. divalent) cation in M3.

manganiandrosite-la.occurrence: In metamorphosed (eclogite facies) lenses near Mn deposits associated with ophiolite.
manganiandrosite-la.etymology: The Ce analogue of manganiandrosite-(La). An epidote-group mineral in which Mn2+ is dominant in A1, REE are dominant in A2, Mn3+ in M1, Al in M2, and in which Mn2+ is the dominant charge-compensating (i.e. divalent) cation in M3.

manganiceladonite.occurrence: Associated with manganesiferous deposits in metacherts of an ophiolitic sequence.
manganiceladonite.etymology: As the Mn3+ analogue of celadonite.

manganilvaite.occurrence: From the retrograde, hydrothermal alteration of manganiferous minerals in Pb-Zn-(Mn) contact metamorphic rocks (skarns).

manganite.occurrence: Formed in low-temperature hydrothermal or hot-spring manganese deposits; replacing other manganese minerals in sedimentary deposits; a component in some clay deposits and laterites.

manganlotharmeyerite.occurrence: In discordant veinlets formed by late-stage remobilization of arsenic during retrograde metamorphism of a carbonate-hosted, syngenetic exhalative massive braunite deposit.
manganlotharmeyerite.etymology: The prefix, mangano, alludes to the Mn3+ dominance within the lotharmeyerite subgroup of the tsumcorite group.

manganneptunite.occurrence: A late segregation mineral found in almost all rock types, including most of the pegmatites, in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
assoc_parsed: in miarolitic cavities in a nepheline syenite sill
manganneptunite.etymology: For the preponderance of manganese in this chemical variant of the neptunite structure.

manganoarrojadite-kna.etymology: Arrojadite indicates a member of the group with Fe2+ dominant at the M site; two suffixes indicate the dominant cation of the dominant valence state at the A and B sites. The prefix, mangano, indicates Mn2+ dominant at the C site. Honors Miguel Arrojado Ribeiro Lisbôa (1872- 1932), Brazilian geologist.

manganochromite.occurrence: From an extension gash vein in a metamorphosed hydrothermal pyrite deposit (Nairne deposit, South Australia); in a metamorphosed iron sulﬁde deposit associated with submarine felsic volcanism (S¨ atra mine, Sweden); in sulﬁde nodules in an iron meteorite (Burkhala meteorite).
manganochromite.etymology: For MANGANese in its composition, and relation to magnesiochromite.

manganocolumbite.occurrence: As an accessory and primary constituent of granite pegmatites; detrital in placers.
manganocolumbite.etymology: For its dominant MANGANese content and its relation to ferroCOLUMBITE.

manganoeudialyte.occurrence: An interstitial phase in nepheline syenite (khibinite).
manganoeudialyte.etymology: As a member of the eudialyte group with dominant manganese in the M2 structural sites and silicon dominant in M3 and M4 sites.

manganogrunerite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in metamorphosed iron-poor manganiferous rocks.
manganogrunerite.etymology: For the original locality, Dannemora, Sweden.

manganokaskasite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in fenites formed by a peralkaline fluid, as a source of Nb, reacting with a xenolith of alumina-rich metamorphic rocks (metapelites) in agpaitic nepheline syenite.
manganokaskasite.etymology: As the manganese analog of kaskaite.

manganokhomyakovite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in nepheline syenite in an alkaline intrusive complex.
manganokhomyakovite.etymology: Honors Dr. Alexander Petrovich Khomyakov (b. 1933), of the Institute of Mineralogy, Geochemistry and Crystal Chemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia, for his contributions to the mineralogy and geochemistry of alkaline rocks, in particular those of agpaitic character. The prefix, mangano, indicates dominant Mn in the M(2) site.

manganokukisvumite.occurrence: A late mineral formed by hydrothermal dissolution of titanium-bearing minerals in an albite-rich syenite breccia in an intrusive alkaline complex.
manganokukisvumite.etymology: As the manganese-dominant analogue of kukisvumite.

manganolangbeinite.occurrence: In a cavern in lava, in thenardite and halite stalactites, formed by fumarolic action.
manganolangbeinite.etymology: As a manganese compound analogous to langbeinite.

manganonaujakasite.occurrence: In lovozerite-lomonosovite nepheline syenite in an alkaline massif.
manganonaujakasite.etymology: The prefix, mangano, indicates the manganese analog of naujakasite.

manganonordite-ce.occurrence: In sodalite syenites and in ussingite veins in an alkaline massif.
manganonordite-ce.etymology: Prefix, mangano, indicates the Mn2+-dominant analog of nordite-Ce.

manganoquadratite.occurrence: In a complex vein-type polymetallic hydrothermal deposit.
manganoquadratite.etymology: For the essential manganese content and the close analogy of the formula and unit-cell dimensions with quadratite.

manganosegelerite.etymology: As the manganese analog of segelerite.

manganosite.occurrence: An alteration product of rhodochrosite or other manganese minerals, formed during oxygen-deﬁcient metamorphism of manganese-bearing deposits; in marine manganese nodules.

manganostibite.occurrence: In late-stage hydrothermal veins in manganese deposits in limestone.
manganostibite.etymology: For MANGANese and antimony, STIBium, in the composition.

manganotapiolite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in a lithium-rich granite pegmatite dike.
manganotapiolite.etymology: For its dominant MANGANese content and relation to ferroTAPIOLITE.

manganotychite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral formed in pegmatite veins in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif (Mt. Alluaiv, Kola Peninsula, Russia).
manganotychite.etymology: As the manganese analog of tychite.

manganvesuvianite.occurrence: In calc-silicate lenses formed by hydrothermal alteration of primary sedimentary and low-grade metamorphic manganese ores.
manganvesuvianite.etymology: Prefix, mangan, indicates a vesuvianite group mineral with the five-coordinated (Y′) position occupied by Mn3+.

mangazeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral along the margins of quartz-arsenopyrite veins in the weathering zone of an intensively sericitized and pyritized granodiorite.
mangazeite.etymology: For Mangazeya Creek, eastern Yakutsk (Sakha Republic), Russia, near the first described locality.

manitobaite.occurrence: A primary phase in phosphate pods in a zoned granitic pegmatite.
assoc_parsed: interior-wall zone of the pegmatite: fluorapatite
manitobaite.etymology: For the province of Manitoba (Canada) in which the mineral was discovered.

manjiroite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of metamorphosed bedded manganese deposits.
manjiroite.etymology: Honors Dr. Manjiro Watanabe (1891-?), Emeritus Professor of Mineralogy, Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan.

mannardite.occurrence: In late-stage quartz-carbonate veins cutting shale and siltstone (Rough claims, Canada); in an orebody in faulted metasediments and iron formation (Bathurst, Canada); in a silver-bearing polymetallic deposit (Kantsi, China); in kimberlite (Star mine, South Africa).
mannardite.etymology: Honors Dr. George William Mannard (1932–1982), formerly President of Kidd Creek Mines, Ltd., Toronto, Canada, for his interest in the mineral deposits of British Columbia.

mansfieldite.occurrence: A hydrothermal product in altered and mineralized andesitic pyroclastic rocks (Hobart Butte, Oregon, USA).
mansfieldite.etymology: Honors Dr. George Rogers Mansﬁeld (1875–1947), U.S. Geological Survey.

mantienneite.occurrence: Replacing minerals in and forming the matrix of sandy layers in lacustrine shale.
mantienneite.etymology: Honors Dr. Joseph Mantienne (1929– ), Bureau de Recherches G´ eologiques et Mini` eres, Orl` eans, France.

maohokite.occurrence: Formed from subsolidus decomposition of Fe-Mg carbonate via a self-oxidationreduction reaction at impact pressure and temperature of 25-45 GPa and 800-900 °C. In meteorite impact breccia composed of fragments of moderately shocked gneiss, amphibolite, and marble in fine-grained matrix.
assoc_parsed: shocked ankerite decomposed into a mixture of magnesioferrite
maohokite.etymology: Honors Hokwang Mao (b. 1941) Geophysical Laboratory, Carnegie Institution of Washington, USA, for his contributions to high pressure research.

maoniupingite-ce.occurrence: In fractures in lamprophyre veins and along the contact between lamprophyre and a later quartz-alkali feldspar syenite dike with REE mineralization.
maoniupingite-ce.etymology: For the occurrence near the Maoniuping REE deposit, China.

mapimite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of an arsenic-rich hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
mapimite.etymology: For the Mapim´ ı mining district in Mexico that produced the ﬁrst specimens.

mapiquiroite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins cutting schist and dolostone.
mapiquiroite.etymology: An acronym from the surnames of the discoverers of the first specimens, Riccardo MAzzanti (b. 1953), Luigi PIerotti (b. 1953), Ugo QUIlici (b. 1946), and Moreno ROmani (b. 1949).

marathonite.occurrence: In heavy mineral separates from olivine gabbro.
assoc_parsed: an fe-rich chlorite-group mineral. distribution from the w horizon
marathonite.etymology: For Marathon, Ontario, Canada, after which the Marathon Cu-PGE deposit (Coldwell complex) is named.

marcasite.occurrence: Typically formed under low-temperature highly acidic conditions, both in sedimentary environments (shales, limestones, and low rank coals) and in hydrothermal veins formed by ascending solutions.
marcasite.etymology: A word of Arabic or Moorish origin, early applied to pyrite and other substances.

marcobaldiite.occurrence: In quartz extension veins in a baryte+pyrite±(Pb-Zn-Ag) ore deposit within a metavolcanic-metasedimentary rock sequence, that was metamorphosed to greenschist facies.
marcobaldiite.etymology: Honors mineral collector Marco Baldi (b. 1944), for his contribution to the knowledge of the mineralogy of the pyrite±baryte±iron oxide ore deposits in the southern Apuan Alps.

marecottite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of selenian digenite in the oxidation zone of a uranium-bearing Cu–Co hydrothermal ore deposit.
marecottite.etymology: To honor Aim´ e Marthoz (1894–1962), former Director of the Union Mini` ere de Haut-Katanga, Congo.

margaritasite.occurrence: As pore ﬁllings and phenocryst casts in felsic volcanic tuﬀs, which have been altered by high-temperature hydrothermal ﬂuids.
margaritasite.etymology: For the Margaritas deposit, Mexico, that produced the ﬁrst specimens.

margarite.occurrence: From low- to medium-grade metamorphic rocks, as in emery deposits, chlorite and mica schists, and glaucophane- bearing rocks.
margarite.etymology: From the Greek for pearl, for its pearly luster on cleavage.

margarosanite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
margarosanite.etymology: From the Greek for pearl and tablet, in reference to its luster and lamellar habit.

marialite.occurrence: Typically in regionally metamorphosed rocks, especially marbles, calcareous gneisses, granulites, and greenschists. Also in skarns, some pegmatites, pneumatolytically or hydrothermally altered ma¯c igneous rocks, and ejected volcanic blocks.
marialite.etymology: For Maria Rosa vom Rath, wife of Gerhard vom Rath, German mineralogist, who named the species.

marianoite.occurrence: A primary mineral in phlogopite-calcite silicocarbonatite emplaced in ijolite.
marianoite.etymology: Honors Anthony Nicola Mariano (b. 1930) for contributions to the study of alkaline rocks and carbonatites.

maricite.occurrence: In phosphatic nodules in sideritic ironstones.
maricite.etymology: Honors Dr. Luka Mari´ c (1899–?), Professor of Mineralogy and Petrology, University of Zagreb, Croatia.

maricopaite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal Pb-Cu ore vein, coating and ¯lling fractures in quartz.
maricopaite.etymology: For Maricopa Co., Arizona, USA, where it was discovered.

mariinskite.occurrence: Replacing low-Al chromite of chromitite lens in serpentinite, probably of metasomatic origin.
mariinskite.etymology: For the locality from which the first specimens were collected.

marinaite.occurrence: A sublimate around an active volcanic fumarole.

marinellite.occurrence: In a highly-reacted xenolith of evaporitic rock as volcanic ejecta.
marinellite.etymology: Honors Giorgio Marinelli (1922-1993), Earth Science Department, University of Pisa, Italy.

markascherite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by weathering of a mineralized (molybdenite, bornite, chalcocite, chalcopyrite) breccia pipe.
markascherite.etymology: Honors Mark Goldberg Ascher, a mineral collector and engineer in Tucson, Arizona, USA, who found the first specimen.

markcooperite.occurrence: A secondary phase on fracture surfaces and in small vugs in quartz veins. Formed from the partial oxidation of primary sulfides (e.g., galena) and tellurides (e.g., hessite) during or following brecciation of the quartz veins.
markcooperite.etymology: Honors Mark A. Cooper (b. 1963), University of Manitoba, for his contributions to mineralogy. He has been involved in the description of many new minerals (~35), and the determination of the crystal structures of many minerals containing uranium and tellurium.

markeyite.occurrence: As efflorescent crusts on the surfaces of mine walls in a Colorado Plateau-type, roll front uranium deposit.
markeyite.etymology: For the locality, the Markey mine.

markhininite.occurrence: Product of fumarolic activity around a volcanic vent.
markhininite.etymology: Honors Professor Evgeniy Konstantinovich Markhinin (b. 1926), Institute of Volcanology, Russian Academy of Sciences, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskiy, Russia.

marokite.etymology: For the ﬁrst occurrence in Morocco, Maroc in French.

marrite.etymology: In honor of Dr. John Edward Marr (1857–1933), Professor of Geology, Cambridge University, Cambridge, England.

marrucciite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal assemblage, within small calcite veinlets crosscutting dolomitic lenses interstratified in a Ba-Fe deposit (Buca Della Vena).
marrucciite.etymology: Honors mineral collector Angelo Marrucci (1956-2003), for his contributions to the mineralogy of Tuscany.

marshite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized zone of a metamorphosed Pb–Zn–Ag deposit (Broken Hill, Australia); in the oxidized zone of a porphyry copper deposit (Chuquicamata, Chile); in tills over a copper anomaly, introduced by brackish seawater (L¨ oyt¨ osuo, Finland).
marshite.etymology: For Charles W. Marsh, who ﬁrst noted the mineral at Broken Hill, Australia.

marsturite.occurrence: Implanted on manganaxinite and epitaxially overgrown on rhodonite in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA).
marsturite.etymology: For MARion STUart, of Bellevue, Idaho, USA, benefactress of fossil and mineral collections in the USA.

marthozite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of selenian digenite in the oxidation zone of a uranium-bearing Cu-Co hydrothermal ore deposit.
marthozite.etymology: To honor Airne Marthoz (1894-1962), former Director of the Union Miniere de Haut-Katanga, Congo.

martinandresite.occurrence: In quartz veins cutting zoisite-, celsian-, and armenite-bearing gneiss.
martinandresite.etymology: Honors Martin Andres (b. 1965), the Swiss mineral collector and amateur mineralogist, who discovered the armenite vein locality of Wasenalp.

martyite.occurrence: Product of groundwater leaching and oxidation of vanadium oxides in a post-mining environment.
martyite.etymology: Honors Joe Marty (b. 1945) for his contributions to mineralogy.

marumoite.occurrence: In a high-sulfidation, epithermal, Cu-Pb-Zn disseminated , massive sulfide deposit (Japan).
marumoite.etymology: Honors Fumiyuki Marumo (b. 1931), professor of mineralogy and crystallography at Nihon University, Tokyo, Japan, a specialist on the structures of sulfosalt minerals.

maruyamaite.etymology: Honors Professor Shigenori Maruyama (b. 1949), Earth-Life Science Institute, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Japan, for his work on regional tectonics.

mascagnite.occurrence: A sublimation product in fumaroles and solfataras; formed by burning coal seams.
mascagnite.etymology: Honoring Paolo Mascagni (1755–1815), Professor of Anatomy, University of Siena, Siena, Italy, who provided the original description.

maslovite.occurrence: In galena-rich portions of massive cubanite-chalcopyrite and mooihoekite ores.
maslovite.etymology: Honors Georgii Dmitrievich Maslov (1915–1968), geologist, one of the discoverers of the Talnakh deposits.

massicot.occurrence: As an oxidation product of galena, bournonite, boulangerite, and other lead-bearing minerals.
massicot.etymology: From early Arabic, through the Spanish mazacote and the French for oxide of lead.

masutomilite.occurrence: In a druse in a granite pegmatite, as the core of a crystal zoned with manganoan zinnwaldite (Tanakamiyama, Japan); as reaction rims coating spessartine-rich garnets in manganese-rich parts of a lithium pegmatite (Ctidru·zice, Czech Republic).
masutomilite.etymology: For Dr. Kazunosuke Masutomi, Japanese amateur mineralogist.

masuyite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in the oxidized zone of uranium-bearing deposits.
masuyite.etymology: For Gustave Masuy (1905–1945), Belgian geologist, who studied Congolese (Zairian) minerals.

mathesiusite.occurrence: A rare post-mining, secondary mineral in the underground workings in a polymetallic hydrothermal vein type deposit.
mathesiusite.etymology: Honors Johannes Mathesius (1504-1565), Lutheran priest and theologian. Mathesius lived and served in Jáchymov, first as a teacher at the Latin lyceum, then as a pastor. His publications on mining include “Sarepta oder Bergpostil”.

mathewrogersite.occurrence: In cavities of corroded Pb-Zn ores in the lower oxidation zone of a polymetallic mineral deposit.
mathewrogersite.etymology: To honor Mathew Rogers, the ¯rst European prospector at Tsumeb, Namibia.

mathiasite.occurrence: A primary mantle-derived phase found in heavy-mineral concentrates from metasomatized kimberlite (South Africa).
mathiasite.etymology: Honors Professor Frances Celia Morna Mathias (1913– ), University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa, for her contributions to studies of mantle-derived rocks.

matildite.occurrence: Formed in hydrothermal deposits at medium to high temperatures and in pegmatites.
matildite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Matilda mine, Peru.

matioliite.occurrence: A secondary hydrothermal mineral in granite pegmatite.
matioliite.etymology: Honors Paulo Anselmo Matioli (b. 1975), mineral collector, founder, and curator of the Museu de Ciências Naturais Jobas “José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva”, Santos, SP, Brazil. Matioli collected the samples used to describe the new Brazilian minerals coutinhoite and matioliite.

matlockite.occurrence: In the oxide zone of some lead-bearing mineral deposits.
matlockite.etymology: For the ﬁrst occurrence near Matlock, England.

matraite.etymology: For the Matra Mountains locality in Hungary.

matsubaraite.occurrence: From a boulder of Ti-bearing jadeitite, the product of late stage high-P/T metamorphism.
matsubaraite.etymology: Honors Dr. Satoshi Matsubara, Department of Geology, National Science Museum, Tokyo, Japan, in recognition of his work on strontium-dominant minerals from Japan.

mattagamite.occurrence: In a small telluride zone in a massive zinc-rich stratiform deposit in Archaen volcanics (Mattagami Lake mine, Canada).
