mattagamite.etymology: For its occurrence at Mattagami Lake, Canada.

matteuccite.occurrence: In stalactites formed in a volcanic crater.
matteuccite.etymology: Honors Vittorio Matteucci (1862–1909), Director of the Vesuvius Laboratory, Vesuvius, Italy.

mattheddleite.occurrence: Lining cavities in quartz which contain other oxidized lead minerals.
mattheddleite.etymology: For Matthew Forster Heddle (1828{1897), Scottish mineralogist.

matulaite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of phosphatic iron deposits.
matulaite.etymology: Honors Margaret Mary Matula (b. 1925), Allentown, Pennsylvania, USA, who supplied some of the first specimens.

matyhite.occurrence: In an angrite meteorite as well-defined domains associated with Fe sulfide near the contact between fayalite-kirschsteinite overgrowth/symplectite and hedenbergite.
matyhite.etymology: Honors Professor Ting-Ying Hsüeh Ma (1899-1979), a palaeontologist who pioneered research into relations between coral growth rate, sea-water temperature, paleoclimate, and paleogeography. He was an early advocate of continental drift. Joint Director of the Department of Geology and the Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University (1946-1950).

maucherite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other nickel arsenides and sulﬁdes.
maucherite.etymology: To honor Wilhelm Maucher (1879–1930), metallugical chemist and mineral dealer of Munich, Germany.

mauriziodiniite.occurrence: A secondary alteration phase formed by the oxidation of native arsenic and other As-bearing primary phases, followed by later alteration by saline fluids derived from evaporating meteoric water under hyperarid conditions. The frequent dense coastal camanchaca fogs probably also played a role in the alteration of the veins and the formation of the secondary minerals.
mauriziodiniite.etymology: Honors Maurizio Dini of La Serena, Chile (b. 1968), an Italian amateur mineralogist who has lived in Chile since 1998 and is a Professor of Sociology at both Universidad Pedro de Valdivia and Universidad Central de Chile. He recognized the studied material as a potentially new mineral and provided the holotype specimen.

mawbyite.occurrence: In an arsenic-rich reaction halo in fractures and cavities in a spessartine-quartz rock in the oxidization zone of a metamorphosed stratiform Pb–Zn orebody (Broken Hill, Australia); in the oxidization zone of Ag–Pb–Cu–Bi mineralization in ﬂuorite–barite–quartz veins (Moldava, Czech Republic).
mawbyite.etymology: To honor Sir Maurice Alan Edgar Mawby (1904–1977), Chairman of CRA, Ltd., for his contribution to the Australian mining industry and preservation of Broken Hill minerals.

mawsonite.occurrence: In massive to disseminated hydrothermal copper ores within highly altered volcanic rocks; in skarns; disseminated in altered granites; rare in copper porphyry deposits.
mawsonite.etymology: Honoring Sir Douglas Mawson (1882–1958), noted English-Australian geologist and Antarctic explorer.

maxwellite.occurrence: Rarely formed in miarolitic cavities in rhyolite adjacent to high-temperature veins in hydrothermal tin deposits.
maxwellite.etymology: Honors Charles Henry Maxwell (1923– ), geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, who studied the Taylor Creek district.

mayenite.occurrence: In thermally metamorphosed limestone blocks included in volcanic rocks (near Mayen, Germany); common in high-temperature, thermally metamorphosed, impure limestones (Hatrurim Formation, Israel).
mayenite.etymology: For Mayen, Germany, near where the mineral was ﬁrst described.

mayingite.occurrence: In chromite ore and placer concentrates.

mazzettiite.occurrence: A rare mineral in a hydrothermal telluride deposit.
mazzettiite.etymology: Honors Giuseppe Mazzetti (1942-2003), curator in chief of the Mineralogy Section, Museum of Natural History, University of Florence, Italy.

mazzite-mg.occurrence: In cavities in a porphyritic olivine basalt.
mazzite-mg.etymology: Honors Professor Fiorenzo Mazzi, mineralogist, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy, and the suffix indicates the dominance of magnesium.

mazzite-na.occurrence: Filling cavities in basalt overlain by layers of silt and clay that are overlain by lacustrine deposits of silt and sodium borate with a few interbeds of rhyolite tuff. Likely affected by extensive sodium cation exchange.
mazzite-na.etymology: Suffix, Na, signifies the sodium-dominant analog of mazzite-Mg.

mbobomkulite.occurrence: A rare product of oxidation and leaching of Ni–Cu from sulﬁdes in the cave roof, reacting with aluminum from phyllosilicates and nitrate from bat guano (Mbobo Mkulu Cave, South Africa); in a sedimentary U–V deposit (Jomac mine, Utah, USA).
mbobomkulite.etymology: For the Mbobo Mkulu Cave, South Africa, the mineral’s ﬁrst-noted occurrence.

mcallisterite.occurrence: A secondary mineral derived from colemanite and priceite veins in altered basalt (Furnace Creek district, California, USA); a primary mineral in a metamorphosed borate playa deposit (Tincalayu deposit, Argentina); at a saline lake (China).
mcallisterite.etymology: To honor James Franklin McAllister (1911–2000), geologist, U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California, USA, who collected the originally described material.

mcalpineite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral, formed by alteration of tellurides and tellurium-bearing sulfides.
mcalpineite.etymology: For the locality at which the mineral originally was found, the McAlpine mine.

mcauslanite.occurrence: A very rare non-oxidized secondary mineral along joints beneath the erosional surface of a greisen-hosted stockwork tin mine.
mcauslanite.etymology: Honors Dr. David A. McAuslan (1943– ), Exploration Manager for Shell Canada Resources Ltd., developers of the East Kemptville tin mine, Canada.

mcbirneyite.occurrence: Very rare in the sulfate zone of sublimates around a fumarole in a composite volcano, likely formed between 100 ◦C–200 ◦C.
mcbirneyite.etymology: Honors Professor Alexander Robert McBirney (1924– ), Volcanologist, University of Oregon, Corvallis, Oregon, USA.

mcconnellite.occurrence: In ﬁne-grained intergrowth with other chromium oxide-hydroxide minerals in alluvial cobbles.
mcconnellite.etymology: For Dr. Richard Bradford McConnell, formerly Director, British Guyana Geological Survey.

mccrillisite.occurrence: A rare product of late-stage hydrothermal alteration of primary zirconium-bearing minerals, in a complex granite pegmatite.
mccrillisite.etymology: Honors the McCrillis family, principally Dean (1931–1989) and his son, Phillip, pegmatite miners from Oxford Co., Maine, USA.

mcgillite.occurrence: As open-space fracture ¯llings in a manganese-rich section of quartzite and argillite in a metamorphosed Pb{Zn orebody (Sullivan mine, Canada).
mcgillite.etymology: For McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada.

mcgovernite.occurrence: As the principal ¯lling of a vein in massive zinc ore in a metamorphosed stratiform Zn-Mn deposit.
mcgovernite.etymology: For J.J. McGovern (?{1915), of Franklin, New Jersey, USA, prominent collector of Franklin minerals.

mcguinnessite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral, typically formed in serpentinized peridotite.
mcguinnessite.etymology: Honors Albert Leo McGuinness (1926–1990), amateur mineral collector and dealer, San Mateo, California, USA, for his contributions to scientiﬁc mineralogy.

mckelveyite-y.occurrence: A rare mineral formed near trona beds in the Green River Formation (Wyoming, USA); in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia).
mckelveyite-y.etymology: To honor Vincent Ellis McKelvey (1916–1985), Director of the U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C., USA, for his studies of the Phosphoria Formation of Wyoming and Idaho, USA.

mckinstryite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal or supergene origin; probably formed below 94.4 ◦C, the upper stability limit for mckinstryite.
mckinstryite.etymology: In honor of Hugh Exton McKinstry (1896–1961), Professor of Geology at Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

mcnearite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of an arsenic-bearing deposit.
mcnearite.etymology: Honors Elizabeth McNear, mineralogist and crystallographer, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.

medaite.occurrence: Formed at low temperature and low H2O fugacity in veinlets cutting manganese ores.
medaite.etymology: Honors Dr. Francesco Meda (1926{1977), an amateur mineralogist from Turin, Italy.

medenbachite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in a weathered polymetallic sulﬁde vein.
medenbachite.etymology: Honors Olaf Medenbach (1949– ), mineralogist, Ruhr University, Bochum, Germany.

megacyclite.occurrence: In unweathered ultra-alkalic pegmatites in an alkalic massif.
megacyclite.etymology: From the Greek for large and cyclical, with reference to the large ringlike groups of silica tetrahedra in the structure.

megawite.occurrence: Occurs as minute inclusions in rock-forming minerals in altered ignimbrite xenoliths in a caldera. Probably formed by contact metamorphism at low pressure and >800ºC.
megawite.etymology: Honors British crystallographer Helen Dick Megaw (1907-2002) for significant contributions to our understanding of the perovskites.

meieranite.occurrence: Probably a result of a hydrothermal event during metamorphism under conditions of 270-420 °C at 0.2-1.0 kb.
meieranite.etymology: Honors Dr. Eugene Stuart Meieran (b. 1937), a member of the U.S. National Academy of Engineering, an avid mineral collector, who donated several important specimens to major museums, for his work in mineral preservation and education.

meierite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal Pb-Zn deposit in lenses of pyroxene-quartz skarn.
assoc_parsed: alters to a mixture of cerchiaraite-  and hedenbergite
meierite.etymology: Honors Walter M. Meier (1926-2009) who among numerous other contributions to zeolite science determined the atomic structure of zeolite ZK-5, which has the same structure as meierite.

meionite.occurrence: Typically in regionally metamorphosed rocks, especially marbles, calcareous gneisses, granulites, and greenschists. Also in skarns, some pegmatites, pneumatolytically or hydrothermally altered ma¯c igneous rocks, and ejected volcanic blocks.
meionite.etymology: From the Greek for less, referring to its less acute pyramidal form compared with vesuvianite.

meisserite.occurrence: As efflorescences on sandstone in the underground workings of a roll-front type uranium deposit, the product of weathering and oxidation of primary uraninite.
meisserite.etymology: Honors Nicolas Meisser (b. 1964), Swiss mineralogist and Curator of Mineralogy and Petrography, Cantonal Museum of Geology, Lausanne, Switzerland.

meitnerite.occurrence: As efflorescent crusts on the surfaces of mine walls by oxidation in the humid underground environment of a Colorado Plateau type, roll-front uranium deposit in organic-rich former stream channel sediment.
meitnerite.etymology: Honors Austrian-Swedish physicist Lise Meitner (1878-1968) who, with Otto Hahn and his assistant Fritz Straßmann, discovered nuclear fission (of uranium) in 1938 and explained the physical process. Chemical element 109 was named meitnerium in her honor.

meixnerite.etymology: To honor Professor Heinrich Hermann Meixner (1908–1981), Austrian mineralogist, University of Salzburg, Salzburg, Austria.

mejillonesite.occurrence: Formed at the contact between granite and what is now a fine-grained, completely altered siliceous layer at the base of a Pliocene (ca. 2.5 Ma) coastal bird guano deposit.
mejillonesite.etymology: For the locality that provided the first specimen.

melanarsite.occurrence: As sublimates on scoria around an active fumarole.
melanarsite.etymology: A prefix from the Greek μέλαν (black) for the mineral color and its identity as an arsenate.

melanocerite-ce.occurrence: In nepheline syenite pegmatites (Langesundsfjord, Norway); in alkalic granite pegmatites (Russia).
melanocerite-ce.etymology: From the Greek for black or dark and cerium in its composition.

melanophlogite.occurrence: A late-stage, low-temperature mineral in sulfur deposits (Racalmuto, Sicily, Italy); in low-temperature hydrothermal veins associated with metamorphosed sedimentary manganese deposits (Chvaletice, Czech Republic); in carbonate-bearing serpentinites (Fortullino, Italy; Mt. Hamilton, California, USA).
melanophlogite.etymology: From the Greek for black and to be burned, in allusion to the fact that some specimens of the mineral turn black when heated.

melanostibite.occurrence: A very rare mineral in ﬁssures in banded dolomite, in a small Fe–Mn orebody in manganoan dolomite.
melanostibite.etymology: From the Greek for black, for its color, and antimony, STIBium, in its composition.

melanotekite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed Fe{Mn deposit, from which over one ton was removed (Lºangban, Sweden); in oxidized Pb{Cu ores (Artillery Peaks, Arizona, USA).
melanotekite.etymology: From the Greek black and to melt or glass, for the black bead formed under the blowpipe.

melanothallite.occurrence: Sublimed on crater walls formed in 1868 and 1906 (Vesuvius, Italy); in volcanic ﬁssures (Tolbachik volcano, Russia).
melanothallite.etymology: From the Greek for black and a young shoot, for the mineral’s property of turning green on exposure.

melanovanadite.occurrence: In altered black shale in a very rich vanadium deposit (Minasragra, Peru); in Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits.
melanovanadite.etymology: From the Greek for black, for the color, and V ANADium in the composition.

melanterite.occurrence: A post-mine product of oxidation of pyrite and marcasite ores; rarely a volcanic sublimate.
melanterite.etymology: From the Greek for a black metallic dye.

melcherite.occurrence: In a vug in dolomitic carbonatite.
melcherite.etymology: Honors Geraldo Conrado Melcher (1924-2011), a pioneer in Jacupiranga carbonatite studies.

meliphanite.etymology: From the Greek for honey-yellow and to appear, in allusion to its color.

melkovite.occurrence: Localized along joints in sandstone, formed by alteration of molybdenite in the oxidized zone of small molybdenite-fluorite deposits.
melkovite.etymology: Honors Professor Vyacheslav Gavrilovich Melkov (1911-1991), Russian mineralogist specializing in uranium minerals, of the All-Union Research Institute of Mineral Resources, Moscow, Russia. Existing name retained instead of ‘mendozavilite-CaCa’ by group nomenclature.

melliniite.etymology: Honors Marcello Mellini, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Siena, Italy, for his contributions to the study of meteorites.

mellinzinkalite.occurrence: A sublimate around a volcanic fumarole.
mellinzinkalite.etymology: From Latin words, mellis (honey), zinkum, and kalium for its color and species-defining cations, zinc and potassium.

mellite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in brown coal and lignite deposits, aluminum typically derived from clay.
mellite.etymology: From the Greek for honey, in allusion to the color.

melonite.occurrence: With other tellurium minerals in the late stages of hydrothermal veins formed at medium to low temperatures. Also in high-temperature Ni–Cu–PGE magmatic sulﬁde deposits.
melonite.etymology: For the Melones mine in California, USA, where it was discovered.

melonjosephite.occurrence: Replacing an alluaudite group mineral in a complex granite pegmatite (Angarf-Sud pegmatite, Morocco).
melonjosephite.etymology: To honor Professor Joseph M´ elon (1898–1991), Institute of Mineralogy, University of Li` ege, Li` ege, Belgium.

menchettiite.occurrence: In a polymetallic (Ag-Mn-Pb-Zn) vein, replacement, and contact metamorphic mineral district.
menchettiite.etymology: Honors Silvio Menchetti (b. 1937), Professor of Mineralogy and Crystallography, University of Florence, Italy, in recognition of his contributions to the systematics of sulfosalt minerals.

mendeleevite-ce.occurrence: In a massif composed of a variety of granitic, alkaline granitic and syenitic pegmatites, various hydrothermal rocks (albitites, fenites) and carbonatites.
mendeleevite-ce.etymology: Honors Dmitriy Ivanovich Mendeleev (1834-1907), the Russian chemist who among other accomplishments created the Periodic Table of Elements.

mendeleevite-nd.occurrence: In a pectolite aggregate in quartz-rich rock associated with a complex alkaline massif.
mendeleevite-nd.etymology: Honors Dmitri Mendeleev (1834-1907), the Russian chemist and author of the periodic table of the chemical elements. The suffix indicates the dominant rare earth element.

mendigite.occurrence: A pneumatolitic phase in miarolitic cavities in sanidinite.
mendigite.etymology: For Mendig, the town in Germany, near the quarry that produced the first specimens.

mendipite.occurrence: In nodules in manganese oxide ores (Somerset, England).
mendipite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Mendip [Myne-deepes, Old English] Hills, England.

mendozavilite-kca.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a porphyry copper deposit.
mendozavilite-kca.etymology: Honors Heriberto Mendoza Avila (b. 1924), Phelps Dodge exploration geologist, who found the first specimen. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

mendozavilite-nacu.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of porphyry copper deposit as thin vein fillings and well-formed crystals in cavities.
mendozavilite-nacu.etymology: Honors Heriberto Mendoza Avila (b. 1924), Phelps Dodge exploration geologist, who found the first specimen. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

mendozavilite-nafe.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of some molybdenum-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
mendozavilite-nafe.etymology: Honors Heriberto Mendoza Avila (b. 1924), Phelps Dodge exploration geologist, who found the first specimen. Two suffixes correspond to the dominant cations in the two different types of non-framework cation sites.

mendozite.occurrence: Rarely formed by oxidation of pyrite in reaction with clays; may occur in volcanic fumaroles.
mendozite.etymology: For its originally described occurrence in Mendoza Province, Argentina.

meneghinite.occurrence: Uncommon, but widespread in hydrothermal veins, also contact metasomatic, volcanogenic sulﬁde, Cu–Mo porphyry, and rarely, Kuroko deposits.
meneghinite.etymology: Honors Professor Giuseppi Meneghini (1811–1889) of Pisa, Italy, who ﬁrst observed the species.

menezesite.occurrence: In a vug in the contact zone between dolomite carbonatite and “jacupirangite” (a pyroxenite).
menezesite.etymology: Honors Luiz Alberto Dias Menezes Filho (b. 1950), mining engineer, mineral collector and merchant.

mengeite.occurrence: In a heavily brecciated hydrothermal vein.
mengeite.etymology: Honors Johann Menge (1788-1852), German geologist and linguist whose 1841 booklet, The Mineral Kingdom of South Australia, highlighted the mineral wealth of South Australia and aided the discovery of major copper deposits at Burra and Kapunda.

mengxianminite.occurrence: In a hsianghualite-bearing vein in the exocontact of a contact metamorphic rock.
mengxianminite.etymology: Honors “Meng Xianmin” (1900-1969), a Chinese geologist, who made significant contributions to our understanding of ore deposits in China.

meniaylovite.occurrence: A product of the alteration of volcanic rocks by fumarole gases.
meniaylovite.etymology: Honors Russian volcanologist Igor Aleksandrovich Meniayloy (1937-1993), for his study of the geochemistry of exhalations of the Tolbachik Main Fracture Eruption; Institute of Volcanology, Far East Branch, Russian Academy of Sciences, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Russia.

menshikovite.occurrence: In a mineralized pod in altered gabbronorite (Lukkulaisvaara intrusion, Russia); in heavy-mineral concentrates from quartz-feldspar sandstones in contact with base-metal sulﬁdes (Chiney intrusion, Russia).
menshikovite.etymology: To honor Dr. Yurii Pavlovich Men’shikov (1934– ), Geological Institute, Kola Science Center, Russian Academy of Sciences, Apatity, Russia, for his extensive work on descriptions of new minerals.

menzerite-y.occurrence: As cores and remnants in composite almandine crystals in a felsic granulite.
menzerite-y.etymology: Honors Gregor Menzer (1897-1989), German crystallographer who solved the garnet structure first and for the dominant rare earth component.

mercallite.etymology: To honor Giuseppe Mercalli (1850–1914), a Director of the Vesuvius Observatory, Italy.

mercury.occurrence: In hydrothermal deposits formed at low temperature and associated with hot springs.
mercury.etymology: From the Latin Mercurius, the mythological messenger of the gods, in allusion to its mobility in liquid form; the chemical symbol from the Latin hydrargyrum, liquid silver.

mereheadite.occurrence: A secondary low-temperature mineral formed in lenses and cavities, in a Mississippi Valley type lead deposit in limestone, by a hydrothermal event that caused the decomposition of the galena and created the conditions which led to the formation of this rare oxychloride mineral.
mereheadite.etymology: For the first locality, Merehead Quarry, England.

mereiterite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral imbedded in gypsum, formed by decomposition of sulﬁdes in a hydrothermal Pb–Zn–Cu ore deposit.
mereiterite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Kurt Helmut Mereiter (1945– ), Professor of Mineralogy, Technical University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria, in recognition of his work on iron sulfates.

merelaniite.occurrence: In crevices loosely attached to alabandite crystals, intimately associated with masses of loosely aggregated graphite crystals. In a region of granulite-facies metamorphism of organic-rich black-shales rich in vanadium. No specimens collected in situ.
merelaniite.etymology: Honors the local miners, past and present, living and working in the township of Merelani.

merenskyite.occurrence: A principal Pd–Pt-bearing mineral, associated with numerous other Pt–Pd species; typically in disseminated interstitial segregations of Cu–Fe–Ni sulﬁdes and enclosing silicates.
merenskyite.etymology: To honor Dr. Hans Merensky (1871–1952), who was instrumental in the discovery of the “Reef” also named for him.

meridianiite.occurrence: In a pocket near the surface of a frozen pond that allowed evaporation, concentration of dissolved matter, and crystallization at temperatures well below the freezing point of water. In sea ice inclusions and Antarctic ice.
meridianiite.etymology: For the locality where the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) Opportunity observed crystal molds in sedimentary rock that may be caused by minerals that have since dehydrated or dissolved.

merlinoite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in veins and cavities of silica-undersaturated volcanic rocks (Cupaello, Italy); an alteration product of cataclastized p egmatitic rocks in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Russia); in manganese nodules (Indian Ocean).
merlinoite.etymology: In honor of Stefano Merlino (1938{ ), Professor of Crystallography, University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy.

merrihueite.occurrence: Rare, in a few chondules of a chondrite, as inclusions in clinopyroxenes.
merrihueite.etymology: For Craig M. Merrihue (?{1965), meteoriticist, of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA.

mertieite-i.occurrence: As ﬁne grains in precious metal placer concentrates, apparently derived from ultramaﬁc source rock.
mertieite-i.etymology: To honor John Beaver Mertie, Jr. (1888–1980), geologist, U.S. Geological Survey, who provided the original material; “I” to distinguish its unique composition and crystallography from that of mertieite-II and isomertieite.

mertieite-ii.occurrence: As ﬁne grains in precious metal placer concentrates, apparently derived from an ultramaﬁc source rock (Goodnews Bay, Alaska, USA); above massive cubanite–mooihoekite ore (Oktyabr mine, Russia).
mertieite-ii.etymology: To honor John B. Mertie, Jr. (1888–1980), geologist, U.S. Geological Survey, who provided the original material; “II” to distinguish its unique composition and crystallography from that of mertieite-I and isomertieite.

merwinite.occurrence: In siliceous dolomitic limestone in contact metamorphic zones, formed at relatively elevated temperatures, locally in substantial quantities.
merwinite.etymology: For Dr. Herbert Eugene Merwin (1878{1963), American mineralogist and petrologist, Carnegie Institute, Washington, D.C., USA.

mesaite.occurrence: Formed on asphaltum blocks in a mine tunnel in sandstone by the oxidation in a moist environment of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a roll-front U-V-deposit.
mesaite.etymology: For the county in Colorado in which the Packrat mine is located.

mesolite.occurrence: In cavities of volcanic rocks, typically basalt, also in andesites, porphyries, and hydrothermal veins.
mesolite.etymology: From the Greek for middle, alluding to its composition intermediate between natrolite and scolecite.

messelite.occurrence: Principally as a late stage hydrothermal alteration product in zoned complex granite pegmatites.
messelite.etymology: For the locality that produced the ﬁrst specimens, Messel, Germany.

meta-aluminite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral formed by dehydration of alunogen; found in sulfate-rich hydrothermal deposits and geothermal fields.
meta-aluminite.etymology: For meta, indicating a lower hydrate, and alunogen.

meta-alunogen.occurrence: An uncommon mineral formed by dehydration of alunogen; found in sulfate-rich hydrothermal deposits and geothermal fields.
meta-alunogen.etymology: For meta, indicating a lower hydrate, and alunogen.

meta-ankoleite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral formed by dehydration of alunogen; found in sulfate-rich hydrothermal deposits and geothermal fields.
meta-ankoleite.etymology: For meta, indicating a lower hydrate, and alunogen.

meta-autunite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral formed by dehydration of alunogen; found in sulfate-rich hydrothermal deposits and geothermal fields.
meta-autunite.etymology: For meta, indicating a lower hydrate, and alunogen.

metaaluminite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by reaction of acid sulfate solutions from oxidizing pyrite reacting with clay minerals (Fuemrole mine, Utah, USA).
metaaluminite.etymology: The preﬁx, from the Greek meta, indicates a lower hydrate than aluminite.

metaalunogen.occurrence: An uncommon mineral formed by dehydration of alunogen; found in sulfate-rich hydrothermal deposits and geothermal ﬁelds.
metaalunogen.etymology: For meta, indicating a lower hydrate, and alunogen.

metaankoleite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the weathered zone of a complex granite pegmatite (Mungenyi pegmatite, Uganda) and the sericitic matrix of a quartz sandstone (Sebungwe district, Zimbabwe).
metaankoleite.etymology: For the Ankole district, Uganda, from which it was ﬁrst characterized.

metaautunite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, formed as dehydration pseudomorphs after autunite.
metaautunite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of autunite.

metaborite.occurrence: In ﬁne-grained halite in a salt dome (Chalkar salt dome, Kazakhstan).
metaborite.etymology: From the Greek meta, as a lesser hydrate than orthoboric acid.

metacalciouranoite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a U-Mo deposit, replacing "pitchblende", and being replaced by uranophane.
metacalciouranoite.etymology: As a lower hydrate of calciouranoite.

metacinnabar.occurrence: In mercury deposits formed under low-temperature near-surface conditions.
metacinnabar.etymology: From the Greek for with, plus cinnabar, in allusion to its common association.

metadelrioite.occurrence: An eﬄorescence on sandstone of the Salt Wash member of the Jurassic Morrison Formation associated with a U–V deposit.
metadelrioite.etymology: For its relation to delrioite and its lesser H 2O content.

metaheinrichite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral derived by the weathering of primary uranium minerals.
metaheinrichite.etymology: The prefix meta indicates the dehydration product of heinrichite.

metahewettite.occurrence: As an impregnation in sandstone (Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits).
metahewettite.etymology: For its relation to hewettite and its lesser H 2O content.

metahohmannite.occurrence: Formed by the partial dehydration of hohmannite.
metahohmannite.etymology: The prefix, from the Greek, meta, indicates a lower hydrate than hohmannite.

metakahlerite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of U–As bearing deposits.
metakahlerite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of kahlerite.

metakirchheimerite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral formed in the oxidized zone of a U–As deposit.
metakirchheimerite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates membership of this species in the meta-autunite group; the name honors Professor Franz Waldemar Kirchheimer (1911– ), former Director of the Geological Survey of Baden-W¨ urttemberg, Germany.

metakottigite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral from the oxide zone of an arsenic-rich polymetallic mineral deposit, formed by oxidation and concomitant dehydrogenization of ferroan k¨ ottigite.
metakottigite.etymology: For its dimorphous relation to k¨ ottigite, and by analogy to metavivianite.

metalodevite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by alteration of arsenic-bearing minerals.
metalodevite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates membership in the meta-autunite group; the name is for Lod` eve, France, near which the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

metamunirite.occurrence: Extremely rare, in cavities in vanadium-bearing sandstone.
metamunirite.etymology: For its relation to munirite, from which it may form by dehydration.

metanatroautunite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit in a granodiorite massif (Tajikistan). In a miarolitic cavity in granite (Lake Boga).
metanatroautunite.etymology: The prefix meta indicates the dehydration product of “sodium autunite”, the transitory sodium analog of meta-autunite.

metanovacekite.occurrence: Typically a dehydration product of nov´ aˇ cekite.
metanovacekite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of nov´ aˇ cekite.

metarauchite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in strongly oxidized polymetallic vein material.
metarauchite.etymology: Honors Czech mineral collector Luděk Rauch (1951-1983) who died prospecting in the Jáchymov mines.

metarossite.occurrence: In veinlets in carnotite-bearing sandstone (Bull Pen Canyon, Colorado, USA).
metarossite.etymology: For its relation to rossite, from which it may form by dehydration.

metaschoderite.occurrence: Typically a dehydration product of schoderite.
metaschoderite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of schoderite.

metaschoepite.occurrence: An irreversible alteration product of schoepite from the oxidized zone of uranium-bearing mineral deposits.
metaschoepite.etymology: From the Greek meta, for a lower hydration state, and its relation to schoepite.

metasideronatrite.occurrence: An uncommon alteration product of pyrite, typically formed in arid climates but stably formed in sea-shore environments.
metasideronatrite.etymology: From the Greek meta, signifying a lower hydrate, and its relation to sideronatrite.

metastibnite.occurrence: Appears to be of primary hydrothermal origin around fumarolic centers (The Geysers, California; Steamboat Springs, Nevada, USA); and the result of oxidation of stibnite (Copiap´ o, Chile).
metastibnite.etymology: From the Greek for with, plus stibnite, in allusion to its composition.

metastudtite.occurrence: Extremely rare, on museum specimens of dolomite and uraninite, from the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit.
metastudtite.etymology: As a dehydration product of studtite.

metaswitzerite.occurrence: Forms by irreversible dehydration of switzerite on exposure to air.
metaswitzerite.etymology: Emphasizes the close chemical and structural relations to switzerite.

metatamboite.occurrence: In the interstices of silicified epithermal hydrothermal breccias of dacitic tuff.
assoc_parsed: native tellurium. distribution from the tambo mine
metatamboite.etymology: Prefix, meta, indicates the lower hydration state compared to tamboite.

metatorbernite.occurrence: Typically a secondary mineral, a dehydration product of torbernite formed during weathering; formed directly above 75 °C.
metatorbernite.etymology: The prefix meta indicates the dehydration product of torbernite.

metatyuyamunite.occurrence: A common dehydration product of tyuyamunite in Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits.
metatyuyamunite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of tyuyamunite.

metauranocircite-i.occurrence: Typically a secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some uranium deposits; may be primary in low-temperature veins.
metauranocircite-i.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of “uranocircite”, named for its content of uranium, and from the Greek for falcon, for its occurrence at the Falkenstein, Germany.

metauranopilite.occurrence: On a museum specimen from a uranium-bearing hydrothermal ore deposit [may = j´ achymovite].
metauranopilite.etymology: From the Greek meta, for a lower hydrate, and its relation to uranopilite.

metauranospinite.occurrence: A secondary mineral of the oxide zone in a hydrothermal polymetallic barite–ﬂuorite deposit.
metauranospinite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of uranospinite.

metauroxite.occurrence: A post-mining secondary phase found in efflorescent crusts on mine walls on asphaltum-quartz matrix in bedded or roll-front U-V deposits in sandstone. Oxalate, C2O4 2-, likely derived from the asphaltum matrix (probably fossilized wood) and the uranyl, UO2 2+, from primary (esp. uraninite) and/or secondary uranium-bearing minerals.
metauroxite.etymology: The prefix meta indicates the compositional similarity to uroxite, with one less H2O group per formula unit. Uroxite identifies a uranyl (UR) oxalate (OX).

metavandendriesscheite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a uranium-bearing mineral deposit.
metavandendriesscheite.etymology: As a dehydration product of vandendriesscheite.

metavanmeersscheite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the uraniferous zone of an altered granite pegmatite, formed by dehydration of vanmeersscheite.
metavanmeersscheite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of vanmeersscheite.

metavanuralite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a lead-bearing U–V deposit, formed as a reversible dehydration product of vanuralite.
metavanuralite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of vanuralite.

metavariscite.occurrence: Commonly a product of weathering phosphatic rocks; may form as concretions by the phosphatization of kaolin during weathering; probably a reaction product of phosphate fertilizer in acid soil.
metavariscite.etymology: For the dimorphous relation with variscite.

metavauxite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of tin mines.
metavauxite.etymology: In allusion to the chemical relation to vauxite.

metavivianite.occurrence: A secondary mineral typically formed from oxidizing vivianite, in complex granite pegmatites; authigenic, in bogs and soils.
metavivianite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of vivianite.

metavoltine.occurrence: Typically an alteration product of pyrite in arid climates; formed as a fumarolic sublimate and solfataric precipitate; may be a post-mining product.
metavoltine.etymology: From the Greek for with and voltaite, as originally associated with that species.

metazellerite.etymology: From the Greek meta, for a lower hydrate of zellerite.

metazeunerite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of arsenic-bearing hydrothermal uranium deposits.
metazeunerite.etymology: The preﬁx meta indicates the dehydration product of zeunerite.

meurigite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral, rare at all localities. Along fault gouge in the oxidized zone of a copper sulﬁde deposit (Santa Rita mine, New Mexico, USA); by alteration of triphylite in granite pegmatite (Hagendorf, Germany); in the oxidized zone of a low-temperature sediment-hosted Carlin-type hydrothermal gold deposit (Gold Quarry mine, Nevada, USA).
meurigite.etymology: Honors Professor John Meurig Thomas (1932– ), crystal chemist, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, England.

meurigite-k.occurrence: A late-stage mineral, rare at all localities. Along fault gouge in the oxidized zone of a copper sulﬁde deposit (Santa Rita mine, New Mexico, USA); by alteration of triphylite in granite pegmatite (Hagendorf, Germany); in the oxidized zone of a low-temperature sediment-hosted Carlin-type hydrothermal gold deposit (Gold Quarry mine, Nevada, USA).
meurigite-k.etymology: Honors Professor John Meurig Thomas (1932– ), crystal chemist, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, England.

meurigite-na.occurrence: A late-stage, low-temperature, secondary mineral in complex phosphate assemblages rich in Fe3+ and Na.
meurigite-na.etymology: Honors Professor John Meurig Thomas (b. 1932), crystal chemist, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, England. The suffix, Na, indicates dominant sodium rather than potassium.

meyerhofferite.occurrence: Typically a minor component of sedimentary or lake-bed borate deposits.
meyerhofferite.etymology: Honoring Professor Wilhelm Meyerhoﬀer (1864–1906), German chemist, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound.

meymacite.occurrence: An alteration product in tungsten deposits.
meymacite.etymology: Originally applied to a mineral from Meymac, France, an alteration product of scheelite, later found to be ferritungstite. The name was, however, reinstated by the IMA CNMMN for this mineral, ﬁrst described from Congo (Zaire), but which also occurs at Meymac, France.

meyrowitzite.occurrence: On calcite-veined asphaltum as efflorescent crusts on the surfaces of mine walls in a sand-hosted uranium deposit of the Colorado Plateau type.
meyrowitzite.etymology: Honors American analytical chemist Robert Meyrowitz (1916-2013), who at the U.S. Geological Survey developed innovative methods for analyzing small and difficult to study mineralogical samples and formulations of high-index immersion liquids (1.74 to 2.00) that are still in use for optical determinations. He collaborated on the descriptions of many new minerals from the uranium deposits of the western U.S., including zellerite, the dimorph of the meyrowitzite.

mgriite.etymology: From the ﬁrst letters of Moscow Geological Exploration Institute [Moskovskogo Geologro Razvedounogo Instituta (MGRI)] the laboratory in which the mineral was discovered.

mianningite.occurrence: In fractures within lamprophyre veins and their contacts with a later quartz-alkali feldspar syenite dike containing REE, U, and Th mineralization.
mianningite.etymology: For the county in China that provided the first specimens.

miargyrite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins of low-temperature origin.
miargyrite.etymology: From the Greek for less and silver, as it contains less silver than other red silver sulfosalt minerals. All rights reserved.
