miassite.occurrence: In heavy-mineral concentrates from fluvial placer deposits derived from ophiolites or layered mafic intrusions.
miassite.etymology: For the Miass River, Russia. Similar material formally named “prassoite”.

michalskiite.occurrence: Secondary alteration product probably formed at low temperature under oxidizing conditions in a uranium deposit.
assoc_parsed: mica. distribution from the dump of the lichtenberg open pit
michalskiite.etymology: Honors German mineral collector and dealer Dipl. Min. Steffen Michalski (b. 1974), who discovered this mineral and provided the studied material.

micheelsenite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal product in alkaline pegmatite.
micheelsenite.etymology: Honors Professor Emeritus of Mineralogy, Harry Ingvar Micheelsen (b. 1931) of the University of Copenhagen, Denmark. He discovered the Nanna pegmatite.

michenerite.occurrence: A principal palladium mineral in Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposits.
michenerite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Charles Edward Michener (1907– ), Canadian geologist for the Canadian Nickel Company, who discovered the mineral.

microcline.occurrence: Common in plutonic felsic rocks, as granites, granite pegmatites, syenites; in metamorphic rocks of the greenschist and amphibolite facies; in hydrothermal veins. A detrital component in sedimentary rocks and as authigenic overgrowths.
microcline.etymology: From the Greek for little and inclined, for the small deviation of the cleavage planes from 90±.

microsommite.occurrence: In ejected volcanic masses and in leucitites.
microsommite.etymology: From the Greek for small, in allusion to crystal size, and for the original locality at Monte Somma, Italy.

middendorfite.occurrence: A late hydrothermal mineral in a hyperperalkaline pegmatite.
middendorfite.etymology: Honors Aleksandr Fedorovich von Middendorf (1815–1894), Academician of the Imperial Russian Academy of Sciences, who carried out the first mineralogical study of the Khibiny Mountains.

middlebackite.struct_group: Not in a structural group, Oxalate
middlebackite.occurrence: A supergene mineral in a weathered Precambrian manganiferous sedimentary iron ore deposit. A source of oxalate was probably decaying organic matter. Copper from weathering of Cu sulfides with dissolution of Cu possibly facilitated by oxalic acid.
middlebackite.etymology: For the Middleback Range, in which the Iron Monarch quarry is located.

mieite-y.occurrence: In a block of granitic pegmatite collected from a talus slope.
mieite-y.etymology: For the prefecture in Japan that produced the first specimens.

miersite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized zone of some Pb–Zn–Cu–Ag deposits, especially in arid regions.
miersite.etymology: Honors Henry Alexander Miers (1858–1942), Professor of Mineralogy, Oxford University, Oxford, England.

miessiite.occurrence: With gold and PGM nuggets in a placer sample from a river draining glaciofluvial gravels, sands, terraces, poorly-sorted sandy till and weathered bedrock.
miessiite.etymology: After the locality, the Miessijoki river (in Saami language, Miessijohka).

miguelromeroite.occurrence: In secondary oxidation zones of arsenic-rich base metal deposits.
miguelromeroite.etymology: Miguel Romero Sanchez (1926-1997) for his dedication to documenting and preserving Mexico’s rich mineral heritage.

miharaite.occurrence: As disseminations in a hedenbergite-garnet-epidote contact metamorphic deposit (Mihara mine, Japan); in a mineralized quartz vein through granite (Imooka mine, Japan); in a bornite vein in copper skarn ore (Ulsan mine, Korea).
miharaite.etymology: For the type locality at the Mihara mine, Japan.

mikasaite.occurrence: A sublimate around a burning coal-gas escape fracture, formed at > 300 ◦C.
mikasaite.etymology: For its occurrence near Mikasa, Japan.

mikehowardite.occurrence: A secondary mineral (previously misidentified as fervanite) in a vanadium deposit formed by potassic fenitization near an alkaline intrusion.
mikehowardite.etymology: Honors James Michael (Mike) Howard (b. 1949), staff economic geologist and field mineralogist, Arkansas Geological Commission for 39 years. Mr. Howard is a specialist in Arkansas species and collecting, particularly micro-mineral crystals.

milanriederite.occurrence: By hydrothermal and metasomatic replacement and fracture-filling of dolostones.
milanriederite.etymology: Honors Czech mineralogist Professor Milan Rieder (b. 1940), for his contributions to mineralogy and service to the international mineralogical community.

milarite.occurrence: In alpine and low-temperature hydrothermal veins; in aplites, syenites, and granite pegmatites.
milarite.etymology: After a spurious type locality, the Val Milµ a(Milar), Switzerland [originally from the nearby Val Giuv, but later found in Val Milµ a also].

millerite.occurrence: Most commonly as a low-temperature mineral, in cavities in limestones and carbonate veins and in barite; an alteration product of other nickel minerals; also in sedimentary rocks, associated with coal measures, and rarely in serpentines.
millerite.etymology: Honors William Hallowes Miller (1801–1880), British mineralogist, Cambridge University, Cambridge, England, who ﬁrst studied crystals of the mineral.

millisite.occurrence: As finely banded crusts on variscite nodules (Little Green Monster mine, Utah, USA); in phosphatic laterite (Taiba mine, Senegal); as cement in weathered phosphorite (Homeland mine, Florida, USA).
millisite.etymology: Honors F.T. Millis, of Lehi, Utah, USA, who collected the first specimens.

millosevichite.occurrence: Precipitated at high temperature from gasses originating from solfataric activity or burning coal measures.
millosevichite.etymology: To honor Professor Federico Millosevich (1875–1942), Italian mineralogist, University of Rome, Rome, Italy.

millsite.occurrence: A secondary mineral found within vugs, interstices and along cracks in granular quartz from a single boulder of quartz-rich granite, probably a glacial erratic. Oxidation of primary sulfides and tellurides under near-surface, wet, oxidizing conditions created the secondary assemblage.
millsite.etymology: Honors Dr. Stuart J. Mills (b. 1982), currently Senior Curator of Geosciences, Museums Victoria, Melbourne, Australia.

milotaite.occurrence: A low-temperature mineral in fractures in selenium-rich uraninite in calcite veins.
milotaite.etymology: Honors Milota Makovicky (b. 1941), Geological Institute, University of Copenhagen, for her outstanding investigations of sulfide and sulfarsenide systems with platinum-group elements.

minamiite.occurrence: In a hydrothermally altered labradorite andesite (Okumanza, Japan); deposited from fumarolic gasses (Mt. Rainier, Washington, USA); in volcanic-hosted argillic alteration (Barton Peninsula, Antarctica).
minamiite.etymology: In honor of Dr. A.E. Minami (1899–1977), who studied the hot springs around the Kusatsu-Shirane volcano, Japan.

minasgeraisite-y.occurrence: A late-stage accessory mineral in a zoned complex granite pegmatite.
minasgeraisite-y.etymology: For the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil, and yttrium in the composition.

minasragrite.occurrence: An alteration product of patronite in a rich deposit of vanadian materials in ﬁssures that cut red shales and that were probably ﬁlled by a remobilized asphaltite deposit (Minasragra, Peru); in a siliciﬁed tree, formed as an oxidation product of pyrite reacting with vanadium-rich organic material (Temple Mountain district, Utah, USA).
minasragrite.etymology: For its occurrence at Minasragra, Peru.

mineevite-y.occurrence: Very rare in pegmatites in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
mineevite-y.etymology: Honoring Professor Dmitry Andreevich Mineev (1935–1992), Russian geochemist and mineralogist, founder of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

minehillite.occurrence: A secondary low-temperature hydrothermal mineral formed by replacement of associated minerals in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
minehillite.etymology: For Mine Hill, at Franklin, New Jersey, USA, where the Franklin deposit was exposed at the surface.

minguzzite.occurrence: Rare, in an oxidized gossan formed in a calcareous dolomite.
minguzzite.etymology: To honor Professor Carlo Minguzzi (1910–1953), Italian mineralogist, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy.

minium.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in some highly oxidized lead-bearing mineral deposits; may form during mine ﬁres.
minium.etymology: From the Latin, through Spanish, for cinnabar, which was once adulterated with red lead oxide, now applied exclusively to that compound.

minjiangite.occurrence: In fractures cutting montebrasite, as a late hydrothermal secondary mineral in a Be-rich, zoned pegmatite.
minjiangite.etymology: For the Minjiang River, located near the Nanping pegmatite.

minnesotaite.occurrence: In banded iron formations subjected to low-grade regional metamorphism.
minnesotaite.etymology: For the State of Minnesota, USA, from which it was ¯rst described.

minohlite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a Cu Zn sulfide deposit.
minohlite.etymology: For Minoh City, from where the first specimens were collected.

minrecordite.occurrence: In a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia); from the wallrock of a carbonate-hosted Pb–Zn orebody (Navan deposit, Ireland).
minrecordite.etymology: For the MINeralogical RECORD magazine, in recognition of that journal’s contributions to a beneﬁcial interaction between professional and amateur mineralogists.

minyulite.etymology: For Minyulo Well, Western Australia, near the source of the ﬁrst specimens.

mirabilite.occurrence: Typically in salt pans, playas, and saline lakes, where deposition may be seasonal, and bedded deposits formed therefrom; rarely in caves and lava tubes; in volcanic fumaroles; a product of hydrothermal sericitic alteration; a post-mining precipitate.
mirabilite.etymology: From the Latin sal mirable, for miracle salt , expressing Glauber’s surprise on its synthesis.

misakiite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by reaction between seawater and primary ore minerals (hausmannite, tephroite, alleghanyite, rhodonite, rhodochrosite, copper, chalcocite) in greenschist facies, metamorphosed, volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits.
misakiite.etymology: For the Sea of Misaki, located near the Sadamisaki Peninsula, Japan.

misenite.occurrence: Very rarely formed under fumarolic conditions.
misenite.etymology: For its occurrence on Cape Miseno, Italy.

miserite.occurrence: In banded metamorphosed shales at the contact with a dike of nepheline syenite (Wilson Springs, Arkansas, USA); in a carbonatite vein (Kipawa Lake, Canada); in quartz-albiteaegirine veinlets and in albitites in syenites (Dara-i-Pioz massif, Tajikistan).
miserite.etymology: For Dr. Hugh Dinsmore Miser (1884-1969), geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey.

mitridatite.occurrence: A common stain or crust on minerals near oxidizing ferrous phosphate minerals, typically triphylite or vivianite in granite pegmatite; a component of cement or fossil replacements in some ferruginous o¨ olitic sediments; in phosphatic soils.
mitridatite.etymology: For Mt. Mithridat [named for King Mithridates], within the city of Kerch, Ukraine, near which the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

mitrofanovite.occurrence: In low-sulfide disseminated Cu-Ni-PGE ore in olivine-bearing gabbronorite in a layered igneous complex.
mitrofanovite.etymology: Honors Dr. Felix P. Mitrofanov, a Russian geologist who was among the first to discover platinum-group element mineralization in the Fedorova-Pana complex.

mitryaevaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in fractures and veinlets, in altered and oxidized vanadium-bearing phosphatic black shales.
mitryaevaite.etymology: To honor Dr. Nonna Mikhailovna Mitryaeva (1920– ), for her contributions to the mineralogy of Kazakhstan.

mitscherlichite.occurrence: A volcanic sublimate (Vesuvius, Italy); an alteration product of ponomarevite (Tolbachik volcano, Russia).
mitscherlichite.etymology: Honors Eilhardt Mitscherlich (1794–1863), German crystallographer and chemist, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound.

mixite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of copper deposits.
mixite.etymology: Honors Anton Mixa, a mining oﬃcial from Pˇ r´ ıbram, who found the mineral at J´ achymov, Czech Republic.

miyahisaite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed (low grade) bedded Mn and chert deposit.
miyahisaite.etymology: Honors Michitoshi Miyahisa (1928-1983) for his contribution to the study of ore deposits on Kyushu.

moctezumite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal Au–Te deposit.
moctezumite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Moctezuma mine, Mexico.

modderite.occurrence: In heavy mineral concentrates (Witwatersrand, South Africa).
modderite.etymology: Derivation not given; presumably named for the Modderfontein mine, South Africa.

mogovidite.occurrence: In a nepheline-pectolite vein within ijolite.
mogovidite.etymology: For the mountain, Mogo-Vid, near the locality from which the first specimens were collected.

mohite.etymology: In honor of Professor G¨ unter Harald Moh (1929–1994), University of Heidelberg, Heidelberg, Germany, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound.

mohrite.etymology: To honor Karl Friedrich Mohr (1806–1879), German analytical chemist, for whom the synthetic compound has long been named.

moissanite.occurrence: Rare: formed in an iron meteorite; as inclusions in diamond; in diamondiferous kimberlites and lamproites, and in eclogite; in volcanic breccias and rhyolite; in alluvium.
moissanite.etymology: For Ferdinand F. Henri Moissan (1852-1907), French chemist, who noted the species in the Canyon Diablo meteorite.

mojaveite.occurrence: A secondary copper mineral formed by decomposition of hessite and chalcopyrite under mildly acidic conditions.
mojaveite.etymology: For the Mojave Desert, USA, where the first specimens were collected.

moluranite.occurrence: In ﬁne ﬁssures in granulated albite, in part replacing brannerite.
moluranite.etymology: For MOLybdenum and URANium in the composition.

molybdenite.occurrence: In high-temperature hydrothermal veins. In disseminated deposits of the porphyry type, both with and without associated major copper mineralization. Also in contact metamorphic deposits in limestone with calcium silicate minerals as well as in pegmatites, granites, and aplites. Rarely in meteorites.
molybdenite.etymology: A word derived from the Greek molybdos, lead.

molybdite.occurrence: In cavities and coating molybdenite in a weathered quartz vein near its contact with topaz-quartz greisen.

molybdofornacite.occurrence: In the deep oxidation zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia).
molybdofornacite.etymology: For its predominance of molybdenum and relation to fornacite.

molybdomenite.occurrence: A rare species in the oxidized zone of selenium-bearing hydrothermal base metal deposits.
molybdomenite.etymology: From the Greek for lead and moon, for its composition, selenium being named for the moon.

molybdophyllite.occurrence: In skarns in granular limestone or dolostone.
molybdophyllite.etymology: From the Greek molybdos, for lead, and phyllos, for leaf, in allusion to its lead content and foliated habit.

molysite.etymology: From the Greek for a stain , as it stains the host rock.

momoiite.occurrence: Product of the metamorphism of siliceous manganese-bearing rocks.
momoiite.etymology: Honors Hitoshi Momoi (1930-2002), who first recognized Mn 3V2Si3O12 molecules in garnet.

monazite-ce.occurrence: An accessory mineral in granites, syenites, and their pegmatites; in carbonatites and volcanoclastic rocks; in ﬁssure veins and high-grade metamorphic rocks; commonly detrital in river and beach sands; rarely authigenic in shales and intense weathering zones.
monazite-ce.etymology: From the Greek for solitary, for its initial apparent rarity, and dominant cerium.

monazite-la.occurrence: In ﬁssure veins, granite and gneissic metamorphic rocks.
monazite-la.etymology: For the member of the monazite group with dominant lanthanum.

monazite-nd.occurrence: In ﬁssures in aplitic veins through white-mica gneiss (Pta. Glogstafel, Italy); replacing brindleyite in bauxite (Marmara deposit, Greece); in volcanic-associated marine cherts (Kokˇ s´ ın, Czech Republic).
monazite-nd.etymology: For the member of the monazite group with dominant neodymium.

monazite-sm.occurrence: From the inner intermediate zone of a lepidolite-subtype granitic pegmatite.
monazite-sm.etymology: The suffix designates the Sm-dominant analog of monazite-(Ce), monazite-(La), and monazite-(Nd).

moncheite.occurrence: Typically in small amounts in Pt–Pd-bearing massive Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposits.
moncheite.etymology: For the locality at Monche Tundra in Russia.

monchetundraite.occurrence: From sulfide-bearing, metasomatically altered orthopyroxenite of a layered mafic intrusion, formed in post-magmatic conditions, at temperatures <500 °C.
monchetundraite.etymology: For the locality, the Monchetundra intrusion, Kola Peninsula, Russia. In the Sámi language, monchetundra means “beauty of the tundra” or “beautiful mountain”.

monetite.occurrence: As coatings and cements resulting from guano-induced phosphatization of sedimentary rocks; a coating on phosphate minerals in granite pegmatite.
monetite.etymology: For Moneta (now Monito) Island, which contains a notable occurrence.

mongolite.occurrence: In the quartz-rich core zone of an alkalic pegmatite, as a late-stage alteration product of a niobium silicate.
mongolite.etymology: For Mongolia, the country where the mineral was discovered.

monimolite.occurrence: In calcite veins in an iron and manganese deposit.
monimolite.etymology: From the Greek for stable, as it is decomposed chemically only with great diﬃculty.

monipite.occurrence: As a single grain in the Allende meteorite, that either crystallized from an immiscible P-rich melt that had exsolved from an Fe-Ni-enriched alloy melt that formed during melting of the host CAI or that exsolved from a solidified alloy.
monipite.etymology: An acronym composed of the chemical symbols of the three essential components.

monohydrocalcite.occurrence: In lake-bed sediments and as tuﬀaceous deposits on lake margins, formed by precipitation at pH > 8.0 and high Mg:Ca or by biological activity; in caves, in speleothems, crusts, and “moonmilk,” probably formed from an aerosol, possibly in the presence of organic matter; rarely in hydrothermal mineral deposits.
monohydrocalcite.etymology: For having the composition of calcite and the Greek for one, as with an additional H 2O.

montanite.etymology: For its occurrence in Montana, USA.

montbrayite.occurrence: With other tellurides, sulﬁdes, and gold in coarsely crystalline masses almost free from gangue (Robb-Montbray mine, Canada).

montebrasite.occurrence: A late primary and secondary mineral in zoned granite pegmatites; may be an ore of lithium.
montebrasite.etymology: For the locality, Montebras, France, from which it was ﬁrst described.

monteneroite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in thin stratiform manganese ores located near the base of a chert sequence. Crystallized from As-, Cu- and Mn-rich fluids that circulated through fractures during the final stage of tectono-metamorphism.
monteneroite.etymology: For its type locality, the abandoned Monte Nero mine.

monteneveite.occurrence: Formed near peak metamorphism (at ~600 °C) during partial breakdown of tetrahedrite-(Fe) by reactions with carbonate, under relatively oxidizing conditions.
monteneveite.etymology: For the type locality, the Monteneve (Schneeberg) mine.

monteponite.occurrence: As a coating over “calamine” (Genarutta mine, Sardinia, Italy); in sulfide ore (Verkhoyan’ya, Russia). In altered pyrometamorphic rocks (Jordan).
monteponite.etymology: For Monteponi, near the locality on Sardinia, Italy.

monteregianite-y.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities, metamorphosed inclusions, and rheomorphic breccias in nepheline syenite in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex.
monteregianite-y.etymology: For the Monteregian Hills, of which Mont Saint-Hilaire is one, and yttrium in the composition.

montesommaite.etymology: For Monte Somma, the volcano ancestr al to Vesuvius, Italy, in the remnants of which the mineral occurs.

montetrisaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed near oxidizing sulfide minerals.
montetrisaite.etymology: For the first described locality, Monte Trisa, Italy.

montgomeryite.occurrence: In sedimentary phosphatic nodules (Fairﬁeld, Utah, USA); a late mineral in highly oxidized phosphate nodules in granite pegmatite (South Dakota, USA).
montgomeryite.etymology: To honor Dr. Arthur Montgomery (1909–1999), American mineralogist, Professor of Geology, Lafayette College, Easton, Pennsylvania, USA, who collected the ﬁrst specimens.

monticellite.occurrence: Formed during metamorphism of siliceous dolostones; in contact metamorphic deposits between limestones and olivine gabbros; in skarns at granite-dolomitic limestone contacts; rarely in kimberlites.
monticellite.etymology: For the Italian mineralogist Teodoro Monticelli (1759{1845).

montmorillonite.occurrence: An alteration product of volcanic tu® and ash, forming bentonite beds, and of pegmatite dikes and wall rocks bordering hydrothermal mineral deposits. Forms under alkaline conditions of poor drainage, with Mg, Ca, Na, and K remaining in the soil.
montmorillonite.etymology: After the occurrence at Montmorillon, France.

montroseite.occurrence: In relatively unoxidized Colorado Plateau-type U–V ores in sandstones; thought to be a primary mineral (Colorado, Utah, and Arizona, USA); in vanadiferous anthraxolite bitumen (Guangxi, China).
montroseite.etymology: For Montrose Co., Colorado, USA, where it was ﬁrst found.

montroyalite.occurrence: In cavities in a silicocarbonate sill.
montroyalite.etymology: For the Monteregian Hill, Mont Royal, prominent landmark in Montreal, Canada, from which the city’s name was derived.

montroydite.etymology: Honors Montroyd Sharp, an owner of the mercury deposit at Terlingua, Texas, USA.

mooihoekite.occurrence: In massive sulﬁde from a pipe-shaped dunite pegmatite in the Norite Zone of the Bushveld complex (Mooihoek mine, South Africa); in troctolite from the basal Duluth Gabbro complex (Minnesota, USA).
mooihoekite.etymology: For the locality on Mooihoek Farm, South Africa.

moolooite.occurrence: On an outcrop of quartz, thought to have formed by reaction between bird guano and soluble secondary copper minerals (Mooloo Station, Australia); in a mine shaft near tree roots (Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, France).
moolooite.etymology: For the original locality on Mooloo Station, Australia.

mooreite.occurrence: Rarely in cavities and veinlets in franklinite–willemite–calcite ore from a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody.
mooreite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Gideon Emmet Moore (1842–1895), University of California, Berkeley, California, USA, American chemist, an early investigator of Franklin and Sterling Hill minerals.

moorhouseite.occurrence: As eﬄorescences with sulﬁdes (probably cobaltian and nickelian pyrite) on siderite–barite matrix from a hydrothermal Pb–Zn–Cu orebody associated with a large barite deposit (Magnet Cove mine, Canada); as crusts on sandstone (near Cameron, Arizona, USA).
moorhouseite.etymology: To honor Dr. Walter Wilson Moorhouse (1913–1969), Canadian Professor of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada.

mopungite.etymology: For the Mopung Hills, Nevada, USA, where it was ﬁrst found.

moraesite.occurrence: A rare late-stage hydrothermal mineral in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
moraesite.etymology: Honors Dr. Luciano Jacques de Moraes (1896–1968), Brazilian mineralogist and geologist.

moraskoite.occurrence: A primary mineral in an IAB-MG iron meteorite, in a graphite-troilite inclusion enclosed in a kamacite-taenite matrix.
moraskoite.etymology: For the host meteorite and Morasko village, near the location of the original discovery .

mordenite.occurrence: In veins and amygdules in various igneous rocks; a hydration product of volcanic glasses; an authigenic mineral in sediments.
mordenite.etymology: For the locality at Morden, Nova Scotia, Canada.

moreauite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized uraniferous zone of a complex granite pegmatite.
moreauite.etymology: Honors Professor Jules Moreau (1931– ), Belgian mineralogist, Catholic University of Louvain, Louvain, Belgium.

morelandite.occurrence: On a museum specimen from a metamorphosed manganese deposit.
morelandite.etymology: Honors Grover C. Moreland (1912–1978), Supervisor of sample preparation, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., USA.

morenosite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of nickel-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits, formed from H 2O solution below 31.5 ◦C.
morenosite.etymology: To honor Se˜ nor Antonio Moreno Ruiz (1796–1852), Spanish pharmacist and chemist, Academy of Natural Sciences, Madrid, Spain.

morinite.occurrence: An uncommon late-stage mineral in complex granite pegmatites.
morinite.etymology: Honors Mr. E.A. Morineau, Director of the tin mine, Montebras, France, who supplied the ﬁrst specimens.

morozeviczite.occurrence: In epigenetic veinlets and metasomatic replacement zones replacing sandstone and older sulﬁdes, in brecciated sandstones underlying copper-bearing shales.
morozeviczite.etymology: To honor Josef Morozewicz (1865–1941), Professor of Mineralogy, Jagellonian University, Krak´ ow, Poland.

morrisonite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by the oxidation of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a moist environment.
morrisonite.etymology: For the Morrison Formation, in which the Packrat mine and other U-V mines of the Uravan mineral belt occur.

moschelite.occurrence: In a sandstone-hosted mercury deposit, the iodine thought to be provided from underlying coal beds.
moschelite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Moschel-Landsberg mines, Germany.

moschellandsbergite.etymology: For the locality at Landsberg, near Obermoschel, Germany.

mosesite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed at low temperature in hydrothermal mercury deposits.
mosesite.etymology: Honors Alfred J. Moses (1859–1920), American mineralogist, Professor of Mineralogy, Columbia University, New York City, New York, USA, who described several other mercury minerals from Terlingua.

moskvinite-y.occurrence: In a boulder of coarse-grained, reedmergnerite-bearing pegmatite in the moraine of the Dara-i-Pioz glacier, Alai mountain ridge, Tien-Shan Mountains, northern Tajikistan. Replacing an undetermined mineral of the britholite group in arfvedsonite lujavrite (Greenland).
moskvinite-y.etymology: Honors the Russian geologist, A.V. Moskvin (1897-1974), a member of the Pamirs- Tadjikskaya expedition and author of numerous scientific papers on the geology of Central Asia.

mottanaite-ce.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities and voids in feldspathoid-bearing alkali-syenitic pyroclastic ejecta. Formed by late-stage post-magmatic hydrothermal fluids enriched in Zr, Ti, REEs, and actinide elements.
assoc_parsed: a phase with composition near cheralitebrabantite
mottanaite-ce.etymology: Honors Annibale Mottana, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Roma Tre (Italy), for his leadership and support of investigations and cataloguing of Latium minerals, during which the mottanaite-(Ce) sample was found; the suffix indicates the dominant REE.

mottramite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of vanadium-bearing base metal deposits.
mottramite.etymology: For an occurrence in England, ore stockpiled at Mottram St. Andrew, Cheshire; likely mined from the nearby Pim Hill mine, Shrewsbury, Shropshire.

motukoreaite.occurrence: Relatively common in assemblages formed by reaction of basalt volcanoclastics with sea-water; in cavities in a ha¨ uyne-nephelinite.
motukoreaite.etymology: From Motukorea, island of cormorants, the Maori name for Brown’s Island, New Zealand.

mounanaite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized zone of a sediment-hosted U–V deposit.
mounanaite.etymology: For the Mounana mine, Gabon, the locality that produced the ﬁrst specimens.

mountainite.occurrence: In a kimberlite pipe (Kimberley, South Africa); in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
mountainite.etymology: For Edgar Donald Mountain, Professor of Geology, Rhodes University, Grahamstown, South Africa.

mountkeithite.occurrence: Rare in a vein in serpentinite in a disseminated nickel sulﬁde deposit, formed by low-temperature alteration of stichtite by sulfate-rich solutions.
mountkeithite.etymology: For the Mount Keith deposit, Australia, in which it occurs.

mourite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a U–Mo deposit (Kyzylsai deposit, Kazakhstan); in a sandstone-hosted uranium deposit (Boso-Hackney prospect, Texas, USA).
mourite.etymology: For MOlybdenum and URanium in the composition.

assoc_parsed: honghe hani and yi autonomous prefecture

moydite-y.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in quartz in a zoned granite pegmatite.
moydite-y.etymology: To honor Louis Moyd (1916– ), Canadian mineralogist, Emeritus Curator, National Museum of Natural Sciences, Ottawa, Canada, for his contributions to mineralogy.

mozartite.occurrence: In veins cutting massive braunite in ophiolitic metacherts.
mozartite.etymology: For Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756{1791), discovered in the 200th year after his death.

mozgovaite.occurrence: Very rare, as a sublimate in a volcanic fumarole, deposited at about 600 ◦C.
mozgovaite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Nadezhda Nikolaevna Mozgova (1931– ), Russian mineralogist, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrography, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia, who has contributed especially to the knowledge of sulfosalt minerals.

mpororoite.occurrence: An alteration product of primary tungsten minerals.
mpororoite.etymology: For the Mpororo deposit, Uganda, where it was ﬁrst found.

mrazekite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by oxidization of polymetallic sulﬁdes.
mrazekite.etymology: Honors Zdenek Mr´ azek (1952–1984), who collected the ﬁrst specimens and recognized their unusual characteristics.

mroseite.occurrence: Very rare in a hydrothermal Au–Te deposit (Moctezuma mine, Mexico).
mroseite.etymology: To honor Mary Emma Mrose (1910–2003), American mineralogist, U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C.

muckeite.occurrence: In dump material at a polymetallic hydrothermal deposit, topotactically relacing lapieite.
muckeite.etymology: Honors Dr. Arno M¨ ucke (1937– ), German mineralogist, Mineralogical-Petrological Institute, G¨ ottingen University, G¨ ottingen, Germany, for his work in systematic and ore mineralogy.

muirite.occurrence: In sanbornite-quartz-bearing metamorphic rock (Fresno Co., California, USA).
muirite.etymology: For John Muir (1834{1914), American mountaineer, conservationist, and naturalist, whose name is intimately associated with the California Sierra Nevada.

mukhinite.occurrence: In marble associated with an iron deposit (Tashelginskoye deposit, Russia); a late-stage mineral in garnet-bearing metamorphic rocks (Kuznetsk, Kazakhstan).
mukhinite.etymology: In honor of Aleksei Stepanovich Mukhin (1910{1974), geologist with the West Siberian Geological Survey.

mullerite.occurrence: A secondary, oxidation-zone mineral presumed to be formed by oxidation of earlier formed tellurides, most likely hessite, with chalcopyrite and galena.
mullerite.etymology: Honors Franz-Joseph Müller, Freiherr von Reichenstein or Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein (1740 or 1742 to 1825 or 1826), an Austrian mineralogist and mining engineer who discovered tellurium in 1782.

mullite.occurrence: In fused argillaceous inclusions in Tertiary eruptive rocks (Isle of Mull, Scotland); as microscopic inclusions in sillimanite in pelitic inclusions in a tonalite (Val Sissone, Italy); in a complex assemblage of emerylike rocks (Sithean Sluaigh, Scotland).
mullite.etymology: For its type locality on the Isle of Mull, Scotland.

mummeite.occurrence: In hydrothermal base-metal sulﬁde vein deposits.
mummeite.etymology: To honor Dr. William Gustav Mumme (1936– ), Australian mineralogist, C.S.I.R.O., Melbourne, Australia, who ﬁrst studied the mineral, for his work with sulfosalts.

munakataite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the weathering zone of a polymetallic sulfide deposit.
munakataite.etymology: For the city of Munakata, where the Kato mine, source of the first specimens, is located.

mundite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized uraniferous zone of a complex granite pegmatite.
mundite.etymology: Honors Professor Walter Mund (1892–1956), radiochemist, Catholic University of Louvain, Louvain, Belgium.

mundrabillaite.occurrence: Derived from bat guano and urine in caves.
mundrabillaite.etymology: For Mundrabilla Station, nearby the Petrogale Cave, Western Australia.

munirite.occurrence: On sandstone, presumably formed from oxidation of vanadium-bearing primary uranium minerals.
munirite.etymology: Honors Munir Ahmad Khan, Chairman, Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission.

murakamiite.etymology: Honors Professor Emeritus Nobuhide Murakami (1923-1994) Department of Geology and Mineralogical Sciences, Faculty of Science, Yamaguchi University, Japan for his contributions to petrology and mineralogy, particularly the discovery of sugilite and katayamalite at Iwagi Islet.

murashkoite.occurrence: In a phosphide assemblage related to the Fe-Ni-P system in pyrometamorphic rocks (Hatrurim Formation).
murashkoite.etymology: Honors Mikhail Nikolaevich Murashko (b. 1952), for his contributions to the mineralogy of the Hatrurim Formation.

murataite-y.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in samples from the dump of a prospect in a pegmatite subjected to alkali metasomatism (St. Peters Dome, Colorado, USA); in pegmatite in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif (Burpala massif, Russia).
murataite-y.etymology: To honor Kiguma Jack Murata (1909– ), geochemist, U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California, USA, for his work on rare-earth chemistry.

murchisite.occurrence: A low-temperature phase (~327 °C in the Cr-S system), probably formed from higher temperature Cr1-xS exsolved or expelled from a Cr-S-bearing, metal-rich spherule included in forsteritic olivine grains that were probably derived from chondrule fragments.

murdochite.etymology: In honor of Professor Joseph Murdoch (1890–1973), American mineralogist, University of California, Los Angeles, California, USA.

murmanite.occurrence: In pegmatites and associated igneous rocks of alkalic complexes, as a primary magmatic mineral or altered from lomonosovite.
murmanite.etymology: For the Murman coast on the northern side of the Kola Peninsula, Russia.

murunskite.occurrence: In rocks that have undergone intensive potassium metasomatism.
murunskite.etymology: For the locality in the Murun massif, Russia.

muscovite.occurrence: A common rock-forming mineral, in phyllites, schists, and gneisses; in granites, granite pegmatites, and aplites. Formed from other minerals under hydrothermal conditions; may be detrital or authigenic.
muscovite.etymology: From \Muscovy glass," for an occurrence in the old province of Muscovy, Russia.

museumite.occurrence: Fills cavities and vugs in nagyágite with which its contacts are sharp with evidence of replacement. Found on a museum specimen from a hydrothermal gold-telluride deposit.
museumite.etymology: Honors all museums in the world that preserve their old samples with care and accuracy.

mushistonite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a tin deposit, replacing stannite (Mushiston deposit, Tajikistan); from a zoned pegmatite (Etta mine, South Dakota, USA).
mushistonite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Mushiston deposit, Tajikistan.

muskoxite.occurrence: In thin veinlets in serpentinite from a layered ultramaﬁc complex.
muskoxite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Muskox intrusion, Canada.

muthmannite.occurrence: In close intergrowths with other tellurides, especially krennerite, in epithermal hydrothermal veins, and in ores enriched by secondary processes (S˘ ac˘ ar ˆ ımb, Romania); replacing calaverite (Baia-de-Arie¸ s, Romania).
muthmannite.etymology: To honor the chemist and crystallographer, Professor Friedrich Wilhelm Muthmann (1861–1913), Technische Hochschule, Munich, Germany.

mutinaite.etymology: From Mutina, the ancient Latin name of Modena, Italy, a center of modern zeolite research. Type: Museum of Natural History, University of Pisa, Italy (15520).

nabalamprophyllite.occurrence: In peralkaline pegmatite dikes cutting alkaline ultramafic rocks.
assoc_parsed: it forms aggregates with pectolite and cancrinite
often intergrown with lorenzenite. in nepheline-bearing pegmatite
it forms radial aggregates of lamellar crystals with lorenzenite
nabalamprophyllite.etymology: For its composition (Na and Ba) and relation to other lamprophyllite-group minerals; a suffix indicates the monoclinic polytype.

nabalamprophyllite -2o.etymology: For its composition (Na and Ba) and relation to other lamprophyllite-group minerals; a suffix indicates the orthorhombic polytype.

nabalamprophyllite-2m.occurrence: In peralkaline pegmatite dikes cutting alkaline ultramafic rocks.
assoc_parsed: it forms aggregates with pectolite and cancrinite
often intergrown with lorenzenite. in nepheline-bearing pegmatite
it forms radial aggregates of lamellar crystals with lorenzenite
nabalamprophyllite-2m.etymology: For its composition (Na and Ba) and relation to other lamprophyllite-group minerals; a suffix indicates the monoclinic polytype.

nabaphite.occurrence: A rare late-stage hydrothermal mineral in cavities in ijolite-urtite pegmatite in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
nabaphite.etymology: For sodium, NAtrium, BArium, and PHosphorus in the composition.

nabesite.occurrence: In albite-lined cavities within tugtupite-bearing albitites.
nabesite.etymology: Comprised of the chemical symbols of the mineral’s three essential cations - Na, Be, Si.

nabiasite.occurrence: In an upper-greenschist-facies metamorphosed syn-sedimentary exhalative Mn deposit in radiolarian cherts along veinlets mineralized by hydrothermal remobilization.
nabiasite.etymology: For the hamlet of Nabias near the deposit.

nabimusaite.occurrence: High-temperature syn-pyrometamorphic alteration of primary ye’elimite-larnite rocks during combustion events as a result of the reaction of potassium-enriched, sulfate-bearing melt with larnite and ellestadite.
nabimusaite.etymology: For the village, Nabi Musa, near the locality that produced the first specimens.

nabokoite.occurrence: A rare sublimate formed in a volcanic fumarole.
nabokoite.etymology: Honoring Sof’ya Ivanovna Naboko (1909– ), Institute of Volcanology, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskii, Russia, Russian volcanologist who ﬁrst collected the mineral.

nacaphite.occurrence: A rare late-stage hydrothermal mineral in ijolite-urtite pegmatite.
nacaphite.etymology: For sodium, NAtrium, CAlcium, and PHosphorus in the composition.

nacareniobsite-ce.occurrence: In alkaline undersaturated igneous rocks and oversaturated peralkaline granites.
nacareniobsite-ce.etymology: For sodium, NAtrium, CAlcium, Rare Earths, NIOBium, and Silicon in its composition; a suffix indicates that cerium is the dominant rare earth element.

nacrite.etymology: From the French nacre, for mother of pearl, in allusion to its appearance.

nadorite.occurrence: As an alteration product of other antimony-bearing minerals in hydrothermal mineral deposits.
nadorite.etymology: For its original occurrence at Djebel Nador, Algeria.

nagashimalite.occurrence: In ¯ssures cutting massive rhodonite ore in a bedded manganese deposit.
nagashimalite.etymology: For pioneer Japanese amateur mineralogist, Otokichi Nagashima (1890{1969).

nagelschmidtite.occurrence: In a complex assemblage of high-temperature contact metamorphosed sedimentary rocks.
nagelschmidtite.etymology: For Guenther Nagelschmidt, chemist who ¯rst reported the synthetic compound in slags.

nagyagite.etymology: For the S˘ ac˘ ar ˆ ımb (Nagy´ ag), Romania locality.

nahcolite.occurrence: A precipitate from hot springs; as eﬄorescences around saline lakes and in brines; formed at a late stage in diﬀerentiated alkalic massifs; as a solid in liquid inclusions in a variety of other mineral species.

nahpoite.occurrence: An alteration product of mari´ cite in nodules in phosphatic ironstone (Yukon Territory, Canada); in sodalite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in diﬀerentiated alkalic massifs (Kola Peninsula, Russia).
nahpoite.etymology: For the principal chemical components, sodium, NAtrium, Hydrogen, Phosphorus, and Oxygen.

nakauriite.occurrence: As fracture ﬁllings in serpentinite (Nakauri, Japan); on chromatite from serpentinite (Hagdale quarry, Scotland).
nakauriite.etymology: For the original material found at Nakauri, Japan.

naldrettite.occurrence: In drill core through the contact zone between massive and disseminated sulfide mineralization hosted by amphibolite and serpentinite replacing pyroxenite and peridotite.
naldrettite.etymology: Honors Professor Anthony J. Naldrett (b. 1933), University of Toronto and past President of both the Mineralogical Association of Canada and the International Mineralogical Association for significant contributions to our understanding of platinum-group element (PGE) deposits.

nalipoite.occurrence: Very rare in sodalite syenite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex.
nalipoite.etymology: For the principal chemical components in the composition, sodium NAtrium, LIthium, Phosphorus, and Oxygen.

nalivkinite.occurrence: In fenitized amphibole-quartz-feldspar rock from a complex alkaline massif.
nalivkinite.etymology: Honors Dmitry Vasiljevich Nalivkin (1889-1982), participant of the Pamiro-Tadjik expedition (1920-1930) and author on the geology, stratigraphy and paleontology of Central Asia.

namansilite.occurrence: In low-grade metamorphosed and highly oxidized Mn, Na-rich sediments.
namansilite.etymology: For sodium, NAtrium; MANganese; and SILicon in the formula.

nambulite.occurrence: In veinlets cutting braunite ores in chert (Funakozawa mine, Japan).
nambulite.etymology: For Professor Matsuo Nambu, Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan.

namibite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in bismuth-bearing hydrothermal polymetallic mineral deposits and granite pegmatites.
namibite.etymology: For the Namib Desert, along the coast of Namibia.

namuwite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral formed in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal Cu–Zn bearing mineral deposits; may be derived from metallic slags.
namuwite.etymology: For the NAtional MUseum of Wales, Cardiﬀ, Wales, in the collection of which the type specimen was noted.

nanlingite.occurrence: Along a contact between greisenized granite and dolomitic limestone.
nanlingite.etymology: For the locality, Nanling area, China, that produced the first samples.

nanpingite.occurrence: In veinlets in the pollucite-rich middle zone of a muscovite-albite-s podumene pegmatite.
nanpingite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Nanping area, China.

nantokite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in hydrothermal copper-bearing deposits; rarely in volcanic sublimates.
nantokite.etymology: For its occurrence near Nantoko, Chile.

naquite.occurrence: In the heavy mineral fraction of a podiform chromitite deposit in the peridotite of an ophiolitic harzburgite. Likely the product of a strongly reducing environment and possibly are xenocrysts derived from a mantle source.
naquite.etymology: For Naqu (Nagchu) Prefecture, Tibet, near the locality that produced the first samples .

narsarsukite.occurrence: In pegmatite (Narss^ arssuk, Greenland); in quartz veins in syenite intruding limestone (Sweetgrass Hills, Montana, USA); in hornfels, igneous breccia, and marble xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
narsarsukite.etymology: For the Greenland locality at Narss^ arssuk (Narsarsuk).

nashite.occurrence: As efflorescences on sandstone in the underground workings of a roll-front type uranium vanadium deposit, from the oxidation of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a moist environment, possibly controlled by the presence of organic matter and phases such as pyrite.
nashite.etymology: Honors Dr. Barbara P. Nash (b. 1944), Professor of Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA., for her many contributions to the geochemistry and petrogenesis of volcanic systems, as well as, for her contributions to the description of several new minerals.

nasinite.occurrence: As scales on piping in a geothermal ﬁeld.
nasinite.etymology: To honor Rafaello Nasini (1854–1931), Italian chemist.

nasledovite.occurrence: A rare fracture ﬁlling in oxidized granodiorite porphyry which also hosts polymetallic ores.
nasledovite.etymology: To honor Professor Boris Nikolaevich Nasledov (1885–1942), geologist, for his investigations of the mineral resources of the Chatkal-Kuramin region, Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan.

nasonite.occurrence: A rare mineral, formed under hydrothermal conditions, cutting franklinitewillemite ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit (Franklin, New Jersey, USA); in calcite-¯lled veins in a metamorphosed Fe{Mn deposit (Lºangban, Sweden).
nasonite.etymology: For Frank Lewis Nason (1856{1928), American geologist, Geological Survey of New Jersey, USA.

nastrophite.occurrence: In pegmatitic veinlets in cancrinite and nepheline syenites.
nastrophite.etymology: For sodium, NAtrium, STROntium, and PHosphorus in the composition.

nataliakulikite.occurrence: In high-temperature, pyrometamorphic, larnite-gehlenite rock (HT-region of the spurrite-merwinite facies).
nataliakulikite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Natalia Artyemovna Kulik (b. 1933), Emeritus Professor of Mineralogy, Novosibirsk State University, an expert in mineralogical descriptions of granitic pegmatites, minerals of radioactive and rare-earth elements, and archaeometry.

nataliyamalikite.etymology: Honors Natalja Alexandrovna Malik (b. 1981), Institute of Volcanology and Seismology of the Far Eastern Branch of The Russian Academy of Sciences in Petropavlovsk -Kamchatsky, Russia. She studies fumarolic activity, volcanic gases, explosive eruptions, tephra, and ash leachates .

natalyite.occurrence: In Cr, V-rich diopside-quartz rocks that are part of a Precambrian metamorphic complex (Slyudyanka complex, Russia).
natalyite.etymology: In honor of the geologist Nataliya Vasil'evna Frolova (1907{1960), geologist, Irkutsk University, Irkutsk, Russia.

natanite.occurrence: Formed by oxidation of earlier tin sulﬁdes in tin deposits.
natanite.etymology: Honors Professor Natan (Antolii) Il’ich Ginzburg (1917–1984), mineralogist and geologist, All-Union Research Institute of Mineral Resources, Moscow, Russia, student of oxidized tin deposits.

natisite.occurrence: In natrolite-ussingite veins cutting alkalic rocks in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
natisite.etymology: For sodium, NAtrium, TItanium, and SIlicon in the composition.

natrite.occurrence: Locally abundant in deep drillholes in pegmatites occurring in diﬀerentiated alkaline massifs (Kola Peninsula, Russia); in sodalite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
natrite.etymology: For sodium, natrium, the sole cation in the chemical formula of the mineral.

natroalunite.occurrence: Less common than alunite, formed by solfataric or hydrothermal sulfate-bearing solutions reacting with clays, rarely with sillimanite; may be in laterites and as an authigenic sedimentary mineral.
natroalunite.etymology: As the sodium, natrium, analog of alunite.

natroaphthitalite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
natroaphthitalite.etymology: The prefix indicates the analogue of aphthitalite with total Na > K and in the Y site.

natroapophyllite.occurrence: In skarns, banded between granite and marble, of a contact metamorphic mineral deposit.
natroapophyllite.etymology: For sodium, natrium, in the composition, and its relation to other apophyllite species.

natrochalcite.occurrence: A rare mineral typically formed in an arid climate in the oxidized zone of copper deposits.
natrochalcite.etymology: From the Latin for sodium, natrium, and the Greek for copper, chalkos, in the composition.

natrodufrenite.etymology: For essential sodium, natrium, and its relation to dufr´ enite.

natrofairchildite.occurrence: In a carbonatite complex, at depths below 70 m.
natrofairchildite.etymology: As the sodium, natrium, analog of fairchildite.

natrojarosite.occurrence: Formed typically in the oxidized zone of mineral deposits by alteration of pyrite in the presence of sodium; rarely as a volcanic sublimate.
natrojarosite.etymology: As the sodium, natrium, analog of jarosite.

natrolemoynite.occurrence: Late stage in pegmatite cutting nepheline syenite.
natrolemoynite.etymology: Alludes to the Na dominance (natro) and polymorphic relationship to lemoynite. Type: Canadian Museum of Nature, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada (81534).

natrolite.occurrence: In cavities in amygdaloidal basalts and related igneous rocks, one of the last minerals to form; ¯lls seams in granite, gneiss, and syenite.
natrolite.etymology: From the Latin natron, for the sodium content.

natromarkeyite.occurrence: Secondary phase on asphaltum in sandstones by oxidation of primary uraninite, montroseite, and coffinite in a humid underground environment.
natromarkeyite.etymology: The prefix indicates the sodium-analogue of markeyite, named for the Markey mine.

natromontebrasite.etymology: For its content of sodium, natrium, and relation to montebrasite.

natron.occurrence: Formed on the margins around soda-rich lakes, or as a precipitate on lake bottoms during cold weather; as an eﬄorescence on lavas; rare in diﬀerentiated alkaline massifs.
natron.etymology: From nitrum, a name from antiquity.

natronambulite.occurrence: In banded ore of a contact metamorphosed bedded manganese deposit, and as an accessory mineral in an albite-microcline-qu artz pegmatite cutting the ore (Tanohata mine, Japan).
natronambulite.etymology: For sodium, natrium, in its composition, and its relation to nambulite.

natroniobite.occurrence: Replacing perovskite and pyrochlore in dolomite carbonatites.
natroniobite.etymology: For sodium, NATRium, and NIOBium in the composition.

natropalermoite.occurrence: In a complex, phosphate-bearing granitic pegmatite, formed by hydrothermal alteration of primary triphylite pods in the core-margin zone of the pegmatite.
natropalermoite.etymology: Reflects the presence of sodium (natrium) and the structural isomorphism to palermoite.

natropharmacoalumite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in cavities and fractures in quartz in an epithermal gold-bearing alunite deposit.
natropharmacoalumite.etymology: As the Na (natro) and Al (alum) end-member in the pharmacosiderite supergroup.

natrophilite.occurrence: A rare mineral, replacing lithiophilite, in a complex granite pegmatite.
natrophilite.etymology: For its content of sodium, natrium, and from the Greek for a friend.

natrophosphate.occurrence: A rare mineral in ijolite-urtite pegmatite in a diﬀerentiated alkaline massif (Kola Peninsula, Russia); in sodalite xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada); in miarolitic cavities in phonolite (Aris quarry, Namibia).
natrophosphate.etymology: For sodium, natrium, and phosphate in the composition.

natrosilite.occurrence: In pegmatites in nepheline syenites in di®erentiated alkalic massifs (Kola Peninsula, Russia); in sodalite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
natrosilite.etymology: For sodium, NATRium, and SILicon in the composition.

natrosulfatourea.occurrence: On rock surfaces as the result of evaporation under the conditions prevailing underground (Rowley mine).
natrosulfatourea.etymology: Reflects its composition: sodium (natro), sulfate (sulfato), urea (urea).

natrotantite.occurrence: In albite units of granite pegmatites.
natrotantite.etymology: For sodium, NATRium, and TANTalum in the composition.

natrotitanite.occurrence: In the wall rock zone of an alkaline granite associated with a granitic massif.
natrotitanite.etymology: For a titanite structure with Na(Y,REE)-dominant in the Ca site.

natrowalentaite.occurrence: On fracture surfaces in iron-stained heavily weathered rock as a product of supergene alteration of primary sulfide and arsenide minerals.
natrowalentaite.etymology: The prefix, natro, indicates dominant sodium replacing calcium in walentaite.

natroxalate.occurrence: In a hydrothermally altered pegmatite in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
natroxalate.etymology: For sodium, natrium, in the composition, and as a naturally occurring oxalate.

naujakasite.etymology: For the locality of original discovery, Naujakasik, Greenland.

naumannite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins deﬁcient in sulfur, associated with other selenides, quartz, and carbonates.
naumannite.etymology: For German mineralogist and crystallographer Carl Friedrich Naumann (1797–1873).

navajoite.occurrence: In the highly oxidized portion of a Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposit, in a stream channel ﬁlled with conglomeratic and silty sandstone; thought to be an oxidation product of corvusite.
navajoite.etymology: For the Navajo Indians, on whose reservation the mineral was ﬁrst found.

nechelyustovite.formula_html: (Na   )   2Ba4Ti4Nb4(Na11   )Ti4(Si2O7)8O8(OH)8(H2O)12
nechelyustovite.occurrence: From the natrolite core of hydrothermally altered pegmatite emplaced in nepheline syenites near their contact with ijolite-urtites.
nechelyustovite.etymology: Honors Georgii N. Nechelyustov (b. 1939), Russian electron microprobe analyst.

nefedovite.occurrence: In pegmatitic segregations in nepheline syenite in a diﬀerentiated alkalic massif.
nefedovite.etymology: To honor Dr. Yevgeny I. Nefedov (1910–1976), Russian mineralogist, St. Petersburg, Russia, involved in the discovery of a number of Kola minerals.

negevite.occurrence: In a phosphide assemblage related to the Fe-Ni-P system in a pyrometamorphic complex (Hatrurim Formation).
negevite.etymology: For the locality, the Negev Desert, Israel, were the mineral was found.

neighborite.occurrence: An authigenic mineral, formed under aluminum-deficient conditions in dolomitic oil shale (South Ouray, Utah, USA); in metamorphosed tuff and clayey carbonate sediments (Ural Mountains, Russia); in miarolitic cavities in peralkalic granite (Lake Gjerdingen, Norway); in cavities in pegmatite and hornfels in an alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint- Hilaire).
neighborite.etymology: Honors Frank Neighbor, district geologist of Sun Oil Co., Salt Lake City, Utah, USA, for his assistance in providing samples.

nekoite.occurrence: In a contact metamorphosed limestone deposit (Crestmore, California, USA).
nekoite.etymology: An anagram of OKENite, for which it was originally mistaken.

nekrasovite.occurrence: In ore aggregates within propylitic andesites and dacites (Khayragatsch deposit, Uzbekistan).
nekrasovite.etymology: To honor Ivan Yakovlevich Nekrasov (1929– ), Russian mineralogist, Institute of Experimental Mineralogy, Moscow, Russia.

nelenite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit, within pegmatitic textured masses, and as calcite-cemented fragments in a breccia probably derived from the pegmatitic material.
nelenite.etymology: In honor of Joseph A. Nelen, chemist at the Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., USA.

neltnerite.occurrence: In a vein with minerals containing manganese and calcium (Tachgagalt, Morocco).
neltnerite.etymology: For Louis Neltner, pioneer student of mineral deposits of the High Atlas Mountains, Morocco.

nenadkevichite.occurrence: Between crystals of microcline in a natrolite-albite-rich pegmatite in nepheline syenite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia); in pegmatites, cavities in igneous breccia, hornfels, and marble xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
nenadkevichite.etymology: For Konstantin Avtonomovich Nenadkevich (1880{1963), Russian mineralogist and geochemist, A.E. Fersman Mineralogical Museum, Moscow, Russia.

neotocite.occurrence: An alteration product of manganese-bearing silicate minerals.
neotocite.etymology: From the Greek, meaning of recent origin, as it is an alteration product.

nepheline.occurrence: Characteristic of alkalic rocks as nepheline syenites and gneisses, alkalic gabbros; in sodium-rich hypabyssal rocks, tu®s and lavas, and pegmatites; as a product of sodium metasomatism.
nepheline.etymology: From the Greek for cloud, as it becomes cloudy when treated with strong acid.

nepouite.occurrence: An alteration product of nickel-rich ultrama¯c rocks.
nepouite.etymology: After the locality, N¶epoui, New Caledonia.

nepskoeite.occurrence: In anhydrite-halite rock in a salt deposit.
nepskoeite.etymology: For the locality, the Nepskoye salt deposit.

neptunite.occurrence: In natrolite veins cutting a glaucophane schist inclusion in a serpentinite body (San Benito Co., California, USA).
neptunite.etymology: For Neptune, sea-god of Roman mythology; so named because of its close association at the type occurrence with aegirine, the name of which derives from Àgir, the Scandinavian sea-god.

neskevaaraite-fe.occurrence: In alkaline igneous rocks sometimes intergrown with labuntsovite-Fe or in hydrothermally altered carbonatite veins.
neskevaaraite-fe.etymology: For the locality (Neskevaara Hill) and Fe-dominant composition of the D structural site.

nesquehonite.occurrence: Typically recently formed under near-surface conditions, as eﬄorescences in coal mines; in fractures in serpentinites; deposits around springs; in caves due to loss of CO 2 in waters.
nesquehonite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence at Nesquehoning, Pennsylvania, USA.

nestolaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit of the Colorado Plateau type.
nestolaite.etymology: Honors Fabrizio Nestola (b. 1972), Italian mineralogist and crystallographer , Department of Geosciences, University of Padua, Italy.

neustadtelite.occurrence: In vugs in quartz collected on waste piles from mining activity.
neustadtelite.etymology: For the locality, Schneeberg-Neustädtel, near where the studied samples were collected.

nevadaite.occurrence: A weathering-derived mineral above a low grade, disseminated gold deposit in hydrothermally altered sedimentary rocks.
assoc_parsed: intermediate members of the strengite-variscite series
nevadaite.etymology: For the US state from which the first specimens were collected.

nevskite.etymology: For the Nevskoye deposit in Russia.

newberyite.occurrence: In caves, formed directly from bat guano.
newberyite.etymology: To honor James Cosmo Newbery (1843-1895), geologist, Melbourne, Australia, who initially found the mineral.

neyite.occurrence: In late-forming crosscutting hydrothermal quartz veins in a quartz-molybdenite stockwork (Lime Creek deposit, Canada); in mesozonal synmetamorphic quartz veins (Johnny Lyon Hills, Arizona, USA).
neyite.etymology: To honor Charles Stuart Ney (1918–1975), geologist in charge of early exploration at the Lime Creek deposit.

niahite.occurrence: A rare mineral, derived from the breakdown of bat guano (Niah Great Cave, Sarawak, Malaysia).
niahite.etymology: For the place of its ﬁrst-noted occurrence, the Niah Great Cave, Malaysia.

niasite.occurrence: Secondary, likely formed from the breakdown of primary nickeline under dry (low relative humidity) and oxidizing (high oxygen fugacity) conditions.
niasite.etymology: For the elements (excluding oxygen) in the mineral's composition: nickel (Ni) + arsenic (As).

nickel.occurrence: In serpentinized ultramaﬁc rocks as a result of low-temperature hydrothermal activity.
nickel.etymology: From the German nickel, demon, from a contraction of kupfernickel,o r Devil’s copper, as the mineral was believed to contain copper but yielded none.

nickelaustinite.etymology: For the predominance of nickel in the composition and relation to austinite.

nickelbischofite.occurrence: As an alteration product on the surface of drill core from an ultramaﬁc intrusion containing low-grade nickel mineralization, formed after storage (Amos, Canada); as a volcanic sublimate (Mt. Shirane, Japan).
nickelbischofite.etymology: As the compositional nickel analog of bischoﬁte, with which it is, however, not isostructural.

nickelblodite.occurrence: By evaporation of ﬂuids containing Na, Ni, and SO 4.
nickelblodite.etymology: For its relation to bl¨ odite, with Ni> Mg.

nickelboussingaultite.occurrence: In an underground nickel ore stockpile, around and on a wooden timber, and on “limonite” (Noril’sk, Russia).
nickelboussingaultite.etymology: As the nickel-bearing analog of boussingaultite.

nickelhexahydrite.occurrence: Precipitated from mine waters in the bottom of an open-pit nickel mine, and on nickel-bearing gabbro-dolerite rocks in the oxidation zone (Noril’sk region, Russia); in shear zones in talc overlying ultramaﬁc rocks (Lahnaslampi deposit, Finland); formed from H 2O solution below 31.5 ◦C.
nickelhexahydrite.etymology: As the nickel-dominant analog of hexahydrite.

nickeline.occurrence: A minor component of Ni–Cu ores in high-temperature hydrothermal veins; massive and in disseminations in peridotite and norite.
nickeline.etymology: From the German kupfernickel,o r Devil’s copper, as the mineral was believed to contain copper but yielded none.

nickellotharmeyerite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of polymetallic ore deposits.
nickellotharmeyerite.etymology: The prefix, nickel, indicates the nickel analog of lotharmeyerite.

nickelpicromerite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the fractures of slightly weathered actinolite-talc schist containing partially vermiculitized biotite and partially altered, nickle-bearing sulfides.
nickelpicromerite.etymology: For a member of the picromerite group with essential nickel.

nickelschneebergite.etymology: For the essential presence of nickel in the compound and relation to schneebergite.

nickelskutterudite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins deposited at medium temperature.
nickelskutterudite.etymology: As the nickel member of the series; skutterudite from its locality at Skutterud, Norway.

nickeltalmessite.occurrence: Secondary in the weathered zone of a hydrothermal arsenopyrite-glaucodot-cobaltite deposit.
assoc_parsed: a mineral of the chromite - manganochromite series
nickeltalmessite.etymology: Identifies the nickel-dominant analogue of talmessite.

nickeltsumcorite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal deposit containing gersdorffite and galena.

nickeltyrrellite.occurrence: As fracture fillings in krut’aite-penroseite by oxidizing, low-T, Cu-Ni-Co-Pb-bearing fluids altering quijarroite-hansblockite-watkinsonite-clausthalite-penroseite aggregates.
nickeltyrrellite.etymology: The prefix identifies the Ni-analogue of tyrrellite.

nickelzippeite.occurrence: Typically as secondary coatings on mine walls, derived from oxidation of uranium-bearing primary Ni–Co sulﬁdes.
nickelzippeite.etymology: For its dominant content of nickel and relation to other zippeite group species.

nickenichite.occurrence: In a cavity in volcanic scoria.
nickenichite.etymology: For the village of Nickenich, Germany, nearby the Nickenicher Sattel volcano.

nickolayite.occurrence: An accessory phase in fused clinopyroxene-plagioclase rocks. Probably connected to co-reduction of molybdenum- and phosphorus-bearing minerals during high-temperature pyrometamorphism.
assoc_parsed: powellite. distribution from the jizah district
nickolayite.etymology: Honors Dieter Nickolay (b. 1941), German mineral collector and mineralogist, for his contributions to systematic mineralogy.

nicksobolevite.occurrence: In crusts deposited from gases escaping an active fumarole on a basaltic volcano.
nicksobolevite.etymology: Honors Academician Nikolay (Nick) Vladimirovich Sobolev (b. 1935), for his contributions to mineralogy and petrology.

niedermayrite.occurrence: Very rare in the oxidation zone of a zinc-rich hydrothermal orebody in brecciated marble, formed as an alteration product of chalcopyrite and greenockite.
niedermayrite.etymology: To honor Dr. Gerhard Niedermayr (1941– ), Curator, Natural History Museum, Vienna, Austria.

nielsbohrite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed near oxidizing uraninite.
nielsbohrite.etymology: Honors Niels Hendrik David Bohr (1885-1962), Danish physicist.

nielsenite.occurrence: As the crystallized products of immiscible melts in thoelitic gabbro and that form ed at temperatures at of below 508° C, in a highly differentiated layered intrusion.
assoc_parsed: bornite with trace ni-co and zn sulfides
nielsenite.etymology: Honors Troels F.D. Nielsen (b. 1950), a geologist with the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland.

nierite.occurrence: A very rare component of enstatite chondrite and chondrite meteorites, probably formed by exsolution during metamorphism.
nierite.etymology: Honors Alfred Otto Carl Nier (1912-1994), Professor of Chemistry at the University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA, a founder of mass spectroscopy.

nifontovite.occurrence: In a skarn formed by quartz diorite intruding limestone (Novofrolovo mine, Russia); near gehlenite-spurrite skarn formed by hydrothermal alteration (Fuka, Japan).
nifontovite.etymology: Honors Roman Vladimirovich Nifontov (1901-1960), Russian geologist who studied sedimentary and placer deposits.

niggliite.etymology: In honor of Professor Paul Niggli (1888–1953), Swiss mineralogist, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland.

nikischerite.occurrence: On and within clay matrix in a hydrothermal vein polymetallic tin deposit.
nikischerite.etymology: Honors American geologist and mineral dealer Anthony (Tony) J. Nikischer (b. 1949), who discovered the mineral and who has for many years supplied rare minerals for scientific study.

nimite.occurrence: In a small tabular body of nickeliferous serpentinite, probably a contact deposit, along the junction of quartzite and an ultrama¯c intrusive; it appears to have formed at »730 ±C and < 2 kbar during thermal metamorphism, possibly of a nickel-rich meteorite.
nimite.etymology: An acronym for the National Institute of Metallurgy of South Africa.

ningyoite.occurrence: The principal uranium mineral, as coatings and ﬁlling cavities in carbonaceous conglomerate (Ningyo mine, Japan); in uranium deposits in organic-rich conglomerate-sandstone-mudstone (British Columbia, Canada).
ningyoite.etymology: For Ningyo Pass, Japan, where the mine in which the mineral was ﬁrst found is located.

niningerite.occurrence: In less extensively metamorphosed enstatite chondrite meteorites.
niningerite.etymology: In honor of Harvey Harlow Nininger (1887–1986), of Sedona, Arizona, USA, for his contributions to meteoritics.

nioboaeschynite-ce.occurrence: In quartz-arfvedsonite veinlets cutting fenites (Vishnevy Mountains, Russia); in heavy-mineral concentrates (Tofty tin belt, Alaska, USA).
nioboaeschynite-ce.etymology: For similarity to aeschynite but with NIOBium greater than titanium, with cerium as the dominant rare-earth element.

nioboaeschynite-y.occurrence: In calcite veins in regionally metamorphosed metasedimentary rocks that may have undergone fenitization-like metasomatism.
nioboaeschynite-y.etymology: For the dominant B-site cation (Nb) and principal rare earth element (Y) in a member of the aeschynite group.

niobocarbide.occurrence: In hydrothermal uranium deposits (Saskatchewan, Canada); in gold deposits in metamorphosed greenstones (Kalgoorlie, Western Australia).
niobocarbide.etymology: To honor Dr. Thomas Brennan Nolan (1901–1992), formerly Director of the U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C., USA.

nioboheftetjernite.etymology: The prefix identifies the Nb-analogue of heftetjernite.

nioboholtite.occurrence: In the internal portion of a complex zoned granitic pegmatite.
nioboholtite.etymology: For the composition and the relationship to holtite.

niobokupletskite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in nepheline syenite pegmatite in an alkaline complex.
niobokupletskite.etymology: The prefix, niobo, indicates the niobium analog of kupletskite.

niobophyllite.occurrence: As discontinuous seams and polycrystalline aggregates within a paragneiss intruded by an alkalic syenite (Seal Lake, Canada).
niobophyllite.etymology: For its niobium content and the Greek word phyllite, meaning leaf, in allusion to its micaceous habit.

niocalite.etymology: For NIObium and CALcium in the composition.

nipalarsite.occurrence: In sulfide-bearing, intercumulus orthopyroxenite of a layered ultramafic intrusion.
nipalarsite.etymology: Derived from the names of the essential components: nickel, paladium and arsenic.

nisbite.occurrence: Very rare in a high-grade base-metal sulﬁde deposit in altered maﬁc rock (Trout Bay, Canada); in Pb–Zn–Cu–Ag ore deposits remobilized by hydrothermal solutions from younger granite emplacement (Bergslagen, Sweden).
nisbite.etymology: For the composition, NIckel and SB, from the chemical symbol for antimony, stibium.

nishanbaevite.occurrence: A sublimates at an active volcanic fumarole.
assoc_parsed: hematite. distribution from the arsenatnaya fumarole
second scoria cone of the northern breakthrough of the great tolbachik fissure eruption
nishanbaevite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Tursun Prnazorovich Nishanbaev (1955-2017), former Head of the Natural History Museum, Ilmen Natural Reserve, Miass, Russia, for contributions to the mineralogy of anthropogenic counterparts of volcanic fumaroles formed on the burning dumps of coal mines.

nisnite.occurrence: In a rodingite dike in an asbestos deposit.
nisnite.etymology: For the chemical symbols of the essential components nickel, Ni, and tin, Sn.

nissonite.occurrence: A very rare mineral in a copper prospect (Panoche Valley, California, USA); in a Precambrian sedimentary iron deposit (Iron Monarch quarry, Australia).
nissonite.etymology: To honor William H. Nisson (1912–1965), amateur mineralogist, mineral collector and dealer, of Petaluma, California, USA, who ﬁrst noted the mineral.

niter.occurrence: In some caves, typically formed by bacterial action on animal matter, as bat guano, or from vegetable matter, such as humus, exposed to seeping groundwater; an eﬄorescence on soils or cliﬀ faces in arid regions.
niter.etymology: A name from antiquity, used to distinguish potassium nitrate from sodium nitrate.

nitratine.occurrence: Principally in bedded deposits formed in playas; in caves, deposited from seeping groundwater leaching nitrates from overlying rocks, especially in very dry and cold climates.

nitrobarite.occurrence: Noted on a museum specimen, probably from a nitrate deposit.
nitrobarite.etymology: For NITRate and BARium in the composition.

nitrocalcite.occurrence: Typically formed in caves and on alkaline soils, which may be seasonal.
nitrocalcite.etymology: For NITROgen and CALCium in the composition.

nitromagnesite.occurrence: A rare cave deposit in humidities up to 78%, typically formed as a leachate of bat guano; may be a component of mixed salts.
nitromagnesite.etymology: For NITROgen and MAGNESium in the composition.

nitroplumbite.occurrence: Underground in a secondary efflorescent assemblage on asphaltite and montroseiteand corvusite-bearing sandstone in a Colorado Plateau-type, roll-front, uranium deposit.
nitroplumbite.etymology: For its chemical composition, a basic nitrate (nitro) of lead (plumbum).

nitscheite.occurrence: Secondary, associated with post-mining oxidation of asphaltum-rich sandstone beds laced with uraninite and sulfides in a damp underground environment.
nitscheite.etymology: Honors German/American nuclear chemist Heino Nitsche (1949-2014) for his work on nuclear and radiochemistry of heavy elements, nuclear forensics, the chemistry of irradiated materials, and the confirmation of elements 114 (flerovium, Fl) and 117 (tennessine, Ts). In 2014, Nitsche received the Hevesy Medal, the premier international award of excellence for his achievements in radioanalytical and nuclear chemistry.

niveolanite.occurrence: A late stage mineral in cavities in the core of a hydrothermally altered peralkaline pegmatite.
niveolanite.etymology: From the Latin niveus, snow white, and lana, wool, in allusion to the typical habit.

nixonite.occurrence: In a heavily metasomatized pyroxenite xenolith in kimberlite, perhaps produced by a fractionated Na-rich kimberlitic melt that infiltrated a mantle-derived garnet pyroxenite and reacted with rutile during kimberlite crystallization.
nixonite.etymology: Honors Peter H. Nixon (b. 1935) retired Professor of Mantle Geology at Leeds University, U.K., for significant contributions to scientific knowledge on kimberlites and their mantle- and deep crustal-derived xenoliths. Nixon discovered the Letseng kimberlite, a world-famous source of large high-quality diamonds. He contributed to the model of orogenically emplaced mantle rocks from the diamond stability field, providing the first strong evidence for this process in the form of graphitized diamonds from the Beni Bousera peridotite massif.

nizamoffite.occurrence: A relatively late-formed phase from secondary alteration of primary triphylite and associated sphalerite in the core margin of a granitic pegmatite.
nizamoffite.etymology: Honors James W. Nizamoff (b. 1971) for his research on pegmatite mineralogy in general and on the phosphate mineralogy of the Palermo pegmatites. Nizamoff is one of the discoverers of this new mineral and provided the specimens used for its characterization.

nobleite.occurrence: Typically a recent incrustation produced by weathering of colemanite and priceite veins in altered olivine basalt and basaltic clastic rocks (near the De Bely mine, California, USA).
nobleite.etymology: To honor Dr. Levi Fatzinger Noble (1882-1965), geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, who studied the Death Valley borate deposits.

nolanite.occurrence: In hydrothermal uranium deposits (Saskatchewan, Canada); in gold deposits in metamorphosed greenstones (Kalgoorlie, Western Australia).
nolanite.etymology: To honor Dr. Thomas Brennan Nolan (1901-1992), formerly Director of the U.S. Geological Survey, Washington, D.C., USA.

nollmotzite.occurrence: Formed by precipitation from U-containing aqueous solutions under partially reducing conditions most probably enhanced by consumption of oxygen during the oxidation of abundant pyrite present in the gangue.
nollmotzite.etymology: Honors two German mineral collectors who found this new mineral. It combines the first four letters of their surnames: Markus Noller (b. 1977) and Reinhard Motzigemba (b. 1952).

nolzeite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral likely formed under alkaline conditions in vugs in altered sodalite syenite.
nolzeite.etymology: Honors Dr. Gert Nolze (b. 1960), a crystallographer at the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (BAM), Berlin, Germany, notably for his part in the development of the extensively used program Powdercell.

nontronite.occurrence: A weathering product of basalts, kimberlites, and other ultrama¯c igneous rocks; in poorly-drained volcanic ash soils; in some hydrothermally altered mineral deposits, midocean ridge basalts, and contact metamorphosed limestones. An authigenic mineral in recent marine sediments.
nontronite.etymology: For the occurrence near Saint-Pardoux, Nontron Arrondissement, France.

noonkanbahite.occurrence: Lines the walls of cavities in alkaline syenite, also a rock-forming mineral in syenite.
noonkanbahite.etymology: For Noonkanbah sheep station, Wolgidee Hills, West Kimberley District, Australia, near the locality that produced the first specimens.

norbergite.occurrence: In contact metamorphic zones in limestones and dolostones into which plutonic rocks or pegmatites have introduced °uorine.
norbergite.etymology: From its ¯rst locality at Norberg, Sweden.

nordenskioldine.occurrence: Very rare in an alkalic pegmatite (Arø Island, Norway); in a hydrothermal deposit in metasomatized marble (Arandis, Namibia); in skarns (China).
nordenskioldine.etymology: Honors Nils Adolf Erik Nordenski¨ old (1832–1901), Swedish mineralogist, geologist, and explorer.

nordgauite.occurrence: A late stage secondary hydrothermal mineral in altered zwieselite-triplite masses in a zoned granite pegmatite.
nordgauite.etymology: For Nordgau, the oldest name for that part of northeastern Bavaria in which Hagendorf is situated, and where mining has taken place since the 13th century.

nordite-ce.occurrence: In the ussingite core of hyperagpaitic pegmatite.
nordite-ce.etymology: A member of the nordite group with Zn dominant in the Z structural site and with a suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

nordite-la.occurrence: Extremely rare in pegmatites in sodalite syenite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
nordite-la.etymology: From the mineral's \northern origin" and lanthanum content.

nordstrandite.occurrence: Commonly in residual soils derived from limestones; in dolomitic oil shale, marine siltstone, chalk; in pegmatite, miarolitic cavities, and xenoliths in nepheline syenites.
nordstrandite.etymology: For Robert A. Van Nordstrand, Sinclair Research Laboratories, Harvey, Illinois, USA, who synthesized the compound, later named for him, then transferred to the natural mineral.

nordstromite.etymology: To honor T. Nordstr¨ om (1843–1920), Swedish mining engineer who ﬁrst studied the sulfosalts from Falun.

norilskite.occurrence: Formed in a differentiated mafic intrusion.
norilskite.etymology: For the mining district in Russia that provided the first specimens.

norrishite.occurrence: A major to minor component of manganiferous schists , formed through metamorphism of a stratiform manganese deposit.
norrishite.etymology: In honor of Dr. Keith Norrish of the Division of Soils, Commonwealth Scienti¯c and Industrial Research Organization, Australia. All rights reserved. norsethite.occurrence: A rare authigenic mineral in and underlying the Green River Formation; a primary mineral in carbonatites; uncommon in metamorphosed hydrothermal mineral deposits.
norsethite.etymology: Honors Keith Norseth (1927–1991), American engineering geologist, Westvaco trona mine, Wyoming, USA, for his assistance in mineralogical studies.

northstarite.occurrence: An oxidation-zone mineral in a vug in massive quartz-baryte-enargite-pyrite in a polymetallic (Au-Ag-Cu-Pb) vein deposit emplaced in contact-metamorphosed dolomite.
northstarite.etymology: For the mine that contained the studied material.

northupite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral, formed probably between 20 ◦ C and 50 ◦ C, as a lacustrine deposit or at depth in mud and clay; may be primary or a replacement of earlier saline minerals.
northupite.etymology: To honor Charles H. Northup (1861–?), grocer of San Jose, California, USA, who found the ﬁrst examples.

nosean.occurrence: In silica-de¯cient alkalic volcanic rocks, principally phonolites.
nosean.etymology: After Karl Wilhelm Nose (1753?{1835), German mineralogist, of Brunswick (now Lower Saxony), Germany.

novacekite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of uranium-bearing polymetallic hydrothermal mineral deposits.
novacekite.etymology: To honor Dr. Radim Nov´ aˇ cek (1905–1942), Czech mineralogist, for his contributions to the mineralogy of uranium.
