stichite.occurrence: An alteration product of chromite in serpentinite.
stichite.etymology: To honor Robert C. Sticht (1857-1922), formerly General Manager of the Mount Lyell Mining and Railway Company, Tasmania, Australia.

stichtite.occurrence: An alteration product of chromite in serpentinite.
stichtite.etymology: To honor Robert C. Sticht (1857–1922), formerly General Manager of the Mount Lyell Mining and Railway Company, Tasmania, Australia.

stilbite-ca.occurrence: A low-temperature hydrothermal mineral, in amygdules and cavities in basalts, andesites, and various metamorphic rocks. Formed in hot springs deposits, and as a cementing agent in some sandstones and conglomerates.
stilbite-ca.etymology: From the Greek for luster, in reference to its pearly luster.

stilbite-na.occurrence: A low-temperature hydrothermal mineral, in amygdules and cavities in basalts, andesites, and various metamorphic rocks. Formed in hot springs deposits, and as a cementing agent in some sandstones and conglomerates.
stilbite-na.etymology: From the Greek for luster, in reference to its pearly luster.

stilleite.occurrence: Included in linnaeite (Shinkolobwe, Congo); intermixed with other selenides (Santa Brigida mine, Argentina).

stillwaterite.etymology: For the Stillwater maﬁc complex, Montana, USA.

stillwellite-ce.occurrence: Locally abundant as a metasomatic replacement of metamorphosed calcareous sediments (Mary Kathleen mine, Australia); in alkalic pegmatites in syenite in an alkalic massif (Dara-i-Pioz massif, Tajikistan).
stillwellite-ce.etymology: For Dr. Frank Leslie Stillwell (1888{1963), Australian ore mineralogist, and its predominant cerium content.

stilpnomelane.occurrence: In banded iron formations and enclosing slates and schists. In metamorphic rocks of the blueschist and greenschist facies, and in some metamorphosed massive sul¯de deposits.
stilpnomelane.etymology: From the Greek for shining and black, in allusion to its luster and color.

stishovite.occurrence: At sites of meteorite impact, formed by shock metamorphism of quartz at temperatures ¸ 1200 ±C and pressures »100 kbar; then metastable, alters to glass or cristobalite at ¸ 300 ±C.
stishovite.etymology: In honor of the Russian crystallographer Sergei Mikhailovich Stishov, who, with S.V. Popova, ¯rst synthesized the compound.

stistaite.occurrence: In concentrates from placer deposits from a region of Silurian shaly-sandy sediments (Elkiaidai River, Uzbekistan); in concentrates from precious metal placers (Rio Taman´ a, Colombia).
stistaite.etymology: For the composition, from Greek STIbium, antimony, and STAnnum, tin.

stoiberite.occurrence: A very rare mineral, deposited in vanadium-bearing sublimates in fumaroles on a basaltic volcanic cone.
stoiberite.etymology: To honor Dr. Richard Edwin Stoiber (1911–2001), Emeritus Professor of Geology, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, USA, who has studied Central American volcanoes and their mineralogy.

stokesite.occurrence: On axinite (Roscommon Cli®, England); in miarolitic cavities in a quartz-albite pegmatite (V·e·zn¶ a,Czech Republic).
stokesite.etymology: For Sir George Gabriel Stokes (1819{1903), Professor of Mathematics, Cambridge University, Cambridge, England.

stolperite.occurrence: In metal assemblages in a carbonaceous chondrite meteorite.
stolperite.etymology: Honors Edward M. Stolper, California Institute of Technology, USA, for his fundamental contributions to petrology and meteorite research.

stolzite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal tungsten-bearing lead deposits.
stolzite.etymology: To honor Dr. Joseph Alexis Stolz (1803–1896), Teplice, Czech Republic, who provided the ﬁrst specimen.

stoppaniite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in syenitic volcanic ejecta.
stoppaniite.etymology: Honors Dr. Francesco Saverio Stoppani (b. 1947), an amateur mineral collector active in the volcanic regions of Latium.

stottite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed in an oxidized zone of a germanium-rich dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
stottite.etymology: To honor Charles E. Stott (1896–1978), geologist and formerly General Director of the Tsumeb mine, Tsumeb, Namibia.

stracherite.occurrence: In pyrometamorphic spurrite marbles and formed under the influence of by-products (gases, fluids) of combustion metamorphism.
stracherite.etymology: Honors American geologist, Glenn Blair Stracher (aka “The Firewalker”) (b. 1949), Professor Emeritus of Geology, East Georgia State College, Swainsboro, Georgia, USA. Stracher is the author and editor of many scientific works on coal combustion and chemical thermodynamics.

straczekite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral, in seams in argillaceous gangue, in vanadium-rich alkalic igneous and metamorphosed sedimentary rocks (Wilson Springs, Arkansas, USA).
straczekite.etymology: To honor John A. Straczek, Chief Geologist, Union Carbide Corporation.

stranskiite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
stranskiite.etymology: Honoring Professor Iwan N. Stranski (1897–1979), German chemist and physicist, Berlin, Germany.

strashimirite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of Cu–As-bearing mineral deposits.
strashimirite.etymology: To honor Strashimir Dimitrov, Bulgarian petrographer.

stratlingite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed limestone xenolith in basalt (B ellerberg volcano, Germany); within metamorphosed clay xenoliths in phonolite (Montalto di Castro, Italy).
stratlingite.etymology: For W. StrÄ atling, who synthesized the mineral.

strelkinite.occurrence: Along seams and fractures in carbonaceous-siliceous shales.
strelkinite.etymology: To honor Professor Mikhail Fedorovich Strelkin (1905–1965), Russian mineralogist, Institute of Geology of Ore Deposits, Petrology, Mineralogy, and Geochemistry, Moscow, Russia, who studied uranium ores.

strengite.occurrence: A late secondary mineral in complex granite pegmatites; in “limonite” iron ores and gossans; with magnetite iron ores; rarely a cave mineral.
strengite.etymology: To honor Johan August Streng (1830–1897), German mineralogist, University of Giessen, Giessen, Germany.

stringhamite.occurrence: A retrograde reaction product between copper-bearing solutions and diopside in diopside-magnetite tactites (Bawana mine, Utah, USA).
stringhamite.etymology: In honor of Bronson Ferrin Stringham (1907{1968), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA.

stromeyerite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins, formed most commonly by secondary processes, although it also forms as a primary mineral.
stromeyerite.etymology: In honor of Professor Friedrich Stromeyer (1776–1835), chemist and mineralogist, University of G¨ ottingen, G¨ ottingen, Germany, who ﬁrst analyzed the mineral.

stronadelphite.occurrence: From hydrothermal alteration of peralkaline pegmatite is a sinuous and branched vein cross-cutting inequigranular nepheline syenite in an alkaline massif.
stronadelphite.etymology: After the chemical element strontium and adelfós, Greek for ‘‘brother’’, as the full strontium analogue of fluorapatite, the most widespread member of the apatite supergroup .

stronalsite.occurrence: A secondary alteration mineral in veins cutting ma¯c metatu® xenoliths (Rendai, Japan); in veinlets and grains in jadeitic aggregates within serpentinite (Mt. Ohsa, Japan).
stronalsite.etymology: For STRONtium and ALuminum in its composition.

strontianite.occurrence: An uncommon low-temperature hydrothermal mineral formed in veins in limestone, marl, and chalk; in geodes and concretions; rarely occurs in hydrothermal metallic veins; common in carbonatites.
strontianite.etymology: For Strontian, Scotland, source of the ﬁrst specimens.

strontio-orthojoaquinite.occurrence: In an amphibole-albitite block embedded in serpentinite.
strontio-orthojoaquinite.etymology: For its ORTHOrhombic symmetry, and relation to strontiojoaquinite.

strontioborite.occurrence: In the insoluble residue from a salt dome.
strontioborite.etymology: For STRONTIum and BORate in the essential composition.

strontiochevkinite.occurrence: In the more ma¯c bands of fenite dikes formed radially around carbonatite plugs.
strontiochevkinite.etymology: For the strontium content and relation to chevkinite.

strontiodresserite.occurrence: As a rare crystalline coating in vugs in a silicocarbonatite sill.
strontiodresserite.etymology: As the strontium analog of dresserite.

strontiofluorite.occurrence: In lenses of sodalite-microcline-aegirine rock within an apatite-rich urtite; produced by intense alteration of primary Sr-bearing minerals by F-rich hydrothermal fluids in a peralkaline parageneses.
strontiofluorite.etymology: As a Sr-dominant analogue of fluorite.

strontioginorite.occurrence: A rare insoluble residue in salt beds (Königshall-Hindenburg mine, Germany).
strontioginorite.etymology: As the strontium analog of ginorite.

strontiohurlbutite.occurrence: In a highly-evolved zoned pegmatite, likely from reactions between late hydrothermal fluids and primary beryl.
strontiohurlbutite.etymology: As a strontium-dominant analog of hurlbutite.

strontiojoaquinite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed and metasomatized basalt lens in serpentinite (Mina Numero Uno, California, USA); in veins cutting metagraywacke (prospect, San Benito Co., California, USA).
strontiojoaquinite.etymology: For its strontium content and its relation to joaquinite in contrast to strontio-orthojoaquinite.

strontiomelane.occurrence: A primary mineral in meta-ophiolite rocks (amphibolite-eclogite facies), the Mn deposit originally of seafloor hydrothermal origin .
strontiomelane.etymology: The strontium analog of cryptomelane. The name alludes to the composition , strontio , and the Greek melas, -anos, for black.

strontioorthojoaquinite.occurrence: In an amphibolite-quartz-albitite dike cutting serpentinite.
strontioorthojoaquinite.etymology: For its strontium content, ORTHOgonal crystal system, and relation to joaquinite.

strontioperloffite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in cavities in quartz veins from low-temperature hydrothermal solutions.

strontiopharmacosiderite.etymology: Indicates the strontium analog of pharmacosiderite.

strontiopiemontite.occurrence: As veinlets in a low-temperature metamorphosed manganese ore deposit (Val Graveglia, Italy).
strontiopiemontite.etymology: From its strontium content and similarity to piemontite.

strontioruizite.occurrence: On chemically weathered metamorphosed manganese ore.
strontioruizite.etymology: Prefix, strontio, indicates the Sr-dominant analog of ruizite.

strontiowhitlockite.occurrence: Very rare, in cavities in a dolomite carbonatite vein cutting pyroxenites in an alkalic massif.
strontiowhitlockite.etymology: As the strontium analog of whitlockite.

strontiumapatite.occurrence: In alkalic pegmatite veins in a zoned ultramaﬁc intrusion (Inagli massif, Russia).
strontiumapatite.etymology: As a strontium-dominant member of the apatite group; see ﬂuorapatite.

strunzite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, typically altered from triphylite, in zoned complex granite pegmatites.
strunzite.etymology: To honor Dr. Hugo Strunz (1910– ), Professor of Mineralogy, Technical University, Berlin, Germany, for his work on pegmatite phosphate minerals, especially those of Hagendorf, Germany.

struverite.occurrence: A late primary mineral in granite pegmatites; rarely detrital.
struverite.etymology: Honors Professor Giovanni Str¨ uver (1842–1915), mineralogist, University of Rome, Rome, Italy.

struvite.occurrence: In peaty earth intermixed with cattle dung (Hamburg, Germany); typically formed in bird or bat guano in caves and surface deposits.
struvite.etymology: To honor Heinrich Christoph Gottfried Struve (1772–1851), German mineral collector, serving as Russian Consul at Hamburg, Germany when the mineral was discovered.

struvite-k.occurrence: Of either late hydrothermal or secondary origin (Switzerland); an alteration product of animal bones and circulating fluids (Austria).
struvite-k.etymology: As the potassium equivalent of struvite.

studenitsite.occurrence: As lenses in clay and carbonate-bearing volcanogenic-sedimentary borate deposits.
studenitsite.etymology: For the Studenitsa Cloister near the ﬁrst occurrence.

studtite.occurrence: A very rare mineral in the oxidized zone of some uranium-bearing mineral deposits.
studtite.etymology: Honors Franz Edward Studt, geologist, who published a geological map of Shaba (Katanga) Province in 1913.

stumpflite.occurrence: In platinum concentrates from an ultramaﬁc pipe deposit (Driekop mine, South Africa).
stumpflite.etymology: Honors Professor Eugen Friedrich Stumpﬂ (1931– ), University of Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany, who ﬁrst described the mineral.

sturmanite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in cavities in metamorphosed bedded manganese deposits.
sturmanite.etymology: Honors Bozidar Darko Sturman (1937– ), Canadian mineralogist, Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto, Ontario, Canada.

stutzite.occurrence: As replacement masses in hydrothermal deposits associated with other tellurides and sulﬁdes.
stutzite.etymology: To honor Andreas Xavier St¨ utz (1747–1806), mineralogist of Vienna, Austria.

suanite.occurrence: In a contact metasomatic hydrothermal boron deposit in diopside–clinohumite– dolomite–calcite skarn (Hol Kol mine, North Korea).
suanite.etymology: For Suan Co., the North Korean region from which the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

sudburyite.occurrence: As tiny inclusions, commonly in cobaltite or maucherite, in mechanical concentrates of platinum-group minerals (Sudbury, Canada).
sudburyite.etymology: For the localities at Sudbury, Canada.

sudoite.occurrence: Disseminated in hematite ore, probably of hydrothermal origin (Negaunee, Michigan, USA); an authigenic mineral in aeolian sandstones (Kesselberg, Germany); in low-grade metamorphic assemblages (Ottr¶e, Belgium).
sudoite.etymology: For Professor Toshio Sudo (1911{ ), University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan.

suessite.occurrence: In a highly reduced brecciated meteorite (North Haig meteorite); in amygdaloidal basaltic porphyrite (Chatkal Range, Russia).
suessite.etymology: To honor Dr. Hans E. Suess (1909–1993), Austrian-American geochemist, Professor of Chemistry, University of California at San Diego, La Jolla, California, USA, for his work in cosmochemistry and meteoritics.

sugakiite.occurrence: An intergranular exsolved phase in sulfide aggregates in lherzolite in a peridotite massif.
sugakiite.etymology: Honors emeritus professor Asahiko Sugaki (b 1923), Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan, for his studies on sulfide phase equilibria.

sugilite.occurrence: In an aegirine-bearing syenite stock in biotite granite (Iwagi Islet, Japan); in bedded manganese deposits (near Kuruman, South Africa).
sugilite.etymology: For Professor Ken-ichi Sugi (1901{1948), Japanese petrologist, who discovered the mineral.

sulfhydrylbystrite.occurrence: As metasomatic lenses in dolomitic marble replacing lazurite.
sulfhydrylbystrite.etymology: Reflects the chemical relationship with bystrite and by analogy to carbobystrite, a prefix sulfhydryl, for its distinctive chemical difference from other members of the group.

sulfoborite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in marine salt deposits.
sulfoborite.etymology: In allusion to sulfur and boron in the composition.

sulphohalite.occurrence: In evaporite deposits (Searles Lake, California, USA; Otjiwalundo salt pan, Namibia); a volcanic sublimate (Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia).
sulphohalite.etymology: In allusion to sulfur and sodium chloride, ( halite), in the composition, neglecting ﬂuorine, the presence of which was unnoticed in the original analysis of type material.

sulphotsumoite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, with other bismuth tellurides.
sulphotsumoite.etymology: In allusion to the chemical relation to tsumoite.

sulphur.occurrence: A sublimation product at volcanic fumaroles; a product of the activity of biological micro-organisms; as a result of low oxidation potential and highly acidic chemical reactions in mineral deposits; formed by the decomposition of sulfides, especially pyrite, during mine fires; found in sedimentary rocks.

sulphur-beta.occurrence: A sublimation product at volcanic fumaroles; a product of the activity of biological micro-organisms; as a result of low oxidation potential and highly acidic chemical reactions in mineral deposits; formed by the decomposition of sulfides, especially pyrite, during mine fires; found in sedimentary rocks.

sulvanite.occurrence: In hydrothermal copper deposits which contain vanadium as a primary sulﬁde.
sulvanite.etymology: For the composition: SULfur and V ANadium.

sundiusite.occurrence: On fracture surfaces in a museum specimen of manganese ore from a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody.
sundiusite.etymology: To honor Nils Sundius (1886–1976), Swedish mineralogist, who made numerous contributions to L ˚ angban mineralogy.

suolunite.occurrence: In veins cutting harzburgites in an ultramafic intrusive (Suolun, China); as a precipitate from an alkaline spring in a fault zone in basalts above an ultramafic intrusive (Al Khawd, Oman).
suolunite.etymology: For the original locality, Suolun, China.

suredaite.occurrence: In a symmetrical banded, hydrothermal vein Ag-Sn deposit.
suredaite.etymology: Honors Ricardo Sureda Leston, head of the Department of Mineralogy and Economic Geology, University of Salta, Argentina.

surinamite.occurrence: In mylonitic mesoperthite gneiss, probably formed during high-pressure granulite facies metamorphism of aluminous rocks (Bakhuis Mountains, Surinam); in sillimanite-rich segregations in pegmatites (Casey Bay, Antarctica); as pseudomorphs after cordierite (Chimwala area, Zambia).
surinamite.etymology: For Surinam, the country of ¯rst occurrence.

surite.occurrence: As ¯ssure ¯llings in the oxidized zone of a Pb-Zn deposit.
surite.etymology: For the type locality, the Cruz del Sur mine, Argentina.

surkhobite.occurrence: In a zoned alkaline syenite pegmatite replacing astrophyllite and bafertisite.
surkhobite.etymology: For the Surkhob river, in the basin of which the first specimens were collected.

sursassite.occurrence: As vein ¯llings in manganese deposits in low-grade metasediments.
sursassite.etymology: From the Roman name for Oberhalbstein, Sursass, Switzerland.

susannite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal lead-bearing deposits, formed at temperatures above 80 ◦C.
susannite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence in the Susanna mine, Leadhills, Scotland.

suseinargiuite.occurrence: Formed by hydrothermal and/or supergene alteration of a primary Mo-Bi mineral assemblage.
suseinargiuite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens, Su Seinargiu, Italy.

sussexite.occurrence: A rare hydrothermal mineral typically in veinlets in boron-bearing metamorphosed Mn–Fe–Zn deposits.
sussexite.etymology: For Sussex Co., New Jersey, USA, within which the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

suzukiite.occurrence: In massive rhodonite-rhodochrosite ores of a bedded manganese deposit, formed in very weakly metamorphosed Triassic cherts.
suzukiite.etymology: For Dr. Jun Suzuki (1896{1970), petrologist and mineralogist, Professor at Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan.

svabite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in calcsilicate contact metamorphic rocks (skarns).
svabite.etymology: Honors Anton Svab (1703-1768), Swedish mining oﬃcial.

svanbergite.occurrence: In aluminous medium-grade metamorphic deposits; from bauxite deposits; a product of sulphatic argillic wall-rock alteration in hydrothermal vein and disseminated ore deposits, replacing apatite.
svanbergite.etymology: Honoring Lars Fredrik Svanberg (1805–1878), Swedish chemist, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Uppsala, Uppsala, Sweden.

sveinbergeite.occurrence: A late forming mineral in cavities in syenite pegmatite in an alkaline plutonic complex.
sveinbergeite.etymology: Honors Svein Arne Berge (b. 1949), the Norwegian amateur mineralogist who observed and collected the first specimens.

sveite.occurrence: As crusts and eﬄorescences precipitated from solutions trickling onto cave roofs and walls.
sveite.etymology: From the ﬁrst letters of the Sociedad Venezolana de Espeleolog ´ ıa, whose members collected the original material studied.

svenekite.occurrence: A secondary mineral coating granite near a polymetallic hydrothermal vein.
svenekite.etymology: Honors Dr. Jaroslav Švenek (1927-1994), the former curator of the mineralogical collection of the National Museum in Prague, Czech Republic.

sverigeite.occurrence: Found on a mine dump; possibly part of a vein assemblage.
sverigeite.etymology: For the country where the mineral was found, Sweden, Sverige in Swedish.

svetlanaite.occurrence: In quartz veins in a high-sulfidation, volcanic hosted, epithermal gold deposit.
svetlanaite.etymology: Honors Dr. Svetlana Konstantinovna Smirnova, a Russian mineralogist, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Academy of Sciences of Uzbekistan, for her contributions to understanding the geology of epithermal Au-Ag deposits of the Tien-Shan region.

svornostite.occurrence: As weathering products from the post-mining alteration of uraninite and sulfides in a Ag-Bi-Co-Ni-U bearing hydrothermal vein deposit.
svornostite.etymology: For the Svornost mine, the locality that produced the first specimens.

svyatoslavite.occurrence: In burning dumps, as a sublimate on fracture walls in coal, formed at about 700 ◦C–900 ◦C.
svyatoslavite.etymology: For Svyatoslav Nestorovich Ivanov (1911– ), Soviet geologist, Ural Scientiﬁc Center, Yekaterinburg (Sverdlovsk), Russia.

svyazhinite.occurrence: A weathering product in fractures cutting pyrite–ﬂuorite-bearing pyroxene–amphibole fenites.
svyazhinite.etymology: Honors Nikolai Vasil’evich Svyazhin (1927–1967), Russian mineralogist, Ural Mining Institute, Sverdlovsk, Russia.

swaknoite.occurrence: Formed from bat guano and urine by reaction with cave walls.
swaknoite.etymology: From Suid Wes Africa Karst Navorsing Organisasie (SWAKNO), a speleological exploration organization, the members of which noted the species.

swamboite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed during the weathering of uranium deposits.
swamboite.etymology: For the occurrence at Swambo, Congo (Zaire).

swamboite-nd.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed during the weathering of uranium deposits.
swamboite-nd.etymology: For the occurrence at Swambo, Congo (Zaire).

swartzite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in oxidized portions of a polymetallic sulﬁde deposit, the source of uranium undetermined.
swartzite.etymology: Honors Charles K. Swartz (1861–1949), Professor of Geology and Mineralogy, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland, USA.

swedenborgite.occurrence: In skarn from a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody.
swedenborgite.etymology: Honors Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772), Swedish philosopher and theologian.

sweetite.occurrence: In an oxidized vein in limestone.
sweetite.etymology: To honor Jessie May Sweet (1901–1979), Curator of the mineral collections of the British Museum (Natural History), London, England.

swinefordite.occurrence: Deposited from ground water, as coatings on the walls of fracture zones and ¯ssures, or replacing spodumene, in a Li-Sn-rich pegmatite.
swinefordite.etymology: For Dr. Ada Swineford (1917{1993), clay mineralogist and Professor of Geology at Western Washington State College, Bellingham, Washington, USA.

switzerite.etymology: To honor Dr. George Shirly Switzer (1915– ), Chairman Emeritus, Department of Mineral Sciences, United States National Museum, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., USA.

sylvanite.occurrence: Most commonly in low-temperature hydrothermal veins; also in medium- and high-temperature deposits, typically among the last minerals formed.
sylvanite.etymology: From TranSYL V ANia, Romania where it was ﬁrst found, and in allusion to the element tellurium ( sylvanium, a name early proposed for the element), which the mineral contains. sylvite.occurrence: In sedimentary basins, forming thick bedded deposits with halite; as a sublimate in volcanic fumaroles; in nitrate beds and cave deposits; a product of burning coal; may be included in other minerals as a product of intermediate-grade metamorphism.
sylvite.etymology: From the alchemical Sal digestivus Sylvii or Salt of Sylvius , the digestive salt of Fran¸ cois Sylvius de le Bo¨ e (1614–1672), Dutch physician and chemist of Leiden, Netherlands.

symesite.occurrence: A secondary low-temperature mineral formed from metalliferous brines moving along fractures through Mn and Fe-oxide mineral deposits in limestone.
symesite.etymology: Honors Robert Symes (1937–) of the Department of Mineralogy, the Natural History Museum (London, England), in recognition of his many contributions to the mineralogy of the ore deposits of South-West England.

symplesite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some arsenic-rich hydrothermal mineral deposits.
symplesite.etymology: From the Greek for with and to be associated, in allusion to the other rare arsenates accompanying it in the original occurrence.

synadelphite.occurrence: A rare low-temperature hydrothermal mineral cutting hausmannite ores in dolomitic marble (Moss mine, Sweden).
synadelphite.etymology: From the Greek for with and brother, as it is commonly associated with several other chemically similar minerals.

synchysite-ce.occurrence: An uncommon hydrothermal accessory mineral in granites and alkalic syenites.
synchysite-ce.etymology: From the Greek for confounding, as originally thought to be parisite, and dominant cerium.

synchysite-nd.occurrence: An authigenic minerals in cement in sandstone (Holiˇ cky deposit, Czech Republic); ﬁlling cavities in the base of a bauxite deposit in contact with limestone (Grebnik deposit, Yugoslavia).
synchysite-nd.etymology: For its relation to synchysite-(Ce) and dominant neodymium.

synchysite-y.occurrence: A rare hydrothermal accessory mineral in alkalic granites and granite pegmatites.
synchysite-y.etymology: For its relation to synchysite-(Ce) and dominant yttrium.

syngenite.occurrence: An uncommon diagenetic component of marine salt deposits; a volcanic sublimate or pneumatolytic reaction product; a hydrothermal vein ﬁlling in a geothermal ﬁeld; derived from bat guano in caves.
syngenite.etymology: From the Greek for related, for the chemical resemblance to polyhalite.

szaibelyite.occurrence: Uncommon in marine evaporite deposits; in boron-bearing contact metasomatized dolomitic marbles and skarns, and metamorphosed banded iron formation.
szaibelyite.etymology: Honors Istv´ an´Ad´ am Rudolf Szaib´ ely (1777–1855), R´ ezb´ anya, Hungary [now B˘ ai¸ ta, Romania], mine surveyor, who collected the ﬁrst specimens.

szenicsite.occurrence: A uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a copper–molybdenum deposit in granite.
szenicsite.etymology: Honors husband and wife Marissa Szenics (1950– ) and Terry Szenics (1947– ), mineral collectors and dealers who found the ﬁrst specimens.

szklaryite.occurrence: In the internal portion of a complex zoned granitic pegmatite.
szklaryite.etymology: For the locality (Szklary pegmatite) in Poland, where the first specimens were collected.

szmikite.etymology: Honors Ignaz Nathaniel Szmik (1815–1881), Hungarian mining oﬃcial at Fels˝ ob´ anya, Hungary (now Baia Sprie, Romania), who discovered the mineral.

szomolnokite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral formed in pyrite-rich oxidized sulﬁde deposits, typically under highly acid and arid conditions.
szomolnokite.etymology: For the ﬁrst recognized occurrence at Szomolnok, Hungary (now Smoln ´ ık, Slovakia).

szymanskiite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a mercury–nickel-bearing sulﬁde deposit in silicate–carbonate rock hydrothermally altered from serpentinite.
szymanskiite.etymology: Honors Dr. Jan T. Szyma´ nski (1938– ), X-ray crystallographer, Canadian Centre for Mineral and Energy Technology (CANMET), Ottawa, Canada.

tacharanite.occurrence: In amygdules and fractures in metabasalts and basaltic breccias; in hydrothermally altered quartzite inclusions in basalt (Bramburg, Germany).
tacharanite.etymology: From the Gaelic tacharan for changeling, as the mineral converts to others on exposure to air.

tachyhydrite.occurrence: A rare mineral in bedded salt deposits of oceanic origin.
tachyhydrite.etymology: From the Greek for quick and water, remarking on its deliquescence.

tadzhikite-ce.occurrence: In the replacement units of zoned pegmatite dikes (Dara-i-Pioz massif, Tajikistan).
tadzhikite-ce.etymology: For the occurrence in Tajikistan (Tadzhikistan), and its yttrium content.

tadzhikite-y.occurrence: In the replacement units of zoned pegmatite dikes (Dara-i-Pioz massif, Tajikistan).
tadzhikite-y.etymology: For the occurrence in Tajikistan (Tadzhikistan), and its yttrium content.

taenite.occurrence: Important in meteorites. As spherules in lunar rocks. In serpentinized nickeliferous ultramafic rocks, as particles or spherules in placer sands, and as loose, detached masses which give few clues as to their ultimate origin. In mafic igneous rocks that assimilated carbon under reducing conditions.
taenite.etymology: From the Greek for band or strip, in allusion to its platy structure.

taikanite.occurrence: In hydrothermal manganese ores related to alkalic dikes intruding limestones and siliceous rocks (Irnimi deposit, Russia); in a bedded manganese deposit (Wessels mine, South Africa).
taikanite.etymology: For the occurrence in the Taikan Mountains, Russia.

taimyrite-i.occurrence: As grains and veinlets near the contact between sulﬁde and rock-forming minerals in gabbro-diabase; in massive sulﬁde ores.
taimyrite-i.etymology: For the type locality on the Taimyr Peninsula, Russia.

tainiolite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral in nepheline syenite pegmatites.
tainiolite.etymology: From the Greek for ribbon in reference to the mineral's tabular crystals.

taipingite-ce.occurrence: In a hydrothermal vein-type REE deposit.
assoc_parsed: calcite. distribution from the taipingzhen rare earth element   deposit in the north qinling orogen
taipingite-ce.etymology: For the locality, Taiping town, from which the studied material was collected.

takanawaite-y.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens and a suffix for the dominant rare earth element.

takanelite.occurrence: Formed in the oxide zone of a bedded manganese deposit in metamorphosed cherts (Nomura mine, Japan); a secondary mineral derived from alteration of rhodochrosite in a manganese deposit (Janggun mine, South Korea).
takanelite.etymology: To honor Dr. Katsutoshi Takane (1899–1945), Professor of Mineralogy, Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan.

takedaite.occurrence: A rare mineral probably formed by boron-rich ﬂuids reacting between crystalline limestone and gehlenite-spurrite skarns.
takedaite.etymology: Honors Professor Hiroshi Takeda (1934– ), mineralogist, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan.

takeuchiite.occurrence: Very rare in museum specimens from a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody.
takeuchiite.etymology: Honors Professor Yoshio Tak´ euchi (1924– ), University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan, who predicted the existence of the species and its crystal structure.

takovite.occurrence: In a karstitic bauxite at the contact of limestone and metamorphosed serpentinite (Takovo, Serbia); an alteration product of nickel sulﬁdes (Western Australia).
takovite.etymology: For Takovo, Serbia, from which it was ﬁrst described.

talc.occurrence: In talc-rich schists or steatite through hydrothermal alteration of ma¯c rocks (steatitization) subsequent to serpentinization during greenschist facies metamorphism. Also formed by thermal low-temperature metamorphism of siliceous dolostones.

talmessite.occurrence: A rare secondary species formed typically in the oxidized zone of some hydrothermal mineral deposits, an alteration product of realgar, orpiment, or Cu–Ni arsenides.
talmessite.etymology: For the Talmessi mine, Iran, in which the mineral was ﬁrst found.

talnakhite.occurrence: In concentrations of up to 70% in zones to 12 m thick, in hydrothermal ores (Talnakh area, Russia); in the layered ultramaﬁc Stillwater complex (Nye, Montana, USA); a component of undersea black smokers.
talnakhite.etymology: For the Talnakh area, Russia, where it occurs.

tamaite.occurrence: In veinlets to 1.5 mm in width in a weakly metamorphosed Mn ore deposit.
tamaite.etymology: For the locality, the Tama district, where the first samples were collected.

tamarugite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in oxidized sulﬁde-bearing alkali-rich aluminous rocks, with sodium supplied from hydrothermal solutions or sea-spray; as eﬄorescences in active geothermal systems; may be formed by reaction between acid sulfate solutions or fumarolic gas and wall rock.
tamarugite.etymology: For the originally-noted occurrence at Cerro Pintados, in the Tamarugal Pampa, Chile.

tamboite.occurrence: In the interstices of silicified epithermal hydrothermal breccias of dacitic tuff.
assoc_parsed: native tellurium. distribution from the tambo mine
tamboite.etymology: For the Tambo mine, where the studied material was collected.

tamuraite.occurrence: In a fluvial placer deposit derived from ultramafic rocks of a layered complex.
assoc_parsed: ir-bearing members of the laurite-erlichmanite series
tamuraite.etymology: Honors Dr. Nobumichi Tamura (b. 1966), senior scientist at the Advanced Light Source, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, USA, for his innovative investigations of minerals and materials by synchrotron microdiffraction.

tancaite-ce.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in the oxidation zone of a sulfide ore vein in granite.
tancaite-ce.etymology: Honors Giuseppe Tanca (b. 1943), an Italian amateur mineralogist, who discovered the mineral. A suffix indicates the dominant rare-earth element.

tancoite.occurrence: In cavities in dump material from a complex granite pegmatite.
tancoite.etymology: For the Tanco mine, Canada, its original locality.

taneyamalite.occurrence: In cracks in ferruginous chert, ma¯c rocks, and limestone subjected to blueschist facies metamorphism (Taneyama mine, Japan); in bedded manganese ores in weakly metamorphosed chert and greenstone of the prehnite-pump ellyite metagraywacke facies (Iwaizawa mine, Japan).
taneyamalite.etymology: For the Taneyama mine, Japan, where the mineral was ¯rst noted.

tangdanite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of an As-bearing Cu sulfide deposit.
tangdanite.etymology: For the Tangdan mine, the locality that produced the first specimens.

tangeite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in vanadium-bearing mineral deposits in sandstone.
tangeite.etymology: For its initially noted occurrence in the Tange Gorge, Fergana Valley, Alai Range, Kyrgyzstan.

taniajacoite.occurrence: On chemically weathered metamorphosed manganese ore.
taniajacoite.etymology: Honors its finders, Tania Janse van Nieuwenhuizen (b. 1973) and Jacobus “Jaco” Stephanus Janse van Nieuwenhuizen (b. 1973), mineral collectors and the owners of ‘‘Crystal Spring s Minerals CC’’ in South Africa.

tanohataite.occurrence: In lens-like veins in a sediment-hosted Mn-ore deposit in contact metamorphic rocks near a granodiorite intrusion.
tanohataite.etymology: For a village close to the location from which the first specimens were collected.

tantalaeschynite-y.etymology: For an aeschynite with TANTALum greater than titanium in the composition and with yttrium as the dominant rare-earth element.

tantalcarbide.occurrence: In placer concentrates from a “gold-washing operation”. Suspected to be a synthetic compound mixed with natural placer concentrate. No in situ localities known.
tantalcarbide.etymology: For the essential chemical components, tantalum and carbide.

tantalite-fe.occurrence: As an accessory and primary constituent of granite pegmatites.
tantalite-fe.etymology: Suffix for dominant Fe in the composition and relation to tantalite-(Mg) and tantalite-(Mn), named for the Greek mythical Tantalus, for the difficulty in bringing the mineral into solution.

tantalite-mg.occurrence: As replacement rims on tantalite-(Mn) crystals in deeply desilicated granite pegmatite that cuts serpentinite near its contact with marble.
tantalite-mg.etymology: Suffix for dominant Mg in the composition and relation to tantalite-(Fe) and tantalite-(Mn), named for the Greek mythical Tantalus, for the difficulty in bringing the mineral into solution.

tantalite-mn.occurrence: An accessory and primary constituent of granite pegmatites; detrital in placers.
tantalite-mn.etymology: Suffix for dominant Mn in the composition and relation to tantalite-(Fe) and tantalite-(Mg), named for the Greek mythical Tantalus, for the difficulty in bringing the mineral into solution.

tanteuxenite-y.occurrence: A detrital mineral in tin placers (Western Australia); in a granite pegmatite (Craveggia, Italy).
tanteuxenite-y.etymology: For its relation to euxenite, with TANTalum greater than niobium.

tantite.occurrence: In a granite pegmatite cutting amphibolites (Mt. Vasin-Myl’k, Russia); in a highly fractionated pegmatite (Animikie Red Ace pegmatite, Wisconsin, USA).

tapiaite.occurrence: A late-stage, low-temperature, secondary mineral that occurs in narrow seams and vugs in the oxidized upper portion of a hydrothermal sulfide vein hosted by volcanoclastic rocks.
tapiaite.etymology: Honors Enrique Tapia (1955-2008), an accomplished Chilean field mineral collector.

taramellite.occurrence: In metamorphic rocks rich in barium silicates, in contact with granitic rocks (Candoglia, Italy); in a metamorphosed Fe{Mn orebody (Lºangban, Sweden).

taramite.occurrence: In sodium-metasomatized alkalic gneisses and nepheline syenite dikes; in eclogite metamorphosed to the amphibolite facies.
taramite.etymology: For the type locality, the Vali-Tarama Valley, Ukraine.

taranakite.occurrence: Formed from phosphatic solutions derived from bird or bat guano reacting with clays or aluminous rocks under perenially damp conditions; the most common phosphate mineral in caves.
taranakite.etymology: For its ﬁrst recognized occurrence on the Taranaki Peninsula, New Zealand.

tarapacaite.occurrence: A minor accessory mineral in nitrate deposits.
tarapacaite.etymology: For its ﬁrst noted occurrence in the Tocopilla Pampa, 170 km north of Antofagasta, Tarapac´ a, Chile.

tarbagataite.occurrence: In pegmatite veins and fenite associated with alkaline granitic massifs.
tarbagataite.etymology: For the Tarbagatai mountain range where the Verkhnee Espe deposit that produced the first specimens is located.

tarbuttite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of zinc-bearing deposits.
tarbuttite.etymology: Honoring Percy Coventry Tarbutt, Director of the Broken Hill Exploration Company, who early provided material for characterization.

tarkianite.occurrence: In a heavy mineral concentrate derived from a serpentinized, disseminated sulfide and PGM-bearing, ultramafic intrusion.
tarkianite.etymology: Honors Prof. Mahmud Tarkian (b. 1941) of the University of Hamburg, Germany , who earlier described an occurrence of the mineral.

taseqite.occurrence: In a cavity in a late-stage hydrothermal albitite vein in alkaline igneous complex.
taseqite.etymology: For the Taseq slope of the Ilímaussaq alkaline complex near which the first specimens were collected.

tashelgite.occurrence: In skarn-like rocks anomalously enriched with Al2O3.
tashelgite.etymology: For the Taghelga River valley, in which the species was first collected.

tassieite.occurrence: A late-stage, low-temperature mineral formed by hydrothermal alteration of stornesite-(Y), wagnerite and fluorapatite in the core of a fluorapatite nodule in regionally metamorphosed and fractured gneissic rocks.
tassieite.etymology: For a lake, Tassie Tarn, near the site from which the first specimens were collected.

tatarinovite.occurrence: In cavities in a rodingite body at the contact between a dike of partly rodingitized gabbroic rock and hosting serpentinite.
tatarinovite.etymology: Honors Russian geologist and petrologist Pavel Mikhailovich Tatarinov (1895-1976), a specialist in deposits of chrysotile asbestos.

tatarskite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral found in drill core in a marine salt deposit.
tatarskite.etymology: Honors Professor Vitalii Borisovich Tatarskii (1907–1993), mineralogist, St. Petersburg University, St. Petersburg, Russia.

tausonite.occurrence: In aegirine-kalsilite rock in an alkalic massif (Murun massif, Russia); in a rheomorphic fenite dike in a carbonatite complex (Sarambi, Paraguay).
tausonite.etymology: To honor Academician Lev Vladimirovich Tauson (1917–1989), Russian geochemist, Director of the Geochemical Institute, Irkutsk, Russia.

tavagnascoite.occurrence: Within vugs in hydrothermal veins, in association with secondary Bi-minerals from the alteration of a bismuthinite ± Bi-sulfosalt assemblage .
tavagnascoite.etymology: For the district that produced the first specimens.

tavorite.occurrence: A secondary oxidation product of earlier phosphates in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
tavorite.etymology: To honor Dr. Elysiario Tavora (1911– ), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Brazil, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

tazheranite.occurrence: In calciphyres banding periclase-brucite marble xenoliths in an alkalic massif (Tazheran massif, Russia). In a CV3 carbonaceous chondrite meteorite.
tazheranite.etymology: For the Tazheran massif, Russia, where it was first noted.

tazieffite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
tazieffite.etymology: Honors Haroun Tazieff (1914-1998), Belgian/French volcanologist, a pioneer in the field study of volcanoes who devoted his life to the study of volcanic gases.

tazzoliite.occurrence: As part of skarn and calc-silicate metamorphic rocks with rare sanidine xenoliths near the contacts with rhyolite and trachite.
tazzoliite.etymology: Honors Professor Vittorio Tazzoli (b. 1938), Department of Earth Science, University of Pavia, Italy, in recognition of his contribution to the fields of mineralogy and crystallography, particularly in the area of pyroxenes.

teallite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral in tin veins; may be an important ore mineral.
teallite.etymology: To honor Jethro Justinian Harris Teall (1849–1924), Director of the Geological Survey of Great Britain and Ireland.

tedhadleyite.occurrence: On the wall of a vug in quartz, likely formed, in situ, as a replacement of native mercury, during a period of high activity of I (with lower Cl and Br) in the fluid or vapor phase.
tedhadleyite.etymology: Honors Ted A. Hadley (b. 1961) of Sunnyvale, California, who participated in the collection of the holotype specimen and for his contributions to mineralogy generally.

teepleite.occurrence: Formed by reaction of boron-rich brines with halite in an extremely desiccated lake (Borax Lake, California, USA).
teepleite.etymology: Honors John Edgar Teeple (1874–1931), for his work on the chemistry of Searles Lake, California, USA.

tegengrenite.etymology: Honors Felix Tegengren (1884-1980), Finlandic-Swedish economic geologist.

teineite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by oxidation of copper- and tellurium-bearing sulﬁdes.
teineite.etymology: For the Teine mine, Japan, in which specimens were ﬁrst found.

telargpalite.occurrence: In metasomatically altered Cu–Ni sulﬁde ores (Talnakh area, Russia); in the layered ultramaﬁc Stillwater complex (Nye, Montana, USA).
telargpalite.etymology: For the constituent chemical elements, TELlurium, ARGentum silver, and PALladium.

tellurantimony.occurrence: In a zinc-rich stratiform massive sulﬁde deposit of volcanogenic origin in Archean volcanics (Mattagami Lake mine, Canada).

tellurite.occurrence: An alteration product of tellurium and tellurides in the oxide zone of some hydrothermal mineral deposits.
tellurite.etymology: For its composition as a TELLURium dioxide.

tellurium.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins; may be of both primary and secondary origin; a sublimate in volcanic fumaroles.
tellurium.etymology: Latin name for the earth , tellus.

tellurobismuthite.occurrence: Typically formed in hydrothermal gold-quartz veins of low sulfur content.

tellurohauchecornite.etymology: Alludes to its chemical relation to the hauchecornite group.

telluromandarinoite.occurrence: Of epithermal hydrothermal origin, found in the interstices of silicified dacitic tuff breccia.
telluromandarinoite.etymology: By a prefix, the name indicates the Te4+ (tellurium) analogue of mandarinoite.

telluronevskite.occurrence: In opal-quartz veinlets and as disseminated grains in ‘secondary quartzite’ that was formed by contact metamorphism or hydrothermal alteration of volcanic rocks .
telluronevskite.etymology: Alludes to the chemical relationship to nevskite, through substitution of tellurium for selenium.

telluropalladinite.occurrence: As tiny grains in mineral concentrates.

telluroperite.occurrence: A secondary phase on fracture surfaces and in small vugs in quartz veins. Formed from the partial oxidation of primary sulfides (e.g., galena) and tellurides (e.g., hessite) during or following brecciation of the quartz veins. The Cl may be sourced in part from primary phases; however, it is most likely from salty brines interacting with primary tellurides.
telluroperite.etymology: Indicates the structural analogy to perite with essential tellurium in the composition.

telyushenkoite.etymology: Honors petrographer and teacher Tamara Matveyevna Telyushenko (1930-1997) for her contributions to understanding the geology of Central Asia and service as head of the Young Geologists’ School of Ashkhabad for over thirty years.

temagamite.occurrence: Cogenetic with moderately high-temperature invasive chalcopyrite magma (Temagami Mine, Canada).
temagamite.etymology: For the Temagami mine in Canada, where the mineral was ﬁrst found.

tengchongite.occurrence: In the oxidized portions of a uranium deposit in migmatite and gneiss.
tengchongite.etymology: For Tengchong Co., China, where the ﬁrst specimens were found.

tengerite-y.occurrence: An alteration coating on yttrium-bearing minerals.
tengerite-y.etymology: To honor C. Tenger, Swedish chemist who studied the mineral.

tennantite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins and contact metamorphic deposits.
tennantite.etymology: In honor of Professor Smithson Tennant (1761–1815), English chemist of Oxford University, Oxford, England.

tennantite-cu.occurrence: In an epithermal hydrothermal vein deposit by replacement of enargite under decreasing fS2.
tennantite-cu.etymology: Honors the English chemist Smithson Tennant (1761-1815) with a suffix for the dominant divalent cation in the C site.

tennantite-fe.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins and contact metamorphic deposits.
tennantite-fe.etymology: In honor of Professor Smithson Tennant (1761–1815), English chemist of Oxford University, Oxford, England.

tennantite-hg.occurrence: Formed by late-stage hydrothermal fluids within metadolostone.
tennantite-hg.etymology: Honors the English chemist Smithson Tennant (1761-1815) with a suffix for the dominant divalent cation in the C site.

tennantite-mn.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins and contact metamorphic deposits.
tennantite-mn.etymology: In honor of Professor Smithson Tennant (1761–1815), English chemist of Oxford University, Oxford, England.

tennantite-zn.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins and contact metamorphic deposits.
tennantite-zn.etymology: In honor of Professor Smithson Tennant (1761–1815), English chemist of Oxford University, Oxford, England.

tenorite.occurrence: Commonly in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal copper deposits; a volcanic sublimate.
tenorite.etymology: To honor Professor Michele Tenore (1781–1861), Italian botanist, University of Naples, Naples, Italy.

tephroite.occurrence: In Fe{Mn ore deposits, related skarns, and metamorphosed manganese-rich sediments.

terlinguacreekite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by alteration of cinnabar or native mercury as granular crusts.
terlinguacreekite.etymology: Named after Terlingua Creek, which flows in the Terlingua mining district, Texas.

terlinguaite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in hydrothermal mercury deposits.
terlinguaite.etymology: For its occurrence at Terlingua, Texas, USA.

ternovite.occurrence: As a very rare late-formed mineral in fractures in lithium-rich pegmatite (Foote mine, North Carolina, USA); on a museum specimen from a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L ˚ angban, Sweden).
ternovite.etymology: As the TETRAgonal dimorph of wickmanite.

terrywallaceite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins that contain sulfosalt mineralization.
terrywallaceite.etymology: Honors Terry C. Wallace Jr., former professor of geosciences and mineral museum curator at the University of Arizona, Tucson, USA. Since 2003, Wallace is the Principal Associate Director for science, technology, engineering, and educational activities at Los Alamos National Laboratory.

terskite.occurrence: In veins in pegmatites in alkalic massifs.
terskite.etymology: For the Tersk shore of the White Sea, southeastern Kola Peninsula, Russia.

tertschite.etymology: Honors Professor Hermann Tertsch (1880–1962), Austrian mineralogist, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria.

teruggite.occurrence: In lacustrine borate deposits, typically associated with volcanic hot springs and diagensis of playa sediments.
teruggite.etymology: Honors Mario E. Teruggi, Professor of Sedimentology and Petrology, National University, Plata, Argentina.

teschemacherite.etymology: To honor Frederick Edward Teschemacher (1791–1863), English chemist, who ﬁrst described the species.

testibiopalladite.occurrence: In a Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposit in a serpentine body intruded into a Permian formation of metamorphic rocks (Locality “Y”, China); in Cu–Ni sulﬁde deposits in clinopyroxenite intruding sandy shales and volcanics (Locality “W”, China).
testibiopalladite.etymology: For TEllurium, antimony (STIBium), and PALLADium in the composition.

tetraauricupride.occurrence: In maﬁc to ultramaﬁc rocks that also contain platinum group elements.
tetraauricupride.etymology: In allusion to the composition and symmetry.

tetradymite.occurrence: In hydrothermal gold-quartz veins of medium to high temperature of formation; also in contact metamorphic deposits.
tetradymite.etymology: From the Greek for fourfold and twin, an allusion to the twin crystals.

tetraferriannite.occurrence: In low-grade metamorphosed banded iron formation.
tetraferriannite.etymology: Prefixes, tetra for the tetrahedral coordination sites in which Fe3+ cations (identified by ferri), reside in a compound analogous to annite.

tetraferroplatinum.occurrence: In a hortonolite dunite (Mooihoek, South Africa); in Uralian ultramaﬁcs and placers derived therefrom.
tetraferroplatinum.etymology: For crystallization in the TETRAgonal system, and iron, FERRum, and PLATINUM in its composition.

tetrahedrite.occurrence: Typically in hydrothermal veins or contact metamorphic deposits of low to medium temperature of formation.
tetrahedrite.etymology: In allusion to the tetrahedral crystal shape. All rights reserved.
