tugarinovite.occurrence: Formed as a primary mineral, by metasomatism in a reducing environment deﬁcient in sulfur.
tugarinovite.etymology: For Aleksei Ivanovich Tugarinov (1917–1977), geochemist, Moscow University, Moscow, Russia.

tugtupite.occurrence: Replaces chkalovite in hydrothermal veins cutting sodalite syenite and syenite (Il¶³maussaq intrusion, Greenland); an alteration product in pegmatites in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia).
tugtupite.etymology: For the occurrence at Tugtup agtak^ or¯a,Greenland.

tuhualite.occurrence: A primary igneous mineral and in vesicles of some silicic lavas, as comendites and pantellerites.
tuhualite.etymology: For the type locality, Mayor Island, New Zealand, which is called Tuhua by the native Maori.

tuite.occurrence: Formed by solid state transformation of whitlockite in a vein of shock-melted material in a chondritic meteorite.
tuite.etymology: Honors Professor Guangzhi Tu, the founding director of the Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS).

tulameenite.occurrence: In placers (Canada); in Uralian ultramaﬁcs (Nizhni Tagil, Russia); in Cu–Ni–PGM deposits in dunite-troctolite-gabbro (Ioko-Dovyren massif, Russia).
tulameenite.etymology: For the Tulameen River, Canada, from the vicinity of which the mineral was ﬁrst noted.

tuliokite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins in nepheline syenite pegmatite.
tuliokite.etymology: For the Tuliok River, Kola Peninsula, Russia, near where the mineral was ﬁrst found.

tululite.occurrence: An abundant accessory mineral in combustion metamorphic (800-850 °C) spurritefluorellestadite marbles derived from bitumen-rich chalky marine sediments.
tululite.etymology: After Tulul Al Hammam (Arabic for “Pigeon Hills”) where the mineral was found.

tumchaite.occurrence: As a lens-like segregation in a core sample from a bore hole, which crosscuts veined dolomite-calcite carbonatites occurring in pyroxenites. Formed by hydrothermal alteration of carbonatite.
assoc_parsed: a mineral of the serpentine group
tumchaite.etymology: For the Tumcha river near the Vuoriyarvi massif.

tundrite-ce.occurrence: In pegmatite veins associated with nepheline syenites.
tundrite-ce.etymology: After the Lovozero massif (formerly the Lovozero tundra), Kola Peninsula, Russia, where it was discovered, and a suffix for the cerium content.

tundrite-nd.occurrence: In pegmatite veins associated with layered nepheline syenite.
tundrite-nd.etymology: For its relation to tundrite-(Ce), and its neodymium content.

tunellite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed in borate deposits.
tunellite.etymology: To honor Dr. George Gerard Tunell, Jr. (1900–1996), Professor of Geology, University of California, Los Angeles, California, USA.

tungsten.occurrence: From gold placers in a river valley and in heavy concentrates from crushed quartz.
tungsten.etymology: From tung sten for ‘heavy stone’ in Swedish.

tungstenite.occurrence: In a deposit replacing limestone (Emma mine, Utah, USA); replacing scheelite (Angokitsk deposit, Russia); in high-temperature fumaroles (Kudryavyy volcano, Russia).

tungstibite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal polymetallic barite–ﬂuorite deposit.
tungstibite.etymology: For TUNGsten and antimony, STIBium, in the composition.

tungstite.occurrence: An alteration product of tungsten minerals, especially wolframite and ferberite, in hydrothermal tungsten-bearing deposits.

tungusite.occurrence: A secondary mineral forming crusts lining cavities and amygdules in hydrothermally altered basalts.

tunisite.occurrence: A very rare hydrothermal mineral, ﬁlling cavities in calcite (Sakiet Sidi Yousseﬀ mine, Tunisia).
tunisite.etymology: For Tunisia, the country in which it was ﬁrst found to occur.

tuperssuatsiaite.occurrence: A late-stage, low-temperature, hydrothermal mineral in veins cutting nepheline syenite and in sodalite-nepheline syenite pegmatite (Tuperssuatsiait Bay, Greenland); in miarolitic cavities in phonolite (Windhoek, Namibia).

turanite.occurrence: A rare secondary oxidation mineral in vanadium-bearing mineral deposits.
turanite.etymology: For the Turan region, Kyrgyzstan, where the mineral was first found.

turkestanite.etymology: For the region, Turkestan Ridge, where the studied material was collected.

turneaureite.occurrence: A rare component of manganiferous ores in high-grade marbles.
turneaureite.etymology: Honors Dr. Frederick Stewart Turneaure (1899-1986), Professor Emeritus of Geology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA.

turquoise.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in the potassic alteration zone of hydrothermal porphyry copper deposits; a vein-ﬁlling in volcanic rocks and phosphate-rich sediments.
turquoise.etymology: From the French Turquie, as Iranian material was early imported through Turkey.

turtmannite.occurrence: In metamorphosed (upper greenschist facies) jacobsite-rich Fe-Mn ores in paleokarst.
turtmannite.etymology: For the Turtmann Valley that hosts the type locality.

tuscanite.occurrence: Within ejected blocks of metasomatized carbonate rocks in a pumice deposit.
tuscanite.etymology: For the Tuscany region of Italy where the mineral was ¯rst found.

tusionite.occurrence: Of late-stage hydrothermal origin, rare in granite pegmatites, typically in miarolitic cavities.
tusionite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence along the upper Tusion River, Tadjikistan.

tuzlaite.occurrence: In a saline evaporite deposit, as veins in dolomitic marl between salt layers.
tuzlaite.etymology: For Tuzla, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the town near the salt mine in which the species was found.

tvalchrelidzeite.etymology: In honor of Academician Aleksander Antonovich Tvalchrelidze (1881–1957), founder of the Georgian Mineralogical-Petrographic School, Tbilisi University, Tbilisi, Georgia.

tvedalite.etymology: For the Tvedalen area in Norway, which has produced many interesting minerals from the nepheline syenites.

tveitite-y.occurrence: In a pegmatite dike in amphibolites, probably formed by inversion of yttroﬂuorite.
tveitite-y.etymology: Honors John Tveit, in whose quarry in Norway the mineral was ﬁrst found.

twinnite.occurrence: In marble with other lead sulfantimonides (Madoc, Canada).
twinnite.etymology: In honor of Robert Mitchell Thompson (1918–1967), Canadian mineralogist, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada. Thompson is “son of Thomas”; the latter is Aramaic for “a twin”. The name is doubly appropriate in alluding to the polysynthetic twinning present in the mineral.

tychite.etymology: From the Greek for good fortune, as the first and one of the last ten crystals examined were of this species, from a lot of about 5000 examined.

tyretskite1a.occurrence: Very rare, in a cavity in dolomitic saline rock, in drillcore from a depth of 1233 m.
tyretskite1a.etymology: For its initial occurrence near the Tyret station, Russia.

tyrolite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal copper deposits, typically formed by alteration of tennantite.
tyrolite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Tirol (Tyrol), Austria.

tyrrellite.occurrence: With other selenides, as the youngest hydrothermal replacements and open space ﬁllings in sheared Precambrian rocks, which also contain uraninite deposits (Goldﬁelds district, Canada).
tyrrellite.etymology: Honors Joseph Burr Tyrell (1858–1957), American geologist, ﬁrst to visit the area of discovery in Canada.

tyuyamunite.occurrence: An uncommon mineral in the oxidized zone of U–V deposits, especially those of the Colorado Plateau-type.
tyuyamunite.etymology: For the Tyuya-Muyun Cave, Kyrgyzstan, its original locality.

uakitite.occurrence: An accessory phase in an iron meteorite. Formed due to high-temperature (>1000 °C) separation of Fe-Cr-rich sulfide liquid from Fe-metal melt.
assoc_parsed: in troilite-daubreelite   inclusions   and in troilite-daubreelite nodules   in fe-ni-metal  . distribution from the uakit iron meteorite   found in 2016 in the baunt evenk district

uchucchacuaite.occurrence: In a telescoped polymetallic hydrothermal deposit (Peru).
uchucchacuaite.etymology: For the Uchuc-Chacua deposit in Peru.

udinaite.occurrence: A sublimate at an active volcanic fumarole.
assoc_parsed: powellite. distribution from the arsenatnaya fumarole
second scoria cone of the northern breakthrough of the great tolbachik fissure eruption
udinaite.etymology: For the Udina volcano situated near the discovery locality.

uedaite-ce.etymology: Honors Tateo Ueda (1912–2000), who was the first to solve the crystal structure of allanite.

uhligite.etymology: To honor Alfred Lewis Johannes Uhlig (1883–1919), German geologist, who lead the expedition on which the mineral was discovered.

uklonskovite.occurrence: Of very rare occurrence in cavities in clays above the salt strata (Kushkanatau salt deposit, Uzbekistan); on gypsum, sulfate derived from oxidizing sulﬁdes, the other elements from limestones and clays (Cetine mine, Italy).
uklonskovite.etymology: Honors Aleksandr Sergeevich Uklonskii (1882–1972), mineralogist, Tashkent University, Tashkent, Uzbekistan, who studied central Asian mineral deposits.

ulexite.occurrence: Typically in playa and salt-marsh deposits in arid regions and bedded sedimentary deposits formed from these, the boron supplied from surrounding hot springs. Some occurrences contain upwards of one billion tons of ulexite.
ulexite.etymology: Honors George Ludwig Ulex (1811–1883), German chemist who obtained the ﬁrst reliable analysis of the mineral.

ulfanderssonite-ce.occurrence: A primary mineral in metasomatic Fe-REE skarn mineralization of the Bastnäs-type.
ulfanderssonite-ce.etymology: Honors Ulf B. Andersson (b. 1960), a Swedish geologist-petrologist for his contributions to the understanding of the genesis of REE deposits of the Bastnäs type.

ullmannite.occurrence: With nickel minerals in hydrothermal veins.
ullmannite.etymology: In honor of Johan Christoph Ullmann (1771–1821), German chemist and mineralogist, who ﬁrst discovered the mineral.

ulrichite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in miarolitic cavities in pegmatoidal granite.
ulrichite.etymology: To honor George Henry Frederick Ulrich (1830–1900), for his contributions to the mineralogy of Victoria, Australia.

ulvospinel.occurrence: A common component of titaniferous magnetite iron ores; in kimberlites; in strongly reduced iron-bearing basalts, terrestrial and lunar.
ulvospinel.etymology: For the occurrence on the Ulv¨ o Islands, Sweden, and as a member of the spinel group.

umangite.occurrence: With other selenides in hydrothermal veins, formed below 112 ◦C.
umangite.etymology: For the Sierra de Umango, Argentina, place of ﬁrst discovery.

umbite.occurrence: In pegmatite in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
umbite.etymology: For Lake Umbozero, which separates the Khibiny massif from the Lovozero massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

umbozerite.occurrence: In pneumatolytic-hydrothermal veins cutting alkalic rocks in the upper part of a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
assoc_parsed: niobium-bearing minerals of the lomonosovite group
umbozerite.etymology: For Lake Umbozero, Kola Peninsula, Russia, near where the mineral was discovered.

umbrianite.occurrence: Essential groundmass, late-magmatic mineral in vesicular melilitolite, unstable under post-magmatic hydrothermal conditions and alters to Ba-rich hydrated phases.
umbrianite.etymology: For Umbria, the region of Central Italy where the studied material was collected.

umohoite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral, typically in sediment-hosted uranium-bearing deposits, formed in the oxidation zone above the water table.
umohoite.etymology: For Uranium, MOlybdenum, Hydrogen, and Oxygen in the composition.

ungavaite.occurrence: As grains in heavy-mineral concentrates derived from drill-core from ultramafic rocks. Likely the product of hydrothermal remobilization of Pd (and possibly Sb) from pre-existing sulfides. Probably developed below 400°C; possibly through a solid state, order-disorder transformation.
ungavaite.etymology: For the Ungava region, in which it was discovered.

ungemachite.occurrence: Rarely formed by the oxidation of pyrite in an arid climate, in veins and cavities in other massive iron sulfates.
ungemachite.etymology: Honors Henri L´ eon Ungemach (1879–1936), Belgian crystallographer who studied the natural sulfates of Chile.

upalite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized uraniferous zone of a complex granite pegmatite.
upalite.etymology: For Uranium, Phosphorus, and ALuminum in the composition.

uralborite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in boron-rich iron-ore skarns (Novofrolovskoye deposit, Russia); in a vein cutting limestone (Fuka, Japan).
uralborite.etymology: For the original locality in the URAL Mountains, Russia, and BORate in its composition.

uralolite.occurrence: In complex zoned granite pegmatites (Boevskoye deposit, Russia; Dunton quarry, Maine, USA); in a spodumene-rich pegmatite in high-grade metamorphic rocks (Weinebene Pass, Austria).
uralolite.etymology: For the Ural Mountain region, Russia, in which it was ﬁrst found.

uramarsite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of pitchblende-sulfide mineralization in highly-fractured , hydrothermally-altered felsite porphyry and tuff breccia.
uramarsite.etymology: An acronym for the major chemical components URanium, AMmonium, ARSenate .

uramphite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a uranium-coal deposit, in fractures in the coal at depths between 20 and 50 m.
uramphite.etymology: For its content of URanium, AMmonium, and PHosphate.

urancalcarite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of uranium deposits.
urancalcarite.etymology: For URANium, CALcium, and CARbonate in the composition.

uraninite.occurrence: In granite and syenite pegmatites; in hydrothermal high-temperature tin and moderate-temperature Co–Ni–Bi–Ag–As and other sulﬁde veins; in Colorado Plateau-type sandstone-hosted U–V deposits; in uraniferous conglomerates; a detrital mineral.

uranoclite.occurrence: In efflorescent crusts on mine walls by postmining oxidation of asphaltum-rich sandstone beds laced with uraninite and sulfides in a damp underground environment .
uranoclite.etymology: For its composition as the first uranyl chloride mineral with no other anions other than hydroxyl.

uranophane-alpha.occurrence: A common secondary mineral in uranium deposits and pegmatites, formed by alteration of uraninite; as coatings, presumably through deposition from meteoric waters.
uranophane-alpha.etymology: From URANium and the Greek for to appear.

uranophane-beta.occurrence: A secondary mineral, altering from other uranium minerals under oxidizing conditions.
uranophane-beta.etymology: In allusion to its dimorphous relation to uranophane.

uranopilite.occurrence: A locally abundant secondary mineral formed under acid conditions by the oxidation of sulﬁdes in the presence of uraninite; may be of post-mining origin.
uranopilite.etymology: From its content of URANium and the Greek for felt, for its texture.

uranopolycrase.occurrence: In a zoned pegmatite vein near the contact with granodiorite.
uranopolycrase.etymology: For its content of URANium and relation to polycrase-(Y).

uranosilite.etymology: For URANium and SILicon in the chemical composition.

uranospathite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of uranium-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
uranospathite.etymology: For its content of uranium and the Greek for a “broad blade”, an allusion to the bladed character of its crystals.

uranosphaerite.occurrence: An oxidation product of uraninite in a Co-Ni-Bi-bearing hydrothermal vein (Schneeberg, Germany).
uranosphaerite.etymology: For URANium in the composition, and the Greek for sphere, for the typical habit.

uranospinite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxide zone of U -As-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
uranospinite.etymology: A prefix for its uranium content and from the Greek for siskin, in allusion to its typical color.

uranotungstite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed in polymetallic base metal deposits.
uranotungstite.etymology: For its content of URANium and TUNGsten.

urea.occurrence: Derived from bat guano and urine, stable only under very arid conditions.
urea.etymology: From the Greek for urine, in which urea was ﬁrst found.

uricite.etymology: For its composition, anhydrous uric acid.

uroxite.occurrence: As post-mining, secondary efflorescent crusts on asphaltum-quartz matrix of mine walls. Hosted in deposits of the Colorado Plateau type with uranium mineralization in intimate association with carbonaceous plant material.
assoc_parsed: uranopilite  . distribution from the burro mine
uroxite.etymology: Identifies a mineral with essential uranyl (UR) and oxalate (OX) components.

urusovite.occurrence: A sublimate at a volcanic fumarole.
urusovite.etymology: Honors crystal chemist Vadim Sergeevich Urusov (b. 1936), Corresponding Member of the Russian Academy of Sciences and Chair of the Department of Crystallography and Crystal Chemistry, Moscow State University, Russia.

urvantsevite.occurrence: In massive zoned Cu–Ni sulﬁde ores (Talnakh area, Russia).
urvantsevite.etymology: Honors Professor Nikolai Nikolaevich Urvantsev (1893–1985), of St. Petersburg, Russia, one of the discoverers of the Noril’sk deposits.

ushkovite.occurrence: In granite pegmatites, as an alteration product of triplite formed by weathering.
ushkovite.etymology: To honor Sergei L’vovich Ushkov (1880–1951), Russian naturalist, student of the Il’men National Forest, Russia.

usovite.occurrence: In a ﬂuorite vein in quartz-mica schists.
usovite.etymology: Honors Academician Mikhail Antonovich Usov (1883–1939), geologist, Karpinskii All-Union Research Institute of Geology, St. Petersburg, Russia.

ussingite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in pegmatites associated with sodalite syenite (Il¶³maussaq intrusion, Greenland); in sodalite xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
ussingite.etymology: For Professor Niels Vigo Ussing (1864{1911), of Copenhagen, Denmark.

ustarasite.etymology: For the locality of ﬁrst discovery, the Ustarasai deposit, Uzbekistan.

usturite.occurrence: In the cuspidine zone of high-temperature skarns in a carbonate-silicate xenolith at the contact with ignimbrites.
usturite.etymology: Formerly bitikleite-(ZrFe). For Ustur Mountain near the type locality.

utahite.occurrence: A very rare secondary mineral found on dump material from the oxidized zone of a Cu–Zn–Te-bearing hydrothermal ore deposit.
utahite.etymology: After the state of Utah, USA, where the mineral was discovered.

uvanite.occurrence: In a Colorado Plateau-type uranium deposit in asphaltic sandstone.
uvanite.etymology: For Uranium and V ANadium in the composition.

uvarovite.occurrence: From hydrothermal alteration of serpentinite containing chromite; in metamorphosed limestones and skarns from the reaction of dolomite and chromite.
uvarovite.etymology: For Count Sergei Semenovich Uvarov (1786{1855), Russian nobleman, President of Academy of Sciences.

uvite.occurrence: Typically in calcium-rich rocks sub jected to contact metamorphism and metasomatic processes which added boron.
uvite.etymology: For the occurrence in Uva Province, Sri Lanka.

uytenbogaardtite.occurrence: In low-temperature hydrothermal Au–Ag quartz veins, in part of supergene origin.
uytenbogaardtite.etymology: To honor Willem Uytenbogaardt (1918– ), Professor of Geology, Technical University, Delft, The Netherlands, prominent ore microscopist.

uzonite.occurrence: As intergrowths with realgar in the pore spaces of tuﬀaceous sediments 10–30 cm deep in a caldera.
uzonite.etymology: For the type locality, Uzon caldera, Russia.

vaesite.occurrence: Disseminated through dolostone (Kasompi mine, Congo); an alteration product of arsenic-deﬁcient nickel-skutterudite (Germany).
vaesite.etymology: In honor of Johannes F. Vaes (1902–1978), mineralogist for the Union Mini` ere du Haut Katanga.

vajdakite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in a highly oxidized uraninite-arsenide-sulfarsenide deposit (Czech Republic).
vajdakite.etymology: Honors Josef Vadjak (b. 1930), of Pequa Rare Minerals, Massapequa, New York, USA, who drew attention to the species, and in recognition of his contributions to mineralogical research on the Jáchymov ore district.

valentinite.occurrence: An alteration product of antimony-bearing minerals in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal antimony deposits.
valentinite.etymology: To honor Basilius Valentinus, 15th century alchemist, who early wrote concerning antimony.

valleriite.occurrence: An alteration product of chalcopyrite in chromitites and dunites (Cyprus); in copper-bearing carbonatites, replacing magnetite (Phalaborwa, South Africa); in Cu–Ni sulﬁde-bearing serpentinized and uralized ultramaﬁc rocks.
valleriite.etymology: In honor of Johan Gottschalk Wallerius (Vallerius) (1709–1785), Swedish chemist and mineralogist.

valleyite.occurrence: An oxidation product of basaltic glass, on the surface of vesicles, formed during the early stage of the scoria formation (Idaho) and in paralava, fused sedimentary rock (Wyoming).
valleyite.etymology: Honors John W. Valley (b. 1948) of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Valley was the President of the Mineralogical Society of America during 2005-2006. His groundbreaking contributions to mineralogy, petrology, and geochemistry have led to a deeper understanding of Earth’s crustal evolution from early Earth to the Anthropocene.

vanackerite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted, polymetallic, hydrothermal ore deposit.
vanackerite.etymology: Honors Georges Vanacker (1923-1992) of Bruges, Belgium, whose systematic mineral collection includes many specimens from the Tsumeb deposit, in one of which, vanackerite was first identified. His collection was donated to the Natural Sciences Institute, Brussels, Belgium.

vanadinite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of lead-bearing deposits, the vanadium leached from wall-rock silicates.

vanadio-oxy-chromium-dravite.occurrence: A primary mineral in metaquartzite (granulite facies) in marble.
vanadio-oxy-chromium-dravite.etymology: As an oxy-chromium-dravite with dominant vanadium in the Y site and V 3+ contents between 5 and 1.5 atoms per formula unit.

vanadio-oxy-dravite.occurrence: A primary mineral in metaquartzite (granulite facies) in marble.
vanadio-oxy-dravite.etymology: As an oxy-dravite with dominant vanadium in the Y site and V 3+ contents between 5 and 1.5 atoms per formula unit.

vanadio-pargasite.occurrence: Formed during prograde (granulite-facies) metamorphism of Cr-V-bearing calcite-dolomite and siliceous sediments.
vanadio-pargasite.etymology: As a vanadium-bearing analog of pargasite, a monoclinic amphibole with Ca dominant as the B cation.

vanadiocarpholite.occurrence: Remobilized components were concentrated in veins and open fissures in silicified wood during metamorphism of Mn-ore bearing cherts.
vanadiocarpholite.etymology: Prefix, vanadio, identifies essential vanadium in the composition of a phase of the carpholite group.

vanadium.occurrence: In sublimates from high-temperature (550-680 ° C) volcanic gases at active fumaroles.
vanadium.etymology: The chemical element named for Vanadis, a Scandinavian goddess.

vanadoallanite-la.occurrence: In a vein cutting a stratiform ferromanganese deposit.
vanadoallanite-la.etymology: For a member of the allanite group with dominant vanadium in the M1 site and suffix for the dominant rare earth element, lanthanum.

vanadoandrosite-ce.occurrence: In quartz-rhodochrosite-sulfide veins cross-cutting massive rhodochrosite ore, as well as in the ore itself, in quartz grains rimmed by chalcopyrite.
vanadoandrosite-ce.etymology: An epidote-group mineral in which Ce3+ is dominant in A2, Mn2+ in A1, V3+ in M1, Al in M2, and in which Mn2+ is the dominant charge-compensating (i.e. divalent) cation in M3.

vanalite.occurrence: Incrusting joints and cavities in weathered shales.
vanalite.etymology: For V ANadium and ALuminum in the composition.

vanarsite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by the oxidation of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a moist environment.
vanarsite.etymology: An acronym based on the composition and specifically the fact that it contains vanadate, arsenite, and arsenate groups.

vandenbrandeite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxide zone of hydrothermal copper-bearing uranium deposits.
vandenbrandeite.etymology: To honor Pierre Van den Brande (1896–1957), Belgian geologist, who discovered the uranium deposit at Kalongwe, Congo.

vandendriesscheite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of uranium-bearing mineral deposits.
vandendriesscheite.etymology: Honors Adrien Vandendriessche (1914–1940), Belgian mineralogist and geologist, University of Ghent, Ghent, Belgium.

vanderheydenite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a highly weathered recrystallized sulfide ore as a result of the release of Zn, S, As, and P from the breakdown of sphalerite, galena, and fluorapatite.
vanderheydenite.etymology: Honors Arnold van der Heyden, mine geologist at the Broken Hill mine for the former Minerals Mining and Metallurgy Ltd (December 1985 until June 1991) in recognition of his contribution to the understanding of the secondary mineralogy of the Broken Hill ore body by the systematic collecting of mineral specimens from the oxidized zone.

vanmeersscheite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the uraniferous zone of an altered granite pegmatite.
vanmeersscheite.etymology: To honor Professor Maurice Van Meerssche (1923–1990), Belgian crystallographer, Catholic University of Louvain, Louvain, Belgium.

vanoxite.occurrence: A replacement of fossil wood and cementing sandstone in Colorado Plateau-type U–V deposits.

vantasselite.occurrence: On dumps in a quartzite quarry, in quartz veinlets or lining schistosity planes.
vantasselite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Ren´ e Van Tassel (1916– ), mineralogist, Royal Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels, Belgium, for his work on Belgian mineralogy.

vanthoffite.occurrence: Restricted to evaporite deposits of oceanic origin.
vanthoffite.etymology: To honor Professor Jacobus Henricus van’t Hoﬀ (1852–1911), German physical chemist, University of Berlin, Berlin, Germany, who elucidated the equilibria involved in formation of oceanic salt deposits.

vanuralite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a lead-bearing U–V deposit (Mounana mine, Gabon).
vanuralite.etymology: For VANadium, URanium, and ALuminum in the composition.

vapnikite.occurrence: In the Hatrurim Formation (“Mottled Zone”). Formed by pyrometamorphism due to combustion of organic-rich material at temperatures above 800 °C., during a retrograde stage by fluids/melts of high alkalinity.
vapnikite.etymology: Honors Yevgeny Vapnik of Ben Gurion, University of the Negev, Beer Sheva, Israel, for his mineralogical studies of the Hatrurim Formation.

variscite.occurrence: Typically deposited from phosphate-bearing waters in contact with aluminous rocks. On islands and in caves, the phosphate provided by decomposition of guano.
variscite.etymology: From Variscia, an old name for Vogtland, the district in Germany which was the original source for the mineral.

varulite.occurrence: In complex granite pegmatites, either as a primary mineral or an alteration product of triphylite–lithiophilite; as nodules in shale.
varulite.etymology: For its initially noted occurrence in the Varutr¨ ask pegmatite, Sweden.

vashegyite.occurrence: Filling cavities in boxwork “limonite” from an iron mine ( ˇZelezn´ ık, Slovakia).
vashegyite.etymology: For its occurrence at Vashegy, Hungary (now ˇZelezn´ ık, Slovakia).

vasilseverginite.occurrence: A volcanic sublimate on basaltic scoria in the walls of a fumarole at temperatures higher than 380 °C.
vasilseverginite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist, geologist, and chemist Vasiliy Mikhailovich Severgin (1765- 1826), Academician of the Russian Academy of Sciences. His books on geology and mineralogy were the first in Russia and presented the first chemical nomenclature in Russian. Severgin was one of the founders of the Russian Mineralogical Society in 1817.

vasilyevite.occurrence: A rare mineral replacing native mercury in vugs in hydrothermal quartz veins.
vasilyevite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist, Vladimir Ivanovich Vasilyev (b. 1929), Institute of Geology, Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Novosibirsk, Russia, for his discovery of numerous new mercury minerals.

vaterite.occurrence: A major constituent of a carbonated calcium silicate hydrogel complex formed from larnite (Ballycraigy, Ireland); a rock-forming mineral formed at low temperatures by hydration of metamorphic calc-silicate rocks in the presence of atmospheric CO 2, in slightly metamorphosed marls and conglomerates, and in weathering crusts (Hatrurim Formation, Israel).
vaterite.etymology: To honor Heinrich Vater (1859–1930), Professor of Mineralogy and Chemistry, Tharandt, Germany.

vaughanite.occurrence: A very rare primary mineral found in drill core from an epithermal-hydrothermal gold deposit.
vaughanite.etymology: To honor Professor David John Vaughan (1946– ), Manchester University, Manchester, England, for his contributions to ore mineralogy.

vauquelinite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the oxidized zones of some hydrothermal base-metal deposits.
vauquelinite.etymology: Honoring Professor Louis Nicolas Vauquelin (1763–1829), French chemist, University of Paris, Paris, France, who discovered chromium.

vauxite.occurrence: A secondary mineral derived from alteration of apatite.
vauxite.etymology: Honoring George Vaux, Jr. (1863–1927), American lawyer and mineral collector, Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania, USA.

vayrynenite.occurrence: An alteration product of beryl and triphylite in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
vayrynenite.etymology: To honor Professor Heikki Allan V¨ ayrynen (1888–1956), Technical Institute, Helsinki, Finland.

veatchite.occurrence: Uncommon in evaporite borate deposits formed by volcanic activity.
veatchite.etymology: Honors John A. Veatch (1808–1870), American physician and geologist, who ﬁrst detected boron in mineral waters in California, USA in the late 1800’s.

veatchite-a.occurrence: Uncommon in evaporite borate deposits formed by volcanic activity.
veatchite-a.etymology: As a polytype of veatchite, crystallizing in the anorthic (triclinic) system.

veatchite-p.occurrence: A very rare component of marine evaporite salt deposits.
veatchite-p.etymology: The preﬁx “p” used to represent a primitive unit cell, and for its close relation to veatchite.

veblenite.formula_html: K2   2Na(Fe2+5Fe3+4Mn7   )Nb3Ti(Si2O7)2(Si8O22)2O6(OH)10(H2O)3
veblenite.etymology: Honors of David R. Veblen (b. 1947), Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA, in recognition of his outstanding contributions to the fields of mineralogy and crystallography.

veenite.occurrence: As small masses, stringers, and disseminated grains in marbles developed in a sequence of Precambrian metasediments near a contact with plutonic granitic gneiss (Madoc, Canada).
veenite.etymology: To honor R.W. van der Veen (1883–1925), Dutch economic geologist and metallographer.

vendidaite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a weathered copper sulfide deposit.
vendidaite.etymology: For the La Vendida mine, from which the first samples were collected.

verbierite.etymology: For the town near where the studied samples were collected.

vergasovaite.occurrence: A rare sublimation product in fumaroles.
vergasovaite.etymology: Honors Dr. Lidia Pavlovna Vergasova (1941– ), Institute of Vulcanology, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskii, Russia, for her contributions to the mineralogy of that volcanic region.

vermiculite.occurrence: An alteration product of biotite or phlogopite, by weathering or hydrothermal action. Formed at the contact between felsic and ma¯c or ultrama¯c rocks such as pyroxenites and dunites; in carbonatites and metamorphosed limestones; a clayey constituent of soils.
vermiculite.etymology: From the Latin to breed worms, alluding to the mineral's exfoliation upon rapid heating.

vernadite.occurrence: A weathering product of other manganese oxides, carbonates, and silicates; easily formed by the action of Fe, Mn-oxidizing bacteria.
vernadite.etymology: For Professor Vladimir Ivanovich Vernadsky (1863–1945), Russian naturalist and geochemist, Moscow University, Moscow, Russia.

verneite.etymology: Honors French author Jules Verne (1828-1905), for his promotion of science. His Voyage au center de la Terre (1864), describes a journey through Earth’s underground started through Snæfell crater in Iceland and finished by ejecting the travelers with eruption of Stromboli in Italy.

verplanckite.occurrence: In thin layers in a metamorphic sanbornite-quartz rock.
verplanckite.etymology: For William E. Ver Planck (1916{1963), geologist of the California Division of Mines & Geology, California, USA.

versiliaite.occurrence: In an iron ore deposit in barite formed by metasomatic processes at the contact between phyllites and dolostones.
versiliaite.etymology: For the Versilia Valley, Apuan Alps, Italy, where it was found.

vertumnite.occurrence: As late-forming crystals inside a small cavity in phonolite.
vertumnite.etymology: For Vertumnus, the god worshipped by the ancient Etruscan people who inhabited the region where the mineral was found.

vesignieite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed in copper-bearing U–V deposits.
vesignieite.etymology: Honoring Colonel Jean Paul Louis V´ esigni´ e (1870–1954), noted French mineral collector.

vestaite.occurrence: In two titanium-rich, shock melt pockets (20-30 mm in size), which are enclosed by former plagioclase (now maskelynite, plagioclase, and tissintite), augite and ilmenite in a basaltic eucrite meteorite.

vesuvianite.occurrence: In skarns formed during contact or regional metamorphism of limestones; in garnetized gabbros, ma¯c and ultrama¯c rocks, and serpentinites; uncommon in alkalic igneous rocks.
vesuvianite.etymology: For its occurrence at Vesuvius, Italy.

veszelyite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of some base-metal mineral deposits.
veszelyite.etymology: Honoring A. Veszelyi (1820–1888), Hungarian mining engineer, who discovered the species.

viaeneite.etymology: To honor Professor Willy A. Viaene (1940– ), Catholic University, Louvain, Belgium, who has made important contributions to geological sciences in Belgium.

vicanite-ce.occurrence: As crystals in miarolitic cavities in volcanic ejecta of syenitic composition.
vicanite-ce.etymology: For the Vican volcanic complex (Italy) where the mineral was found. Type: Mineralogical Museum, University of Rome, Italy.

vigezzite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in an albitized pegmatite in amphibolite and biotite gneiss (Orcesco, Italy).
vigezzite.etymology: For Val Vigezzo, Italy, where the mineral occurs.

vigrishinite.occurrence: In a zoned peralkaline pegmatite located in foyaite and lujavrite rocks of a layered alkaline igneous complex. Found at the periphery of the ussingite core near its contact with the aegirine-eudialyte zone.
vigrishinite.etymology: Honors the Russian amateur mineralogist and mineral collector Viktor G. Grishin (b. 1953) for his significant contribution to the mineralogy of the Lovozero complex, Russia.

viitaniemiite.occurrence: An inclusion in eosphorite and rimming morinite, from a complex zoned granite pegmatite (Viitaniemi pegmatite, Finland); in druses in granite (Greifensteine, Germany).
viitaniemiite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Viitaniemi pegmatite, Finland.

vikingite.occurrence: Associated with cosalite and as lamellae in galena in the gustavite-galena paragenesis (Ivigtut, Greenland).
vikingite.etymology: For the Vikings, early settlers of Greenland.

villamaninite.occurrence: As subhedral disseminated grains in black bituminous dolostone; in white coarse-grained recrystallized dolostone; as nodular aggregates in vuggy dolomite veinlets (Providencia mine, Spain).
villamaninite.etymology: For the town of Villaman ´ ın, Spain.

villiaumite.occurrence: In nepheline syenite and nepheline syenite pegmatites; in lake-bed deposits.
villiaumite.etymology: Honors Maxime Villiaume, French explorer, in whose collections of rocks from Guinea the mineral was ﬁrst found.

villyaellenite.occurrence: A rare post-mine low-temperature reaction product of carbonate gangue with arsenical solutions derived from arsenic (Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, France); on a museum specimen from the oxidized zone of an arsenic-rich base metal deposit (Mapimí, Mexico); on a single specimen from a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Sterling Hill, New Jersey, USA).
villyaellenite.etymology: Honors Dr. Villy Aellen, Director, Natural History Museum, Geneva, Switzerland.

vimsite.occurrence: In boron-rich copper-bearing skarn (Novofrolovskoye deposit, Russia); in iron-bearing skarn (Solongo deposit, Russia).
vimsite.etymology: For the 50th anniversary of the All-Union Scientiﬁc Research Institute of Mineral Resources [an acronym for Vses. Nauch.-Issled. Inst. Mineral. Syr’ya], Moscow, Russia.

vincentite.occurrence: As inclusions in Fe-bearing palladium grains in sediment concentrates from the Riam Kanen River, S.E. Borneo.
vincentite.etymology: Honors Professor E. A. Vincent of Oxford University, England.

vinciennite.occurrence: In a porphyry copper deposit with other tin-bearing sulfides (Maggie deposit, Canada) .
vinciennite.etymology: To honor Professor Henri Vincienne (1898-1965), who first called attention to the mineral. Type Ma<;erial: National School of Mines, Paris, France.

vinogradovite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in cavities and veins, and replacing titanium-bearing minerals, in alkalic pegmatites in di®erentiated alkalic massifs (Kola Peninsula, Russia).
vinogradovite.etymology: In honor of Academician Aleksander Pavlovich Vinogradov (1895{1975), Russian geochemist, Director of the Vernadsky Institute of Geochemistry and Analytical Chemistry, Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia.

violarite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin, with other sulﬁdes.
violarite.etymology: From the Latin for violet, its color on a polished surface.

virgilite.occurrence: As inclusions in stream cobbles of peraluminous volcanic glass.
virgilite.etymology: In honor of Professor Virgil Everett Barnes (1903{ ), University of Texas, Austin, Texas, USA, prominent worker on tektites, impactites, and other natural glasses.

viseite.occurrence: Presumably as a secondary mineral in phosphatic sedimentary rocks, and from the weathering or low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of aluminous skarn deposits.
viseite.etymology: For the locality where the mineral was discovered, Vis¶e, Belgium.

vishnevite.occurrence: In poikilitic aegirine-nepheline-sodalite syenites and associated p egmatites.
vishnevite.etymology: For the locality in the Vishnevy Mountains, Russia.

vismirnovite.occurrence: Formed by oxidation of earlier tin sulﬁdes in tin deposits.
vismirnovite.etymology: Honors Academician Vladimir Ivanovich Smirnov (1910–1988), Moscow University, Moscow, Russia, an early investigator of tin deposits in Central Asia.

vistepite.occurrence: In a rhodonite vein in biotite-quartz hornfels at the margin of a tin-bearing granite massif.
vistepite.etymology: For the mineralogist and systematic mineral collector Victor Ivanovich Stepanov (1924{1988), A.E. Fersman Mineralogical Museum, Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia.

viteite.occurrence: In a heavy mineral concentrate from the oxidized ore of a sulfide-bearing orthopyroxenite body of a layered intrusion.

viteite.etymology: For the Vite River, which flows near the Monchetundra intrusion.

vitimite.occurrence: A low-temperature hydrothermal mineral in veinlets in a skarn-type boron deposit.
vitimite.etymology: For the Vitim plateau, in the southern part of which the first specimens were collected.

vittinkiite.etymology: For the Vittinki iron mines, Isokyrö, Western and Inner Finland Region, Finland, from where the studied material was collected (Fersman Museum #15061).

vitusite-ce.occurrence: An alteration product of steenstrupine in diﬀerentiated alkalic massifs (Il´ ımaussaq massif; Kola Peninsula, Russia); in sodalite xenoliths associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
vitusite-ce.etymology: To honor Vitus Bering (1681–1741), Danish-Russian explorer of the Arctic seas, and the dominant rare earth, cerium.

vivianite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of metallic ore deposits and complex granite pegmatites; replacing organic material in fossil bones, lake sediments, and in bog-iron ores and peat bogs; rarely in caves.
vivianite.etymology: Honoring John Henry Vivian (1785–1855), Welsh-Cornish mineralogist, of Truro, Cornwall, England, who discovered the species.

vladimirite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of arsenic-bearing mineral deposits.
vladimirite.etymology: For its first-noted occurrence in the Vladimirovskoye deposit, Russia.

vladimirivanovite.occurrence: In highly metamorphosed rocks of granulite facies at the contacts of dolomitic marbles with granites.
vladimirivanovite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist and geochemist Vladimir Georgievich Ivanov (1947-2002).

vladkrivovichevite.occurrence: Most likely a late-stage, low-temperature hydrothermal (epigenetic) reworking of primary Pb-Cu-Zn-Ag sulfides. Known from a single specimen purchased commercially.
vladkrivovichevite.etymology: Honors Professor Vladimir Gerasimovich Krivovichev (b. 1946), Head of the Mineralogy Department, Geological Faculty, St. Petersburg State University, Russia.

vladykinite.occurrence: An early magmatic phase in a dike of coarse-grained feldspathoidal syenite (lujavrite) in an alkaline igneous complex.
vladykinite.etymology: Honors Nikolay V. Vladykin (b. 1944), Vinogradov Institute of Geochemistry, Irkutsk, Russia, for his contributions to the study of alkaline rocks.

vlasovite.occurrence: A late phase in nephelin e syenites, syenitic pegmatites, and along the contact zone of a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Lovozero massif, Russia); in miarolitic cavities in ejected blocks of peralkalic granite (Ascension Island).
vlasovite.etymology: In honor of the Russian mineralogist and geochemist Kuz'ma Alekseevich Vlasov (1905{1964), founder of the Institute of Mineralogy, Geochemistry, and Crystal Chemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia.

vlodavetsite.occurrence: A product of low-temperature hydration of minerals on the fracture walls of volcanic fumaroles.
vlodavetsite.etymology: Honors Vladimir Ivanovich Vlodavets (1893–1993), volcanologist who founded the Kamchatka volcanological station.

vochtenite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a uranium-bearing Cu–Sn hydrothermal mineral deposit.
vochtenite.etymology: Honoring Professor Renaud F.C. Vochten (1933– ), State University, Antwerp, Belgium, uranium mineralogist, who discovered the mineral.

voggite.occurrence: Very rare, in cavities in an altered amygdaloidal basalt dike intruding a zirconium-bearing silicocarbonatite sill in a limestone quarry.
voggite.etymology: Honoring Adolf Vogg (1931– ), Canadian amateur mineralogist who collected the original specimens.

voglite.occurrence: A rare oxidation product of uraninite.
voglite.etymology: Honors Josef Florian Vogl (1818–1896), Austrian mining oﬃcer and mineralogist, who studied the minerals of J´ achymov, Czech Republic and ﬁrst described this species.

volaschioite.occurrence: An oxidation product of pyrite in tunnels through a magnetite-pyrite deposit.
volaschioite.etymology: Derived from the ancient name for the first known locality, believed to be derived from forno (furnace) and Volaschio (a locally significant proper noun).

volborthite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of vanadium-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
volborthite.etymology: To honor Aleksandr Fedorovich von Volborth (1800–1876), Russian paleontologist, who ﬁrst noticed the mineral.

volkonskoite.occurrence: An epigenetic mineral in sandstones, conglomerates, and red beds, commonly ¯lling voids from the decomposition of organic matter (Okhansk region, Russia); a weathering product of serpentinite (Gotse Delchev, Bulgaria).
volkonskoite.etymology: For Prince Petr Mikhailovich Volkonskii (1776{1852), Minister of the Imperial Court, Russia, patron of the natural sciences.

volkovskite.occurrence: Uncommon in water-insoluble residues from salt domes and potash deposits.
volkovskite.etymology: To honor A.I. Volkovskaya, petrographer, who ﬁrst noted the mineral.

voloshinite.occurrence: In veinlets or pods inside pollucite aggregates found in rare-element granitic pegmatites, a late-stage mineral formed after pollucite.
voloshinite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist A. V. Voloshin (b. 1937).

voltaite.occurrence: In volcanic fumaroles, solfataras, and mud volcanos; an alteration product in mineral deposits high in pyrite, especially in arid climates, where it may also be a post-mining product.
voltaite.etymology: To honor Alessandro Giuseppe Antonio Anastasio Volta (1745–1827), Italian physicist, early experimenter with electricity.

volynskite.occurrence: As complex intergrowths with other tellurides in gold ores.
volynskite.etymology: For Igor Sergeevich Volynskii (1900–1962), former Director of the Mineragraphic Laboratory, Institute of Mineralogy and Geochemistry of Rare Elements, Moscow, Russia.

vonbezingite.occurrence: A very rare mineral formed during a period of evaporation of surface or ground waters at ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure.
vonbezingite.etymology: To honor Karl-Ludwig von Bezing (1945– ), Austrian-South African mineral collector, for his contributions to knowledge of mineralogy of the Kalahari manganese ﬁeld.

vonsenite.etymology: Honors Magnus Vonsen (1879–1954), amateur mineralogist and mineral collector of Petaluma, California, USA, who discovered the mineral.

vorlanite.occurrence: In a calcareous skarn xenolith in ignimbrite probably transformed by radiation damage to CaUO4 (Russia). In larnite-spurrite metacarbonate rocks formed by combustion metamorphism at very high temperature (> 1000° C) and low pressure (Israel).
vorlanite.etymology: After the locality that produced the first specimens, Mt. Vorlan.

voronkovite.occurrence: In a lenticular zoned pegmatite hosted by poikilitic nepheline-sodalite syenite in the middle part of a differentiated alkaline complex.
voronkovite.etymology: Honors Russian crystallographer Alexander Alexandrovich Voronkov (1928-1982).

vorontsovite.occurrence: In mineralized limestone breccias (calcite-dolomite, up to 85% of volume) in the ores of the sulfide-carbonate type in a gold deposit of uncertain origin.
vorontsovite.etymology: Honors mining engineer Vladimir Vasilyevich Vorontsov (1842-later than 1908) for whom the city and mine are named where the new mineral was discovered.

voudourisite.occurrence: A secondary mineral from the weathering of primary hawleyite and greenockite.
voudourisite.etymology: Honors Professor Panagiotis Voudouris (b. 1962), Department of Mineralogy and Petrology, Faculty of Geology and Geoenvironment, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Greece, in recognition of his groundbreaking work on the Lavrion deposits.

vozhminite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Vozhmin massif, Karelia, Russia.

vrbaite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal deposit with other As–Tl sulﬁde minerals.
vrbaite.etymology: For Professor Karel Vrba (1845–1922), University of Prague, Prague, Czechoslovakia, Czech mineralogist.

vuagnatite.occurrence: In rodingitized dikes of pegmatitic anorthositic gabbro crosscutting harzburgite-serpentines in an ophiolite (Taurus Mountains, Turkey); in rodingitized metagabbro dikes in serpentinized peridotite (Red Mountain, California, USA); all occurrences suggest formation under conditions of relatively low temperature and high pressure.
vuagnatite.etymology: For Professor Mark Bernard Vuagnat (1922{ ), student of ophiolites, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.

vulcanite.etymology: After the locality, Vulcan, Colorado, USA.

vuonnemite.occurrence: In albitized alkalic rocks in di®erentiated alkalic massifs (Kola Peninsula, Russia); in a transition zone between two nepheline syenites (Il¶³maussaq intrusion, Greenland); in sodalite xenoliths in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
vuonnemite.etymology: For the occurrence near the Vuonnemiok River, Khibiny massif, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

vuorelainenite.occurrence: In a metamorphosed iron sulﬁde deposit associated with submarine felsic volcanism (S¨ atra mine, Sweden); in quartzite schists (Ol’khon Gate Straits, Lake Baikal, Russia).
vuorelainenite.etymology: To honor Yrj¨ o Vuorelainen (1922– ), Finnish exploration geologist, formerly with the Outokumpu Company, Finland.

vurroite.occurrence: As encrustations around fumaroles (400-600 °C) in an active volcanic crater.
vurroite.etymology: Honors Filippo Vurro, (b. 1940), Professor of mineralogy, University of Bari, Italy, and specialist in the mineralogy and geochemistry of modern volcanic deposits.

vyacheslavite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in uranium deposits.
vyacheslavite.etymology: To honor Vyacheslav Gavrilovich Melkov (1911–1991), Russian mineralogist specializing in uranium minerals, Russian Research Institute of Mineral Resources, Moscow, Russia.

vysotskite.occurrence: In andesine diabases (Noril’sk region, Russia) and in ultramaﬁc layered intrusives elsewhere. As disseminations that probably are crystallized products, at magmatic temperatures, of a residual immiscible sulﬁde melt.
vysotskite.etymology: For Nikolai Konstaninovich Vysotskii (1864–1932), Soviet geologist, who ﬁrst found platinum at Noril’sk, Russia.

vyuntspakhkite-y.occurrence: Two generations of crystals occur in °uorite in \amazonite" pegmatites.
vyuntspakhkite-y.etymology: For Mt. Vyuntspakhk, 5 km southeast of Mt. Ploskaya, Kola Peninsula, Russia, and its yttrium content.

wadeite.occurrence: In veins in leucite lamproites (Wolgidee Hills, Western Australia); in nepheline-feldspathoid and natrolite veins in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Russia).
wadeite.etymology: For Dr. Arthur Wade, Australian geologist who ¯rst collected the mineral.

wadsleyite.occurrence: In fragments within a vein in a \hypersthene"-olivine chondritic meteorite, believed to have formed during an extraterrestrial shock event.

wagnerite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in metamorphic rocks of moderate to high grade; uncommon in pegmatites.
wagnerite.etymology: Honoring F.M. von Wagner (1768–1851), mining oﬃcial in Munich, Germany.

waimirite-y.occurrence: In veins cutting A-type granite formed by reaction with fluorine and REE-rich fluids.
waimirite-y.etymology: For the Waimiri-Atroari people of Roraima and Amazonas, Brazil.

wairakite.occurrence: In pores and cavities in rocks in geothermal areas, deposited from hydrothermal °uids; may replace feldspar. In tu®aceous sand stones and breccias, vitric and welded tu®s, and in clay.
wairakite.etymology: For the ¯rst-noted locality at Wairakei, New Zealand.

wairauite.occurrence: In a dominantly lizardite serpentine at the western contact of an ultramaﬁc intrusion; thought to have formed under low-sulfur reducing conditions during the serpentinization process (Wairau Valley, New Zealand).
wairauite.etymology: For the Wairau Valley locality in New Zealand.

wakabayashilite.occurrence: As ﬁbers in druses of quartz or embedded in calcite.
wakabayashilite.etymology: For Yaichiro Wakabayashi (1874–1943), mineralogist for the Mitsubishi Mining Company, Japan.

wakefieldite-ce.occurrence: In siliciﬁed limestone (Kusu deposit, Congo); in vesicles with zeolites (Yellow Lake, Canada).
wakefieldite-ce.etymology: Originally described as “kusuite”; the name later changed to reﬂect its identity as the cerium analog of wakeﬁeldite-(Y).

wakefieldite-la.occurrence: A low temperature mineral in a hydrothermal barite vein.
wakefieldite-la.etymology: As the La analogue of wakefieldite-(Ce) and wakefieldite-(Y).

wakefieldite-nd.occurrence: From metamorphism-induced recrystallization and dehydration of Fe- and Mnoxyhydroxide in a stratiform ferromanganese deposit. Hydrothermal in rhyolitic ash flow tuff.
wakefieldite-nd.etymology: Indicates the Nd-dominant analogue of wakefieldite-(Y) and wakefieldite-(Ce).

wakefieldite-y.occurrence: In quartz in a zoned granite pegmatite (Evans-Lou quarry, Canada).
wakefieldite-y.etymology: For Wakeﬁeld Lake, nearby the Evans-Lou quarry, Canada, and the dominant rare earth, yttrium.

walentaite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in a complex zoned pegmatite, probably formed by alteration of l¨ ollingite and triphylite–lithiophilite (White Elephant mine, South Dakota, USA); a secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a gold mine in granulite (Griﬃn’s Find mine, Australia).
walentaite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Kurt Walenta (1927– ), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Stuttgart, Stuttgart, Germany, for his contributions to the mineralogy of arsenates and phosphates, especially from the Black Forest, Germany.

walfordite.occurrence: Very rare in the brecciated oxidized zone of a tellurium-bearing hydrothermal gold deposit.
walfordite.etymology: Honors Phillip Walford (1945— ), Chief Geologist, LAC Minerals Ltd., who noted the ﬁrst specimens.

walkerite.etymology: Honors Canadian geologist Thomas Leonard Walker (1867-1942) for his contributions to mineralogy in general and to the study of borates from the Minas Basin, Nova Scotia, in particular.

wallisite.etymology: For Wallis, the German name for the Swiss Canton in which the Lengenbach quarry is located.

wallkilldellite.occurrence: Extremely rare in massive granular franklinite-willemite ore from a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Sterling Hill).
wallkilldellite.etymology: For the dell of the Wallkill River, in which both the Sterling Hill and the Franklin deposits were discovered.

wallkilldellite-fe.occurrence: Secondary in the oxidation zone of copper arsenide deposits.
wallkilldellite-fe.etymology: The suffix, Fe, indicates the iron analog of wallkilldellite.

walpurgite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of Bi–U–As-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
walpurgite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence in the Walpurgis vein, Schneeberg, Germany.

walstromite.occurrence: Disseminated in a sanbornite-quartz gneissic metamorphic rock, especially where the quartz content is high. In small veins of pyrometamorphic rankinite paralava within gehlenite hornfelses (Israel).
walstromite.etymology: For Robert E. Walstrom, mineral collector of Fresno, California, USA, who first recognized the distinctive character of the mineral.

walthierite.occurrence: Rare, in open-space ﬁlling of a fault, formed by reaction of hydrothermal ﬂuids with barite.
walthierite.etymology: To honor Dr. Thomas Nash Walthier (1923–1990), American economic geologist, St. Joseph Minerals Co., who worked in the Tambo district, Chile.

wampenite.occurrence: On a specimen of fossilized conifer wood.
wampenite.etymology: For the locality that produced the first specimens, Wampen, Germany.

wangdaodeite.occurrence: In or adjacent to shock-melt veinlets in chondritic parts of a meteorite, P-T conditions of formation estimated to be 20-24 GPa and >1200 °C.
wangdaodeite.etymology: Honors Professor Daode Wang (1932-2012) Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences for his contributions to systematic study of meteorites of China and Antarctica.

wardite.occurrence: A component of low-temperature phosphatic nodules; an uncommon species in complex zoned pegmatites.
wardite.etymology: Honoring Henry Augustus Ward (1834–1906), American collector and dealer in natural history objects (Ward’s Natural Science Establishment) Rochester, New York, USA.

wardsmithite.occurrence: A rare weathering product of priceite and colemanite.
wardsmithite.etymology: In honor of Ward Cromwell Smith (1906–1998), geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California, USA, who studied southwestern U.S. borate occurrences.

warikahnite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by alteration of tennantite in an oxidized zone in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
warikahnite.etymology: Honoring WAlter RIchard KAHN (1911– ), Bayersoien, Germany, dealer and collector specializing in Tsumeb minerals, for his support of research into rare secondary minerals.

warkite.occurrence: In ultra-refractory Ca, Al-rich inclusions (UR CAIs) from CM, CV, CO, and CH chondrite meteorites.
assoc_parsed: either perovskite or kangite in cores mantled and rimmed by davisite and/or sc-diopside
grossite in cores mantled by grossite ± gehlenite
warkite.etymology: Honors David Wark (1939-2005), an Australian cosmochemist, for contributions to research in meteoritics, especially, CAIs in carbonaceous chondrites.

warwickite.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in boron-metasomatized limestone and associated skarns; in lamproitic rocks and carbonatitelike veinlets cutting them.
warwickite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence near Warwick, New York, USA.

wassonite.occurrence: In a barred olivine (BO) chondrule, thought to have formed in the solar nebula by melting fine-grained precursor dust, in an enstatite chondrite meteorite.
wassonite.etymology: Honors Professor John Taylor Wasson (b. 1934), University of California Los Angeles (UCLA), USA, Departments of Chemistry and Biochemistry, and Earth and Space Sciences , for achievements across a broad swath of meteorite and impact research.

watanabeite.occurrence: In a hydrothermal quartz vein (Teine mine); in a high sulfidation epithermal deposit (Kamchatka).
watanabeite.etymology: Honors Professor Takeo Watanabe (1907-1986), University of Tokyo (1944-1968), Nagoya University (1968-1971), President of the Akita University (1971-1976), who first reported native tellurium and sylvanite at the Teine mine.

watatsumiite.occurrence: In veinlets in a metamorphosed Mn deposit.
watatsumiite.etymology: For Watatsumi, the Japanese god of the sea, in recognition that the mineral is the V and Mn analog of neptunite, whose name alludes to Neptune, the Roman god of the sea.

waterhouseite.occurrence: In cavities in the carbonate-rich beds of a Precambrian banded iron formation.
waterhouseite.etymology: Honors Frederick George Waterhouse (1815-1898), first Director of the South Australian Museum (Adelaide), in recognition of his contribution to the preservation of the natural history of South Australia, and in celebration of the continuing work of the Waterhouse Club in their support of the South Australian Museum.

watkinsonite.occurrence: In vein-type uranium deposits with other tellurides and selenides.
watkinsonite.etymology: For Professor David H. Watkinson, Carleton University, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada.

wattersite.occurrence: A rare mineral in a mercury deposit in silicate–carbonate rock hydrothermally altered from serpentinite.
wattersite.etymology: Honors Lu Watters (1911–1989), American mineral collector, musician, and environmentalist, specializing in the mineralogy of the California Coast Ranges.

wattevilleite.etymology: Honors Oscar de Watteville, Paris, France.

wattevillite.etymology: Honors Oscar de Watteville, Paris, France.

wavellite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in low-grade metamorphic rocks and phosphate deposits; rare in hydrothermal veins.
wavellite.etymology: For William Wavell (?–1829), physician, of Horwood Parish, Devon, England, discoverer of the species.

wawayandaite.occurrence: A late-stage vein mineral on willemite-franklinite ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
wawayandaite.etymology: From wawayanda, meaning many or several windings in the language of the Lenni Lenape Indians, early inhabitants of the Franklin area, in allusion to the grossly curved and winding habit of most crystals.

waylandite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral replacing primary bismuth minerals.
waylandite.etymology: Honors Edgar James Wayland, ﬁrst Director of the Uganda Geological Survey.

wayneburnhamite.occurrence: As a metasomatic mineral on fracture surfaces in vesuvianite/wollastonite rock.
wayneburnhamite.etymology: Honors the American geochemist-petrologist C. Wayne Burnham (1922-2015), Professor at Pennsylvania State University from 1955-1986 and Adjunct Professor of Geology, Arizona State University for many years. Best known for his seminal research on the role of volatiles in igneous systems, Burnham received the 1998 Roebling Medal from the Mineralogical Society of America.

weberite.occurrence: In the cryolite deposit and overlying pegmatite (Ivigtut, Greenland).
weberite.etymology: Honors Theobald Weber (1823–1886), active in the early development of the Ivigtut cryolite deposit.

weddellite.occurrence: Authigenic in bottom muds and in peat sediments; in calcareous lake-bottom sediments; may be formed by reaction of calcite with oxalic acid produced by lichens.
weddellite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence in the Weddell Sea, Antarctica.

weeksite.occurrence: In “opal" veinlets in rhyolite, agglomerates, sandstones and limestones.
weeksite.etymology: Honors Dr. Mary Alice Dowse Weeks (1909-1988), mineralogist with the U.S. Geological Survey, noted specialist in the mineralogy of uranium and vanadium.

wegscheiderite.occurrence: As a replacement of trona in a lacustrine deposit.
wegscheiderite.etymology: In honor of Rudolf Franz Johann Wegscheider (1859–1935), Austrian chemist, who ﬁrst synthesized the compound.

weibullite.occurrence: Intimately intergrown with laitakarite and bismuthinite in a “hornblende” rock.
weibullite.etymology: For Mats Weibull (1856–1923), who ﬁrst described the mineral.

weilite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of arsenic-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
weilite.etymology: To honor Professor Ren´ e Weil (1901– ), French mineralogist, University of Strasbourg, Strasbourg, France.

weinebeneite.occurrence: In fractures in a spodumene-rich pegmatite in high-grade metamorphic rocks.
weinebeneite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Weinebene Pass, Austria.

weishanite.occurrence: In the siliciﬁed zone of the silver-rich part of an Au-Ag deposit in biotite granulite.

weissbergite.occurrence: In late-stage hydrothermal veins that brecciate siliciﬁed dolomitic carbonate rocks. The assemblage appears to ﬁll open space between breccia fragments and to have been formed during the boiling stage at the end of the hydrothermal episode.
weissbergite.etymology: For Dr. Byron G. Weissberg, Chemistry Division, D.S.I.R., New Zealand.

weissite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other tellurides.
weissite.etymology: For Louis Weiss, owner of the Good Hope mine and discoverer of rickardite.

welinite.occurrence: In small amounts, as ¯llings in ¯ssures with other minerals cutting hausmannite ore (Lºangban, Sweden).
welinite.etymology: For Dr. Eric Welin, mineralogist and geochronologist, Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm, Sweden.

weloganite.occurrence: In an alkalic sill (Francon quarry, Canada); associated with an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
weloganite.etymology: To honor William Edmond Logan (1798–1875), ﬁrst Director of the Canadian Geological Survey.

welshite.etymology: For Wilfred R. Welsh, amateur mineralogist of Upper Saddle River, New Jersey, USA.

wendwilsonite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in cobalt-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits.
wendwilsonite.etymology: To honor Dr. Wendell Eugene Wilson, Jr. (1946– ), Editor and Publisher of the Mineralogical Record, for his contributions to specimen mineralogy.

wenjiite.occurrence: In podiform chromitite, perhaps by crystallization of a ternary Ti-Si-P melt during cooling.
wenjiite.etymology: Honors Bai Wenji (1935-2019), Research Professor, Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, for his research on suture zone ophiolite chromitites in China, including Dongqiao, Hegenshan and Sartuohai, and the description of seven new mineral species.

wenkite.occurrence: Formed between barite layers and calc-silicate rock, a product of strong metamorphism of marbles (Candoglia, Italy).
wenkite.etymology: For Professor Eduard Wenk (1907{ ), mineralogist and petrologist, University of Basel, Basel, Switzerland.

werdingite.occurrence: In granulite facies metamorphosed metasediments and metavolcanic cordierite-sillimanite and biotite gneisses.
werdingite.etymology: For Dr. GÄunter Werding, of the Mineralogical Institute, Ruhr University, Bochum, Germany.

wermlandite.occurrence: Very rare in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody in a low-temperature ﬁssure-ﬁlling assemblage among large calcite crystals.
wermlandite.etymology: For Wermland, an earlier spelling of the Swedish province V¨ armland, in which the L ˚ angban deposit is located.

wernerbaurite.occurrence: As efflorescences on sandstone in the underground workings of a roll-front type uranium vanadium deposit, from the oxidation of montroseite-corvusite assemblages in a moist environment, possibly controlled by the presence of organic matter and phases such as pyrite.
wernerbaurite.etymology: Honors Professor Werner H. Baur (b. 1931), Geological Sciences Department, University of Illinois, Chicago, for his distinguished career in mineralogical crystallography.

wernerkrauseite.occurrence: A late-stage mineral formed during retrograde metamorphism of strongly altered xenoliths within alkaline basalt.
wernerkrauseite.etymology: Honors Dr. Werner Krause (b. 1949), a chemist with a special interest in the crystal chemistry and morphology of secondary minerals, many new species of which he discovered.

wesselsite.occurrence: In a hydrothermally-altered sedimentary manganese deposit.
wesselsite.etymology: Named for the Wessels mine, South Africa, where the first specimens were collected.

westerveldite.occurrence: As minute inclusions in maucherite which occurs in chromite-nickeline ores. The chromite ores and associated cordierite rock are schlieren veins through serpentinized ultramaﬁc rocks (La Gallega mine, Spain).
westerveldite.etymology: For Dr. Jan Westerveld (1905–1962), Professor of Geology and Mineralogy, University of Amsterdam, The Netherlands.

wetherillite.occurrence: As efflorescent crusts, on the surfaces of mine walls, derived from the oxidation of primary minerals (uraninite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, bornite and covellite) in a relatively humid underground environment.
wetherillite.etymology: Honors John Wetherill (1866-1944), discoverer of the deposit that was exploited as the Blue Lizard mine, and for George W. Wetherill (1925-2006) for his seminal work on the spontaneous fission of uranium which led to techniques for dating of rocks based on radioactive decay.

wheatleyite.occurrence: Very rare, on a specimen found on the mine dumps of a Pb–Zn vein deposit.
wheatleyite.etymology: For the type locality, the Wheatley mine, Pennsylvania, USA.

whelanite.occurrence: In a copper-rich, diopside-garnet-magnetite contact metamorphic rock (skarn).
whelanite.etymology: Honors James A. Whelan (1928- 2003), professor of mineralogy (1958 to 1992), University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA.

whewellite.occurrence: Of uncommon occurrence as a low-temperature primary hydrothermal mineral in carbonate-sulfide veins, geodes, or septarian nodules; may be associated with coal measures or formed by oxidation of organic material in surrounding rocks; in some uranium deposits.
whewellite.etymology: Honors William H. Whewell (1794-1866), English naturalist and philosopher.

whiteite-cafemg.occurrence: In a complex zoned granite pegmatite (Lavra da Ilha pegmatite, Brazil); in an iron-formation (Blow River, Canada).
whiteite-cafemg.etymology: Honoring John Sampson White, Jr. (1933– ), Associate Curator of Mineralogy, Department of Mineral Sciences, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., USA; the suﬃx indicates sequentially the dominant atom in the X, M(1), and M(2) structural positions.

whiteite-camgmg.occurrence: A low-temperature secondary mineral presumed to have formed as a result of hydrothermal alteration of phosphate nodules derived from the sediments.
whiteite-camgmg.etymology: For a member of the whiteite group with the M3 site occupied by Al3+ and the suffix indicates the dominance of Ca at the X site and Mg at both the M1 and M2 sites.

whiteite-camnmg.occurrence: Along fracture surfaces in beryl and quartz in a zoned complex granite pegmatite.
whiteite-camnmg.etymology: For its relation to sl whiteite-(CaFeMg); the suﬃx indicates sequentially the dominant atom in the X, M(1), and M(2) structural positions.

whiteite-camnmn.occurrence: A secondary mineral in cavities within zwieselite crystals or as coronas (up to 1 mm in diameter) around cubic crystals of uraninite in the core zone of a complex granitic pegmatite that was altered and leached by low-temperature oxidizing hydrothermal solutions.
whiteite-camnmn.etymology: For the chemical composition, in accordance with nomenclature for the whiteite group.

whiteite-mnfemg.etymology: For its relation to whiteite-(CaFeMg); the suﬃx indicates sequentially the dominant atom in the X, M(1), and M(2) structural positions.

whiteite-mnmnmg.occurrence: From a Mn-rich, carbonate-rich zone, in a deeply weathered, Precambrian sedimentary iron ore deposit (Monarch quarry), likely as a late-stage, low-temperature hydrothermal phase.
whiteite-mnmnmg.etymology: Root name, whiteite, indicates a member of the group with M(3) = Al3+; the suffix indicates sequentially the dominant atom in the X, M(1), and M(2) structural positions.

whiteite-mnmnmn.occurrence: In tertiary phosphate mineralisation formed in cavities left behind by leached primary fluorapatite, in partially oxidized pegmatite.
whiteite-mnmnmn.etymology: Base name whiteite indicates a member of the jahniste supergroup with M3 = Al3+ and a suffix with the dominant cation in the X, M1 and M2 site respectively.

whitlockite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in complex zoned granite pegmatites; in phosphate rock deposits; may be formed in caves from leached guano; in chondrite meteorites.
whitlockite.etymology: To honor Herbert Percy Whitlock (1868–1948), American mineralogist, Curator, American Museum of Natural History, New York City, New York, USA.

whitmoreite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
whitmoreite.etymology: Honoring Robert William Whitmore (1936– ), Weare, New Hampshire, USA, American collector of microscopic minerals and owner of the Palermo #1 mine.

wickenburgite.occurrence: In oxidized hydrothermal veins, carrying galena and sphalerite, in quartz and fluorite gangue (near Wickenburg, Arizona, USA).
wickenburgite.etymology: For Wickenburg, Arizona, USA, the community near which it was discovered.

wickmanite.occurrence: A rare late-stage, low-temperature mineral in magnetite ore and jacobsiterichterite-manganoan biotite skarn in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody (L ˚ angban, Sweden); in a nepheline syenite pegmatite (Tvedalen, Norway); in a hydrothermal mineral deposit in altered garnet skarn (Pitk¨ aranta district, Russia).
wickmanite.etymology: To honor Professor Franz-Erik Wickman (1915– ), Swedish-American mineralogist, for his contributions to L ˚ angban mineralogy.

wicksite.occurrence: In nodules in shale beds in an iron formation.
wicksite.etymology: To honor Dr. Frederick John Wicks (1937— ), Curator of Mineralogy, Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto, Canada.

widenmannite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal As–Pb-bearing deposit (Michael mine, Germany); an alteration product of sulﬁdes by sea water (Loe Warren zawn, England).
widenmannite.etymology: To honor Johann Friedrich Wilhelm Widenmann (1764–1798), German mineralogist who discovered uranium in the Black Forest.

widgiemoolthalite.occurrence: In a stockpile of weathered ore from a hydrothermal nickel deposit.
widgiemoolthalite.etymology: For its occurrence near Widgiemooltha, Western Australia.

wightmanite.occurrence: Very rare in contact metamorphosed limestone.
wightmanite.etymology: Honors Randall H. Wightman (1915–1969), Director of Exploration and Mining of the Riverside Cement Co., Riverside, California, USA.

wiklundite.occurrence: In a Fe-Mn-(Ba-As-Pb-Sb) deposit in dolomite-rich skarn, probably formed shortly after peak metamorphism at temperatures above 600° C and pressures < 3.5 kbars.
wiklundite.etymology: Honors Swedish mineral collectors Markus Wiklund (b.1969) and Stefan Wiklund (b. 1972), the brothers who jointly found the specimen containing the mineral.

wilancookite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in phosphate nodules near the quartz core of a complex granitic pegmatite, formed during late stages by reaction between montebrasite and beryl.
wilancookite.etymology: Honors American mineralogist and crystallographer William R. Cook Jr. (1927-2006) and his wife Anne. Bill and Anne endowed the mineralogy chair at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History (Ohio, USA) and were founding members of the Mineralogical Society of Cleveland.

wilcoxite.occurrence: A rare post-mine mineral deposited from solutions derived from an oxidizing breccia zone (Lone Pine mine, New Mexico, USA); in intensely oxidized cassiterite–tourmaline–quartz–polysulﬁde ore (Deputatskoye deposit, Russia).
wilcoxite.etymology: To honor William Wilcox (?–1880), discoverer of the Wilcox district, New Mexico, USA.

wildcatite.occurrence: From the oxidation of primary Te phases. Occurs on late fractures, as vug fillings and filling open-space in breccia matrix.
wildcatite.etymology: For the type locality, the Wildcat prospect, named for the area it lies within, Wildcat Hill.

wildenauerite.occurrence: ‘Fingers’ of porous wildenauerite penetrate into rockbridgeite from its surface, as an oxidation product of a precursor, green, mixed-valence iron-bearing species in granitic pegmatite.
wildenauerite.etymology: From the old name for the Hagendorf-Süd quarry, Wildenauer-Grube, named for the mining family, Wildenauer, and their long-time activities in feldspar mining at the Hagendorf Süd pegmatite.

wilhelmkleinite.occurrence: Very rare from a deep oxidation zone in a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
wilhelmkleinite.etymology: To honor Wilhelm Klein (1889–1939), Manager of the Otavi Mining and Railroad Company mines in Namibia (1916–1939), an early collector of Tsumeb minerals.

wilhelmramsayite.occurrence: A late hydrothermal phase in the core of an ultra-agpaitic pegmatite dominated by aegirine, microcline, sodalite, natrolite, pectolite, villaumite, ± natrite, thermonatrite, lomonosovite.
wilhelmramsayite.etymology: Honors Finnish geologist Wilhelm Ramsay (1865-1928), who did the first detailed study of the Khibiny-Lovozero alkaline complexes.

wilhelmvierlingite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in a complex zoned granite pegmatite.
wilhelmvierlingite.etymology: To honor Wilhelm Vierling (1901–1995), Weiden, Germany, a longtime student of Hagendorf minerals.

wilkinsonite.occurrence: In an eruptive peralkaline trachyte (Warrumbungle volcano, Australia); in syenite ejecta (Wonchi volcano, Ethiopia).
wilkinsonite.etymology: For John Frederick George Wilkinson, Emeritus Professor of Geology, University of New England, Armidale, Australia.

wilkmanite.occurrence: A primary phase and an alteration product of sederholmite, in albite diabase sills that cut a schist formation, associated with low-grade uranium mineralization.

willemite.occurrence: Of secondary origin, especially in zinc deposits developed in limestones; while uncommon, locally an important ore of zinc.
willemite.etymology: For William I (1772{1843), King of the Netherlands (1815{1840).

willemseite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a nickel-bearing layered igneous sill.
willemseite.etymology: For Johannes Willemse, Professor of Geology, University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa.

willhendersonite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed by low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of potassic basaltic lavas (San Venanzo quarry, Italy); by contact metasomatism of limestone xenoliths in basalts (Ettringer Bellerberg volcano, Germany).
willhendersonite.etymology: For Dr. William A. Henderson, Jr. of Stamford, Connecticut, USA.

willyamite.etymology: For the locality in Willyama Township, New South Wales, Australia.

wiluite.occurrence: In metasomatized skarn (Russia). In fragments of metasomatized carbonate-rich xenoliths in volcanic ejecta (Italy).

winchite.occurrence: In schists with low-grade metamorphosed manganese deposits; in metabasalts of the jadeite-glaucophane and amphibolite-eclogite facies; in manganiferous cherts that have undergone blueschist facies metamorphism.
winchite.etymology: For H.J. Winch, who ¯rst found the mineral.

windhoekite.occurrence: In miarolitic cavities in alkaline phonolite.
windhoekite.etymology: For Windhoek, the district of Namibia where the studied samples were collected.

windmountainite.occurrence: In vesicles within a phonolite dike in a zoned, alkaline laccolith. Formed from latestage fluids that were alkaline, oxidized, and rich in Fe 3+ and H2O.
windmountainite.etymology: For Wind Mountain where the studied material was collected.

winstanleyite.occurrence: Very rare in strongly altered and pyritized granodiorite from the dump of a hydrothermal Au–Te-bearing ore deposit.
winstanleyite.etymology: To honor Betty Jo Winstanley Williams (1934– ), who collected the ﬁrst specimen.

wiserite.occurrence: An accessory mineral in stratiform manganese deposits.
wiserite.etymology: For David Friedrich Wiser (1802{1878), Swiss mineralogist who ¯rst analyzed the mineral.

witherite.occurrence: Usually in minor amounts in low-temperature hydrothermal veins, typically an alteration product of barite; may be of anoxic sedimentary origin, barium supplied by volcanic hot-spring activity; uncommon in coal measures.
witherite.etymology: In honor of Dr. William Withering (1741–1799), English physician and mineralogist, who ﬁrst noted the mineral.

wittichenite.occurrence: In hydrothermal veins with other bismuth minerals (Wittichen, Germany); with Cu-Fe sulﬁdes (Seathwaite Tarn, England); with secondary uranium minerals and selenides of Cu, Pb, and Bi (Kletno, Poland).
wittichenite.etymology: After the type locality, Wittichen, Germany.

wittite.occurrence: In an amphibolite rock (Falun, Sweden); in garnet tactite (Middlemarch Canyon, Arizona, USA).
wittite.etymology: For T. Witt, Swedish mining engineer.

witzkeite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a guano deposit in an arid climate.
witzkeite.etymology: Honors Thomas Witzke (b. 1963), a German mineralogist whose study of alteration processes and products has resulted in the discovery and description of several new minerals.

wodginite.occurrence: In a complex zoned pegmatite in amphibolite (Tanco pegmatite, Canada).
wodginite.etymology: For its occurrence at Wodgina, Western Australia.

wohlerite.occurrence: A late phase in alkalic pegmatites; an accessory mineral in neph eline syenites; in fenites associated with alkaline intrusives; and in carbonatites.
wohlerite.etymology: For Professor Friedrich WÄ ohler(1800{1882), German chemist, GÄ ottingen,Germany.

wolfeite.occurrence: A secondary mineral, formed by hydrothermal alteration of triphylite in complex zoned granite pegmatites; rarely in hydrothermal veins; in phosphatic nodules in shales.
