wolfeite.etymology: To honor Professor Caleb Wroe Wolfe (1908–1980), American crystallographer, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts, USA.

wollastonite.occurrence: Common in thermally metamorphosed siliceous carbonates, the intruding igneous rock, and skarn deposits along their contact; also in some alkalic igneous rocks and carbonatites.
wollastonite.etymology: For William Hyde Wollaston (1766{1828), English chemist and mineralogist.

wolsendorfite.occurrence: A rare alteration product of uraninite in the oxide zone of uranium-bearing mineral deposits.
wolsendorfite.etymology: For the mineral’s ﬁrst-noted occurrence at W¨ olsendorf, Germany.

wonesite.occurrence: In metavolcanics with high Mg:Fe, moderate sodium, and very little calcium, metamorphosed at an estimated 535 ±C.
wonesite.etymology: To honor petrologist David R. Wones (1932{1984), Professor of Geology, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA.

woodallite.occurrence: In a low-grade, disseminated nickel sulfide deposit in lizardite+brucite-altered dunite formed by hydrothermal alteration of primary magmatic chromite by Cl-rich solutions at temperatures < 320oC.
woodallite.etymology: Honors Australian geologist Roy Woodall (b. 1930) who was instrumental in the initiation and development of the nickel and alumina industries in Western Australia.

woodhouseite.occurrence: In quartz veins in an andalusite deposit (Champion mine, California, USA); a product of sulphatic argillic wall-rock alteration in hydrothermal vein and disseminated ore deposits, replacing apatite (Summitville, Colorado, USA); rarely a cave deposit, formed from guano.
woodhouseite.etymology: To honor Professor Charles Douglas Woodhouse (1888–1975), University of California, Santa Barbara, California, USA, American mineralogist and mineral collector.

woodruffite.occurrence: In the oxidized portion of a metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebody (Sterling Hill, New Jersey, USA); in massive manganese ores (Sandur, India); in the oxidized zone of a Ag-Pb-Zn ore deposit (Lardeau, Canada); a component of ocean-floor Fe-Mn nodules.
woodruffite.etymology: Honors Samuel Woodruff, American miner for the New Jersey Zinc Company, and prolific mineral collector of Franklin-Sterling Hill minerals.

woodwardite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of copper deposits.
woodwardite.etymology: Honors Samuel Pickford Woodward (1821–1865), English geologist and naturalist.

wooldridgeite.occurrence: A rare weathering product of primary sulﬁdes, the source of phosphorus enigmatic.
wooldridgeite.etymology: Honoring James Wooldridge (1923–1995), amateur mineralogist and gemologist, who discovered the mineral.

wopmayite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in a phosphate-carbonate assemblage formed after the dissolution of primary lithiophosphate by hydrothermal solutions. From a spodumene-rich boulder found in the dumps of a zoned petalite-subgroup pegmatite.
wopmayite.etymology: Honors Wilfrid Reid “Wop” May (1896-1952) who was born in Carberry, Manitoba, Canada. “Wop” May was a pioneering aviator who created the role of the bush pilot, and opened the Canadian North to mineral exploration and mining.

wrightite.occurrence: As sublimates on basaltic scoria near a volcanic fumarole vent (500-6000 °C.).
wrightite.etymology: Honors Adrian Carl Wright (b. 1944), Emeritus Professor, University of Reading, UK, a well-known expert in structural studies of glass-forming systems.

wroewolfeite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of copper-bearing hydrothermal mineral deposits; may be post-mine or formed in dumps and in slags.
wroewolfeite.etymology: To honor Professor Caleb Wroe Wolfe (1908–1980), American crystallographer, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts, USA.

wulfenite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal lead deposits, the molybdenum commonly introduced externally.
wulfenite.etymology: To honor Franz Xavier Wulfen (1728–1805), Austrian–German Jesuit, who wrote a monograph on the lead ores of Bleiberg, Austria.

wulffite.occurrence: As sublimates at a fumarole as incrustations on the surface of basalt scoria or on tenorite or aphthitalite crusts.
wulffite.etymology: Honors Russian crystallographer Georgiy Viktorovich Wulff (1863-1925), who suggested the model of X-ray interference in crystals (1913) and published fundamental works showing the relationships between the crystal structure and physical properties of minerals.

wulfingite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed by weathering of zinc-bearing slag (Richelsdorf, Germany).
wulfingite.etymology: Honors Dr. Ernst Anton W¨ ulﬁng (1860–1930), Professor of Mineralogy and Petrography, Heidelberg University, Heidelberg, Germany.

wumuite.occurrence: In a biotite-quartz monzonite pluton near the contact zone with gabbro and nearby quartz-vein-type Au mineralization. Formed by metasomatic reaction of high-temperature fluids rich in W and Te with potassium feldspar in the monzonite.

wupatkiite.occurrence: A rare post-mine oxidation product of sooty U–Co–Ni–Mo primary mineralization (Cameron district, Arizona, USA).
wupatkiite.etymology: For the prehistoric Wupatki Indian pueblos, now a National Monument, nearby the Cameron district, Arizona, USA.

wurtzite.occurrence: Of hydrothermal origin in veins with other sulﬁdes. Also along shrinkage fractures in clay-ironstone concretions, of low-temperature origin.
wurtzite.etymology: For Charles Adolphe Wurtz (1817–1884), French chemist, of Paris, France.

wustite.occurrence: Formed as an alteration product of other iron-bearing minerals at high temperatures in a highly reducing environment; in highly-reduced iron-bearing basalts; as inclusions in diamonds in kimberlites; in precipitates from deep-sea hot brines and in Fe–Mn nodules; in microspherules of likely extraterrestrial origin found in a variety of geological environments; in some meteorites.
wustite.etymology: The artiﬁcial compound was named for Friedrich W¨ ust (1860–1938), German metallurgist and Director for Iron Research of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute, D¨ usseldorf, Germany; the name was then later transferred to the naturally-occurring equivalent.

wyartite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed as an alteration product of uraninite in the oxide zone of a uranium deposit.
wyartite.etymology: Honors Dr. Jean Wyart (1902–1992), French crystallographer, Professor of Mineralogy, Sorbonne, Paris, France.

wycheproofite.occurrence: Filling cavities in pegmatitic veins in a granite quarry.
wycheproofite.etymology: For the occurrence at Wycheproof, Australia.

wyllieite.etymology: To honor Dr. Peter John Wyllie (1930– ), Professor of Petrology and Geochemistry, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA.

xanthiosite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in hydrothermal Ni–As–U ore deposits.
xanthiosite.etymology: From the Greek for yellow and sulfur, in allusion to its distinctive sulfur-yellow color.

xanthoconite.occurrence: Typically associated with other silver sulfosalts in hydrothermal veins.
xanthoconite.etymology: From the Greek for yellow and powder in allusion to its color.

xanthoxenite.occurrence: An uncommon alteration product of triphylite in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
xanthoxenite.etymology: From the Greek for yellow and supposed chemical resemblance to cacoxenite.

xenophyllite.occurrence: In phosphide-phosphate assemblages confined to troilite nodules of an iron meteorite (medium octahedrite, IIIAB).
xenophyllite.etymology: From the Greek, xénos (stranger) and fýllo (leaf), for its extraterrestrial origin and perfect cleavage.

xenotime-y.occurrence: An accessory mineral in alkalic to granitic rocks, well-developed in associated pegmatites; in gneiss and Alpine veins; a common detrital mineral in placers.
xenotime-y.etymology: From the Greek for vain and honor, as the contained yttrium had been mistaken for a new element.

xenotime-yb.occurrence: A primary phase in the saccharoidal albite unit of a gadolinite subtype of the NYF family of rare-element granitic pegmatite.
xenotime-yb.etymology: Xenotime from the Greek for vain and honor, as the contained yttrium had been mistaken for a new element. The suffix, Yb, identifies the dominant rare earth element.

xiangjiangite.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of a uranium deposit.
xiangjiangite.etymology: For the Xiang Jiang (Hsiang Chiang) River, China.

xieite.occurrence: In a shock vein in a L6 chondrite meteorite, formed by solid-state transformation of chromite under shock-induced high pressure and temperature (Suizhou).
xieite.etymology: Honors Professor Xiande Xie, former president of the International Mineralogical Association (1990 to 1994) for his contributions to mineralogy and shock effects on minerals.

xifengite.occurrence: Innermost in spheres, surrounded by nickel-iron minerals and their oxidation products, apparently of extraterrestrial origin, found in placers.
xifengite.etymology: For an eastern passageway, Xifengkou, of the Great Wall of China.

xilingolite.etymology: For the Xilingola locality in China.

ximengite.occurrence: An alteration product of bismuthinite in a tin deposit.
ximengite.etymology: For Ximeng Co., China, in which it was ﬁrst noted to occur.

xingzhongite.occurrence: In dunite-hosted platinum ores, related to chromium mineralization (China).
xingzhongite.etymology: Presumably for the undeﬁned Chinese type locality.

xitieshanite.occurrence: Formed in the oxidation zone of a pyrite-rich orebody in a very arid climate.
xitieshanite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Xitieshan mine, China.

xocolatlite.occurrence: From the weathering of an epithermal quartz-tellurium-gold vein system.
xocolatlite.etymology: After the word xocolatl used by the Aztecs for a sacred beverage, known in English as chocolate, made by mixing cocoa, water, vanilla, pepper, and chili. The name alludes to the mineral’s chocolate-brown color and Mexican provenance.

xocomecatlite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of hydrothermal Au–Te deposits.
xocomecatlite.etymology: From the Nahua language xocomecatl, for grape, in allusion to its appearance as a bunch of grapes.

xonotlite.occurrence: In contact metamorphic deposits within limestones, serpentinites, and metavolcanic rocks.
xonotlite.etymology: For the Mexican locality at Tetela de Xonotla, from which it was ¯rst described.

xuite.occurrence: In basaltic scoria, formed by oxidation of Fe-bearing pyroclasts at high temperatures. Undergoes dehydroxylation to form brownmillerite from ~236 to ~396 °C.
assoc_parsed: calcite. distribution from the menan volcanic complex
xuite.etymology: Honors Huifang Xu, University of Wisconsin, Madison, USA and Hongwu Xu, Los Alamos National Laboratory, USA, for their contributions to minerals research, including the discovery of two other Fe-bearing nanominerals, luogufengite and valleyite.

yafsoanite.occurrence: Very rare in a tellurium-bearing gold quartz deposit in dolomite–calcite (Kuranakh deposit, Russia); in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal ore deposit (Empire mine, Arizona, USA).
yafsoanite.etymology: For the Yakutskii Filial Sibirskogo Otdeleniya Akademii Nauk (Yakut Filial, Siberian Branch, Academy of Sciences, YAFSOAN in Russian).

yagiite.occurrence: In silicate inclusions of an iron meteorite, crystallized in a magnesium-rich environment.
yagiite.etymology: For Dr. Kenzo Yagi, Professor of Geology, Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan.

yakhontovite.occurrence: As veins and coatings in deeply oxidized sul¯de-cassiterite ores.
yakhontovite.etymology: For Liya Konstantinova Yakhontova (1925{ ), Russian mineralogist, Moscow Univesity, Moscow, Russia.

yakovenchukite-y.occurrence: In voids in a thin (3.4 cm) sodalite-aegirine-microcline veinlet cutting ijolite-urtite.
yakovenchukite-y.etymology: Honors Victor Nesterovich Yakovenchuk (b. 1950), researcher at the Laboratory of Self- Organization in Mineral Systems, Geological Institute of the Kola Science Centre, Russian Academy of Sciences, for his contributions to the study of minerals of alkaline and alkaline-ultrabasic massifs.

yancowinnaite.occurrence: Secondary in the weathering zone of a Cu-Pb-Zn sulfide deposit.
yancowinnaite.etymology: For Yancowinna County, New South Wales, where the studied samples were collected.

yangite.occurrence: In rhodochrosite-bearing epithermal veins of a polymetallic sulfide deposit.
yangite.etymology: Honors the contributions of Hexiong Yang, Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, to the fields of chain silicates in particular and mineralogy in general, and his stewardship of the RRUFF project’s attempt to characterize the known minerals chemically, structurally, and spectrographically.

yangzhumingite.occurrence: Formed in metamorphosed carbonate rock in the transition zone between dolomite and slate in a rare earth-bearing deposit.
yangzhumingite.etymology: Honors Professor Yang Zhuming (b. 1951), mineralogist and crystallographer, for his contributions to the mineralogy of the Bayan Obo deposit.

yanomamite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral replacing arsenopyrite in quartz-topaz greisen veins in granite.
yanomamite.etymology: For the Yanomami Indians, residents of the Amazon basin.

yarlongite.occurrence: In heavy mineral separates from an ophiolitic podiform chromitite.
yarlongite.etymology: From the first part of the name of the river, Yarlong Zangbo River, near the Luobusha ophiolite.

yaroshevskite.occurrence: In sublimates around a volcanic fumarole.
yaroshevskite.etymology: Honors Russian geochemist, Professor Alexei Andreevich Yaroshevsky (b. 1934), Department of Geochemistry at the Faculty of Geology, Moscow State University, Russia.

yaroslavite.occurrence: From the oxidized zone of a banded sellaite-tourmaline-ﬂuorite deposit.
yaroslavite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Yaroslavsk deposit, Russia.

yarrowite.occurrence: As weathering-produced lamellar replacements of other copper sulﬁdes in stratabound red-bed copper deposits (Yarrow and Spionkop Creeks, Canada).
yarrowite.etymology: For the type locality at Yarrow Creek, Canada.

yarzhemskiite.occurrence: In a halite-sylvite evaporitic rock in a salt dome. Formed by diagenesis or postdiagenetic processes.
assoc_parsed: quartz. distribution from the chelkar salt dome
yarzhemskiite.etymology: Honors Russian geologist, petrologist, and mineralogist Yakov Yakovlevich Yarzhemskii (1901-?), a specialist in the petrology of evaporite rocks and mineralogy and genesis of boron deposits related to evaporites.

yavapaiite.occurrence: In the ﬁre zone of a pyritic orebody, formed under fumarolic conditions.
yavapaiite.etymology: For the Yavapai Indian tribe who inhabit the region around Jerome, Arizona, USA.

yazganite.occurrence: A hydrothermal mineral in fissures cutting porphyritic andesite in a stratovolcano.
yazganite.etymology: Honors Dr. Evren Yazgan (b. 1943), a geologist who found the first specimens.

yeatmanite.occurrence: In veins in massive granular ore in a metamorphosed stratiform zinc deposit.
yeatmanite.etymology: For Pope Yeatman (1861{1953), mining engineer at Franklin, New Jersey, USA.

yecoraite.occurrence: In fractures in a quartz vein emplaced in quartz monzonite, an oxidation product of tetradymite and pyrite.
yecoraite.etymology: For the proximity of its ﬁrst occurrence to Yecora, Sonora, Mexico.

yedlinite.occurrence: A very rare late-stage secondary mineral in an oxidized polymetallic hydrothermal ore deposit.
yedlinite.etymology: To honor Leo Neal Yedlin (1908–1977), American mineral collector of microscopic specimens, of New Haven, Connecticut, USA, who ﬁrst noted the mineral.

yeelimite.occurrence: In a high-temperature ( > 900 ◦C) metamorphic assemblage in cobbles in a pseudo-conglomerate.
yeelimite.etymology: For Har Ye’elim and Nahal Ye’elim, the most conspicuous hill and wadi in the Hatrurim Basin, Israel.

yegorovite.occurrence: Late hydrothermal, low temperature paragenesis in peralkaline pegmatite.
yegorovite.etymology: Honors Russian crystallographer and crystal-chemist Yurii Kavdievich Yegorov-Tismenko (1938-2007), Faculty of Geology, Moscow State University.

yeomanite.occurrence: In cavities in manganese oxide pods.
yeomanite.etymology: Honors Angela Yeoman (b. 1931) and her company, Foster Yeoman, which operated the quarry until 2006, for her personal interest in mineral collecting, conservation and research at Merehead and for her company that supported these activities for nearly 50 years.

yimengite.occurrence: A metasomatic alteration product of chromian spinel in kimberlites.
yimengite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Yimeng Mountain area, China.

yingjiangite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in an oxidized zone of a uranium deposit (Tongbiguan village, China).
yingjiangite.etymology: For Yingjiang Co., China, within which it was ﬁrst noted.

yixunite.occurrence: In a contact metasomatic Co–Cu–Pt-bearing vein in garnet-amphibole pyroxenite in contact with anorthosite and granite.
yixunite.etymology: For its occurrence near the Yixun River, China.

yoderite.occurrence: A major phase in quartz-kyanite-talc schist formed under conditions of »10 kbar H2O pressure and 800 ±C.
yoderite.etymology: For Hatten Schuyler Yoder, Jr. (1921{ ), petrologist with the Geophysical Laboratory, Washington, D.C., USA.

yofortierite.occurrence: A late-stage hydrothermal mineral in pegmatite veins within nepheline syenite in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada);
yofortierite.etymology: For Yves Oscar Fortier (1914{ ), former Director of the Geological Survey of Canada (1964{1972).

yoshimuraite.occurrence: In the border facies of an alkalic pegmatite cutting a stratiform manganese deposit (Noda-Tamagawa mine, Japan).
yoshimuraite.etymology: In honor of Professor Toyofumi Yoshimura, Kyushu University, Hakozaki, Japan.

yoshiokaite.occurrence: A metastable phase, as shocked crystal fragments and in devitri¯ed glasses in a regolith breccia. The glass may have resulted from shock melting of alkali anorthite on the ancient lunar highlands.
yoshiokaite.etymology: For T. Yoshioka (1935{1983), who studied the synthetic phase.

yttriaite-y.occurrence: In fluvial placer sediment derived from older inter-layered sandstones, alevrites and pebbly sands.
assoc_parsed: native tungsten with inclusions of quartz and “phengite”
yttriaite-y.etymology: Based on the common name for the equivalent chemical compound, yttria.

yttrocolumbite-y.occurrence: [A rare accessory mineral in granite pegmatites.]
yttrocolumbite-y.etymology: As the niobium ( columbium) analog of yttrotantalite.

yttrocrasite-y.etymology: From a dominance of YTTRium in the composition, and the Greek for a mixing,a s there are many other elements in addition to yttrium.

yttrotantalite-y.occurrence: A rare accessory mineral in granite pegmatites.
yttrotantalite-y.etymology: For YTTRium in its composition and relation to tantalite.

yttrotungstite-ce.occurrence: In eluvial cassiterite mines, probably altered from wolframite or scheelite.
yttrotungstite-ce.etymology: For YTTRium and TUNGSTen in the composition.

yttrotungstite-y.occurrence: In eluvial cassiterite mines, probably altered from wolframite or scheelite.
yttrotungstite-y.etymology: For YTTRium and TUNGSTen in the composition.

yuanfuliite.occurrence: In metamorphosed magnesian marble in a boron deposit (Zhuanmiao deposit, China); in ultramaﬁc rocks (Ingleﬁeld Land, Greenland).
yuanfuliite.etymology: In honor of Professor Yuan Fuli (1893–1987), Chinese geologist, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, China.

yugawaralite.occurrence: As crystals lining cavities, and veinlets, typically deposited in active geothermal areas.
yugawaralite.etymology: For the locality where ¯rst found, Yugawara Hot Spring, Japan.

yukonite.occurrence: A secondary mineral typically altered from arsenopyrite.
yukonite.etymology: For Yukon Territory, Canada, within which the mineral was ﬁrst found.

yuksporite.occurrence: In veins in nepheline syenite in a differentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Russia).
yuksporite.etymology: For the localities near Mt. Yukspor, Kola Peninsula, Russia.

yurgensonite.occurrence: As sublimates at an active volcanic fumarole.
yurgensonite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist, geochemist, and specialist in studies of ore deposits Professor Georgiy Aleksandrovich Yurgenson (b. 1935) for contributions to the mineralogy and geochemistry of tin deposits of the Transbaikal Region, South Siberia and the geochemistry of arsenic in the oxidation zone of ore deposits.

yurmarinite.occurrence: Formed as sublimates on basaltic scoria around an active volcanic fumarole.
yurmarinite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist, and specialist in the study of ore deposits, Yuriy Borisovich Marin (b. 1939), Professor of Mineralogy and Petrology, Saint Petersburg Mining University, Vice-President of the Russian Mineralogical Society (since 1992) and Editor- in-Chief of Zapiski Rossiiskogo Mineralogicheskogo Obshchestva.

yushkinite.occurrence: In quartz-carbonate veins in carbonate rocks.
yushkinite.etymology: For Academician Nikolai Pavlovich Yushkin (1936– ), Russian mineralogist, Director of the Institute of Geology, Syktyvkar, Russia.

yusupovite.occurrence: In glacial moraine derived from an alkaline igneous complex.
yusupovite.etymology: Honors Rustam Gumirovich Yusupov (b. 1935), a Uzbek mineralogist and curator at the Geological Museum, Tashkent, Uzbekistan.

yvonite.occurrence: A secondary mineral formed on specimens from mine dumps at a gold-bearing arsenic sulﬁde deposit.
yvonite.etymology: To honor Klaus Yvon (1943– ), Professor of Crystallography, Geneva University, Geneva, Switzerland.

zabuyelite.occurrence: Imbedded in halite in rock salt, and precipitated on the margins of a lithium-rich salt lake (Zabuye Salt Lake, Tibet, China); as solid inclusions in ﬂuid inclusions in spodumene.
zabuyelite.etymology: For its initially-noted occurrence at the Zabuye Salt Lake, Tibet, China.

zaccagnaite.occurrence: In cavities in calcite veins in marble formed through alteration of sphalerite by aluminum-rich hydrothermal fluids (Italy). By diagenesis of Zn- and Al-rich ferromanganese speleo-stromatolites (Spain).
zaccagnaite.etymology: Honors scholar Domenico Zaccagna (1851-1940), who published the first geological map of the Apuan Alps and was a competent collector of minerals from the Carrara marble.

zaccariniite.occurrence: A low temperature mineral formed during alteration of ophiolite, now in heavymineral concentrate derived from ophiolitic chromitite.
zaccariniite.etymology: Honors Professor Federica Zaccarini (b. 1962), University of Leoben, Austria, in recognition of her contributions to the mineralogy of platinum-group elements and their deposits.

zadovite.occurrence: In paralava veins cutting gehlenite-rich pyrometamorphic rock formed by the combustion of organic matter in the sedimentary protolith or methane released by tectonic forces.
zadovite.etymology: Honors Russian mineralogist Aleksandr Efimovich Zadov (1958-2012), author or co-author of more than 90 new mineral species.

zagamiite.occurrence: In shock-melt veinlets and pockets in basaltic shergottite meteorites.
zagamiite.etymology: For Zagami, Nigeria, where the Zagami meteorite fell.

zaherite.occurrence: In veinlets in a kaolinite-b¨ ohmite rock (Punjab Salt Range, Pakistan); an alteration product of natroalunite or directly by hydrothermal sulfatization of sillimanite in massive sillimanite veins (Hotson farm, South Africa).
zaherite.etymology: In honor of Mohammed Abduz Zaher (1935– ), Geological Survey of Bangladesh, who discovered the mineral.

zairite.occurrence: A rare mineral in the weathering zone of quartz wolframite deposits.
zairite.etymology: For the country, Zaire (now Congo), where the ﬁrst specimens were collected.

zakharovite.occurrence: In ussingite veinlets cutting foyaite in di®erentiated alkalic massifs (Kola Peninsula, Russia).
zakharovite.etymology: For Professor Evgeii Evgen'evich Zakharov (1902{1980), Director of the Moscow Geological Exploration Institute, Moscow, Russia.

zanazziite.occurrence: In a simply zoned granite pegmatite with other phosphates (Lavra da Ilha pegmatite, Brazil).
zanazziite.etymology: To honor Dr. Pier Francesco Zanazzi (1939– ), Professor of Mineralogy, University of Perugia, Perugia, Italy, for his structural studies of many minerals, including this one.

zangboite.occurrence: In a heavy mineral separate from mining podiform chromitites hosted in harzburgite in an ophiolite complex.
zangboite.etymology: For the Yarlong Zangbo River (also known as the Brahmaputra River) that flows near the first described locality.

zapatalite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal base-metal prospect in siliciﬁed brecciated limestone.
zapatalite.etymology: To honor Emiliano Zapata (1879–1919), Mexican revolutionary.

zaratite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral formed by alteration of chromite, pentlandite, pyrrhotite, and millerite in serpentinites and ultramaﬁc rocks.
zaratite.etymology: To honor Antonio Gil y Zarate (1793–1861), Spanish dramatist.

zavaritskite.occurrence: An alteration product of bismuthinite in bismuth-bearing hydrothermal ore deposits in quartz-topaz-siderophyllite greisens cutting a granite pluton (Mt. Sherlova, Russia); in a quartz-muscovite-topaz greisen (Torrington, Australia).
zavaritskite.etymology: To honor Academician Aleksandr Nikolayevich Zavaritskii (1884-1952), Russian petrographer.

zaykovite.occurrence: In heavy mineral concentrates from a placer deposit, possibly derived from serpentinised dunite-harzburgite or gabbro-clinopyroxenite-dunite complexes nearby.
zaykovite.etymology: Honors Victor Vladimirovich Zaykov (1938-2017), Russian geologist and geo-archaeologist, for contributions to the study of PGE minerals from gold placers of the Urals and other regions.

zdenekite.occurrence: A rare post-mining mineral formed in the oxidized zone of a red-bed sandstone Pb–Cu deposit (Cap Garonne mine, France).
zdenekite.etymology: Honoring Dr. Zdenek Johan (1935– ), mineralogist and Director of Scientiﬁc Aﬀairs, Bureau de Recherches G´ eologiques et Mini` eres, Orl` eans, France.

zektzerite.occurrence: Rarely in miarolitic cavities in a riebeckite granite (Washington Pass, Washington, USA).
zektzerite.etymology: For Jack Zektzer (1936{ ), of Seattle, Washington, USA, who presented the mineral for study.

zellerite.occurrence: A rare weathering product of uranium ores, formed at low pH in the presence of oxidizing pyrite.
zellerite.etymology: To honor Howard Davis Zeller (1922– ), geologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, who discovered the mineral.

zemannite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a hydrothermal Au–Te deposit.
zemannite.etymology: To honor Dr. Josef Zemann (1923– ), Austrian crystallographer, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria, specialist in tellurium minerals.

zemkorite.occurrence: Filling fractures and as inclusions in unserpentinized but sodium metasomatized kimberlite at about 400–450 m depth.
zemkorite.etymology: For Institute of the Earth’s Crust (Institut ZEMnoy KORY in Russian), Russian Academy of Sciences, Siberian Branch, Irkutsk, Russia, where the mineral was studied.

zenzenite.occurrence: In a carbonate-phyllosilicate skarn rock, in a metamorphosed Fe–Mn orebody.
zenzenite.etymology: For Dr. Nils Zenz´ en (1883–1959), formerly Senior Curator of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm, Sweden.

zeophyllite.occurrence: In cavities, as a secondary mineral from hydrothermal alteration of basalt (Litom·e·rice, Czech Republic); a late-stage mineral in low-temperature hydrothermal veins cutting alkalic intrusive rocks in a di®erentiated alkalic massif (Khibiny massif, Russia); in marble xenoliths in nepheline syenite in an intrusive alkalic gabbro-syenite complex (Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada).
zeophyllite.etymology: From the Greek to boil and a leaf, in allusion to its habit.

zeravshanite.occurrence: A pegmatite mineral in a quartz rock fragment in glacial sediment derived from an alkaline massif.
zeravshanite.etymology: For the locality, Zeravshan Range, that produced the first specimens.

zeunerite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of arsenic-bearing hydrothermal uranium deposits.
zeunerite.etymology: Honoring Gustav Anton Zeuner (1828-1907), Director, School of Mines, Freiberg, Germany.

zhanghengite.occurrence: In the matrix of a chondrite meteorite.
zhanghengite.etymology: Honors Zhang Heng (79-139), a famous Chinese astronomer.

zhanghuifenite.occurrence: Attributed to veining, produced possibly by a late-stage, fluid-rich peraluminous melt in a zoned granitic pegmatite.
zhanghuifenite.etymology: Honors Chinese mineralogist, Professor Huifen Zhang (1934-2012), Institutes of Geochemistry in Guiyang and Guangzhou, China.

zhangpeishanite.occurrence: As inclusions in fluorite in a polymetallic Nb–REE–Fe deposit.
zhangpeishanite.etymology: Honors Professor Zhang Peishan (b. 1925) for his contributions to the mineralogy of Bayan Obo.

zharchikhite.occurrence: In cavities in hydrothermally mineralized fault breccia in trachyte in a stockwork molybdenum deposit.
zharchikhite.etymology: For its occurrence in the Zharchikha deposit, Russia (the name simpliﬁed in transliteration).

zhemchuzhnikovite.occurrence: In veinlets found at a depth of 230 m in a drill core in the permafrost zone, in brown coal naturally saturated with acetic acid.
zhemchuzhnikovite.etymology: Honors Yurii Apollonovich Zhemchuzhnikov (1885–1957), specialist in coal geology and petrology, Karpinskii Russian Research Institute of Geology, St. Petersburg, Russia.

zhiqinite.occurrence: In podiform ophiolite. In a polymineralic spheroid 20 µm across inferred to have crystallized from a droplet of Ti-Si-P intermetallic melt.
zhiqinite.etymology: Honors Chinese structural geologist Xu Zhiqin (b. 1941), an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

ziesite.occurrence: In vanadium-bearing sublimates in fumaroles on a basaltic volcanic cone.
ziesite.etymology: To honor Dr. Emanuel G. Zies, Carnegie Institute, Washington, D.C., USA.

zigrasite.occurrence: One of the last minerals formed in a tourmaline-bearing pocket in a complex rare-element granitic pegmatite.
zigrasite.etymology: Honors James Zigras (b. 1981) of Paramus, New Jersey, USA., the mineral collector who discovered the mineral.

zimbabweite.occurrence: In a hydrothermally altered kaolinized zone of a complex rare-metal and ﬂuorine-rich granite pegmatite.
zimbabweite.etymology: For Zimbabwe, the country where it was ﬁrst found.

ziminaite.occurrence: As fumarole sublimates on volcanic scoria.
ziminaite.etymology: For the Zimina volcano, located 12 km south of the Bezymyannyi volcano, Russia.

zinc.occurrence: In the oxidized zone of Pb-Zn-Ag deposits, derived from sphalerite by oxidation (Elsa mine, Canada); coatings on fibrous volcanic glass, as a volcanic sublimate (Mount Elbrus, USSR); in platinum concentrates (Aurora deposit, USSR).
zinc.etymology: From the German zink, of obscure origin.

zincalstibite.occurrence: In cavities in marble likely an alteration product of different sulfides (sphalerite, zinkenite, stibioluzonite) by low-temperature Al-rich hydrothermal fluids (1T); a secondary mineral is the weathering zone of a tetrahedrite-tennantite, galena, sphalerite and pyrite deposit (9R).
zincalstibite.etymology: For the composition, as a mineral with essential zinc, and structurally related to cualstibite.

zincaluminite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a Ag–Zn mine.
zincaluminite.etymology: For zinc and aluminum in the composition, and its similarity to aluminite.

zincgartrellite.occurrence: In the oxidized portion of a polymetallic deposit.
zincgartrellite.etymology: For the essential zinc content and relationship to the isostructural mineral gartrellite.

zincite.occurrence: A primary mineral in metamorphosed stratiform zinc orebodies (New Jersey, USA); a secondary mineral altered from other zinc minerals in oxidized zinc-rich ore deposits; a product of volcanism.

zinclipscombite.occurrence: Secondary in the oxidation zone of a hydrothermal vein-type silver and base metal sulfide deposit.
zinclipscombite.etymology: The prefix identifies the zinc-dominant analogue of lipscombite.

zincmelanterite.occurrence: A rare mineral formed in the oxidation zone of pyritic ore deposits.
zincmelanterite.etymology: As the zinc-dominant member of the melanterite group.

zincoberaunite.occurrence: In a zoned phosphatic granitic pegmatite.
zincoberaunite.etymology: As the analogue of beraunite with zinc dominant among essential bivalent cations.

zincobotryogen.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of Pb-Zn ore bodies hosted in marble and greenschists.
zincobotryogen.etymology: As the zinc-dominant analog of botryogen.

zincobradaczekite.occurrence: A sublimate in active volcanic fumaroles.
zincobradaczekite.etymology: Indicates the zincian analogue of bradaczekite.

zincobriartite.etymology: Prefix, zinco, indicates the Zn-analogue of briartite.

zincochromite.occurrence: Replacing chromian aegirine in micaceous metasomatites.
zincochromite.etymology: For ZINC and CHROMium in the composition.

zincocopiapite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral formed in the oxidation zone of a Pb–Zn deposit in a very arid climate (Xitieshan mine, China); a precipitate from thermal hot springs (Kopet-Dag Mountains, Turkmenistan); an alteration product of pyrite and sphalerite in schists (Les Vallettes, Switzerland).
zincocopiapite.etymology: For its dominant content of zinc and relation to copiapite.

zincolibethenite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of a polymetallic mineral deposit.
zincolibethenite.etymology: For its composition and relationship to libethenite.

zincolivenite.etymology: The prefix identifies the zinc-dominant analogue of olivenite. Formerly ‘cuproadamite’.

zincomenite.etymology: An allusion to its chemical composition: zinc selenite (the Greek μηναζ means moon, indicating selenium).

zincospiroffite.occurrence: A secondary mineral in an oxidized Te- and Au-bearing quartz vein.
zincospiroffite.etymology: As the zinc-dominant analogue of spiroffite.

zincostaurolite.occurrence: In metabauxite formed during regional metamorphism.
zincostaurolite.etymology: The prefix, zinco, indicates the zincian analog of staurolite.

zincostrunzite.occurrence: In zoned phosphatic granitic pegmatite (Hagendorf). In vugs in a secondary phosphate assemblage from altered triplite-zwieselite in wolframite-bearing quartz lens (Sitio do Castelo).
assoc_parsed: in a former triphylite nodule replaced by phosphophyllite and apatite
zincostrunzite.etymology: As the Zn analogue of strunzite.

zincovoltaite.occurrence: In the oxidation zone of a Zn–Pb–Fe sulﬁde deposit, formed in an arid climate.
zincovoltaite.etymology: As the zinc analog of voltaite.

assoc_parsed: the 3r and 1t polytypes commonly are intergrown. serpierite

zincrosasite.occurrence: In an oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit (Tsumeb, Namibia).
zincrosasite.etymology: For its predominance of zinc content over copper content, and its relation to rosasite.

zincroselite.occurrence: A rare secondary mineral in an oxidized zone of a dolostone-hosted hydrothermal polymetallic ore deposit.
zincroselite.etymology: For its content of zinc and relation to roselite.

zincsilite.occurrence: In the zone of oxidation of a galena-sphalerite-chalcopyrite skarn deposit, as a pseudomorph after diopside.
zincsilite.etymology: For ZINC and SILicon in the composition.

zinczippeite.occurrence: In quartzose ore containing uraninite and disseminated sulﬁdes.
zinczippeite.etymology: For its content of zinc and relation to other zippeite group species.

zinkenite.occurrence: A constituent of hydrothermal veins, associated with base metal and tin sulﬁdes and sulfosalts.
zinkenite.etymology: For J.K.L. Zinken (sometimes Zincken) (1798–1862), German mineralogist and mining geologist.

zinkgruvanite.occurrence: From a metamorphosed, stratiform, sphalerite and galena-dominated deposit in a succession of interbedded metatuffite, marble, and skarn. Likely syngenetic-exhalative in origin.
zinkgruvanite.etymology: For the type locality, the Zinkgruvan mine, Sweden.

zinnwaldite.occurrence: In tin-bearing pneumatolytic deposits in greisen; more rarely in granites, granite pegmatites, and high-temperature quartz veins.
zinnwaldite.etymology: For the locality C¶³novec (Zinnwald), Czech Republic.

zippeite.occurrence: An uncommon secondary mineral, in part post-mine, in oxidized uranium deposits.
zippeite.etymology: Honors Dr. František Xaver Maximillian Zippe (1791-1863), Austrian mineralogist and geologist.

zircon.occurrence: An accessory mineral in igneous and metamorphic rocks, with crystals reaching large size in ma¯c pegmatites and carbonatites; in sedimentary rocks and alluvial heavy-mineral sands.
zircon.etymology: Thought to be derived from the Persian zar, for gold, and gun, for color, through the Arabic zarqun.

zirconolite.occurrence: In alkaline rocks, as carbonatites, kimberlites, syenites, sanidinites; more rarely in ultramaﬁc rocks; in felsic pegmatite in gabbro; a detrital mineral.

zirconolite2m.occurrence: In alkaline rocks, as carbonatites, kimberlites, syenites, sanidinites; more rarely in ultramaﬁc rocks; in felsic pegmatite in gabbro; a detrital mineral.

zirconolite3o.occurrence: In alkaline rocks, as carbonatites, kimberlites, syenites, sanidinites; more rarely in ultramaﬁc rocks; in felsic pegmatite in gabbro; a detrital mineral.

zirconolite3t.occurrence: In alkaline rocks, as carbonatites, kimberlites, syenites, sanidinites; more rarely in ultramaﬁc rocks; in felsic pegmatite in gabbro; a detrital mineral.

zircophyllite.occurrence: In the natrolite zone of alkalic pegmatites.
zircophyllite.etymology: For ZIRCOnium in the composition and the Greek for leaf, in reference to its foliated, micaceous habit.

zircosulfate.occurrence: In a cavity in intensely hydrothermally altered nepheline syenite pegmatite, perhaps formed by acid sulfatic solutions attacking eudialyte.
zircosulfate.etymology: For zirconium and sulfate in its composition.

zirkelite.occurrence: In a magnetite-pyroxenite carbonatite (Jacupiranga, Brazil); a late-stage diﬀerentiate in a layered intrusion (Rhum, Scotland).
zirkelite.etymology: Honors Ferdinand Zirkel (1838–1912), German petrographer, Professor of Mineralogy, University of Leipzig, Leipzig, Germany.

zirklerite.occurrence: As the principal constituent of a rock composed of halite, anhydrite, quartz, and clay minerals, in brecciated layers intercalcated with halite and potash layers.
zirklerite.etymology: For Dr.-Ing. Zirkler, General Director of the Aschersleben Potash Works, Germany.

zirsilite-ce.occurrence: In the quartz core of a zoned pegmatite in the Dara-i-Pioz alkaline massif.
zirsilite-ce.etymology: For the essential composition, zirconium silicate and the suffix indicates cesium as the dominant rare earth element.

zirsinalite.occurrence: In pegmatitic veinlets cutting alkalic rocks in di®erentiated alkalic massifs.
zirsinalite.etymology: For ZIRconium, SIlicon, and sodium, NAtrium, in the composition.

zlatogorite.etymology: To honor Academician Vladim ´ ır Zoubek, former Director of the Geological Survey and Geological Institute of the Czechoslovak Academy of Science, Prague, Czech Republic.

znucalite.occurrence: A rare secondary species at carbonate-hosted polymetallic veins, and nearby oxidizing uranium veins; on dump material and coating mine walls, apparently of post-mine origin.
znucalite.etymology: For Zn, U, and Ca in the composition.

zodacite.occurrence: Initially found on a museum specimen from a complex zoned granite pegmatite.
zodacite.etymology: To honor Peter Zodac (1894–1967), American founder of Rocks and Minerals magazine.

zoisite.occurrence: Typically in medium-grade regionally metamorphosed crystalline schists formed from igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic rocks relatively high in calcium; in eclogites and blueschist facies metamorphic rocks.
zoisite.etymology: For Siegmund Zois, Baron von Edelstein (1747{1819), Austrian supporter of mineralogy who supplied the ¯rst specimens.

zoisite-pb.occurrence: Typically in medium-grade regionally metamorphosed crystalline schists formed from igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic rocks relatively high in calcium; in eclogites and blueschist facies metamorphic rocks.
zoisite-pb.etymology: For Siegmund Zois, Baron von Edelstein (1747{1819), Austrian supporter of mineralogy who supplied the ¯rst specimens.

zolenskyite.occurrence: From an EH4 enstatite chondrite meteorite. Probably formed from daubréelite at highshock pressures during collisions on the parent body.
zolenskyite.etymology: Honors Michael E. Zolensky (b. 1955), planetary scientist, cosmochemist, and mineralogist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, USA, for his contributions to research on extraterrestrial materials, including enstatite chondrites.

zolotarevite.occurrence: In leucocratic nepheline syenite (foyaite) of an alkaline massif.
assoc_parsed: a mineral of the kazakovite-isinalite series
zolotarevite.etymology: Honors Dr. Andrey A. Zolotarev (b. 1982), Russian crystallographer, St. Petersburg State University, for his contributions to the crystal chemistry and mineralogy of titano- and zirconsilicates.

zoltaiite.occurrence: A metamorphic mineral formed under greenschist-facies P-T conditions.
zoltaiite.etymology: Honors Tibor Zoltai (1925-2003) for contributions to mineralogical research and education.

zorite.occurrence: On walls of fractures ¯lled with nepheline in the central natrolite region of a pegmatite vein in a di®erentiated alkalic massif.
zorite.etymology: In reference to the Russian for \the rosy radiance of the sky at dawn" for the color.

zoubekite.etymology: To honor Academician Vladimir Zoubek, former Director of the Geological Survey and Geological Institute of the Czechoslovak Academy of Science, Prague, Czechoslovakia.

zubkovaite.occurrence: A sublimate or, more likely, crystallized by the interaction between fumarolic gas and adjacent basalt scoria.
assoc_parsed: aphthitalite. distribution from the arsenatnaya fumarole
second scoria cone of the northern breakthrough of the great tolbachik fissure eruption
zubkovaite.etymology: Honors Russian crystallographer and crystal chemist Natalia Vital’evna Zubkova (b. 1976), Associate Professor of Geology, Moscow State University, a specialist in structural mineralogy and a co-author of the descriptions of 101 new mineral species.

zugshunstite-ce.occurrence: Formed by evaporative precipitation during weathering of pyritiferous phyllite, the rare earths probably derived from monazite and xenotime.
zugshunstite-ce.etymology: Derived from the Cherokee Indian term for the Great Smoky Mountains, source of the mineral.

zuktamrurite.occurrence: In a phosphide assemblage related to the Fe-Ni-P system in pyrometamorphic rocks (Hatrurim Formation).
zuktamrurite.etymology: For Zuk-Tamrur cliff (Dead Sea) nearby the locality (Halamish Wadi) where the studied specimens were collected.

zunyite.occurrence: In highly aluminous shales and hydrothermally altered volcanic rocks.
zunyite.etymology: For the Zu~ni mine, Colorado, USA, where it was discovered.

zussmanite.occurrence: In an exotic block of metamorphosed shales, siliceous ironstones, and impure limestones, probably representing deep ocean sediments subjected to blueschist facies metamorphism.
zussmanite.etymology: For Jack Zussman (1924{ ), mineralogist-crystallographer, Manchester University, Manchester, England.

zvyaginite.occurrence: In a hydrothermally-altered peralkaline pegmatite lens in a peripheral part of the ussingite core near its contact with the aegirine-eudialite zone; the pegmatite is part of a larger complex alkaline igneous intrusion. Possibly the product of a cation exchange reaction between epistolite and low-alkali aqueous (late hydrothermal) solutions enriched in Zn 2+.
zvyaginite.etymology: Honors Russian crystallographer, crystal chemist and physicist Boris Borisovich Zvyagin (1921-2002), who was a pioneer and expert in electron diffraction studies of materials.

zvyagintsevite.occurrence: As small irregular grains and veinlets in copper sulﬁdes, associated with diﬀerentiated gabbro-diabase intrusives (Noril’sk region, Russia).
zvyagintsevite.etymology: For Professor Orest Evgen’evich Zvyagintsev (1894–1967), who did geochemical research on the platinum metals, Institute of General andInorganic Chemistry, Moscow, Russia.

zwieselite.occurrence: A primary phosphate in complex zoned granite pegmatites.
zwieselite.etymology: For its ﬁrst-noted occurrence at H¨ uhnerkobel, nearby Zwiesel and Rabenstein, Germany.

zykaite.occurrence: An alteration product of arsenopyrite and pyrite in ancient mine dumps.
zykaite.etymology: To honor Dr. V´ aclav Z´ yka (1926– ), Director, Institute of Raw Materials, Kutn´ a Hora, Czech Republic.
